Defined by intricately-programmed beat construction often using complex polyrhythms and microtimings impossible for human-drummers, microtonal-and-detuned pitch design rejecting equal-temperament defaults, ambient-and-pad textural foundations underlying the rhythmic foreground, song-form built on long-form sectional development rather than dance-floor-functional vamp construction, and home-listening-oriented (album-format, headphone-aware) production aesthetic. Subgenres include Braindance (Rephlex label specialty), drill-and-bass (extreme-fast Squarepusher-Aphex Twin style), and ambient-IDM. Distinguished from straight techno or house by absence of dance-floor functionality; distinguished from ambient by retention of rhythmic-pulse foreground; distinguished from glitch (later subgenre) by greater commitment to song-form structure.

items.name: Synthwave
items.lineage: Late-2000s onward electronic genre evocative of 1980s film-soundtrack and synth-pop production aesthetics — characterized by gated-reverb drums, analog-poly-synth pads and leads, FM-electric-piano harmonic foundation, and explicit 1980s-cinema reference — codified through Kavinsky (Nightcall 2010, soundtrack to Drive), College, Mitch Murder, Power Glove, FM-84, Carpenter Brut, and the broader online retrowave-aesthetic scene
items.description: Synthwave (codified 2009 onward through internet-era electronic music subgenre, with parallel French electro-and-darksynth scenes and 2010s mainstream visibility through Stranger Things and other 80s-revival media), the 1980s-soundtrack-styled electronic music subgenre. Defined by analog-synth pads (or analog-modeling soft-synth equivalents) carrying the sound, gated-reverb drum-machine programming (the 1980s-drum-sound treatment of Lexicon-or-AMS-RMX16-gated-reverb-snare), neon-nostalgia visual-and-audio aesthetics (synthwave often paired with 80s VHS-aesthetic visual material — Miami sunset palettes, neon-grid imagery, retro-futurist car-and-cityscape themes), midtempo around 100-120 BPM with characteristic 80s-pop offbeat-emphasis groove, and lyric content (when present, often instrumental) drawing on 80s film-and-television soundtrack-aesthetic. Distinguished from straight 80s pop revival by post-2009 timestamp and digital-DAW production despite analog-aesthetic; distinguished from chillwave by 80s-soundtrack-specific reference and brighter-not-hazier mood; distinguished from outrun (related subgenre) by less-aggressive aesthetic and absence of darksynth-distortion foreground.

items.name: Boom bap
items.lineage: East Coast 1990s sample-based hip-hop production aesthetic — codified through DJ Premier (Gang Starr, Jay-Z’s Reasonable Doubt 1996), Pete Rock, Large Professor, and Q-Tip’s A Tribe Called Quest production work; characterized by 90-95 BPM tempo, hard-snare-and-kick "boom bap" drum signature, jazz and soul sample loops, and East Coast lyrical-virtuoso emcee tradition
items.description: Boom bap (1986-1996 New York City East Coast hip hop golden age, with later revival/throwback movements 2010 onward), the sample-based hip-hop production aesthetic that defined the genre's golden-era sound. Defined by sample-based beat construction with chopped soul-jazz-funk loops as the harmonic-and-melodic foundation, drums sampled from breakbeat records and processed with sub-bass-emphasizing low-end and crispy SP-1200-or-MPC60-filtered top-end, MC-foreground vocal mix delivering complex multisyllabic-rhyme-scheme lyrics over the beat, four-bar loop structure with verse-chorus song organization, and tempos around 88-96 BPM. Distinguished from Southern hip-hop by sample-based-not-808-based foundation; distinguished from West Coast G-funk by absence of synth-bass and live-instrument re-recording; distinguished from later trap by tempo and snare-snare-not-high-hat-roll percussion focus.

items.name: G-funk
items.lineage: Early-1990s Los Angeles gangsta-funk hip-hop subgenre codified by Dr. Dre on The Chronic (1992) and Snoop Doggy Doggs Doggystyle (1993), built on Parliament-Funkadelic samples, talkbox lead, high-pitched synth lead lines, and slow-tempo (90-100 BPM) syncopated drum machine programming
items.description: G-funk (1990-1996 California, codified through Dr. Dre's The Chronic and Snoop Dogg's Doggystyle establishing the West Coast hip-hop sound), the early-90s West Coast hip-hop subgenre. Defined by P-Funk-derived sample foundation (Parliament-Funkadelic, Bootsy Collins, and Roger Troutman talkbox samples and re-played interpolations forming the harmonic foundation), high-pitched whining-synth lead lines (often Moog or DX7) replacing East-Coast-style sample-flips, melodic-sung hook chorus sections delivered by guest R&B singers, laid-back tempos around 90-100 BPM with prominent slow swing-feel, and lyrical content around West-Coast-Compton-and-Long-Beach gang-life, cruising, and party narratives. Distinguished from East Coast boom-bap by P-Funk-source palette and synth-foreground; distinguished from earlier West Coast hip-hop (Ice-T, NWA) by sung-hook structure and slower tempo; distinguished from later Hyphy by pre-2000 timestamp and absence of slow-and-low car-culture aesthetic.

items.name: Trap (southern)
items.lineage: Southern trap subgenre codified through Atlanta’s 2000s street-rap scene — T.I.’s Trap Muzik (2003), Young Jeezy’s Let’s Get It: Thug Motivation 101 (2005), Gucci Mane, and Three 6 Mafia’s earlier Memphis groundwork; characterized by 70-80 BPM-doubled trap-hi-hat patterns, 808-bass-and-kick programming, and street-narrative lyrical subject matter
items.description: Southern trap (codified 2000-2008 Atlanta through Three 6 Mafia precursor work and crystallizing through T.I., Young Jeezy, Gucci Mane, and Shawty Lo as foundational figures), the 2000s Atlanta-originated hip-hop subgenre. Defined by 808 sub-bass foundation (the trap-genre signature deep-and-pitched bass note carrying the harmonic foundation, used both as drone-bass and as melodic-bass-line), hi-hat triplet rolls (the trap-fast-hi-hat-pattern programmed at double-time over halved-tempo grid), atmospheric synth pads providing ambient harmonic underpinning, MC vocal verses delivered over the beat with characteristic Atlanta-flow drawl, lyric content addressing trap-house drug-trade narratives, hustler-flex subjects, and Atlanta-specific cultural references, and tempos around 130-150 BPM with halved-tempo perception. Distinguished from earlier Southern hip-hop (Houston chopped-and-screwed, New Orleans bounce) by 808-sub-bass-foreground; distinguished from later cloud-rap by retention of aggressive-hard-hitting trap-foundation; distinguished from drill by Atlanta-not-Chicago-and-UK lineage and absence of sliding-808.

items.name: Drill
items.lineage: Chicago modern drill subgenre codified through Chief Keef ("I Don’t Like" 2012, Finally Rich 2012), Lil Durk, King Louie, and the Glory Boyz Entertainment (GBE) scene — characterized by 140-160 BPM doubled trap-hi-hat patterns, ominous-minor-key piano sample beds, and aggressive south-side-Chicago narrative content
items.description: Drill (2010-2012 Chicago South Side, codified through Chief Keef and Lil Reese's Glory-Boyz-Entertainment recordings, with UK Drill 2012-onward and Brooklyn drill 2017-onward as major regional offshoots), the dark-aggressive hip-hop subgenre. Defined by sliding 808 sub-bass patterns moving through bass-line-melodic phrasing rather than static kick-and-808-drop construction, sparse minor-key piano-or-synth melodies often using single-note repetition or two-note ostinato, deadpan or aggressively-delivered MC vocals over the beat without melodic embellishment, lyric content treating gang rivalry, retaliatory violence, and Chicago South Side neighborhood specificity, and tempos around 140-150 BPM but read at half-speed by the listener due to 808-drop placement. Distinguished from earlier Chicago hip-hop by darker subject matter and 808-foreground production; distinguished from trap by sliding-808 melodic-line rather than static-bassline; distinguished from later UK drill by Chicago vocabulary and slower tempo.

items.name: Cloud rap
items.lineage: Atmospheric-trap subgenre codified through early-2010s East Coast underground hip-hop — washed-out reverbed beats with extended ambient pads, hi-pass-filtered drums, atmospheric-vocal-treatment with heavy reverb-and-delay; A$AP Rocky’s LiveLoveA$AP (2011), Lil B, and the broader Soundcloud-era post-blog-rap aesthetic
items.description: Cloud rap (2009 onward, originating with Lil B, Main Attrakionz, and the SpaceGhostPurrp / Raider Klan Memphis-influenced Tumblr-era internet hip-hop scene), the atmospheric ambient-sample-driven hip-hop subgenre defined by dreamy production palette and melodic-leaning vocals. Defined by reverb-and-chorus-drenched ambient-pad source samples (often pulled from new-age, vaporwave-adjacent corporate background music, or video-game soundtracks), drum patterns sparse and washed-back in the mix rather than driving the track, vocal delivery floating over the production rather than locking to the kick-snare grid, lyrical content of internet-mysticism, fashion-aesthetic, drug-haze, and emotional vulnerability, and a SoundCloud-and-Tumblr distribution ecosystem with bedroom-DAW production. Distinguished from Memphis horrorcore (which was a sonic source) by post-internet aesthetic and absence of horror imagery; distinguished from trap by absence of hard 808 foundation; distinguished from later experimental hip-hop by retention of song-form rather than collage construction.

items.name: Palm-wine guitar
items.lineage: West African coastal acoustic-guitar songcraft tradition, codified through the early-twentieth-century Sierra Leonean and Liberian port-city repertoire and the Ghanaian Koo Nimo and the Sierra Leonean S.E. Rogie 1950s-1960s acoustic-guitar lineage — characterized by relaxed two-finger picking patterns over Krio/English-Creole melodic vocal lines, played at outdoor gatherings drinking the eponymous fermented palm sap
items.description: Palm wine music (codified late-19th and early-20th century onward across Sierra Leone, Liberia, Ghana, and Nigeria coastal-Anglophone West Africa, with Ghanaian highlife, Nigerian juju, and Sierra Leonean maringa as later descendants), the West African acoustic-guitar tradition. Defined by fingerpicked-acoustic-guitar accompaniment in conversational-strumming style with rolling thumb-and-fingers patterns drawing on Spanish-Portuguese-trader-and-sailor repertoire encountered through coastal port-trading networks, conversational vocal performance often by guitarist-singer with English-Krio-Pidgin or local-language lyrics, optional second-voice harmony and small percussion (shaker, hand-drum), informal performance contexts of palm-wine bar (the genre name from the rural-bar setting where this music was performed), and lyric content addressing romantic-and-social subjects. Distinguished from later highlife and juju by acoustic-not-electric instrumentation and informal-bar setting; distinguished from Mande griot music by Anglophone-coastal-not-Mande-savanna lineage; distinguished from American country-blues despite shared fingerpicking-guitar by West African vocal-and-melodic vocabulary.
exemplars: S. E. Rogie — Palm Wine Sounds of Africa

items.name: Highlife
items.lineage: West African dance-band popular music tradition codified through E.T. Mensah and the Tempos (Ghanaian highlife pioneer, 1947-onward), Bobby Benson (Nigerian highlife pioneer), Victor Olaiya, the Black Beats, the Cardinal Rex Lawson dance band, then extended through the 1960s-70s Lagos-Accra recording boom — built on a fusion of Caribbean calypso, ballroom dance-band horn-section orchestration, and West African rhythmic foundations (Akan, Ga, Yoruba percussion patterns)
items.description: Highlife (codified 1920s-1930s coastal Ghana and Nigeria from the encounter of European colonial-era brass-and-string ensemble music with West-African Akan and Yoruba rhythmic-and-melodic traditions, with golden eras 1948-1962 in Ghana and 1960s in Nigeria), the West African popular music genre that became the modernization-era dance music of urban West Africa. Defined by horn-section (trumpet, saxophone, trombone) call-and-response with vocal lead, electric-guitar lead-and-rhythm voicings drawing on Akan-and-Yoruba multi-tonic melodic vocabulary, rhythm section of electric bass and drum-kit, congas and shekere or shaker percussion, and song-form built on extended verse-chorus with instrumental dance-break sections. Lyrical content in English, Akan, Twi, Yoruba, and other West African languages addressing romantic, social, and political subjects. Distinguished from later afrobeat by song-form-and-pop-tempo over extended-vamp-and-political-polemic; distinguished from juju by Ghanaian-and-pan-West-African origin and brass-section foreground; distinguished from soukous by West-African-not-Congolese lineage and slower tempo.

items.name: Mbira tradition
items.lineage: Zimbabwean Shona spiritual mbira-dzavadzimu (ancestor-spirit lamellophone) ceremonial tradition, codified through the bira ritual context — Stella Chiweshe and Ephat Mujuru as the canonical 1970s-1980s exponents bringing Shona mbira to international audiences, with interlocking kushaura (first part) and kutsinhira (second part) patterns played at all-night ceremonies
items.description: Mbira dzavadzimu / mbira huru (continuous tradition pre-colonial onward in Zimbabwe Shona contexts, with continuous spiritual ceremonial practice through colonial-era suppression and post-independence revival), the Zimbabwean Shona spirit-possession music for thumb-piano. Defined by interlocking-parts performance on multiple mbiras (typically two or three players, one playing kushaura lead-pattern, another playing kutsinhira response-pattern, the two interlocking to produce a composite melodic-rhythmic texture), the mbira instrument itself (22-25 metal keys mounted on wooden soundboard, played by two thumbs and right index-finger, often placed inside a deze gourd-resonator for amplification), hosho gourd-rattle providing additional rhythmic layer, lead-vocal-and-call-and-response group response carrying mahonyera melodic-spirit-call material, and ceremonial function as spirit-possession music for bira ancestor-veneration ceremonies. Distinguished from later electric-band chimurenga (which adapts mbira patterns to electric guitar) by acoustic-mbira-foreground; distinguished from other African lamellophone traditions (kalimba, sanza) by Shona-specific 22-25-key configuration and ceremonial function.

items.name: Tuareg desert blues (Ishumar / Tishoumaren / Assouf)
items.lineage: Saharan Tamasheq ishumar / tishoumaren electric-guitar tradition codified through Tinariwen (formed 1979 in Algerian refugee camps among Tuareg exiles) — characterized by hypnotic modal pentatonic guitar figures, call-and-response Tamasheq vocals, and dry desert-room production aesthetic; Bombino, Mdou Moctar, and Etran Finatawa extending the lineage post-2000s
items.description: Tuareg desert blues (1979 onward, codified through Tinariwen's Algerian-refugee-camp formation in the post-Tuareg-rebellion exile, with broader West African Sahara-region adoption through the 1990s-2000s; canon spans three production eras — cassette-trading culture from Tamanrasset/Libyan-training-camp/Bamako/Kidal 1980-1998, the 1999-2000 Radio Tisdas Sessions in Kidal recorded by Justin Adams and Jean-Paul Romann under solar-power-only nocturnal-tracking constraint and mixed at Real World Studios Wood Room, and post-2004 Bamako/Tessalit/Joshua Tree diaspora studios), the Tuareg and Saharan electric-guitar music tradition. Defined by single-coil electric guitar playing modal pentatonic melodies derived from traditional Tuareg one-string imzad and tehardent lute repertoire (pentatonic 1-2-3-5-6 with frequent raised 4th producing the misleading "blues" surface that is genealogically Saharan-modal, not Atlantic-delta), electric bass providing low-end foundation, inverted half-calabash gourd-percussion struck with bare hands and finger-rings as the defining percussion sound (NOT djembe — that conflation must be resisted), hypnotic two-chord cyclic vamps across 8-15 minute songs in cyclical-camel-gait tempo 95-115 BPM, vocal delivery in Tamasheq with male solo lead and female responsorial chorus including offbeat handclap layer, capo-named keys (2nd, 3rd, 5th, 7th-fret capos with absolute pitch as separate convention), and lyric content addressing Tuareg-nationalist political themes, exile, and desert landscape. Vox DA5 battery-powered modeling combos are documented Tuareg-touring gear because they survive the Sahara. Distinguished from West African Mande-griot music by Tuareg-not-Mande language and electric-guitar-not-kora lead; distinguished from American blues despite naming convention by African-not-African-American lineage and modal-not-12-bar-blues structure; distinguished from later Tinariwen-influenced Western indie-rock by direct Saharan source and political-protest framing.
exemplars: Tinariwen — Aman Iman: Water Is Life

items.name: Reggae roots
items.lineage: Jamaican roots reggae genre that emerged in the early-to-mid 1970s as the Rastafarian-political-prophetic extension of ska and rocksteady — recordings tracked at Channel One Studios (the Sly and Robbie / Roots Radics house band era), Studio One, and Treasure Isle through Bob Marley and the Wailers (Catch a Fire 1973, Natty Dread 1974, Rastaman Vibration 1976), Peter Tosh, Bunny Wailer, Burning Spear (Marcus Garvey 1975), Culture (Two Sevens Clash 1977), the Mighty Diamonds, the Abyssinians, Israel Vibration
items.description: Roots reggae (codified 1968-1983 Jamaica, with Bob Marley & the Wailers, Burning Spear, Culture, Black Uhuru, and the Studio One-and-Trojan-and-Channel-One studio era establishing the sound), the Rastafari-themed Jamaican reggae tradition. Defined by one-drop drumming pattern (kick on beat 3 with rim-click or hi-hat on beat 1, the inverse of standard rock backbeat), off-beat skanking-guitar or keyboard-organ chops on beats 2 and 4, deep bass guitar carrying the song's primary melodic foundation in syncopated low-register phrases, lead-vocal-and-chorus call-and-response with backing-vocal harmony groups (Wailers' I-Threes the example), and lyric content centered on Rastafari religious-philosophical subjects (Jah-praise, Babylon-critique, repatriation-to-Africa themes, biblical-prophetic register, marijuana-as-sacrament). Distinguished from rocksteady (its predecessor) by slower tempo and one-drop drumming; distinguished from later dancehall by acoustic-and-analog-band production over digital-riddim; distinguished from later lovers-rock by Rastafari-political content over romantic-personal subject.

items.name: Dub
items.lineage: Jamaican instrumental remix-and-effects genre invented by King Tubby (Osbourne Ruddock) in the late 1960s through the early 1970s in his Waterhouse-district Kingston home workshop — created by taking the rhythm tracks (riddims) of existing reggae recordings and live-re-mixing them through tape delay (Roland Space Echo), spring reverb, and dropout-mute manipulation; codified through King Tubby, Lee Scratch Perry (his Black Ark studio canon), Augustus Pablo (King Tubby Meets Rockers Uptown 1976), Scientist (Hopeton Brown, Tubbys protégé)
items.description: Dub (codified 1968-1975 Jamaica through King Tubby, Lee Scratch Perry, and Errol Thompson establishing the genre's mixing-board-as-instrument approach), the Jamaican production-aesthetic-as-genre that emerged from reggae instrumentals reworked at the mixing console. Defined by reggae-instrumental foundation (the dub track is typically built from the existing reggae multitrack rather than recorded fresh), heavy spring-reverb-and-tape-delay processing of individual elements (vocal, snare, guitar chops processed with extreme delay-and-reverb feed-back), dropping-vocal-in-and-out technique (vocal track muted-and-unmuted across the song to highlight the rhythm-section), bass-and-drums-foreground mixing (the riddim section pushed up while melodic elements get periodically removed), and live-mix performance aesthetic where the engineer's real-time mixing-console manipulation IS the performance. Distinguished from straight reggae by mixing-board-foreground-as-genre and absence of fixed-vocal-arrangement; distinguished from later dub-techno by Jamaican-not-Berlin/Cologne lineage and reggae-rhythm foundation; distinguished from later dancehall by analog-mixing-board production over digital-riddim foundation.

items.name: Jamaican dancehall
items.lineage: Jamaican dancehall genre emerging in the early 1980s as the post-roots-reggae evolution toward digital-rhythm computer-riddim DJ-toasting tradition — breakthrough recordings the Sleng Teng riddim 1985 (Wayne Smith Under Mi Sleng Teng, the first all-computer-generated reggae riddim), then through Yellowman, Eek-A-Mouse, Shabba Ranks, Buju Banton, Beenie Man, Bounty Killer, Vybz Kartel, and the broader 1990s-2000s Greensleeves / VP Records dancehall catalog
items.description: Jamaican dancehall (1979 Junjo Lawes era through present), the digital riddim-based successor to roots reggae. Defined by the 1985 Sleng Teng riddim shift to Casio-MT-40 digital production, faster tempos than roots reggae (95-110 BPM), sing-jay vocal delivery alternating between rhythmic toasting and melodic chant, and the riddim-versioning ecosystem where dozens of artists record over the same instrumental. Standard production: programmed drum-machine kick-and-snare patterns, prominent sub-bass, electric piano or organ stabs, sampler-triggered horn or vocal hits, dropouts and rewinds. Distinguished from reggae roots by digital-not-analog instrumentation and aggressive-not-meditative vocal posture; distinguished from ragga and bashment by era boundaries (early dancehall pre-1990, ragga 1990s-onward digital intensification).
exemplars: Wayne Smith — Under Mi Sleng Teng

items.name: Flamenco
items.lineage: Andalusian gitano-and-payo song-dance-guitar tradition codified across the southern Spanish provinces (Seville, Cádiz, Granada, Córdoba, Jerez de la Frontera, Málaga) with origins in the 18th-century Romaní migration through Andalusia, formalized as concert-stage repertoire from the 1840s Café de Chinitas era through the mid-20th-century commercial recording canon and into the modern Camarón de la Isla / Paco de Lucía / Tomatito flamenco-nuevo era
items.description: Flamenco (codified 18th-19th century Andalusia, particularly Seville, Cádiz, and Jerez de la Frontera, through Roma-Andalusi convergence with Moorish-and-Sephardic regional traditions), the Andalusian Romani vocal-and-guitar tradition. Defined by the cante (singing) at the center, with vocal performance using phrygian-derived modes (Andalusian mode E-F-G#-A-B with a flat-second cadence) and microtonal melisma decoration that draws on Arab maqam vocabulary, classical-nylon-string flamenco guitar accompaniment using rasgueado strumming and golpe percussive-tap-on-the-soundboard, palmas hand-clapping providing rhythmic foundation, the compás (rhythmic-cycle) system organizing different palos (song forms — soleá in 12, alegría in 12, tangos in 4, bulerías in 12-fast), and performance contexts spanning peña (private singing club), tablao (commercial flamenco venue), and family gathering. Distinguished from Sephardic Romance and Romani non-Andalusian song traditions by specific Andalusian compás-and-palos system; distinguished from later flamenco-pop and flamenco-fusion by traditional cante-foreground.

items.name: Hawaiian slack-key (kī hōʻalu)
items.lineage: Hawaiian fingerstyle guitar tradition that emerged after 1832 when Spanish-Mexican vaquero cowboys brought to Hawaii by King Kamehameha III to manage the new ranching industry left their guitars behind as gifts to Hawaiian musicians — who slackened the strings (kī hōʻalu literally means loosen the key) into open tunings and developed the fingerstyle vocabulary; 20th-century figures Gabby Pahinui (1921-1980, the voice, his Sons of Hawaii ensemble preserving the tradition), Sonny Chillingworth, Atta Isaacs, Raymond Kane, Leonard Kwan, Keola Beamer, the modern Cyril Pahinui and Ledward Kaapana lineage
items.description: Hawaiian kī hōʻalu (slack-key guitar) tradition (1830s onward), the open-tuned fingerstyle acoustic guitar idiom developed by Hawaiian paniolo (cowboys) after Mexican-vaquero introduction of Spanish guitars during the Kamehameha-III ranching period. Defined by its open tunings (G major taro patch, F-wahine, mauna loa, and dozens of family-secret variants once held closely within ohana lineages), thumb-bass-and-fingers melodic counterpoint, and the slack-string detuning that gives the idiom its name. Originally a private family-and-paniolo tradition; codified for performance and recording from the 1947 Gabby Pahinui sessions onward, with the 1970s Hawaiian Renaissance under Atta Isaacs, Sonny Chillingworth, and Ledward Kaapana bringing the form to commercial recording. Distinguished from American fingerstyle blues by Hawaiian-language vocals and ohana-tuning catalog; distinguished from Hawaiian steel-guitar (kīkākila) by hands-on-fretboard-not-bar technique.

items.name: Qawwali
items.lineage: Indian-subcontinental Sufi devotional song tradition rooted in 13th-century South Asian Chishti Sufi practice, codified through the dargah (Sufi shrine) qawwal tradition at the Nizamuddin Auliya shrine in Delhi, the Khwaja Moinuddin Chishti shrine in Ajmer, and continuing through the Pakistani qawwali lineage of the Sabri Brothers, Aziz Mian, and Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan (whose 1985 Real World Records release brought qawwali to global audiences)
items.description: Qawwali (codified 13th-14th century South Asian Sufi tradition, with Amir Khusrau's compositional foundation establishing the repertoire and continuous tradition through Pakistani and Indian dargah-shrine performance to present, with international visibility through the Sabri Brothers and Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan recording legacies), the Sufi devotional ensemble singing genre. Defined by harmonium drone-and-melody accompaniment, tabla two-headed drum-pair providing tala metric foundation, lead-vocalist (mukhya) and chorus (party — supporting vocalists) call-and-response performance, building intensity through repeated mantra-and-poem refrain, lyric repertoire drawing on Persian-Urdu Sufi mystical poetry (Rumi, Bulleh Shah, Amir Khusrau, Iqbal), handclapping providing rhythmic foundation alongside tabla, and ceremonial performance contexts at Sufi shrines (dargahs) on saint-veneration occasions. Distinguished from ghazal by larger ensemble (chorus-and-clappers) and Sufi-devotional-not-lyric-poetic framing; distinguished from Hindustani classical khayal by devotional-ceremonial function and qawwali-specific repertoire; distinguished from contemporary Pakistani-and-Indian Sufi-pop by ceremonial-shrine performance context.

items.name: Fado
items.lineage: Lisbon urban song tradition emerging in the early 19th-century Alfama / Bairro Alto / Mouraria quarters, codified through Amália Rodrigues mid-20th-century commercial recordings and extended into the modern Mariza / Camané / Mísia revival — characterized by the unique guitarra portuguesa (Portuguese 12-string pear-shaped lute) accompanying solo voice singing of saudade (untranslatable Portuguese longing/nostalgia)
items.description: Fado (codified 1830s onward in Lisbon's Mouraria and Alfama working-class neighborhoods, with parallel Coimbra university tradition and golden era 1939-1969 through Amália Rodrigues's recordings), the Portuguese urban folk vocal tradition. Defined by lead vocal performance carrying the saudade emotional register (the Portuguese-specific affect of melancholic longing for absent past or distant homeland), Portuguese guitar (12-string steel-strung pear-shaped guitar) playing arpeggiated countermelody figures, classical (viola) guitar providing harmonic accompaniment, tavern-and-fado-house performance contexts (small intimate rooms with attentive listeners), and song-form alternating fixed melodic frames (estilos) with newly-composed lyric texts. Distinguished from Coimbra fado by Lisbon-not-university tradition and female-singer-foreground; distinguished from Spanish flamenco by Portuguese-language and Portuguese-guitar instrumentation; distinguished from Cape Verdean morna (a related Portuguese-Atlantic genre) by Lisbon-not-Cape-Verde lineage.

items.name: Morna
items.lineage: Cape Verdean Lusophone-archipelago melancholic ballad tradition — codified through the late-19th-century Brava and São Vicente island repertoire and through Cesária Évora’s international career from the 1990s onward (Miss Perfumado 1992), characterized by Crioulo-language poetic-confessional lyrics on themes of saudade and emigration, accompanied by cavaquinho, violão, violin, and clarinet ensemble in slow 2/4 meter
items.description: Morna (codified 19th-century origin on Boa Vista and later São Vicente; standardized 1940s-onward through Bana and Ildo Lobo as performers and Eugénio Tavares / B. Léza / Manuel de Novas songwriting tradition; pre-canon 1960s-Mindelo-radio-station mono field recordings preserved in the Lusafrica archive; international breakthrough through Cesária Évora's 1991 Mar Azul and 1992 Miss Perfumado albums under producer José da Silva's Lusafrica Paris infrastructure with engineers Christian Echaïb, Didier Le Marchand, and Gérard Kourtchian and arranger Paulino Vieira at Studio Bastille, Studio de la Madeleine, Studio Music dAnge, and Studio Harry Son), the Cape Verdean Lusophone-archipelago melancholic ballad tradition that constitutes the national music of Cape Verde. Defined by Cape Verdean Kriolu (São Vicente variant) lyric language carrying the sodade affect — distinct from Portuguese saudade by Atlantic-creole inflection — chest-voice contralto delivery without melisma or vibrato (NOT fado-melismatic, NOT bolero-melismatic), small acoustic-ensemble accompaniment built around classical-nylon-string violão (steel-string also documented, fingerstyle thumb-and-pick hybrid), Cape Verdean cavaquinho (the 16-fret variant distinct from Brazilian and Portuguese cavaquinhos, reentrant D-G-B-D steel tuning, brighter and more piercing than its cousins), violin in the obligato-fill role between vocal phrases, B♭ clarinet as primary counter-melody voice (Mindelo military-band lineage), occasional accordion and piano color, and upright bass (electric P-bass with flatwounds is the studio substitute). Slow tempo 60-85 BPM in 2/4 or 4/4 (NOT 3/4 waltz — the meter has been historically misclassified). Harmonic motion: i-iv-V-i with secondary dominants and characteristic ♭VI-V-i cadence borrowed from fado; a subset of mornas use Phrygian-tinged ♭2 in melody. Lyric content: departure for diaspora (Portugal, US New England, France, Netherlands), the sea as both passage-of-departure and hope-of-return, love-and-loss, colonial-and-post-colonial homeland experience. Minimal percussion (light shaker, brushed snare); the funaná ferrinho scraper is explicitly forbidden on slow morna tempos. Distinguished from Portuguese fado by Kriolu language and cavaquinho-foreground vs Portuguese-language and Portuguese-guitar; distinguished from coladeira by slow-tempo vs upbeat-dance-tempo; distinguished from funaná by acoustic-string-foreground vs accordion-and-ferrinho groove. Cigarette-on-mic articulation is a documented vocal-texture signature in the Évora canon.

items.name: Irish trad session
items.lineage: Irish traditional instrumental dance-tune session tradition — modal melodies (Dorian and Mixolydian dominant) played on fiddle, tin whistle, flute, uilleann pipes, button accordion, concertina, bodhrán, and (in the post-Bothy-Band revival era) bouzouki and guitar in DADGAD tuning — revived from the 1960s-70s through Sean Ó Riada, Ceoltóirí Chualann, the Chieftains, the Bothy Band, Planxty, Altan, and the broader Doolin / Clare / Galway pub-session circuit
items.description: Irish traditional session music (codified from 1950s onward through Comhaltas Ceoltóirí Éireann revival). Standard session ensemble: fiddle, tin whistle or low whistle, flute (wooden simple-system), uilleann pipes, button accordion (B/C system), bodhrán, sometimes guitar (DADGAD tuning). Repertoire: reels (4/4 fast), jigs (6/8), slip jigs (9/8), hornpipes (4/4 dotted), polkas, slides, airs (slow modal melodies). Modal harmonic vocabulary (Mixolydian, Dorian) with characteristic ornaments: rolls, cuts, triplets, cranns. Distinguished from Scottish Highland tradition by uilleann-pipe-not-Highland-pipe and by session-format-not-pipe-band. Seán Ó Riada, The Chieftains, Planxty, De Dannan codified the modern recording-era form.

items.name: Klezmer
items.lineage: Eastern European Ashkenazi Jewish wedding-band tradition that was the central popular-celebratory music of the Yiddish-speaking world from the 16th-early-20th centuries before the Holocaust decimated its practitioner community; revived from the 1970s onward through The Klezmer Conservatory Band, Andy Statman, the Klezmatics, Brave Old World, and the Margot Leverett-Klezmer-Mountain-Boys lineage
items.description: Klezmer tradition (Eastern European Ashkenazi, 16th-century court-musician origin; American revival 1970s onward). Standard ensemble: clarinet (post-1880s replacement of historical zither, lead voice), violin, accordion, upright bass, sometimes trumpet, tsimbl (Yiddish hammered dulcimer), drums. Repertoire: bulgar (4/4 dance), freylekhs (4/4 celebratory), khosidl (3/4-or-4/4 hasidic), doinas (free-meter improvised lament). Modal vocabulary: freygish (altered Phrygian), Ahava Rabbah, Adonoi Molokh. Characteristic krekhts vocal-cry ornaments translated to clarinet (Naftule Brandwein) and violin. Distinguished from neighboring Romanian and Hungarian gypsy-music by Yiddish-language vocal repertoire and freygish modal foundation.

items.name: Field hollers and work songs
items.lineage: African-American vernacular work-song tradition of the agricultural and prison-labor south — including field hollers (solo melismatic vocal under physical labor), call-and-response group work songs (cotton-chopping, railroad-tie-laying, levee-construction), and the related prison work-song tradition documented at Mississippi State Penitentiary at Parchman Farm and Louisiana State Penitentiary at Angola through Alan Lomax's field-recording campaigns of the 1930s-40s
items.description: African-American work-songs and field-hollers tradition (post-emancipation through mid-20th-century, prison-camp and agricultural labor contexts). Solo or call-and-response unaccompanied vocal practice, sometimes with implement-as-percussion (axe-blow on wood, hammer-on-iron). Repertoire: prison work-songs (Parchman Farm, Angola), levee-camp songs, agricultural field-hollers, river-song lineage. Free-meter melismatic vocal style retaining West-African praise-song influence. Distinguished from later electric-blues by acoustic-non-instrumental form and pre-commercial-recording-era origin. Documented through Alan Lomax’s Library of Congress recordings (1933-1942), Vera Hall, Bessie Jones, Jelly Roll Morton recollections of New-Orleans-precedent forms.
exemplars: Lomax field recordings of Mississippi prison work songs
Bessie Jones & the Georgia Sea Island Singers

items.name: Americana
items.lineage: Post-1980s amalgamation of country, folk, rock, blues, and Appalachian string-band traditions into a roots-music umbrella — codified through No Depression magazine (1995-onward), Uncle Tupelo / Wilco / Son Volt, Lucinda Williams, Steve Earle, Gillian Welch, Jason Isbell, Drive-By Truckers
items.description: Americana tradition (1990-present), emerging from Uncle Tupelo (1987-1994) and No Depression magazine community. Ensemble: acoustic-and-electric guitar, pedal steel or lap steel, fiddle or mandolin, upright or electric bass, drum kit with country-rock backbeat. Repertoire mixes country, folk-revival, garage-rock, and singer-songwriter idioms. Distinguished from mainstream-country by deliberate-roughness and rejection of Nashville production; distinguished from country-rock by 1990s-onward timeline and indie-label distribution. Wilco, Drive-By Truckers, Lucinda Williams, Whiskeytown codified the regional sound; Americana Music Association founded 2000.
exemplars: Lucinda Williams — Car Wheels on a Gravel Road

items.name: Funk
items.lineage: African-American rhythmic-displacement genre codified by James Brown 1965 onward (Out of Sight, Papas Got a Brand New Bag, Cold Sweat, Funky Drummer) and extended through Sly and the Family Stone, the Meters, Parliament-Funkadelic, Earth Wind and Fire, Tower of Power, Ohio Players, Bootsy Collins, the entire JBs / Maceo / Fred Wesley horn-section canon
items.description: Funk (codified 1965-1971 through James Brown's Out of Sight / Cold Sweat / There Was a Time recordings establishing the genre's rhythmic foundation, with parallel and successor traditions through Sly Stone, P-Funk, and the broader 70s funk industry), the African-American rhythmic-music genre built on one-chord vamp foundation. Defined by one-chord vamps where the entire song stays on a single tonic chord without harmonic motion, syncopated 16th-note rhythmic foundation in the rhythm section (the 16th-note hi-hat-and-guitar comping that gives funk its push), percussive horn stabs punctuating the vocal-and-rhythm groove, bass-and-drum interlock built on the one (the strong-beat downbeat of beat 1), and vocal performance alternating between James-Brown-style scream-and-shout lead and call-and-response group response. Distinguished from soul by groove-foreground over song-foreground; distinguished from disco by absence of four-on-floor and string-orchestration; distinguished from rock by absence of distorted-electric-guitar foreground.

items.name: Southern soul (Stax / FAME / Muscle Shoals tradition)
items.lineage: African-American gospel-belt vocal soul tradition codified through Stax Records Memphis (Otis Redding, Sam and Dave, Wilson Pickett, Eddie Floyd, Booker T and the MGs), FAME Studios Muscle Shoals (Aretha Franklin I Never Loved a Man, Wilson Pickett Mustang Sally, Etta James Tell Mama), and Muscle Shoals Sound Studio (Aretha Franklin Spirit in the Dark, Bob Seger, Wilson Pickett)
items.description: Southern soul (codified 1959-1972 across Memphis-Stax-Records, Muscle Shoals (FAME and Muscle Shoals Sound studios), and parallel Atlantic-Records-distributed Southern-tracking sessions, with golden era 1965-1969), the Memphis/Muscle-Shoals soul tradition. Defined by horn-section foreground (Memphis Horns at Stax, the Muscle Shoals Horns at FAME providing the Southern soul brass-section sound), gritty-and-blues-inflected vocal performance with gospel-derived melismatic ornamentation (the Southern soul vocalist trained in Black-Pentecostal-church singing tradition), back-line interplay between bass-guitar-and-drum-kit-and-rhythm-guitar (Booker T & the MGs at Stax, the Muscle Shoals Rhythm Section at FAME providing the rhythm-section foundation), Hammond B-3 organ pad providing harmonic underpinning, and song-form built on tight 2:30-3:00 single-format with horn-line breaks and bridge-modulation craft. Distinguished from Northern Soul/Motown by gritty-Southern-grit over pop-polish; distinguished from later Philadelphia soul by absence of orchestrated-string-foreground; distinguished from R&B by Southern-tracking-room production specificity and gospel-vocal-rooted foreground.

items.name: Northern soul and Motown
items.lineage: Detroit-based African-American pop-soul codified at Hitsville USA Motown 1959-1972 (the Supremes, Temptations, Four Tops, Marvin Gaye, Stevie Wonder, Smokey Robinson, Martha and the Vandellas) with the Funk Brothers as house rhythm section; the term Northern Soul refers to the UK club-DJ revival of mid-1960s Detroit and Chicago and Philadelphia uptempo soul records that found a second life on the British Midlands and Northern dance-floor circuit from 1969 onward
items.description: Northern soul / Motown (codified 1959-1972 Detroit through Berry Gordy's Motown Records and parallel Stax-Memphis and Atlantic-New York Southern soul scenes, with the Motown Detroit assembly-line production model establishing the genre's polished pop-soul aesthetic), the Detroit-produced pop-soul tradition. Defined by backbeat-forward four-on-floor or 2-and-4 backbeat percussion with prominent drum-kit and tambourine, polished arrangements with vocal-hooks and string-and-horn overdubs, the Funk Brothers session-musician house-band providing the rhythm-section foundation across all Motown recordings, gospel-derived lead-vocal performances often supported by tightly-arranged backing-vocal harmony groups (the Andantes, the Vandellas, the Supremes), and song-form built on tight 2:30-3:00 single-format with hook-foreground craft. Northern soul refers to the UK 1968-onward club-revival of obscure 1960s American soul records from Motown and parallel labels. Distinguished from Stax-Southern soul by Detroit-not-Memphis lineage and pop-polish over gritty-Southern-grit; distinguished from later Philadelphia soul by pre-1971 timestamp and absence of orchestrated-string-foreground; distinguished from disco by song-foreground over groove-foreground.

items.name: Philadelphia International soul
items.lineage: Lush orchestral soul codified at Sigma Sound Studios Philadelphia 1971-1980 under Kenny Gamble and Leon Huffs Philadelphia International Records label with the MFSB rhythm section (Mother Father Sister Brother) as house band — The OJays Backstabbers and Love Train, Harold Melvin and the Blue Notes If You Dont Know Me by Now, MFSB TSOP, Spinners, Three Degrees, Patti LaBelle
items.description: Philadelphia International Records orchestrated soul (1971-1985), the Gamble & Huff production house responsible for the lush-strings-and-tight-rhythm-section sound that bridged Motown-era polish with disco-era four-on-the-floor. Defined by the MFSB house band (Mother Father Sister Brother) at Sigma Sound Studios — Earl Young drums with the four-on-the-floor pattern that prefigured disco, Anthony Jackson and Ronnie Baker on bass, Norman Harris and Bobby Eli on guitar — over which Thom Bell and Bobby Martin laid orchestral string charts and horn overdubs. Distinguished from Motown by the larger orchestral palette and Philadelphia rhythm-section vamp foundation; distinguished from disco by song-form-not-12-inch-vamp construction and pre-1977 era boundary.
exemplars: Harold Melvin & the Blue Notes — If You Don’t Know Me By Now
Billy Paul — Me and Mrs. Jones

items.name: Classic R&B (1948-1962 era)
items.lineage: Atlantic Records New York 1948-1962 small-combo R&B canon — Ruth Brown, LaVern Baker, the Drifters, Ray Charles I Got a Woman and What Did I Say, Big Joe Turner Shake Rattle and Roll, the Coasters — tracked by Tom Dowd at Atlantic Studios 11 West 60th Street with a recurring NYC session rhythm section, distinct from later Stax / Motown / Philly Soul subgenres
items.description: Classic R&B (mid-1960s through late-1970s African-American popular music continuum sitting between gospel, blues, and pop), the broad rhythm-and-blues lineage that bridged Stax-Memphis Southern soul, Chess Chicago electric blues, and Atlantic-New York urban soul. Defined by horn-driven mid-tempo arrangements with electric-guitar-bass-drums-piano rhythm section and Hammond-organ pad, vocal performance prioritizing gospel-derived melismatic ornamentation over operatic line-work, lyric content alternating love-and-heartbreak themes with social-consciousness 'Message Music' (post-What's-Going-On 1971 lineage), and song-form built on tight three-minute single arrangement with horn-line breaks and bridge modulations. Distinguished from later contemporary R&B by analog-tracking-not-DAW production and live-band-not-programmed rhythm; distinguished from Northern-soul-Motown by Southern-and-Atlantic studio lineage and more gospel-rooted vocal weight; distinguished from funk by song-foreground over groove-foreground.

items.name: Doo-wop
items.lineage: Late-1940s through early-1960s African-American (originally) and Italian-American (East Coast urban) vocal-harmony group teen-pop R&B tradition built on the I-vi-IV-V chord cycle and non-lexical vocal syllables (shooby-doo-wop) — the Orioles, the Ravens, the Five Satins, the Penguins (Earth Angel, 1954), the Platters, Frankie Lymon and the Teenagers (Why Do Fools Fall in Love, 1956)
items.description: Doo-wop (codified 1953-1963 in African-American urban centers, with the New York / New Jersey / Philadelphia / Cincinnati / Chicago / Los Angeles vocal-group scenes producing the recordings, and the form fading from popular foreground after the British Invasion of 1964 and the rise of Motown soul superseded the simpler vocal-group template), the African-American vocal-harmony group tradition that bridges the late-1940s jubilee-and-gospel-quartet lineage with the early-1960s soul vocal-group lineage. Defined by lead-vocal-and-backing-quartet-or-quintet ensemble configuration with the lead singer carrying melody-and-narrative-lyric while three or four backing voices supply harmony underpinning, the syllabic-nonsense-vocable backing-line device (the "doo-wop", "shoo-be-doo", "shoo-doo-de-doo" patterning that names the genre) functioning as harmonic-and-rhythmic foundation in place of and in addition to instrumental rhythm-section, light rhythm-section accompaniment (electric guitar, electric bass replacing upright bass through the era, drum kit with brush-or-stick subdued backbeat, occasional saxophone solo break, occasional piano, never overly busy — the vocals carry the song), I-vi-IV-V ("doo-wop progression") and similar simple cyclic chord changes that became the foundational template for early rock-and-roll and pop ballad writing, and lyric content centered on adolescent romantic experience (the "teenager"-as-cultural-category emerging exactly contemporaneous with the genre, both as marketing target and as the subjects the songs depicted). Cultural origin: jubilee-quartet sacred-vocal lineage rerouted toward secular romantic material via the late-1940s rhythm-and-blues vocal-group transition (the Mills Brothers, the Ink Spots), with mid-1950s urban-storefront and street-corner amateur quartets supplying the bulk of the era's recording roster (one-hit-wonder economics characteristic of the genre — most groups recorded only one or two records before dissolving). Distinguished from contemporaneous classic R&B by vocal-group-foreground over instrumental-band-foreground and by harmonic-vocable backing over horn-section backing; distinguished from preceding jubilee quartet by secular-romantic over sacred-spiritual subject matter; distinguished from following Motown soul by simpler cyclic chord vocabulary and by absence of orchestral-pop production scale. Lineage forward feeds the 1960s soul vocal-group tradition (the Drifters bridge group), the 1960s girl-group tradition (the Brill Building songwriters who scored doo-wop hits also wrote for the Crystals and Ronettes), and through them the broader pop-vocal-harmony lineage extending to street-corner-revival a-cappella movements of the 1970s onward.

items.name: 1960s girl group
items.lineage: Early-1960s teen-pop female-vocal-group genre centered on the Brill Building songwriter ecosystem — codified through The Shirelles ("Will You Love Me Tomorrow" 1960, Goffin-King), The Ronettes ("Be My Baby" 1963, Phil Spector-Wall of Sound), The Crystals, The Marvelettes, Martha and the Vandellas; characterized by lead-and-backing-vocal arrangements, professional-songwriter material, and small-studio production aesthetic of the era
items.description: Early-1960s girl group / teen-pop tradition (codified 1958-1964 in New York Brill-Building songwriting circuit and Los Angeles Spector-and-Phil-Spector-orbit production circuit, with the contemporaneous Detroit Motown girl-group lineage operating as parallel African-American extension of the form), the female-vocal-group teen-pop tradition that bridged the late-1950s doo-wop vocal-group template with the 1964-onward British-Invasion-and-Motown era. Defined by female lead-and-harmony vocal-group ensemble (typically three or four voices, occasionally five), Brill-Building professional-songwriting craft (Carole King and Gerry Goffin, Jeff Barry and Ellie Greenwich, Burt Bacharach and Hal David, Doc Pomus and Mort Shuman, Cynthia Weil and Barry Mann supplying the material), Spector-style Wall-of-Sound production aesthetic (multiple overdubbed guitar layers, doubled-and-tripled keyboard parts, full orchestral string-section additions, ensemble percussion including castanets-and-tambourine-and-handclap layers, all crushed together via heavy-compression mono-mix into a unified hyper-density sonic mass) on the Spector roster (the Crystals, the Ronettes, Darlene Love), with parallel Detroit production aesthetic (the Funk Brothers rhythm-section foundation, lighter and dryer than Spector) on the early Motown roster (the Marvelettes, the Vandellas), AABA or verse-chorus song forms with prominent hook-driven choruses, and lyric content centered on adolescent romantic experience (mirroring doo-wop's subject focus but from female-gendered perspective). Cultural origin: late-1950s teen-pop economics combined with the rapid-amateur-to-professional pipeline of New York singing groups (mostly recruited from urban high schools and vocal-coach-and-amateur-radio circuits) feeding professional Brill-Building songwriting and Spector / Motown / Lieber-and-Stoller production infrastructure. Distinguished from contemporaneous doo-wop by female-vocal-group-foreground over male-vocal-group-foreground and by professional-production-scale over street-corner-amateur-economics; distinguished from following Motown soul by lighter teen-pop subject matter and by less explicit gospel-vocal-technique deployment; distinguished from later female-singer-songwriter pop by composed-not-self-written professional songwriting practice. Lineage forward feeds the 1965-onward Motown female solo-vocal lineage (Diana Ross emerging from the Supremes), the 1980s girl-group revival (the Bangles, the Go-Gos), and the broader female-pop-vocal-group commercial template extending through Destiny's Child to contemporary K-pop girl groups.

items.name: Western swing
items.lineage: 1930s-1940s Texas-Oklahoma string-band swing-era jazz hybrid — codified through Bob Wills and His Texas Playboys (formed 1934, hits "San Antonio Rose" 1938, "New San Antonio Rose" 1940), Milton Brown and His Musical Brownies, Spade Cooley’s Orchestra; characterized by fiddle-and-steel-guitar lead, big-band swing-rhythm-section, and Texas-roadhouse repertoire blending country, jazz, blues, and polka idioms
items.description: Western swing (codified 1934-1955 across Fort Worth, Tulsa, Los Angeles dance-hall ballroom circuits, with Bob Wills and His Texas Playboys as the reference and Light Crust Doughboys as the earlier prototype), the Texas-Oklahoma string-band tradition that fused fiddle-foreground country instrumentation with swing-era jazz harmony, arrangement, and ensemble texture. Defined by twin-fiddle and steel-guitar lead voices over a rhythm section combining upright bass, drum kit, tenor banjo or rhythm guitar, and piano (Al Stricklin Texas Playboys pianist), saxophone-and-trumpet horn additions on larger ensembles (the Tiffany Transcriptions and 1940s Texas Playboys peak), repertoire crossing country fiddle tunes with Tin Pan Alley pop standards, swing-era jazz-band charts, and original Bob Wills compositions, all rendered with Wills's spoken hollers and call-outs (the "ah-haa" the genre is famous for) functioning as in-performance bandleader-to-band communication, and dance-functional 4/4 swing-feel rhythm with backbeat shuffle and Western two-step lineage. Distinguished from contemporaneous big-band swing by string-band foreground over horn-section foreground; distinguished from honky-tonk by big-band-arrangement scale over small-combo intimacy and by jazz-harmonic-vocabulary over country-I-IV-V framework; distinguished from later Bakersfield country by jazz-not-rock rhythmic foundation. Lineage forward feeds Asleep at the Wheel's 1970s revival and the broader Texas-and-California country-jazz hybrid template.
exemplars: Bob Wills and His Texas Playboys
Milton Brown and his Musical Brownies

items.name: African-American spirituals
items.lineage: Pre-Emancipation through Reconstruction African-American sacred song tradition with origins in enslaved-people Christian conversion encounter — codified through the Fisk Jubilee Singers (formed 1871) bringing arranged spirituals to international audiences, then through the Tuskegee Institute Singers and Hampton Singers; the foundational repertoire of "Swing Low Sweet Chariot," "Go Down Moses," "Wade in the Water" entering the American hymn canon
items.description: African-American spirituals (foundational pre-Emancipation through Reconstruction era African-American sacred-song tradition, with first systematic transcription in the 1867 Slave Songs of the United States compilation by Allen, Ware, and Garrison documenting 136 songs, and post-Reconstruction concert-hall popularization through the Fisk Jubilee Singers 1871-onward tour repertoire), the foundational sacred song tradition combining West-African vocal practice (call-and-response leader-and-chorus structure, melismatic-vocal-ornament tradition, polyrhythmic-foot-and-handclap rhythmic foundation) with Christian biblical-narrative content adopted from Protestant hymnody. Defined by communal call-and-response leader-and-chorus organization, unaccompanied-voice or hand-percussion arrangement (no instrumental foreground in the traditional folk-form; concert-arranged spirituals from 1871-onward Fisk Jubilee Singers tradition added piano accompaniment), biblical-narrative-and-hidden-meaning lyric tradition (Wade in the Water, Steal Away, Follow the Drinking Gourd as examples of the dual-coding of religious-content as both spiritual-message and coded escape-and-resistance instructions), pentatonic-and-blues-scale tonal language with characteristic minor-third blue-note inflection, and free-meter or duple-meter rhythmic foundation. Distinguished from later black gospel by absence of formal song-structure-and-chord-progression (gospel-proper begins with Thomas A. Dorsey 1930s composing tradition); distinguished from white shape-note Sacred Harp by call-and-response structure vs SATB-part-singing; distinguished from white Protestant hymnody by African-derived vocal practice. Lineage forward feeds black gospel, blues, jazz vocal tradition, soul, and through them the entire trajectory of African-American secular and sacred popular music.
exemplars: 1867 Slave Songs of the United States

items.name: Jubilee quartet
items.lineage: Late-19th-century African-American close-harmony sacred quartet tradition originating from the Fisk Jubilee Singers (Fisk University Nashville, founded 1871 to raise funds for the historically Black university through their groundbreaking 1871-onward concert tours of spirituals) — established the male-quartet template that became foundational for both Black gospel quartet tradition and the secular-derivative doo-wop tradition. Notable groups include the Hampton Institute Quartet, Tuskegee Institute Singers, the Fisk Jubilee Quartet recordings 1909-onward
items.description: Jubilee quartet (codified late-1870s through 1940s African-American close-harmony quartet tradition emerging from post-Reconstruction-era Fisk Jubilee Singers 1871-onward concert-tour heritage and adopted by historically-Black-college choirs and traveling gospel-quartet ensembles; tradition codified in commercial recording from the 1920s through Norfolk Jubilee Quartet, Birmingham Jubilee Singers, Tuskegee Institute Singers, and dozens of similar groups recording for OKeh, Columbia, and Paramount race-records labels), the late-19th-century-and-early-20th-century African-American close-harmony quartet tradition that arranges spirituals-repertoire material into formal four-voice harmonized concert presentation. Defined by four-voice male-quartet arrangement (the bass-baritone-second-tenor-first-tenor configuration with each voice carrying an independent harmonic line — distinguished from earlier folk-spiritual call-and-response unison-with-improvised-harmony performance), arranged-not-improvised harmonic vocabulary, repertoire of arranged-spirituals plus jubilee-original compositions (Swing Low Sweet Chariot, Steal Away, Wade in the Water in formalized concert arrangement), unaccompanied-or-light-piano accompaniment, and formal-concert-presentation performance context (HBCU campus concerts, traveling-tour concert halls, race-records studios). Distinguished from preceding folk-spiritual oral tradition by formal arrangement and concert-presentation practice; distinguished from later mid-1930s-onward black-gospel quartet (Golden Gate Quartet, Soul Stirrers, Dixie Hummingbirds) by less-rhythmically-driving and less-blues-derived vocal-style; distinguished from white barbershop quartet by African-American sacred-and-spiritual repertoire and formal academic-tour origin. Lineage forward feeds black-gospel quartet (Golden Gate Quartet bridges the eras), doo-wop (the four-voice close-harmony quartet format with rhythmic backing), and through them the broader African-American vocal-group continuum.

items.name: Disco
items.lineage: Mid-1970s through 1980 dance-floor evolution of Philly Soul orchestral pop, NYC club culture, and 4/4 thump rhythm — codified through Donna Summer / Giorgio Moroder collaborations (I Feel Love 1977, Munich Musicland), Chic (Nile Rodgers and Bernard Edwards at Atlantic / Power Station NYC), Bee Gees Saturday Night Fever (RSO 1977), KC and the Sunshine Band, Sister Sledge, the entire Studio 54 NYC era catalog
items.description: Disco (codified 1973-1979 New York City Manhattan club-scene-and-Philadelphia-International-Records production lineage, with parallel European Munich-Sound Donna-Summer-and-Giorgio-Moroder development, and golden era 1976-1979), the dance-soul genre that defined late-70s American pop. Defined by four-on-the-floor kick-drum foundation (the disco-kick on every beat with hi-hat 16ths providing the propulsive forward-motion), string-laden orchestral production with full string-section overdubs and brass-section punctuation, syncopated bass lines often using octave-jumping or extended-vamp patterns, lead-vocal performances often by female singers delivering soulful-melismatic vocal lines, song-form built on extended 12-inch-single arrangements (5-8 minute extended remixes for DJ-club use), and tempos around 110-130 BPM. Distinguished from earlier soul by four-on-floor kick foundation and orchestral-string emphasis; distinguished from later post-disco and house by retention of live-orchestra-and-live-rhythm-section foundation; distinguished from funk by song-form and string-arrangement orientation over groove-foreground.

items.name: Spiritual jazz
items.lineage: Late-1960s/1970s African-American jazz movement combining modal-and-free harmonic vocabulary with explicit religious / political / Afro-diasporic content — Pharoah Sanders, Alice Coltrane, Don Cherry, Lonnie Liston Smith, the Strata-East and Impulse! catalogs
items.description: Spiritual jazz (codified 1965-1975 through John Coltrane's late-period A Love Supreme and Meditations records establishing the genre's devotional-intent foundation, with successor work through Pharoah Sanders, Alice Coltrane, Don Cherry, Sun Ra, and the broader Black-spiritual-jazz movement), the late-1960s/70s modal and free-leaning jazz with devotional intent. Defined by African and Asian instrumental incorporation (sitar, tabla, kalimba, mbira, talking-drum, sruti-box drone, and other non-Western instruments adopted into the jazz-ensemble), modal and free-leaning improvisation extending Coltrane's late-period vocabulary, devotional-and-cosmic-spiritual lyric content (when present) and song-titles invoking Black-spiritual-tradition material, extended-form composition stretching past 15-30 minutes, and Pan-African and Black-Power-era political-spiritual framing. Distinguished from straight modal jazz by devotional-intent-foreground over secular jazz-improvisation; distinguished from straight free-jazz by retention of melodic-and-harmonic foundation; distinguished from later world-music-and-jazz fusion by Black-spiritual-tradition lineage rather than ethnomusicological-eclectic-collection.

items.name: Thrash metal
items.lineage: Mid-1980s through early 1990s fast-tempo aggressive metal genre fusing NWOBHM melodic-twin-guitar vocabulary with hardcore-punk tempo and aggression — codified through the Big Four (Metallica Kill Em All 1983 and Master of Puppets 1986, Slayer Reign in Blood 1986, Megadeth Peace Sells But Whos Buying 1986, Anthrax Among the Living 1987), then extended through Exodus, Testament, Overkill, Death Angel, Kreator (German Teutonic thrash), Sodom, Sepultura (Brazilian)
items.description: Thrash metal (codified 1981-1986 across San Francisco Bay Area and broader US-and-international thrash scene, with foundational Big Four — Metallica, Megadeth, Slayer, Anthrax — and parallel work through Exodus, Testament, Death Angel, Overkill, Sepultura, and the broader thrash community), the fast-palm-muted-riffing extreme metal subgenre. Defined by fast-palm-muted riffing foundation (palm-muted right-hand technique on downtuned electric guitars producing the chunky-muted thrash-riff sound), tempos around 180-220 BPM, dual-guitar harmony lead-lines drawing on NWOBHM melodic-harmony heritage, shouted-and-aggressive-clean vocal delivery (alternating shouted-verse with clean-or-rough-sung chorus depending on band), galloping-rhythm rhythm-guitar foundation with double-bass-drum gallop, lyric content addressing political-and-social subjects, war-and-violence imagery, and personal-aggression themes, and tight-arrangement song-form with extended-instrumental break-and-solo sections. Distinguished from earlier hard rock and NWOBHM by tempo and palm-muted aggression; distinguished from later death and black metal by retention of clean-rough-sung vocal and absence of growl/shriek; distinguished from speed metal by retention of song-form melodic-harmony foreground.

items.name: Death metal
items.lineage: Mid-1980s onward extreme metal subgenre characterized by down-tuned humbucker guitar, palm-muted chug riffs, blast-beat drumming, growl-vocal delivery, and morbid thematic content — codified through Florida-tampa-bay (Death — Scream Bloody Gore 1987, Morbid Angel — Altars of Madness 1989, Obituary, Deicide), and Stockholm (Entombed — Left Hand Path 1990, Dismember, Grave) with the genre splitting into technical, brutal, and melodic substreams by the mid-1990s
items.description: Death metal (1985 onward, codified 1989-1993 through Florida (Tampa-Death-Obituary) and Stockholm (Entombed-Dismember-Grave) regional scenes), the downtuned blast-beat-driven extreme metal subgenre. Defined by guitars tuned down (D, C, B, A standard or further), tremolo-picked dissonant riffs in mid-low register exploiting half-step and tritone intervals, blast-beat percussion alternating bass-drum-and-snare at 200+ BPM, growled or guttural-grunted vocal delivery far below conversational pitch (the death-growl that names the genre), song-form built on riff-juxtaposition rather than verse-chorus and frequent metric-modulation, and lyrical content treating mortality, gore, occult, and existential-philosophical material. Distinguished from black metal by mid-low-not-treble emphasis and growled-not-shrieked vocal; distinguished from doom by blast-beat tempo; distinguished from grindcore by song-length and progressive-metal structural ambition; distinguished from thrash by absence of major-key punk-derived vocabulary.

items.name: Hardcore punk
items.lineage: Early-1980s American underground extension of punk into faster tempos, shorter song lengths, screamed vocals, and a developed touring-and-DIY-record-label network — codified through the Washington DC scene (Bad Brains Bad Brains 1982, Minor Threat — Out of Step 1983), the Boston scene (SS Decontrol, DYS), the Los Angeles scene (Black Flag — Damaged 1981, Circle Jerks, Suicidal Tendencies), and the New York hardcore scene (Agnostic Front, Cro-Mags, Sick of It All)
items.description: Hardcore punk (codified 1979-1985 American suburban-and-urban punk-evolution scenes — Black Flag's Los Angeles, Minor Threat's Washington DC, Bad Brains's DC-and-NYC, Dead Kennedys's San Francisco), the faster-and-angrier-than-punk underground subgenre. Defined by tempos pushed to 180-220 BPM (faster than first-wave punk's 140-180 BPM), shouted-vocal delivery without melodic singing, song-lengths often under 2 minutes with extreme economy of structure, breakdowns mid-song where the rhythm halves and the riff opens (the breakdown that fed forward into metalcore), DIY-zine-and-fanzine distribution and small-club tour circuit, and lyric content addressing political-radical-anarchist themes, suburban-malaise, and confrontational-social-commentary. Distinguished from first-wave punk by speed and tighter performance economy; distinguished from later metalcore by absence of metal-derived guitar-tone; distinguished from grindcore by retention of punk-rock structural conventions over extreme-short-form fusion.

items.name: Krautrock
items.lineage: West German experimental rock genre that emerged in 1968-1980 — codified through Can (Tago Mago 1971, Ege Bamyasi 1972, Future Days 1973), Kraftwerk (Autobahn 1974, Trans-Europe Express 1977 — the electronic-pop founding albums), Neu! (Neu! 1972, Neu! 2 1973 — the motorik-rhythm-foundation albums), Faust, Amon Düül II, Tangerine Dream, Cluster, Harmonia, Popol Vuh; characterized by repetitive motorik rhythm (the Klaus Dinger drumbeat), tape-loop and tape-delay manipulation, modular-synthesizer sequencing, and a deliberate philosophical break from Anglo-American rock idiom
items.description: Krautrock (codified 1968-1976 in West Germany, descending from psychedelic-rock and avant-garde art-music encounters in the post-1968-protest cultural moment, with Hamburg-Berlin-Düsseldorf-Cologne regional centers), the German experimental rock genre. Defined by motorik drum patterns (the steady-eighth-note kick-snare-and-hi-hat pattern at 120-130 BPM forming the rhythmic foundation, named for its mechanical-machine quality), drone-and-meter harmonic basis where pieces stay on a single tonal center for extended durations rather than moving through chord-changes, electronic textures from early modular synthesizers and effects-processing, song-forms regularly extending past 15 minutes, and a refusal of Anglo-American blues-rock vocabulary in favor of European classical and avant-garde reference points. Distinguished from progressive rock by absence of jazz-fusion-and-classical-virtuosity orientation and presence of motorik metric foundation; distinguished from psychedelic-rock by post-1968 timestamp and German experimental commitments; distinguished from later post-punk by retention of long-form jam-derived structure.

items.name: Math rock and post-rock
items.lineage: Late-1980s onward underground rock movement deploying odd time signatures, polymetric and angular guitar interplay, instrumental-or-near-instrumental song form, and crescendo-based arrangement — codified through Slint (Spiderland 1991), Tortoise (Millions Now Living Will Never Die 1996), Mogwai (Mogwai Young Team 1997), Godspeed You Black Emperor (F♯ A♯ ∞ 1997), Don Caballero (American Don 2000), Battles (Mirrored 2007)
items.description: Math rock and post-rock (codified 1990s onward, with math-rock through Slint, Don Caballero, and June of 44 establishing the irregular-meter foreground style, and post-rock through Tortoise, Mogwai, and Godspeed You! Black Emperor establishing the long-crescendo dynamics-driven instrumental subgenre), the instrumental-rock subgenres built on irregular meters and through-composed forms. Defined by irregular-meter compositional foreground (5/8, 7/8, 11/8, and other unusual time signatures, with frequent metric-modulation mid-piece), long-crescendo dynamics-driven structures (post-rock specialty of building from quiet acoustic-guitar-and-piano introduction over 5-10 minutes through to fully-distorted climax), through-composed song-forms abandoning verse-chorus pop structure, often-instrumental focus with vocals appearing only as textural elements when present, and clean-tone guitar tapping-and-finger-picking technique foreground. Distinguished from progressive rock by indie-rock lineage rather than 70s-prog-rock heritage; distinguished from emo (related parallel) by instrumental-foreground over confessional-vocal; distinguished from straight indie-rock by structural ambition and tempo-and-meter complexity.

items.name: Industrial
items.lineage: Late-1970s onward experimental-electronic genre using harsh noise textures, found-sound and concrete materials, deconstructed song-form, and explicitly transgressive thematic content — codified through Throbbing Gristle (Second Annual Report 1977, the founding industrial recording), Cabaret Voltaire, Einstürzende Neubauten, SPK, and continuing through the post-industrial commercial breakthrough (Ministry — Land of Rape and Honey 1988, Nine Inch Nails — Pretty Hate Machine 1989)
items.description: Industrial (codified 1976 onward through Throbbing Gristle's Industrial Records establishing the Sheffield-and-London first-wave, with second-wave 1980s codification through Cabaret Voltaire, Einstürzende Neubauten, and Skinny Puppy), the mechanical-processed-percussive electronic music genre. Defined by sampled metal-and-machinery sound sources (factory-percussion, found-sound, scrap-metal hits, processed industrial-noise textures), heavy distortion processing pushing source materials past recognizability, often shouted-or-distorted vocal delivery foregrounding aggressive-confrontational delivery, percussion built on irregular-and-pounding patterns rather than danceable-grid (though later EBM-and-aggrotech industrial subgenres adopted dance rhythms), and lyric and visual themes of dystopia, mechanization, transgression, and confrontational anti-mainstream stance. Distinguished from later EBM (electronic body music) by absence of dance-floor-functional structure and four-on-floor; distinguished from noise-music by retention of song-form vestiges; distinguished from industrial-metal (later subgenre) by absence of metal-derived guitar foundation.

items.name: Noise music
items.lineage: Late-1960s onward experimental-music genre foregrounding harsh-noise, feedback, and non-musical sound as primary material — codified through the Japanese noise canon (Merzbow — Pulse Demon 1996, Hijokaidan, Masonna, Boredoms), the European industrial-noise scene, and the American academic-experimental tradition extending from John Cage through the contemporary noise-festival circuit
items.description: Noise music (codified 1970s-1980s onward through Italian Futurism precursors and the Japanese Noise (Japanoise) and American/UK industrial-noise lineages, with Merzbow, The Haters, and Hijokaidan as practitioners), the abrasive distortion-saturated electronic music genre. Defined by absence of fixed pitch or meter (the music exists as pure timbre-and-intensity rather than pitched-and-rhythmic-organized music), distortion-saturated sound sources pushed past the threshold of recognizability through chained-effects-pedal processing, found-sound and feedback as compositional sources, performance contexts spanning small-DIY venue, art-gallery installation, and home-listening-album format, and an aesthetic stance of pushing sound-as-such past genre-conventional limits into pure-sonic-experience. Distinguished from industrial by absence of song-form and rhythmic-pulse vestiges; distinguished from drone-ambient by harsh-loudness rather than sustained-quiet aesthetic; distinguished from free-improvisation by fixed-or-loop-based source material rather than real-time instrumental improvisation.

items.name: Drone and dark ambient
items.lineage: Long-form sustained-tone genre family descending from early-20th-century minimalist composition (La Monte Young, Tony Conrad, Charlemagne Palestine), Brian Eno post-Roxy ambient canon (Ambient 1: Music for Airports 1978), the Eno-and-Lanois ambient-textural canon (Apollo: Atmospheres and Soundtracks 1983), and the 1990s-onward dark ambient extension into ritualistic-occult mood (Lustmord, Coil, Raison dÊtre, the Cold Meat Industry label catalog)
items.description: Drone-dark ambient (1980s onward, codified through Lustmord, Kammarheit, Coil, and the larger industrial-and-experimental dark-electronic lineage), the sustained drone-based dark electronic music subgenre. Defined by long-form sustained low-frequency drone tones (often deep into sub-bass register, sometimes reinforced through processed synth or processed acoustic-instrument source), processed field-recordings of industrial machinery, abandoned spaces, and natural environment phenomena layered as ambient textural elements, absence of metric pulse or meter — the music exists as evolving textural environment rather than rhythmic-organized music, and lyrical and visual themes of decay, abandoned-space, post-apocalyptic landscape, and occult ritual. Distinguished from straight ambient by darker palette and industrial-source aesthetic; distinguished from drone metal by absence of metal-derived guitar and percussion; distinguished from early industrial by absence of percussion and song-form vestiges.

items.name: Hyperpop
items.lineage: Late-2010s onward maximalist pop subgenre fusing the production language of EDM-Bigroom, mainstream-pop, online-fandom-internet-culture, and bedroom-DAW-production aesthetics — codified through the PC Music label (A.G. Cook, SOPHIE), 100 gecs (1000 gecs 2019), Charli XCX (Pop 2 2017, how i'm feeling now 2020), Dorian Electra, Hannah Diamond, and the broader Discord-and-SoundCloud-distributed scene
items.description: Hyperpop (codified 2015-2020 internet-and-streaming-platform, with PC Music label and SOPHIE production output crystallizing the genre and 100 gecs as the breakthrough commercial expression), the post-2010s electronic-pop maximalism subgenre. Defined by pitched-up female-vocal-or-androgynous-vocal performance often heavily auto-tuned and digitally processed, sound-design-forward production where unconventional synth and sample sources foreground over traditional song instrumentation, abrupt section-edits and sudden dynamic shifts (whisper-to-full-blast within seconds), extreme-saturation and clipping aesthetic embracing distortion-as-feature, BPMs varying widely (90-160 within a single track), and song-content of internet-meme references, queer-femme aesthetics, and self-conscious genre subversion. Distinguished from straight EDM by absence of dance-floor-functional structure; distinguished from chillwave by maximalist-not-relaxed register; distinguished from earlier glitch-pop by post-2015 timestamp and TikTok-era distribution context.

items.name: Modern R&B
items.lineage: Modern neo-soul breath-admixed contemporary-r&b vocal aesthetic codified through D’Angelo (Brown Sugar 1995, Voodoo 2000), Erykah Badu (Baduizm 1997), Maxwell, Lauryn Hill (The Miseducation of Lauryn Hill 1998), and the Soulquarians collective with Questlove and J Dilla — characterized by jazz-chord harmonic vocabulary, drum-machine-and-live-band hybrid production, and intimate-confessional vocal performance
items.description: Modern R&B (codified 2010 onward, descending from contemporary-R&B and crystallizing through Frank Ocean, The Weeknd, Miguel, and the post-2010 PBR&B/alt-R&B movement), the post-2010 R&B fused with hip-hop production. Defined by sparse arrangements rejecting the lush-string-and-orchestral mid-2000s contemporary-R&B production maximalism in favor of stripped-back synth-and-drum-machine textures, melismatic-vocal-and-melodic-rapping vocal hybrid where artists alternate sung-melody and rap-cadence within the same vocal performance, lyric content often confessional-personal addressing relationships, mental-health, drug-experience, and self-doubt, hip-hop-derived production with prominent 808 sub-bass and trap-derived hi-hat patterns, and tempos varying widely (60-100 BPM perception, with hip-hop-style halved-time grids). Distinguished from contemporary 2000s R&B by sparse-not-lush arrangement; distinguished from straight hip-hop by sung-melodic vocal foreground; distinguished from cloud-rap by retention of song-form rather than vamp-based construction.

items.name: Tango
items.lineage: Argentine bandoneón-and-violin orquesta-típica tradition codified through the Buenos Aires studio canon from Carlos Gardel onward
items.description: Tango (codified 1880s onward in Buenos Aires and Montevideo riverside-port working-class neighborhoods, with golden era 1935-1955 establishing the orquesta-típica big-tango-band sound through Carlos di Sarli, Aníbal Troilo, and Osvaldo Pugliese as bandleaders), the Argentine urban dance and song tradition. Defined by bandoneón-led ensemble (the bandoneón button-accordion is the tango-defining lead instrument, providing both melodic line and harmonic-stab punctuation), violin and cello string-section providing additional melodic and harmonic foundation, piano and double-bass rhythm-section, dramatic dynamics and rubato within strict tempo (the orquesta-típica tension between dramatic-dynamic-and-rubato performance and steady-tempo rhythmic foundation), partnered close-embrace dance choreography, and tango-canción (sung-tango) variant with foregrounded vocal-narrative lyrics. Distinguished from milonga by faster tempo and absence of milonga-specific habanera-rhythm; distinguished from later nuevo tango by retention of orquesta-típica conventions; distinguished from broader Latin-American tango by Buenos-Aires-Montevideo specific origin.

items.name: Milonga
items.lineage: Argentine-Uruguayan rural-pampas tango-precursor and parallel folk genre 1870s-onward with habanera-derived dotted-eighth-sixteenth ostinato bass and characteristic 2/4 milonga-clave. Originated in Rio-de-la-Plata gaucho-payada improvisatory-sung-poetry combined with Afro-Cuban habanera rhythm imported via 19th-century maritime ship-traffic between Buenos Aires and Havana. The milonga-campera rural form remains payada-derived (guitar-accompanied gaucho ballads), while the milonga-ciudadana urban form 1920s-onward fed directly into orquesta-típica tango via the 6/8-against-2/4 polyrhythmic dance variant played at faster tempo than mainline tango.
items.description: Milonga (codified mid-19th-century Argentine-and-Uruguayan rural-pampas folk-and-popular song-and-dance form pre-dating-and-parallel-to tango, with documented continuous-tradition from 1870s-onward rural-payada-troubadour performance practice; flowering through early-20th-century Buenos-Aires-and-Montevideo urban-milonga adaptation that fed directly into tango; mid-20th-century folkloric-revival through Atahualpa Yupanqui milonga-camp era 1940s-1970s, Mercedes Sosa parallel folklore-argentino lineage; 1990s contemporary continuation through Eduardo Falú, Jorge Cafrune, and contemporary Argentine folklore-singer-poet tradition), the Argentine-and-Uruguayan rural-pampas tango-precursor and parallel folk genre.
