items.description: Nashville sound (codified 1957-1970 through Chet Atkins's RCA-Nashville and Owen Bradley's Decca-Nashville production lineages, with the Music Row recording-industry consolidation establishing Nashville as the country-music industry capital), the postwar commercial country production aesthetic. Defined by string-section orchestration (the Nashville Strings session-musician union providing string-quartet-and-larger ensembles for country tracking sessions), smooth vocal-harmony arrangements (the Anita Kerr Singers and Jordanaires providing background-vocal smoothing), removal of fiddle-and-pedal-steel honky-tonk markers in favor of pop-orchestral instrumentation, lush mid-tempo arrangements designed for adult-pop crossover, and song-content of sophisticated romantic-narrative themes shifted away from honky-tonk-bar-room subject matter. Distinguished from honky-tonk by absence of fiddle-and-pedal-steel and presence of string-orchestra; distinguished from later countrypolitan (which extends the aesthetic further) by post-1957 to 1970 timestamp; distinguished from Bakersfield sound (the parallel California country-rebellion) by Nashville-pop orientation rather than honky-tonk retention.

items.name: Red Dirt
items.lineage: Oklahoma-Texas roots-country movement that emerged in 1970s-80s Stillwater Oklahoma as a regional alternative to the Nashville Music Row commercial-country machine — codified through the figures Bob Childers (the Red Dirt poet who became the genres elder statesman), the Red Dirt Rangers, Cross Canadian Ragweed, Stoney LaRue, Jason Boland and the Stragglers, Turnpike Troubadours, and the broader 21st-century Texas Country / Red Dirt circuit (Robert Earl Keen, Ray Wylie Hubbard, Hayes Carll) that maintains a parallel infrastructure to Nashville commercial country
items.description: Red Dirt (codified 1985 onward in Stillwater Oklahoma through the post-Cain's-Ballroom and Eskimo-Joe's-bar-scene songwriter community, with Bob Childers as the genre-foundational figure and second-wave continuation through Cross Canadian Ragweed, Stoney LaRue, and Jason Boland), the Stillwater-Oklahoma songwriter scene. Defined by songwriter-forward focus where original-personal-text composition foregrounds over performance-craft or commercial polish, country-rock instrumentation (electric guitar, bass, drums, fiddle, pedal-steel, occasional acoustic-guitar) with band-arrangement, working-class lyric narratives addressing Oklahoma-rural-and-college-town subjects (cattle-ranching, oil-field work, university-bar life, Oklahoma-specific landscape and culture), live-bar circuit centering on Stillwater venues and the Cain's Ballroom and Tulsa-and-Oklahoma-City regional scenes, and DIY-and-independent-label distribution. Distinguished from Texas country by Oklahoma-not-Texas centrality despite cultural overlap; distinguished from straight outlaw country by post-1985 timestamp and college-town setting; distinguished from Americana by retention of Oklahoma-specific cultural framing.

items.name: Gothic country
items.lineage: Dark-themed americana subgenre with Old Testament / Southern Gothic / murder-ballad subject matter — Sixteen Horsepower, Wovenhand, Murder by Death, the Handsome Family, early Johnny Cash American Recordings IV
items.description: Gothic country (1990s onward, codified through 16 Horsepower, Slim Cessna's Auto Club, Wovenhand, and the broader Denver-and-Tennessee scene of dark-Americana songwriters), the murder-ballad-leaning Americana sub-style. Defined by sparse instrumentation built on acoustic-or-electric guitar, upright bass, banjo, fiddle, and minimal drums (often brushes-on-snare or single-floor-tom rather than full kit), dark minor-key tonalities and modal-Aeolian-or-Phrygian melodic vocabulary, Southern-gothic-literary narrative content (rural murder ballads, religious-fundamentalist visions, generational curses, decaying Southern-towns), vocal delivery often baritone-or-lower with deliberate gravitas and anti-pop projection, and aesthetic kinship with cowpunk and dark-folk. Distinguished from straight Americana by darker tonal-and-thematic register; distinguished from cowpunk by less-aggressive-and-more-literary aesthetic; distinguished from murder-ballad-revival folk by retention of country-and-Americana instrumentation rather than pure-folk acoustic palette.

items.name: American primitive guitar
items.lineage: Instrumental fingerpicked steel-string solo-acoustic tradition pioneered by John Fahey on Blind Joe Death (1959, Takoma Records, Takoma Park MD) fusing Mississippi Delta blues, Appalachian hymnody, ragtime, Indian raga (especially via Robbie Basho who studied with Ali Akbar Khan), and 20th-century minimalist classical into a personal compositional vocabulary — extended through Leo Kottke (6 and 12 String Guitar, 1969), Peter Lang, Sandy Bull, Bola Sete; revived from the mid-2000s onward through Tompkins Square Records (Josh Rosenthal) via Jack Rose, William Tyler, James Blackshaw, Daniel Bachman, Glenn Jones, Sarah Louise
items.description: American primitive guitar (1959-onward, originating with John Fahey's self-released Blind Joe Death on Takoma Records, Takoma Park MD), the instrumental fingerstyle steel-string acoustic tradition Fahey coined as American Primitive — a term borrowed from painting referring to self-taught visionary work. Defined by solo steel-string acoustic guitar in open or altered tunings (DADGAD, open D, open C variants, custom-derived tunings), Travis-derived alternating-bass-plus-melody fingerpicking with the thumb often holding a sustained drone pedal, harmonic vocabulary fusing Mississippi Delta blues vamps, Appalachian hymnody, ragtime cadential figures, Indian raga modal-suspension (especially in Robbie Basho's 12-string raga adaptations after his study with Ali Akbar Khan), and 20th-century minimalist-classical ostinato influence, forms ranging from short blues-frame pieces through long-form raga arcs (Basho Visions of the Country, 30 Days) to virtuosic melody-foregrounded showpieces (Leo Kottke 6 and 12 String Guitar, 1969), and characteristic Fahey-era recording aesthetic of intimate parlor or home-studio tracking with single-mic-or-stereo-pair purist setups (no overdubs, no compression). Distinguished from folk-revival singer-songwriter open-tunings by exclusive instrumental focus and compositional ambition; distinguished from contemporary acoustic fingerstyle (Tommy Emmanuel et al.) by interior introspective register over technique-foregrounded entertainment; distinguished from delta blues by self-conscious composer-driven structural ambition over song-form vernacular. Modern revival (2005-onward) through Tompkins Square Records (Josh Rosenthal) revived the tradition via Jack Rose (whose pre-2009 death cemented his foundational status), William Tyler, James Blackshaw, Daniel Bachman, Glenn Jones, Sarah Louise, Steve Gunn.
exemplars: John Fahey — Blind Joe Death (1959, Takoma Records)
Jack Rose — Two Originals of Jack Rose (2008)

items.name: Gothic Americana (Southern Gothic literary tradition)
items.lineage: Broader Southern Gothic literary tradition (Faulkner, Flannery OConnor, Cormac McCarthy) rendered in folk-country-blues instrumentation with Pentecostal / Old Testament / frontier-violence thematic vocabulary — encompasses the Denver gothic-country canon (Sixteen Horsepower, Wovenhand, Slim Cessna Auto Club, the Reverend Glasseye) plus broader practitioners like Nick Cave (Murder Ballads, The Boatmans Call), late-period Tom Waits (Bone Machine onward), R.L. Burnside, the Handsome Family, the Bad Livers — distinct from gothic_country in scope (encompasses non-country instrumentation) and from folk_noir in literary lineage (Southern Gothic vs Victorian/Pre-Raphaelite)
items.description: Gothic Americana — the broader Southern Gothic literary tradition (Faulkner, Flannery O'Connor, Cormac McCarthy, Carson McCullers, Eudora Welty) rendered in folk-country-blues-rock instrumentation with Pentecostal / Old Testament / frontier-violence thematic vocabulary. Encompasses the Denver gothic-country scene (16 Horsepower, Wovenhand, Slim Cessna's Auto Club, the Reverend Glasseye), the literary-narrative branch (Murder by Death, Handsome Family), late-period Nick Cave (Murder Ballads, The Boatman's Call, Skeleton Tree), post-Bone-Machine Tom Waits (Bone Machine onward, especially Mule Variations and Alice), R.L. Burnside's late-period electrified Hill Country blues, and the broader dark-folk-rock songwriter tradition working with Southern Gothic source material. Defined by minor-key default tonal vocabulary (Aeolian-default with Dorian and Phrygian touches), declamatory Pentecostal-derived or Baptist-revival-derived vocal delivery (David Eugene Edwards' Nazarene upbringing audibly shapes Wovenhand), instrumentation crossing the country-folk-rock boundary (banjo and fiddle from gothic_country side, distorted hurdy-gurdy or distorted guitar from rock side, hammered dulcimer and harmonium from chamber-folk side), and lyrical content drawn from rural violence, divine judgment, sin, Old Testament narrative, the South's buried histories, the rural-American Gothic literary tradition. Distinguished from gothic_country in scope (broader instrumentation, more rock-leaning practitioners included); distinguished from folk_noir in literary lineage (Southern Gothic / Pentecostal versus Victorian / Pre-Raphaelite / chamber).
exemplars: Nick Cave and the Bad Seeds — Murder Ballads (1996)
The Handsome Family — Through the Trees (1998)
R.L. Burnside — A Ass Pocket of Whiskey (1996)

items.name: Folk noir (contemporary dark chamber-folk songwriter tradition)
items.lineage: Contemporary dark chamber-folk songwriter tradition centered around Marissa Nadler (six-album catalog from Ballads of Living and Dying 2004 through Strangers 2016), Espers (Greg Weeks / Meg Baird / Helena Espvall, Philadelphia), and the broader Kemado / Mexican Summer / Hexham Head circle — with Victorian, Pre-Raphaelite, surrealist-poetry (Nadler set Pablo Neruda on her debut), and cinematic-noir literary roots; the term was originally coined by Tony Wakeford for Sol Invictus to distance from the neofolk umbrella, but contemporary usage names the Nadler-Espers chamber-folk lineage. Distinct from gothic_americana (Southern Gothic / Pentecostal roots) and from neofolk-apocalyptic (Current 93, Death in June, post-industrial / Romantic-traditionalism lineage)
items.description: Folk noir — the contemporary dark chamber-folk songwriter tradition centered around Marissa Nadler (six-album catalog from Ballads of Living and Dying, 2004, through Strangers, 2016, and onward), Espers (the Philadelphia trio of Greg Weeks, Meg Baird, Helena Espvall who released Espers I, II, III on Wichita and Drag City 2004-2009), and the broader Kemado / Mexican Summer / Hexham Head circle of dark American chamber-folk songwriters (Diane Cluck, Hannah Cohen, Sharon Van Etten's earliest work, Meg Baird solo, Cat Power's pre-Greatest Hits period). Defined by fingerpicked acoustic-guitar foreground often in open or altered tunings, minor-key chamber arrangements with cello / viola / harmonium / piano supporting the song-form rather than expanding it, characteristic long-tail reverb processing on lead vocals as a defining production gesture (Greg Weeks at Hexham Head in rural Pennsylvania pioneered this aesthetic, with Marissa Nadler tracked there for Songs III: Bird on the Water, 2007), Aeolian and Phrygian modal vocabulary with suspended-fourth and sustained-resolution voicings, female-vocal-led canon (though not exclusively female), and lyrical content drawing from Victorian and Pre-Raphaelite imagery, gothic-novel atmosphere, surrealist poetry (Nadler set Pablo Neruda on her 2004 debut), cinematic film-noir reference, and personal-confessional content rendered through indirect imagery rather than direct confession. The term "folk noir" was originally coined by Tony Wakeford for Sol Invictus in the early 1990s to distance his project from the broader neofolk-apocalyptic umbrella (Current 93, Death in June), but contemporary usage has shifted to name the Nadler-Espers chamber-folk lineage. Distinguished from gothic_americana in literary lineage (Victorian / Pre-Raphaelite versus Southern Gothic / Pentecostal) and instrumentation (chamber-folk versus country-folk-rock); distinguished from neofolk-apocalyptic in production aesthetic (acoustic-chamber intimate versus martial-and-synth post-industrial) and thematic content (introspective-cinematic versus pagan-apocalyptic-traditionalist); distinguished from singer-songwriter folk by reverb-soaked vocal atmosphere and chamber instrumentation versus dry-vocal-and-band setup.
exemplars: Marissa Nadler — Ballads of Living and Dying (2004)
Marissa Nadler — Songs III: Bird on the Water (2007)
Diane Cluck — Black with Green Leaves (2005)

items.name: Ethio-jazz
items.lineage: Ethiopian Golden Age 1969-1974 Amha-Kaifa-Philips label canon — codified through Mulatu Astatke’s Berklee-and-NYC training brought back to Addis Ababa, the Roha Band and Walias Band as the canonical recording ensembles, Mahmoud Ahmed (Ere Mela Mela 1975), Alemayehu Eshete, and Tilahun Gessesse (also romanized Tlahoun Gèssèssè) as canonical singers; characterized by Ethiopian kignit-modal vocals over jazz-and-soul instrumental beds
items.description: Ethio-jazz (1969-1975 Addis Ababa Golden Age production, codified through Mulatu Astatke and the Hager Fikir Theatre / Imperial Bodyguard / Police Orchestra / Army Band / Walias Band house ensembles for the Amha Records, Kaifa Records, and Philips Ethiopia label catalog; tracked at Addis private studios and clandestinely at the Empire-era radio station that until 1969 had held a Hagere Fikir Maheber government monopoly on recording, with lacquers and masters shipped abroad for pressing to India, Lebanon, Greece, and West Africa — foreign-pressing-plant mid-forward signature is part of the canon and NOT generic vintage-warm; revival from 2005 onward via European reissue labels; Mulatu Astatke specifically has THREE distinct production contexts the codex must separate — 1965 London/Trinity College, 1966-1972 New York Worthy-label Latin-jazz, and 1969-1974 Addis Amha sessions), the Ethiopian musical genre pairing Ethiopian pentatonic kignit modes with American jazz horn arrangement and back-line. Defined by Ethiopian kignit (tezeta major/minor for nostalgia, bati major/minor for laments, ambassel for historical/heroic, anchihoye for slow-danceable) tuned in pure temperament NOT 12-TET, motor-on vibraphone introduced by Mulatu Astatke to Ethiopian popular music with slow tremolo, 1960s combo-organ (Farfisa / Vox / Hammond M-series spinet — NOT full Hammond B-3 which was rare in period), Selmer Mark VI or Eastern-European Amati/Lignatone baritone saxophone as the signature horn voice, trumpet and trombone section, 1960s hollowbody/semi-hollow electric guitar comping the Ethio-jazz chord stab on beats 2 and 4 or syncopated, Höfner 500/1 violin bass or similar flatwound European bass, small drum kit with calfskin or early plastic heads and papery snare, LP-style congas and bongos introduced by Astatke, and traditional Ethiopian instruments (krar bowl lyre, masenqo spike fiddle, washint bamboo flute, kebero conical drum) on azmari recordings issued by the same labels. Vocal delivery in Amharic with characteristic ejective consonants (p' t' s' q' k'), melismatic upper-register ornamentation, and microtonal inflection within the kignit. Tempo 65-95 BPM for tezeta ballads, 110-140 BPM for chik-chika / James-Brown-influenced uptempos. Ethiopian shuffle is a delayed-and on beats 2 and 4 — NOT swing-eighth. Distinguished from straight Ethiopian traditional music by jazz instrumentation and harmonic vocabulary; distinguished from American jazz by kignit modes and pure-temperament tuning; distinguished from Afrobeat by Ethiopian-not-Yoruba lineage and shorter-form song construction.
exemplars: Mulatu Astatke — Ethiopian Modern Instrumentals Hits

items.name: Samba-jazz
items.lineage: Rio de Janeiro 1962-1970 small-group jazz-samba tradition centered on the Forma and Som Maior label catalog — codified through Sergio Mendes’s Bossa Rio (1964) and Brasil 66, Tamba Trio (Luiz Eça-Bebeto-Helcio Milito), Sambalanço Trio, Edu Lobo, and Milton Banana Trio; characterized by piano-trio-plus-singer instrumentation, advanced-harmonic vocabulary, and energetic-up-tempo samba-derived rhythmic foundation
items.description: Samba jazz (codified 1962 onward through Bossa Três, Sambalanço Trio, and Tamba Trio establishing the small-combo Brazilian-jazz-fusion genre, with parallel international visibility through 1962-onward Brazilian-jazz exports), the Brazilian samba-and-jazz fusion subgenre. Defined by Brazilian samba back-line foundation (the samba rhythmic-percussion vocabulary translated to small-combo drum-kit and percussion) with bebop harmonic vocabulary (extended-chord ii-V-I cycles, altered dominants, modal-jazz mode-foundations), instrumental-foreground with improvising horn-front-line (saxophone, trumpet, flute) over piano-bass-drums-and-percussion rhythm-section, song-form built on tight head-solos-head structure with extended vamp-and-improvisation sections, and tempos around 100-140 BPM. Distinguished from straight bossa nova by jazz-instrumental-improvisation foreground over intimate-vocal-and-acoustic-guitar foundation; distinguished from cool jazz by Brazilian samba rhythmic foundation; distinguished from later Brazilian fusion-and-MPB by retention of acoustic-jazz-instrumentation over electric-band.

items.name: Cajun
items.lineage: South Louisiana Cajun French dance-hall music tradition rooted in the 1755 Acadian expulsion from Nova Scotia, codified through the Hackberry Ramblers (1930s commercial recordings), Iry LeJeune (post-WWII accordion revival), Nathan Abshire, Dewey Balfa and the Balfa Brothers, the Savoy Family Band (Marc and Ann Savoy and their sons), and the modern continuation (Steve Riley and the Mamou Playboys, BeauSoleil with Michael Doucet)
items.description: Cajun music (mid-19th century onward, originating with Acadian-French exiles deported from Nova Scotia 1755 and resettled in southwest Louisiana parishes Lafayette, Vermilion, Acadia, and Saint-Landry), the Louisiana Cajun French-Acadian dance music tradition that fused French ballad lineage with Anglo-Celtic fiddling and African-Caribbean rhythmic feel. Defined by the diatonic single-row Cajun accordion (a German-built instrument adopted ca. 1880 that displaced fiddle as lead), fiddle (often two playing in parallel thirds), iron triangle keeping time, and French-language vocal delivery in archaic Louisiana French preserving 17th-century vocabulary. Repertoire centered on waltzes (valses) and two-steps for fais-do-do dance hall, with high-pitched plaintive vocal style. Distinguished from zydeco by white-Creole-not-Black-Creole tradition and accordion-not-piano-accordion lead; distinguished from Quebecois fiddle by accordion presence and Louisiana-not-Quebec lineage; distinguished from straight Anglo-American old-time by French language and triangle percussion.

items.name: Zydeco
items.lineage: Black Creole French Louisiana dance-music tradition codified through Clifton Chenier (the King of Zydeco, the Houston-based bandleader from the 1950s through his death in 1987), Boozoo Chavis (the originator of the genre name with his 1954 Paper in My Shoe), Buckwheat Zydeco, Rockin Dopsie, Beau Jocque, Geno Delafose; characterized by piano accordion (the larger more harmonically capable cousin of the Cajun single-row accordion) plus frottoir rubboard (the metal washboard-derived percussion worn over the shoulders, the Clifton Chenier and welder Willie Landry innovation (c. 1946), popularized by Cleveland Chenier), distinct from Cajun (which is white Acadian French Louisiana with single-row diatonic accordion)
items.description: Zydeco (codified 1940s-1950s onward in Black-Creole Louisiana communities of southwest Louisiana, descending from earlier juré chant tradition and parallel-Cajun white-Creole tradition through cross-cultural mixing, with golden era through Clifton Chenier's lineage from 1955 onward), the African-American Creole counterpart to Cajun music. Defined by piano-accordion lead voice (rather than the Cajun-diatonic single-row accordion — the piano-accordion's wider note-range enables more harmonic-and-melodic flexibility), frottoir washboard scrubbed with thimbles or spoons providing percussive foundation, R&B-influenced groove and harmonic vocabulary (zydeco's blues-and-rhythm-and-blues lineage distinguishes it from Cajun's older string-band heritage), French-Creole-language vocal performance often with English code-switching, electric-bass and drum-kit foundation in modernized zydeco, and dance-hall performance context. Distinguished from Cajun by African-American-Creole-not-white-Creole tradition, piano-accordion-not-diatonic-accordion, and frottoir-not-triangle percussion; distinguished from straight blues by accordion-foreground and Louisiana-Creole-French-language; distinguished from R&B by accordion-and-frottoir folk-instrumentation.

items.name: Katajjaq (Inuit throat-singing game)
items.lineage: Inuit Arctic throat-singing game tradition preserved across Nunavik (northern Quebec), Nunavut, Greenland, and the Inuit Russian Far East — two women face each other in close proximity (often forehead to forehead) and alternate inhale-exhale vocal patterns at high speed, attempting to break each others rhythm until one laughs or runs out of breath; modern revival through Tanya Tagaq (the solo katajjaq performer who extended the tradition into solo electronic-collaboration work, Animism 2014 Polaris Music Prize), Susan Aglukark, the Pirurvik Centre cultural preservation infrastructure
items.description: The Inuit katajjaq (throat-singing) tradition continuous from premodern Inuit-Arctic-hunter-gatherer practice across Northern Canada (Nunavut, Nunavik, Nunatsiavut) and Greenland through colonial-era continuous performance (including a documented period of missionary-suppression in the late-19th-and-early-20th-century) into modern Inuit-cultural-revival; the katajjaq is performed as a vocal-game-and-competition between two women face-to-face, with characteristic interlocking-throat-sound arrangement evoking Arctic-environment sounds (wind, geese, dogs, walrus, mosquitoes). Defined by unaccompanied two-women-face-to-face hocket-and-throat-percussion arrangement, Inuktitut text register with characteristic vocables-and-ideophones, characteristic interlocking-percussive-vocal architecture.
exemplars: Madeleine Allakariallak — traditional Inuit katajjaq canonical

items.name: Tin Pan Alley song
items.lineage: American pre-rock popular songwriting tradition centered on the West 28th Street and later Brill Building songwriter-publisher infrastructure (c. 1885-1965) — covering George M. Cohan, Irving Berlin (Alexander s Ragtime Band 1911, the Tin Pan Alley breakthrough), Cole Porter, the Gershwins, Rodgers and Hart (later Rodgers and Hammerstein), Harold Arlen, Hoagy Carmichael, and the post-WWII Brill Building era (Goffin and King, Mann and Weil, Sedaka, Bacharach and David, Leiber and Stoller); foundational repertoire for the 32-bar AABA song form that defined American popular music for half a century
items.description: Pre-rock American songwriting tradition centered on Manhattan publishing houses; functional-harmony songs in 32-measure AABA form, sentimental-romantic-novelty subjects, written for sheet music and stage performance.

items.name: Brill Building pop
items.lineage: American 1958-1965 songwriter-pop industry centered on the Brill Building at 1619 Broadway in Manhattan and the adjacent 1650 Broadway — codified through the Aldon Music writing rooms of Don Kirshner and Al Nevins housing Carole King and Gerry Goffin, Barry Mann and Cynthia Weil, Neil Sedaka and Howard Greenfield, Burt Bacharach and Hal David — assembly-line songwriter pairs producing girl-group and teen-idol hits
items.description: Brill Building pop (1958-1965, named for the 1619 Broadway Manhattan office building that housed songwriting teams under contract to publishing houses), the late-50s-into-mid-60s songwriter-team teen-pop produced through industrial assembly-line craft. Defined by the songwriter-team pairing system writing songs to professional-craft standards then matching them to artists, teenage-romance lyrical subject (high school courtship, parental disapproval, prom-night devotion), Wall-of-Sound-or-girl-group production aesthetic with castanets-handclaps-strings palette, doo-wop-derived vocal-group backing, and a tight 2:30-2:50 single-format duration. Distinguished from Wall-of-Sound proper (which is a production aesthetic) by being a songwriting-and-publishing system; distinguished from Tin Pan Alley by post-rock-and-roll era and teenage subject; distinguished from Greenwich-Village confessional by craft-not-personal songwriting.

items.name: Great American Songbook (vocal jazz pop)
items.lineage: 1920s-1950s American popular-song repertoire from Tin Pan Alley, Broadway, and Hollywood (Gershwin, Berlin, Porter, Kern, Rodgers-and-Hart-and-Hammerstein) as interpreted by mid-century vocal jazz singers — Sinatra, Ella Fitzgerald, Sarah Vaughan, Tony Bennett, Nat King Cole
items.description: Mid-century vocal interpretation of pre-rock standards; jazz-trained singers performing AABA-form songs with rubato verses and swung choruses, typically with piano trio or jazz orchestra accompaniment.

items.name: Easy listening (orchestral pop)
items.lineage: Mid-20th-century instrumental and vocal orchestral-pop tradition — codified through Percy Faith (Theme from A Summer Place 1959), Mantovani (the cascading-strings sound), Henry Mancini (Moon River 1961, the Pink Panther theme 1963), Ray Conniff (the orchestrated-vocal-chorus sound), Lawrence Welk, Mitch Miller; the genre served as the mid-century mass-audience easy-listening AM-radio format before the rock-and-roll era displaced it from commercial-radio dominance
items.description: Easy listening orchestral / mood music (1949 onward, codified through Mantovani's Charmaine recording and the postwar Capitol-RCA-Columbia hi-fi mood-music industry, with golden era 1955-1965), the mid-century orchestral instrumental pop intended as background-suitable suburban-domestic-stereo music. Defined by lush string arrangements with cascading-glissando string-section gestures (Mantovani's signature waterfall sound), gentle Latin-jazz-and-bossa rhythms in the rhythm-section, vocal-free or near-vocal-free instrumental focus, repertoire of Broadway-standard and pop-hit instrumental covers alongside original mood-music compositions, and stereo-spectacular hi-fi production aesthetic designed to showcase the new home stereo equipment. Distinguished from cocktail-jazz by orchestral-not-small-combo instrumentation; distinguished from film score by standalone-not-narrative-tied composition; distinguished from later lounge-music by sincerity rather than ironic-revival framing.

items.name: Dream pop
items.lineage: 1980s-onward atmospheric guitar pop genre codified through the 4AD label catalog (Cocteau Twins, Treasure 1984, Heaven or Las Vegas 1990 the dream pop album), the Mazzy Star California canon (She Hangs Brightly 1990, So Tonight That I Might See 1993 with Hope Sandoval female-vocal-foreground), Galaxie 500 (the New England slowcore-adjacent canon), Beach House (Baltimore modern dream pop, Teen Dream 2010, Bloom 2012)
items.description: Dream pop (1985 onward, with Cocteau Twins, A.R. Kane, and the 4AD label codifying the genre and a second-wave 2010-present revival), the atmospheric guitar-and-vocal-pop subgenre. Defined by reverberant breathy vocal performance often using non-lexical or syllabic-blurred lyrics so vocal becomes another texture rather than language carrier, washes of chorused-or-modulated electric guitar (heavy use of phaser, flanger, and reverb effects creating layered ambient textures), midtempo 4/4 with non-aggressive drum-pattern, song-form retaining verse-chorus structure but stretched and harmonically suspended, and production aesthetic prioritizing atmospheric depth over dynamic punch. Lineage extends through shoegaze (a heavier-distorted subgenre) and slowcore (slower-tempo subgenre). Distinguished from shoegaze by less wall-of-distortion guitar and more vocal-foreground; distinguished from chillwave by post-1985 origin and guitar-band-not-synth-band instrumentation; distinguished from indie pop by reverberant-and-textural-rather-than-bright-and-immediate aesthetic.

items.name: Jangle pop
items.lineage: 1980s indie genre extending the 1960s Byrds twelve-string-electric chimey-guitar sound — codified through R.E.M. (the Athens Georgia voice, Murmur 1983, Reckoning 1984, Fables of the Reconstruction 1985), The dB s, the Smiths (the UK parallel canon, with Johnny Marrs Rickenbacker arpeggios over Morrisseys baritone), the Replacements early period, the Feelies, Game Theory, and the broader Paisley Underground Los Angeles scene (Dream Syndicate, Rain Parade, Three OClock); foundational sound: chiming Rickenbacker 12-string-electric over driving rhythm-section and melodic vocal hooks
items.description: Jangle pop (codified 1980 onward through R.E.M.'s Murmur and the Athens Georgia and Glasgow Scotland college-rock scenes, with second-wave Brian-Wilson-influenced revival in the late-2000s through 2010s), the chimey 12-string guitar pop subgenre descended from 60s folk-rock. Defined by 12-string electric-guitar lead lines providing the chimey-bright signature texture (Rickenbacker 360-12 the instrument), tight three-or-four-part vocal harmony arrangements, melodic clean-tone guitar phrases over rhythm-section foundation, song-form built on tight verse-chorus structures around 3 minutes, lyric content of romantic-frustration, college-aged disaffection, and personal-introspective themes, and production aesthetic preserving guitar-band live tracking with minimal post-production. Distinguished from 60s folk-rock by post-1980 timestamp and indie-college-rock context; distinguished from power pop by jangle-not-power-chord guitar emphasis and absence of British-Invasion-1964-65 lineage; distinguished from straight indie pop by 12-string-guitar centrality.

items.name: Power pop
items.lineage: Late-1960s through 1970s British Invasion-derived guitar-pop subgenre codified through the Who (the term power pop was coined by Pete Townshend to describe the Whos sound), Big Star (the Memphis power-pop band, #1 Record 1972, Radio City 1974), Badfinger (the Apple Records 1970-72 power-pop voice), Cheap Trick (the mainstream-commercial post-Big-Star extension), the Raspberries, the Knack (My Sharona 1979 the commercial breakthrough); foundational sound: melodic-hook-centric three-minute songs with chord-driven electric guitars, harmony vocals, and tight rhythm-section foundation
items.description: Power pop (codified 1972 onward through Big Star and Badfinger establishing the sound, with second-wave 1979-1981 commercial-mainstream era through Cheap Trick, The Knack, and the Cars, and continuing tradition through to present), the hooky guitar-pop subgenre. Defined by hooky melodic-foreground songwriting with tight verse-pre-chorus-chorus pop-craft architecture, full-throated vocal harmonies stacking 2-4 voices in arranged harmony parts, ringing distortion-touched guitars (the power-pop-specific guitar-tone of clean Rickenbacker or Telecaster pushed slightly into amp-overdrive), hard backbeat percussion with prominent fills, song-content addressing teenage-romantic-and-relationship subjects, and tight 3-3:30 song-length. Production lineage descends from late-Beatles-era and Who-and-Move British-Invasion power-pop precursors. Distinguished from straight pop by retention of band-instrumentation foreground over orchestrated arrangement; distinguished from punk by full-vocal-harmony and clean-guitar aesthetic; distinguished from later jangle pop by retention of hard-rock distortion-tinge.

items.name: Sophisti-pop
items.lineage: 1980s British adult-contemporary jazz-pop subgenre characterized by smooth chord-rich production, electric-piano-led harmonic foundation, atmospheric backing vocals — codified through Sade (Diamond Life 1984, Promise 1985), Everything But the Girl (Eden 1984), the Style Council (Café Bleu 1984), Prefab Sprout (Steve McQueen 1985), and the early Swing Out Sister releases
items.description: Sophisti-pop (codified 1984-1989 UK and adjacent adult-contemporary pop scenes through Sade, Style Council, Prefab Sprout, Everything But the Girl, and the post-new-wave-era jazz-leaning pop movement), the mid-1980s British and adjacent adult-contemporary pop genre. Defined by jazz-derived chord vocabulary (extended major-7 and minor-9 voicings, altered-dominants, modal-jazz mode-foundations drawn from American adult-contemporary and bossa-nova sources), smooth fretless-bass and electric piano (Fender Rhodes, DX7) instrumental foundation, sax solo features as melodic-instrumental color, programmed drum-machine percussion alongside or replacing live drum-kit, lyric content addressing sophisticated-adult romantic subjects in literate-poetic register, and production aesthetic prioritizing smooth-and-restrained over post-punk-aggression or new-wave-spike. Distinguished from American adult-contemporary by post-new-wave UK-and-European cultural framing; distinguished from later acid jazz by absence of rare-groove-and-funk-revival sample-based foundation; distinguished from straight smooth-jazz instrumental by retention of song-form vocal-pop-craft.

items.name: Art pop
items.lineage: High-concept songwriter pop with avant-garde production sensibility — Kate Bush, Peter Gabriel, Brian Eno, Talk Talk Spirit of Eden, Bjork, Sufjan Stevens, Joanna Newsom, FKA twigs, Bon Iver
items.description: Conceptually-ambitious pop song that imports techniques from avant-garde, art-rock, or experimental electronic adjacencies; through-composed structures, theatrical vocal performances, often album-as-statement.

items.name: Twee pop
items.lineage: 1980s-onward fey indie-pop subgenre codified through C86 cassette (NME 1986) and the Sarah Records (Bristol 1987-1995) lineage — characterized by jangly minor-key guitar, soft male and female vocals, lo-fi production aesthetic, and twee-romantic lyrical subject matter; Belle and Sebastian, Tullycraft, Stars, and Camera Obscura extending the canon into the 2000s
items.description: Twee pop (codified 1986 onward through the C86 NME-cassette compilation and the British indie-pop scene of the late-1980s, with successor 1990s-2000s American-and-UK indie-pop continuation through the K Records-and-Sarah-Records label communities), the childlike-fey indie-pop subgenre. Defined by tinkly-clean-guitars (the twee-bright-clean electric-guitar tone with chorus and minimal-distortion processing), deliberately-sung vocal performance prioritizing earnestness over sophistication (the twee-aesthetic of unadorned-clear vocal projection), simple two-or-three-chord verse-chorus song structures, lyrical content addressing childhood-nostalgia, gentle-romantic, pastoral-imagery, and fey-aesthetic subjects, and DIY-cassette-and-7-inch-single distribution through small indie labels. Distinguished from later mainstream indie pop by C86-and-Sarah-Records lineage and refusal of commercial polish; distinguished from straight indie-rock by absence of harder-distorted-guitar foreground; distinguished from straight pop by retention of indie-credibility and DIY-aesthetic.

items.name: Indie pop (modern)
items.lineage: Post-2000 streaming-era indie-pop with bedroom-recording aesthetic and DIY production — codified through Vampire Weekend (Vampire Weekend 2008), Beach House (Teen Dream 2010), Grimes (Visions 2012), and the broader Pitchfork-canonical indie ecosystem; characterized by reverb-soaked guitars, drum-machine programming, and confessional first-person lyrical register
items.description: Indie pop modern (2010s onward, the streaming-platform indie-pop developing after the late-2000s indie-rock peak, codified through artists distributing on Spotify, Bandcamp, and TikTok with bedroom-DIY production scaled to mainstream pop polish), the streaming-era hooky guitar-and-synth pop subgenre. Defined by bedroom-DIY production aesthetic scaled up through DAW polish and selective commercial-mastering investment (the post-2015 hybrid where DIY-bedroom-roots remain audible but commercial competitiveness is engineered), prominent hooks designed for TikTok-virality and streaming-playlist attention-economy, blend of acoustic-and-electric guitar with synth-pad and programmed-drum textures, vocal performance often pitched-and-processed with subtle auto-tune and stack-doubling, and lyric content of personal-relatable subject matter optimized for pop crossover. Distinguished from indie pop's earlier 2000s incarnation by streaming-platform distribution context; distinguished from straight bedroom pop by commercial-polish ceiling; distinguished from straight commercial pop by retained indie-credibility-signaling.

items.name: Bubblegum pop
items.lineage: Late-1960s through early-1970s manufactured-pop subgenre targeted at the pre-teen audience — codified through the Buddah Records label catalog produced by Kasenetz-Katz (the 1910 Fruitgum Company Simon Says 1968, Ohio Express Yummy Yummy Yummy 1968), the Archies (the cartoon-derived studio project, Sugar Sugar 1969 the commercial breakthrough), Bobby Sherman, the Partridge Family, the Osmonds, the Jackson 5 early period — built on simple melodic hooks, three-chord harmonic foundation, and lyrical content of pre-adolescent crush-romance and sugar-themed innocence
items.description: Bubblegum pop (1968-1972, originated through Buddah Records' Kasenetz-Katz Singing Orchestral Circus collective and producer-driven studio assembly of fictional bands), the late-60s manufactured teen-pop with deliberate juvenility as its aesthetic stance. Defined by sing-song hooks repeated to memorability, candy-and-sugar imagery in lyrics, simple I-IV-V-vi harmonic progressions without modulation, three-chord verse-chorus-verse-chorus structure under 3 minutes, vocal arrangements alternating lead with choral group response, and Saturday-morning-cartoon-show synergy. Production aesthetic borrowed Wall-of-Sound density without girl-group emotional weight. Distinguished from straight teen-pop by self-conscious juvenility-as-pose; distinguished from psychedelia by absence of mind-expansion lyrical apparatus.

items.name: J-pop (classic mainstream)
items.lineage: Japanese 1980s-1990s mainstream pop tradition codified through Seiko Matsuda, Yumi Matsutoya, the agency-system idol pop infrastructure (Johnny’s Entertainment for male groups, Sun Music for solo idols), and television-tied tie-up song format — characterized by major-key brightness, English-loanword lyric inserts, and tightly-arranged session-musician production
items.description: Classic J-pop (codified 1988 onward through Komuro Tetsuya productions, with golden era 1990-1998 of avex trax and Visual-Kei lineage and second wave 2010-onward through Hello Project and AKB48 idol-group), the Japanese mainstream pop tradition. Defined by extended-harmony chord progressions drawing from kayōkyoku (mid-century Japanese pop) and 70s-80s American AOR vocabulary, prominent key-changes mid-song (often modulating up a semitone or whole-tone for the final chorus), high-pitched and emotive vocal performance often with crying-affect register, tightly-arranged session-band-or-programmed instrumentation with rhythm-section, synth-pads, and string-pad layers, and song-form alternating verse-pre-chorus-chorus with extended bridge-modulation sections. Distinguished from kayōkyoku (its predecessor) by 1980s-onward timestamp and synth-and-rock-band instrumentation; distinguished from later K-pop by Japanese-language and Japan-specific industry framing; distinguished from anison (anime soundtrack pop) by mainstream-pop-not-tied-to-anime-property context.

items.name: Enka
items.lineage: Japanese 20th-century sentimental popular-ballad genre derived from late-Meiji-period (1880s-1912) enka-shi street-political-protest-song tradition, transformed mid-Showa-period (1930s-1960s) into commercial recording-industry sentimental-vocal-pop. The vocal technique stresses kobushi melismatic-ornamental vibrato-and-microtonal-bend, koe-on chest-resonance projected-vocal, and pentatonic-yo minor-leaning melodic-vocabulary (often modulating through 4-cycle key changes per verse). Lyrical themes center on lost-love, distant-homeland, mother-and-rural-nostalgia, and ocean-and-port-imagery. The 1960s-1980s golden-age enka-orchestra featured strings-and-shamisen-and-shakuhachi hybrid-arrangement; 1990s-onward enka declined as a youth-genre but persists as a senior-audience-and-karaoke staple.
items.description: Enka (codified 1950s-onward Japanese sentimental popular-ballad tradition, with foundational figures Misora Hibari and Mori Shin'ichi establishing the genre's 1950s-1960s identity; tradition continues into the 21st century though commercial centrality has shifted to younger pop forms; the Meiji-era predecessor enka song-form developed as political-protest street-song commentary in the 1880s and migrated through 1920s ryūkōka popular-song tradition before crystallizing into the postwar sentimental-ballad form), the postwar Japanese sentimental-ballad tradition centered on melismatic vocal performance, yearning-and-nostalgia lyric subjects, and Western-pop-instrumentation augmented by Japanese-traditional instrumental coloration. Defined by kobushi vocal-ornamentation tradition (the Japanese melismatic-ornament practice involving rapid pitch-bend-and-tremolo embellishment of sustained notes that gives enka its emotionally-saturated vocal signature), Western-tonal-pop-instrumentation foundation (rhythm-section drum-bass-electric-guitar-keyboards-synthesizer plus orchestral-string-section overdubs in mature-era productions) augmented by shamisen-and-koto coloration on signature recordings (the East-meets-West fusion specific to the genre), pentatonic-and-yo-scale melodic vocabulary that grounds the genre in Japanese-traditional tonal language despite Western harmonic framework, lyric content centered on yearning, lost love, hometown-nostalgia (furusato), gendered-suffering subjects, sake-and-rain imagery, and characteristic emotional-saturation register, and song-form built on AABA or verse-chorus structures with prominent vocal-feature climax sections often modulating to a higher key for the final chorus. Recording era: 1950s through 2000s as the dominant commercial mid-elder Japanese popular tradition; 78rpm shellac through vinyl through CD eras of distribution. Distinguished from contemporaneous kayōkyoku (which developed alongside enka and shared many performers and writers) by enka's deeper retention of pentatonic-melodic and traditional-Japanese-vocal-ornamentation practices; distinguished from later 1980s J-pop by traditional-instrumentation-and-lyrical-subjects orientation rather than 80s-Western-rock-pop-vocabulary; distinguished from min'yō folk tradition by composed-not-traditional repertoire and Western-pop-instrumentation framework. Lineage forward feeds the broader Japanese mainstream pop continuum (kayōkyoku to J-pop), and the karaoke phenomenon (enka songs as the karaoke repertoire backbone for older Japanese listeners). Lineage of major exemplars marks the era: Misora Hibari (1937-1989, the foundational enka diva), Mori Shin'ichi (b. 1947), Kitajima Saburō (b. 1936), Ishikawa Sayuri (b. 1958), Itsuki Hiroshi (b. 1948).

items.name: City pop
items.lineage: Japanese 1976-1986 sophisticated urban-adult-pop genre fusing late-1970s American AOR (adult-oriented rock), funk, fusion-jazz, and disco-soul into a distinct Tokyo-bubble-era mature-pop aesthetic. The instrumentation features electric-piano (Rhodes-and-Wurlitzer), fretless-bass, clean-electric-guitar (often with chorus pedal), brass section (often Roland JX-3P synth-brass), and breathy-intimate close-miked vocal-style. Lyrically focused on urban-leisure: nighttime-driving, summer-resort-and-beach, romantic-rendezvous-in-cafes-and-bars, and Tokyo-Yokohama-Shōnan coastal lifestyle. Originally a quiet commercial-niche aimed at the Japanese middle-class consumer-boom audience, city-pop gained massive 2010s-onward Western internet-re-discovery via vaporwave and YouTube-algorithmic-suggestion.
items.description: City pop (codified 1976 onward in late-70s and 80s Japanese urban pop scene, with Sugar Babe and Tatsuro Yamashita as foundational artists and golden era 1980-1986 establishing the sound, with international 2010s vaporwave-revival visibility through YouTube algorithmic discovery), the Japanese urban pop genre importing American AOR, jazz-fusion, and disco-funk vocabularies. Defined by lush extended-chord arrangements with major-7 and minor-9 harmonic vocabulary drawn from American jazz-fusion and adult-contemporary pop traditions, smooth tight-session-band performance (often the same Tokyo session musicians appearing across many artists' records), urban-life lyrical content (Tokyo-skyline-and-bay imagery, late-night-cocktail-bar settings, romantic-intrigue-amid-cosmopolitan-life subjects), Roland-and-Yamaha synthesizer textures alongside Rhodes-and-Wurlitzer electric piano, and high-fidelity-stereo production aesthetic showcasing the new-Japanese hi-fi industry. Distinguished from kayōkyoku by absence of older-Japanese-pop-tradition vocabulary and adoption of American-jazz-fusion language; distinguished from later J-pop classic by pre-1989 timestamp and adult-not-idol-pop orientation; distinguished from American AOR despite shared influences by Japanese-language and Tokyo-urban specificity.

items.name: Shibuya-kei
items.lineage: 1990s Japanese eclectic-pop subgenre centered on Tokyo’s Shibuya district record-store scene — codified through Pizzicato Five, Cornelius (Keigo Oyamada), Fantastic Plastic Machine, and Kahimi Karie; characterized by sampledelic crate-digger production, sixties-French-pop and bossa-nova references, and ironic-cosmopolitan pop sensibility
items.description: Shibuya-kei (codified 1990s onward in Tokyo Shibuya neighborhood music-scene through Pizzicato Five, Cornelius, Cibo Matto, and the broader Shibuya-Tower-Records-and-record-store culture), the 1990s Tokyo neighborhood scene fusion genre. Defined by fusion of French chanson-pop, bossa nova, easy listening, samba-jazz, lounge, electro-pop, and 60s pop-revival source vocabularies (the Shibuya-kei eclectic-record-collector aesthetic of borrowing from disparate retro-and-international source materials), playful-and-ironic pop-craft songwriting with deliberately-eclectic genre-juxtaposition, female-vocal-foreground in many examples, sample-based and live-band production aesthetic combinations, and Tokyo-record-store and Shibuya-club performance contexts. Distinguished from straight Japanese pop and J-pop by Shibuya-neighborhood specificity and retro-eclectic source palette; distinguished from American lounge-revival by Japanese cultural-context and Tokyo industry framing; distinguished from later Japanese electronic genre by retention of song-form pop-craft.

items.name: K-pop (modern)
items.lineage: Korean idol-pop tradition codified through Seo Taiji and Boys (1992) breaking the trot mold, then HOT, Shinhwa, and SES as first-generation idols; second-generation (TVXQ, BIGBANG, Wonder Girls, 2NE1) breaking into Japan 2005-2010; third-generation BTS, Blackpink, EXO, Twice driving global crossover from 2013 onward — characterized by densely-produced multi-genre tracks, synchronized choreography, and integrated visual identity
items.description: Korean idol-pop built on producer-team songwriting and choreographed group performance; genre-collage tracks that shift between hip-hop, EDM, R&B, ballad, and pop sections within single songs; layered group vocals.

items.name: Mandopop
items.lineage: Mandarin-language mainstream Chinese-language pop tradition codified through 1980s Taiwan (Teresa Teng, Liu Wen-cheng) — through Jay Chou’s 2000-2010 Hua Yu pop (Mandarin pop with hip-hop and R&B production), and the contemporary cross-strait Mandarin entertainment industry spanning Taiwan, mainland China, Singapore, and Malaysia
items.description: Mandarin-language pop centered on Taipei production lineage; ballad-oriented, melodically and harmonically rich, vocal-virtuoso-emphasized, often draws on Chinese pentatonic phrasing within western functional harmony.

items.name: Cantopop
items.lineage: Hong Kong Cantonese-language mainstream pop, codified through the late-1970s Sam Hui and the early-1990s Four Heavenly Kings — Jacky Cheung, Andy Lau, Aaron Kwok, Leon Lai — characterized by ballad-heavy repertoire, film-tie-in song format, and the post-handover (1997) industry that absorbed and merged with the mainland Mandarin pop market
items.description: Cantopop (1974 onward, codified through Sam Hui's Cantonese-pop breakthrough records and crystallized in the 1980s-1990s televised entertainment industry centered on TVB and the Heavenly Kings era), the Hong Kong Cantonese-language popular music genre. Defined by Cantonese-tonal-language vocal delivery (the six-tone Cantonese spoken-pitch contour shapes melodic phrasing differently than tonal-language-free Mandopop), ballad-dominant repertoire with melodramatic emotional vocal performance, lush adult-contemporary arrangements with synth-pad-and-string orchestration over electric-bass and programmed drums, frequent use of cover-versions of Japanese kayōkyoku and Western pop songs translated into Cantonese, and a star-making apparatus through televised song contests and karaoke licensing. Distinguished from Mandopop by Cantonese-language and Hong Kong-not-Taiwan/mainland-China industry; distinguished from Hong Kong Canto-rock by ballad-not-band orientation; distinguished from Western adult-contemporary by Cantonese-tonal-melody and Hong Kong cinematic-emotional aesthetic.

items.name: Vocaloid synth-voice pop
items.lineage: Japanese synth-vocal subculture codified through Yamaha’s Vocaloid voice-synthesis software (2004) and the Hatsune Miku (2007) avatar that became the canonical virtual idol — characterized by user-generated music with synthetic-vocal lead, anime-inflected visual identity, and the Nico Nico Douga upload-and-remix ecosystem that fed the genre
items.description: Japanese-origin pop built around synthesized vocal-engine voices (character voicebanks); virtuosic super-fast melodic lines beyond human breath capacity, hyperpop-adjacent timbral aesthetic, internet-distributed authorship.

items.name: Chanson pop (modern)
items.lineage: Modern French songwriter pop tradition extending the chanson lineage past the 1960s yé-yé era — Vanessa Paradis, MC Solaar, Mylène Farmer in the 1990s; Carla Bruni, Cœur de Pirate, Christine and the Queens, Stromae (Belgian) extending the form into the 2000s-2020s with electronic and hip-hop production influences
items.description: Chanson pop modern (1990s onward, descended from mid-century chanson but absorbing post-hip-hop, electronic, and indie-rock production sensibilities), the contemporary French songwriter pop genre that preserves the chanson tradition's spoken-prosody French-text emphasis while modernizing arrangements. Defined by French-language vocal delivery foregrounded in the mix with conversational-rather-than-belted projection, song-form built around literary-text-driven verse structures rather than hook-driven verse-chorus pop, modernized arrangements drawing on indie-rock guitar bands, electronic textures and programmed drums, jazz-tinged piano vamping, or hip-hop-derived sample-based production depending on the artist, and a heritage of cultural prestige and literary respectability inherited from chanson classique. Distinguished from chanson classique by post-1990 timestamp and contemporary production palette; distinguished from French-language pop and Eurovision-style French entries by intellectual-text aesthetic and slow-burn rather than radio-friendly hook construction.

items.name: Cantautore italiano
items.lineage: Italian songwriter tradition codified through the Genoa school (Fabrizio De André, Luigi Tenco, Bruno Lauzi, Gino Paoli, Umberto Bindi), the Milan school (Enzo Jannacci, Giorgio Gaber), the Roman school (Antonello Venditti, Francesco De Gregori, Lucio Dalla, Claudio Baglioni), and the modern continuation (Vinicio Capossela, Cristiano De André), with French chanson and Brazilian bossa nova as primary external lineage influences
items.description: Italian singer-songwriter tradition emphasizing literary lyric authorship and intimate solo-or-compact-ensemble arrangements; descends from 1960s Genoa school, modernized through the 1970s and onward.

items.name: Schlager
items.lineage: German-language popular sentimental song genre with 1920s Weimar cabaret roots, mid-century commercial extension (Heino, Roy Black, Freddy Quinn), and modern continuation (Helene Fischer, Andrea Berg) — major-key sentimental melodies, accordion-and-strings-and-occasional-yodel arrangements, lyrical content concerning love, home country (Heimat), nostalgia, holidays, alpine landscapes; distinct from Liedermacher (politically engaged literary-cabaret tradition)
items.description: Schlager German (codified 1920s onward through Weimar-era Berlin cabaret tradition, with golden eras 1955-1965 and 1972-1985 establishing the sound), the German-language sentimental popular song tradition. Defined by mid-tempo simple-harmonic-progression backbone (typically I-IV-V-vi diatonic functional harmony without complex modulation), prominent melodic singing-along-friendly hooks designed for audience-participation, German-language lyric content addressing romantic-melancholy, sentimental-nostalgia, and pleasant-vacation subjects, lush adult-contemporary arrangements with strings, accordion-or-keyboard, light percussion, and optional brass-and-woodwind accents, and television-variety-show performance context (the German Schlagerfest televised competitions and cruise-ship performance circuit). Distinguished from German rock and pop by sentimental-mainstream commercial-radio orientation; distinguished from earlier Weimar-era cabaret by post-1955 timestamp; distinguished from Eurovision pop by German-language commitment and German-cultural-industry framing rather than pan-European-festival aesthetic.

items.name: Eurovision pop
items.lineage: Pan-European televised song-contest pop tradition tied to the annual Eurovision Song Contest (founded 1956) — codified through the contest’s evolving format: bombastic-power-ballad and key-change-climax conventions in the 1990s-2000s, then post-2010 electronic-and-quirky entries (Conchita Wurst 2014, Måneskin 2021); a stylistic register more than a genre
items.description: Eurovision pop (codified 1956 onward through the annual Eurovision Song Contest televised competition, with successive eras of stylistic conventions through 60s-70s ballads, 80s-pop, 90s-eurodance, 2000s-onward genre-pluralism), the pan-European televised song-contest pop optimized for three-minute spectacle. Defined by tight 3-minute song-format compliance (the contest's strict three-minute time-limit shapes every entry), key-change ballads and dramatic arrangement designed for live-television visual-and-aural impact, choreographed staging with backing-dancers and elaborate costume-and-lighting, English-language vocal performance (a shift from earlier multilingual era post-1999 rule change permitting any language), national-cultural-identity signaling within pop-format conventions, and a peculiar mix of sincere ambition and self-conscious genre-spectacle aesthetics. Distinguished from straight commercial pop by contest-format constraints and televised-spectacle context; distinguished from European national-language pop traditions by pan-European competitive-festival framing; distinguished from American pop by European industry-and-cultural-context centrality.

items.name: Scandi pop
items.lineage: Nordic mainstream pop production school codified through Stockholm-based Cheiron Studios (Max Martin, Denniz PoP) starting mid-1990s — supplying Britney Spears, Backstreet Boys, NSYNC era global pop; later evolving through MNEK, Robyn, Lykke Li, and the broader Swedish songwriter-and-producer export to international pop markets
items.description: Nordic-region pop production school exporting hooky melodic-and-harmonic templates globally since the 1990s; melancholic-major-key affect, polished synth-and-vocal production, songwriter-team authorship.

items.name: Russian estrada
items.lineage: Soviet-era (1940s-1991) and post-Soviet (1991-onward) Russian-language commercial-stage popular song — Edita Piekha, Joseph Kobzon, Lev Leshchenko, Alla Pugacheva (Pesnya goda annual TV festival regular), Sofia Rotaru, Filipp Kirkorov; characterized by sentimental minor-key lyrical content, orchestrated arrangements with strings and brass, and the centralized State-controlled distribution through Melodiya / Soviet TV / Radio infrastructure
items.description: Russian estrada (codified 1930s onward through Soviet-era state-licensed popular-music industry, with continuous tradition through Soviet golden era 1960s-1980s and post-Soviet continuation through to present), the Soviet-era and post-Soviet Russian-language popular song tradition. Defined by large vocal range with operatic-projection or pop-belted vocal performance (the estrada-voice training drawing on conservatory-classical-vocal pedagogy applied to popular material), ballad-dominant repertoire alternating with novelty-numbers and patriotic-songs, lush string-orchestra-and-rhythm-section arrangements drawing on European-easy-listening and American-pop influences, song-form built on tight verse-chorus structures around 3 minutes, and lyric content addressing romantic-melancholy, Soviet-patriotic, and personal-narrative subjects. State-licensed-distribution era from 1930s to 1991 with continued post-Soviet commercial-radio-and-television presence. Distinguished from Russian rock by ballad-and-pop orientation over rock-band; distinguished from chanson-russe by Russian-language and Soviet-industry framing rather than French-tradition lineage; distinguished from American pop by Russian-conservatory-vocal-training and Soviet-cultural-industry context.

items.name: Portuguese pop (modern)
items.lineage: Modern Portuguese mainstream pop tradition extending past the fado canon — codified through Madredeus, Mariza’s fado-fusion, the 2000s Buraka Som Sistema kuduro crossover, and contemporary artists like Sara Tavares, David Carreira; characterized by Portuguese-language vocals over electronic-and-organic hybrid production
items.description: Portuguese pop modern (1990s onward, descending from earlier fado-influenced Portuguese popular song through Madredeus, Mariza, and Salvador Sobral lineages and crystallizing through the post-Eurovision-2017 international-visibility era), the modern Portuguese-language mainstream pop genre. Defined by traces of fado-derived melodic ornament and saudade-affect emotional register layered into modernized pop-song production, Portuguese-language vocal performance with characteristic intimate-conversational delivery rather than belted-projection, instrumentation combining acoustic-Portuguese-guitar lineage with modern pop band-instrumentation (electric-and-acoustic guitar, bass, drums, synth pads, programmed elements), song-form built on tight verse-chorus pop structures with bridge-modulation craft, and lyric content addressing romantic-and-personal subjects with literary-poetic ambition. Distinguished from straight fado by post-1990 timestamp and modernized arrangement; distinguished from Brazilian Portuguese-language MPB by European-Portuguese accent and Lisbon-not-Rio cultural framing; distinguished from Spanish-language Iberian pop by language and Portugal-specific industry context.

items.name: Spanish canción pop
items.lineage: Spanish-language mainstream song tradition centered on Iberian and Latin American crossover — codified through Mecano, Joaquín Sabina, Alejandro Sanz, and Rosalía bringing flamenco-pop and electronic-pop fusions into the international mainstream from the 1980s through 2020s
items.description: Spanish canción pop / Spanish-language Iberian mainstream pop (codified 1960s onward through Spanish-state-era pop-recording industry, with continuous tradition through Spain's transition to democracy and post-1980s mainstream-pop industry), the Spanish-language Iberian mainstream pop song tradition. Defined by copla-derived melodic ornament (traces of traditional Spanish-Andalusian melismatic vocal-decoration carried into modernized pop arrangements), imported Anglo-American pop-rock production conventions (electric-and-acoustic guitar, bass, drums, synth pads, programmed elements) translated into Spanish-language vocabulary, song-form built on tight verse-chorus pop structures with bridge-modulation pop-craft, vocal performance often with operatic-projection or melismatic-pop-belt depending on era and artist, and lyric content addressing romantic-melodrama, personal-narrative, and Spanish-cultural specificity. Distinguished from Latin-American Spanish-language pop by Iberian-Spanish accent and Spain-specific industry; distinguished from flamenco-pop by absence of palmas-and-cajón flamenco-rhythm-section; distinguished from straight Anglo-American pop despite production-overlap by Spanish-language commitment.

items.name: Galician kantautor and folk-pop
items.lineage: Galician-language singer-songwriter tradition emerging from underground anti-Franco protest culture in the late-1960s and flourishing after the 1975 Spanish democratic transition — figures Suso Vaamonde (the 1970s Galician protest voice), Bibiano, Andrés do Barro, the broader Movida galega 1980s post-Franco cultural-flourishing wave, and the modern Mercedes Peón folk-revival lineage; draws on the medieval Galician-Portuguese Cantigas de Santa María corpus (13th-century Alfonso X court) and rural Galician folk substrate
items.description: Galician kantautor / cantautor (1968 onward, codified during late-Franco-era Galician-language cultural revival through Andrés do Barro, Voces Ceibes collective, and successors), the Galician-language regional folk-pop songwriter tradition. Defined by Galician-language vocal delivery (the deliberate political-cultural choice during decades of suppression), folk-derived melodic-and-modal vocabulary drawing on Galician traditional muiñeira (mill-dance) and alborada (dawn-piece) repertoire, gaida (Galician bagpipe) accompaniment occasionally extended with pandeireta tambourine, fiddle, and accordion, lyric content addressing Galician identity, peasant-and-fisherfolk solidarity, and post-Franco democratic transition, and a folk-festival circuit through Galician cultural associations. Distinguished from Basque kantautor by Galician language and gaida-not-txalaparta instrumental signature; distinguished from Spanish-language Castilian protest song by regional-language commitment; distinguished from later Galician folk-rock by acoustic-singer-songwriter rather than band orientation.

items.name: Basque kantautor
items.lineage: Basque-language (Euskera) singer-songwriter tradition emerging from underground anti-Franco protest culture in the late-1960s — codified through Mikel Laboa (the Basque kantautor founder, his 1969 Bost urte and 1974 Gernika releases the founding statements), Benito Lertxundi, Imanol Larzabal, Antton Valverde, Lourdes Iriondo, Xabier Lete; deeply engaged with Basque cultural-linguistic revival under and after Franco-era cultural suppression, with parallel post-1980s extensions through Ruper Ordorika (the post-Franco-era Basque cantautor voice)
items.description: Basque kantautor / Euskal kantautoreak (1965 onward, beginning under late-Franco-era cultural repression and crystallizing through the 1970s Ez Dok Amairu collective), the Basque-language regional songwriter tradition tied to language-revival cultural politics. Defined by Basque-language vocal delivery (a deliberate political act during decades when the language was suppressed), folk-derived solo guitar accompaniment occasionally extended with txalaparta plank percussion or trikitixa accordion, lyrics drawing on Basque mythology, peasant resistance themes, and the abertzale (patriotic) movement vocabulary, and a performance circuit running through bertso-saio improvised-verse competitions and Euskal Herria festival circuit. Distinguished from Galician kantautor by language and txalaparta-percussion lineage; distinguished from Spanish-language Castilian protest song by ETA-era political stakes.

items.name: Bachata
items.lineage: Dominican-Republic guitar-based bolero-derivative couple-dance romantic-song tradition originated 1960s in Santo-Domingo-and-Cibao rural-and-urban barrios. The ensemble: requinto lead-guitar (small-bodied higher-pitched playing arpeggio-and-melodic-fills), segunda rhythm-guitar (six-string playing strum-pattern with güira metallic-scraper), bongos, and bajo electric-bass. The bachata-clave 4-beat pattern emphasizes the second-and-fourth beats with bongo accents. Five historical phases: 1960s-foundational (acoustic-guitar bolero-rural-rhythm), 1970s-marginalized (urban-poor barrio-association), 1980s-electrified (electric-instruments incorporation), 1990s-mainstreamed (bachata-rosa commercial-crossover), and 2000s-onward modern-bachata (urban-bachata fusion with R&B and reggaeton).
items.description: Bachata (1962 onward, originating in Dominican Republic working-class neighborhoods around Santo Domingo and codified through Radhamés Aristy and José Manuel Calderón's amargue song-form), the Dominican guitar-led song form built on lead-and-rhythm-guitar pair over bongo-and-bass back-line. Defined by the lead Dominican-bachata guitar (smaller, higher-tuned) playing arpeggio-and-melodic-fill counterpoint to the rhythm guitar's strummed accompaniment, melismatic-tenor lead vocal trading with second-voice harmony, lyrical content centered on amargue (bitterness, heartbreak), 4/4 meter with a syncopated hand-percussion pattern, and tempos around 120-140 BPM. Late-90s modernization (Aventura, Romeo Santos lineage) added pop-R&B production and English-Spanish bilingual lyrics. Distinguished from merengue by guitar-led-not-accordion-led ensemble and slower-romantic-lyrical register; distinguished from bolero by Dominican-rural-rather-than-Cuban-urban roots and bongos-not-claves percussion.

items.name: Bolero (tropical romantic)
items.lineage: Pan-Latin-American romantic ballad tradition that emerged in late-19th-century Santiago de Cuba (the first bolero Tristezas by José Pepe Sánchez 1883) and codified pan-continentally from the 1930s through Mexican composers Agustín Lara (Solamente Una Vez 1941, Granada 1932), Consuelo Velázquez (Bésame Mucho 1940 — the most-recorded bolero), Armando Manzanero, María Grever, and the trio canon (Trio Los Panchos 1944-onward, Trio Matamoros, Trio Calaveras), with the post-WWII voices Pedro Infante, Lucho Gatica, Lola Beltrán, Olga Guillot, and the late-1940s Cuban filin small-combo intimate-jazz extension
items.description: Pan-Latin-American romantic ballad of Caribbean origin; slow-tempo, extended-harmony chord vocabulary, melismatic vocal interpretation; Cuban-Mexican axis, foundation for international Latin pop ballad.

items.name: Son cubano
items.lineage: Cuban son tradition, the canonical Afro-Cuban song-form that became the foundational template for salsa, mambo, cha-cha-chá, and most Caribbean-Latin popular music 1900s-onward. Originated in eastern Cuban Oriente-province (Santiago de Cuba and Guantánamo region) late-19th-century out of changüí proto-son rural-Afro-Spanish-fusion, with classic ensemble of tres (small three-double-course guitar), Spanish guitar, bass (originally botija jug-bass, later contrabass), bongos, claves, and maracas. Migrated to Havana in the 1920s where the sexteto-and-septeto urban-commercial codification (adding trumpet) made son the international Cuban-music ambassador. The clave 3-2 (or reversed 2-3) two-bar wood-block rhythm anchors all son derivatives; the verse-montuno structure (canto verse-section, montuno call-and-response open-improvisation section) defines all subsequent Caribbean popular-song architectures.
items.description: Eastern Cuban song-and-dance form centered on tres-guitar interlocking with bongos and bass; verse-section followed by call-and-response montuno over clave; foundational template for salsa, mambo, and Latin jazz.

items.name: Salsa (Nuyorican)
items.lineage: New York Puerto Rican-Cuban-Latin diaspora dance-music codified through the Fania All-Stars canon (1968-1977) with Hector Lavoe, Willie Colón, Celia Cruz, Eddie Palmieri, Rubén Blades
items.description: New York-developed dance-band Latin music synthesizing son cubano, mambo, and jazz horn arrangement; sophisticated piano-and-horn arrangements, soneo improvisation over montuno, large-ensemble back-line.

items.name: Salsa cubana (timba)
items.lineage: 1990s Cuban dance-band evolution from son and salsa — characterized by complex multi-meter clave layering, jazz-fusion harmonic vocabulary, heavy electric-bass and synth integration; codified by NG La Banda, Los Van Van late-period, Issac Delgado, and Manolito y Su Trabuco bringing post-Soviet-era Cuban innovation to international Latin music
items.description: 1990s Cuban Latin dance-band evolution incorporating funk-and-jazz-fusion harmonic vocabulary, drum-kit syncopation alongside traditional Cuban back-line, breakdown-and-build dance-section structures, very high intensity.
exemplars: Pupy y Los Que Son Son

items.name: Mambo
items.lineage: Cuban big-band brass-and-saxophone urban-popular-dance music codified 1939-onward in Havana from son-cubano accelerated-and-orchestrated for big-band swing-orchestra adaptation. The mambo-typical ensemble: four-trumpets, five-saxophones (two altos, two tenors, plus baritone), piano, contrabass, congas, bongos, timbales, claves, maracas, and güiro. The mambo-section open-improvisation montuno-equivalent features brass-shouts (mambos), saxophone-and-piano riffs over ostinato-vamp, and percussion-and-vocal call-and-response. The 1947-onward Mexico-City-and-NYC-Palladium mambo-craze made it the international Cuban-dance-music ambassador; the 1950s saw mambo-fused-with-jazz (Afro-Cuban jazz, Latin-jazz), with cha-cha-chá and pachanga emerging as next-generation variants.
items.description: Mambo (codified 1938-1955 through Havana-Mexico-City-New-York Cuban big-band scene, with Pérez Prado, Tito Puente, Tito Rodríguez, and Machito as primary architects and golden era 1950-1955), the Cuban-derived big-band dance music genre. Defined by large jazz-influenced ensemble (5+ trumpets, 4+ saxophones, trombone, piano, bass, congas, bongos, timbales, and vocals), Afro-Cuban rhythm-section foundation built on clave-pattern (forward and reverse 3:2), call-and-response between brass section, sax section, and rhythm section, montuno piano-vamp foundation, and tempos around 140-180 BPM with strong dance-floor-functional pulse. Distinguished from son cubano by larger ensemble and big-band-jazz instrumentation; distinguished from earlier Cuban danzón by faster tempo and absence of slow opening; distinguished from later salsa (which descends from it) by big-band ensemble size and pre-1965 timestamp.

items.name: Cha-cha-chá
items.lineage: Cuban couple-dance and music genre invented 1953-onward in Havana from danzón-de-nuevo-ritmo modernization, named after the characteristic triple-step (one-two-cha-cha-cha) percussive-foot pattern. The canonical orquesta-charanga ensemble: solo flute (typically wooden five-key flute), three-or-four violins, contrabass, piano, timbales, congas, and güiro scraper. The tempo (around 120 BPM, moderate, danceable for non-professionals) and the simplified chord-progressions (typically I-IV-V or II-V-I in major keys) made cha-cha-chá the most accessible Cuban couple-dance for non-Cubans, fueling its massive 1950s-1960s American-and-European mainstream popularity. The structure is verse-and-montuno like son cubano, with the montuno open-improvisation section often featuring extended flute-and-violin solos over coro-pregón call-and-response.
items.description: Cha-cha-chá (codified 1953-1954 in Havana through violinist-bandleader Enrique Jorrín's adaptation of mambo and danzón, named for the three-step foot-pattern's rhythmic articulation), the 1950s Cuban dance form that became the international ballroom dance phenomenon of the late 50s. Defined by the characteristic three-step (1-2-cha-cha-cha) syncopated foot-pattern carried into the rhythm-section's güiro-and-claves articulation, charanga-style flute-and-violin orchestration over piano-bass-tumbadoras (timbales-replacement-by-conga in some bands), tempos around 110-130 BPM, and song forms with vocal montuno call-and-response and instrumental break sections for dance. Performance contexts: Havana dance halls, ballroom dance studios, US Latin-jazz crossover venues. Distinguished from mambo by slower tempo and three-step foot pattern; distinguished from danzón by faster tempo and absence of slow opening section; distinguished from later salsa by charanga instrumentation rather than conjunto brass-and-percussion line.

items.name: Charanga
items.lineage: Cuban orquesta-charanga light-flute-and-violin orchestral-dance ensemble derived from danzón-orquesta-típica modernization 1920s-onward, codified into the canonical charanga-francesa instrumentation by 1930s. The ensemble: solo wooden five-key flute, two-to-four violins, piano, contrabass, timbales, congas, and güiro. Initially attached to danzón-cubano repertoire, charanga expanded into danzonete, cha-cha-chá, mambo-charanga, and pachanga (Eduardo Davidson 1959 innovation) as the genre absorbed son-cubano-and-mambo influences. The charanga-soneando style 1960s-onward incorporated trombone-and-trumpet-and-saxophone via the salsa-Nuyorican charanga-orquesta hybridization. Modern charanga revival 1990s-onward foregrounds the flute-violin texture as the canonical timba alternative-to-brass.
items.description: Cuban dance-ensemble configuration with five-key flute and violins as melodic-front, piano and bass mid, timbales and guiro percussion; played danzón, danzonete, cha-cha-chá, mambo across the 20th century.

items.name: Guaracha
items.lineage: Cuban up-tempo song-and-dance form, the satirical-comic cousin to son cubano, prominent in the Sonora Matancera repertoire and the Celia Cruz canon
items.description: Cuban up-tempo song-and-dance with sharply-syncopated melodic-vocal phrasing, satirical-narrative lyric mode, and call-and-response montuno; sibling form to son with faster tempo and looser narrative structure.

items.name: Rumba cubana
items.lineage: Afro-Cuban secular drum-and-vocal folkloric tradition (yambú / guaguancó / columbia subforms) originating in Havana and Matanzas tenement-courtyard contexts
items.description: Afro-Cuban secular drum-and-vocal tradition; conga-trio interplay (quinto soloing, tumba grounding, conga middle) over claves, lead-and-chorus call-and-response vocals; three regional styles yambú, guaguancó, columbia.

items.name: Guaguancó
items.lineage: Cuban couple-dance rumba subform with the characteristic vacunao symbolic-pursuit-and-evasion choreographic structure, codified 1880s-onward in Havana-and-Matanzas Afro-Cuban barrios out of solar-tenement-courtyard improvised drumming. Built on three-conga interlocking pattern (tumbador low-pulse, tres-dos middle-syncopation, quinto high-improvisation lead), clave 3-2 or 2-3 wood-block timekeeper, and palitos cáscara stick-on-drum-shell pattern. Vocal structure follows decimas Spanish-poetic-form opening (canto), coro-call-and-response chorus, and montuno open-improvisation section. The faster-tempo rumba-columbia and slower-tempo rumba-yambú are the sibling subforms.
items.description: Guaguancó (codified 19th century Havana and Matanzas, the most internationally-known of the three rumba sub-styles — yambú, guaguancó, columbia), the mid-tempo Afro-Cuban rumba sub-style. Defined by clave-3:2 (forward) rhythmic foundation with prominent quinto improvisational drumming (the smallest-and-highest-pitched conga drum carrying the improvisational-virtuosic line over the foundational tumbadora-and-tres-golpes pattern), couple-dance choreography of male-pursuit-and-female-vacunao-deflection (the flirtatious-pursuit narrative giving the dance its sexual-charged energy), call-and-response between lead-vocalist and chorus, claves and palitos sticks providing additional rhythmic foundation, and lyric content addressing daily-life subjects, romantic boast, and barrio-neighborhood references. Distinguished from yambú by mid-tempo rather than slow tempo and presence of vacunao dance-figure; distinguished from columbia (the third rumba sub-style) by couple-dance rather than solo-male-display format; distinguished from later salsa by acoustic-percussion-only ensemble.

items.name: Danzón
items.lineage: Cuban late-19th-century elegant-couple-dance tradition derived from European-contradanza imported through Haitian-French Saint-Domingue refugees 1791-onward, codified 1879-onward in Matanzas-and-Havana by orquesta-típica orchestral ensembles. The dance unfolds through ABACA rondo-form (introduction-and-paseo-promenade, A-section, B-section, A-return, C-trio-section, A-return), allowing partner-couples to alternate between dancing and resting during instrumental-trio-sections. The classic charanga-francesa ensemble: two flutes (one wooden, one metal), two violins, contrabass, piano, timbales (with cáscara stick-rhythm-on-shell), and güiro scraper. The danzón seeded the cha-cha-chá 1953-onward and danzonete vocal-variant 1929-onward and remains a living tradition through danzonera dance-hall events in Havana, Mérida, and Mexico-City.
items.description: Formal-court couple-dance form of the late 19th and early 20th centuries; charanga-ensemble instrumentation, sectional ABACA structure with elaborated thematic sections, ancestor of cha-cha-chá and mambo.

items.name: Cumbia colombiana
items.lineage: Colombian Caribbean-coast cortejo-procession couple-dance tradition originating mid-17th-century onward in Cartagena-and-Barranquilla Atlantic-coastal-region from Afro-Indigenous-Spanish fusion (enslaved-Africans-of-the-Bantu-Yoruba diaspora + Zenú-Wayuu Indigenous-coast + Spanish colonial Catholic-feast-day procession). The canonical conjunto-de-cumbia ensemble: gaitas Indigenous-Wayuu vertical-clay-and-cane flutes (gaita-macho lead, gaita-hembra accompaniment), tambor-mayor low-bass-drum (African-derived), llamador high-pulse-drum, alegre middle-improvisation-drum, maracas-and-guache shakers. The cumbia-clave 4-beat pattern emphasizes beats 1 and 3 (the conga-pattern echo). The 1940s-1960s commercial-mainstream cumbia adaptation by big-band-with-accordion-and-brass (cumbia-de-orquesta) spread Colombian-cumbia internationally; the 1960s-onward Peruvian-Mexican-and-Argentine cumbia-variants emerged from this diaspora.
items.description: Colombian Caribbean-coast dance music descended from indigenous-African-Spanish triple-heritage; gaita flute or accordion lead over tambora drum and bass, characteristic dotted-eighth back-line; spread continent-wide.

items.name: Cumbia peruana (chicha)
