Recordings include the Sugar Hill Gang Rappers Delight 1979 (the commercial breakthrough, built on a session-band recreation of Chics Good Times bassline), Grandmaster Flash and the Furious Five The Message 1982 (the socially-conscious hip-hop breakthrough), Afrika Bambaataa Planet Rock 1982 (the Kraftwerk-Trans-Europe-Express-derived electro-funk hip-hop fusion), Run-DMC self-titled debut 1984
items.description: Founding-decade hip-hop (1979–1985), pre-sample-based-production. Live-band-backing recreates disco breaks while MCs rap over the rhythm. Party-record formats (12-inch single dominant), call-and-response between MCs, foundational lyric vocabulary (boasts, party-rocking, social commentary, neighborhood pride). The pre-recorded canon of the genre — recordings before this period don’t exist commercially.
exemplars: Grandmaster Flash & The Furious Five — The Message (1982)
Afrika Bambaataa & Soul Sonic Force — Planet Rock (1982)

items.name: Golden-age sample-collage hip-hop (1986-1991)
items.lineage: The golden-age sampler-defined era of hip-hop, codified by the E-mu SP-1200 (released 1987) and Akai S950 (released 1988) drum-and-sampler workstations that enabled the boom-bap breakbeat-and-sample-collage production aesthetic — Public Enemy It Takes a Nation of Millions to Hold Us Back 1988 produced by the Bomb Squad (Hank Shocklee), Boogie Down Productions Criminal Minded 1987 produced by KRS-One and Scott La Rock, Eric B and Rakim Paid in Full 1987, EPMD Strictly Business 1988, A Tribe Called Quest The Low End Theory 1991, De La Soul 3 Feet High and Rising 1989, the broader Native Tongues collective
items.description: 1986–1991 sample-based hip-hop era between live-band founding decade and 1990s boom-bap proper. SP-1200 / S900 / S950 sampler-defined production with eclectic sample-source approach (jazz, soul, funk, rock, library music). Native Tongues / D.A.I.S.Y. Age aesthetic centered on positive-Afrocentric expression. Four-bar-loop construction, lyric-forward MC craft, pre-Pro-Tools tracking workflow.
exemplars: De La Soul — 3 Feet High and Rising (1989)
A Tribe Called Quest — The Low End Theory (1991)
Eric B & Rakim — Paid in Full (1987)
Public Enemy — It Takes a Nation of Millions to Hold Us Back (1988)

items.name: Contemporary R&B (late-90s–2000s)
items.lineage: Late-1990s-and-2000s producer-team-era contemporary R&B aesthetic codified by the Darkchild, Jam-and-Lewis (later Flyte Tyme), Timbaland, She'kspere, and Rodney Jerkins production-lineage. Built on the breath-admixed close-miked intimate-vocal-aesthetic with stacked harmony backgrounds (typically 4-to-8 voice layered), neo-soul jazz-extended chord-vocabulary (minor-9, major-7-sharp-11, sus-2, sus-4 voicings), and programmed drum-machine kit (typically Roland TR-909, Akai MPC60-3000, or Korg M1) playing swung-and-shuffled hi-hat-and-snare-with-808-kick. The genre layered Atlanta-Memphis-NYC studio-clusters and bridged classic-Motown-and-Philly-soul lineage to 2010s-modern-R&B and trap-soul.
items.description: Late-1990s into early-2000s contemporary R&B production tradition. Darkchild / Jam-Lewis / Timbaland producer-team era. Programmed beats with syncopated kick patterns, multitracked vocal stacks (lead + harmonies + ad-libs + doublings), melismatic R&B vocal phrasing, sub-bass synthesis, sampled drum hits. Hip-hop-adjacent production aesthetic crossed with traditional R&B vocal performance.
exemplars: Brandy & Monica — The Boy is Mine (1998)

items.name: Garage-rock revival (2001–2010)
items.lineage: 2000s deliberate-vintage garage-rock movement reviving 1960s garage-rock sonic and stylistic vocabulary through fuzz-and-reverb single-coil-guitar production, raw vocal delivery, and short-song-form construction — codified through The White Stripes (White Blood Cells 2001, Elephant 2003), The Strokes (Is This It 2001), The Hives (Veni Vidi Vicious 2000), Yeah Yeah Yeahs, The Vines, with revival-aesthetic continuing through Black Lips and the Burger Records scene
items.description: 2001–2010 international garage-rock revival movement. Deliberate vintage-aesthetic production — tube tape, mono mixing, fewer overdubs, raw simple arrangements, period-correct equipment as artistic choice. Back-to-basics rock-and-roll songwriting with simplified instrumentation, fashion-cohesive scene aesthetic across international cities (NYC, Detroit, London, Stockholm, Sydney).
exemplars: The White Stripes — Seven Nation Army (2003)
The Hives — Hate to Say I Told You So (2002)

items.name: Minneapolis synth-funk-pop
items.lineage: 1980s Minneapolis funk-pop hybrid centered on the Paisley Park studio aesthetic — codified through Prince (1999 1982, Purple Rain 1984, Sign O the Times 1987), the Time (the Morris Day vehicle, What Time Is It 1982), Sheila E (The Glamorous Life 1984), Jesse Johnson, the Family — characterized by drum-machine-led groove construction, dirty-funk synth-bass, falsetto vocal lead, and explicit sexual-and-spiritual thematic mixing
items.description: Early-to-mid-1980s Minneapolis-centered synth-funk-pop hybrid tradition. LinnDrum + Oberheim/Yamaha analog-poly-synth + tight rhythm guitar + electric bass interlock + funk-derived vocal arrangements + dance-pop song structure. Auteur-multitrack production (single creator playing all parts), professional-grade home studio defining the workflow.

items.name: TikTok-era streaming pop
items.lineage: 2020s short-form-platform-native pop crafted for algorithmic discovery on TikTok and Instagram Reels — characterized by hook-foregrounded sub-thirty-second song structures, mid-song genre-and-tempo pivots, viral-dance-and-challenge-targeted composition, and rapid-iteration release cycles — exemplars include Olivia Rodrigo (SOUR 2021), Lil Nas X (Old Town Road 2019), Doja Cat, PinkPantheress, Ice Spice, with the form representing a structural shift from album-era pop construction
items.description: 2020s streaming-platform-native pop tradition. Short-form-video-platform-optimized song construction (sub-2-minute tracks, hooks front-loaded, repetition-friendly choruses). Bedroom-DAW production with sample-flipped breakbeats, pitched-up bedroom-vocal, intimate-but-streaming-loud mastering. Distribution and discovery primarily through algorithmic streaming-platform recommendation rather than radio or critical reception.

items.name: Globalized African-pop crossover
items.lineage: 2020s Africa-meets-Western-pop streaming-era hybrid tradition — codified through Wizkid ("Essence" featuring Tems 2020), Burna Boy (African Giant 2019, Twice as Tall 2020), Tems, Rema, Tiwa Savage, and the broader Afrobeats-to-international-mainstream wave; characterized by Afrobeats / amapiano rhythmic foundations under English-and-Pidgin vocals, major-label distribution, and feature collaborations with North American and European pop artists
items.description: 2020s globalized African-pop crossover tradition. Amapiano log-drum back-line and afrobeats syncopation crossed with Western pop melodic structure, English-language hooks, multi-producer cross-continental workflow. Streaming-era global distribution. Bridges African source-traditions with Western pop architecture — distinct from any single regional source-tradition by virtue of its hybridized production approach.

items.name: British R&B and British Invasion (1962–1968)
items.lineage: Mid-1960s British R&B and blues-rock interpretation of American sources — codified through The Rolling Stones (The Rolling Stones 1964, their early Chess-blues covers), The Animals ("The House of the Rising Sun" 1964, "I’m Crying" 1964), The Yardbirds (Five Live Yardbirds 1964), and Them (Van Morrison’s early band) — characterized by white English musicians performing African-American blues and R&B repertoire with electric-rock-band instrumentation through Marshall amplifiers and the British studio sound
items.description: Mid-60s British R&B and blues-rock tradition (1962–1968): the Soho-club-circuit cohort interpreting American R&B and Chicago-blues source material through a tight-band British engineering aesthetic. Defined by the combo-organ-and-clean-edge-guitar instrumental signature, blues-shouter vocal delivery, single-take small-room tracking, and a specifically British producer-led discipline targeting AM-radio singles rather than album-side construction. The transitional zone between American rhythm-and-blues source material and what became British hard rock — distinct from later British classic-rock by both era (predates 1968 multitrack adoption) and by R&B-cover-orientation rather than blues-rock-original-orientation.
exemplars: The Animals — House of the Rising Sun (1964)
The Yardbirds — Heart Full of Soul (1965)
The Rolling Stones — (I Can't Get No) Satisfaction (1965)
Manfred Mann — Do Wah Diddy Diddy (1964)
The Pretty Things — Don't Bring Me Down (1964)
Spencer Davis Group — Gimme Some Lovin' (1966)
The Kinks — You Really Got Me (1964)

items.name: Khayal (Hindustani classical vocal)
items.lineage: The most common North Indian Hindustani classical vocal genre, replacing dhrupad as the dominant vocal form from the 18th century onward — codified through the Gwalior, Agra, Kirana, Patiala, Atrauli-Jaipur gharana lineages; characterized by the bilampat-laya-vilambit-laya (slow tempo) opening composition (cheez or bandish) followed by improvisation through alap, bol-banav (word-elaboration), tan (rapid melodic runs), and laykari (rhythmic variation)
items.description: Slow-tempo improvisatory vocal genre that became the dominant Hindustani classical form from roughly the 18th century onward, displacing dhrupad as the primary court-art tradition. Two-part structure (badā khyāl / chōṭā khyāl), elaborate raga-exposition (āḷāp) followed by tāl-locked composition. Voice as primary improvisation vehicle with tabla and sarangi as co-improvisers within tabla-bound rhythmic-cycle constraints.

items.name: Tappa (Punjabi-origin Hindustani semi-classical)
items.lineage: Hindustani semi-classical vocal genre originating in late-18th-century Punjab through Mian Ghulam Nabi Shori (Shori Mian), who adapted Punjabi camel-driver folk songs into a fast-melisma classical-vocal genre — characterized by its rapid-fire intricate ornamental melisma patterns (different from khayal sustained-then-fast structure) and continued through the Banaras gharana lineage (Girija Devi, Naina Devi, Shobha Gurtu)
items.description: Fast-melismatic semi-classical North Indian vocal genre derived from Punjabi camel-drivers’ songs, codified for art-music context in the late 18th century by Mian Shori Mian. Defined by extremely rapid taan (melodic-figure) sequences within compact compositions. Hybrid position between khayal and thumri — more rhythmically driven than the former, more melodically agile than the latter.
exemplars: Girija Devi — Tappa in Raga Khamaj
Malini Rajurkar — Tappa in Raga Kafi
Shobha Gurtu — Tappa in Raga Bhairavi

items.name: Dadra (Hindustani semi-classical light-vocal)
items.lineage: Hindustani semi-classical light-vocal genre cast in the dadra tala (six-beat rhythmic cycle, 3+3 grouping) — typically performed at the end of a thumri concert as a lighter-mood companion piece, with romantic-and-devotional Brij Bhasha and Awadhi lyrical content
items.description: Light-classical North Indian vocal genre in dadra-tāl (six-beat cycle), shorter and more song-like than thumri but sharing thumri’s romantic / devotional poetic register. Boundary genre between mehfil-court-music and the regional folk traditions of Uttar Pradesh and Punjab. Often performed as concert closer following a thumri set.
exemplars: Girija Devi — Dadra in Raga Khamaj

items.name: Tarana (Hindustani vocalized-syllable composition)
items.lineage: Hindustani vocal genre using non-lexical vocalized syllables (tom, na, dir, dani, todani, yala, nadiri, drim) attributed by tradition to Amir Khusraus 13th-century court innovation — typically performed at the end of a khayal concert as a fast-tempo rhythmically dazzling concert-closer, with the syllables functioning as vocal-equivalent to tabla bols
items.description: Hindustani vocal genre using meaningless rhythmic syllables (tom, dir, ta, na, ra) as compositional material. Attributed to Amir Khusrau (13th–14th century) but most famously developed in Mughal-court khayal lineage. Typically performed as a fast closer to a khayal set, the syllables enabling extreme rhythmic dexterity that meaningful text would constrain.
exemplars: Pandit Jasraj — Tarana in Raga Bhairav
Rashid Khan — Tarana in Raga Hamsadhwani
Bhimsen Joshi — Tarana in Raga Yaman

items.name: Kriti (Carnatic devotional composition)
items.lineage: The central composition-form of Carnatic classical music, codified by the early-19th-century Trinity (Tyagaraja set Telugu and Sanskrit devotional poetry to ~600 kritis predominantly to Rama; Muthuswami Dikshitar composed in Sanskrit predominantly to various deities; Syama Sastri composed predominantly to the Goddess) — every kriti has the standard pallavi (refrain) / anupallavi (upward-developing second section) / charanam (longer extending section) structure
items.description: Foundational compositional form of Carnatic (South Indian) classical music. Three-section structure (pallavi / anupallavi / charanam) on devotional Hindu poetry, primarily in Sanskrit, Telugu, or Tamil. Attributed compositions of the Trinity (Tyāgarāja, Muthuswāmy Dīkshitar, Śyāma Śāstri, all early 19th century) form the repertoire. Differs from Hindustani forms by being substantially text-bound rather than rāga-improvisation-bound.

items.name: Padam (Carnatic slow-tempo lyrical genre)
items.lineage: Carnatic slow-tempo lyrical genre setting Tamil and Telugu nayika-bhava (heroine-emotion) poetry to elaborated single-line-per-section vocal exposition — typically performed in the second half of a Carnatic kutcheri after the main kriti, with the 17th-century padam composer Kshetrayya (Telugu) and the Tamil padam tradition continued through Subbarama Iyer
items.description: Slow-tempo Carnatic vocal genre, typically setting love-poetry (often shringara-rasa Sanskrit or Telugu verse) addressed to the divine beloved. Performed primarily in concert and bharatanatyam-dance contexts. Extreme tempo dilation enables word-painting and microtonal raga-elaboration on individual syllables that faster forms cannot accommodate.

items.name: Javali (Carnatic light-classical love-song)
items.lineage: Carnatic light-classical romantic-love song genre at faster tempo than padam, setting Telugu and Tamil and Kannada erotic-and-romantic poetry to elaborated vocal performance — emerged in the 19th century at the Mysore and Tanjore courts, codified through Patnam Subramania Iyer and Veene Sheshanna
items.description: Light-classical Carnatic vocal genre treating overtly erotic and worldly themes — distinct from padam by being faster, simpler in structure, and explicit rather than sublimated in religious framing. Late-19th-century courtly origin, sometimes performed by devadasis. Rapid tempo and direct text foregrounded.

items.name: Tillana (Carnatic concert-closer rhythmic showpiece)
items.lineage: Carnatic rhythmic showpiece genre using non-lexical jathi syllables (dhim, tarana, dhirana) alongside short Sanskrit or Telugu praise-text — the Carnatic counterpart of the Hindustani tarana, typically performed as the concert-closer of a kutcheri; composers Swati Tirunal Rama Varma (Maharaja of Travancore, 1813-1846), Pallavi Seshayyar, the modern composer Lalgudi Jayaraman
items.description: Carnatic counterpart to the Hindustani tarana — concert-closer using rhythmic syllables (tana, nom, tom) interspersed with brief text. Faster tempo than typical Carnatic forms, virtuosic display piece. Often choreographed for bharatanatyam dance. Composers Lalgudi Jayaraman and Patnam Subramania Iyer contributed repertoire.
exemplars: Lalgudi Jayaraman — Tillana in Raga Behag
M. Balamuralikrishna — Tillana in Raga Bhairavi
Sudha Ragunathan — Tillana in Raga Kuntalavarali

items.name: Gurmat Sangeet (Sikh devotional)
items.lineage: Sikh sacred-music tradition built on shabad kirtan (singing of the verses of the Guru Granth Sahib scripture), organized by raga across the 31 ragas mentioned in the Granth, performed by trained ragis at gurdwaras worldwide and especially at Harmandir Sahib (the Golden Temple) in Amritsar where the tradition has been performed continuously since the 1604 installation of the Adi Granth scripture by Guru Arjan Dev
items.description: Sikh devotional vocal tradition deriving from the music settings (raga assignments) specified in the Guru Granth Sahib. Performed in gurdwara worship and concert. Shares the musical-grammar of Hindustani classical (raga-bound improvisation, tāl-locked composition) but with Sikh-Punjabi linguistic register and shabad (verse) rather than purely abstract melodic exposition.
exemplars: Bhai Gurmeet Singh Shaant — gurbani kirtan
Bhai Niranjan Singh Jawaddi Kalan — shabad kirtan

items.name: Sufi sama (Indian-subcontinental Sufi devotional ceremony)
items.lineage: Chishti-order Sufi devotional ceremony tradition centered on sama (Arabic for listening), the practice of group listening to qawwali-style devotional poetry-singing as a path toward divine union; performed at dargah (Sufi shrine) settings across the Indian subcontinent, with the Nizamuddin Auliya shrine in Delhi and the Khwaja Moinuddin Chishti shrine in Ajmer as the principal pilgrimage sites
items.description: South Asian Sufi mystical-listening ceremony, distinct from but related to qawwali. Performed at Chishti-order Sufi shrines (dargahs), focused on poetic-mystical-text rendering rather than the stadium-format projection of qawwali. Smaller ensemble, more variable tempo, longer ecstatic-state-cultivation sections. Cultural-context layer beneath the qawwali genre.

items.name: Tropicália
items.lineage: Brazilian late-1960s art-pop counter-cultural movement (1967-1969 peak) emerging in Salvador-Bahia-and-São-Paulo as fusion of bossa-nova harmonic-sophistication, Northeast forró-and-baião rhythmic-vocabulary, Anglo-American psychedelic-rock instrumentation (electric-guitar, fuzz, distortion), Stockhausen-and-Cage avant-garde electroacoustic-experimentation, and Brazilian-modernist-poetry pau-brasil concrete-and-anthropophagic literary-aesthetic. Built politically in opposition to the 1964-1985 Brazilian military dictatorship through ironic-pop subversion. The canonical recordings of the late-1960s tropicália phase shaped Brazilian-mainstream MPB 1970s-onward and influenced global art-rock through the 1990s-onward Western re-discovery wave.
items.description: Late-1960s Brazilian art-music movement (1967–69) collaging bossa nova, MPB, psychedelic rock, electronic experimentation, concrete poetry, and political critique under military dictatorship. Defined by a deliberate juxtaposition aesthetic — kitsch and high-art, indigenous and imported elements, traditional Brazilian and Anglo-American rock all coexisting in the same arrangement.

items.name: MPB (Música Popular Brasileira)
items.lineage: Brazilian MPB (Música Popular Brasileira) post-bossa-nova-and-tropicália sophisticated-popular-music umbrella-tradition emerging 1965-onward from the bossa-nova-tropicália-festival circuit. Built on harmonically-extended chord-vocabulary (minor-7-and-maj-7-and-9-and-11 jazz-extensions), Brazilian-rhythmic foundation (samba, baião, choro, bossa derivatives), and singer-songwriter literary-poetic-lyrical-sophistication. The 1970s mpb-jovem-guarda commercial-pop wave, the 1980s mpb-de-câmara chamber-mpb, and 1990s-onward mpb-as-heritage-institution comprise the genre's historical arc. Canonical instrumentation: violão acoustic-guitar nylon-string fingerstyle-led, with optional flute, piano, cavaquinho, and contemporary-rhythm-section. The MPB-canon overlaps significantly with samba-canção and bossa-nova but retains a distinct singer-songwriter-as-poet aesthetic identity.
items.description: Catchall term for sophisticated post-bossa Brazilian popular music — the artists who emerged from the bossa nova / tropicália generation and became the long-form mainstream of Brazilian song. Acoustic-guitar-and-voice texture preserved from bossa, harmonic vocabulary inherited from jazz, lyric craft inherited from samba lineage, all integrated as the ongoing Brazilian pop format.
exemplars: Djavan — Não É Azul, Mas É Mar (1989)

items.name: Maracatu
items.lineage: Pernambuco (Recife-and-Olinda) Afro-Brazilian cortejo-procession carnival tradition of the nação-de-baque-virado coronation-pageant lineage 1700s-onward, where rei-and-rainha Black-royal-couple-and-court led by maracatu-baque-virado heavy-mid-tempo percussion processions enact symbolic Afro-Catholic-Yoruba-Bantu syncretic-king-coronation ceremony. The baque-virado rhythm features alfaia barrel-drums (two-headed rope-tensioned), caixa snare-with-bottom-strings, gonguê single-cowbell, and ganzá shaker, with calunga doll-and-staff iconography carried by the procession. The baque-solto rural-zonal variant adds woodwind-and-trumpet melodic-elements and faster-tempo agitation. The genre seeded 1990s mangue-beat fusion-rock and remains central to Recife carnival.
items.description: Processional Afro-Brazilian drumming tradition from Pernambuco state, with two distinct sub-traditions: maracatu nação (urban Recife, ceremonial royal-court enactment) and maracatu rural (sugar-cane-region rural). Massive bass-drum (alfaia) ensemble plus call-response vocals. Outdoor processional context — open-air recording captures the tradition more faithfully than studio.
exemplars: Nação Estrela Brilhante do Recife — field recordings
Cordel do Fogo Encantado — Recanto do Sossego (rural maracatu derived)

items.name: Frevo
items.lineage: Brazilian Pernambuco (Recife) carnival fast-tempo brass-band marcha tradition codified 1907-onward as the working-class-and-capoeira-defense response to the elite-elite carnival-club tradition. The canonical frevo-orquestra ensemble: trumpets, trombones, saxophones, and rhythm-section (snare-and-bass-drum military-marching kit, sometimes augmented with percussive surdo-and-tamborim Brazilian-samba percussion). The frevo-de-rua street-version is purely instrumental and very fast (typically 200+ BPM), led by passistas dancers carrying small umbrellas (sombrinhas) executing the characteristic acrobatic-jumping passo-de-frevo footwork. Three sub-genres: frevo-canção (sung-frevo with vocal-lyrics), frevo-de-bloco (more relaxed bloco-carnival-association style), and frevo-de-rua (instrumental-street-version).
items.description: Fast-tempo (140-160 bpm) brass-band carnival music from Recife, Pernambuco. Distinct from Rio-de-Janeiro samba by tempo (much faster), instrumentation (brass-driven rather than string-and-percussion), and the accompanying acrobatic dance form (frevo dance with a distinctive step vocabulary). Carnival processional in origin, with concert and recorded forms developing later.
exemplars: Capiba — Madeira que Cupim Não Rói
Edson Rodrigues e Sua Orquestra — Frevos de Rua de Pernambuco

items.name: Axé
items.lineage: Bahian carnival pop crossover tradition centered on Salvador, Bahia, from the 1980s onward — codified through Margareth Menezes (Elegibo 1989), Daniela Mercury, Banda Mel, and the trio-elétrico amplified-truck performance tradition; characterized by samba-reggae and ijexá Afro-Brazilian rhythmic foundation, pop-rock-band instrumentation, and Bahian-Salvador carnival-circuit canonical context
items.description: Salvador, Bahia carnival pop tradition emerging in the 1980s from the merger of trio-elétrico carnival sound-truck tradition with samba-reggae rhythmic foundation and Anglo-American pop song architecture. Mainstream commercial form rather than rural-or-religious tradition. Defined by big-chorus call-response and the trio-elétrico amplification context (open-air carnival).
exemplars: Chiclete com Banana — A Cor desse Amor

items.name: Sertanejo
items.lineage: Brazilian rural-country pop tradition with two principal eras — sertanejo raiz (rural-roots, 1930s-1960s acoustic duos with double-vocal harmony) and sertanejo universitário (2000s-onward urban-pop crossover) codified through Leandro and Leonardo, Chitãozinho and Xororó (raiz canon), then Michel Teló, Luan Santana, and Marília Mendonça (post-2010 universitário)
items.description: Brazilian rural-country popular music tradition, originating in Goiás and Minas Gerais. Two-voice tight-thirds harmony singing (dupla de irmãos) over guitar-and-accordion accompaniment. Modern sertanejo universitário (1990s onward) added pop-rock production and country-music-Anglo influence, becoming the mainstream Brazilian commercial-radio format.
exemplars: Gusttavo Lima — Balada (Tchê Tcherere Tchê Tchê)

items.name: Capoeira music
items.lineage: Bahian Afro-Brazilian martial-art-and-music ceremonial tradition led by three-berimbau monochord-bow ensemble — gunga lowest-tonic-keeper, médio middle-mid-tone-variation, viola highest-improvisation-lead — with pandeiro frame-drum, atabaque conical-hand-drum, agogô double-bell, and reco-reco scraped-bamboo. The roda circular-game-space is opened by ladainha lament-style sung-prayer-history, transitioned through corrido call-and-response chamada formal-invitation chant, and continues through quadras four-line verse-sections. The Angola-style slower-low-game and Regional-style faster-acrobatic-game subdivide the practice, both built on the eight-toque rhythmic-vocabulary (angola, são-bento-grande, são-bento-pequeno, iuna, miudinho, banguela, cavalaria, samango).
items.description: Afro-Brazilian capoeira-roda music — the call-response singing and berimbau-led percussion that accompanies the capoeira martial-art-game. Berimbau (single-string musical bow) directs tempo and game-style. Multiple distinct rhythmic patterns (toques) signal different game-types. Traditionally Bahian, now globally practiced.

items.name: Baião
items.lineage: Brazilian Northeast rural-pastoral rhythm-and-song-form codified 1946-onward by accordion-zabumba-triangle pé-de-serra trio-instrumentation, named after the rural-stick-dance baião already documented 19th-century in Pernambuco-and-Bahia agreste-interior. The characteristic baião zabumba-pattern emphasizes the third sixteenth (the 'lifted' beat) and the eighth-note dotted accentuation, with sanfona-accordion delivering descant melody-and-chord-accompaniment. Lyrically focused on rural-Northeast everyday-life: drought (seca), cattle-ranching (vaqueiro), migration to Southern Brazilian cities, religious-folkloric culture (cordel literature, feast-days). The 1960s-MPB-tropicalia generation reframed baião as a national-symbol of Brazilian-northeastern identity in opposition to coastal-cosmopolitan bossa-nova-and-Rio-elite.
items.description: Northeast-Brazilian (Pernambuco, Ceará, Bahia) dance-song tradition foregrounding accordion (sanfona) over guitar and zabumba (bass drum) rhythmic foundation. Codified for radio-broadcast scale by Luiz Gonzaga in the 1940s, becoming the Northeast-Brazilian regional sound. Underlying rhythmic pattern shared with forró.
exemplars: Dominguinhos — Eu só quero um xodó

items.name: Embolada
items.lineage: Brazilian Northeast (Pernambuco, Bahia, Paraíba, Ceará) rapid-fire repentista vocal-duel tradition — two emboladores improvise verses over a fast pandeiro rhythmic foundation, alternating in pairs and trying to outdo each other in tongue-twister vocal dexterity, rhymed wit, and topical social satire; closely related to the parallel cantoria de viola (the Northeast repentista poetic-duel tradition with viola caipira accompaniment) and the broader Sertão Brazilian-Northeast vernacular oral-poetic culture, recently recognized by Brazilian cultural heritage authorities and continued through 20th-century figures Caju e Castanha, Mestre Verdelinho, and modern festival circuits
items.description: Northeast-Brazilian (Pernambuco, Ceará) rapid-fire vocal-duel tradition. Two improviser-poets (repentistas) trade rhyming verses at high tempo, accompanied by pandeiro hand-drum. Improvised lyrics with strict-meter constraint. Direct ancestor of Brazilian battle-rap / freestyle-MC tradition. Field-recording-context (street-corner, market, festa).

items.name: Jongo
items.lineage: Afro-Brazilian rural circle-dance tradition of the Vale do Paraíba (Rio-de-Janeiro and São-Paulo border, plantation-Bantu lineage 19th-century onward) characterized by call-and-response chant over candongueiro and tambu friction-drum patterns. Practiced by Kongo-Angolan-descended quilombo communities since colonial sugar-coffee-plantation labor, jongo nights feature umbigada-rotation-dance, riddle-and-spell sung-couplets (pontos), and trance-adjacent participatory circle structure. The tradition survived the post-abolition (1888-onward) rural-to-urban migration and remained the seedbed for early-20th-century samba-rural and samba-de-roda before the carioca-urban samba-canção codification.
items.description: Rural Afro-Brazilian song-and-dance tradition from southeastern Brazil (Rio de Janeiro and Minas Gerais coffee regions), descended from Central African (Angolan/Kongolese) sources brought via the slave trade. Round-dance format with call-response improvised verses (pontos), atabaque-and-tambu drumming. Cousin tradition to samba but with stronger ritual / ancestor-veneration character preserved.
exemplars: Tia Maria do Jongo — historical recordings

items.name: Bomba (Puerto Rican)
items.lineage: Afro-Puerto Rican drum-and-dance ritual tradition traced directly to West African Yoruba and Ashanti rhythmic-drum-and-call-response heritage brought through 17-18th-century enslaved African labor, with Loíza (the Black-majority town on the northeast coast), Mayagüez, Ponce, and Cataño as the bomba towns; played on the bomba barril (single-headed barrel drum carved from rum cask) with the soloist drummer (subidor or primo) tracing the dancers steps in real-time dialogue while a secondary drum (buleador) maintains rhythmic foundation, plus maracas and cuá (struck wood block) — preserved through the Cepeda and Ayala families and modern groups like Los Pleneros de la 21
items.description: Afro-Puerto Rican drum-and-call-response tradition rooted in 17th–19th-century plantation life on the island’s coastal regions. Two-drum (buleador / primo) interaction with primo drum responding to dancer’s movements (drum-follows-dancer rather than dancer-follows-drum). Call-response soloist-and-chorus singing. Multiple regional sub-traditions (Loíza, Mayagüez, Ponce).
exemplars: Cepeda Family — Bomba de Loíza recordings
Modesto Cepeda — Bomba y Plena Workshop

items.name: Plena (Puerto Rican)
items.lineage: Puerto Rican narrative-and-news song tradition originating in Ponce c. 1900 — built on the three sizes of pandereta frame drum (requinto small high-pitched lead, seguidor medium-pitched, segundo bass), plus voice and güiro scraper, performing topical-narrative songs about working-class urban Puerto Rican life and current events (the genres defining periódico cantado newspaper-set-to-music function); codified through Manuel Jiménez Canario (the first commercially-recorded plenero, 1925-onward), Mon Rivera (the mid-20th-century voice), and the modern Plena Libre, Los Pleneros de la 21, and Viento de Agua extensions
items.description: Puerto Rican song-form tradition emerging in early 20th-century Ponce as commentary-and-news-bearing genre. Three different-sized panderetas (handheld frame drums) interlock with cuatro and güiro accompaniment. Topical / commentary-bearing lyric tradition, sometimes called "the singing newspaper of the working class" by ethnomusicologists.
exemplars: Los Pleneros de la 21 — NYC plena revival

items.name: Jíbaro
items.lineage: Rural Puerto Rican mountain (montaña) peasant song tradition rooted in the Spanish décima poetic form (ten-line stanza, 8 syllables per line, ABBAACCDDC rhyme scheme) brought from 17th-century Iberian colonial settlement and preserved in the Puerto Rican mountain interior — performed on the cuatro puertorriqueño (the 10-string national instrument with five double-string courses), classical guitar, güiro, and bongos; figures Ramito (Florencio Morales Ramos, the 20th-century jíbaro voice), Chuíto el de Bayamón, Toño Mayo, and the modern revival through Ecos de Borinquen and the Cuatro Project
items.description: Rural Puerto Rican song tradition (jíbaro: "rural mountain dweller"). Cuatro-and-guitar accompaniment with güiro percussive scrape, décima poetic form (ten-line octosyllabic stanzas), controversia improvised verse-exchange between paired singers, Christmas parranda house-to-house repertoire. 19th-century origins in mountain coffee-and-tobacco-farming culture; codified through 20th-century commercial recordings (Ansonia Records, Disco Hit) and radio broadcast. Distinct from coastal Puerto Rican bomba-and-plena Afro-Caribbean traditions by Andalusian rather than West-African derivation, and by string-trio rather than drum-driven ensemble.
exemplars: Ramito (Florencio Morales Ramos) — El Cantor de la Montaña
Chuíto el de Bayamón — décima recordings

items.name: Parang (Trinidadian)
items.lineage: Trinidadian Spanish-language Christmas-season music tradition descended from the Venezuelan parranda visiting-musician tradition — performed in Trinidad and Tobago by parranderos (door-to-door Christmas-season visiting parang groups) during the Christmas-Epiphany season (early December through January 6), with characteristic cuatro-and-guitar accompaniment, maracas, and Spanish-language religious-and-secular Christmas songs (the parang corpus, including standards like Sereno Sereno and Maria Maria)
items.description: Trinidadian Christmas-and-Epiphany season house-to-house Spanish-language singing tradition descended from Venezuelan migrants in the 19th century. Cuatro-led ensemble with guitar, maracas, and a tenor-led group of singers. Aguinaldo (Christmas) song repertoire predominates; Lent and Easter sub-repertoires also exist. Bridges Latin-American song-form to Anglo-Caribbean island context.

items.name: Punta (Garifuna)
items.lineage: Garifuna (Black-Carib) Honduran-Belizean-Guatemalan-Nicaraguan Caribbean-coast Afro-Amerindian song-and-dance tradition descended from the 1797 British-deportation of the surviving Carib-Arawak-Afro-Caribbean people from St-Vincent to Roatan-island (now eastern-Caribbean-coast Central-America). The canonical punta ensemble: three garaon barrel-drums (primero high-improvisation, segunda middle-rhythm, tercera bass-drum) with maracas (sisira), conch-shell-trumpet, and call-and-response female-vocal-leadership. The 2/4 rapid-tempo punta-rhythm accentuates the dance characterized by virtuosic hip-and-glute movement. (under the broader Garifuna language-music-and-dance category). The 1980s-onward punta-rock electrified-and-commercialized variant brought guitar-and-keyboard to the genre.
items.description: Garifuna ceremonial-and-celebratory drumming tradition practiced in the Garifuna diaspora of Belize, Honduras, Guatemala, and Nicaragua coastal regions. Garifuna people are descendants of Carib-Arawak indigenous and West African (Igbo, Akan) shipwrecked-and-resettled populations on St. Vincent before British relocation to Central America in 1797. Distinct from but related to Caribbean diasporic forms; primero-and-segundo drum interaction with female call-response singing.

items.name: Paranda (Garifuna)
items.lineage: Garifuna (Black-Carib) Spanish-Latin-influenced ballad tradition performed across the Garifuna diaspora in Belize, Honduras, Guatemala, Nicaragua, and the Garifuna emigrant communities in New York and Los Angeles — codified through Andy Palacio (the Belizean Garifuna paranda voice, 2007 Wátina album, his death in 2008 marking the end of the second-generation paranda era), Aurelio Martinez, the broader Stonetree Records catalog
items.description: Garifuna ballad form distinct from punta — slower tempo, Spanish-Latin-influenced acoustic-guitar accompaniment, individual-singer-and-guitarist solo presentation rather than ensemble drum-and-chorus context. Romantic and reflective lyric register. The ballad-tradition counterpart to punta’s celebratory-drum tradition within the same Garifuna culture.

items.name: Cadence-lypso
items.lineage: Dominica creole-French Caribbean dance-band tradition fusing Haitian compas and Trinidadian calypso, codified through Exile One and Grammacks in the 1970s
items.description: Dominica-founded creole-French Caribbean dance-band tradition (1970s onward) developed by Exile One and Grammacks. Combines kompa-direkt rhythmic foundation, calypso lyric-craft, and amplified-Caribbean-band instrumentation. Genre-bridge between French Antilles and Anglo-Caribbean musics. Lyric in Dominica creole and French.

items.name: Kompa-direkt (Haitian)
items.lineage: The original founding Haitian kompa-direkt tradition invented by Nemours Jean-Baptiste in 1955 — characterized by big-band horn-section arrangement, slower 2/4 dance tempo (90-110 BPM), and the meringue Haitian rhythmic foundation; figures Nemours Jean-Baptiste (the founder), his orchestra Ensemble Aux Calebasses, and the parallel cadence-rampa lineage of Webert Sicot
items.description: Haitian dance-band tradition codified by Nemours Jean-Baptiste in 1955. Mid-tempo (90–110 bpm) groove, tanbou-derived rhythmic foundation translated to drum-kit and conga, jazz-derived horn arrangements. The dominant Haitian commercial popular-music form for the second half of the 20th century. Source-tradition for cadence-lypso and modern zouk.
exemplars: Tabou Combo — Mass Compas Mini All-Stars (1973)

items.name: Bouyon
items.lineage: Dominica electronic-hybrid Caribbean dance music codified through WCK and the late-1980s Dominica recording scene — characterized by cadence-lypso roots merged with zouk and dancehall programming, French Creole vocals, and the 100-120 BPM rhythmic foundation distinctive to the genre
items.description: Dominica-founded electronic-hybrid Caribbean dance music developed in the late 1980s by WCK band, combining cadence-lypso, jing ping (Dominica indigenous), zouk, and reggae over drum-machine-and-synth foundation. Bridges acoustic Caribbean traditions with digital-production aesthetics. Generated derivative styles (bouyon-soca, bouyon-gwadda) across the Anglophone-Francophone Caribbean.

items.name: Chouval-bwa
items.lineage: Martinican rural carousel-music (chouval bwa is Martinican Creole for wooden horse, referring to the merry-go-round and travelling fair context where the music traditionally accompanied the carousel ride) — built on accordion (the melodic instrument), tambour bélé (the large Martinican single-headed barrel drum carried on the shoulder), ti-bwa (small bamboo struck-percussion), and chacha (Martinican calabash rattle); codified through 20th-century figures Eugène Mona (the Martinican flute virtuoso who incorporated chouval-bwa elements into his fusion work), Dédé Saint-Prix (the chouval-bwa accordionist), Tipany — distinct from the kindred Martinican biguine and zouk traditions
items.description: Rural Martiniquan carousel-and-festival music tradition. Wooden-horse merry-go-rounds (chouval-bwa = "wooden horse" in Martinican creole) at country fairs are accompanied by accordion-led ensemble with bamboo flute (boula) and tambour-bélé drum. Source-tradition for elements of zouk and biguine. Field-recording context predominates over commercial recording.

items.name: Soca soul
items.lineage: Trinidadian soul-and-soca crossover tradition codified by Lord Shorty’s reinvention of calypso through soca (1973 Endless Vibrations record) — Arrow’s Hot Hot Hot (1982) bringing the form to international audiences, then Machel Montano, Bunji Garlin, Patrice Roberts, and Destra Garcia evolving the canon through the 1990s-2000s
items.description: Sub-tradition of soca with American R&B / soul vocal phrasing and harmonic vocabulary, distinct from "power soca" (uptempo carnival-targeted) or "groovy soca" (slower tempo carnival-targeted). Closer to mainstream Anglo-American R&B in vocal-stylings while preserving the soca rhythmic foundation. Caribbean-pop crossover format.
exemplars: Kes the Band — Trini-pop crossover catalog

items.name: Shaabi (Egyptian)
items.lineage: Cairo working-class popular vernacular music tradition emerging in the 1970s-80s — codified through Ahmed Adaweya (the foundational voice, whose 1972 album Salametha Umm Hassan broke the classical-tarab dominance of Egyptian commercial music), Shaaban Abdel Rehim, Hakim, Saad El Soghayar — built on the Cairo working-class colloquial Egyptian Arabic vocabulary, oud-and-qanun urban-modernized instrumentation, and topical lyrical content addressing daily Cairo street life
items.description: Cairo working-class urban vernacular tradition. Distinct from classical Arabic art-music tradition by being explicitly popular, lyrically vernacular (rather than fusha Arabic), and tied to street-and-wedding performance contexts. Mid-tempo rhythmic foundation, oud-and-darbuka core, characteristic vocal-tahrir (melismatic ornamentation).
exemplars: Shaaban Abdel Rahim — Ana Bakrah Israel (2000)

items.name: Mahraganat (Egyptian)
items.lineage: Cairo working-class digital-electronic shaabi descendant tradition — codified circa 2007-2010 through the working-class districts of Salam City and El-Marg, with DJ Figo, Sadat, Alaa Fifty Cent, Oka, and Wegz as the canonical exponents — characterized by Casio-and-FL-Studio-produced backing tracks, autotuned street-vernacular Arabic vocals, wedding-party performance context, and the Mahraganat festival circuit
items.description: Cairo working-class popular-music genre emerging in the late 2000s — shaabi-derivative but produced entirely on bedroom-DAW and distributed initially via mobile phone and YouTube, bypassing licensed Egyptian commercial recording infrastructure. Heavy autotune, machine-rhythmic foundation, vernacular-Arabic-language explicit lyric content. Censored under successive Egyptian governments. Cousin-tradition to grime, kuduro, and other peripheral-urban-electronic genres.
exemplars: DJ Amr Haha — Cairo street recordings

items.name: Chaabi (Moroccan)
items.lineage: Moroccan-Arabic-language popular wedding-and-celebration music built on the rural Moroccan dance rhythms (haoussa from Casablanca, aita from the Atlantic plains, houara from the Souss valley) with the urban ensemble of oud, violin, the Moroccan-invented banjo (late 1960s), darbuka, voice — codified through Cheikha Rimitti (raï predecessor and chaabi crossover), Najat Aatabou, Stati, Daoudi
items.description: Moroccan urban vernacular tradition, distinct from same-named Algerian chaabi (which has different musical structure). Wedding-and-celebration performance contexts. Moroccan-Arabic and Tamazight (Berber) language. Faster tempo than typical Egyptian shaabi, more pentatonic-modal harmonic vocabulary, more emphasis on chorus-call-response than solo-vocalist focus.

items.name: Tarab (Egyptian classical)
items.lineage: The specifically Egyptian branch of the broader Arab tarab tradition — built on the takht ensemble (oud, qanun, ney, riq, kamancheh) plus the 20th-century Egyptian innovation of adding a large Western violin section for the 1945-1970 Umm Kulthum / Mohammed Abdel Wahab era recordings; pre-WWII figures Sayed Darwish, Mohammed al-Qasabgi, Zakariya Ahmed, then the post-WWII Golden Age anchored by Umm Kulthum (1898-1975), Mohammed Abdel Wahab (1902-1991), Abdel Halim Hafez (1929-1977)
items.description: Egyptian classical-vocal tradition predating mid-20th-century electrification of Arabic popular music. Long-form taqsim (instrumental improvisation) sections framing wasla (vocal compositions) sequences. Audience-and-singer reciprocal call-response (saltana — the cultivated state of mutual ecstatic listening). Pre-microphone-era performance-and-recording aesthetic.
exemplars: Mohammed Abdel Wahab — instrumental taqsim catalog

items.name: Arabesk (Turkish)
items.lineage: Turkish urban-melancholic Egyptian-music-influenced crossover-pop tradition that dominated Turkish mass culture from the 1970s through the 1990s — codified through Orhan Gencebay (the founder, 1968 onward), Müslüm Gürses, İbrahim Tatlıses (the 80s-90s voice), Ferdi Tayfur, Bülent Ersoy; thematically anchored in the urban-rural migration anxiety of Turkish working-class internal-migrant audiences, with characteristic minor-key Egyptian-inspired string arrangements over Turkish-language vocals
items.description: Turkish urban-popular-music tradition emerging in the 1970s. Combines Turkish classical-music makam-modal vocabulary with Arabic-pop production scale, melancholic-lyric register addressing Anatolian urban-migrant experience. Initially marginalized by Turkish state-cultural establishment as inauthentic; now mainstream Turkish commercial radio.

items.name: Mizrahi (Israeli)
items.lineage: Israeli Eastern-Jewish popular tradition descended from Yemenite, Iraqi, Moroccan, and Persian Jewish communities — codified through Zohar Argov, Ofra Haza (whose 1988 Im Nin’Alu became an international crossover), Eyal Golan, and the broader Mizrahi recording scene; characterized by Hebrew vocals over Arabic-maqam-derived melodic vocabulary
items.description: Israeli popular-music tradition associated with Mizrahi (Sephardic / Maghrebi / Iraqi-Jewish) communities. Combines Arabic-makam melodic-vocabulary, Turkish-arabesk lyric register, and Israeli-Hebrew-language pop architecture. Initially marginalized by Ashkenazi-dominated Israeli music establishment; became mainstream Israeli commercial pop from the 1990s onward.

items.name: Tehrangeles Persian pop
items.lineage: Iranian-diaspora Los Angeles-recorded pop tradition (1980-1995) codified by the post-1979-revolution émigré recording industry centered on Westwood / Tarzana — Andy and Kouros, Moein, Dariush, Googoosh’s post-2000 return, with characteristic Farsi-language vocals over Westernized pop-rock production
items.description: Iranian-diaspora popular-music tradition centered in Los Angeles ("Tehrangeles") from 1979 onward, after the Iranian Revolution made commercial pop production within Iran legally restricted. Persian-language pop produced with American studio infrastructure, distributed back into Iran via cassette and later satellite-and-streaming. Hybrid Persian-classical-derived melody with American-pop-production architecture.

items.name: Lebanese tarab-pop
items.lineage: Beirut-centered modern Arabic-pop with classical-tarab roots, melismatic-ornate praise-and-devotional vocal style emerging from 1950s-onward post-Egyptian-classical Levantine regional expansion. The 1960s-1970s Lebanese-orchestral-style integrated rahbani-school theatrical-musical compositional vocabulary with classical maqam modal-foundation (Rast, Hijaz, Bayati, Nahawand), tarab ecstatic-vocal listener-state aesthetic, and Western-string-section-and-electric-instrumentation arrangement-modernization. The 1980s-civil-war-period diaspora-expansion took Beirut-tarab to Paris-and-London recording-studios, transformed in the 2000s-onward via electronic-arabic-pop and house-influenced-arabic-pop into the modern khaleeji-and-shami pan-Arab pop-mainstream.
items.description: Beirut-centered modern Arabic-pop tradition retaining tarab-vocal melismatic ornamentation while incorporating Western pop production-scale and arrangement vocabulary. Diva-singer-led ensemble format. Pan-Arab market reach through Lebanon’s relatively unrestricted recording industry. Distinct from Egyptian shaabi (working-class) and Gulf khaliji (Saudi-Emirati pop) by sophistication-of-arrangement and tarab-tradition continuity.

items.name: Malhun (Maghrebi)
items.lineage: Moroccan-Algerian sung-poetry (al-malhun) tradition originating in 16th-century Tafilalt and codified through 18th-19th-century Fez and Meknes urban poetic circles — preserves a corpus of classical-Maghrebi-Arabic poetry set to elaborate melodic-modal vocal compositions in the Andalusi-derived modal vocabulary; figures: Houcine Toulali, El Haj Houcine Toulali, the post-WWII Fez and Marrakech malhun masters
items.description: Moroccan-Algerian sung-poetry tradition rooted in 16th-century Andalusian-Maghrebi exchange. Strophic verse-form (qasida) in Maghrebi-vernacular Arabic on devotional, ethical, and social-commentary themes. Bridges Andalusian classical-music tradition (al-Ala) with vernacular Moroccan-Algerian musical contexts. Heritage-status genre preserved through specialist performer-scholars.
exemplars: Cheikh El Hadj Houcine Toulali — Casablanca recordings

items.name: Iraqi maqam (al-Maqam al-Iraqi)
items.lineage: Iraqi classical vocal tradition codified in the Baghdadi school as a corpus of 56 canonical maqams (mode-pieces), each with a specific opening tahrir vocal cadenza, body section called miyana, and closing teslim cadence; performed by a solo qari vocalist accompanied by the chalghi small ensemble of santur, jawza Iraqi spike-fiddle, tabla, and riq — figures Mohammed al-Qabbanchi, Yusuf Omar, Hussein Al-Aazami, Hamid al-Saadi
items.description: Iraqi classical-vocal art-music tradition (al-Maqam al-Iraqi), distinct from but related to broader Arabic-maqam tradition. Suite-form structure of fixed sections (tahrir, miyana, jalsa) framing improvisation. Specifically Baghdadi performance-context, with characteristic Iraqi-vernacular lyric register.

items.name: Shōmyō (Japanese Buddhist liturgical chant)
items.lineage: Tendai-school-and-Shingon-school Japanese Buddhist sutra-chant tradition with characteristic neumed-melisma vocal-line preserving Tang-dynasty Chinese-Buddhist liturgical music transmitted via 8th-9th-century Japanese-monastic-pilgrimage. The two surviving lineages — Tendai-shōmyō (anchored at Mount Hiei monastic complex, established 805 CE by Saichō) and Shingon-shōmyō (anchored at Mount Kōya monastic complex, established 816 CE by Kūkai) — preserve separate but related sutra-and-bonbai canonical-chant-vocabulary repertoires. The chant unfolds in free-rhythm ametrical-pulse, layers single-monk solo-leader against full-monastic-choir responsorial sections, and uses three-pitch-level neumed notation (kotsufu) for melodic contour preservation across centuries.
items.description: Japanese Buddhist liturgical chant tradition associated with Tendai and Shingon schools. Two distinct sub-traditions (ryōkyoku, kokyoku) reflecting different scale-systems imported from Tang-Dynasty China in the 9th century and developed locally. Solo-or-monastic-ensemble vocal performance with no instrumental accompaniment. Microtonal pitch-bending, slow tempo, breath-and-silence-shaped phrasing. Ancestor of gagaku and indirectly of much later Japanese vocal aesthetics.
exemplars: Kōmyō Shōmyō Choir — Buddhist liturgy archive

items.name: Theravada Pali chant
items.lineage: Sri Lankan / Burmese / Thai / Cambodian / Lao Theravada Buddhist scriptural-recitation tradition — the liturgical practice of reciting the Tipitaka (the Pali-language scripture-corpus codified at the First Buddhist Council c. 480 BCE) in slow modal melismatic chant; performed by monks in temple wat / vihara contexts at morning and evening services, festival celebrations (Vesak, Kathina), and ceremonial-meditational practice
items.description: Theravada Buddhist sutta-recitation tradition practiced across Sri Lanka, Thailand, Myanmar, Cambodia, and Laos. Pali-language scripture recited in characteristic monastic-vocal register — slow tempo, narrow pitch range, formulaic melodic-cells repeated across sutta-passage breaks. Distinct from Mahayana Chinese-derivative Buddhist chant by both language and melodic-vocabulary. Practical-spiritual function (chanting paritta-protective verses) rather than aesthetic-performance.

items.name: Pure Land Buddhist chant
items.lineage: East-Asian Pure-Land (Jingtu / Jodo) devotional chant tradition centered on the Amitabha nembutsu (recitation of Amitabha’s name) — codified through 5th-century Chinese teacher Tan Luan, formalized as separate school by Shan Tao (613-681), studio-recorded 1960-1980, then Honen (1133-1212) establishing Jōdo-shū in Japan, and Shinran (1173-1263) founding Jōdo Shinshū; characterized by repetitive nianfo / nembutsu name-chanting practice in slow-tempo melismatic delivery
items.description: East-Asian Pure-Land Buddhist devotional chant tradition. Repetition of the Amitabha-recollection formula (nembutsu in Japanese, nianfo in Chinese, yeombul in Korean) — cyclical short-phrase chanting designed for rebirth-aspiration practice. Communal-congregational performance context most common, often hours-long sessions. Distinct from monastic shōmyō by being practiced by laity rather than only monastics.
exemplars: Chinese Pure Land nianfo recordings (Mt. Putuo)

items.name: Beompae (Korean Buddhist chant)
items.lineage: Korean Buddhist liturgical chant tradition with Joseon-era codification, allied to the broader yeombul devotional practice
items.description: Korean Buddhist liturgical-music tradition distinct from both Japanese shōmyō and Chinese fanbei sources, though descended from Tang-period Chinese imports of the same root tradition. Three categories (anchaebi, hossori, ji-eun-chae) corresponding to different ritual-and-text contexts. Monastic-and-layperson-trained specialists (beompaesa) preserve the tradition. Sometimes accompanied by mokeotak (wooden-fish slit-drum) and beopgu (drum).

items.name: Himalayan Vajrayana liturgy
items.lineage: Tibetan / Bhutanese / Ladakhi Vajrayana tantric ritual-music tradition with multiphonic chant and brass-and-percussion liturgical ensemble
items.description: Tibetan-Buddhist tantric ritual-music tradition broader than the specifically Gyutö-school throat-chant subset. Includes monastery-orchestra repertoire (long-trumpets, conch, double-reed, ritual drums and cymbals) and varied vocal-styles across Gelug, Kagyu, Nyingma, Sakya, and Bon schools. Liturgical function (deity-yoga sadhana practice, protector-rituals, mandala consecrations) rather than aesthetic performance. Distinct from the gyuto-throat-chant single-school sub-tradition.

items.name: Bongo flava (Tanzanian)
items.lineage: Tanzanian Swahili-language hip-hop and R&B hybrid tradition codified through Diamond Platnumz, Ali Kiba, Professor Jay, and Lady Jaydee — emerging late 1990s from Dar es Salaam street hip-hop scene, then evolving into mainstream Swahili-pop with R&B crossover; characterized by Swahili vocals over hip-hop and afropop production
items.description: Tanzanian Swahili-language popular-music tradition emerging in the late 1990s. Combines Anglo-American hip-hop / R&B production aesthetics with East-African vocal-melodic phrasing and Swahili-language lyric content. Distinct from West-African afrobeats by language, rhythmic foundation, and East-African / Indian-Ocean cultural-context references. Mainstream Tanzanian and Kenyan commercial-radio format from 2000 onward.

items.name: Genge (Kenyan)
items.lineage: Nairobi Sheng-language hip-hop subgenre codified through Jua Cali, Nonini, P-Unit, and the Calif Records ecosystem (founded by Clemo) starting circa 2003 — characterized by Sheng-slang lyrics (Nairobi Swahili-English code-mix), kapuka-beat foundation, and street-Nairobi lyrical subject matter
items.description: Nairobi Sheng-language (urban Swahili-English creole) hip-hop tradition emerging in the early 2000s. Distinct from broader bongo-flava by being more rhythmically aggressive, more lyric-forward in Sheng vernacular, and tied specifically to Nairobi street-vernacular rather than Tanzanian-Swahili pan-East-African register. Producer collective Calif Records defined the early sound.

items.name: Ethio-pop modern
items.lineage: Modern Amharic-language popular tradition descended from the 1960s-70s Ethio-jazz canon (Mulatu Astatke, Mahmoud Ahmed) — codified through Aster Aweke, Ejigayehu Shibabaw / Gigi, Teddy Afro, and Mahmoud Ahmed’s continued career; characterized by Amharic vocals over kignit-modal-melodic frameworks with Western pop production
items.description: Modern Ethiopian (Amharic-language predominantly) popular-music tradition continuing the lineage of the 1960s-70s Ethio-jazz era. Five-note Ethiopian pentatonic-modal melodic-vocabulary preserved across modernized arrangement scales. Addis-Ababa-centered commercial recording infrastructure expanded post-2000 enables larger-scale production than the cassette-and-vinyl Ethio-jazz era allowed.

items.name: Sahel praise music (Mali, Senegal, Mauritania, Niger)
items.lineage: Contemporary West African Sahel praise-music tradition that extends the Mande jeli vocal-and-praise lineage into the modern electric-band context — Salif Keita (Maninka noble-line singer who broke caste taboo by becoming a commercial musician, 1987 Soro album the Paris-recorded breakthrough), Youssou NDour (Senegalese Wolof, his 1984 Immigrés the Paris recording), Baaba Maal (Senegalese Fulani Pulaar-language), Mory Kanté (Guinean kora-virtuoso, 1987 Yé Ké Yé Ké), Ali Farka Touré, Toumani Diabaté, Khaira Arby, Oumou Sangaré
items.description: Sahelian praise-singing tradition descended from West-African griot (jeli) lineage, in modern band-arranged commercial-recorded form. Mali-Senegalese-Mauritanian regional commercial recording infrastructure (Studio Bogolan, Studio Salif, etc.) supports the production scale. Bridges traditional praise-song genealogical-recitation function with modern festival-and-album distribution context.

items.name: Mandé jeli
items.lineage: Mande hereditary praise-singer caste tradition spanning Mali, Guinea, Senegal, Gambia, Burkina Faso — the Kouyaté, Cissokho, Diabaté, Suso, Konté, Sissoko griot family lineages preserving the Sundiata Keita Mandé epic (13th century) and the broader Mande royal-court genealogical praise-poetry corpus; standard jeli ensemble: kora, ngoni, balafon, tama talking drum, djembe, voice
items.description: Hereditary praise-singing tradition of the Mandé peoples (Mandinka, Bambara, Khassonké), descended from the Mali Empire (1235-1670). Jeli (also jali, géwél, gawlo) are professional specialists transmitting oral history, panegyric, and ceremonial recitation through patrilineal succession. Heptatonic Mande tonal organization with characteristic neutral-third intonation. Traditional ensemble: griot voice, kora (21-string harp-lute), balafon (resonator-gourd xylophone), ngoni (plucked spike-lute). Performance contexts span chiefly courts, life-cycle ceremonies (weddings, naming-days, funerals), and family-compound gatherings. Vocal style features extensive melisma, ornamental flourishes, and sustained high-register declamation. Modern lineage carriers maintain pre-electric instrumental traditions while engaging with international concert and recording infrastructure.
exemplars: Kasse Mady Diabaté — Manden Djeli Kan
Jali Nyama Suso — kora field recordings (Gambia)

items.name: Wassoulou
items.lineage: Malian Wassoulou region (south of Bamako, between the Niger and Sankarani rivers, populated by the Wassoulou Fula and Bambara peoples) popular-music tradition extending the older donso ngoni (hunters harp-lute) hunters-music tradition into modern band format; built on the kamele ngoni (the Wassoulou youth harp-lute, a smaller more melodic adaptation of the donso ngoni), female-vocal foregrounded — codified through Oumou Sangaré (the Wassoulou voice from her 1989 Moussolou breakthrough onward), Sali Sidibé, Coumba Sidibé, Nahawa Doumbia
items.description: Malian popular tradition originating in the Wassoulou region south of the Niger River, distinct from hereditary jeli praise-singing in its communal-rural origin and non-specialist lineage. Pre-modern roots in pentatonic hunters-music (donso); the modern recorded form emerged in the 1970s-1980s through women-led ensembles, with hexatonic-pentatonic melodic frame and djembe-driven rhythmic foundation. Lyrics address love, social commentary, women’s perspectives, and rural-life themes — explicitly outside the genealogical-praise-of-elites repertoire of jeli tradition. Modern arrangements add electric guitar and bass; the kamele ngoni (small youth’s harp-lute, hexatonic) is the genre’s signature instrument.
exemplars: Nahawa Doumbia — La Grande Cantatrice Malienne

items.name: Algerian rap (rap algérien)
items.lineage: Algerian Arabic-and-French hip-hop tradition codified through MBS, Lotfi Double Kanon, Soolking, and the broader Algiers-and-Marseille diaspora circuit — characterized by raï-and-chaabi influence, Arabic-French-Berber trilingual lyrics, and post-1990s war-and-protest political-activist tradition
items.description: Algerian hip-hop tradition emerging in the early 1990s, lyrically code-switching between Algerian Arabic, Tamazight (Berber), and French. Politically-engaged from inception (formed during the Algerian civil war 1991-2002, addressing police violence, economic conditions, religious-political tensions). Distinct from French-mainland hip-hop by language-mix and Algerian cultural-context references, distinct from Maghrebi pop by rap-rhythmic-foundation rather than chaabi.

items.name: ECM-school jazz aesthetic
items.lineage: Eicher-school audiophile-jazz recording-aesthetic codified through ECM Records (founded 1969 Munich by Manfred Eicher) — characterized by close-miked silence, near-zero compression, long natural decay, and the "most beautiful sound next to silence" mastering signature; Keith Jarrett (The Köln Concert 1975), Pat Metheny (Bright Size Life 1976), Arvo Pärt (Tabula Rasa 1984) as canonical exponents
items.description: Recording-aesthetic tradition associated with Manfred Eicher’s ECM Records (Munich, 1969-onward). Defined by concert-hall-or-large-tracking-room recording, minimal-and-precisely-placed close-miking, extended decay-tail preservation, and an audiophile-documentary mix philosophy. Genre-agnostic in catalog scope but recognizable as a unified production aesthetic across jazz, classical, and folk recordings.

items.name: Hyperion-school classical-recording aesthetic
items.lineage: Hyperion Records (British classical label founded 1980) audiophile-canon production aesthetic for Western classical chamber and song repertoire — characterized by intimate close-miked sound stage, transparent capture without console coloration, minimal post-processing, and exploratory programming covering obscure and rediscovered repertoire alongside the standard canon
items.description: British audiophile-classical-recording aesthetic associated with Hyperion Records (founded 1980, London). Documentary-realism approach to chamber-music recording: real concert-hall or church recording-venues, minimal microphone count (often pure stereo pair), no spot-microphone overdubbing in mixing, extended-dynamic-range mastering. Repertoire-focused on the relatively-undocumented edges of Western classical canon (early-music, Romantic-rarities, contemporary).
exemplars: The King's Singers — early Hyperion catalog

items.name: Historically-informed performance recording
items.lineage: Late-twentieth-century classical-performance movement aiming to play pre-1900 Western art-music repertoire on period-appropriate instruments using period-appropriate technique, tuning (typically A=415 Hz baroque, A=430 Hz classical), tempo, articulation, and ornamentation — codified through ensembles including The English Concert (Trevor Pinnock), Concentus Musicus Wien (Nikolaus Harnoncourt), Academy of Ancient Music (Christopher Hogwood), and continuing through generations of period-instrument-trained performers
items.description: Recording tradition rooted in the historically-informed-performance (HIP) movement (1960s onward) — period-correct instruments, performance-practice-research-derived ornamentation, original-source-derived tempo and articulation. Recording approach pairs the performance-aesthetic with appropriate period-or-period-suitable acoustic spaces (parish churches, palace chapels). Distinct from mainstream-classical recording aesthetic by both instrumentation and sonic positioning.
exemplars: Christopher Hogwood — Academy of Ancient Music

items.name: Anglican cathedral-choral recording tradition
items.lineage: English Anglican cathedral choral foundation tradition — a continuous liturgical-music transmission across the cathedral and collegiate-chapel foundations of the Church of England (including the choral foundations at King's College Cambridge, St Paul's London, Westminster Abbey, and the cathedral cities) — characterized by daily evensong service, Anglican-chant psalmody, anthem repertoire, and the boy-treble-led mixed-adult-male voicing convention
items.description: British Anglican cathedral-choral recording tradition. Captures the actual cathedral-as-tracking-space rather than studio-emulating-cathedral. Boys-and-men SATB choir register (or in some 21st-century groups SAATB with girls or women), four-or-five-second decay times, organ-and-voice integration. Distinct from classical-vocal recording (concert-hall-or-studio context) by both performer demographic and venue acoustic.
exemplars: King's College Cambridge — Festival of Nine Lessons and Carols (annual since 1928)
St Paul's Cathedral Choir — daily Evensong recordings

items.name: Manhattan-chamber loft-recording
items.lineage: Manhattan-loft-school chamber-recording aesthetic codified through 1970s-1980s minimalist composers recording in downtown Manhattan converted-warehouse loft spaces — Steve Reich (Music for 18 Musicians 1976), Philip Glass (Glassworks 1982), Meredith Monk, and the Knitting Factory-adjacent ecosystem; characterized by ensemble close-tracking, dry-room aesthetic, and minimalist compositional architecture
items.description: Manhattan-loft-and-small-room contemporary-classical and chamber-jazz recording aesthetic associated with labels like New World, CRI (Composers Recordings Inc.), Cantaloupe Music, and the wider Bang on a Can / new-music collective scene. Smaller spaces than ECM’s preferred concert halls, more compositional-collage workflow than purist-documentary aesthetic. Often features composer-performer-engineer triple-roles in single-creator recordings.
exemplars: Bang on a Can All-Stars — Industry (1995)

items.name: Chinese conservatory traditional ensemble (民乐 minyue)
items.lineage: 20th-century-codified Chinese national-music conservatory ensemble form anchored at the Central Conservatory Beijing and Shanghai Conservatory
items.description: Conservatory-codified Chinese national-music ensemble tradition (民乐 minyue), formalized in mid-20th-century Beijing and Shanghai conservatories. Distinct from literati-amateur wenrenyue and operatic jingju traditions. Standard ensemble: erhu (bowed two-string), pipa (plucked four-string), guzheng (long zither), ruan (moon-bodied lute), sanxian (three-string), dizi (transverse bamboo flute), sheng (mouth organ), yangqin (hammered dulcimer). Repertoire includes adapted folk-tune arrangements, newly-composed concert pieces, and reconstructed historical material. Pentatonic-rooted modal organization (gong, shang, jue, zhi, yu modes); large concert-hall presentation with conductor-led ensemble unison passages alternating with featured soloists.
exemplars: Central Conservatory of Music ensemble recordings

items.name: Vietnamese chamber (nhạc tài tử and ca trù)
items.lineage: Vietnamese traditional chamber-music heritage spanning two distinct regional traditions — nhạc tài tử (Music of the Talented Amateurs), the Southern Vietnamese (Mekong Delta) chamber tradition of the 19th-century educated-amateur scholar-musician class, performed in private homes with đàn tranh (16-string Vietnamese zither), đàn bầu (Vietnamese monochord), đàn nguyệt (moon-shaped lute), đàn tỳ bà (pear-shaped lute), sáo trúc (bamboo flute), with characteristic improvisation and modal variation; ca trù (the Northern Vietnamese sung-poetry tradition), performed by female ca nương vocalist accompanied by đàn đáy (three-string lute) and phách (wooden percussion clapper)
items.description: Vietnamese traditional music covering nhạc tài tử (Mekong-Delta scholar-amateur chamber tradition, late-19th-century onward) and ca trù (older court-and-temple ceremonial form, 15th-century onward). Tonal-language vocal practice with extensive ornament-and-pitch-bending; instruments include đàn bầu (one-string monochord with whammy-bar pitch-bend), đàn tranh (16-string zither), đàn nguyệt (moon lute, related to ruan but distinct). Repertoire structured around mode (điệu) plus rhythmic-pattern (tiết tấu). Distinguished from neighboring Chinese conservatory tradition by tonal-language interaction with melodic line and by smaller-chamber-ensemble scale.
exemplars: Phạm Đức Thành — đàn bầu recital albums
Nguyễn Vĩnh Bảo — Mekong-Delta tài tử recordings
Trần Văn Khê — pedagogical chamber recordings

items.name: Bengali baul (mystic-itinerant song)
items.lineage: Lalon-Shah-lineage Bengali mystic-itinerant tradition, studio-recorded 1970-1990 (Lalon Fakir, c. 1774-1890, the foundational figure) — codified through the Kenduli Mela annual Baul gathering, the Bardhaman district teaching lineages, and the 20th-century preservation work of Purna Das Baul; characterized by ektara-or-dotara-and-khamak accompaniment, Sufi-Vaishnav-Tantric syncretic philosophy, and the wandering-mendicant performance context
items.description: Bengali baul mystic-itinerant song tradition, lineage of 19th-century Lalon Shah and earlier Sufi-and-Vaishnava-syncretic poet-singers. West-Bengal and Bangladesh rural-itinerant practice; baul-fakirs travel between village fairs and ashrams singing self-composed mystical poetry. Instruments: voice with ektara (one-string drone), dotara (two-or-four-string plucked lute), khamak (pitch-bend tension lute), sometimes small percussion. Lyrics address dehatattva (body-as-temple) philosophy; performance contexts include akhra (devotional gathering) and mela (fair). Distinguished from neighboring Bengali Rabindra-Sangeet by oral-non-codified transmission and by mystic-not-literary lyrical content.
exemplars: Paban Das Baul — French Folkways field albums

items.name: Finnish kantele folk and Kalevala-recitation
items.lineage: Karelian-Finnish epic-recitation tradition documented by Elias Lönnrot in compiling the Kalevala national epic (1835 first edition, 1849 expanded), paired with the lap-zither kantele (Finlands national instrument) — performed in Karelian, Ingrian, Estonian, and other Baltic-Finnic language traditions in pre-Christian rune-singing and folk-tale-singing contexts
items.description: Finnish kantele folk and Kalevala epic-recitation tradition. Kalevala (compiled 1835 by Elias Lönnrot from Karelian rune-singers) is the narrative-poetry corpus; kantele (Finnish-Karelian box zither, 5-to-39 strings) is its accompanying instrument. Recitation practiced in trochaic-tetrameter Kalevala-meter; melodic patterns are short, modal, and additive. Distinguished from neighboring Nordic-Atlantic Swedish bowed-string folk by absence-of-bowed-string ensemble and by its specifically epic-recitation focus over dance-tune repertoire. Modern revival since 1970s through Sibelius Academy folk-music department.
exemplars: Folk Music Institute Finland — field recordings of rune-singers

items.name: Swedish nyckelharpa folk
items.lineage: Swedish Uppland regional folk tradition centered on the nyckelharpa (Swedish keyed fiddle with twelve sympathetic resonance strings), performed alongside ordinary fiddle (spelman tradition) for the polska dance forms (slängpolska, åttondelspolska, smedjespolska variants) at midsummer celebrations and folk festivals
items.description: Swedish-Uppland nyckelharpa-and-fiddle ballad-and-polska tradition. Nyckelharpa (keyed bowed instrument, 16+ sympathetic strings) is regional-iconic to Uppland; modern chromatic version codified 1920s by August Bohlin. Repertoire: polskor (3/4 dance tunes with characteristic shifted-second-beat), gånglåtar (walking-tunes), schottis, ballad-singing. Distinguished from Norwegian-fiddle tradition by keyed-not-fingered fingerboard. Performance contexts include spelmansstämma (gathering-of-fiddlers) and modern concert-stage. Folkmusiken revival since 1970s.

items.name: Russian byliny (epic-narrative)
items.lineage: Russian (originally Kievan and Novgorodian) oral-epic recitation tradition of narrative songs about the legendary bogatyri heroes (Ilya Muromets, Dobrynya Nikitich, Alyosha Popovich); preserved through the 19th-20th centuries in the Russian Far North (Onega and White Sea regions) by Old Believer communities and documented by ethnomusicologists Pavel Rybnikov and Alexander Hilferding
items.description: Russian byliny epic-narrative tradition: oral-historical-narrative poetry transmitted by skomorokhi (medieval) and later Old-Believer skaziteli into the 19th-and-20th-century. Subjects: Kievan-Rus heroes (bogatyri), Novgorod merchants, religious-historical events. Performance: solo-male recitation accompanied by gusli (Slavic psaltery, 5-to-25 strings). Recitative melody constrained to 3-to-5 notes per byliny; verses chained without strict-metric repetition. Documented through 19th-century Onega-region collecting expeditions (Hilferding, Rybnikov). Distinguished from Russian-folk-orchestra tradition by solo-narrative-not-ensemble form and by archaic-not-codified repertoire.
exemplars: Olga Sergeyeva — Onega-region byliny field recordings
Anglo-Russian collaborative recordings — Holy Russia: Music of the Northern Folk

items.name: Russian folk balalaika and choral
items.lineage: Vassily Andreyev-codified (late 19th-century) Russian-folk-orchestra tradition — Andreyev standardized the balalaika family (prima, sekunda, alto, bass, kontrabass) and founded the Great Russian Orchestra (Velikorusskiy Orkestr) in St. Petersburg 1888, establishing the concert-stage Russian-folk-instrument ensemble model that the Soviet era institutionalized through state ensembles like the Pyatnitsky Choir
items.description: Russian folk-orchestra-and-choir tradition codified by Vasily Andreyev (1888 onward), who systematized peasant balalaika and developed standardized chromatic instrument family (prima, secunda, alto, bass, contrabass). 20th-century Soviet folk-orchestra format combined balalaika-and-domra ensembles with piano accordion (bayan) and large vocal choir. Repertoire: arranged-folk-song, original-composed concert pieces, Soviet-era patriotic repertoire. Distinguished from byliny epic-recitation by codified-conservatory form and large-ensemble scale; distinguished from Russian-Orthodox-chant by secular-folk content.
exemplars: Osipov State Russian Folk Orchestra — Andreyev anniversary recordings

items.name: Hungarian cimbalom (verbunkos and nóta)
items.lineage: Hungarian-Romani (cigány) urban-restaurant ensemble tradition centered on the primás-led band with concert-pedal cimbalom (Schunda 1874 design), violin, viola (kontra), and bass (bőgő); repertoire spans verbunkos (18th-century military recruiting dance), magyar nóta (Hungarian art-song), csárdás (national dance), and the Liszt Hungarian Rhapsodies / Brahms Hungarian Dances arrangements of this repertoire
items.description: Hungarian-Romani urban-restaurant ensemble tradition: magyar nóta (popular-art song, 19th-century onward) and verbunkos (recruitment-dance, late-18th-century military-recruitment origin). Standard prímás-led ensemble: lead violin (prímás), second violin (kontrás), viola (kontra), cimbalom (hammered dulcimer), double bass. Cimbalom developed by József Schunda (1874 Budapest) into pedaled chromatic concert version. Distinguished from neighboring Eastern-European Jewish ensemble tradition by Hungarian-language vocal repertoire and by verbunkos rhythmic-foundation distinct from freygish-mode dance lineage.
exemplars: Lajos Boross — Budapest restaurant ensemble recordings

items.name: Bulgarian dance traditional (horo, ruchenitsa)
items.lineage: Bulgarian village dance tradition built on aksak additive odd-meter rhythms (7/8 rachenitsa, 9/8 devetorka, 11/8 kopanitsa, 13/8 from Shopluk region) — performed at village celebrations, weddings, and (post-1944) on the State Ensemble stage circuit; characteristic instrumentation: gaida (bulgarian bagpipe), kaval (rim-blown flute), tambura, accordion, gadulka (bowed lute)
items.description: Bulgarian village-and-stage horo-dance tradition. Distinctive irregular-meter-cycle structures: horo (general dance), ruchenitsa (7/8), kopanitsa (11/16), paidushko (5/8), petrunino (13/16). Instruments: gaida bagpipe, kaval end-blown flute, tambura (Balkan long-neck lute), gadulka (bowed lyra), tapan double-headed drum. Mid-20th-century state-folk-ensemble codification (Filip Kutev Ensemble, 1951) created concert-stage versions; village-tradition continues at folk festivals. Distinguished from Greek-and-Romanian neighbors by specifically-Bulgarian asymmetric meters and by characteristic women’s-choir vocal-style (open-throated, parallel-second harmony).

items.name: Breton folk (kan ha diskan, fest-noz)
items.lineage: Breton traditional dance-and-song tradition — comprising kan ha diskan (Breton paired-vocal call-and-response, two singers alternating phrases for unaccompanied dance-song) and the biniou-and-bombarde pipe-couple (biniou koz the small Breton bagpipe, bombarde the Breton shawm, played in parallel octaves for outdoor fest-noz dance contexts); 20th-century revival figures the Goadec sisters (Sœurs Goadec), Alan Stivell (the Celtic-revival harper from 1971 onward), Yann-Fañch Kemener, Tri Yann
items.description: Breton call-and-response and pipe-couple tradition, lineage of pre-modern Breton-language song-and-dance practice. Kan ha diskan (call-and-response unaccompanied vocal duet) accompanies fest-noz (night-festival) dance. Couple-de-sonneurs ensemble: biniou (Breton bagpipe, soprano-pitched) plus bombarde (oboe-class double-reed, tenor-voiced). 20th-century Breton-cultural-revival movements (Breton Federation 1942, Bagad pipe-band tradition modeled on Scottish pipe-band) codified concert-stage forms. Distinguished from neighboring Irish-and-Scottish Celtic traditions by Breton-language repertoire and by biniou-bombarde couple-instrument architecture.
exemplars: Alan Stivell — Renaissance of the Celtic Harp (1971)

items.name: Italian southern folk (tarantella, pizzica)
items.lineage: Southern Italian traditional dance-and-song heritage — tarantella (the broad family of Southern Italian fast 6/8 dance-music, regional variants from Campania, Calabria, Apulia, Sicily), pizzica (the Salentine Apulian variant historically associated with tarantismo, the cultural-spider-bite-ritual of bitten women dancing the trance out of their bodies), and broader Italian southern pastoral tradition with zampogna (Southern Italian bagpipe with two chanters and drones) and ciaramella (the small shawm partner of zampogna in the Christmas-novena outdoor piping-couple); modern revival through the Notte della Taranta festival (Melpignano, since 1998) and the figures Antonio Castrignanò, Mauro Durante, Alla Bua
items.description: Southern-Italian processional and pastorale tradition: tarantella (Apulia and Calabria), pizzica-pizzica (Salento), tammurriata (Campania), saltarello (Lazio). Zampogna-ciaramella pastoral pipe-couple tradition associated with Christmas novena processions through Naples and Rome (18th-century-onward). Tambourine-driven dance-trance practice (pizzica especially) historically connected to tarantismo healing-ritual. Distinguished from Sardinian tradition by mainland-Italian language and by Catholic-ritual-calendar context. Revival movement since 1970s through Notte della Taranta festival and ethnomusicological collecting.
