items.name: Tibetan ache lhamo opera
items.lineage: Tibetan ache lhamo ("sister-goddess") folk-opera tradition. Origin traced by tradition to the fourteenth-century yogi-engineer-saint Thangtong Gyalpo, who is said to have founded the form and organized the first performance-troupe to raise funds for his iron-chain suspension-bridge construction projects across Tibet. The canonical repertoire comprises eight classical plays drawn from Indo-Tibetan Buddhist narrative cycles, including Sukyi Nyima (the deer-girl), Drowa Sangmo (the celestial-bride), Chöyi Nyima, Pema Wöbar, Drimé Künden, Nangsa Wöbum, Gyasa Belsa, and Donyö Dondrup. Performance integrates singing (with distinctive named melodic-modes), stylized dance-and-mime movement, recited dialogue, and percussion accompaniment (rolmo large paired cymbals and damaru double-headed hand-drum the principal instruments — no melodic instruments, the form is essentially voice-and-percussion). The Lhasa-region Kyumolung style and the Shang and Gyenpa regional styles constitute the three main lineages. Performance traditionally outdoors during summer festivals, particularly the Shotön (yogurt-festival) at Norbulingka in Lhasa. The Tibetan Institute of Performing Arts (TIPA, Dharamshala, India) maintains the principal exile-community transmission lineage post-1959. Distinguished from the parallel monastic-liturgical yang chant by ache lhamo's secular-narrative (vs liturgical) functional framework and absence of long-trumpets and double-reed monastic-ensemble instrumentation; distinguished from Chinese jingju by Tibetan-language repertoire and characteristic voice-and-percussion-only ensemble configuration.

items.name: Tibetan multiphonic yang chant
items.lineage: Tibetan Buddhist monastic multiphonic yang chant tradition of the Gelug-school tantric colleges Gyuto and Gyume (founded 1474 and 1485, respectively, by Sherab Sengge, a direct disciple of Tsongkhapa). The yang chant technique produces a chest-register-pitched fundamental enriched with audible upper-partial overtones such that a single voice produces what sounds like a chord — the third, fifth, and sometimes higher partials being amplified into clearly audible voice-leading register. Multiple monks chanting in unison produce a thick texture of fundamental-plus-overtones across the assembly. Repertoire centers on the Lama Chöpa (Guru Puja), the Yamantaka tantric cycles, the Guhyasamaja tantric cycles, and the Chakrasamvara tantric cycles. Accompaniment by the canonical monastic-ensemble percussion: rolmo large paired cymbals, dril-bu small hand-bell, damaru double-headed hand-drum, dung-chen long telescoping copper-or-brass trumpet (the four-meter-long ceremonial instrument, played in pairs, capable of producing the very-low subharmonic that anchors the ensemble), rgya-gling double-reed oboe (the melodic-leading instrument when wind voices are present), and kangling thigh-bone trumpet (for specific wrathful-deity cycles). Huston Smith's 1967 Music of Tibet recordings (GemsTone GT1003-CD reissue 2005) and David Lewiston's 1971 Nonesuch Explorer H-72071 Tibetan Ritual Music constitute the principal Western-distributed documentation. Distinguished from Mongolian khoomei by Tibetan yang chant's ensemble (vs solo) and liturgical (vs secular) framework; distinguished from Sakya-school chant by Gelug-specific tantric-cycle repertoire; distinguished from Bön pre-Buddhist Tibetan chant by Buddhist tantric-text base.

items.name: Japanese gidayū-bushi (Bunraku narration)
items.lineage: Japanese gidayū-bushi sung-and-spoken narration tradition, the canonical narrative-vocal style of ningyō jōruri Bunraku puppet-theater. Named after the founding seventeenth-century narrator Takemoto Gidayū (1651-1714), who codified the style at the Takemoto-za puppet-theater in Osaka beginning in 1684 and whose canonical works (such as the Sonezaki Shinjū love-suicide play, 1703, written by his collaborator Chikamatsu Monzaemon) established the genre's core repertoire. Bunraku-as-form. Performance configuration: a single tayū (narrator) sits on a raised platform stage-right, holding the maruhon scroll-text and shifting between speaking voices for multiple characters and the omniscient narrator, while a shamisen player (three-string plucked lute, specifically the heavy-bodied futozao shamisen reserved for jōruri) sits beside providing accompaniment that is structurally inseparable from the vocal narration — a single composition of tayū-and-shamisen voice. The narrative style spans a vast emotional and acoustic range: from quiet bedchamber confidence to climactic suicide-scene wails, from comedic banter to mortal-injury death-rattle, with the tayū employing a striking range of voice-types and registers. Repertoire genealogically connected to the older Heike-monogatari biwa-narrative and to the medieval Buddhist sermon-chant traditions. Twentieth-century canonical tayū include Toyotake Yamashiro-no-Shōjō, Takemoto Tsudayū, and contemporary masters of the National Bunraku Theatre lineage. Distinguished from gagaku court music by gidayū's narrative-theatrical (vs ceremonial-orchestral) functional framework; distinguished from kabuki nagauta by jōruri's puppet-theater accompaniment context.

items.name: Rajasthani Manganiyar tradition
items.lineage: Rajasthani Manganiyar hereditary musician tradition of the Thar Desert region of western Rajasthan, India (Jaisalmer, Barmer, and Jodhpur districts), with the parallel Langa community sharing many features. The Manganiyar are Muslim-by-religion-but-Hindu-by-patron-relation hereditary musicians whose performance-economic configuration centers on the jajmani patron-relationship: each Manganiyar family is bound to specific Rajput patron-families across generations, performing at patron weddings, births, and funerals as the ritual-and-aesthetic specialist providers. Canonical instrumentation: kamaicha (gourd-bowled bowed lute with sympathetic strings) as the primary melodic carrier in deeper-register sustained-tone repertoire, plus khartal wooden-castanet-pair, dholak two-headed barrel drum, and sometimes algoza double-flute or sarangi. Repertoire spans devotional Sufi qawwali-adjacent material, Rajput court-praise repertoire, panihari water-bearer women's-song accompaniment, and the canonical drone-and-narrative-improvisation pieces such as Niambat Khan and Padharo Mhare Des. Modal vocabulary draws on regional raga-frameworks distinct from Hindustani classical but related — the Manganiyar mode-system uses approximately just-intonation tonal hierarchies. Komal Kothari's Rupayan Sansthan in Borunda (founded 1960s) and the Archives & Research Center for Ethnomusicology (AIIS Gurugram, Shubha Chaudhuri) provide the principal scholarly documentation; Daniel Neuman & Shubha Chaudhuri's Bards, Ballads and Boundaries (Seagull 2006) anchors the contemporary scholarship. Sakar Khan and Anwar Khan among the canonical twentieth-century kamaicha and singing masters. Distinguished from Hindustani classical by Manganiyar's jajmani-patron-relationship economic structure and folk-classical hybrid modal system; distinguished from Langa (the parallel Sindhi-influenced hereditary community) by Manganiyar-Marwari dialect and Rajput-patron-relationship base.

items.name: Croatian klapa Dalmatian close-harmony
items.lineage: Croatian klapa Dalmatian close-harmony multipart-singing tradition of the Adriatic coastal region (Split, Šibenik, Zadar, Dubrovnik and the Adriatic islands). The classical klapa configuration is a male a-cappella quartet or quintet: lead tenor (prvi tenor), second tenor (drugi tenor), baritone (bariton), and bass (bas), with the optional addition of a second bass voice for fuller texture. Vocal architecture features close-harmony chordal-block writing (almost always homophonic, with all voices moving together rhythmically), characteristic Mediterranean modal-tonal ambiguity (major-mode tonic with frequent flattened-seventh and minor-mode plagal cadences), and the canonical klapa "Dalmatian" intonation with slightly stretched intervals producing a bright, resonant ensemble sound when sung in stone-walled outdoor narrow-street alleys (the canonical performance acoustic). Repertoire spans the dramatic Mediterranean-coastal love-and-loss ballad cycles, the religious-procession-and-feast-day repertoire, sea-and-fishing lament cycles, and the contemporary klapa-festival-composed repertoire of newer pieces in the traditional style. Klapa Cambi, Klapa Šufit, and Klapa Sebenico among the canonical twentieth-century ensembles. The annual Omiš Festival of Dalmatian Klapa (founded 1967) constitutes the principal performance-and-competition venue. Distinguished from Sardinian cantu a tenore by Croatian klapa's close-harmony tonal-chord-block (vs Sardinian drone-and-overtone) architecture; distinguished from Corsican paghjella by Croatian's four-or-five-voice quartet-with-bass (vs Corsican's three-voice male-trio) configuration; distinguished from Albanian iso-polyphony by Croatian's tonal-chord-block (vs Albanian iso-drone) foundation.

items.name: Croatian Istrian two-part-in-Istrian-scale
items.lineage: Croatian Istrian two-part-in-Istrian-scale (dvoglasno pjevanje na tijesno) tradition of the Istrian peninsula (northwestern Croatian Adriatic coast, with related material in adjacent Slovenian Istria). The form is a two-voice male diaphonic vocal practice in which the two voices move in characteristic parallel-second-and-minor-third intervals, ending each phrase strictly in unison-or-octave cadence, all within the non-tempered six-tone Istrian scale codified in the 1920s by composer-theorist Ivan Matetić Ronjgov (1880-1960). The Istrian scale is a regional folk-tonal system with paired-second intervallic structure and characteristic non-tempered intonation that no Western equal-tempered transcription captures faithfully. Performance involves the lead voice (kantadur) and the answering voice (kontradur), with the two singers standing close together and projecting outward in unison facing the audience or open landscape. Parallel instrumental form exists in the sopele (paired large-and-small conical-bore double-reed shawms playing the same intervallic vocabulary as the two voices) and the šurla (similar paired shawms in the southern Istrian dialect). Performance contexts include outdoor village squares, processions, and the contemporary folk-festival circuit. Distinguished from broader Croatian klapa by Istrian's two-voice diaphonic (vs four-voice close-harmony) architecture and non-tempered Istrian-scale (vs twelve-tet tonal-chordal) vocabulary; distinguished from Slovenian-folk-singing by Istrian-specific Croatian regional dialect.

items.name: Macedonian Glasoechko male diaphonic
items.lineage: Macedonian Glasoechko male two-voice diaphonic singing tradition of the Dolni Polog and Drimkol-Golo Brdo regions of western North Macedonia. The form features two-voice male singing in characteristic parallel-second and minor-third intervals over a sustained drone-tone (often an organ-point sustained by the second voice while the lead voice elaborates the melodic content), with most phrases cadencing on a unison-or-octave close. Distinguished from neighboring Balkan two-voice traditions by Glasoechko's Mijak-and-Šop dialect-specific cadential vocabulary and the characteristic Macedonian-pastoral functional context. The melodic vocabulary draws on regional pastoral-and-shepherd-call modal frameworks with characteristic narrow-range melodic-contour conventions. Accompanying instrumental contexts sometimes include the kaval end-blown shepherd-flute and the gajda Balkan bagpipe with double-reed chanter and drone-pipe. Performance traditionally outdoors in mountain-pasture contexts during summer transhumance, with the long-distance acoustic projection of the two-voice configuration suited to mountain-valley environments. The mid-twentieth-century rural depopulation of the Polog and Drimkol regions reduced active practitioners. Distinguished from Croatian Istrian diaphonic by Macedonian Glasoechko's drone-and-melody (vs Istrian's strict-two-voice-parallel) configuration and Macedonian-pastoral functional context; distinguished from Albanian iso-polyphony by Glasoechko's two-voice (vs Albanian three-or-four-voice) configuration; distinguished from neighboring Bulgarian male diaphonic by Macedonian-Mijak-dialect-specific cadential conventions.

items.name: Armenian duduk-accompanied chant
items.lineage: Armenian duduk-accompanied vocal-and-instrumental chant tradition, with the duduk (apricot-wood double-reed cylindrical-bore aerophone). The duduk produces a deep, plangent, melancholic tone with characteristic vibrato-and-pitch-bend articulation and a fundamental pitched in the human-vocal mid-register, allowing the instrument to function as a "second voice" alongside the singer in lament and ceremonial contexts. Traditional duduk performance is in pairs: the dam duduk holds a sustained drone-tone (the dam, equivalent to the Sufi-Persian damam pedal-point), while the lead duduk plays the melodic content above. Vocal repertoire spans Armenian Apostolic liturgical sharakan hymns (the Armenian Orthodox church's canonical hymn cycles, in eight modes after the Byzantine oktoechos but with Armenian-language and characteristic ornamental conventions), folk-lament repertoire (the patkerazard genre of bride-departure laments), and the historical-narrative ballad cycles tied to the Armenian Genocide commemoration. Modal vocabulary draws on Armenian regional modal systems with quarter-tone and three-quarter-tone microtonal inflections shared with broader Anatolian and Caucasus regional modal traditions. Djivan Gasparyan (1928-2021) and Vatche Hovsepian among the twentieth-century canonical duduk masters. Performance contexts include Apostolic Church liturgical settings (the canonical context for sharakan), funeral and commemoration ceremonies, and the post-1990 international-touring concert-circuit. Distinguished from Azerbaijani mugham by Armenian duduk's sharakan-liturgical (vs dastgah-classical) repertoire base and Armenian-Apostolic-rite framework; distinguished from Turkish ney by duduk's double-reed cylindrical-bore (vs Turkish end-blown-flute) construction.

The duduk produces a deep, plangent, melancholic tone with characteristic vibrato-and-pitch-bend articulation. Traditional duduk performance is in pairs: the dam duduk holds a sustained drone-tone, while the lead duduk plays the melodic content above. items.name: Lithuanian sutartinės multipart
items.lineage: Lithuanian sutartinės multipart-singing tradition of northeastern Lithuania (Aukštaitija region). Sutartinės are female-group (occasionally mixed-or-male) polyphonic songs in characteristic parallel-second intervals — two-or-three voices moving in tight major-second-and-minor-second clusters, with strict canonical-imitative entry-patterns at the second or fourth. The genre includes vocal-only (sutartinės-as-song) and instrumental variants performed on kanklės (board zither, finger-plucked) and skudučiai (multiple-tube pan-pipes played by multiple players in hocketed pattern, with each player blowing only one tube and the melodic line resulting from the rapid alternation across players). Sutartinė structure typically alternates between an opening-formula sung by one voice, an answering response from the second voice, and the eventual building-up of the canonical two-or-three-voice texture. Repertoire spans work-song accompaniment, calendar-rite celebrations, wedding-cycle songs, and the broader Baltic narrow-range narrative-poetic tradition. Modal vocabulary draws on the Lithuanian sutartinės parallel-seconds vocabulary, considered one of the most archaic tonal systems in Europe with possible deep Indo-European ritual-music continuity. Zenonas Slaviūnas's three-volume 1820-sutartinė edition (1958-1959) is the foundational corpus-documentation; Stasys Paliulis's instrumental-sutartinė collection complements the vocal corpus; Distinguished from Latvian dainas by Lithuanian sutartinės parallel-seconds polyphonic configuration (vs Latvian-dainas-as-mostly-monophonic-or-heterophonic); distinguished from Estonian Setu leelo by Lithuanian's strict-canonical-imitation (vs Setu's call-and-response-with-drone-bourdon) architecture.

items.name: Estonian Setu leelo polyphonic song
items.lineage: Estonian Setu leelo polyphonic women's-song tradition of the Setu region (southeast Estonia and adjacent Pechory district of Russia). The Setu are a distinct Estonian-and-Russian-borderland Finno-Ugric ethnic group whose linguistic-cultural identity preserves archaic Finno-Ugric features lost in mainstream Estonian. Leelo is performed by a women's group with the lead singer (sõnoline, "the word-singer") improvising the verse text and melodic line, answered by the choral group (torrõ, "the resonators") in unison or in a sustained drone-bourdon below the melodic line. The drone configuration distinguishes leelo from neighboring Baltic polyphonic traditions: the torrõ chorus holds a sustained pedal-tone while the sõnoline elaborates above, producing a drone-and-melodic-elaboration register more akin to certain Slavic and Central-Asian traditions than to the parallel-second sutartinė style. Vocabulary draws on a regional Estonian-Setu pentatonic-leaning modal system. Verse-form is Kalevala-meter (the canonical Finno-Ugric four-stress eight-syllable line shared with the Finnish-Karelian Kalevala epic). Repertoire spans calendar-rite celebrations, wedding-cycle songs (Setu weddings featured the most elaborated leelo repertoire, with sung-confrontation-and-praise sequences between bride-and-groom parties), funeral-lament cycles, and the contemporary Värska-Obinitsa Setu cultural-festival circuit. Mipu Music MIPUCD 104 — Setusongs (1991, recorded May 1990) provides the canonical Western-distributed documentation. Distinguished from Lithuanian sutartinės by Setu leelo's drone-and-melody (vs Lithuanian parallel-seconds) configuration; distinguished from Karelian rune-singing by Setu's antiphonal-with-drone (vs Karelian's strict-alternation) architecture; distinguished from mainland Estonian regilaul by Setu-dialect-specific vocabulary and Estonian-Russian-borderland regional context.

items.name: Swedish kulning herding-call
items.lineage: Swedish kulning (and the cognate Norwegian kuløkk and laling) high-volume female herding-call tradition of the mountain-pasture fäbod summer-grazing settlements of central and northern Sweden (Dalarna, Hälsingland, Härjedalen, and Jämtland provinces) and adjacent western Norway. Performed by women (the milkmaids who managed cattle and goats at the summer pastures) as a long-distance projecting call to bring grazing animals home at evening milking-time, kulning developed as a specialized vocal-projection technique using a tightly-focused upper-chest-and-head register that can carry several kilometers across mountain valleys. The technique employs characteristic ornamentation: a rapid initial pitch-glide upward to the calling-pitch, characteristic falling-fourth and falling-fifth interval ornaments, and a distinctive crystalline high-register timbre produced by tight glottal-and-supralaryngeal compression. Repertoire spans the practical herding-calls (lockrop) used to summon specific animals, calling-songs (lockläte) sung to entertain or comfort the cattle, and the broader corpus of fäbod-related work-song. The Svenskt visarkiv (Swedish Folk Music Archive) field-recordings beginning in the 1940s, and Susanne Rosenberg's twenty-first-century scholarship and performance, anchor the documentation. The mid-twentieth-century industrialization of Swedish dairy-farming eliminated the fäbod system as functional infrastructure; kulning persists as a heritage-art practice with active transmission through folk-music schools and concert-revival performers including Jonna Jinton in the post-2010 social-media revival. Distinguished from Norwegian kuløkk by Swedish-dialect-specific vocabulary and Dalarna-Härjedalen regional fäbod context; distinguished from Sámi yoik by kulning's pastoral-call functional context (vs yoik's personal-and-ancestor-evocation function) and tight-focused projection technique (vs yoik's nasal-resonance and narrow-range vocabulary).

items.name: Northern Sámi luohti yoik
items.lineage: Northern Sámi luohti yoik tradition of the Sápmi region of northern Norway, Sweden, Finland, and the Russian Kola Peninsula. Luohti is the principal yoik subgenre of the Northern Sámi (Davvisámegiella-speaking) population — a sung-vocal form whose conceptual orientation is fundamentally different from Western lyric song: a yoik does not sing "about" its subject but rather is the subject — to yoik a person, a place, or an animal is to evoke and bring-present that subject through the act of yoiking. Vocal style features narrow-range melody (two-to-five pitches typically), characteristic nasal-resonant timbre, characteristic descending-melodic-contour shapes, repeated melodic-formula cycling, and a strikingly non-strophic open-ended performance temporality (a yoik does not have a definite beginning or ending — the singer enters and exits a yoik mid-phrase). Pre-tempered tonal system with characteristic fourth, fifth, and octave intervals as the structural skeleton. Repertoire is personal: each Sámi person traditionally has an assigned-or-received luohti that names them, and natural-feature luohti exist for specific mountains, lakes, and reindeer-herd boundaries. The Sámi Christian-mission suppression-era 1850s-1950s pushed the tradition underground; the post-1970s Sámi cultural revival (anchored in the founding of the Sámi Parliament and the Sami University College) has restored public-performance space, with figures such as Nils-Aslak Valkeapää, Mari Boine, and Wimme Saari among the canonical twentieth-century revival figures. Arnt Bakke's 1949-1972 field-recording collection at UiT The Norwegian Arctic University Museum (Tromsø) and Ola Graff's continued 1982-2019 collection constitute the principal documentary anchor. Distinguished from Skolt and Southern Sámi yoik by Northern-Sámi-Davvisámegiella dialect; distinguished from Finnish joiku by language-specific cadential and intonation vocabulary.

items.name: Skolt Sámi leuʹdd
items.lineage: Skolt Sámi leuʹdd vocal tradition of the Skolt Sámi (Nuõrttsää'mǩiõll-speaking) population of the easternmost Sámi homeland — historically the Pechenga (Petsamo) region of the Russian Kola Peninsula, displaced post-1944 to the Sevettijärvi-Nellim region of northeastern Finland. Leuʹdd differs from the Northern Sámi luohti in functional orientation: rather than the open-ended personal-or-natural-feature evocation of luohti, leuʹdd are narrative-personal-history songs telling the life-stories of specific individuals (the singer's own life, or the life of a deceased relative). The leuʹdd repertoire thus constitutes an oral-historical archive of the Skolt Sámi community, particularly significant given the community's displacement-trauma history. Vocal style features narrow-range melody (often even narrower than Northern Sámi luohti, sometimes restricted to three pitches), with characteristic micro-pitch-inflection on syllables, narrative-strophic structure (longer narratives extending across many strophes with melodic-formula return), and a more text-bearing register than luohti's pure-sound-evocation. The Skolt Sámi were converted to Russian Orthodoxy (not Lutheran like the Northern Sámi), so leuʹdd survived alongside Orthodox liturgical chant rather than under the suppression-pressure of the Lutheran Sámi-mission. The Marko Jouste-led Saami Culture Archive at the University of Oulu maintains the primary documentation; the Sevettijärvi leuʹdd ensemble continues active transmission. Distinguished from Northern Sámi luohti by Skolt-dialect-specific narrative-personal-history (vs luohti-evocation) functional framework; distinguished from Southern Sámi vuelie by Skolt-Sámi Kola Peninsula regional origin and post-1944 Finnish-displacement context.

items.name: Southern Sámi vuelie
items.lineage: Southern Sámi vuelie yoik tradition of the Southern Sámi (Åarjelsaemien gïele-speaking) population of central Norway and adjacent Swedish Härjedalen and Jämtland. Vuelie ("yoik" in the Southern Sámi language) features differ from the Northern Sámi luohti and Skolt leuʹdd: typically a slightly wider melodic range, a more strophic-and-cyclical formal structure, and characteristic ornamental conventions distinct from the Northern Sámi vocabulary. The Southern Sámi homeland is the most geographically southern and linguistically distinct of the Sámi communities, with the language considered the most endangered of the Sámi languages. Repertoire spans the personal-evocation yoik (parallel to Northern Sámi luohti), the place-and-reindeer-herd vuelie, and the narrative-historical sequences. The Southern Sámi mid-twentieth-century cultural-revival lineage — including Frode Fjellheim, whose contemporary vuelie composition "Eatnemen Vuelie" featured in the 2013 Disney film Frozen, bringing international visibility — has restored public-performance space for the tradition. Heikki Laitinen's scholarship in Folkmusik i Sverige (Lundberg & Ternhag 2005) provides Swedish-side documentation; the Norwegian Sami Center maintains parallel institutional infrastructure. Distinguished from Northern Sámi luohti by Southern-Sámi dialect and characteristic wider-range cyclical-strophic structure; distinguished from Skolt leuʹdd by Southern Sámi's evocation-and-place (vs Skolt narrative-personal-history) functional framework; distinguished from Lule and Pite Sámi (the intermediate dialect-regions) by southern-most-geographic origin and the distinct Åarjelsaemien linguistic-cultural identity.

items.name: Mapuche tayil genealogical chant
items.lineage: Mapuche (Araucanian) tayil women's genealogical-ritual chant tradition of the Mapuche communities of southern Argentina (Neuquén, Río Negro, Chubut provinces) and adjacent southern-central Chile (Araucanía Region). Tayil is a sung-evocation of a kin-group's tayil-spirit (each Mapuche kin-group / küpan has its own tayil-spirit-melody, inherited matrilineally), with the singer's voice bringing-present the spiritual essence of the ancestor-line during the ngillatún collective-ceremony (the central Mapuche public ritual cycle, held over multiple days in a sacred clearing). Performance involves a single woman singer-evocator (tayilfe) in melismatic-narrow-range melodic style with characteristic descending-contour cadential conventions and Mapuche pentatonic-leaning modal vocabulary, accompanied by kultrún (the one-headed shamanic frame-drum with cosmological-diagram-painted goat-skin or horse-skin head, struck with a curved beater) and sometimes trutruka long-trumpet or pifüllka end-blown whistles. The tayil tradition is distinct from but adjacent to the machi shamanic ülkantun (the curing-songs of the machi shaman, a separate role and repertoire). Carol E. Robertson-DeCarbo's 1976 Indiana doctoral dissertation (Tayil: Musical Communication and Social Organization Among the Mapuche of Argentina), her 1979 Ethnomusicology article Pulling the Ancestors (23/3), and María Ester Grebe Vicuña's 1973 Revista Musical Chilena article on the kultrún constitute the foundational scholarship. Distinguished from neighboring Tehuelche and Huilliche vocal traditions by Mapuche-Mapudungun language and tayil-spirit-evocation functional framework; distinguished from broader South American indigenous ritual-music by the specific küpan-spirit-inheritance kin-group structure.

items.name: Shipibo-Conibo icaros healing songs
items.lineage: Shipibo-Conibo icaros healing-song tradition of the Ucayali river basin of the Peruvian Amazon, with cognate forms across the broader Western Amazonian shamanic-tradition area (Asháninka, Shuar, Yagua, and Cocama-Cocamilla parallel forms). Icaros are sung-spells learned by shamans (onaya in the Shipibo language) through master-apprentice transmission and through dieta-restricted-diet plant-spirit communications, then deployed during nocturnal ayahuasca-ceremony healing sessions in the maloca palm-thatch ceremonial hut. Each icaro is associated with a specific plant-spirit (the icaro of ayahuasca, the icaro of chacruna, the icaro of toé, the icaro of bobinsana, and so on), a specific therapeutic function (cleansing icaros, protective icaros, vision-amplifying icaros, calling-the-spirits icaros, mareación-managing icaros), and a specific named master-shaman lineage. Performance occurs in near-darkness with the shaman singing close to the individual patient, the icaro lasting from a few minutes to over an hour depending on therapeutic context. Vocal style features narrow-range melodic vocabulary, characteristic glissando-and-descending-cadence ornaments, the use of phlegmatic-rasp voice quality for certain icaros, and the optional accompaniment of shacapa leaf-bundle rattle (the canonical Amazonian shamanic-rhythm instrument). Bernd Brabec de Mori's 2015 monograph Die Lieder der Richtigen Menschen (Helbling) and the Phonogrammarchiv of the Austrian Academy of Sciences Shipibo collection constitute the principal scholarly documentation; the 2008 Peruvian INC Resolución 836 declared traditional ayahuasca practice as cultural-heritage at the national level. Distinguished from Mestizo-Peruvian ayahuasquero icaros by the Shipibo-Conibo language repertoire and indigenous-community ceremonial-functional context; distinguished from Yawanawa and Huni Kuin healing songs by Shipibo-specific dieta-and-plant-spirit lineage.

items.name: Cape Verdean batuko of Santiago Island
items.lineage: Cape Verdean batuko (also tabanka and finaçon) Afro-Atlantic women's percussive-vocal tradition of Santiago Island, the historically-and-demographically central island of the Cape Verde archipelago. Batuko configuration: a circle of women seated, each playing a tchabeta — a tightly-rolled cloth bundle held between the legs and struck with the open hand to produce a deep slap-tone — while one woman in the center (the txabetadeira-lead or "the one who is dancing batuko") sings the verse-text and dances in the center of the circle, with the surrounding women responding antiphonally and clapping in cross-rhythmic patterns over the tchabeta pulse. The tradition is genealogically connected to the West-African Mandinka and Wolof women's drum-and-dance circles that the Portuguese slave-trade transported to Santiago Island in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries; the absence of true membrane drums in the post-arrival diaspora (slave-traders banned drums in transport and on early plantations) led to the substitution of the cloth-bundle as percussion surface, an organological adaptation of considerable interest. Vocal repertoire spans batuko (the strophic dance-rhythm song), finaçon (the slower more elaborated solo-singer-with-circle improvisatory-praise form), and txabeta (the rhythm-only instrumental cycles between vocal sections). Modal vocabulary draws on the broader Cape Verdean-creole regional folk tonal system. Santiago Island batuko ensembles such as Finaçon-bidjus and the women's associations of the Santa Catarina and Tarrafal municipalities maintain active transmission. Distinguished from morna and coladera (Cape Verde's other principal traditions) by batuko's women-only Santiago-Island-specific Afro-Atlantic percussive-vocal (vs the morna's acoustic-guitar-and-cavaquinho ballad) functional configuration; distinguished from Guinea-Bissau Manjak women's drum-circles by Cape Verdean-creole linguistic-cultural identity.

items.name: Brazilian samba de roda do Recôncavo
items.lineage: Brazilian samba de roda Afro-Brazilian circle-dance tradition of the Recôncavo Baiano region (the coastal-inland area surrounding the Bay of All Saints in the state of Bahia, northeastern Brazil). Samba de roda is the most direct surviving ancestral form of all later Brazilian sambas — the Recôncavo Baiano region's population descended from West-African (Yoruba and Bantu) enslaved peoples brought to Bahia during the seventeenth-and-eighteenth-century Portuguese slave-trade, and samba de roda preserves the most direct Afro-Brazilian linguistic and rhythmic continuity. Performance configuration: a circle (roda) of participants, with one or two dancers moving into the center of the circle in turn to perform the characteristic samba-de-roda footwork (the umbigada navel-bump greeting an iconic moment in each turn), while the surrounding circle plays the percussion battery — atabaque barrel-drums, pandeiro frame-drum-with-jingles, viola machete small five-string lute (the genealogically older ancestor of all later Brazilian violas), reco-reco ridged scraper, and clapping. Vocal style features a lead singer (the puxador) singing the verse with chorus response from the circle, with characteristic Yoruba-derived linguistic substrate in many of the older repertoires. Repertoire connects to the broader Afro-Brazilian Candomblé religious-context (the terreiro yard being the canonical performance space) and to the secular festive-cycle repertoire. The 2007 IPHAN nomination dossier (Carlos Sandroni and Sant'Anna) and the Samba de Roda de São Felix ensemble constitute the principal documentation. Distinguished from Rio-de-Janeiro samba (the urban-twentieth-century descendant tradition) by samba-de-roda's rural-Bahia Recôncavo-specific and pre-urban-tradition configuration; distinguished from candomblé Afro-Brazilian ritual-music by samba-de-roda's secular-festive (vs orixá-ritual) functional framework.

items.lineage: Tongan lakalaka combines occasion-specific sung poetry, choral polyphony and coordinated standing dance. A punake directs the words, music and movements. This seed uses the documented vocal-and-handclap configuration.

items.name: Māori karanga and pōwhiri ritual call
items.lineage: Māori karanga and pōwhiri formal-welcome ceremonial vocal tradition of Aotearoa New Zealand. The karanga is the high-pitched extended-pitch-glide formal call performed by senior women (the kaikaranga) at the opening of a pōwhiri formal welcome ceremony as visiting parties approach the marae (carved meeting-house and forecourt). The kaikaranga of the host iwi (tribe) initiates the karanga with a long sustained high-pitched call extending across many seconds, which the kaikaranga of the visiting party answers, and the call-response continues across phases as the visitors physically approach the carved whare-nui meeting-house. The karanga functions to acknowledge the dead, identify the visitors, invoke the ancestors, and ritually-spatially admit the visitors onto sacred ground. Vocal architecture features extended-pitch-sustain, high-register projection (the kaikaranga voice carrying across a wide outdoor distance), characteristic pitch-bend ornament, and a strikingly non-strophic open-ended duration determined by ceremonial context. Following the karanga, the broader pōwhiri sequence proceeds through whaikōrero (formal oratory by senior men, the kaikōrero), waiata (sung songs accompanying or responding to the oratory), and finally hongi (forehead-and-nose-pressing ritual greeting). The pūtātara conch-shell trumpet sometimes signals the opening of the karanga sequence. Performance contexts include marae-welcome of guests, tangihanga funerals, school and parliament openings, and any other formal-ceremonial gathering at a marae. Mervyn McLean's Maori Music (Auckland University Press 1996) is the principal English-language scholarly documentation. Distinguished from Māori waiata sung-song by karanga's extended-pitch-glide ceremonial-call (vs strophic-melodic-song) configuration; distinguished from Tongan lakalaka by karanga's women-only call-and-response (vs Tongan large-group choreographed-poetry) functional framework.
items.description: Māori karanga and pōwhiri formal-welcome ceremonial vocal tradition of Aotearoa New Zealand. The karanga is the high-pitched extended-pitch-glide formal call performed by senior women (the kaikaranga) at the opening of a pōwhiri formal welcome ceremony as visiting parties approach the marae (carved meeting-house and forecourt). The kaikaranga of the host iwi (tribe) initiates the karanga with a long sustained high-pitched call extending across many seconds, which the kaikaranga of the visiting party answers. The karanga functions to acknowledge the dead, identify the visitors, invoke the ancestors, and ritually-spatially admit the visitors onto sacred ground. Vocal architecture features extended-pitch-sustain, high-register projection, characteristic pitch-bend ornament.

items.name: Māori haka taparahi
items.lineage: Māori haka taparahi war-and-ceremonial-chant tradition of Aotearoa New Zealand. Haka is a general category encompassing several sub-types: haka taparahi (ceremonial-without-weapons, the most commonly performed contemporary form), haka peruperu (with-weapons war-haka, performed before battle in pre-contact context), ngeri (vigorous-spontaneous response-haka), and tūtūngārahu (rehearsal-haka before peruperu). Performance involves a male (or sometimes mixed-gender) group in characteristic posture — feet planted shoulder-width, knees bent, body lowered into a slight crouch — performing a vigorous percussive-chant with characteristic facial expression (pukana eye-bulging, whetero tongue-protrusion in male haka), stamping-and-slapping-the-body rhythmic percussion (the performers' own thighs and chests producing the percussion-track), and shouted-rhythmic verse-text alternating between solo-leader verses and choral group response. The most internationally famous haka, Ka Mate Ka Mate (composed c.1820 by Ngāti Toa chief Te Rauparaha), now in worldwide circulation through the All Blacks rugby team's pre-match performance, illustrates the form. The verse-text is poetic-narrative and often connects to ancestor-praise, war-history, or current-ceremonial-occasion. Performance contexts include marae welcoming and farewell ceremonies, tangihanga funeral concluding rites, sports-team pre-match rituals, school and university kapa haka performance, and the Te Matatini National Kapa Haka Festival (held biennially since 1972, the premier competitive haka venue). Mervyn McLean's Maori Music (Auckland University Press 1996) is the canonical scholarly documentation. Distinguished from karanga-and-pōwhiri by haka's vigorous-percussive-stance-with-shouted-text (vs sustained-high-call) configuration; distinguished from Tongan lakalaka and Samoan sasa by haka's characteristic Māori-language verse-text and pukana-whetero facial-expression vocabulary.

items.name: Yemeni Sanaani song
items.lineage: Yemeni al-ghinā' al-Ṣanʻānī ("the song of Sana'a") classical urban-chamber-song tradition of the Yemeni highlands. Origin in the medieval Yemeni-Rasulid period (thirteenth-fifteenth centuries) with development through the Qasimid and Mutawakkilite imamate periods (seventeenth-twentieth centuries) into the modern form. Performance configuration: a male singer (the singer holds the social role of muṭrib, a respected community-cultural-figure rather than a paid entertainer) accompanies himself on the qanbus (the short-neck skin-bellied Yemeni-Arabian lute — distinct from the more familiar oud, with characteristic deep buzzing-resonance from the skin belly), or on the small-frame turbi drum or sahn metal-tray-as-percussion-surface. Performance contexts center on the qat-chew majlis (the afternoon-into-evening social gathering at a private home where male participants consume the mildly stimulant qat leaf while engaging in literary-philosophical-political conversation and song). Repertoire spans three movement-categories within a typical qomah ("setting"): das'ah (the slow opening movement), wasṭ (the middle movement), and ghinā' al-bāṣ (the lively concluding movement). Lyric base draws on classical Arabic poetry and especially the seventeenth-century Yemeni mystic-philosopher poet Muhammad ibn Sharaf al-Dīn (1559-1607). Modal vocabulary draws on the Arabic maqam framework with Yemeni-specific cadential and ornamental conventions. The Yemen Music House field-recording archive constitutes the principal documentation. Distinguished from Iraqi maqam by Yemeni-Sanaani's qanbus (vs Iraqi joza-and-santur) instrumental signature and Yemeni-Arabian regional dialect; distinguished from Hejazi and Najdi Arabian song by Yemeni-Sanaani's qat-majlis-chamber (vs court-or-bedouin) functional context.

items.name: Coptic Orthodox liturgical chant
items.lineage: Coptic Orthodox liturgical chant tradition of the Egyptian Christian community, the canonical sacred-music tradition of the Coptic Orthodox Church (founded by tradition by Saint Mark in Alexandria in the first century, with continuous liturgical-music transmission from at least the Hellenistic-late-antique period). The Coptic liturgical year follows an eight-mode oktoechos modal-cycle structure (parallel to but distinct from the Byzantine and Syriac oktoechoi), with mode-specific cadential formulae governing each of the canonical liturgical hours and the principal cycles of the Sundays of Lent, the Holy Week, the Easter season, and the regular Sunday Divine Liturgy. Performance configuration: a male choir of cantor-and-chorus (the muallim head-cantor with his assistant cantors and the broader congregation), with characteristic percussion-only instrumental accompaniment — sanj small bronze paired hand-cymbals, muthallath metal triangle struck with rod, and the canonical kūz pottery-jar struck on specific Lenten and funeral hymns. Vocal architecture features microtonal modal-melodic vocabulary with characteristic shifted-third intervals and quarter-tone-and-three-quarter-tone microtonal inflections that no Western tempered transcription captures faithfully — Ragheb Moftah (1898-2001) led the twentieth-century institutional preservation project at the Institute of Coptic Studies (Cairo, 1926-2001), with English transcription-and-notation collaborator Ernest Newlandsmith (Cairo transcriptions 1926-1936) and Hungarian musicologist Margit Tóth (from 1970 onward) producing the canonical published documentary corpus, culminating in the 1998 AUC Press publication The Coptic Orthodox Liturgy of St. Basil: With Complete Musical Transcription. Distinguished from Byzantine chant by Coptic's Egyptian-Arabic-and-Coptic-Bohairic liturgical-language base (vs Greek), characteristic Coptic cymbal-and-triangle percussion accompaniment, and Egyptian-specific modal vocabulary; distinguished from Ethiopian Tewahedo zema by Coptic's eight-mode oktoechos system (vs Tewahedo's threefold ge'ez-ezel-araray); distinguished from Syriac and Maronite chant by Coptic's Egyptian regional rite and characteristic instrumental percussion presence.

items.name: Tigrinya music (Eritrean / northern Ethiopian)
items.lineage: Tigrinya vocal-and-string tradition of Eritrea and the Tigray region of northern Ethiopia, sharing the qenet pentatonic mode-system with broader Habesha practice but with Tigrinya-language poetic-meter and Eritrean-highland melodic-contour conventions. Performance ranges from solo wata one-string spike-fiddle to ensembles with krar bowl-lyre, masenqo, kebero drum, and washint flute. Distinguished from Amhara azmari by Tigrinya-language repertoire and Asmara-Mendefera-Massawa dialect.

items.name: Oromo music (Ethiopian Cushitic)
items.lineage: Oromo vocal-and-instrumental tradition of central-southern Ethiopia and northern Kenya, the largest Cushitic-language-speaking community in the Horn of Africa. Repertoire spans geerarsa men's heroic chant, weedduu wedding songs, irreecha thanksgiving songs at Lake Hora Arsadi, and contemporary Afaan Oromoo political-protest song. Performance integrates voice-led melodic content with krar, masenqo, and kebero accompaniment. Modal vocabulary draws on qenet pentatonic with Borana-Macha-Tulama-Arsi regional cadential vocabulary.

items.name: Somali qaraami song
items.lineage: Somali qaraami art-song tradition emerging in 1940s Mogadishu and Hargeisa as urban-classical Somali popular music, incorporating Arabian peninsular oud and qanun with Somali-language poetic-meter. The genre matured through the Somali Republic golden-age 1960s-1970s with Radio Mogadishu broadcasting the canonical Hargeisa-school singers. Vocal style features melismatic ornament over Arabic maqam vocabulary with Somali-Cushitic vocal-inflection. The post-1991 civil war disrupted institutional transmission; diaspora-revival in Minneapolis, London, and Toronto sustains contemporary practice.

items.name: Sudanese aghani al-banat ("girls' songs")
items.lineage: Sudanese aghani al-banat women's vocal-and-percussion tradition of central and northern Sudan, performed at women's gatherings (subhia mid-morning gatherings, henna ceremonies, weddings). Performance configuration: lead singer (haggaaba) with all-female chorus and tar frame-drum in characteristic 6/8 swing. Lyric base spans courtship, marriage-celebration, and political-protest. Modal vocabulary draws on Sudanese seven-mode pentatonic-leaning system. The Khartoum-radio golden-age 1950s-1970s anchored documentation. Featured prominently in the 2018-2019 Sudanese revolution protest contexts.

items.name: Nubian music (Egyptian-Sudanese Nile Valley)
items.lineage: Nubian music of the Mahas and Kunuz communities of the Nile Valley between Aswan and Dongola, with post-1964 Aswan High Dam relocation extending diaspora to Cairo and Khartoum. Performance integrates Nubian-language responsorial chorus with tar frame-drum and darbuka, plus twentieth-century urban-oud incorporation. Modal vocabulary draws on Nile Valley pentatonic-leaning tradition with distinct Nubian intervals. The post-1964 diaspora produced an exile-mourning lyric corpus addressing the loss of villages submerged by Lake Nasser. The aragid wedding-dance repertoire constitutes the core ceremonial layer.

items.name: Sabar drumming (Senegalese Wolof)
items.lineage: Senegalese Wolof sabar drumming tradition, the canonical drum-language and ceremonial-dance percussion-form of Senegal and The Gambia. The sabar ensemble centers on the open-bottomed wood-and-hide sabar drum played with curved stick in right hand and bare left hand, with several drum-types (nder lead, mbung-mbung mid, tugne low, gorong bottom) constructing polyrhythmic dialogue. The bakk drum-language is a quasi-linguistic communication system encoding named messages. Doudou N'Diaye Rose consolidated the contemporary repertoire and trained the largest performing ensemble.

items.name: Donsongoni hunter's harp (Mande)
items.lineage: Mande donsongoni ("hunter's harp") vocal-and-instrumental tradition of the Wassoulou region of southern Mali and adjacent eastern Guinea, performed by initiated hunters at hunter-society gatherings and at funerals. The donsongoni is a six-string calabash harp distinct from the larger courtly kora — associated with the rural-egalitarian hunter's society (donso-tòn) rather than the hereditary griot caste. Repertoire spans hunting-praise, ancestor-evocation, and esoteric hunter-society initiation material. The Wassoulou modernization brought the donsongoni into popular music through Oumou Sangaré.

items.name: Apàlà (Yoruba Muslim percussion-song)
items.lineage: Yoruba apàlà percussion-and-vocal genre originating in 1930s-1940s Ibadan as a Muslim-Yoruba devotional-and-praise music for post-Ramadan ìdí-l-Fitr celebrations. Performance centers on male lead singer with a battery of dùndún talking-drums (iyaalu mother-drum plus gangan pressure-drums), agogo bell, sekere shaker, and chorus response. The talking-drum lineage carries percussive-and-melodic-allusion content through standardized Yoruba drum-language. Distinguished from sákárà by apàlà's dùndún-talking-drum (vs sákárà's frame-drum-with-shawm) instrumental signature. Direct ancestor of later fuji genre.

items.name: Sákárà (Yoruba Muslim frame-drum song)
items.lineage: Yoruba sákárà Muslim-Yoruba vocal-and-percussion tradition of southwestern Nigeria, predating both apàlà and fuji as the earliest documented Yoruba urban-Muslim popular music — emerging in 1930s Lagos and Ibadan from rural Muslim-Yoruba devotional song. Performance: male lead singer with sákárà frame-drums (clay-bowled, single-headed, struck with curved stick) and goje one-string spike-fiddle providing melodic-counter-voice. Lyric base draws on Islamic-devotional praise, Yoruba moral-philosophical commentary, and social-political commentary on Nigerian urban life.

items.name: Were music (Yoruba Ramadan procession)
items.lineage: Yoruba were music: pre-dawn Ramadan-procession devotional song-and-drumming tradition of southwestern Nigerian Muslim-Yoruba communities, performed by ajiwere groups moving through Muslim neighborhoods before the suhoor pre-dawn meal during Ramadan. Performance combines unison or call-and-response chorus singing in Yoruba and Arabic (Quranic phrases interpolated into Yoruba praise-poetry) with sákárà frame-drums and small bells. Direct ancestor of fuji music — Alhaji Ayinde Barrister brought the were aesthetic into post-Ramadan secular commercial performance contexts.

items.name: Coupé-décalé (Ivorian dance music)
items.lineage: Coupé-décalé Ivorian dance-pop genre emerging in early-2000s Paris among the Ivorian diaspora club scene and rapidly transferred back to Abidjan. The name derives from Nouchi street-slang ("couper" to grab money, "décaler" to slip away) describing the get-rich-and-flee aspirational lifestyle. Production centers on hard four-on-the-floor digital kick with Nouchi-French lyrical content, simple call-and-response chorus, and electronic synth-bass. The death of founding figure Stéphane Hamidou Doukouré (Douk Saga) in 2006 mythologized the Paris-Abidjan founder-generation.

items.name: Zouglou (Ivorian student music)
items.lineage: Zouglou Ivorian student-and-popular music emerging in 1990 at the University of Abidjan dormitories as a participatory call-and-response song-and-dance form expressing political commentary. The genre arose from the older bidakouro Bété percussion-and-vocal tradition adapted with French-language and Nouchi-slang lyrics. Performance grew from a-cappella dormitory-circle form into commercial studio recording from 1992 onward. Magic System's 1ère Gaou (1999) became the first international-crossover zouglou hit.

items.name: Singeli (Tanzanian high-tempo electronic)
items.lineage: Singeli ultra-high-tempo Tanzanian electronic dance music emerging in 2000s in the Manzese neighborhood of Dar es Salaam from convergence of traditional ngoma drumming with PC-software production. Runs typically at 180-300 BPM with chopped vocal samples, accelerated taarab loops, and aggressive synth riffs over hyper-fast machine-drum kicks. Performance contexts: street-corner sound-system parties, weddings, and post-2017 international festival circuit through Nyege Nyege Tapes Kampala. MC calls out hyper-fast Swahili-Bongo-slang lyrical phrases.

items.name: Kapuka (Kenyan urban pop)
items.lineage: Kapuka Kenyan urban-pop genre emerging in early-2000s Nairobi from the Ogopa DJs and Calif Records production camps. Characterized by mid-tempo beat with Swahili-Sheng (Nairobi street-slang) and English lyrical content over R&B-influenced synthesizer-and-drum-machine production. Distinguished from parallel genge by kapuka's slower-tempo R&B-leaning (vs genge's faster-hardcore-hip-hop-leaning) aesthetic targeting middle-class urban-Nairobi commercial-radio. Producer Lucas Bikedo at Ogopa DJs formed the production-hub anchor.

items.name: Kabyle music (Algerian Berber)
items.lineage: Kabyle music of the Tamazight-speaking Berber population of the Kabylie mountains of northern Algeria. Performance integrates classical Kabyle-language poetic-meter (the asefru four-line verse-form developed by seventeenth-century poet Si Mohand) with Berber pentatonic-leaning modal vocabulary distinct from Andalusi-Arab. The mid-twentieth-century Paris-emigration produced an exile-and-protest corpus through Slimane Azem; 1970s-1980s cultural-revival under Idir and Lounès Matoub. The 1998 Matoub assassination politicized the genre. Instrumentation: oud, mandole (Algerian electric-mandolin), bendir frame-drum.

items.name: Algerian chaabi (Algiers urban folk)
items.lineage: Algerian chaabi ("popular") urban-folk tradition of Algiers and broader Algerian coastal region, emerging in 1920s-1930s Algiers Casbah as working-class popular reinterpretation of older malhun classical-Arabic poetic tradition, with simplified modal structures and accessible Algerian-Arabic dialect lyrics. Founding figure El Hadj M'Hamed El Anka codified the genre, establishing instrumentation of oud, mandole, banjo (introduced through American jazz exposure), darbuka, and tar frame-drum. Repertoire spans poetic-philosophical reflection (qsida), urban-life observation, and post-1962 independence cultural-pride themes.

items.name: Tunisian malouf (Andalusi classical)
items.lineage: Tunisian malouf classical Andalusi-Arabic art-music tradition, the Tunisian recension of the broader Maghrebi-Andalusi nuba descended from medieval al-Andalus through the post-1492 expulsion-diaspora settlement (with Testour as a principal Andalusi-refugee settlement). The Tunisian repertoire comprises thirteen canonical nubat. The early-twentieth-century Rachidia Institute (Tunis, 1934) consolidated the canon. Performance integrates male choir-and-soloist with oud, rebab, qanun, nay, and darbuka. Distinguished from Moroccan al-Āla by Tunisian-specific suite-cycle and Rachidia-Institute-canonized repertoire.
items.description: Tunisian malouf classical Andalusi-Arabic art-music tradition, the Tunisian recension of the broader Maghrebi-Andalusi nuba descended from medieval al-Andalus through the post-1492 expulsion-diaspora settlement (with Testour as a principal Andalusi-refugee settlement). The Tunisian repertoire comprises thirteen canonical nubat. The early-twentieth-century Rachidia Institute (Tunis, 1934) consolidated the canon. items.name: Libyan maluf (Andalusi classical)
items.lineage: Libyan maluf classical Andalusi-Arabic art-music tradition of Tripoli and Benghazi, the Libyan recension of broader Maghrebi-Andalusi nuba descended from the post-1492 al-Andalus expulsion-diaspora. The Libyan repertoire is the smallest of the Maghrebi recensions, comprising suite-cycles shared with Tunisian malouf with Libyan-Arabic poetic-meter and dialect cadential conventions. The post-2011 civil-conflict period disrupted institutional transmission; diaspora-recovery at Royal Conservatory of Music Tripoli is the contemporary anchor.

items.name: Saidi music (Upper Egyptian)
items.lineage: Saidi music of Upper Egypt (south of Cairo extending to Aswan), the canonical pre-modern rural musical tradition of the Egyptian Nile Valley peasant Saidi communities. Performance centers on the mizmar pair (loud double-reed conical-bore aerophone played in heterophonic-melodic-elaboration) over tabla baladi or tabla dohola two-headed barrel-drum. Repertoire spans wedding-celebration cycles, mawwal vocal-lament solo declamations (free-rhythm extended-melismatic-ornament register), and tahtib stick-dance accompaniment cycles for which Saidi music is particularly known.

items.name: Sufi inshad (Egyptian devotional song)
items.lineage: Egyptian Sufi inshad devotional vocal tradition, comprising the canonical liturgical-and-devotional song repertoire of the Egyptian Sufi orders (Shadhili, Qadiri, Rifa'i, Burhani). Performance contexts include the mawlid annual saint-celebrations (especially at Sayyida Zaynab and Hussein in Cairo, and Tanta and Desouk), the dhikr collective remembrance-of-God sessions, and the nightly hadra circle-gatherings. The munshid Sufi-singer-specialist trains in classical Arabic poetic meter, Egyptian maqam modal system, and the canonical mystical-poetic corpus of Ibn al-Farid and al-Busiri.

items.name: Khaliji (Arabian Gulf music)
items.lineage: Khaliji ("Gulf") urban popular music of the Arabian Peninsula Gulf states — Kuwait, Bahrain, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, UAE, Oman — characterized by mid-tempo 2/4 or 4/4 metric base with syncopated 2-and-4 backbeat and distinctive Khaliji-modal vocabulary between maqam-Arabic and Persian-dastgah. The genre developed from the older sawt classical urban-chamber Bahraini-and-Kuwaiti tradition into contemporary Khaliji-pop through the post-1970s petroleum-era recording industry centered in Bahrain, Kuwait, and Riyadh.

items.name: Sawt (Bahraini-Kuwaiti chamber song)
items.lineage: Sawt classical Arabian-Gulf urban-chamber song tradition of Bahrain and Kuwait, developed in eighteenth-nineteenth centuries through cultural and trade connections between Gulf merchant-class urban centers and Yemen (with Yemeni-Sanaani musical influence) and East Africa (Zanzibari merchant-class exchange). Performance configuration: male solo singer accompanying himself on oud, with mirwas small drum and hand-clapping from a small audience. Repertoire organizes around sawt arabi (longer, complex modal cycle) and sawt shami (shorter, lighter modal cycle).

items.name: Bahraini fjiri (pearl-divers' song)
items.lineage: Bahraini fjiri pearl-divers' work-song tradition, performed by the all-male crews of dhow boats conducting the annual ghaws pearl-diving season in the Persian Gulf during the pre-petroleum era (eighteenth-mid-twentieth centuries). Repertoire structured around the diving voyage cycle: departure songs, anchor-hauling songs, noon-prayer-pause songs, diver-hauling songs, homeward-return songs. Architecture features male lead singer (nahham) with chorus response, hand-clapping, tar frame-drum, and jahla clay-jar percussion. The 1930s-1950s closure of natural-pearl industry terminated functional context.

items.name: Kurdish dengbêj (bardic singer-tradition)
items.lineage: Kurdish dengbêj ("voice-bearer") solo male-bardic vocal tradition of southeastern Turkey, northern Iraq, northwestern Iran, and northeastern Syria. The dengbêj sings unaccompanied narrative-epic, lament (heyranok), and historical-political commentary songs in Kurdish (Kurmanji, Sorani, or Zaza), in free-rhythm extended-melisma style with wide melodic range. The post-1923 Turkish-Republican suppression nearly extinguished public-performance space; post-1991 partial liberalization and dedicated dengbêj coffee-houses in Diyarbakır restored continuity. Canonical repertoire centers on Mem û Zîn (Ehmedê Xanî, seventeenth century).

items.name: Syriac Orthodox liturgical chant
items.lineage: Syriac Orthodox liturgical chant, the canonical sacred-music tradition of the Syriac Orthodox Church (Oriental Orthodox alongside Coptic, Armenian, Ethiopian). Follows the Beth Gazo ("Treasury") eight-mode oktoechos system with hundreds of canonical melodies. Performance: male choir of cantor-and-chorus chanting in Syriac (the ancient Aramaic liturgical language preserved unchanged from early-Christian period), with Maronite, Syrian Catholic, Assyrian Church of the East, and Indian Malankara Syrian Orthodox sharing overlapping recensions. The post-1915 Sayfo and late-twentieth-century Middle East displacement dispersed tradition across diaspora.

items.name: Maronite liturgical chant
items.lineage: Maronite Catholic liturgical chant of the Maronite Church (the largest Eastern Catholic Church, in full communion with Rome, centered in Lebanon). Lineage descends from the broader West-Syriac Antiochene rite. The Beth Gazo eight-mode oktoechos system is shared with Syriac Orthodox but with Maronite-Lebanese recension and Latin-rite influences from post-twelfth-century communion with Rome. The Quzhaya monastery in the Qadisha Valley (founded sixteenth century) and Patriarchal seat at Bkerké anchor institutional transmission. Liturgical language is Syriac for the Eucharistic anaphora and Arabic for most other content.

items.name: Assyrian Church of the East Beth Gazo chant
items.lineage: Assyrian Church of the East liturgical chant, the canonical sacred-music tradition of the East-Syriac (Edessene) rite, descending from the Mesopotamian early-Christian community at Edessa and Nisibis. The Assyrian Beth Gazo collection comprises canonical melodies organized through an eight-mode system distinct from but related to the West-Syriac (Antiochene) Beth Gazo. Liturgical language is classical Syriac (Eastern dialect). The post-1915 Sayfo and Iraqi-Syrian displacement disrupted Hakkari-Mesopotamian transmission infrastructure; the Patriarchate (currently seated in Erbil) and diaspora communities in Chicago, Detroit, and Sydney sustain practice.

items.name: Uyghur On Ikki Muqam (Twelve Muqams)
items.lineage: Uyghur On Ikki Muqam ("Twelve Muqams") classical Central Asian art-music tradition of the Uyghur Turkic-Muslim population of the Tarim Basin (Xinjiang). The twelve canonical muqamat — Rak, Chebbiyat, Mushavrek, Charigah, Pengigah, Ozhal, Echeh, Ushshaq, Bayat, Nava, Sigah, Iraq — each comprises three sections: chong naghma free-rhythm great-song suite; dastan metrically-bound narrative-song; faster mashrap social-dance section. Turdi Akhun in the 1950s codified recensions; the Xinjiang Muqam Ensemble anchors institutional transmission.

items.name: Kazakh küy (instrumental dombyra art)
items.lineage: Kazakh küy classical instrumental art-music tradition of Kazakhstan, performed on dombyra two-string long-necked fretted plucked lute as solo virtuoso narrative-programmatic compositions. Each küy narrates a historical-mythological story through purely instrumental means: the canonical "Aksak Kulan" tells of a son's death announced through dombyra after no one dared speak the news. Two regional schools: Western tökpe (more rhythmically vigorous) and Eastern shertpe (more lyrical-contemplative). Kurmangazy Sagyrbayuly (1818-1889) and Tattimbet Kazangapuly (1815-1862) are canonical composers.

items.name: Kazakh aitys (improvisational poetic contest)
items.lineage: Kazakh aitys improvisational poetic-contest tradition: a competitive verbal-dueling form in which two akyn improvising poet-singers face off in extempore Kazakh-language verse exchange, each responding to the previous while introducing new poetic-philosophical material, accompanied by akyn's own dombyra. Performance traditionally at weddings, autumn-harvest celebrations, and festival days, with audience reaction signaling who is winning. Survived Soviet period as sanctioned-folk practice and entered post-1991 cultural revival as national-cultural symbol. Annual televised aitys competitions broadcast since the 1990s.

items.name: Rabindra sangeet (Tagore songs)
items.lineage: Rabindra sangeet ("Tagore songs") Bengali art-song repertoire composed by Nobel-laureate poet-philosopher Rabindranath Tagore (1861-1941), comprising approximately 2,232 documented songs in the canonical Gitabitan collection across categories: puja, prem, prakriti, swadesh, bichitra. The compositional language synthesizes Hindustani-classical raga-and-tala framework with Bengali kirtan-and-baul folk inflections, Carnatic melodic gestures, and late-period Western-tonal-harmonic elements absorbed through Tagore's European travels. The Visva-Bharati transmission lineage maintains canonical melodic-and-textual readings.

items.name: Nazrul geeti (Nazrul songs, Bengali)
items.lineage: Nazrul geeti Bengali art-song repertoire composed by Kazi Nazrul Islam (1899-1976, Bidrohi Kobi "Rebel Poet" and national poet of Bangladesh), comprising approximately three thousand documented songs: Islamic-devotional (Hamd-and-Naat in Bengali), Hindu-devotional Shyamasangeet (Bengali Kali songs), love and longing, revolutionary-political (anti-British-colonial Karar Oi Louho Kapat), and ghazal. Compositional language draws on Hindustani-classical raga vocabulary with strong influences from Persian-Urdu ghazal melodic-line aesthetic and Bengali folk-kirtan rhythmic conventions. The post-1976 Bangladeshi Nazrul Institute consolidated canonical standards.

items.name: Lavani (Marathi women's song-dance)
items.lineage: Lavani Marathi women's song-and-dance tradition of Maharashtra, characterized by powerful and often erotically suggestive female lead-singer-dancer performance accompanied by dholak two-headed barrel drum and tabla. Two main streams: nirguni lavani (philosophical-devotional) and shringari lavani (romantic-erotic, more popularly known). Performance traditionally occurs in folk-theatre tamasha contexts in nineteenth-and-twentieth-century rural Maharashtra, with the kalavantin dancer-singer holding a respected (if socially marginalized) professional role. Mid-twentieth-century Marathi-cinema adopted lavani as iconic regional cultural-form.

items.name: Powada (Marathi heroic-ballad)
items.lineage: Powada Marathi heroic-ballad tradition of Maharashtra, celebrating military and historical-political figures through declamatory narrative-and-call-and-response song. The canonical core centers on the seventeenth-century Maratha-Empire founder Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj — the powada of Tanaji Malusare's heroic death at the 1670 Battle of Sinhagad is most internationally circulated. Performance: male lead-singer-narrator (shahir) with chorus and dholak percussion, vigorous declamatory delivery, and audience call-and-response. The shahir is historically a respected community-poet-historian; nineteenth-century social-reformer Jyotirao Phule used powada for political consciousness-raising.

items.name: Borgeet (Assamese Neo-Vaishnavite devotional)
items.lineage: Borgeet ("noble songs") Assamese Neo-Vaishnavite devotional vocal tradition composed in the fifteenth-sixteenth centuries by Srimanta Sankardev (1449-1568) and his disciple Madhavdev (1489-1596), the founders of the Ekasarana Dharma neo-Vaishnavite reform movement in Assam. The canonical corpus comprises approximately 250 songs in the Brajavali language (a literary-religious mix of Brajabhasha and Assamese). Performance configuration: solo voice with khol two-headed barrel-drum and taal small cymbals, in slow-tempo melismatic-melodic style. The naamghar (Sankardev-tradition village-temple) and sattra (monastic institution) circuits maintain transmission infrastructure.

items.name: Divya Prabandham (Tamil Vaishnavite hymns)
items.lineage: Nalayira Divya Prabandham ("Four Thousand Divine Hymns") canonical Tamil Vaishnavite devotional poetry collection compiled in the eleventh century by Nathamuni from the earlier seventh-tenth century compositions of the twelve Alvar poet-saints. Performance: solo or small-group chanting in classical Tamil at Vaishnavite temple liturgical occasions (especially in the 108 Divya Desam temples), with strict cantillation traditions transmitted through hereditary Bhattar priest lineages and the Madhura Kavi Alvar disciples. The Srivaishnavite community considers these hymns equal to the Sanskrit Vedas as sacred scripture. Performance follows specific raga-mode assignments preserved through unbroken oral transmission.

items.name: Thiruvaachakam (Tamil Shaivite hymns)
items.lineage: Thiruvaachakam ("Sacred Utterance") canonical Tamil Shaivite devotional poetry composed in the ninth century by Manikkavachakar, comprising 51 hymns expressing intense personal-devotional anguish and longing for Shiva. The collection forms part of the Tirumurai canonical Tamil Shaivite scriptural corpus and is integral to liturgy at the Chidambaram Nataraja Temple and the broader Tamil Shaivite temple circuit. Performance follows strict Tamil cantillation tradition transmitted through hereditary Othuvar singer lineages. The popular saying "Thiruvaachakathukku urugaar oru vaachakathukkum urugaar" ("those unmoved by Thiruvaachakam are unmoved by anything") captures the corpus's emotional power.

items.name: Telugu kirtana (Carnatic devotional song)
items.lineage: Telugu kirtana devotional-song genre within the broader Carnatic classical tradition of South India, with Telugu serving as the dominant lyrical language of the Carnatic kriti repertoire. The Telugu-language compositions of the Carnatic Trinity Tyagaraja (1767-1847), Muthuswami Dikshitar (1775-1835), and Syama Sastri (1762-1827) form the canonical core of the entire Carnatic concert repertoire. Performance follows the standard Carnatic kriti structure (pallavi-anupallavi-charanam) with raga-and-tala framework. The Tyagaraja Aradhana annual festival at Tiruvaiyaru constitutes the central institutional anchor of the kriti performance tradition.

items.name: Sinhala vannama (Sri Lankan court dance-song)
items.lineage: Sinhala vannama Sri Lankan classical court dance-song tradition, comprising eighteen canonical pieces composed in the seventeenth-eighteenth centuries at the Kandyan royal court for performance at state ceremonies. Each of the eighteen vannamas evokes a specific subject (gaja-vannama elephant, ashva-vannama horse, mayura-vannama peacock, sinha-vannama lion, etc.) through characteristic melodic-and-rhythmic gesture and stylized choreographic movement. Performance combines solo male voice with geta-bera double-headed barrel drum and elaborate choreography. The Sri Lankan Cultural Department and Royal Asiatic Society preserve the canonical transmission.

items.name: Nepali lok (folk-popular song)
items.lineage: Nepali lok geet ("folk songs") encompass the broad popular-and-traditional song repertoire of Nepal, including regional variants from the Newari, Tharu, Gurung, Magar, Tamang, Rai, Limbu, and other ethnic communities, plus the urban Kathmandu Valley pan-Nepali pop synthesis. The genre developed through the twentieth-century Radio Nepal (founded 1951) commercial-recording era. Standard instrumentation centers on madal two-headed barrel-drum, tabla, sarangi (Nepali, four-string short-neck bowed lute distinct from Hindustani sarangi), and bansuri flute. Repertoire spans selo (Tamang call-and-response), tappa (regional ballad), and roila (Karnali region).

The genre developed through the twentieth-century Radio Nepal (founded 1951) commercial-recording era. Standard instrumentation centers on madal two-headed barrel-drum, tabla, sarangi (Nepali, four-string short-neck bowed lute distinct from Hindustani sarangi), and bansuri flute. Repertoire spans selo (Tamang call-and-response), tappa (regional ballad), and roila (Karnali region).

items.name: Huangmei opera (Anhui regional opera)
items.lineage: Huangmei opera (Huangmei xi) Chinese regional opera tradition originating in the late nineteenth century in the Huangmei county of Hubei province and developing through the early-twentieth century in Anhui province (especially Anqing region) into one of the five major Chinese opera traditions. Distinguished from the elite kunqu and jingju by accessible vernacular Anhui-and-Hubei dialect language, simple rural-folk melodic vocabulary (developed from tea-picking and rice-planting work songs), and more naturalistic theatrical-realism in staging. The Tianxianpei ("Heavenly Match") play is the canonical type-specimen. The post-1949 Anhui Provincial Huangmei Opera Theatre consolidated the modern repertoire.

items.name: Sichuan opera (chuanju)
items.lineage: Sichuan opera (chuanju) Chinese regional opera tradition of the Sichuan basin (Chengdu, Chongqing, and broader province), synthesizing five distinct musical styles: gaoqiang (high-pitched), kunqiang (kunqu-derived), huqin (string-led), tanxi (clapper-style), and dengdiao (Sichuan-folk-derived) into a single eclectic theatrical tradition. The chuanju is particularly known for the "face-changing" (bian lian) stagecraft technique where the performer switches painted masks in fractions of a second through hidden mechanisms. Performance integrates voice, stylized dance-movement, recited dialogue, percussion-led ensemble, and elaborate face-painting and costume conventions.

items.name: Yueju (Shaoxing / Shanghai opera)
items.lineage: Yueju Shaoxing opera, a Chinese regional opera tradition originating in the rural Sheng County of Zhejiang province at the turn of the twentieth century and crystallizing in 1920s-1930s Shanghai as an all-female-cast operatic form (yueju is one of only a handful of Chinese operas traditionally performed exclusively by female actors playing both male and female roles). Distinguished from kunqu and jingju by its lyrical, romance-focused dramaturgical orientation, accessible Wu-dialect Shaoxing-area linguistic register, and the all-female casting convention. The 1953 film adaptation of the canonical Liang Shanbo and Zhu Yingtai butterfly-lovers legend (with Yuan Xuefen and Fan Ruijuan in the principal roles) consolidated the national audience.

items.name: Pingju (Northern Chinese opera)
items.lineage: Pingju Northern Chinese regional opera tradition emerging in late-nineteenth-century Hebei province from the lianhualao folk-song-and-storytelling form. Distinguished from jingju by accessible vernacular Mandarin language, naturalistic realistic staging, and contemporary-life dramaturgical content (vs jingju's classical historical-and-mythological repertoire). The genre became a major popular-theatrical form in northern China through the early-twentieth-century commercial-theatre period. The post-1949 Beijing Pingju Theatre and Hebei Provincial Pingju Theatre consolidated the modern repertoire. Canonical play Yang Sanjie Gao Zhuang (The Story of Yang Sanjie) constitutes the type-specimen.

items.name: Qinqiang (Shaanxi opera, "the ancestor of bangzi")
items.lineage: Qinqiang Northwest Chinese regional opera tradition of Shaanxi province, considered the ancestor of the broader bangzi (wooden-clapper) opera family that includes jin opera (Shanxi), yu opera (Henan), and Hebei bangzi. Origin traced to the Qin and Han dynasty court music of the Wei River basin. Performance features powerful declamatory vocal projection (characteristically loud and emotionally intense, reflecting the Loess Plateau aesthetic), the bangzi wooden-clapper as principal percussion-pulse keeper, and pi-pa accompanied martial-arts and historical-warrior repertoire. The post-1949 Shaanxi Provincial Qinqiang Theatre and the Yi Su She troupe (founded 1912 in Xi'an) anchor institutional transmission.

items.name: Yu opera (Henan bangzi)
items.lineage: Yu opera Henan provincial Chinese opera tradition, the largest of the bangzi (wooden-clapper) opera family by audience and the second-largest Chinese opera tradition after jingju by aggregate national reach. Origin in seventeenth-eighteenth century Henan from earlier folk-music synthesis with qinqiang influences. Distinguished from neighboring qinqiang by softer, more lyrical vocal register and accessible Henan-dialect Mandarin language. Canonical play Hua Mulan (the female-warrior legend) constitutes the type-specimen of yu opera's strong female-protagonist tradition. The post-1949 Henan Yu Opera Theatre under Chang Xiangyu consolidated the modern repertoire.

items.name: Japanese min'yō (regional folk-song)
items.lineage: Japanese min'yō ("folk song of the people") encompasses the regional-traditional song repertoire of Japan, with distinct regional canons across Tohoku (northern Honshu, distinctive for vigorous work-song and sake-brewing-song lineages), Kyushu (with the Itsuki Lullaby and broader Kyushu-folk repertoire), Okinawa (separate from mainland Japanese min'yō with sanshin-and-ryuka-poetic-meter tradition), and Hokkaido (Soran Bushi the canonical Hokkaido min'yō, originally an Okhotsk Sea herring-fishing work-song). Performance configuration: solo voice with shamisen, shakuhachi flute, and taiko drum accompaniment. The post-1920s commercial-recording period at Nippon Columbia and Polydor Japan documented canonical regional repertoires.

items.name: Noh utai (Noh theatre chant)
items.lineage: Japanese Noh utai sung-and-chanted vocal tradition of the canonical Noh theatre form, codified in the fourteenth-fifteenth centuries by Zeami Motokiyo (1363-1443). Performance integrates the male shite-actor's utai chant (the central narrative-and-character voice) with the jiutai chorus (typically eight male singers seated stage-right), supported by the hayashi instrumental ensemble (nohkan flute, ko-tsuzumi shoulder-drum, o-tsuzumi hip-drum, taiko stick-drum). Vocal architecture features extremely slow tempi, characteristic narrow-range melodic vocabulary in the yowagin "weak-style" and tsuyogin "strong-style" registers, with strictly codified breath-pause and vibrato conventions.

items.name: Nagauta (Kabuki long-song)
items.lineage: Japanese nagauta ("long song") sung-and-shamisen narrative tradition serving as the principal musical accompaniment for Kabuki theatre dance-and-action sequences. Codified in mid-Edo period eighteenth century, with the canonical compositional lineages tracing to Kineya Kangoro and Kineya Saburousuke. Performance configuration: a row of male singers seated upstage on a raised platform (typically four-to-eight singers), with a parallel row of shamisen players, plus hayashi percussion ensemble (drums, flutes) on stage-right. Repertoire spans dance-piece accompaniment, dramatic-scene underscore, and standalone concert pieces (the gozen-engaku "music for the lord" reception genre). Kineya guild lineages maintain hereditary transmission.

items.name: Okinawan sanshin-and-eisa music
items.lineage: Okinawan sanshin-and-eisa music of the Ryukyu archipelago (southwestern Japan), historically and culturally distinct from mainland Japanese music. The sanshin (Okinawan three-string snake-skin-bellied long-neck plucked lute, the direct ancestor of the mainland shamisen) anchors the melodic content of solo-and-ensemble Okinawan classical (kunkunshi-notated court music), folk min'yō, and the contemporary popular Okinawan-pop forms. Eisa is the Okinawan summer Bon-festival ancestor-honoring dance-drum-and-chant tradition, with paranku frame-drum and odaiko large drum ensembles processing through Okinawan villages during the lunar-Bon mid-August period.

items.name: Korean sanjo (solo virtuoso instrumental)
items.lineage: Korean sanjo ("scattered melody") solo virtuoso instrumental tradition emerging in late-nineteenth-century southwestern Korea (Jeolla provinces) and crystallizing into the canonical concert form through Kim Chang-jo (1865-1919) for the gayageum zither and subsequent adaptations for geomungo, daegeum, ajaeng, and haegeum. Performance is a continuous suite of progressively accelerating sections (jinyangjo, jungmori, jungjungmori, jajinmori, hwimori, danmori), with janggu hourglass-drum accompaniment marking the rhythmic-cycle changgu. The sanjo grew from sinawi shaman-ensemble heterophony into a self-standing virtuoso art-music form parallel to but distinct from pansori vocal narrative.

items.name: Korean sinawi (shaman ensemble improvisation)
items.lineage: Korean sinawi shamanic-ensemble improvisational tradition of southwestern Korea (Jeolla provinces and adjacent Chungcheong region), serving as the ritual-music accompaniment for the gut Korean shaman ceremony. Performance integrates a mudang shaman-priestess with an instrumental ensemble of daegeum bamboo flute, piri double-reed pipe, haegeum two-string fiddle, ajaeng bowed zither, and janggu hourglass-drum percussion in collective improvisational heterophony over the canonical sinawi modal-and-rhythmic framework. Distinguished from sanjo by sinawi's collective-ensemble (vs solo virtuoso) configuration; distinguished from pansori by sinawi's instrumental-ensemble (vs solo vocal narrative) framework. Direct historical ancestor of sanjo solo art-music.
