items.name: Chongmyo jeryeak (royal ancestral shrine music)
items.lineage: Korean Chongmyo jeryeak (Royal Ancestral Shrine Music) Joseon-dynasty court ritual music for the spring-and-autumn ancestor-veneration ceremony at the Chongmyo Royal Shrine in Seoul. Composed in 1463 by King Sejo (reigned 1455-1468) from earlier Goryeo-and-Tang-derived material, the suite comprises two parts: Botaepyeong (eleven movements praising civil virtue, performed during the literary-rite portion of the ceremony) and Jeongdaeeop (eleven movements praising martial virtue, performed during the military-rite portion). Performance configuration: a large court ensemble of approximately fifty musicians plus sixty-four dancers performing the strict ilmu line-dance choreography.

items.name: Korean trot (twentieth-century popular ballad)
items.lineage: Korean trot (teuroteu) twentieth-century popular ballad genre emerging in 1920s-1930s colonial-period Korea from the synthesis of Japanese enka (then dominant on the colonial-Korean recording market) with native Korean folk vocal-inflection. Characterized by the canonical 2/4 "trot rhythm" (a swung syncopated pulse derived ultimately from foxtrot dance-band music), characteristic Korean vocal-vibrato called kkeokgi ("bending"), and emotionally direct sentimental-romantic-and-loss lyrical register. The genre survived multiple cycles of cultural-policy suppression (especially the 1965 anti-Japanese-influence purge) and remains a major mainstream Korean popular-music form today. The 2010s trot-revival under Korean cable-television trot-contests reinvigorated the genre with young audiences.

items.name: Vietnamese cải lương (renovated opera)
items.lineage: Vietnamese cải lương ("renovated theatre") southern-Vietnamese popular-and-classical theatrical tradition emerging in 1917 in Mekong Delta region as a modernization of the older hát bội classical-court-opera tradition, incorporating Western-style spoken dialogue and naturalistic staging while retaining the đờn ca tài tử southern-amateur-music instrumental tradition as musical foundation. The genre flourished through the colonial-period Mekong Delta and post-1945 Saigon as the dominant southern Vietnamese popular-theatre form. Performance integrates đàn tranh sixteen-string zither, đàn bầu one-string monochord, đàn nguyệt moon-lute, and đàn tỳ bà pear-lute with stylized melodic-recitative vocal-narrative content.

items.name: Vietnamese đờn ca tài tử (southern amateur music)
items.lineage: Vietnamese đờn ca tài tử ("music of talented amateurs") southern-Vietnamese chamber-music tradition emerging in late-nineteenth-century Mekong Delta from the synthesis of the older nhã nhạc court-music tradition with southern-Vietnamese folk-music. Performance configuration: small intimate amateur-ensemble of literate-class male and female musicians playing đàn tranh sixteen-string zither, đàn bầu one-string monochord, đàn nguyệt moon-lute, đàn tỳ bà pear-lute, đàn cò two-string fiddle, plus singer. Repertoire organized around the twenty bản tổ canonical melodic patterns. The form is the direct musical ancestor of cải lương southern-popular theatre.

items.name: Vietnamese hát chèo (northern folk opera)
items.lineage: Vietnamese hát chèo northern-Vietnamese folk-opera tradition of the Red River Delta region (Hà Nam, Nam Định, Thái Bình, Hải Dương, and Hưng Yên provinces). Origin traced to tenth-eleventh century rural-Vietnamese village-temple ceremonial performance, with the canonical literary repertoire codified in seventeenth-nineteenth centuries. Distinguished from cải lương by northern-Vietnamese (vs southern-Vietnamese) regional identity and rural-village (vs urban-commercial) traditional functional context. Performance integrates dramatic recitation, melodic-song, dance, mime, and small-ensemble accompaniment. The Vietnam National Chèo Theatre in Hanoi anchors institutional preservation; rural village-ensemble transmission continues in original Red River Delta communities.

items.name: Lao lam saravane (southern-Lao folk genre)
items.lineage: Lao lam saravane: Southern-Lao (Champasak-region) variant of the broader Lao lam (sung-and-spoken folk-narrative-and-courtship) tradition that includes the Thai cognate mor lam. Lam saravane is the lighter, more melodic-and-flirtatious variant compared to the heavier philosophical-and-narrative lam siphandone of the southernmost Lao region. Performance: lead singer (mor lam) with khaen bamboo-pipe-mouth-organ accompaniment, in extempore versified Lao-language verse-exchange with characteristic pentatonic-modal vocabulary and the rhythmic-pulsed khaen drone. The mid-twentieth-century Vientiane and Bangkok commercial-recording era spread the saravane variant nationally.

items.name: Thai lûk thûng ("child of the field," country song)
items.lineage: Thai lûk thûng ("child of the field") country-song genre emerging in mid-twentieth-century Thailand from the synthesis of Central Thai folk-music with Latin (Cuban, Mexican) rhythmic-influences imported through 1950s-1960s American military presence and Western commercial pop. Characterized by strong vibrato-laden vocal projection, slow-to-mid-tempo orchestral-with-electric-instruments arrangement, and rural-life-and-romantic-loss lyrical content addressing the experience of the rural-Thai migrant worker class. Suraphol Sombatcharoen (1930-1968) is considered the foundational artist; Pumpuang Duangjan (1961-1992) consolidated the modern form. Distinguished from Thai mor lam by lûk thûng's Central Thai (vs Isan northeastern) regional base.

items.name: Thai lûk krung ("child of the city," urban song)
items.lineage: Thai lûk krung ("child of the city") urban-popular song genre emerging in 1930s-1940s Bangkok from the synthesis of Thai melodic-and-poetic-vocabulary with Western-jazz harmonic-instrumentation framework. Performance: solo voice with Western jazz-orchestra accompaniment (piano, double-bass, drum-kit, brass section), in smooth, romantic register addressing urban Bangkok middle-class concerns. Sunthraporn ensemble (founded 1939 by Eua Sunthornsanan) consolidated the canonical sound; the parallel post-war Suchin Phaisarnyaphirom and Charin Nantanakorn lineages extended the repertoire. Distinguished from lûk thûng by lûk krung's urban-Bangkok (vs rural-migrant) cultural orientation and Western-jazz-harmonic (vs Thai-folk-pentatonic) musical framework.

items.name: Indonesian keroncong (Lusophone-derived urban folk)
items.lineage: Indonesian keroncong urban-folk genre emerging in sixteenth-seventeenth century Portuguese-trading-post communities of Tugu (north Jakarta) and Maluku from the Portuguese moresco and fado-precursor folk-music brought by Portuguese and Indo-Portuguese settlers, then absorbed into the Malay-Indonesian musical-cultural sphere over four centuries. Performance configuration centers on the cuk (small ukulele-like four-string lute) and cak (smaller four-string), plus violin, flute, cello (played pizzicato), and acoustic guitar. Vocal style features mid-tempo wide-vibrato male-or-female lead with characteristic Indonesian-Malay melodic-line aesthetic over Western-tonal-harmonic framework. The mid-twentieth-century Lokananta Records era anchored commercial-recording preservation.

items.name: Indonesian dangdut (classical era)
items.lineage: Indonesian dangdut classical-era popular-music genre emerging in late-1960s-early-1970s Jakarta from the synthesis of Indian-filmi melodic-vocal aesthetic (transmitted through Indonesian audiences' exposure to Bollywood cinema), Malay folk-ballad melodic-vocabulary, and Arabian peninsular orkes melayu instrumental conventions. The name derives from the canonical onomatopoeic "dang...dut" rhythmic-figure played on the tabla-derived gendang drum. Rhoma Irama (born 1946) is the canonical king-of-dangdut figure whose 1970s-1980s recordings consolidated the genre; Elvy Sukaesih (born 1951) is the queen-of-dangdut counterpart. Distinguished from broader Malay orkes melayu by dangdut's Indian-filmi-influenced vocal-ornament style.

items.name: Indonesian jaipongan (Sundanese popular)
items.lineage: Indonesian jaipongan Sundanese popular-music genre developed in 1974 by Gugum Gumbira in Bandung (West Java) as a modernization of the older ketuk tilu Sundanese folk-dance-music. The form incorporates the traditional kendang Sundanese drum-set, gamelan degung metallophone framework, and Sundanese-language vocal repertoire, but with substantially energized faster-tempo rhythmic pulse and assertive female-singer-dancer presentation. The genre became culturally significant during the late-1970s Indonesian-cultural-nationalism period as an alternative to Western-influenced popular music. Distinguished from broader Sundanese gamelan by jaipongan's mid-1970s commercial-popular crystallization and the assertive vocal-and-dance performance register.

items.name: Balinese kecak (monkey chant)
items.lineage: Balinese kecak Indonesian collective-male-chorus a-cappella ritual-and-tourist-performance tradition of the village of Bona (south-central Bali) and surrounding villages, developed in the 1930s by Walter Spies and Wayan Limbak in collaboration with local Balinese performers, drawing on the older sanghyang trance-ceremony chorus tradition. Performance configuration: a circle of 50-150 male performers seated cross-legged, chanting interlocking "chak-chak-chak" rhythmic patterns in characteristic seven-or-more-part hocketed polyrhythm, while a single performer in the center enacts scenes from the Ramayana narrative. The form is one of the most internationally recognized Balinese performance traditions through twentieth-century tourist circuit.

items.name: Balinese gamelan gong kebyar (twentieth-century virtuosic gamelan)
items.lineage: Balinese gamelan gong kebyar Indonesian virtuosic gamelan ensemble form crystallizing in early-twentieth-century north Bali (Buleleng region) from the older gamelan gong gede court-ensemble form. The kebyar style is characterized by sudden dynamic-and-tempo contrasts (the term "kebyar" means "burst of flame"), virtuoso metallophone-player technique, and a more compressed performance duration suited to the post-colonial Balinese village-and-tourist performance economy. Performance configuration: ensemble of approximately 25-30 musicians playing tuned bronze metallophones (gangsa, ugal, jegogan, calung), gong chimes (reyong, trompong), kendang drums, and gong-cymbals. The annual Bali Arts Festival in Denpasar features kebyar competitions across all Bali regencies.

items.name: Filipino kundiman (romantic art-song)
items.lineage: Filipino kundiman romantic art-song genre emerging in the nineteenth century from the Tagalog-Visayan folk-courtship-song tradition, codified into formal art-song repertoire by Spanish-period and early-American-period composers. Characterized by the canonical kundiman structure: opening minor-key verse followed by major-key chorus, in slow 3/4 meter with characteristic rubato. Lyrical content addresses love, loss, devotion, and (in the Philippine Revolution period) covert nationalist-political symbolism (the beloved as metaphor for the Philippine homeland). Francisco Santiago, Nicanor Abelardo, and Antonio Molina constitute the early-twentieth-century compositional canon; Atang de la Rama and Sylvia La Torre are the canonical mid-twentieth-century interpreters.

items.name: Filipino harana (serenade)
items.lineage: Filipino harana ("serenade") nineteenth-and-twentieth-century romantic-courtship vocal tradition of the Tagalog and broader lowland-Christian Philippine communities, in which young men serenaded young women at their windows accompanied by acoustic guitar. The form derives from Spanish-colonial seventeenth-eighteenth century romance song-tradition adapted with Tagalog-Visayan language and Philippine-tropical sensibility. Performance: small-group of male singers (often with the principal suitor) with acoustic-guitar accompaniment, performing standard repertoire of harana-classics or improvising. The form survived as a vestigial-cultural practice through the twentieth century and entered post-2000s urban-revival contexts through documentary projects and folk-music ensembles.

items.name: Burmese mahagita (classical canon)
items.lineage: Burmese mahagita ("great song") classical Burmese art-music canon, comprising the codified repertoire of the late-Konbaung-dynasty (eighteenth-nineteenth century) royal court at Mandalay. The mahagita corpus is organized through several song-categories (kyò devotional-style, bwèh ceremonial-style, thachingan classical-song-form, etc.) with distinct modal-and-rhythmic conventions per category. Performance configuration ranges from solo voice with saung gauk arched-harp accompaniment (the most refined chamber form) to fuller ensembles with pat-tala xylophone, hsaing-waing drum-circle, and additional wind-instruments. The post-1885 British annexation of Burma terminated the royal-court patronage; the post-1962 Burma Socialist Programme cultural-policy and the State School of Music and Drama anchor modern transmission.

items.name: Burmese hsaing waing (drum-circle ensemble)
items.lineage: Burmese hsaing waing percussion-led ensemble tradition, the canonical Burmese folk-and-ceremonial instrumental form. The ensemble centers on the pat waing tuned-drum-circle (twenty-one tuned drums arranged in a horseshoe around the seated lead player) plus kyi waing tuned-gong-circle, hne double-reed shawm, chauk lon bat double-headed drum-pair, si small cymbals, and wa wooden-clappers. The pat waing drum-circle player is the de-facto ensemble leader, with the player simultaneously delivering melodic, rhythmic, and ensemble-cueing functions. Performance contexts span weddings, religious-festival celebrations, theatrical accompaniment (zat pwe), and the classical mahagita repertoire performance. Distinguished from neighboring Thai pi phat and Khmer pinpeat ensembles by Burmese hsaing waing's tuned-drum-circle (vs gong-circle-led) instrumental hierarchy.

items.name: Singaporean xinyao (Mandarin youth folk)
items.lineage: Singaporean xinyao ("Singapore songs") Mandarin-language singer-songwriter youth-folk movement emerging in early-1980s Singapore among ethnic-Chinese tertiary-education students at the National University of Singapore, Nanyang Technological Institute, and the major junior colleges. The form developed as a youth-cultural alternative to Cantopop and Mandopop commercial-pop dominance, with simple acoustic-guitar-accompanied original Mandarin-language compositions addressing youth concerns, campus life, and Singaporean identity. The Liang Wern Fook ensemble and Singapore Youth Festival 1983-1985 xinyao competitions consolidated institutional visibility. Distinguished from Taiwan campus-folk min-ge yundong (1970s) by Singaporean specific cultural-context and Singlish-inflected Mandarin register.

items.name: Acehnese saman
items.lineage: Acehnese saman seated-rhythmic-dance-and-song tradition of the Gayo people of central Aceh province, northern Sumatra, Indonesia. Performance configuration: a tightly packed row of 10-20 male dancers seated cross-legged on the floor, performing extremely fast and precise synchronized hand-clapping, chest-slapping, thigh-slapping, and arm-movement choreography while singing Islamic-devotional verse in the Gayo language. The form emerged in the thirteenth-fourteenth century with Islamic missionary activity in Aceh; the canonical genre features rapid acceleration through the performance and characteristic call-and-response between the leader-syech and the body of dancers.

items.name: Samoan siva and fagufagu (Polynesian dance-song)
items.lineage: Samoan siva (formal dance) and fagufagu (drum-led collective dance) Polynesian-cultural-performance traditions of the Samoan archipelago (Independent State of Samoa and American Samoa). The siva manaia is the standard performance featuring a single dancer (often the daughter of the host family in a fa'alavelave ceremonial gathering) accompanied by sung verses and slit-drum (pate) and rolled-mat (papa) percussion. The taualuga formal high-chief's-dance is the culminating ceremonial-form. Vocal repertoire features distinct fa'aluga (verse) and fa'amalama (refrain) structural sections. The post-twentieth-century Pacific-festival circuit and Polynesian Cultural Center anchor international circulation.

items.name: Fijian meke (chant-and-dance)
items.lineage: Fijian meke collective chant-and-dance tradition of the Fijian iTaukei (indigenous Fijian) population. The meke comprises several sub-forms: meke wesi (spear-dance, male-warriors), meke iri (fan-dance, women), meke ni vakatara (sitting-dance), and seasea (women's standing-dance), each with distinct choreographic vocabulary and song-accompaniment. Performance involves a vakatara dance-troupe with parallel singing chorus and slit-drum-and-bamboo-stamping-tube percussion. The canonical post-independence Fiji-1970 cultural-revival under the Fiji Museum and the Pacific Theatre formed institutional preservation infrastructure. Distinguished from neighboring Tongan lakalaka by Fijian meke's warrior-and-women parallel-track choreographic structure and Fijian-language repertoire.

items.name: Tahitian himene rū'au (chant of the elders)
items.lineage: Tahitian himene rū'au ("chant of the elders") slow-tempo unaccompanied chant tradition of the Society Islands (French Polynesia), distinct from the better-known himene tarava festival-chorus form. Performance: elders sing slow-tempo Tahitian-language sacred-or-genealogical verse in unison or two-part configuration, with characteristic free-rhythm phrasing and chest-register projection. The form survived the post-1810 Christianization period as a sanctioned-folk-cultural practice and entered the twentieth-century Polynesian-cultural-revival as a marker of pre-contact tradition. The annual Heiva i Tahiti festival hosts himene competitions across multiple categories. Distinguished from himene tarava by himene rū'au's slow-tempo elder-led (vs festival-chorus mass-participation) functional context.

items.name: Aboriginal didgeridoo solo songlines (extended)
items.lineage: Aboriginal Australian songlines tradition embedding the didgeridoo (Yolngu yiḏaki) as both instrument and oral-historical-mnemonic system mapping landscape across Arnhem Land (Northern Territory) and the broader Top End. The yiḏaki is a hollowed eucalyptus-trunk natural-trumpet played with constant-airflow circular-breathing technique. Performance contexts span the manikay public ceremonial-song tradition (which is sung-vocal with clapsticks plus yiḏaki accompaniment) and the more specialized initiation-ceremony repertoire restricted to initiated men. Each manikay cycle maps a specific songline-route across the country, encoding geographic and ancestral knowledge. Distinguished from the broader generic didgeridoo-solo by manikay's ceremonial-functional context and Yolngu-specific yiḏaki performance lineage.

items.name: Papua New Guinean panpipe and polyphonic singing
items.lineage: Papua New Guinean polyphonic vocal-and-panpipe traditions across the New Guinea Highlands (Eastern Highlands, Western Highlands, Chimbu, Enga regions), with each linguistic-cultural group preserving distinct multi-part vocal-or-instrumental polyphonic conventions. The Huli yodel-and-cyclic-clap, the Hagen courtship-chants, the Enga sandalu and tee public-ceremony chants, and the Chimbu collective-flute ensembles each represent distinct contributions to the broader New Guinea polyphonic-music register. Performance contexts span bridewealth-negotiation ceremonies, mourning-rituals, harvest-festivals, and (post-1975 independence) the National Cultural Commission and University of Papua New Guinea ethnomusicology archive preservation work. Distinguished from neighboring Melanesian musical traditions by New Guinea Highlands-specific polyphonic-density and dialect-specific intonation vocabularies.

items.name: Solomon Islands panpipe ensemble
items.lineage: Solomon Islands panpipe ensemble tradition of the Are'are people of southern Malaita island and adjacent Solomons communities, featuring large coordinated ensembles of stopped-bamboo-pipes-arranged-in-rafts played in interlocking hocketed polyphonic patterns. The au tahana (raft-panpipe) and au kuita (bundle-panpipe) instrumental categories support distinct repertoire layers. Performance contexts span feast-day celebrations, mourning-rituals, and (post-1978 independence) international-festival and recording-circuit work through the canonical Narasirato Pan Pipers ensemble formed in the 1990s. The genre is one of the most internationally circulated Melanesian musical traditions through twentieth-century ethnomusicological recording.

items.name: Vanuatu women’s water music
items.lineage: Northern Vanuatu women create interlocking rhythms by striking and moving water with their hands. This seed selects the water-percussion portion of a performance; accompanying songs and other dances are separate configurations.

items.name: Lakota peyote songs (Native American Church)
items.lineage: Lakota peyote-meeting songs of the Native American Church tradition: the canonical liturgical-song repertoire for the all-night peyote-sacrament ceremony shared across many North American Native nations through the post-1900 Native American Church organization. Performance: a singer using gourd-rattle and water-drum (small drum with water inside producing a distinctive pitched-glissando-able sound), in seated-circle configuration with the participants taking turns leading songs through the night. Repertoire combines Lakota-language songs with vocables-only material and (post-1920s) songs incorporating English-language Christian themes. Distinguished from broader powwow song by peyote-meeting's sacrament-specific liturgical context and the water-drum-and-gourd-rattle (vs powwow-drum) instrumental configuration.

items.name: Navajo healing chantways
items.lineage: Navajo (Diné) healing chantways tradition: the canonical body of Navajo ceremonial-healing rituals, each comprising multi-day complex ceremonies with hundreds of associated songs, sandpaintings, and prayer-recitations performed by trained hataalii (medicine-singer-priests). The major chantways include Blessingway (Hózhójí), Enemyway (Anaa'jí), Nightway (Tł'éé'jí), Mountainway (Dziłk'iji), Beautyway (Hózhóójí), and Flintway (Béésh Yikʼájí). Each ceremony involves specific song-cycles tied to specific mytho-cosmological narratives, with strictly canonical-fixed melodic content transmitted through hataalii apprenticeship. Distinguished from broader Native American liturgical traditions by Navajo-specific cosmology and the elaborate multi-night ceremonial-cycle structure.

items.name: Apache crown dance (Mountain Spirit songs)
items.lineage: Apache crown dance (Gaan or Mountain Spirit dance) ceremonial-performance tradition of the Western Apache and broader Apachean (Mescalero, Jicarilla, Chiricahua, San Carlos, White Mountain) communities. Performance features four masked dancers representing the Gaan Mountain Spirits accompanied by song-leader-and-drummer plus chorus, with the Gaan dancers wearing tall slatted wooden crowns and yucca-fiber kilts. Performance contexts include the Sunrise Ceremony (the four-day female puberty rite, the most important Apache ceremony) and various social-and-healing occasions. Repertoire is restricted in non-Apache circulation; the public-demonstration crown-dance performances at the annual Apache fairs (San Carlos, White Mountain) constitute the principal external-cultural visibility.

Repertoire is restricted in non-Apache circulation; the public-demonstration crown-dance performances at the annual Apache fairs (San Carlos, White Mountain) constitute the principal external-cultural visibility.
exemplars: White Mountain Apache Tribal Cultural Center

items.name: Yaqui pascola and matachín (northern Mexican Easter dance-cycle)
items.lineage: Yaqui (Yoeme) pascola-and-matachín Easter Week ceremonial dance-cycle of the Yaqui communities of Sonora (Mexico) and southern Arizona, integrating pre-contact Yaqui ceremonial structure with sixteenth-century Spanish-Jesuit liturgical introductions into a syncretic Yaqui-Catholic Easter cycle. The pascola "old men of the fiesta" dancers wear carved-wood masks and dance to harp-and-violin music in the village dance-ramada throughout the multi-day ceremonial cycle; the matachín soldiers-of-the-Virgin dance-society performs in colorful crown-and-staff regalia. Performance: continuous days-long ceremonial-cycle with multiple specialized music-and-dance functions including the canónigos solemn liturgical procession, the venado-deer-dance hunting ceremony, and the matachín-soldier-of-the-Virgin processional.

items.name: Maya marimba (Guatemalan Highland)
items.lineage: Maya marimba tradition of the Guatemalan Highlands (Quetzaltenango, Sololá, Huehuetenango departments) and adjacent Chiapas (Mexico), featuring large wooden-resonator marimba ensembles played by three-to-four marimberos simultaneously on a single instrument (marimba doble or marimba grande). The instrument arrived in the New World through West-African enslaved-population introduction and was adopted by the Maya highland communities as a distinctly Guatemalan-cultural-marker. Repertoire spans the canonical son chapín nineteenth-and-twentieth-century Guatemalan national-popular forms, religious-procession music for the cofradía saint-society celebrations, and contemporary popular and dance-band material. The Marimba de Concierto formal-conservatory tradition operates parallel to the village-marimba folk-tradition.

items.name: Quechua wayno (traditional Andean)
items.lineage: Traditional Quechua wayno (also huayno, huayño) Andean folk-music form of the Quechua-and-Aymara-speaking populations of highland Peru, Bolivia, and Ecuador. The wayno is the canonical Andean dance-and-song form, in 2/4 meter with characteristic syncopation pattern, slow-to-medium tempo, and pentatonic-to-modal melodic vocabulary. Performance: small ensemble of quena end-blown notched flute, charango armadillo-shell ten-string-paired lute, bombo bass-drum, and voice — with the lyric content addressing rural-Andean life, love, mourning, and Quechua-cultural-identity. The mid-twentieth-century Cusco-and-Ayacucho-and-Huancayo regional canonical traditions are the most institutionally preserved; the Bolivian Cochabamba-and-Potosí lineages constitute the parallel highland-Bolivian tradition.

items.name: Mapuche ülkantun (sung-poetry beyond tayil)
items.lineage: Mapuche ülkantun ("singing") sung-poetry tradition of the Mapuche communities of southern Argentina and central-southern Chile, distinct from the more specialized tayil women's genealogical-ritual chant. The ülkantun encompasses the broader Mapuche song-repertoire spanning everyday-occasion songs, mourning-laments, war-songs, courtship-songs, and political-resistance songs. Performance: solo singer often accompanying themselves on kultrun shallow-frame-drum (the canonical Mapuche ceremonial-percussion-instrument), with characteristic narrow-range Mapuche pentatonic melodic vocabulary and the Mapudungun language base. The post-1990 Chilean-democratic-transition cultural-revival under the Mapuche cultural-policy organizations consolidated institutional visibility; the Mapuche post-2010 political-mobilization period has reinvigorated the genre.

items.name: French musette (Parisian accordion-led)
items.lineage: French musette accordion-led popular-folk genre developed in early-twentieth-century Paris from the convergence of Auvergnat-immigrant cabrette-bagpipe dance-music with Italian-immigrant accordion-playing in the working-class Parisian guinguette dance-hall and bistro scenes around Bastille and the rue de Lappe. Characterized by waltz-and-java rhythmic base, virtuoso accordion-melodic lead, and the canonical valse musette dance-floor accompaniment. The interwar 1920s-1930s period at Bal Tabarin and Balajo dance-halls anchored institutional crystallization. Distinguished from later French chanson by musette's instrumental-dance (vs literary-lyrical) primary functional orientation.

items.name: Bal-folk (French folk-dance revival)
items.lineage: French bal-folk folk-dance-revival movement emerging in 1970s post-1968 French counter-cultural folk-music revival, reconstructing the regional folk-dance repertoires (bourrée Auvergnate, mazurka, scottish, polka, valse Aveyronaise) for participatory ballroom-style social-dance contexts. Performance: small ensemble of hurdy-gurdy, cabrette or veuze bagpipe, vielle à roue, fiddle, accordion, acoustic guitar, plus voice for sung-dance pieces. Distinguished from earlier French bal-musette by bal-folk's regional-folk-revival (vs Parisian-urban-cabaret) functional context. The Bal-Folk association network and the annual Saint-Chartier (later renamed Le Son Continu) festival anchor institutional continuity.

items.name: Chanson réaliste (Parisian working-class song)
items.lineage: French chanson réaliste working-class-life-and-loss song genre emerging in turn-of-the-twentieth-century Parisian cabaret-and-music-hall as a Naturalist-literary parallel to the urban-realist novel of Émile Zola. Characterized by dramatically delivered ballad-form solo-vocal narratives addressing prostitution, working-class poverty, doomed romance, and street-life themes, with simple piano-or-accordion accompaniment. The mid-twentieth-century crystallization through Édith Piaf consolidated the international visibility; the parallel Damia and Fréhel lineages anchored the canonical interwar register. Distinguished from later existentialist Rive-Gauche chanson by chanson réaliste's working-class-explicit (vs intellectual-philosophical) thematic orientation.

items.name: Gwerz Breton (Brittany narrative-lament)
items.lineage: Breton gwerz long-narrative-lament tradition of Brittany (Lower Brittany, Breton-language region), comprising the canonical Breton-language sung-narrative corpus addressing historical-tragic events, supernatural-encounters, and personal-moral-cautionary tales. Performance configuration: solo unaccompanied female-or-male voice in characteristic free-rhythm extended-melismatic style with narrow-range modal vocabulary and the strict Breton-Celtic-meter four-line stanza form. The nineteenth-century Théodore Hersart de La Villemarqué Barzaz-Breiz collection (1839) consolidated the literary-historical canon. The post-1970 Breton-language-revival under Yann-Fañch Kemener and Nolwenn Korbell sustained institutional transmission. Distinguished from Breton kan ha diskan dance-singing by gwerz's sung-narrative-without-dance functional orientation.

items.name: Alpine yodel (Austrian-Swiss-Bavarian Jodel)
items.lineage: Alpine Jodel ("yodel") vocal tradition of the Austrian Tyrol, Swiss German-speaking cantons, and Bavarian Alps, characterized by rapid alternation between chest-register and falsetto-register on extended vowel-only melodic phrases (without text). Developed historically as a cattle-herder long-distance signaling system in the high mountain pastures, with parallel survival as social-celebration song in village gathering contexts. Performance ranges from solo Naturjodler unaccompanied lyrical-melodic form to multipart Jodler-with-Stubenmusik chamber-ensemble accompanied versions. The Swiss Yodel Festival (Eidgenössisches Jodlerfest, founded 1924) constitutes the institutional anchor; the parallel Austrian-Tyrolean and Bavarian regional traditions maintain village-level transmission.

items.name: Tyrolean Schuhplattler (slap-dance with music)
items.lineage: Tyrolean Schuhplattler folk-dance-and-music tradition of the Austrian Tyrol, South Tyrol (Italy), and Bavarian Alps, in which male dancers perform synchronized choreography involving rhythmic slapping of thighs, knees, and shoe-soles in characteristic accelerating patterns, accompanied by Stubenmusik chamber-ensemble of zither, hammered dulcimer (Hackbrett), accordion, double-bass, and voice. The tradition crystallized in seventeenth-eighteenth century Alpine villages from earlier courtship-display dance-forms. Performance contexts span the Heimatabend folkloric-evening tourist-demonstrations, village-festival celebrations, and the canonical Schuhplattlerverein dance-association competitions. Distinguished from broader German Alpine music by Schuhplattler's specific male-percussive-choreographic register.

items.name: Tarantella napoletana (Neapolitan)
items.lineage: Tarantella napoletana Southern Italian folk-dance-and-song tradition of the Naples region (Campania), characterized by fast 6/8 meter (or compound-duple), virtuoso mandolin-and-acoustic-guitar instrumental lead, and tambourine percussion (the tammorra and tamburello). Historically connected to the tarantismo ritual-healing dance-cure tradition of southern Italian rural communities (the dance ostensibly cured tarantism, the psychosomatic illness attributed to tarantula-bite). Performance contexts span village-festival celebrations, weddings, and the canonical Neapolitan urban-popular concertina contexts. Distinguished from pizzica salentina by tarantella napoletana's Campanian regional cadential-conventions and the broader Neapolitan canzone connection.

items.name: Pizzica salentina (Salento spider-dance)
items.lineage: Pizzica salentina Southern Italian folk-dance-and-music tradition of the Salento peninsula (southern Puglia), historically tied to the tarantismo ritual-healing tradition where the pizzica dance ostensibly cured tarantism. Characterized by fast 12/8 or 6/8 meter, virtuoso tamburello frame-drum lead, and characteristic call-and-response courtship-and-warrior-dance choreography. Performance contexts include the annual Notte della Taranta festival in Melpignano (founded 1998, now drawing 200,000+ attendees), the canonical Salento-village wedding-and-festival cycle, and (post-2000) the international neo-folk revival circuit. Distinguished from Neapolitan tarantella by pizzica's Salentine regional dialect register and slower tempo-of-instrumental-acceleration arc.

items.name: Saltarello (central Italian leaping dance)
items.lineage: Saltarello central-and-southern Italian folk-dance-and-music tradition of Lazio, Abruzzo, Marche, and Molise regions, characterized by fast triple-meter or 6/8 leaping-dance with characteristic accelerating tempo. Origin documented in fourteenth-century Italian musical manuscripts (the Saltarello primo and secondo in the Add MS 29987 British Library manuscript) and preserved in continuous folk-tradition through the medieval-Renaissance-modern transition. Performance: tambourine-led ensemble with accordion, fiddle, organetto button-accordion, and chorus. Distinguished from tarantella by saltarello's central-Italian regional base and characteristic standing-leap (vs spinning) choreographic register. The post-1970s Italian-folk-revival reactivated the genre in the original regional contexts.

items.name: Stornelli (Italian improvised rural couplets)
items.lineage: Italian stornelli improvised-couplet folk-song tradition of central Italy (Tuscany, Umbria, Lazio, Marche, Abruzzo) and adjacent regions, in which singer-poets improvise short rhymed verse-couplets (typically tripartite three-line stanzas) on assigned topics, often in competitive dialogic-exchange between two singers. Performance: unaccompanied or minimally-accompanied solo voice, with the canonical poetic-meter conventions strictly governing the improvisation. The genre survived the twentieth-century rural-urbanization period as a vestigial folk practice and entered the post-1970s Italian folk-revival under researchers Roberto Leydi and Diego Carpitella. Distinguished from broader Italian regional-folk-song by stornelli's specifically-improvisational structural framework.

items.name: Cante jondo siguiriya (deepest flamenco)
items.lineage: Andalusian cante jondo siguiriya: the deepest, most tragic-emotional palo (song-form) of the cante jondo "deep song" flamenco core repertoire. Characterized by the canonical siguiriya twelve-beat compás (3+3+2+2+2), extended free-rhythm extended-melismatic introductory passages, and intense vocal-emotional projection registering the genre's anguished-lament aesthetic. Lyric content addresses death, the loss of loved ones, the pain of incarceration, the suffering of the Roma-Andalusian historical experience. Distinguished within the cante jondo palos by siguiriya's tragic-anguish (vs the soleá's graver-philosophical or the martinete's a-cappella-direct) emotional register. The canonical siguiriya repertoire descends through hereditary cantaor lineages with strict transmission-conservation conventions.

items.name: Soleá (flamenco "mother of cante")
items.lineage: Andalusian soleá flamenco palo (song-form), considered the "mother of cante" foundational form from which much of the broader flamenco palo system derives. Characterized by the canonical twelve-beat soleá compás (with accents on beats 3, 6, 8, 10, 12), grave-philosophical lyrical content addressing solitude, the existential condition, and contemplative resignation. Performance: solo cantaor voice with sole flamenco guitar accompaniment, in slower tempo than siguiriya with characteristic falsetas (guitar-instrumental-interludes) between vocal sections. The Triana neighborhood of Seville and the Jerez de la Frontera lineages constitute the canonical regional sub-traditions of soleá. Distinguished from siguiriya by soleá's more contemplative-philosophical (vs anguished-tragic) emotional register.

items.name: Bulería (flamenco festive fast palo)
items.lineage: Andalusian bulería flamenco palo, the fast-tempo festive-celebratory form developed in late-nineteenth-century Jerez de la Frontera from the older soleá tradition. Characterized by the canonical twelve-beat bulería compás (accents shifted from soleá to beats 12, 3, 6, 8, 10 with characteristic rhythmic-displacement-and-suspension play), fast tempo, and improvisational-virtuosic vocal-and-guitar-and-palmas (hand-clapping) interplay. Lyric content spans humorous, romantic, and celebratory themes — much lighter than the cante jondo deep-songs. The bulería closes most flamenco performance sets as the festive-final palo. Distinguished from soleá by bulería's faster tempo, lighter emotional register, and the canonical Jerez-rhythmic-displacement-and-virtuosity practice.

items.name: Alegría (flamenco "happiness" of Cádiz)
items.lineage: Andalusian alegría ("happiness") flamenco palo of the cantiñas family, developed in nineteenth-century Cádiz from the older Castilian jota and northern-Spanish folk-dance-forms adapted to Andalusian flamenco-compás framework. Characterized by twelve-beat alegría compás (accents on 3, 6, 8, 10, 12 like soleá but with major-key feel and bright tempo), upbeat lyrical content addressing happiness, the sea, the city of Cádiz, and Andalusian regional pride. Performance integrates the canonical alegría dance (one of the foundational baile flamenco choreographic forms) with vocal and guitar accompaniment. Distinguished from soleá by alegría's major-key brighter (vs Phrygian-mode darker) tonal register and Cádiz-regional cultural-identity.

items.name: Catalan sardana (national-folk circle-dance)
items.lineage: Catalan sardana circle-dance-and-music tradition of Catalonia (Spain), the canonical Catalan national-folk-dance form. Performance configuration: a cobla ensemble of eleven musicians playing tenora (Catalan oboe), tible (smaller oboe), trumpets, fiscorn (flugelhorn-like brass), trombone, contrabass, and the flabiol-and-tambori one-handed flute-and-drum combination played simultaneously by a single musician. Dancers stand in a circle holding hands, performing the precise counting-of-steps Catalan choreographic vocabulary. The sardana became politically significant during the Franco-period (1939-1975) suppression of Catalan culture, and post-1975 democratic-Catalonia consolidation. Distinguished from other Iberian circle-dance forms by sardana's eleven-instrument-cobla and precise-counted-step structural conventions.
items.description: Catalan sardana circle-dance-and-music tradition of Catalonia (Spain), the canonical Catalan national-folk-dance form. Performance configuration: a cobla ensemble of eleven musicians playing tenora (Catalan oboe), tible (smaller oboe), trumpets, fiscorn (flugelhorn-like brass), trombone, contrabass, and the flabiol-and-tambori one-handed flute-and-drum combination played simultaneously by a single musician. Dancers stand in a circle holding hands, performing the precise counting-of-steps Catalan choreographic vocabulary. The sardana became politically significant during the Franco-period (1939-1975) suppression of Catalan culture, and post-1975 democratic-Catalonia consolidation. Distinguished from other Iberian circle-dance forms by sardana's eleven-instrument-cobla and precise-counted-step structural conventions.

items.name: Balkan brass (fanfara, Roma-Serbian-Macedonian)
items.lineage: Balkan brass ensemble tradition of southern Serbia (Vranje, Užice regions), western Bulgaria, and northern Macedonia, performed by predominantly Roma musicians at weddings, funerals, and the canonical annual Guča Brass Band Festival in southern Serbia (founded 1961). Performance configuration: ensemble of 6-12 brass instruments (trumpets, trombones, tubas, flugelhorns) plus tapan large double-headed cylindrical drum, playing characteristic Balkan asymmetrical-meter (5/8, 7/8, 9/8, 11/8) rhythmic-cycles with virtuosic ornamental melodic-line. The genre crystallized in nineteenth-century Ottoman-period military-band tradition adapted into the post-Ottoman Balkan civilian-popular-celebration context. Distinguished from neighboring Albanian saze and Greek nisiotika by Balkan brass's brass-ensemble (vs string-and-clarinet) instrumental signature.

items.name: Romanian lăutari (Roma tavern-band tradition)
items.lineage: Romanian lăutari (Roma professional-musician-class) tavern-band-and-wedding-music tradition of Romania and Moldova, performed by predominantly Roma musicians serving the broader Romanian agricultural-and-urban communities. The taraf ensemble centers on violin (sometimes multiple violins in heterophonic relationship), cimbalom hammered-dulcimer (the larger Hungarian-Romanian concert variant of the broader dulcimer family), accordion, double-bass, and voice. Repertoire spans the canonical doina free-rhythm lament solo-vocal-or-violin form, the hora circle-dance, the brâu chain-dance, and the broader Romanian regional-folk repertoire. The post-1989 international circulation through the Taraf de Haïdouks ensemble brought the lăutari tradition into the world-music circuit.

items.name: Romanian doina (free-rhythm lament)
items.lineage: Romanian doina free-rhythm extended-melismatic lament-and-pastoral solo vocal-or-instrumental tradition of Romania and Moldova. Performance: solo unaccompanied voice (or solo violin, solo wooden-flute caval, or solo wooden-clarinet) in characteristic free-rhythm parlando-rubato style with extensive ornamental-melismatic figuration on long vowels. The doina has multiple regional sub-traditions: doină de jale (lament-doina), doină ciobănească (shepherd-doina), doină haiducească (outlaw-doina), and doină de dragoste (love-doina), each with characteristic regional intonation conventions. Distinguished from broader Romanian folk-song by doina's strict free-rhythm extended-melismatic structural requirement.

items.name: Hungarian verbunkos (military-recruitment dance)
items.lineage: Hungarian verbunkos military-recruitment dance-music tradition emerging in late-eighteenth century Habsburg-Hungarian military-recruitment practice (the verbunk recruitment-event featured local musicians playing energetic dance-music to inspire young men to enlist). The genre developed canonical compositional conventions: characteristic dotted-rhythm (kuruc rhythm) opening, augmented-fourth Hungarian-Gypsy-scale modal coloring, and characteristic accelerating tempo arc. The verbunkos became the foundational nineteenth-century Hungarian art-music style (informing Franz Liszt's Hungarian Rhapsodies and Béla Bartók's ethnographic-research), and through Brahms's Hungarian Dances entered the broader European musical consciousness. Distinguished from later magyar nóta urban-popular form by verbunkos's late-eighteenth-century historical-recruitment-context origin.

items.name: Hungarian magyar nóta (urban Hungarian song)
items.lineage: Hungarian magyar nóta ("Hungarian song") urban-popular song-form developing in nineteenth-century Hungarian cities as composed-popular-song with Hungarian-Gypsy-scale modal characteristics, performed by Roma cigányzenekar bands at coffee-houses, restaurants, and private parties. Distinguished from authentic peasant népdal folk-song (which Bartók and Kodály championed against magyar nóta as ethnographic-cultural-purity) by magyar nóta's composed-individual-author (vs anonymous-collective-folk) compositional framework. Performance: solo singer with cigányzenekar ensemble of first-violin (prímás), second-violin and viola accompaniment, cimbalom, clarinet, and double-bass. The genre remained dominant in twentieth-century Hungarian urban popular culture and continues today as a sentimental cultural form.

items.name: Polish góralski (Tatra highlander)
items.lineage: Polish góralski Tatra-Mountain highlander music-and-dance tradition of the Podhale region in southern Poland, performed by the Polish góral mountain-folk community. The kapela góralska ensemble centers on the prymista (lead violinist) accompanied by sekund (second-violin) and basy (three-string Tatra-style upright-bass), with characteristic open-string drone-and-shifted-tonal-center modal vocabulary distinct from broader Polish lowland folk-music. Performance contexts span village-festival celebrations, wedding ceremonies, and (since 1968) the international Folk-Music Festival in Zakopane. The post-1980 Tatra-cultural-revival under the local Highlander Union has consolidated institutional preservation. Distinguished from Slovak fujara solo and Czech moravian folk by Polish góralski Podhale-Tatra specific stylistic-conventions.

items.name: Greek nisiotika (island music)
items.lineage: Greek nisiotika ("island music") folk-popular music tradition of the Greek Aegean Sea islands — Naxos, Mykonos, Tinos, Andros, Skyros, Lesbos, Chios, Samos, and adjacent islands — distinguished from mainland Greek demotic music by characteristic island-dance-rhythm repertoire (the syrtos, sousta, ballos), instrumental signature (lyra Cretan-style three-string fiddle on some islands, violin elsewhere, laouto long-neck lute, and santouri hammered-dulcimer), and the broader Aegean-island maritime-cultural orientation. The mid-twentieth-century commercial-recording era at Columbia, HMV, and Pathé Athens documented the canonical island repertoire. Distinguished from the parallel Cretan lyra tradition by nisiotika's broader-Aegean-island-network and lighter dance-emphasis register.

items.name: Cretan lyra (Cretan pear-shaped fiddle)
items.lineage: Cretan lyra solo-and-ensemble music tradition of Crete (Greece), centered on the pear-shaped three-string upright-played fiddle of unique Cretan construction (with the fingers stopping the strings from the side rather than pressing down, allowing characteristic Cretan-style pitch-glide ornament). Performance configuration: lyra leading with laouto long-neck-lute rhythmic-and-harmonic accompaniment, plus voice for sung repertoire. Repertoire spans the canonical Cretan dance-forms (pentozali fast-warrior-dance, syrtos slow-circle-dance, sousta), mantinada improvised-couplet form, and the rizitika hilltop-mountain-village ritual-song tradition. The post-twentieth-century Anogeia village and the Psarantonis-Xylouris family lineage anchor the canonical contemporary tradition. Distinguished from broader Greek nisiotika by Cretan-specific lyra-instrument signature.

items.name: Pontic Greek music (Black Sea Greek)
items.lineage: Pontic Greek music tradition of the Pontic Greek ethnic community originating in the Black Sea coast of Anatolia (Trabzon, Sinop, Samsun regions, now Turkey), displaced post-1923 Greek-Turkish population exchange to mainland Greece (especially northern Greece, Athens, and Thessaloniki). Performance configuration centers on the Pontic kemenche (three-string upright-fiddle, distinct from Cretan lyra in tuning and playing technique), often accompanied by daouli large frame-drum and angeion bagpipe. Repertoire features fast asymmetrical-meter dance-music (omal, tik, dipat, tromakton) and slow narrative-and-lament forms (Pontic dialect of Greek with characteristic Anatolian-Greek phonological features). Distinguished from broader Greek demotic music by Pontic-Black-Sea regional identity, kemenche-instrument signature, and post-1923 diaspora-cultural-memory orientation.

items.name: Cypriot tsiattista (improvised dueling couplets)
items.lineage: Cypriot tsiattista improvised-couplet poetic-dueling tradition of Cyprus (Greek-Cypriot communities), Performance: two poet-singers face off in extempore Greek-Cypriot-dialect rhymed-couplet exchange, each turn answering the previous while introducing new poetic-and-philosophical-and-humorous-and-mocking material, accompanied by violin and laouto. The genre is structurally parallel to other improvised-poetic-dueling Mediterranean traditions (Basque bertsolaritza, Italian stornelli, Sardinian gara poetica, Sicilian mottetto), but with Cypriot-Greek dialect register and tetraposyllabos-fifteen-syllable-line characteristic poetic-meter. Performance contexts: weddings, agricultural festivals, and the annual Tsiattistakia festivals in Cyprus.

items.name: Latvian dainas (folk-song quatrains)
items.lineage: Latvian dainas folk-quatrain song tradition: the canonical Latvian oral-poetic-and-song corpus comprising over 1.2 million collected four-line quatrains in trochaic-tetrameter or dactyl-tetrameter form, documenting the entire Latvian rural-life-cycle from birth-rituals through wedding-cycle through funeral-rites. Compiled by Krišjānis Barons (1835-1923) in the canonical six-volume Latvju Dainas (1894-1915), the largest single-author folklore-collection in any language. Performance configuration: unaccompanied solo or small-group female-voice in characteristic narrow-range pentatonic-or-modal melodic vocabulary with strict daina meter. The post-1991 Latvian-independence cultural-revival under the Song-and-Dance Celebration (Latvian: Dziesmu un deju svētki) has consolidated institutional transmission. Distinguished from broader Baltic vocal music by daina's strict quatrain-form and Krišjānis Barons canonical-corpus reference.

items.name: Karelian rune-singing (Kalevala-meter)
items.lineage: Karelian rune-singing tradition of the Karelian (Karjala) ethno-linguistic region straddling the Finnish-Russian border (eastern Finland, Russian Karelia), comprising the canonical Finno-Karelian narrative-and-magical-incantation oral-poetic corpus from which Elias Lönnrot compiled the Kalevala national-epic (first edition 1835, expanded second edition 1849). Performance: solo or duo unaccompanied voice in strict Kalevala-meter (four-stress eight-syllable trochaic line), often performed antiphonally with one singer providing a low-register drone or echo to the other's melodic line. The Karelian-Finnish runo-singer historical tradition was nearly extinguished by twentieth-century Soviet-and-Finnish modernization; documentary collection by Lönnrot and subsequent collectors preserved approximately 200,000 verses. Distinguished from broader Finnic vocal-music by rune-singing's strict Kalevala-meter and oral-epic-narrative orientation.

items.name: Faroese kvæði (ballad chain-dance)
items.lineage: Faroese kvæði Faroe Islands ballad-and-chain-dance tradition, the canonical surviving medieval-Scandinavian narrative-ballad chain-dance form that has persisted in continuous practice on the Faroes since the medieval period. Performance configuration: a circle of dancers holding hands, moving in characteristic slow-stepping pattern, with the lead-singer (skipari) singing the narrative-stanzas while the dancer-chorus responds with refrain-lines. Repertoire centers on long narrative-cycles including the Sjúrðar kvæði (Sigurd-the-dragon-slayer cycle, the canonical Faroese epic, 200+ stanzas), and other historical, mythological, and ballad-narrative cycles in classical Faroese language. The post-1948 Faroese cultural-autonomy period under the Føroya Fróðskaparfelag (Faroese Society) consolidated institutional preservation.

items.name: Icelandic rímur (epic-chant)
items.lineage: Icelandic rímur (singular ríma) epic-chant narrative tradition of Iceland, comprising sung-narrative cycles based on Old Norse sagas, Continental medieval romance, and biblical-and-classical sources. Origin documented from late fourteenth-century onward, with continuous transmission through Icelandic farmstead winter-evening-entertainment context (the kvöldvaka evening-vigil reading-and-singing gathering) into the twentieth century. Performance: solo unaccompanied chanting in characteristic narrow-range Phrygian-and-related modes, with the canonical poetic-meter ferskeytt four-line stanza form and elaborate alliterative-and-internal-rhyme conventions inherited from skaldic verse. The Iðunn society (founded 1929) and the Kvæðamannafélagið Iðunn (Iðunn Rímur-singer Society) anchor institutional preservation; the post-2000s neo-folk revival has reactivated the genre.

items.name: Norwegian stev (solo singing-game)
items.lineage: Norwegian stev solo-singing tradition of inland-Norway (Setesdal, Telemark, and adjacent mountain regions), comprising short improvised-or-traditional four-line quatrains sung unaccompanied. Two main streams: gamlestev ("old stev") canonical fixed-traditional-stanzas, and nystev ("new stev") improvised-on-occasion stanzas often performed in competitive-dialogic exchange between two singers. Performance: solo unaccompanied voice in characteristic narrow-range Norwegian-pentatonic-and-modal vocabulary with strict stev-meter four-stress-line. The Hilme inland-Norway lineage and the canonical nineteenth-century stev-singers (Jorunn Hilme, Talleiv Røysland) consolidated institutional documentation; the post-1970s Norwegian folk-music revival re-established practice.

items.name: Hardingfele slått (Hardanger-fiddle dance-tunes)
items.lineage: Norwegian Hardanger-fiddle slått dance-tune tradition of western-Norwegian mountain valleys (Hardanger, Voss, Telemark, Setesdal, Numedal regions). The hardingfele Hardanger-fiddle has four bowed melody strings plus four-or-five sympathetic resonant strings beneath the fingerboard, producing characteristic shimmering-overtone resonance. Slått (singular slått, plural slåttar) are solo virtuoso dance-tunes with strict regional-stylistic-conventions: springar three-beat asymmetric dance-tune, gangar two-beat walking-dance, halling acrobatic-male-display-dance, and rull rolling-tune. Performance: solo Hardanger-fiddle, with each regional sub-tradition (Setesdal, Hallingdal, Numedal, Valdres, Telemark) maintaining distinctive playing-conventions and ornamental-vocabulary.

items.name: Swedish polska (traditional fiddle-dance)
items.lineage: Swedish polska traditional fiddle-dance tradition of Sweden, comprising several regional sub-types: åttondelspolska (eighth-note-pulse polska), sextondelspolska (sixteenth-note-pulse polska), Slängpolska (swing-polska), and several regional named variants. Performance configuration: solo fiddle, twin-fiddles (svenska låtspel), nyckelharpa (keyed fiddle), or small ensembles of these instruments. Distinguished by the canonical Swedish-fiddle ornamental conventions and the asymmetrical-triple-meter dance-pulse where the second beat is shortened. The post-1970s Swedish folk-music revival under the spelmanslag fiddler-group network consolidated institutional preservation; the annual Riksspelmansträff and Bingsjöstämman fiddle-festivals anchor performance circuit.

items.name: Asturian gaita (Iberian Celtic bagpipe)
items.lineage: Asturian gaita Iberian Celtic-bagpipe tradition of Asturias (northern Spain), the canonical Asturian regional-folk-music instrumental signature. The gaita asturiana is a mouth-blown single-drone bagpipe distinct from the larger Galician gaita gallega and the Scottish Highland pipes in tuning and ornament-vocabulary. Performance: solo gaita or gaita-and-tambor (drum-pair) accompanying voice, dance, or solo instrumental display. Repertoire spans foliada wedding-celebration repertoire, vaqueirada cattle-herder dance-music, and the canonical Asturian-Celtic revival-period compositions of the late-twentieth century. Distinguished from Galician gaita gallega by Asturian-specific tuning and ornamental conventions. items.description: Asturian gaita Iberian Celtic-bagpipe tradition of Asturias (northern Spain), the canonical Asturian regional-folk-music instrumental signature. The gaita asturiana is a mouth-blown single-drone bagpipe distinct from the larger Galician gaita gallega and the Scottish Highland pipes in tuning and ornament-vocabulary. Performance: solo gaita or gaita-and-tambor (drum-pair) accompanying voice, dance, or solo instrumental display. items.name: Basque bertsolaritza (improvised verse-dueling)
items.lineage: Basque bertsolaritza improvised-verse tradition of the Basque Country (Euskal Herria, northern Spain and southwestern France), in which bertsolari poet-singers improvise extempore verses in the Basque language on assigned topics, often in competitive-dueling exchange. Performance: solo unaccompanied voice in characteristic narrow-range Basque-folk melodic vocabulary, with strict Basque-poetic-meter conventions governing the improvisation. The annual Bertsolari Txapelketa Nagusia (Bertsolari Grand Championship, held every four years) constitutes the central institutional anchor; the Mintzola Foundation (founded 1996) and Xenpelar Dokumentazio Zentroa preserve the institutional archive. Distinguished from other Mediterranean improvised-poetic traditions by Basque-language base and Euskara-specific meter conventions.

items.name: Corsican paghjella modern revival
items.lineage: Corsican paghjella three-voice male polyphonic singing tradition of Corsica (France). Performance: three male singers in close-position polyphonic configuration: a bassu low-register foundational voice, a sicunda middle-register voice, and a terza high-register ornamental voice, all male-only, performing sacred (especially the canonical Mass-of-the-Dead repertoire) and secular repertoire. The genre nearly disappeared by the mid-twentieth century but was revived through the 1970s riacquistu Corsican-cultural-revival movement under the canonical group A Filetta. Distinguished from Sardinian cantu a tenore by Corsican paghjella's three-voice-male (vs four-voice-with-guttural-bass) configuration.

items.name: Banda sinaloense
items.lineage: Mexican brass-band tradition of Sinaloa state, derived from late-nineteenth-century German-immigrant military-band tradition adapted to Mexican-rural-popular celebration-music. Large ensemble of clarinets, trumpets, trombones, sousaphone, tambora, tarola, voice — entirely brass-and-percussion. Repertoire spans ranchera, corrido, cumbia. Banda El Recodo (founded 1938) anchors the canonical sound.

items.name: Norteño (northern Mexican)
items.lineage: Northern-Mexican popular-music of border states (Tamaulipas, Nuevo León, Coahuila, Chihuahua), accordion-and-bajo-sexto-led with bass-drum-kit. Origin in late-nineteenth-century German-Czech-Polish-immigrant accordion music synthesized with Mexican forms. Repertoire: corrido, ranchera, polka, cumbia. Falcon Records (McAllen, 1948 onward) anchored commercial circulation.

items.name: Sonidero (Mexican cumbia sound-system)
items.lineage: Mexican cumbia DJ-and-sound-system tradition of Mexico City and northern-Mexican border-cities, emerging 1960s-1970s. The sonidero plays cumbia records on large mobile sound-systems at outdoor street-parties, interspersed with extempore MC-shoutouts dedicated to attendees by name and Mexican-immigrant family members in the US. Slowed-down cumbia rebajada emerged through accidental incorrect-speed playback.

items.name: Cumbia rebajada (Monterrey slowed)
items.lineage: Slowed-down Mexican cumbia variant emerging accidentally in Monterrey 1980s-1990s when sonidero DJs played records at slower speed, producing characteristically lowered-pitch hypnotic-droning. Deliberate cultural practice followed, with sound-systems and bedroom-producers crafting deliberately slowed versions. Intersected with 2010s "tribal guarachero" Monterrey electronic-cumbia.

items.name: Son huasteco (Huasteca trio)
items.lineage: Regional Mexican son tradition of the Huasteca cultural region (Veracruz, Hidalgo, San Luis Potosí, Tamaulipas, Querétaro). Trio of huapanguero violin (with high-falsetto vocal ornament and improvisatory melodic-doubling), quinta huapanguera five-string acoustic-bass-guitar, and jarana huasteca five-string rhythm-guitar. Alternating violin-improvisation and falsetto-vocal-improvisation sections define the canonical huapango.

items.name: Son istmeño (Oaxaca Isthmus)
items.lineage: Regional Mexican son tradition of the Isthmus of Tehuantepec (southeastern Oaxaca), the Zapotec-cultural-region southern-Mexican-Pacific lowland. Zapotec-language vocal repertoire alongside Spanish, characteristic 6/8 alternating-with-3/4, and Tehuana-feminine cultural register. Marimba ensemble (parallel to but distinct from Guatemalan Maya marimba), acoustic-guitar, voice. La Sandunga (Andrés Gutiérrez 1853) is the unofficial Zapotec anthem.

items.name: Trío romántico (Mexican bolero trio)
items.lineage: Mexican trío romántico bolero-trio tradition emerging in 1930s-1940s Mexico City. Three-male-voice harmonized chorus with two acoustic guitars and one requinto (smaller higher-tuned lead guitar). Trio Los Panchos (founded 1944, New York) crystallized the form, established the requinto-lead-with-three-voice-harmony as canonical, and exported the genre internationally throughout Latin America.

items.name: Bolero mexicano
items.lineage: Mexican adaptation of the broader Latin-American bolero, developed in mid-twentieth-century Mexico City through Agustín Lara (born 1897) and the 1940s-1950s Mexican-cinema golden-age. Solo voice with piano-or-trio accompaniment, slow 2/4 meter with the canonical bolero rhythmic figure, intensely romantic-melancholic register. Distinguished from Cuban bolero by Mexican-Spanish lyrical register and elaborate harmonic-vocabulary.

items.name: Trova cubana
items.lineage: Cuban troubadour-song tradition emerging in late-nineteenth-century Santiago de Cuba and Havana from synthesis of Spanish romance ballad with Cuban son and bolero. Solo voice or duo with one or two acoustic guitars, intimate-confessional register. Trova tradicional (1890s-1920s, Sindo Garay, Manuel Corona) crystallized the genre; nueva trova (post-1968, Silvio Rodríguez, Pablo Milanés) integrated revolutionary-political content.

items.name: Filin (Cuban jazz-trova)
items.lineage: Cuban jazz-influenced song genre developed in late-1940s-early-1950s Havana. Young composer-performers (José Antonio Méndez, Cesar Portillo de la Luz, Frank Domínguez, Marta Valdés, Frank Emilio Flynn) integrated American-jazz extended-chord harmony, blue-note vocabulary, and intimate-confessional vocal-style with the older trova canon. Havana nightclub and bohemian-cafe contexts.

items.name: Descarga (Cuban jam session)
items.lineage: Cuban improvisational ensemble-form developed in 1950s Havana through after-hours jam sessions at Tropicana, Sans Souci, Habana Hilton hotel-clubs. Combines son montuno rhythmic framework with jazz-improvisational solos over canonical guajeo ostinato. Cachao y Su Ritmo Caliente sessions (1957, Israel "Cachao" López) are the foundational recorded document. Post-1960 exile to Miami and New York extended into broader Latin-jazz.

items.name: Songo (Cuban 1970s fusion)
items.lineage: Cuban dance-music developed in 1970s-1980s Havana by Los Van Van under Juan Formell, synthesizing son montuno, changüí, North American funk, and Cuban folkloric rumba. Introduced drum-kit alongside canonical timbales and congas, electric-bass with funk-derived ostinato, extended sectional structures. Directly informed subsequent 1990s timba emergence.

items.name: Salsa dura (hard 70s NY salsa)
items.lineage: Aggressive virtuoso style of New York salsa developed in 1970s through Fania All-Stars and broader Fania Records roster. Intense rhythmic-and-instrumental projection, virtuoso solo improvisations, extended compositional structures, politically-conscious socially-realist lyric content addressing immigration, poverty, Latin-American social-justice. Fania Records (1964, Johnny Pacheco, Jerry Masucci) constitutes the institutional anchor.

items.name: Salsa romántica (80s romantic)
items.lineage: Softer-romantic style of salsa developed in mid-1980s Miami and New York from older salsa dura. Reduced rhythmic-aggression, simpler arrangements, slower-mid-tempo, explicit romantic-love-and-relationship lyric content. Emerged through Latin-Caribbean commercial-radio-targeting and became dominant late-1980s-and-1990s salsa-mainstream. RMM Records and producer Sergio George consolidated canonical sound.

items.name: Salsa colombiana (Cali)
items.lineage: Colombian regional variant of salsa centered in Cali (Valle del Cauca, southwestern Colombia, "world capital of salsa"). Distinguished from New York and Puerto Rican salsa by faster-tempo, more aggressive-rhythmic-pulse, and the Cali dance-school choreographic culture emphasizing fast complex footwork. Grupo Niche (1980, Jairo Varela) and Orquesta Guayacán anchor canonical Cali sound.

items.name: Merengue urbano
items.lineage: Electronic-and-rap-influenced Dominican merengue variant emerging in 1990s-2000s. Synthesis of traditional merengue rhythmic pulse with hip-hop production and reggaeton harmonic-rhythmic vocabulary. Drum-machine-and-sampler production, faster 2/4 tempo than traditional merengue, simpler chord-progressions, explicit MC-rapped vocal sections alongside sung verse-and-chorus. Omega "El Fuerte" and El Cata anchored the 2000s commercial sound.

items.name: Merengue típico (Cibao traditional)
items.lineage: Traditional Dominican merengue variant of the Cibao region (Santiago, La Vega, Moca, San Francisco de Macorís). Button-accordion (German-immigrant introduction, adopted as canonical), tambora double-headed drum, güira metal-scraper, marímbula or electric-bass, voice. Tatico Henríquez (1944-1976) is the canonical tipico accordionist; Fefita La Grande (born 1943) is the canonical female lead.

items.name: Chutney (Indo-Caribbean)
items.lineage: Indo-Caribbean Trinidadian-and-Guyanese popular-music developed in late-twentieth-century Trinidad from synthesis of Bhojpuri-Hindi folk-song of the post-indenture Indian-laborer community with Trinidadian calypso-and-soca. Voice (often female), dholak, dhantal, tassa, electric-instruments. Sundar Popo's 1968 "Nana and Nani" is the canonical foundational chutney recording.

items.name: Twoubadou (Haitian troubadour)
items.lineage: Haitian rural-and-popular acoustic-song tradition emerging in early-twentieth-century Haiti from synthesis of Cuban son and bolero, Dominican merengue tipico, and Haitian rural folk-song. Acoustic-guitar, marímbula, mandolin, accordion, manouba scraper, voice. Working-class counterpart to elite-class urban kompa direct big-band tradition. Post-1980 acoustic-revival under Ti Coca, Manno Charlemagne, Beethova Obas.

items.name: Rasin (Haitian roots-Vodou rock)
items.lineage: Haitian rock-and-Vodou-fusion genre developed in late-1970s-1980s Haiti. Fusion of Haitian Vodou ceremonial-drumming-and-singing with rock-and-roots-music aesthetic. Emerged through Boukman Eksperyans (founded 1978 in Port-au-Prince by Theodore "Lolo" Beaubrun) and parallel groups Boukan Ginen, Sanba Yo, Rara Machine. Electric guitars-bass-drum-kit alongside Vodou-ceremonial percussion. The 1990 Vodou Adjae album consolidated international visibility.

items.name: Garifuna punta-rock (Belize/Honduras modern)
items.lineage: Modern-popular variant of older Garifuna punta dance-tradition, developed in 1970s-1980s Belize and Honduras. Pen Cayetano (born 1954, Dangriga) developed the punta-rock sound in mid-1970s; Andy Palacio (born 1960) extended internationally through his 2007 Wátina album (Stonetree Records). Electric instruments alongside Garifuna traditional drums (primero, segunda, tercero) and shaker.

items.name: Aguinaldo (Puerto Rican Christmas)
items.lineage: Puerto Rican Christmas-and-Three-Kings-Day song tradition performed during canonical Christmas season at parrandas door-to-door musical-visits. Cuatro puerto-rico (ten-string-paired Puerto Rican lute), acoustic-guitar, güiro scraper, percussion, voice. Repertoire spans religious-devotional Christmas content, picaresque parranda material, and patriotic-cultural Puerto-Rican content. Décima ten-line stanza characteristic of jíbaro music.

items.name: Chamamé
items.lineage: Folk-popular music of Argentine Mesopotamia region (Corrientes, Misiones, Entre Ríos, Formosa, Chaco) and adjacent eastern Paraguay. Synthesis of indigenous Guaraní vocal-melodic conventions, German-immigrant accordion-tradition, and Spanish-colonial folk-music inheritance. Voice with button-accordion, acoustic-guitar, contrabass. Lyrics draw on Guaraní and Castilian-Spanish, often bilingual.

items.name: Chacarera (Argentine northwest)
items.lineage: Argentine folk-dance-and-song tradition of northwestern provinces (Santiago del Estero, Tucumán, Salta, La Rioja). Characteristic 6/8 meter, fast-tempo paired-couple dance with handkerchiefs, lyrical content addressing rural-northwestern Argentine life. Voice with acoustic-guitar and bombo legüero large-frame-drum. Atahualpa Yupanqui and Los Hermanos Ábalos (founded 1932) consolidated canonical repertoire.

items.name: Zamba (Argentine slow-romantic)
items.lineage: Argentine slow-romantic folk-dance-and-song tradition of northwestern provinces, derived from Peruvian zamacueca (which also derived Chilean cueca and Andean tondero). Slow 6/8 meter, melancholic register addressing romance, loss, and northwestern-Argentine pampas-mountain landscape. Mid-twentieth-century commercial-folklore revival under Yupanqui, Cuchi Leguizamón, Mercedes Sosa consolidated canonical zamba repertoire.

items.name: Cueca (Chilean national)
items.lineage: Chilean national folk-dance-and-song tradition derived from broader Peruvian-Spanish zamacueca lineage, codified in mid-nineteenth-century Chile (formally declared national dance 1979). Characteristic 6/8 meter alternating with 3/4 polymeter, fast tempo with paired-couple handkerchief-and-stomping choreography. Post-1973 dictatorship period featured the dissident "cueca sola" performed solo by widows of disappeared persons.

items.name: Festejo (Afro-Peruvian celebration)
items.lineage: Afro-Peruvian folk-popular dance-and-song tradition of coastal Peru (Lima, Chincha, El Carmen, Ica regions), descended from West-African-enslaved-population cultural memory through colonial-Peruvian slavery period. Fast 6/8 meter, virtuoso cajón lead, quijada jawbone-rattle, acoustic-guitar. Nicomedes Santa Cruz (1925-1992) and Victoria Santa Cruz (1922-2014) consolidated twentieth-century cultural revival. Susana Baca, Eva Ayllón anchor contemporary scene.

items.name: Landó (Afro-Peruvian slow groove)
items.lineage: Afro-Peruvian slow-tempo groove-based form characterized by slow 12/8 with strong off-beat accent and characteristic syncopated cajón pattern. Distinguished from festejo by landó's slower-meditative-melancholic register. Addresses melancholy-romance, the experience of enslavement and its memory (canonical "María Landó" by Chabuca Granda with poetry of César Calvo, recorded by Susana Baca).

items.name: Currulao (Colombian Pacific)
items.lineage: Afro-Colombian marimba-and-percussion ensemble tradition of Pacific coastal region (Chocó, Valle del Cauca, Cauca, Nariño departments) and adjacent Ecuadorian Pacific coast. Marimba de chonta (wooden marimba with bamboo resonators), bombo and cununo drums, guasá tubular shakers, voice (often female-lead with chorus).

items.name: Champeta (Cartagena Afro-Colombian)
items.lineage: Afro-Colombian dance-music genre of Cartagena and the Colombian Caribbean coast, emerging in 1980s from synthesis of African soukous, juju, and highlife (transmitted through cassette-and-vinyl trade with Africa via maritime sailors) with local Colombian Caribbean costeño rhythmic-vocabulary. Performed at picós large mobile sound-systems in working-class barrios. Distinguished from cumbia by champeta's African-pop-derived (vs cumbia's indigenous-Afro-Spanish-syncretic) lineage.

items.name: Sertanejo universitário (Brazilian pop-country)
items.lineage: Brazilian sertanejo subgenre emerging in late-2000s as a urban-modern revival of the older sertanejo country-music tradition, targeted at younger university-student audiences. Characterized by pop-country-influenced harmonic vocabulary, slower mid-tempo love-ballad register, and twin-male-vocal-harmony presentation. Goiânia, Brasília, and São Paulo studios anchored the canonical sound. Michel Teló's 2011 "Ai Se Eu Te Pego" became the international-crossover hit.

items.name: Forró pé-de-serra (traditional forró)
items.lineage: Traditional Brazilian forró sub-form preserving the canonical Luiz Gonzaga-era 1940s-1960s northeastern Brazilian dance-music form. Trio configuration: sanfona button-accordion lead, zabumba double-headed bass-drum, triangle, plus voice. Distinguished from later forró eletrônico and forró universitário by pé-de-serra's acoustic-trio (vs full-band-electronic) instrumental signature. Repertoire centers on Luiz Gonzaga's canonical compositional corpus and parallel northeastern forró composers.

items.name: Brega and tecnobrega (Belém-Pará)
items.lineage: Brega and tecnobrega Brazilian popular-music genres of the northern Brazilian Amazonian Pará state (especially Belém). Brega ("kitsch") originated as a mid-late-twentieth-century commercial sentimental-popular music; tecnobrega is its 2000s-onward electronic-DIY remix-and-production reformulation, with characteristic synthesizer-and-808-drum-machine production, fast tempo, and an outdoor-aparelhagem sound-system street-party performance context. Distinguished from sertanejo by brega's northern-Amazonian-Brazilian regional base.

items.name: Pisadinha and arrocha (northeastern romantic)
items.lineage: Brazilian arrocha and pisadinha contemporary northeastern-Brazilian romantic-popular music genres. Arrocha (Bahian, 1990s-2000s) is a slow-tempo romantic ballad with Brazilian-pop-influenced harmonic-vocabulary. Pisadinha (Pernambuco/Bahia, 2010s-2020s) is the faster-tempo dance-derivative incorporating electronic-production. Both share the working-class northeastern-Brazilian cultural orientation distinct from sertanejo universitário's middle-class-university-targeting.

items.name: Repente and embolada (NE Brazilian improvised)
items.lineage: Brazilian repente and embolada improvised-poetic-dueling traditions of the northeastern Brazilian sertão (Pernambuco, Paraíba, Ceará, Rio Grande do Norte states). Repente is the canonical extended-improvised-verse form of cantadores (poet-singers) performing in pairs, often using rabeca (Northeastern fiddle) or viola (Brazilian ten-string lute) accompaniment. Embolada is the faster-tempo subform with characteristic mocking-and-humorous-couplet improvisation, typically over a pandeiro frame-drum beat.

items.name: Lambada and carimbó (Amazonian Pará)
items.lineage: Brazilian carimbó traditional Afro-Pará dance-music of the Amazonian Pará state, descended from West-African enslaved-population cultural memory. Lambada is the 1980s commercial-pop derivative of carimbó that achieved international fame through Kaoma's 1989 hit "Chorando se Foi" and the Brazilian Lambada dance-craze. Distinguished from broader Brazilian samba-and-forró by carimbó's Amazonian-Pará regional base and characteristic ass-jiggling tribal-rhythmic-pulse.

items.name: Coco brasileiro (NE Brazilian work-song)
items.lineage: Brazilian coco northeastern-Brazilian song-and-dance tradition of Pernambuco, Paraíba, and Alagoas, descended from the African-Brazilian colonial-period rural-work-song tradition (coco was originally a coconut-husking work-song with stamping-rhythm accompaniment). Performance: lead singer with chorus response, hand-clapping or ganzá-shaker rhythm, occasional pandeiro frame-drum. Repertoire spans rural-worker thematic content, coastal-fishing themes, and romantic-couplet improvisation. Genre revival under Nação Zumbi and Chico Science in 1990s integrated coco with rock-and-electronic-production.

items.name: Classical period (1750-1820)
items.lineage: European art-music period c.1750-1820 centered on Vienna, codifying balanced sonata-form, periodic-phrase symmetry, and the Classical orchestra (strings, paired woodwinds and brass, timpani). The Haydn-Mozart-Beethoven trinity established the canonical symphony, string quartet, sonata, and piano concerto repertoires. Distinguished from preceding Baroque by Classical period's homophonic textures, clear cadential punctuation, and dramatic-rhetorical phrase structure.

items.name: Early Romantic (1800-1850)
items.lineage: European art-music period c.1800-1850 emerging from late Beethoven through the first generation of explicitly Romantic composers. Characterized by expanded chromatic harmony, programmatic narrative content, virtuoso performer-composer figures, and the lieder cycle as song-form. Schubert's 600+ songs, Schumann's piano-cycles, Chopin's piano-études-and-nocturnes, and Mendelssohn's symphonies constitute the canonical core.

items.name: Late Romantic (1850-1910)
items.lineage: European art-music period c.1850-1910 expanding the Romantic vocabulary into extreme chromaticism (Wagner), massive orchestral forces (Mahler, Strauss, Bruckner), nationalist-folk integration (Dvořák, Smetana, Borodin), and the gradual approach to tonal dissolution. Wagner's Tristan chord (1859) is often cited as the precipitating moment of tonal crisis. The German-Austrian symphonic tradition reached its maximum extent with Mahler's 1000-performer Eighth Symphony (1910).

items.name: The Mighty Handful (Russian nationalist five)
items.lineage: Nineteenth-century Russian nationalist-composer collective in Saint Petersburg (Mily Balakirev, César Cui, Modest Mussorgsky, Nikolai Rimsky-Korsakov, Alexander Borodin), articulating a distinct Russian art-music identity through folk-melodic integration, modal-and-pentatonic vocabulary, programmatic-nationalist narrative content, and characteristic Russian-orchestration-color techniques. Mussorgsky's Boris Godunov (1869, revised 1872) and Pictures at an Exhibition (1874) constitute the canonical type-specimens. Direct precursor to Stravinsky's pre-1914 ballet trilogy.
