The sound is thin bright guitar played in chords rather than riffs, chorused melodic bass, dry gated drums and detached Spanish lyrics that used camp and irony where earlier Argentine rock used protest directness. It differs from British post-punk in its warmer dance-pop pulse and from later rock latino in its deliberate refusal of anthemic scale.

items.name: J-Pixie
items.lineage: Tokyo kawaii-electropop idiom crystallized around 2011-2016 in Yasutaka Nakata's Harajuku productions and the Kyary Pamyu Pamyu records — 128-135 BPM four-on-the-floor with sidechained saw-supersaw chords, pitched-up and heavily formant-shifted girlish lead vocals stacked in unison, toy-timbre glockenspiel and music-box countermelodies, abrupt key-lifting bridges, and dense chopped vocal-sample fills replacing conventional drum breaks.
items.description: J-pixie is the hyper-bright, toy-timbred wing of 2010s Japanese electropop, produced almost entirely in the box around a small circle of Tokyo auteurs and their Harajuku-styled idol vocalists. It is defined by pitch-shifted, hard-tuned childlike vocals layered many deep, candy-colored supersaw chords, music-box and glockenspiel hooks, and structural whiplash — a chorus can modulate, drop out or splinter into chopped vocal confetti within four bars. Where mainstream J-pop keeps a band-shaped arrangement and enka-inflected phrasing, this style is fully synthetic and deliberately weightless.
exemplars: Kyary Pamyu Pamyu — Pamyu Pamyu Revolution

items.name: Cantautora Mexicana
items.lineage: Mexican women's singer-songwriter lineage running from Guadalajara and Mexico City in the late 1990s through the 2000s-2020s Natalia Lafourcade and Carla Morrison records — nylon-string or small-body acoustic guitar with accordion, jarana and requinto colorings, moderate 3/4 vals and 2/4 bolero-son frames beside plain pop 4/4, close-miked conversational mezzo vocals with minimal vibrato, and first-person lyric writing that reclaims son jarocho and bolero repertoire rather than importing Anglo folk-rock forms.
items.description: Cantautora mexicana names the women-led singer-songwriter current that consolidated in Mexico from the late 1990s, distinct both from the male nueva canción troubadours and from the rock en español bands its authors often emerged out of. The sound is intimate and acoustic-centred — nylon guitar, accordion, jarana and light string writing under a close, unforced voice — with harmonic vocabulary drawn from bolero and son jarocho rather than Anglo folk. It differs from Latin pop balladry by keeping arrangements small and lyric-first, and from traditional son by treating those forms as authorial material.

items.name: Nouvelle Chanson Française
items.lineage: French song renewal launched in Nantes, Brest and Paris in the early 1990s by Dominique A and Miossec and extended through Vincent Delerm, Benjamin Biolay, Camille and Keren Ann — spare drum-machine or brushed-kit pulses at 70-110 BPM, single electric guitar or upright piano harmony with occasional string quartet, near-spoken low-dynamic French diction placed loud and dry in the mix, and Gainsbourg-descended prosody applied to indie-rock and electronic textures rather than orchestral variété.
items.description: Nouvelle chanson française is the post-1990 reinvention of French art-song, begun when Dominique A and Miossec recorded literate French lyrics over lo-fi drum machines and single guitars instead of the orchestras of classic variété. Its markers are austere arrangements, dry close vocals delivered at speaking volume and near the bottom of the range, and harmony borrowed from indie rock, minimalism and electronics. Compared with classic chanson it is quieter, less theatrical and structurally looser; compared with French indie rock it never subordinates the text to the band.

items.name: Operatic Pop
items.lineage: Cross-over idiom commercialized from Milan, London and Los Angeles in the mid-1990s by producers Mauro Malavasi, Frank Peterson, David Foster and Simon Cowell — classically trained legit or bel canto vocal production mounted on slow 6/8 and 4/4 pop-ballad harmony at 60-80 BPM, full studio string orchestra plus choir with sustained-pad reinforcement, key-lift final choruses, and Italian, Latin or pseudo-liturgical text sung with continuous vibrato over close-miked pop-scale dynamics.
items.description: Operatic pop, or popera, is the studio-built crossover style that put classically trained voices on top of pop ballad structures, commercially fixed by Andrea Bocelli's mid-1990s records and the Il Divo and Josh Groban projects that followed. Sonically it combines a full orchestral string-and-choir bed, sustained synthesizer reinforcement and a modern compressed pop mix with continuous operatic vibrato and legit vocal placement. It is distinguished from actual opera by its through-mixed close-miking, fixed pop song form and absence of drama, and from orchestral pop ballads by the vocal technique itself.
exemplars: Sarah Brightman — Time to Say Goodbye
Charlotte Church — Voice of an Angel

items.name: Celtic Rock
items.lineage: Ireland and Scotland, 1970-1985, codified by Horslips, Moving Hearts, Runrig and the Pogues — traditional reel and jig melodies in Dorian and Mixolydian modes transferred to distorted twin electric guitars and uilleann pipes or fiddle in unison, bodhrán doubling a rock kit in cut-time 4/4 and 6/8 at 120-160 BPM, Hammond-style combo organ pads, and unornamented shouted-chorus singing of Irish- and Scots-language or ballad-derived texts.
items.description: Celtic rock formed in Ireland and Scotland in the early 1970s when bands took session-repertoire reels, jigs and ballads and played them on amplified rock instrumentation without smoothing the modal melodies into blues shapes. The defining texture is pipes, whistle or fiddle carrying the tune in unison with distorted guitar over a bodhrán-reinforced rock kit, with long instrumental set-medleys standing in for solos. It differs from British folk rock in leaning on dance-tune repertoire rather than balladry, and from trad revival in accepting distortion, volume and rock song form outright.
exemplars: Runrig — The Cutter and the Clan
The Pogues — Rum Sodomy & the Lash
Thin Lizzy — Whiskey in the Jar

items.name: Etherpop
items.lineage: North American and northern-European bedroom-to-label electronic pop of 2011-2016 — Purity Ring, Grimes, Chvrches and Sylvan Esso — built at 90-125 BPM on pitched vocal samples, reverb-drenched bell and marimba-timbre synth leads, sub-bass and trap-derived hi-hat rolls under a high, breathy, heavily reverbed and layered female lead, arrangements assembled in the box with almost no acoustic sourcing and no live drum performance.
items.description: Etherpop is the airy, reverb-saturated strain of electronic pop that surfaced around 2011 out of laptop production and blog culture, sitting between synthpop songwriting and post-witch-house sound design. Its signatures are a high breathy lead vocal multiplied and drowned in long reverbs, glassy bell-and-mallet synth patches, trap-inherited hi-hat subdivision and a heavy sub-bass floor, all rendered entirely in the box. Unlike dream pop it has no guitars and no band performance; unlike hyperpop it stays smooth and consonant rather than distorted and maximal.
exemplars: Chvrches — The Bones of What You Believe

items.name: Türkçe Drill
items.lineage: Istanbul and Turkish-diaspora Berlin, 2019 onward, adapting UK and Brooklyn drill to Turkish — 138-145 BPM half-time patterns with sliding 808 glides, triplet hi-hat rolls and skeletal snare on the third beat, melodic hooks sampled or replayed from arabesk and saz lines in Phrygian-dominant colour, and a low, clipped, heavily consonant Turkish flow tracked on an SM7B in home rooms and mixed entirely in the box.
items.description: Türkçe drill is the Turkish-language branch of drill, taking shape from roughly 2019 among Istanbul rappers and Turkish-German producers who fed arabesk and saz melody into the UK drill template. The beats keep drill's sliding 808 glides, third-beat snare placement and triplet hat rolls, but the top line is usually a minor or Phrygian-dominant plucked motif rather than a dark piano or bell, and darbuka fills sometimes replace stock percussion. It is separated from Turkish trap by its slower half-time feel and menacing sparseness, and from UK drill by its melodic sourcing and vocal cadence.

items.name: Música de Fondo
items.lineage: Hispanophone easy-listening orchestral idiom produced in Mexico City, Madrid and Buenos Aires from the mid-1950s to the late 1970s for radio, hotel and film-interlude use — bolero, vals and light-Latin themes at 60-100 BPM arranged for massed muted strings, wordless mixed choir, vibraphone, harp glissandi and brushed kit, with melody always doubled at the octave and dynamics compressed flat so the music sits under speech.
items.description: Música de fondo is the Spanish-language wing of orchestral easy listening: instrumental arrangements of boleros, valses and pop themes made in Mexico City, Madrid and Buenos Aires between the mid-1950s and the 1970s expressly to play beneath conversation, radio programming and film scenes. The scoring is massed violins doubled at the octave with harp, vibraphone, wordless choir and brushes, recorded warm and mastered with almost no dynamic range. It differs from the bolero orquestado it draws on by removing the singer and the drama, and from American mood music by keeping Latin dance forms and phrasing intact.

items.name: Dancefloor Drum and Bass
items.lineage: London and Bristol, 2007 onward, consolidated by Hospital Records, Sub Focus and Wilkinson — 174 BPM two-step breaks with a hard-quantized kick-snare grid rather than chopped amen edits, supersaw and reese-hybrid bass riffs written as pop hooks, an eight-bar build-and-drop structure imported from EDM, and sung topline vocals in full pop song form mixed loud over heavily sidechained sub.
items.description: Dancefloor drum and bass is the festival-facing, vocal-led branch of D&B that took over UK dance charts from about 2010, largely through the Hospital and RAM rosters. It keeps the 174 BPM two-step break but replaces chopped breakbeat editing with a clean quantized grid, and builds tracks around sung choruses and melodic supersaw drops arranged on the eight-bar build-and-release logic of big-room EDM. Against liquid D&B it is brighter and more compressed, against neurofunk it is consonant and hook-driven rather than sound-design driven, and against jungle it discards the breakbeat as an editing surface entirely.

items.name: Scenecore
items.lineage: American MySpace-era post-hardcore hybrid of roughly 2006-2011 centred on Ohio, Arizona and Florida bands like Attack Attack!, blessthefall and Brokencyde — down-tuned seven-string breakdowns at half-time against 170-200 BPM double-kick verses, alternating unclean screams and Auto-Tuned clean choruses, trance-derived supersaw and arpeggiated synth layers sitting on top of the guitars, and fully grid-edited digital tracking with replaced drum samples.
items.description: Scenecore is the late-2000s MySpace subculture's music: metalcore breakdowns and screamed verses spliced onto trance synths and Auto-Tuned pop choruses, made by American bands between roughly 2006 and 2011. Production is uniformly digital and grid-locked — sample-replaced triggered drums, quad-tracked down-tuned seven-string guitars, brickwalled masters — and songs cut abruptly between screamed half-time breakdowns and euphoric electronic hooks. It is distinguished from contemporary metalcore by the sincerity of its dance-pop material and from crunkcore by retaining real band instrumentation throughout.
exemplars: Asking Alexandria — Stand Up and Scream
I Set My Friends on Fire

items.name: Preschool Children's Music
items.lineage: North American commercial repertoire for children under six, professionalized from the 1950s Ella Jenkins and Mister Rogers broadcasts through Raffi's late-1970s Canadian albums and the 1990s Wiggles and Laurie Berkner catalogues — narrow-range diatonic melodies inside an octave at 90-120 BPM, strummed acoustic guitar or ukulele with glockenspiel and toy-piano color, four-square phrases with built-in call-and-response and gesture cues, and a bright, clearly enunciated adult voice doubled by a children's chorus.
items.description: Preschool children's music is the professional recorded repertoire written for under-sixes, distinct from playground-transmitted nursery rhyme in that it is composed, copyrighted and produced for records and television. The sound is deliberately transparent: one clear adult lead voice, a strummed guitar or ukulele, small tuned percussion, and melodies that stay inside an octave with heavy repetition and built-in participation cues. It differs from school-age kids' pop by avoiding drum programming and contemporary chart production, and from lullaby by its bright tempo and call-and-response function.
exemplars: Raffi — Singable Songs for the Very Young
Ella Jenkins — You'll Sing a Song and I'll Sing a Song
Fred Rogers — Won't You Be My Neighbor?

items.name: Tagalog Rap
items.lineage: Manila-centred Filipino-language hip hop that broke commercially in 1990 when Francis Magalona's 'Mga Kababayan Ko' and Andrew E's 'Humanap Ka Ng Panget' put Tagalog and Taglish flow over imported boom-bap and new-jack breaks, later hardened by Gloc-9's rapid multisyllabic socio-political verses and the 2010s FlipTop battle-league and Ex Battalion trap wave — typically 85-100 BPM sampled or programmed beats, a sung Tagalog hook over the chorus, and rhyme schemes exploiting the language's abundant open-vowel and -an/-in suffix endings.
items.description: Filipino-language rap that emerged in Metro Manila around 1990 and has stayed a mass-market pop form there rather than a niche, with Tagalog and Taglish verses over sampled boom-bap, later trap and drill production. Its signature is the density of syllables per bar that Tagalog's vowel-final words permit, paired with a melodic sung chorus drawn from OPM ballad convention. It differs from other Asian hip hop scenes in its battle-rap infrastructure (FlipTop) and from US rap in the near-universal presence of a full-voiced sung hook.

items.name: Torch Song
items.lineage: American cabaret-and-popular ballad of unrequited love, named for 'carrying a torch' and codified in the late-1920s Broadway and speakeasy revues by Helen Morgan and Libby Holman, then perfected on record between 1935 and 1960 by Billie Holiday, Judy Garland, Frank Sinatra and Julie London — slow rubato 32-bar AABA or verse-and-chorus forms at roughly 55-75 BPM, lush strings and muted brass or a solo piano, a spoken-to-sung verse preamble, and a conversational, near-confessional vocal that trades vibrato for microphone intimacy.
items.description: A slow, harmonically rich American ballad of thwarted love that grew out of 1920s Broadway and nightclub singing and reached its recorded apex on 1950s LPs by Sinatra, Holiday and London. It is defined by extreme rhythmic freedom against a plush orchestral or trio bed, a low dynamic floor exploiting close-microphone technique, and a lyric addressed to an absent lover. Unlike the blues it sits on Tin Pan Alley chromatic changes rather than a 12-bar frame, and unlike vocal-jazz standards generally it treats the melody as text delivery rather than a springboard for improvisation.
exemplars: Judy Garland — 'The Man That Got Away'
Frank Sinatra — 'In the Wee Small Hours'

items.name: J-Pop Rock
items.lineage: Japanese band-format pop-rock that crystallised in the early 1990s as the 'Big Beat' TV-tie-up era, driven by Being Inc. and Tsunku production and by Mr. Children, Spitz and B'z selling millions of singles — mid-tempo 100-140 BPM four-piece guitar-bass-drums arrangements with layered synth and string pads, dense pre-chorus modulations and abrupt key lifts into the sabi (hook), and a high, clear, near-vibratoless Japanese-language lead vocal sitting well forward of a heavily compressed digital-multitrack mix.
items.description: The band-driven mainstream of Japanese pop from roughly 1990 onward, where rock instrumentation serves an extremely developed pop songwriting grammar of long pre-choruses, secondary-dominant chains and last-chorus key changes. Production is bright, dry and digital, with the vocal placed unusually loud and clean relative to Western rock mixing. It is distinguished from Western pop-rock by that harmonic restlessness and vocal placement, and from J-rock proper by prioritising tie-up-single hooks over distortion and scene identity.

items.name: Ectofolk
items.lineage: An ethereal, largely female-fronted art-folk strain named after the 'Ecto' internet mailing list that formed around Happy Rhodes and Kate Bush in the early 1990s, drawing on Bush's 1980s art-pop, Celtic revival modality and 4AD's dream-pop production — free-flowing or slow 4/4 songs built on grand piano or fingerpicked acoustic guitar with harp, bowed strings and string-machine pads, multi-octave stacked wordless vocal choirs, and literary, mythic or interior lyrics delivered with a wide, cathedral-scale reverb.
items.description: A late-1980s-through-1990s singer-songwriter idiom, largely Anglo-American and largely woman-fronted, that fused Kate Bush's art-pop, Celtic-modal folk and 4AD-style reverberant production; the label itself comes from the Ecto listserv community that mapped the affinity. It is marked by piano- or fingerpicked-guitar foundations, minimal or absent drums, stacked wordless vocal choirs, and mythic or introspective texts. It differs from indie folk in its studio grandeur and vocal range, and from dream pop in retaining acoustic songwriter form rather than guitar texture as the primary material.

items.name: Gauze Pop
items.lineage: A soft-focus indie pop strain descended from Cocteau Twins and the 4AD roster of the mid-1980s and rebuilt after 2006 by Beach House, Mazzy Star's inheritors and the Captured Tracks/Sub Pop dream-pop wave — slow to mid 70-110 BPM songs whose guitars are run through chorus and long plate or hall reverb until attack disappears, breathy or reverb-veiled vocals mixed at or below the instruments with lyrics semi-intelligible by design, organ or string-machine pads, and simple two- or three-chord loops in mixolydian or aeolian colour.
items.description: A hazy, texture-first branch of dream pop in which reverb and modulation are used to blur every transient and push the voice into the instrumental bed, first on 4AD records in the 1980s and revived broadly from the mid-2000s. Songs are short and pop-shaped but harmonically static, relying on timbre and slow crescendo rather than chord movement. It is quieter and cleaner than shoegaze, which foregrounds distortion and volume, and more song-bound than ambient, which abandons verse-chorus form entirely.

items.name: Dembow (Dominican)
items.lineage: Dominican street-dance genre built on the 'Pounder'/Dem Bow riddim exported from Kingston in 1990, localised in Santo Domingo barrios through the 2000s by producers such as DJ Scuff and Bubloy and MCs Omega, El Alfa and Chimbala — 110-125 BPM boom-ch-boom-chick two-bar drum pattern with a hard sampled snare or timbal on the offbeat, minimal or absent harmonic content, shouted call-and-response Spanish hooks with heavy vocal chopping and pitch effects, and abrupt sound-effect stabs replacing melodic instrumentation.
items.description: The Dominican Republic's dominant street-pop form, derived from the Jamaican Dem Bow riddim that also seeded reggaeton but developed separately in Santo Domingo from the mid-2000s. It is faster, sparser and more percussive than reggaeton: often little more than the riddim, a sub-bass, sound-effect stabs and a shouted Spanish chant traded between MC and crowd. Compared to reggaeton it largely discards sung melody and chord loops; compared to merengue it keeps the aggressive tempo but replaces the live tambora-and-güira ensemble with sampled drums.

items.name: Aussietronica
items.lineage: The Australian electronic-pop lineage running from Melbourne and Sydney indie-dance of the early 2000s — Cut Copy, The Presets and Pnau on Modular Recordings — into the post-2011 Sydney beat-scene of Flume, Hermitude and Chet Faker; characterised by 100-125 BPM tempos, warm analogue-poly and wavetable pads over crisp sampled drum programming, heavily pitched and chopped vocal samples used as lead melody, hooks built from a single filtered synth swell rather than a chord progression, and a glossy but wide, reverberant mixdown.
items.description: A loosely bounded Australian electronic scene, first as Modular-label indie-dance in Melbourne and Sydney in the 2000s and then as the Flume-centred future-bass and beat production of the 2010s. It is identifiable by melodic synth-lead writing, chopped and pitched vocal fragments in place of a sung topline, and a bright, spatially wide mix. It sits apart from European big-room EDM in its indie-pop songwriting instincts, and from UK bass music in favouring warm harmonic pads over sub-bass weight.

items.name: Rock Cristiano
items.lineage: Spanish-language Christian rock that took shape in Argentina and Mexico from the late 1980s, with Rescate forming in Buenos Aires in 1991 and Marcos Witt's CanZion label industrialising Latin worship recording out of Durango and Houston — mid-tempo 80-130 BPM guitar-band arrangements over pop-rock and rock-nacional forms, congregational-friendly diatonic progressions with a modulated final chorus, doubled distorted and clean guitars, and Spanish devotional or evangelistic lyrics delivered in a full chest voice with a large backing-vocal crowd.
items.description: Spanish-language Christian rock and rock-worship, developed from the late 1980s onward across Argentina, Mexico and the US Latino church, and distributed largely through denominational labels such as CanZion rather than secular radio. Musically it borrows rock nacional and pop-rock arrangement wholesale while keeping congregational singability: diatonic progressions, a single memorable refrain, and a chorus key lift. It differs from Anglo CCM chiefly in absorbing Latin American rock idioms and, at its heavier end, ska and punk; it differs from traditional himnos in using a full amplified band and first-person devotional address.

items.name: Tecnobanda
items.lineage: Jalisco-and-Sinaloa hybrid of the early 1990s in which the acoustic banda sinaloense wind section was partly replaced by synthesizers and a trap kit, popularised by Banda Machos, Banda Maguey and Banda Móvil out of Villa Corona and Guadalajara and tied to the quebradita dance craze of 1992-96 — fast 140-170 BPM polka and cumbia rhythms, a synth patch imitating the tuba bass line, clarinets and trumpets doubling the vocal melody in thirds, tarola-and-tambora backbeat played on drum kit, and shouted gritos punctuating the choruses.
items.description: A Mexican electrified banda variant that emerged around 1990 in Jalisco and spread through the quebradita dance boom in Mexico and the US Southwest. It keeps banda's clarinet-and-brass melodic doubling and breakneck polka tempos but substitutes a keyboard bass for the sousaphone and a drum kit for the tambora-and-tarola pair, producing a lighter, more portable ensemble. It is distinguished from banda sinaloense proper by that synthetic bass and reduced wind roster, and from grupero and technocumbia by retaining the banda wind sound rather than leading with keyboards alone.

items.name: Trap Mexicano
items.lineage: Mexican Spanish-language trap that consolidated after 2015 out of the Guanajuato, Monterrey and Mexico City rap scenes — Santa Fe Klan, Alemán, Gera MX and Neto Peña — over Atlanta-derived production: 130-150 BPM half-time grids, long-decay 808 sub-kicks, triplet and 32nd-note hi-hat rolls, sparse minor-key piano or detuned-bell loops, Auto-Tuned sung-rapped hooks, and barrio-Spanish lyrics that frequently graft cumbia, banda or mariachi samples and guest vocalists onto the beat.
items.description: The Mexican branch of Spanish-language trap, established from roughly 2015 in Guanajuato, Monterrey and Mexico City and now a mainstream chart force. It uses standard Atlanta trap architecture — sustained 808 sub-kicks, rolled hi-hats, minor-key loop hooks — but is marked by nylon-guitar, cumbia and banda interpolations and by heavy collaboration with regional-Mexican singers. It differs from Puerto Rican Latin trap in accent, in that regional-Mexican fusion, and in a more narrative barrio-realist lyric tradition inherited from Mexican rap of the 2000s.

items.name: Sunshine Pop
items.lineage: Los Angeles studio-pop of roughly 1965-1970 made by session-band productions around Curt Boettcher, Gary Usher and Roger Nichols and by vocal groups such as The Association and The Mamas & the Papas — bright major-key songs at 90-130 BPM with jazz-derived major-seventh and added-sixth harmony, four- and five-part close vocal blocks stacked on multitrack, orchestral colour from harpsichord, flutes, French horn and vibraphone, brushed or lightly played drums, and lyrics of pastoral optimism cut with wistfulness.
items.description: A Los Angeles studio-pop idiom of the late 1960s, built by Wrecking Crew sessions and multitrack vocal overdubbing around producers like Curt Boettcher and Gary Usher. Its markers are lush close-harmony vocal blocks, jazz-inflected major-seventh harmony, chamber-orchestral instrumental colour, and a deliberately bright, reverb-chamber sheen. It is distinguished from folk rock by that harmonic and orchestral sophistication, from baroque pop by its sunnier affect and vocal-group centre, and from the surf lineage by abandoning the beach-band instrumentation entirely.
exemplars: Roger Nichols & the Small Circle of Friends

items.name: Disco House
items.lineage: Mid-1990s house subgenre built in Chicago, New York and Paris from looped and filtered 1970s disco records, codified by Daft Punk, DJ Sneak, Armand Van Helden and Basement Jaxx circa 1995-2000 — 118-128 BPM four-on-the-floor with 909 kick and open hat on the upbeat, a chopped string or guitar loop swept through a resonant low-pass filter, sidechained pumping on every bar, and clipped diva vocal snippets used as rhythmic hooks rather than sung verses
items.description: Disco house emerged in the mid-1990s when producers in Chicago, New York and Paris began looping four- and eight-bar chunks of 1970s Philadelphia and Salsoul records over programmed 909 drums. Its signature is the filter sweep: a full-band disco loop opened and closed across sixteen bars so the arrangement is carried by timbre rather than by chord change, with heavy bus compression pumping against the kick. Unlike deep house it keeps the borrowed record audible and celebratory, and unlike Chicago house it is loop-based collage rather than drum-machine-and-keyboard composition.

items.name: Fvnky Rimex
items.lineage: Indonesian bedroom-DJ remix idiom of the late 2010s and 2020s, spread through TikTok, SoundCloud and Joox by producers styling themselves 'DJ [name] fvnky' — descended from funkot and dangdut koplo, it runs 140-160 BPM with a hard four-on-the-floor kick, a stuttering sampled kendang or synthetic tom fill on the turnaround, a shrill sawtooth or FM lead riffing on the pop melody being remixed, and pitch-shifted vocal fragments cut from the source track
items.description: Fvnky rimex ('funky remix' in Indonesian orthographic play) is a bedroom-producer remix culture that took hold across Indonesia and Malaysia in the late 2010s, circulated almost entirely as compressed MP3 and short-form video audio. It takes an existing pop, dangdut or sentimental ballad, strips it to a vocal hook, and drives it with the funkot lineage's fast pounding kick, gated tom rolls and cheap workstation leads, usually clipped into distortion by design. Compared with its parent funkot it is shorter, more melody-forward and built for phone speakers, and unlike Western bootleg house it makes no attempt to hide the preset-library timbres.

items.name: Acid Rock
items.lineage: San Francisco and Los Angeles psychedelic rock of 1966-1970 codified by the Grateful Dead, Jefferson Airplane, Blue Cheer and the 13th Floor Elevators — moderate-tempo blues-derived modal vamps stretched into long extemporised jams, saturated single-coil guitar through fuzz and spring reverb, heavy use of feedback and Leslie-treated organ, wailing declamatory vocals, and a rhythm section that swells and recedes rather than keeping fixed dynamics
items.description: Acid rock formed on the West Coast ballroom circuit in 1966-67 as bands built extended improvisations over one- or two-chord blues and modal vamps to accompany light shows and long dances. The sound is defined by sustained fuzz and feedback guitar, drifting Leslie organ, chamber and spring reverb applied to whole mixes, and structures that abandon verse-chorus timing for open-ended soloing. It is louder and more blues-pentatonic than the ornate studio psychedelia of British bands, and less song-oriented than garage rock, sitting directly upstream of early heavy metal.
exemplars: Grateful Dead — Anthem of the Sun

items.name: Rap DF
items.lineage: Mexico City hip-hop consolidated in the Distrito Federal barrios from the mid-1990s through the 2000s by Cartel de Santa's contemporaries, Control Machete's Monterrey rivals, Sociedad Café and the Neblinna City / Nezahualcóyotl crews — 85-95 BPM boom-bap breakbeats sampled from Mexican rock and bolero LPs, filtered upright-bass loops, turntable cuts on the hook, and a dense chilango slang delivery with clipped consonants and end-of-bar rhyme clusters
items.description: Rap DF is the hip-hop of Mexico City proper and its eastern conurbation, distinct from the Monterrey rap-rock wave that broke nationally first. It is sample-based and stubbornly boom-bap, drawing loops from Mexican rock urbano, bolero and film-score vinyl, cut on cheap samplers in home and basement studios, with scratched hooks and posse cuts kept as standard form well past their US expiry date. What marks it apart is the vocal: fast chilango argot, heavy use of albur wordplay, and lyrics about specific colonias rather than generic street imagery.

items.name: Velha Guarda
items.lineage: Rio de Janeiro's samba old-guard repertory, formalised from the late 1960s when Paulinho da Viola, Cartola, Nelson Cavaquinho and Zé Keti brought the elder composers of Portela and Mangueira into the recording studio — moderate 2/4 samba at 90-105 BPM with telecoteco pandeiro, surdo de marcação on beat two, tamborim and reco-reco, cavaquinho comping against seven-string guitar countermelody, and a plain, unforced chest voice with call-and-response chorus
items.description: Velha guarda names the veteran composers' wings of Rio's samba schools and, by extension, the acoustic samba de terreiro they carried — songs written in the 1930s-50s but preserved and recorded by their authors and by younger disciples from the late 1960s on. The sound is a small circle: hand percussion, cavaquinho, seven-string guitar bass lines, and unamplified singing with a responding chorus, recorded live to tape with minimal separation. Against the escola de samba bateria it is quiet and conversational, and against pagode of the 1980s it keeps older harmonic turns and avoids banjo, tantã and studio gloss.

items.name: Rap Político
items.lineage: Spanish-language political hip-hop formed in the 1990s across Madrid, Santiago, Havana, Caracas and Mexico City — codified by Chile's Tiro de Gracia and Ana Tijoux, Cuba's Orishas and Los Aldeanos, and Spain's Def Con Dos and SFDK — 85-95 BPM sample loops drawn from nueva canción, son and Andean folk records, sparse scratched hooks, and long unhurried verses of denunciatory rhetoric delivered in an oratorical register closer to protest song than to battle rap
items.description: Rap político is the branch of Spanish-language hip-hop that inherited the addressee and rhetoric of nueva canción rather than the boasting conventions of US rap, taking hold in the 1990s in Chile, Cuba, Spain and Mexico. Production is typically sample-based and mid-tempo, often looping Andean flutes, charango or 1970s protest-song LPs so the beat itself carries a political citation, with the vocal mixed forward and dry for intelligibility. It differs from conscious rap in the US by naming specific governments, coups and dictatorships, and from nueva canción by keeping the breakbeat and the rhymed metrical grid.

items.name: Cumbia 420
items.lineage: Argentine subgenre formed circa 2015-2018 in Rosario and the Buenos Aires conurbano, codified by Perro Primo, Papu DJ, DT.Bilardo and popularised by L-Gante from 2020 — cumbia villera's keyboard riffs and güira slowed to roughly 95-100 BPM over a trap-derived 808 sub and triplet hi-hats, with cheap workstation lead patches, plate-heavy vocal reverb, and Auto-Tuned half-sung barrio narration about cannabis, money and neighbourhood life
items.description: Cumbia 420 was assembled in Rosario home studios in the mid-2010s by producers who kept cumbia villera's synth-organ hooks and güira shuffle but replaced the live percussion section with an 808 kick, sub-bass and trap hi-hat rolls. Its records are short, loop-locked and mixed hot for phone playback, with the vocal soaked in Auto-Tune and long plate reverb rather than the dry shouted delivery of 2000s villera. It sits between cumbia and Latin trap: slower and more melodic than trap, harmonically simpler and far more bass-heavy than digital cumbia from the Buenos Aires club scene.

items.name: Social Media Pop
items.lineage: Platform-native pop that consolidated after 2018 as TikTok became the primary discovery channel — written and produced by bedroom auteurs and topline camps around a fifteen-second hook placed in the first eight seconds, typically 110-140 BPM with programmed 808 or trap-adjacent drums, a single sticky vocal motif stacked in octaves and thirds, minimal harmonic movement, and conversational close-miked lead vocals treated with hard tuning and short slap delay
items.description: Social media pop names the songwriting and production practice that grew up around short-form video from roughly 2018 onward, in which the arrangement is engineered backwards from a loopable hook rather than toward a chorus. Records are short, front-loaded, harmonically static, and mixed to survive phone speakers and lossy codecs, with the lead vocal recorded on a dynamic mic in an untreated room and stacked into wide unison. Unlike mainstream radio pop it accepts amateur-sounding capture as an aesthetic, and unlike hyperpop it avoids extreme distortion and formant play in favour of legibility.

items.name: Scorecore
items.lineage: Trailer-music idiom industrialised in Los Angeles from the late 1990s by production libraries such as Immediate Music, Two Steps From Hell and Audiomachine — 70-90 BPM half-time epic cues built on ostinato low strings, wordless Latinate choir, staccato brass stabs, taiko and orchestral bass-drum hits on a rising two-minute arc of statement, breakdown and full-tutti climax, sampled libraries layered with live overdubs and mastered to near-constant peak loudness
items.description: Scorecore is the commercial trailer-cue repertoire that split off from film scoring in the late 1990s, written for licensing libraries rather than for picture. Its conventions are rigid: a slow-building ostinato in divisi low strings, wordless choir on open vowels, brass in unison rhythmic hits, and enormous layered percussion, all compressed and limited far beyond orchestral norms so the cue reads over dialogue and explosions. Compared with concert-hall late-Romantic writing it is harmonically static and structurally formulaic; compared with a film score proper it has no thematic obligation to a narrative and exists purely as a two-minute escalation.

items.name: Redneck Rock
items.lineage: Austin, Texas hybrid of 1972-1979 documented by Jan Reid's 'The Improbable Rise of Redneck Rock' and centred on the Armadillo World Headquarters — codified by Willie Nelson, Jerry Jeff Walker, Michael Martin Murphey and Doug Sahm, it plays honky-tonk and western-swing forms at rock volume with electric guitar and pedal steel trading leads, fiddle over a shuffle or train beat, loose live-in-the-room drumming, and a laconic drawled vocal that keeps country phrasing but rock attitude
items.description: Redneck rock — also called progressive country or cosmic cowboy music — is the Austin scene of the 1970s in which longhaired players and honky-tonk audiences shared the same dance halls. Musically it keeps country song form, pedal steel and fiddle but adds rock rhythm-section weight, extended instrumental sections and looser, less-produced tracking than contemporaneous Nashville records. It is distinguished from outlaw country as a marketing category by being a specific city's live scene, and from country rock by coming from country players moving toward rock rather than from Californian rock bands moving toward country.
exemplars: Michael Martin Murphey — Cosmic Cowboy Souvenir

items.name: Gaming EDM
items.lineage: Copyright-free dance music built for streamers and gameplay video from about 2011 onward, centred on the NoCopyrightSounds, Monstercat and Trap Nation catalogues — 128-150 BPM electro house, future bass and melodic dubstep with a supersaw or vocal-chop build, a filtered eight-bar riser into a snare roll, and a wide detuned lead drop, produced entirely in the box by teenage and early-twenties producers and mastered loud for compressed video audio
items.description: Gaming EDM is the body of royalty-free electronic dance music that grew around YouTube and Twitch after 2011, distributed by labels that license tracks for use in gameplay videos and streams. It follows big-room and future-bass conventions strictly — long risers, a beat-dropout bar, a detuned supersaw or chopped-vocal drop, and sidechained pumping — but is written to sit under commentary rather than to fill a festival field, so mids are scooped and the loudness is constant. It differs from festival big-room EDM chiefly in distribution economics and in the absence of a named DJ persona; from hardstyle it keeps a straight kick and a much brighter melodic register.

items.name: New Jersey Rap
items.lineage: Hip-hop of Newark, East Orange, Jersey City and South Jersey running from Sugar Hill Records' Englewood sessions in 1979 through Naughty by Nature, Redman and the Fugees in the 1990s to the Jersey-club-driven drill of Bandmanrill and Sha EK after 2020 — early phase is East Coast boom bap at 90-95 BPM with dusty soul loops and hard-swung snares; the recent phase runs 140-150 BPM over Jersey club's kick-kick-pause-kick bed-squeak pattern with sliding 808s
items.description: New Jersey rap is a distinct East Coast lineage that predates and then ran parallel to New York's, from Sugar Hill Records in Englewood through the Newark-and-Illtown axis of Naughty by Nature, Redman, Queen Latifah and the Fugees. Its modern form is defined by Newark club music: rappers in the 2020s ride the 140-BPM Jersey club triplet-kick pattern with the signature bed-squeak sample, giving drill-style rhyming a dance-floor tempo no other regional scene uses. Against New York drill it is faster, bouncier and built on a club rhythm rather than a sliding UK-derived 808 pattern, and against Philadelphia rap it foregrounds the DJ-club pulse over the soul loop.
exemplars: Queen Latifah — All Hail the Queen

items.name: Epicore (trailer-music epic)
items.lineage: Los Angeles trailer-music production libraries of the 2000s — Immediate Music, Two Steps From Hell (Thomas Bergersen and Nick Phoenix, founded 2006), Audiomachine — codified a consumer-facing 'epic' idiom sold direct to listeners from 2010 onward: 80-130 BPM ostinato string figures, unison low brass and horn calls, wordless Latinate choir, taiko and orchestral bass-drum hits on a rising two-minute build-to-drop arc, sampled-orchestra libraries layered with synth sub and cinematic braams.
items.description: A production-library idiom that hardened into a listener-facing genre once trailer houses began selling their cues as albums around 2010. It uses full sampled orchestra plus choir strictly as an intensity machine: static or slowly-rotating minor-modal harmony, relentless quaver ostinati, and a percussion floor of taiko, ensemble bass drum and processed sub-hits, all mastered brick-flat. It differs from film scoring proper in having no dramatic function to follow — the entire form is a single monotonic crescendo — and from symphonic metal in carrying no guitars, band, or lead vocalist.

items.name: Chicano rap
items.lineage: Mexican-American rap of Los Angeles, San Diego and South Texas codified by Kid Frost's 'La Raza' (1990) over El Chicano's 'Viva Tirado' and carried on by Cypress Hill, Delinquent Habits, Lil Rob and Mr. Capone-E — mid-tempo 85-95 BPM G-funk-adjacent beats built on East LA oldies and Latin-soul samples, live-feel bass and whining portamento synth leads, Spanglish couplets, lowrider-cruise subject matter and sung Chicano-soul hooks.
items.description: Emerged in Southern California around 1990 as Mexican-American MCs adapted West Coast rap to barrio and lowrider culture, with a parallel Texas stream through Houston. Its signature is the sampled East LA oldie or Latin-soul break under laid-back 90-BPM drums, sung Chicano-soul choruses, and code-switching Spanish-English delivery. It differs from mainstream G-funk in its sample sources and its explicitly Mexican-American identity politics, and from Latin trap in predating trap drum programming entirely.

items.name: Deboxe (Brazilian eletrofunk)
items.lineage: Southern-Brazilian eletrofunk stream named for the Rio Grande do Sul party-and-label brand Deboxe, consolidated from roughly 2018 onward out of gaúcho DJ crews reworking Rio funk montagem practice — 130-150 BPM four-on-the-floor with hard-clipped distorted 808 sub-kicks, gunshot and vocal-chop stabs, radically pitched-down or sped-up MC acapellas, and long automated build-and-drop edits made entirely in the DAW for sound-car and open-air baile playback.
items.description: A DJ-driven eletrofunk style from Rio Grande do Sul and the wider Brazilian south, spread after 2018 through the Deboxe party circuit, YouTube and short-video platforms. It is defined by deliberately overdriven sub-bass kicks, minimal melodic content, chopped MC vocals treated as percussion, and edits engineered for the distortion of car and street sound systems. Against Rio's mandelão it is faster and more four-on-the-floor, and against brega funk it drops the melodic hooks almost entirely.

items.name: Trap chileno
items.lineage: Santiago trap scene that broke nationally around 2017 through Pablo Chill-E's Shishigang, Ceaese, Polimá Westcoast and Gianluca — 130-145 BPM half-time trap programming with rolling triplet hats and long 808 glides, heavy Auto-Tune melodic delivery, and specifically Chilean street slang (coa) and población narrative that separates it from Puerto Rican and Argentine trap.
items.description: Chilean trap consolidated in Santiago's peripheral comunas from about 2016-2017, built in home studios on Atlanta-derived 808 and hi-hat templates but sung in dense Chilean slang with heavy pitch correction. Its production leans darker and sparser than Argentine trap and avoids the dembow pulse that defines reggaeton, while a parallel wing (Polimá Westcoast, Young Cister) pushes toward melodic R&B. The regional marker is lexical and rhythmic-declamatory rather than instrumental.

items.name: Cumbia chilena
items.lineage: Chilean adaptation of Colombian cumbia established in Santiago in the early 1960s by Luis Alberto Martínez's La Sonora Palacios and Los Vikings 5 — faster than its Colombian source at roughly 110-130 BPM, driven by electric organ or piano guajeo, two-trumpet-and-trombone brass riffs, timbales-and-congas kit playing and güiro on the offbeat, with unison chorus refrains; revived from the late 1990s as nueva cumbia chilena by Chico Trujillo and Juana Fe with punk-speed tempos and brass grit.
items.description: Chile localized Colombian cumbia from the early 1960s into a brisk, brass-and-organ dance music known as 'cumbia sound', anchored by La Sonora Palacios and Sonora de Tommy Rey and inseparable from Chilean weddings and Fiestas Patrias. Its markers are a faster tempo than Colombian cumbia, an electric-organ or piano guajeo carrying the harmony, and a compact trumpet-trombone front line rather than gaita or accordion. The 1990s nueva cumbia wave added punk and ska attack while keeping the same rhythmic skeleton.

items.name: Música sonorense (Sonoran regional)
items.lineage: Regional-Mexican strain of the state of Sonora — norteño with alto saxophone and tambora on the Hermosillo-Ciudad Obregón corridor through the later twentieth century, then reoriented after 2019 by Hermosillo's Natanael Cano and Caborca's Luis R Conriquez into corridos tumbados: 80-110 BPM sierreño-style requinto and twelve-string acoustic guitar over tuba or tololoche bass, no drum kit, with speech-close narrative vocal delivery and trap-adjacent song lengths.
items.description: The Sonoran wing of regional Mexican music, historically a saxophone-inflected norteño distinct from Sinaloan banda and Nuevo León accordion conjunto, and since 2019 the epicenter of corridos tumbados through Hermosillo-born Natanael Cano. Current practice strips percussion entirely: two or three acoustic guitars plus tuba or upright bass, cut close-miked in home-professional rooms, with conversational sung-spoken corrido narration. It parts from Sinaloan sierreño mainly in vocal cadence and in its early adoption of hip-hop-length, hip-hop-mixed masters.

items.name: Rawstyle
items.lineage: Dutch hardstyle offshoot codified around 2010-2013 by Radical Redemption, Warface and E-Force out of the Rotterdam-Eindhoven hard-dance circuit — 150-160 BPM with a distorted, heavily overdriven reverse-bass kick whose tail carries the bassline, screech and hoover leads, pitched-down horror or spoken-word vocal samples, and long tension-release breakdowns built for arena hard-dance events.
items.description: Rawstyle split from euphoric hardstyle in the Netherlands in the early 2010s by abandoning melodic uplifting leads in favour of distortion as the primary compositional material. Kicks are multi-stage distorted so the pitched tail supplies the bassline; leads are screeches and detuned hoovers; vocals are almost always pitched-down samples rather than sung toplines. Compared with hardcore and uptempo it sits slower at 150-160 BPM and retains hardstyle's reverse-bass architecture and long breakdown form.

items.name: Afroswing
items.lineage: London-born fusion of Afrobeats, Jamaican dancehall and UK rap that broke between 2015 and 2018 through J Hus, Kojo Funds, Not3s and producers Jae5 and Steel Banglez — 100-108 BPM with a swung dancehall-derived kick-and-rim pattern, log-drum-adjacent percussion, clean plucked guitar and marimba-like synth motifs, and sing-rapped melodic hooks in London-Nigerian-Caribbean slang.
items.description: Afroswing formed in East and South London around 2015 as second-generation West African and Caribbean artists merged Afrobeats percussion and dancehall phrasing with UK rap cadence. Its sound is warm and mid-tempo: swung 100-105 BPM drums, bright plucked guitar and mallet motifs, sub-heavy but uncluttered low end, and hooks delivered half-sung. It differs from grime in tempo and tonality, from drill in its major-key brightness, and from Nigerian Afrobeats in its rap-rooted rhythmic delivery and UK vernacular.

items.name: Rap calme (French mellow rap)
items.lineage: Streaming-era French mellow-rap tendency consolidated in Paris around 2015-2020 by Lomepal, Josman, Nekfeu and Ichon — 70-95 BPM half-time or lightly swung drums, Rhodes and warm sampled loops, low dynamic range, close-mic conversational and half-sung delivery in French with introspective, non-confrontational writing designed for late-night and playlist listening.
items.description: A soft-focus wing of French rap that became a distinct listening category in the late 2010s, defined less by a rhythmic template than by restraint: muted drums, jazz-leaning keyboard loops, intimate vocal miking and lyrics turned inward. It sits between boom-bap-derived French rap and French R&B, and is set apart from the dominant Paris-Marseille street rap by its low intensity and near-absence of aggressive ad-libs. Production is DAW-native and mastered quiet relative to trap-français.

items.name: Rock urbano mexicano
items.lineage: Working-class Mexico City rock forged in the hoyos fonquis of the 1970s-80s by Alex Lora's Three Souls in My Mind and El Tri, then Banda Bostik, El Haragán y Compañía and Liran' Roll — blues-shuffle and mid-tempo hard-rock forms at 90-130 BPM with pentatonic guitar riffs, harmonica, plainspoken chorded Spanish shouted vocals, and lyrics about poverty, police, alcohol and barrio life sold on cassette outside the commercial industry.
items.description: Rock urbano is the barrio rock of Mexico City, hardened after the 1971 Avándaro festival drove Mexican rock underground into improvised hoyos fonquis venues. Musically it stays close to blues-based hard rock and boogie — three chords, harmonica, distorted riffing — but its identity is lyrical: everyday Spanish, chilango slang, and open class grievance. It differs from rock en español of the 1980s in refusing new-wave polish and from Mexican metal in tempo and blues vocabulary.

items.name: Anime lo-fi
items.lineage: YouTube- and Discord-native lo-fi hip-hop variant that formed after 2015 around the ChilledCow / Lofi Girl stream and its anime-styled visual identity, descending musically from Nujabes and Fat Jon's Samurai Champloo score (2004) — 70-85 BPM boom-bap drums with swung, softened transients, jazz-chord Rhodes and upright-piano loops, tape hiss and wow-flutter, vinyl crackle, and spoken anime dialogue samples used as the only vocal element.
items.description: A branch of lo-fi hip-hop whose defining marker is Japanese-animation framing — anime dialogue samples, anime and city-pop source material, and looping illustrated video streams — rather than a separate rhythmic grammar. Tracks are two-minute instrumental loops at 70-85 BPM with deliberately degraded highs, filtered drums and jazz voicings, produced entirely in the box for study and sleep playlists. Against jazzy hip-hop proper it has no MC and no arrangement development; against ambient it retains a hard boom-bap backbeat.

items.name: Rap belge
items.lineage: Francophone Belgian rap centered on Brussels and Liège, internationally established from 2015 by Damso, Hamza, Roméo Elvis and Caballero & JeanJass — 70-100 BPM trap and cloud-rap production with cold synth pads and heavy 808 sub, a markedly slower and more nasal-conversational flow than Paris rap, Brussels-Congolese slang and dry gallows humor, plus a separate Dutch-language Flemish wing.
items.description: Belgian rap grew from 1990s Brussels crews into a distinct, export-strength scene after 2015, disproportionately shaped by Congolese-Belgian artists. Its production is trap-derived but cooler and sparser than French mainstream rap, favouring minor pads, long 808 slides and dry vocal mixes, and its flows are slower with a recognizably Belgian accent and lexicon. Alongside the Francophone core sits a Dutch-language Flemish rap current with its own Antwerp-Brussels axis.

items.name: Stomp and flutter
items.lineage: North American and Icelandic indie-folk-pop tendency of roughly 2009-2016, an algorithmically-named counterpart to stomp-and-holler distinguished by lighter, often female or mixed-gender lead voices — 100-140 BPM four-on-the-floor foot-stomp and handclap percussion, strummed dreadnought guitar with mandolin, glockenspiel and upright piano coloration, group 'hey' shouts and airy multitracked harmony over major-key diatonic progressions.
items.description: A late-2000s to mid-2010s strain of festival-scaled indie folk-pop built on stomped-and-clapped rhythm rather than a drum kit, acoustic string coloration, and communal singalong choruses. It is separated from stomp-and-holler by timbre and affect: brighter, softer-voiced, more often duet or mixed-ensemble, and reverbed toward airiness rather than gruff rasp. Recording practice favours a live room with the ensemble tracking together, then wide harmony overdubs, giving a roomy but modern digital master.

items.name: Bossbeat (programmed bossa-downtempo)
items.lineage: Producer-side fusion emerging in late-1990s Rio–London–Tokyo downtempo circles and consolidated by Bebel Gilberto's Tanto Tempo (2000) and the Ziriguiboom/Far Out labels, setting João Gilberto's nylon-string batida and extended-tertian bossa harmony against programmed 85–105 BPM breakbeats, filtered Rhodes pads, sampled pandeiro and shaker loops, and an unforced close-miked whisper vocal in Portuguese.
items.description: A studio-born hybrid of bossa nova and downtempo electronic production that crystallised around 2000 in the Rio–London axis of the Ziriguiboom and Far Out labels. It keeps bossa's ninth- and eleventh-loaded chord vocabulary, the guitar's syncopated batida, and the breathy near-spoken vocal, but replaces the live drummer with looped breakbeats, filtered pads and sampled hand percussion. Unlike acoustic bossa nova it is grid-locked and non-improvised, and unlike Latin house it stays below 105 BPM with no four-on-the-floor kick.

items.name: Banda jalisciense
items.lineage: Jalisco village wind-band tradition formed in the late nineteenth century out of municipal and military brass instruction, running parallel to mariachi in the same region: 10–20 players of clarinets, cornets/trumpets, valve trombones, alto horns, tuba and tambora-plus-tarola battery, playing sones, jarabes, marches and polkas at 100–140 BPM with 6/8-against-3/4 hemiola, unison clarinet leads, tuba on the downbeat-and-offbeat bass line, and shouted gritos over sung coplas.
items.description: The wind-band music of Jalisco and the surrounding Bajío, developed from late-1800s municipal brass instruction and still played for fiestas patronales, weddings and processions. Its core sound is massed clarinets carrying the melody over valve trombones and alto horns, a tuba bass that alternates root and fifth against the tambora's 6/8 pulse, and the son jalisciense hemiola shared with mariachi. It is distinguished from banda sinaloense by its lighter, clarinet-forward and more march-and-jarabe-oriented repertoire rather than the heavier tuba-and-tambora technobanda drive of Sinaloa.
exemplars: Banda de Tlayacapan-style Jalisco municipal bands
Mariachi Vargas de Tecalitlán (shared Jalisco son repertoire)

items.name: Frauenrap (German women's rap)
items.lineage: German-language women's rap tradition running from Cora E. and Sabrina Setlur in the early 1990s Heidelberg/Frankfurt scenes through the 2010s Berlin queer-feminist wave of Sookee, Ebow and Nura, marked by dense multisyllabic German rhyme over 85–100 BPM boom-bap or, latterly, trap hi-hat triplets and 808 glides, dry close-miked delivery, and explicitly gendered lyrical address answering the male-dominated Straßenrap canon.
items.description: A strand of German hip-hop defined by women MCs, first visible with Cora E. and Sabrina Setlur in the mid-1990s and re-founded as an explicitly political scene in 2010s Berlin around Sookee's Springstoff circle. Sonically it spans dry sample-based boom bap and later trap production with 808 sub-glides and triplet hi-hats, but is consistently vocal-forward with minimal effect on the rap track so German consonant clusters stay legible. It differs from mainstream German Straßenrap less in beat construction than in lyrical stance, and from Anglophone women's rap in its harder-edged, agglutinative rhyme scansion.

items.name: Early modern classical (1890–1930)
items.lineage: The Paris–Vienna–Budapest rupture of roughly 1890 to 1930, codified by Debussy's whole-tone and modal planing, Stravinsky's additive-metre ostinati in the Ballets Russes scores, Bartók's field-collected Magyar and Romanian scales, and Schoenberg's move through free atonality into the twelve-tone method — scored for expanded orchestra with divisi strings, doubled woodwinds, celesta, harp and enlarged percussion, and marked by dissolved functional cadence, shifting bar lengths, and timbre treated as a structural parameter.
items.description: The repertoire of the four decades in which Western common-practice tonality was stretched past its breaking point: Debussy and Ravel's modal and whole-tone planing, Stravinsky's irregular-metre ostinati, Bartók's folk-derived scales, and the Second Viennese School's move from free atonality to serialism. The orchestral sound is large but often chamber-transparent, with celesta, harp, muted brass and an expanded percussion section used for colour rather than reinforcement. It differs from late Romanticism in abandoning functional cadential closure and from postwar modernism in retaining audible pulse, motive and gesture.
exemplars: Igor Stravinsky - Le Sacre du printemps
Charles Ives - Three Places in New England

items.name: Afrofuturismo brasileiro
items.lineage: São Paulo–Salvador movement of the 2010s in which Black Brazilian artists — Rincon Sapiência, Xênia França, Jup do Bairro, BaianaSystem — set candomblé and samba-reggae percussion patterns (atabaque toques, timbau and surdo, berimbau figures) against 808 sub-bass, modular synth pads and sampled Afro-diasporic archive material at 90–110 BPM, with Portuguese lyrics that route Yoruba cosmology and quilombo history through a science-fictional register.
items.description: A Brazilian Afrofuturist current that took shape in São Paulo and Salvador through the 2010s, joining candomblé and samba-reggae drum languages to sub-bass-heavy electronic production and speculative Black-diasporic imagery. The texture layers live atabaque, timbau and berimbau over programmed 808 kicks and wide synth pads, with vocals moving between rapped Portuguese, sung refrains and ritual-derived call-and-response. It differs from baile funk in tempo and harmonic ambition, and from mainstream MPB in placing electronic timbre and Yoruba cosmology at the centre rather than the songwriting tradition.

items.name: Duranguense (pasito duranguense)
items.lineage: Chicago-based Mexican-migrant style codified around 2000 by Grupo Montez de Durango and K-Paz de la Sierra, transplanting the Durango tamborazo repertoire into a small electric ensemble: synthesizer patches replacing the clarinet and brass sections, saxophone and trombone leads, a fast 2/4 polka-derived tempo near 150–170 BPM, tambora-and-tarola battery on top, and a nasal high-tenor lead vocal singing ranchera and cumbia covers, danced as the shuffling pasito duranguense.
items.description: A regional Mexican style invented not in Mexico but among Durangan migrants in Chicago around 1999–2000, taking off nationally with Grupo Montez de Durango. It compresses the large tamborazo wind band into a keyboard-led six- or seven-piece: synth patches carrying the massed-clarinet lines, saxophone and trombone doubling the hook, and a relentless 150–170 BPM tambora-and-tarola polka pulse. Against banda sinaloense it is smaller, faster, synthetic in timbre and built largely on covers of existing ranchera and cumbia hits.

items.name: Trancecore (electronicore)
items.lineage: Late-2000s American and British scene hybrid, codified by Attack Attack!'s Someday Came Suddenly (2008), Enter Shikari's Take to the Skies (2007) and I See Stars, welding metalcore breakdowns on drop-tuned seven-string guitars and blast-adjacent double-kick to full-blown supersaw trance leads and 140-BPM four-on-the-floor synth drops, alternating screamed verses with heavily pitch-corrected clean choruses.
items.description: A 2007–2012 fusion of metalcore and uplifting trance that grew out of the MySpace-era scene circuit in Ohio, Michigan and St Albans. Tracks cut between drop-tuned breakdowns with triggered double-kick and unashamedly euphoric supersaw synth drops at trance tempo, with screamed verses handed to auto-tuned clean choruses. It differs from ordinary metalcore in that the synth is a co-lead rather than atmosphere, and from crossover EDM-rock in keeping the hardcore breakdown as the structural climax.
exemplars: Enter Shikari - Take to the Skies

items.name: Shiver pop
items.lineage: Algorithmically named descriptor for the cold-toned indie synth-pop that coalesced 2009–2014 across Brooklyn, Gothenburg and Toronto — Chromatics, Austra, Niki & The Dove, Purity Ring — built on arpeggiated analog-poly sequences at 100–120 BPM, gated reverb-drenched drum-machine hits, single-coil guitar washed in tremolo and chorus, and a high, breathy, heavily reverberant female lead sung in a narrow, unforced range.
items.description: A cold, reverberant strain of indie synth-pop from roughly 2009 to 2014, gathered under a listener-data label rather than a scene name, running from Chromatics and Glass Candy through Austra, Niki & The Dove and Purity Ring. The sound is arpeggiated analog polysynth over programmed drums with long plate and hall tails, chorused single-coil guitar, and an airy, close-miked high female lead sitting deep in the reverb field. It differs from dream pop in leaning on sequencers rather than guitar layers, and from mainstream synthpop in its deliberately chilly, unbelted vocal delivery and muted dynamic range.

items.name: Jazz trumpet lineage
items.lineage: The soloist tradition running from Louis Armstrong's 1925–28 Hot Five sides through Dizzy Gillespie's bebop upper-register chromaticism, Clifford Brown and Lee Morgan's hard-bop articulation, and Miles Davis's Harmon-muted space — Bb trumpet or flugelhorn fronting piano, bass and drums, phrasing swung eighths across AABA and blues forms at 120–280 BPM, with half-valve smears, terminal vibrato, growl and plunger mutes as core expressive vocabulary.
items.description: The line of trumpet soloing that defines much of jazz's melodic language, from Armstrong's rhythmically displaced New Orleans lead through bebop's chromatic bebop-scale runs to the muted, spacious modal playing of late-1950s Miles Davis. The instrument is typically captured close on a ribbon with a small acoustic rhythm section behind it, so attack transients and half-valve inflections stay audible. It differs from concert-trumpet practice in its vibrato control, mute vocabulary and reliance on improvised chorus-length invention rather than notated line.
exemplars: Louis Armstrong - Hot Fives and Sevens

items.name: American metalcore
items.lineage: New England and Mid-Atlantic hybrid of hardcore punk and Gothenburg melodic death metal, codified 1997–2004 by Converge, Shadows Fall and Killswitch Engage's Alive or Just Breathing: drop-tuned downpicked riffs and harmonised twin-guitar leads over 160–200 BPM double-kick and half-time breakdowns, screamed verse with sung octave-leaping chorus, and triggered click-forward kick drums in a heavily edited multitrack mix.
items.description: The American fusion of hardcore punk structure with Swedish melodic death metal riffing that consolidated in Massachusetts and the Mid-Atlantic between 1997 and 2004. Its markers are harmonised minor-key twin-guitar leads, downtuned downpicked chugging, a screamed-verse/sung-chorus split, and the half-time breakdown inherited from New York hardcore. It differs from melodic death metal in retaining hardcore's breakdown and clean-chorus hook, and from metallic hardcore proper in its explicit melodic and production polish.
exemplars: Killswitch Engage - Alive or Just Breathing
Shadows Fall - The Art of Balance
As I Lay Dying - Shadows Are Security
Hatebreed - Satisfaction Is the Death of Desire

items.name: Barnmusik (Swedish children's song)
items.lineage: Swedish children's-song repertoire founded by Alice Tegnér's Sjung med oss, Mamma! collections from 1892 and re-codified for record and television in the 1960s–80s by Georg Riedel's settings of Astrid Lindgren texts and by Sveriges Radio's children's programming: strophic diatonic melodies in narrow range, moderate 2/4 and 3/4 tempi, acoustic guitar, piano and accordion accompaniment, and unison children's-choir singing with a single adult lead.
items.description: Sweden's institutional children's-song repertoire, beginning with Alice Tegnér's published collections in the 1890s and reaching mass circulation through Astrid Lindgren film and television music set by Georg Riedel from the 1960s onward. Musically it favours short strophic diatonic tunes in a singable range, warm acoustic accompaniment of guitar, piano and accordion, and unison children's voices tracked live in a bright room. Compared with Anglo-American nursery rhyme it is composer-attributed and notated rather than anonymous and oral, and carries a distinctly Nordic pastoral lyric world.
exemplars: Alice Tegnér - Sjung med oss, Mamma!
Georg Riedel & Astrid Lindgren - Emil i Lönneberga

items.name: Visual kei
items.lineage: Japanese rock movement launched by X Japan's Blue Blood (1989) and consolidated in the mid-1990s by Luna Sea, Malice Mizer and Buck-Tick, pairing an androgynous costumed stage identity with speed-metal double-kick, harmonised lead guitar, symphonic keyboard and string-pad layers, abrupt tempo and metre shifts within single songs, and a theatrical Japanese-language vocal that swings between clean high tenor and scream.
items.description: A Japanese rock movement defined as much by elaborate androgynous visual presentation as by sound, beginning with X Japan at the end of the 1980s and spreading through Luna Sea, Malice Mizer, Buck-Tick and later Dir En Grey and the GazettE. Musically it draws on speed metal, glam, goth and symphonic pop in the same song, with harmonised leads, orchestral keyboard beds, sudden metre changes and a lead vocal that alternates operatic clean tenor with screamed passages. It differs from Western glam metal in its through-composed sectional ambition and from J-rock generally in treating band image as a formal component of the genre.

items.name: Piseiro
items.lineage: Brazilian Northeastern dance-pop offshoot of forró that crystallized in Bahia and Pernambuco around 2015-2019 through Barões da Pisadinha, Zé Vaqueiro and João Gomes, built on a MIDI-keyboard 'pisadinha' groove at 95-115 BPM in which a programmed zabumba-and-triangle pattern lands hard on beat one under bright arpeggiated teclado hooks, sanfona countermelody, and plainspoken tenor vocals about rural romance and heartbreak.
items.description: Piseiro emerged in the Brazilian Northeast in the late 2010s as a keyboard-programmed reduction of forró and arrocha, spreading nationally via WhatsApp and YouTube before major-label pickup. Its signature is the pisadinha itself: a stomping zabumba-and-triangle loop generated on a Yamaha-style arranger keyboard, with the bass drum planted on beat one and a thin, glassy synth lead carrying the hook. Compared to traditional forró pé-de-serra it drops the live trio and swings less; compared to arrocha it is faster and more dance-oriented than balladic.

items.name: Ska Mexicano
items.lineage: Mexico City ska-rock hybrid codified between 1989 and 1998 by Maldita Vecindad, Panteón Rococó, Salón Victoria and La Tremenda Korte, marrying a 160-190 BPM offbeat guitar upstroke and walking bass to a Mexican street-band horn section (trumpet, trombone, tenor sax), cumbia and danzón interludes, and shouted barrio-political Spanish vocals delivered by a frontman over a driving one-drop-into-four snare.
items.description: Ska mexicano formed in Mexico City in the late 1980s and early 1990s, when the rock urbano and chavo banda scenes absorbed second-wave British 2 Tone and Jamaican ska records circulating through tianguis markets. It is faster and brassier than 2 Tone, with a horn section written in the parallel-third idiom of Mexican banda and frequent detours into cumbia, danzón or son jarocho within a single track. Where Jamaican ska is loose and studio-mixed, the Mexican strain is played live, hoarse-voiced and explicitly political, aligned with Zapatista and anti-government protest.
exemplars: Maldita Vecindad y los Hijos del Quinto Patio

items.name: Big Beat
items.lineage: British breakbeat dance style codified 1993-1999 around Brighton's Big Beat Boutique and Skint/Wall of Sound by The Chemical Brothers, Fatboy Slim and The Prodigy, running 110-140 BPM over chopped funk and hip-hop breaks layered with acid-303 bass, heavily distorted and filter-swept synths, loud crash-cymbal fills, and rock-scale drum compression with vocal hooks reduced to single sampled shouts.
items.description: Big beat crystallized in mid-1990s Britain as a deliberately unsubtle, rock-club-facing alternative to the accelerating hardcore and jungle scenes, built on mid-tempo funk breakbeats rather than four-on-the-floor. Its defining sound is extreme saturation and compression on a sampled break, with long filter sweeps and stop-start arrangement gestures modelled on stadium rock dynamics. Unlike jungle it keeps the break slow and unchopped, and unlike house it is designed for crowds that never learned to dance to 4/4.
exemplars: The Chemical Brothers - Dig Your Own Hole
Fatboy Slim - You've Come a Long Way, Baby
The Prodigy - The Fat of the Land

items.name: Vapor Soul
items.lineage: Blog-era downtempo electronic R&B named by streaming taxonomies around 2013-2016 and shaped by Rhye, Banks, Chet Faker and Sohn, running 80-100 BPM over soft-attack 808 sub-kicks and finger-snap backbeats under washed reverb-drenched Rhodes and analogue pads, with breathy androgynous close-mic'd vocals sung near a whisper and harmonized in stacked thirds.
items.description: Vapor soul is a mid-2010s convergence of chillwave production aesthetics with contemporary R&B songwriting, circulated first through music blogs and then consolidated as a playlist category. The sound is defined by extreme space and restraint: sparse rounded low end, long-tailed reverbs on electric piano and pads, and a lead vocal recorded so close that breath and lip noise stay in the mix. It is warmer and more song-shaped than chillwave proper, and slower and more atmospheric than the alternative R&B of its immediate neighbours.

items.name: Hardwave
items.lineage: Online-native offshoot of the wave and trap scenes formed roughly 2018-2021 across SoundCloud and Discord through Sidewalks and Skeletons, Hyperforms, Aire Atlantica and Kanuto, pairing 140-160 BPM half-time trap drums and 808 slides with towering distorted supersaw leads, sidechained shoegaze-scale reverb walls, and pitched-up or wordless vocal fragments used as texture rather than lyric.
items.description: Hardwave arose entirely online in the late 2010s when producers in the wave scene pushed its melancholic synth writing through hard-clipped distortion and metal-adjacent loudness. The result keeps wave's half-time trap skeleton and emotional minor-key melody but replaces its icy restraint with saturated supersaw stacks, screaming detuned leads and a mastering ceiling deliberately driven into clipping. It is distinguished from wave by sheer aggression and from dubstep by its lack of bass wobble and its guitar-like, sustained lead voicing.

items.name: Folklore Argentino
items.lineage: Argentine national folk-song repertoire codified in the 1940s-1960s by Atahualpa Yupanqui, Los Chalchaleros, Ariel Ramírez and Mercedes Sosa and centred on the Cosquín festival, comprising the slow 6/8 zamba with handkerchief-dance phrasing, the driving hemiola chacarera, the vidala and the chamamé, scored for nylon-string guitar rasgueado, bombo legüero played on head and rim, charango and quena, with declamatory rubato-heavy solo or duo singing in criollo Spanish.
items.description: Folklore argentino is the codified national folk repertoire consolidated during the mid-twentieth-century boom that ran from provincial peñas to the Cosquín festival and the Buenos Aires recording industry. Its core rhythmic identity is the 6/8-against-3/4 hemiola that underpins zamba and chacarera, articulated by the bombo legüero's alternation between skin and wooden rim and by strummed guitar patterns learned by ear. Unlike Andean huayno it is guitar-led rather than panpipe-led, and unlike nueva canción it began as a conservative rural-nostalgic idiom before Sosa and the Nuevo Cancionero movement politicised it.

items.name: Drumless Hip Hop
items.lineage: New York underground rap approach consolidated in the 2010s by Roc Marciano, Ka, The Alchemist and Griselda-adjacent producers, stripping the boom-bap kit entirely so that a looped soul, library or soundtrack sample carries the beat alone at an implied 80-90 BPM, leaving the rapper's conversational, unhurried, largely unpunched-in delivery to supply the rhythmic grid.
items.description: Drumless hip hop is a 2010s New York underground practice in which producers remove percussion from the loop, leaving a raw sample fragment — often a chamber-soul, spaghetti-western or library cue — cycling unsupported beneath the vocal. Roc Marciano's Marcberg is usually cited as the template, with Ka and later Alchemist and Navy Blue extending it. The absence of a kit shifts every rhythmic responsibility onto the MC, producing a floating, half-spoken cadence that distinguishes it sharply from the snare-locked boom bap it descends from.

items.name: J-Pop Boy Group
items.lineage: Japanese male idol-group pop formalized by Johnny & Associates from the 1980s onward and sustained by SMAP, Arashi, Hey! Say! JUMP and Snow Man, built on 120-135 BPM four-on-the-floor or shuffle-pop backing with dense synth-brass and string-machine arrangements, unison-then-solo-rotation vocal distribution across five to nine members, major-key modulating choruses and choreography-driven sectional form.
items.description: The Japanese boy group format was institutionalized by Johnny & Associates' training and debut system and has defined mainstream male J-pop since the 1980s. Musically it favours bright major-key writing with frequent late-song key changes, thick layered backing vocals and a rotating line distribution that keeps every member audible, all built for televised choreography. It differs from K-pop boy groups in its lighter vocal production, weaker hip-hop and EDM influence, and preference for melodic Showa-descended pop over rap-verse structures.

items.name: J-Acoustic
items.lineage: Japanese acoustic-guitar-led pop lineage descending from 1970s fōku and consolidated in the late 1990s and 2000s by Yuzu, Kobukuro, Ikimonogakari and Miyuki Nakajima's successors, using strummed steel-string guitar and close male duo harmony over unobtrusive drum and bass at 80-130 BPM, with harmonica breaks, diatonic modulating choruses and plainly enunciated Japanese lyrics about hometowns, graduation and perseverance.
items.description: J-acoustic names the acoustic-guitar-centred strand of Japanese mainstream pop that grew out of the 1970s folk boom and returned to chart dominance in the late 1990s through street-performing duos in Yokohama and Osaka. The sound keeps a strummed steel-string and a paired male harmony at the front of the mix, with rhythm section and strings entering only to lift the chorus, and prizes clear diction over vocal ornament. It is distinct from J-pop idol production in its live-band restraint and from Western indie folk in its bright, fully resolved harmonic language and overtly uplifting lyric register.

items.name: Corridos Clásicos
items.lineage: Mexican-Texan narrative ballad tradition rooted in the border conflicts of 1848-1930 and commercially codified on record from the 1930s-1960s by Los Alegres de Terán, Dueto América, Los Cadetes de Linares and later Los Tigres del Norte, set in strophic quatrains sung in parallel thirds by a male duo over a 3/4 or fast 2/4 norteño frame of diatonic button accordion, bajo sexto and tololoche, with formulaic opening and farewell despedida verses.
items.description: The classic corrido is the pre-narcocorrido ballad repertoire of the Mexico-Texas border, carrying news and heroic biography — Gregorio Cortez, Valentín de la Sierra, the Revolution, Prohibition smuggling — in fixed strophic form. Recorded output from the 1930s through the 1960s standardized the norteño accompaniment of accordion, bajo sexto and upright bass behind two voices locked in thirds, with the accordion answering each vocal phrase. It differs from ranchera in its journalistic third-person narrative and unvarying strophe, and from later narcocorridos in its I-IV-V harmonic economy and absence of brass or drum kit.
exemplars: Los Tigres del Norte - Contrabando y Traición

items.name: Rif (Rifian Amazigh Song)
items.lineage: Amazigh song tradition of the Rif mountains of northern Morocco, transmitted as women's izran couplets and codified for record and cassette from the 1970s-1990s by Walid Mimoun, Milouda El Hoceima and Thidrin, set in short antiphonal Tarifit-language quatrains over a fast duple bendir and deff pattern with adjun frame-drum accents, zamar or ghaita double-reed drone melody, and from the 1980s a strummed banjo or cheap synth doubling the vocal line.
items.description: Rifian music is the song tradition of the Tarifit-speaking Amazigh of northern Morocco, historically centred on izran — terse improvised or memorized couplets exchanged between women and men at weddings and harvests over frame drums. From the 1970s a politicized protest strand emerged in the diaspora and at home, adding banjo, guitar and later synthesizer to the drum-and-reed core while keeping the narrow-range modal melody and antiphonal couplet form. It differs from Moroccan chaabi in its language, its unmetered vocal entries and its far more austere instrumentation, and from Kabyle Algerian song in its faster, drier percussion.

items.name: Türkçe Slow Şarkılar
items.lineage: Turkish slow-tempo pop ballad idiom consolidated in Istanbul's Unkapanı record trade between the late 1980s and the 2000s through Sezen Aksu's arrangers, Nilüfer, Kayahan, Sertab Erener and Tarkan, pairing 60-80 BPM ballad drum programming and lush synth-string beds with makam-inflected melodies, a kanun or bağlama obbligato, quarter-tone melismatic vocal ornament and heavily reverbed, arabesk-descended emotional delivery.
items.description: Türkçe slow is the Turkish mainstream ballad repertoire that dominated cassette and radio play from the late 1980s onward, sitting between Western soft-rock arrangement and arabesk affect. Tracks pair Western functional harmony and synthesized string pads with melodies that bend into makam intervals, decorated by a kanun, bağlama or ney figure answering each vocal line, and a singer whose ornamented, tearful delivery is the focus of the mix. It is more harmonically Westernized and better produced than arabesk proper, and slower and more melodramatic than the uptempo Türkçe pop it shares its performers with.

items.name: Hawaiian hip hop
