items.lineage: Oʻahu and Maui scene formed in the early 1990s as Honolulu MCs grafted local pidgin-English rhyming onto reggae-inflected boom-bap, codified by Sudden Rush's Hawaiian-language 'na mele paleoleo' records from 1995 onward and by the Jawaiian-adjacent island-rap circuit — 88-100 BPM half-time drums, one-drop and steppers bass patterns borrowed from roots reggae, ukulele and slack-key guitar samples or live overdubs, and a relaxed conversational flow that switches between English, Hawaiian Pidgin and ʻōlelo Hawaiʻi.
items.description: Hawaiian hip hop emerged in Honolulu in the early 1990s, when local rappers merged mainland boom-bap production with the reggae rhythms already dominant in island radio through Jawaiian. It is marked by laid-back tempos, one-drop or steppers bass movement under sampled drums, ukulele and slack-key guitar textures, and lyrics that code-switch between English, Hawaiian Pidgin and Hawaiian. Unlike mainland West Coast rap it foregrounds sovereignty and land politics rather than street narrative, and unlike Jawaiian reggae proper it keeps the MC, not the singer, at the center.

items.name: Neoperreo
items.lineage: Internet-native reggaeton offshoot that coalesced around 2016 through SoundCloud and Instagram networks linking Santiago, Mexico City, Madrid and Los Angeles, named and organized largely by Tomasa del Real and Ms Nina with DJ Florentino and Chico Sonido supplying beats — 90-100 BPM dembow retained but stripped to a thin skeletal kick-snare, sub-heavy and dry, topped with deliberately deadpan or breathy female vocals, heavy autotune, and lo-fi digital synth stabs replacing the maximal 2000s reggaeton horn hooks.
items.description: Neoperreo formed online around 2016 as a queer- and woman-led rewrite of reggaeton, built in bedrooms and circulated through SoundCloud rather than through Puerto Rican or Colombian label infrastructure. Its dembow is deliberately thin and dry, the low end sits in a clean sub rather than a mastered radio bounce, and vocals are close, flat and heavily pitch-corrected. Where mainstream Latin trap chases polish and features, neoperreo keeps the lo-fi bedroom finish as an aesthetic commitment and centers explicit female sexual agency in the lyrics.

items.name: Rave funk (funk rave)
items.lineage: Rio de Janeiro and São Paulo hybrid that broke nationally around 2021-2022 when funk carioca producers began welding euro-rave and big-room material onto the tamborzão grid, codified by DJ Ramon Sucesso, DJ Guuga and the 'automotivo' producer network — 130-150 BPM, four-on-the-floor kick alternating with syncopated tamborzão fills, screaming detuned supersaw and hoover leads, pitched vocal chops of MC shouts, and abrupt drop-and-silence arrangement borrowed from festival EDM.
items.description: Rave funk crossed over in Brazil in the early 2020s as favela funk producers absorbed European rave and big-room EDM signatures into the tamborzão rhythm bed. It runs far faster than classic funk carioca, leans on detuned supersaw hooks and hoover stabs, and structures tracks around drops and silences rather than a continuous groove. Compared to funk 150 BPM it is more melodic and more overtly European in synth vocabulary, and compared to bruxaria it keeps a euphoric rather than menacing affect.

items.name: Russelåter
items.lineage: Norwegian commissioned-party-music practice in which graduating 'russ' bus groups pay producers for a custom track, industrialized from roughly 2010 onward around Oslo and Bergen production houses and released in a compressed pre-May-17 season — 145-155 BPM, hardstyle-derived reverse-bass or jumpstyle offbeat kick, sawtooth lead riffs, Norwegian-language rap or shouted gang vocals naming the bus, and a build-drop-build architecture optimized for onboard soundsystems.
items.description: Russelåter are bespoke party tracks commissioned by Norwegian high-school graduation bus crews, a market that became a full production industry after 2010. Musically they sit between hardstyle, jumpstyle and Scandinavian club-pop: hard offbeat or reverse bass, bright saw leads, brutal limiting for outdoor bus PA playback, and Norwegian-language rap or chanted crew names. The genre is defined less by a stylistic boundary than by its commissioning economics and its annual May release window, which distinguishes it from generic Scandinavian EDM.

items.name: Cubatón
items.lineage: Havana adaptation of Puerto Rican reggaeton that took hold between 1999 and 2005 through home-computer producers in Alamar and Centro Habana, codified by Cubanito 20.02, Eddy-K, Candyman and the early Gente de Zona — dembow at 92-100 BPM overlaid with son clave, live or sampled congas, timbales and bongó, tumbao bass figures displacing the flat reggaeton sub, and a shouted party-chant delivery alternating with sung soneo-style choruses.
items.description: Cubatón developed in Havana around the turn of the 2000s, when reggaeton reaching the island by informal cassette and CD circulation was rebuilt on home PCs by producers with deep son and timba backgrounds. The dembow remains, but it is cut against son clave and layered with conga and timbal patterns, and the bass moves in anticipated tumbao rather than sitting on the downbeat. That rhythmic layering, plus soneo-derived call-and-response choruses, separates it from Puerto Rican reggaeton and from mainland Cuban timba, which keeps a full horn section and live rhythm section.

items.name: Vapor twitch
items.lineage: Internet-native electronic microgenre that took shape between roughly 2014 and 2019 around livestream and gaming-video culture, feeding off vaporwave's chopped 1980s-90s sample palette but rebuilt for stream-background use — 100-140 BPM, glitch-cut breakbeats and trap hats, FM and wavetable leads over pitched-down mall-jazz and anime-soundtrack samples, heavy sidechain, and short loopable arrangements with no vocal focal point.
items.description: Vapor twitch is a streaming-era microgenre sitting between vaporwave, future funk and glitch-leaning bass music, produced entirely in the box and distributed as royalty-cleared loops for livestream backgrounds and gaming edits. It keeps vaporwave's degraded 1980s sample sources and chroma but adds a firmer trap or breakbeat pulse, brighter FM leads and pumping sidechain, and it is mixed for laptop and phone playback rather than for a soundsystem. Unlike vaporwave proper it is functional and upbeat rather than melancholic and slowed, and unlike future funk it tolerates glitch edits and harsh digital artifacts.

items.name: Mangue beat
items.lineage: Recife, Pernambuco movement launched in 1991 by Fred Zero Quatro's 'Caranguejos com Cérebro' manifesto and realized by Chico Science & Nação Zumbi on Da Lama ao Caos (1994) — maracatu nação alfaia batteries and coco rhythms locked against distorted humbucker guitar, slap and fuzz electric bass, drum kit and hip-hop turntable scratching, with declaimed half-rapped Portuguese vocals over 4/4 maracatu patterns at 100-120 BPM.
items.description: Mangue beat began in Recife in 1991 as an explicit cultural programme, connecting the mangrove swamps of the city's periphery to global information networks, and it produced its defining record with Chico Science & Nação Zumbi's Da Lama ao Caos in 1994. Its sound is the alfaia drum battery of maracatu nação played at full volume against distorted rock guitar, fuzz bass and turntable scratching, with vocals delivered in a clipped declamatory Pernambucan Portuguese. It differs from Tropicália, which absorbed foreign forms into song, by keeping Northeastern percussion as the structural foundation rather than as colour, and from other Brazilian rock by its refusal of Rio-São Paulo idioms.

items.name: Rock uruguayo
items.lineage: Montevideo rock lineage running from the Beatlesque Los Shakers and Los Mockers of 1964-68 through the post-dictatorship boom of 1985 onward, codified by Los Estómagos, Los Traidores and El Cuarteto de Nos and continued by La Vela Puerca and No Te Va Gustar — guitar-bass-drums power trio or quartet format, mid-tempo 100-140 BPM, frequent candombe tambor patterns displaced onto the drum kit, and Rioplatense Spanish lyrics ranging from post-punk political bite to absurdist wordplay.
items.description: Rock uruguayo begins with the mid-1960s beat groups Los Shakers and Los Mockers and returns in force with the 1985 end of the military dictatorship, when a Montevideo post-punk generation used rock as public political speech. The recurring local marker is candombe: the tambor chico, repique and piano patterns of Barrio Sur transposed onto a rock drum kit, which gives the music a lilt absent from Argentine rock nacional. Lyrics in Rioplatense Spanish swing between the sardonic literary voice of El Cuarteto de Nos and the anthemic social address of the later ska-rock bands.

items.name: Rap español
items.lineage: Spanish-language hip hop of Spain, seeded by Madrid and Torrejón breakdance crews in the mid-1980s and codified between 1989 and 1994 by El Club de los Poetas Violentos and the Rap de Aquí compilations, then peaking with Zaragoza's Violadores del Verso and Seville's SFDK around 1999-2006 — 85-95 BPM sampled boom-bap drums, jazz and soul loops, scratched hooks, and dense multisyllabic Castilian rhyming with rolled r's and heavy consonantal attack.
items.description: Rap español is the hip-hop tradition of Spain, distinct from Latin American rap in language register and in its long fidelity to sample-based boom-bap production well past that style's US decline. Its canonical form is a mid-tempo looped jazz or soul break, filtered bass, scratched vocal hook, and a technically dense Castilian flow prizing internal rhyme and battle-derived punchlines. Where French rap absorbed North African and Caribbean production early, Spanish rap stayed closer to the New York 1990s template, and only after 2015 did trap and Latin urbano displace it commercially.
exemplars: El Club de los Poetas Violentos

items.name: Jazz saxophone tradition
items.lineage: American saxophone-led improvising lineage running from Coleman Hawkins's vertical arpeggiated approach and Lester Young's linear behind-the-beat phrasing in the 1930s, through Charlie Parker's bebop vocabulary codified 1945-1950, to the hard-bop and modal saxophone of Sonny Rollins and John Coltrane at Van Gelder's studios between 1955 and 1965 — swing-eighth 4/4 at 120-300 BPM, head-solos-head form over 32-bar and blues frames, and a reed-and-mouthpiece sound culture ranging from Hawkins's wide subtone vibrato to Coltrane's hardened cutting attack.
items.description: The jazz saxophone tradition is the improvising lineage that made the tenor and alto the primary solo voices of American jazz from the 1930s onward. It is defined by a shared vocabulary of chord-scale running, blues inflection and rhythmic displacement, carried through the head-solos-head form over standards and blues, and by a highly individuated tone culture in which mouthpiece, reed and vibrato choices function as personal signature. Distinguished from big-band section playing by its soloist focus, and from later fusion saxophone by its acoustic, unamplified sound and its allegiance to changes-based improvisation.

items.name: Musical impressionism
items.lineage: French art-music current formed in Paris between roughly 1890 and 1920, codified by Claude Debussy from Prélude à l'après-midi d'un faune (1894) and extended by Maurice Ravel — whole-tone and octatonic collections, unresolved parallel ninth and seventh chords, modal borrowings from plainchant and from Javanese gamelan heard at the 1889 Exposition, blurred metric articulation with frequent 9/8 and shifting bar groupings, and orchestration built on divisi strings, solo flute and english horn, harp glissandi and celesta.
items.description: Musical impressionism is the Parisian art-music current of roughly 1890 to 1920 centred on Debussy and Ravel, in which functional tonal progression gives way to chords valued for colour and to whole-tone, pentatonic and octatonic collections. Texture is the primary carrier of meaning: divisi strings, harp glissandi, celesta, muted horns and solo woodwind lines are combined for shimmer rather than for contrapuntal clarity, and metre is deliberately obscured. It differs from late Romanticism in abandoning goal-directed harmonic tension, and from the succeeding neoclassicism in its refusal of clean-edged motivic construction.

items.name: Dinner jazz
items.lineage: American and British background-jazz practice codified for hotel dining rooms, supper clubs and later for radio and streaming programming from the mid-1950s onward, growing out of cocktail piano and the Nat King Cole and George Shearing trio formats — 70-120 BPM medium swing and bossa feels, brushed drums, walking bass at low dynamics, sparse block-chord piano or vibraphone comping, warm subtone tenor obbligato and either wordless or crooned standards delivered without hard attack.
items.description: Dinner jazz is the functional low-dynamic branch of small-group jazz developed for hotel dining rooms and supper clubs, consolidated in the 1950s around the piano trio and the light-toned tenor. Its markers are brushes rather than sticks, a bass kept soft and steady, restrained block-chord comping, and standards taken at medium tempo with the melody left largely intact. It is separated from hard bop by its deliberate refusal of dynamic peaks and extended solo development, and from later smooth jazz by remaining acoustic and standards-based rather than electric and originals-based.

items.name: Funk 150 BPM
items.lineage: Rio de Janeiro funk carioca subgenre that emerged around 2014-2016 out of the North Zone baile circuit and the DJ Rennan da Penha and Baile da Gaiola scene — the tamborzão sample battery accelerated to roughly 150 BPM, snare and atabaque hits pushed into rapid stuttering triplet-feel rolls, an aggressive dry kick with almost no sub tail, minimal melodic content, and MC vocals delivered as short shouted or sung hooks looped over the pattern.
items.description: Funk 150 BPM is the accelerated Rio variant of funk carioca that took over the city's bailes in the mid-2010s, driven by the North Zone DJ circuit and by dance videos circulating on social media. It takes the tamborzão pattern, raises the tempo to around 150, and thins everything else out: dry punchy kick, machine-gun snare and atabaque rolls, almost no bassline or harmony, and a single looped MC hook. Against classic 130 BPM funk it trades groove weight for rhythmic velocity, and against rave funk it stays percussive rather than adding euro-rave synth leads.

items.name: Música Bajacaliforniana
items.lineage: Border-state regional-Mexican idiom of Tijuana, Mexicali and Ensenada consolidated from the 1980s onward as norteño conjunto absorbed banda brass and Sinaloan corrido repertoire, codified commercially by Los Tucanes de Tijuana and later Grupo Firme — diatonic button accordion and bajo sexto over tololoche or tuba bass, 2/4 polka and 3/4 vals subforms at 110-150 BPM, doubled saxophone lines, and paired baritone-tenor vocals delivering narrative corrido verse.
items.description: A Baja California variant of regional Mexican music that formed along the Tijuana-San Diego corridor from the 1980s, blending norteño accordion-and-bajo-sexto conjunto with banda tuba bass, sax doublings and Sinaloan corrido narrative. Recordings are bright, close-miked and DAW-assembled, with the accordion and sax panned hard against a tuba or tololoche root and a stiff polka backbeat. It differs from Sinaloan banda by keeping the accordion conjunto at the centre, and from Texan conjunto by its heavier brass bottom and cross-border corrido subject matter.

items.name: Suomirock
items.lineage: Finnish-language guitar rock consolidated in Helsinki, Tampere and Joensuu across the late 1970s and 1980s — Hurriganes' rhythm-and-blues drive gave way to Eppu Normaali's melodic punk-pop and Hassisen Kone/CMX's darker modal writing, built on Marshall-driven humbucker guitar, straight 4/4 at 120-170 BPM, minor-key Aeolian melody, tonewheel organ or poly-synth pads, and a declamatory baritone singing colloquial Finnish.
items.description: Finnish-language rock that became a mass idiom between the mid-1970s and late 1980s, when Finnish lyrics replaced English across the domestic market. The sound is analog-tracked band rock — overdriven humbucker guitars, a dry room kit, organ or synth padding — with a plain-spoken vocal foregrounded and melodies leaning minor and modal rather than blues-pentatonic. It is distinguished from Anglo-American arena rock by its lyric-first mix, its melancholic Aeolian tunes and, in the Eppu Normaali strand, a punk-derived brevity.

items.name: Alté
items.lineage: Lagos alternative scene named around 2016 by DRB LasGidi affiliates and consolidated by Odunsi (The Engine), Santi and Cruel Santino — laptop-built afrofusion at 90-110 BPM that sets loose, log-drum-free syncopated programming and 808 sub against clean single-coil guitar chords, chorused synth pads, and a breathy, half-sung half-rapped delivery in Nigerian Pidgin and English.
items.description: A Lagos-based alternative strand of Nigerian pop that crystallised after 2015 around a self-consciously non-mainstream, internet-native cohort. Its productions are sparse and hazy — muted guitar loops, wide reverbed pads, soft 808s, unquantised percussion — with vocals mixed intimately and often heavily doubled rather than belted. Against mainstream Afrobeats it trades the hard log-drum/amapiano bounce and hook-first arrangement for slower tempos, R&B and neo-soul harmony, and a deliberately amateurish, lo-fi warmth.

items.name: Roots Worship
items.lineage: Acoustic, Americana-inflected congregational worship that emerged in North American and Northern Irish church-planting circles after 2008 — Rend Collective, All Sons & Daughters and Shane & Shane stripped arena-worship synth pads back to dreadnought guitar, mandolin, upright-toned bass, brushed kit and Hammond, with 70-100 BPM 6/8 and 4/4 hymn-shaped forms, congregational unison choruses and unaffected, slightly rough lead vocals.
items.description: A post-2008 reaction inside contemporary worship music against stadium-scale synth production, returning to acoustic folk and hymn instrumentation while keeping modern congregational song form. Records are cut with live-room bleed, real strummed and picked acoustics, banjo or mandolin colour, brushed drums and group singing that sounds like a room rather than a stacked studio choir. It differs from mainstream modern worship in texture and dynamic restraint rather than theology or harmony, and from Americana proper in its deliberately singable, repeat-friendly chorus writing.

items.name: New Age
items.lineage: Contemplative instrumental music codified in California, Japan and Ireland between 1975 and 1990 through Steven Halpern's untempered keyboard drones, Kitarō's synth-and-flute suites and Windham Hill's acoustic roster — slow or unmeasured pulse, consonant diatonic and pentatonic harmony, long-decay reverb, sustained analog pads and string machines, wordless vocal layering, and near-total avoidance of dissonance or backbeat.
items.description: An instrumental genre built from the mid-1970s around meditation, healing and relaxation contexts rather than concert or dance use, spanning synthesizer suites, solo acoustic playing and world-instrument pastiche. Its markers are unhurried or pulseless time, wholly consonant harmony, very long reverb tails, and timbres chosen for smoothness — pads, string machines, breathy flutes, wordless voices. Where ambient proper is often texturally austere or process-driven, new age is melodically explicit and emotionally directive, and unlike minimalism it avoids rigorous structural procedure entirely.

items.name: New Age Piano
items.lineage: Solo acoustic piano branch of new age crystallised by Windham Hill Records in Palo Alto between 1979 and 1990 — George Winston's seasonal albums and Liz Story's and David Lanz's records established slow rubato tempi, sustained-pedal open-fifth left-hand ostinati, diatonic modal melody over unresolved suspended chords, close ribbon-and-condenser capture of a well-tuned grand, and long natural decay with no percussion or backbeat.
items.description: The solo-piano wing of new age, defined commercially by Windham Hill from 1979 onward and later broadened by European pianists working in the same idiom. It is characterised by rubato phrasing, pedal-heavy sustain, repeating left-hand open intervals, and diatonic or Lydian melodies that circle rather than modulate, captured with minimal processing so the instrument's decay carries the record. Compared with synth-led new age it is entirely acoustic and single-timbre; compared with classical solo repertoire it is harmonically static and largely unnotated in performance practice.

items.name: Scam Rap
items.lineage: Detroit and Flint microgenre that broke out in 2018-2019 through Teejayx6, Kasher Quon and Dank Demoss — rapid, unpunched conversational verses narrating step-by-step credit-card and bank fraud over cheap DAW beats at 130-150 BPM, with detuned bell or piano loops, rattling triplet hats, distorted 808 glides, no hook, and abrupt off-beat entries typical of the Detroit sample-flip style.
items.description: A lyric-defined offshoot of Detroit rap that surfaced on YouTube around 2018, in which entire verses are instructional narratives of financial fraud delivered deadpan and at speed. Musically it inherits the Detroit template — fast, slightly out-of-tune loops, hyperactive hi-hats, a barely mixed vocal recorded in a bedroom and uploaded compressed — with hooks often omitted entirely. It differs from Atlanta trap by tempo, by the absence of melodic ad-libbed choruses, and by a comedic documentary lyric register that has no parallel in gangsta or drill.

items.name: Float House
items.lineage: Melodic, weightless strand of deep and progressive house consolidated after 2015 around the Anjunadeep and This Never Happened labels — Lane 8, Yotto and Ben Böhmer working at 118-124 BPM with soft-attack 909-derived kicks, sidechained sustained pads, filtered Rhodes and piano chords, wide reverbed vocal fragments, and eight-to-sixteen-bar sweeps that replace the drop with continuous swell.
items.description: A post-2015 melodic house style built for headphone and festival-sunset listening rather than club peak time, associated with the Anjunadeep and mau5trap-adjacent orbit. Its signature is buoyancy: rounded kicks, heavy sidechain breathing, chords held through long filter opens, and reverb-drenched vocal chops that function as texture rather than lead. Against deep house proper it is brighter and more chord-forward, and against progressive trance it avoids the sharp build-and-drop architecture in favour of gradual, continuous lift.

items.name: Rock Drums (drum-feature instrumental)
items.lineage: Anglo-American practice of the kit as lead voice, running from Sandy Nelson's 1959 tom-driven instrumental singles through the extended concert solos of Ginger Baker, John Bonham and Cozy Powell in 1966-1980 — large-shell kits tuned low and open, multi-mic close-and-room capture through transformer consoles to 15 ips tape, 4/4 backbeat frames at 100-160 BPM, and structured toms-and-cymbal improvisation over a minimal riff.
items.description: The drum-forward instrumental repertoire of rock — solo features, tom-led singles and extended concert showcases — in which the kit carries melody-function through pitch-tuned toms and cymbal colour rather than accompanying a song. Its sonic identity comes as much from recording practice as playing: open low-tuned shells, distant ribbon room mics compressed hard, and tape saturation giving the ambience a bloom that close-miking alone will not. It sits apart from drumline and ensemble percussion traditions in being a single amplified kit within a rock band frame, and apart from ordinary rock tracks in giving the drums the lead role.

items.name: Levenslied
items.lineage: Dutch sentimental popular song of the Jordaan and Rotterdam working-class districts, commercialised on record from the 1930s and dominant on Dutch radio from the 1950s through Johnny Jordaan, Willy Alberti and later André Hazes — 3/4 waltz and slow 4/4 at 70-110 BPM, accordion and string-section accompaniment, plain major-key harmony with a chromatic passing turn, and a full-throated, heavily rubato Dutch-language vocal on themes of love, drink and loss.
items.description: The Dutch-language sentimental ballad tradition, rooted in Amsterdam's Jordaan quarter and carried onto record and television across the twentieth century. Its sound is accordion-led waltz or slow ballad with light orchestral strings behind a declamatory, tearful lead voice pushed close on a tube mic. It is the Low Countries analogue of German Schlager and French chanson réaliste, but distinguished by the accordion's constant foreground presence, its unabashedly local dialect delivery, and a lyric world of neighbourhood, café and bereavement rather than romance abstracted.

items.name: Rap Cristiano
items.lineage: Spanish-language Christian hip hop developed across Puerto Rico, the Dominican Republic, Mexico and the US Latino church from the mid-1990s, professionalised after 2005 by Redimi2, Funky, Alex Zurdo and Manny Montes — 85-100 BPM boom-bap and reggaeton-inflected programming, sung R&B choruses, piano and string sample beds, and dense doctrinal or testimonial verse delivered with clear diction over 808 sub and clap-driven backbeats.
items.description: Spanish-language Christian rap, built in Caribbean and Mexican evangelical scenes from the 1990s and now a large commercial sector with its own labels and festivals. Production tracks the mainstream Latin urbano timeline — boom-bap, then reggaeton dembow, then trap 808s — while the lyric register stays testimonial and scripture-quoting, and choruses are usually sung in a polished R&B or pop-worship style rather than chanted. It is distinguished from secular Latin trap by the absence of profanity and by hook writing borrowed from congregational worship, and from English-language CHH by its Caribbean rhythmic base.

items.name: Naija Worship
items.lineage: Nigerian Pentecostal congregational worship shaped in Lagos megachurches from the 1990s and exported on record after 2010 through Sinach, Nathaniel Bassey, Dunsin Oyekan and Mercy Chinwo — 70-100 BPM 4/4 and 6/8 forms that build over long repeated refrains, Hammond and synth pad beds under electric bass and kit, talking drum and conga underlay, call-and-response between soloist and choir, and English, Yoruba or Igbo lyrics carried by a belted, melismatic lead.
items.description: The worship repertoire of Nigerian Pentecostal churches, recorded largely live in sanctuaries and released as long-form praise and worship sets. Musically it combines American gospel harmony and organ vamping with West African percussion underneath and highlife-derived guitar figures, and its defining formal trait is extended cyclic repetition of a single refrain that intensifies through key lifts and spontaneous congregational singing. It differs from African-American gospel in its rhythmic base and language mixing, and from Afrobeats in tempo, function and the priority of choir over programmed track.

items.name: Rap Marocain
items.lineage: Moroccan hip hop that emerged in Casablanca, Salé and Meknes in the late 1990s, breaking commercially with Fnaïre, Don Bigg and Muslim in the mid-2000s and going pan-Arab with ElGrandeToto after 2017 — Darija-language verse over 80-145 BPM trap and boom-bap programming, frequent chaabi and Gnawa borrowings (guembri ostinato, qraqeb metal-castanet 12/8), maqam-coloured sung hooks, and a nasal, hard-consonant delivery cutting across the beat.
items.description: Moroccan rap in Darija, formed in coastal-city youth scenes from the late 1990s and now one of the largest hip-hop markets in the Arabic-speaking world. Beats are DAW-built trap or boom-bap that regularly quote local material outright — guembri riffs, qraqeb patterns, chaabi violin and maqam-inflected sung refrains — while the vocal exploits Darija's clipped consonants for percussive attack. It parts from Egyptian mahraganat by keeping rap-verse structure rather than shaabi keyboard-and-chant form, and from French banlieue rap by its Amazigh and Gnawa sound sources despite shared diaspora ties.

items.name: Bass Trap
items.lineage: Festival-circuit hybrid of Southern hip-hop's 808 vocabulary and EDM sound-design that formed 2011-2014 through Baauer, RL Grime, and the Trap City / Mad Decent blog economy — 140-150 BPM half-time drum programming, long-decay tuned 808 kicks, triplet and 32nd-note hi-hat rolls, detuned supersaw or metallic Massive lead stabs on the drop, pitched vocal chops and airhorn stingers in place of a rapped verse.
items.description: Bass trap is the instrumental EDM offshoot of Atlanta trap that crystallized around 2012 on Mad Decent, Fool's Gold, and the SoundCloud blog circuit, built for main-stage festival systems rather than car audio. Its signature is a half-time 140-150 BPM grid where the tuned 808 sine carries both bass and kick duty, hi-hats subdivide into machine-gun triplet rolls, and a heavily sound-designed synth or vocal-chop lead replaces the MC. Unlike Atlanta rap trap it is voice-free or vocal-sample-only and structured around EDM build-and-drop architecture; unlike dubstep it keeps the 808 rather than the wobble bass as its central voice.

items.name: Jazz Piano (trio and solo idiom)
items.lineage: The piano-led American jazz idiom codified between the 1930s and 1960s by Art Tatum, Bud Powell, Bill Evans, and Thelonious Monk — left-hand rootless voicings and shell chords under a right-hand bebop line, swung eighths at anywhere from ballad rubato to 300 BPM, walking bass and brushed or ride-led drums in the trio format, and improvisation over 32-bar AABA standards and blues.
items.description: Jazz piano as a distinct performance tradition runs from Harlem stride through Tatum's virtuoso arpeggiation to the Powell-Evans conception of the piano trio as three equal conversational voices, consolidated in the New York and Englewood Cliffs sessions of 1955-1965. Its defining sound is extended tertian harmony voiced rootlessly in the left hand, a horn-derived single-note right-hand line, and interactive bass and brush work rather than timekeeping accompaniment. It differs from stride and boogie-woogie in abandoning the metronomic striding left hand, and from later fusion keyboard playing in staying acoustic and tied to the standard-repertoire chorus form.
exemplars: Bill Evans Trio - Sunday at the Village Vanguard

items.name: Tierra Caliente
items.lineage: Regional Mexican string tradition of the hot lowlands of Michoacán, Guerrero, and the Balsas basin, professionalized on record from the 1950s through conjuntos de arpa grande and later the Tierra Caliente banda-and-tamborita ensembles — 6/8 sones and gustos in sesquialtera hemiola, a large arpa grande played with percussive cajón-of-the-soundbox tapping, twin violins in parallel thirds, vihuela and guitarra de golpe rhythm, and high nasal duet singing.
items.description: Tierra Caliente names the music of the Balsas depression straddling Michoacán and Guerrero, documented commercially from the 1950s in Mexico City studios and still played at rural jaripeos and bailes. Its classic conjunto de arpa grande sets a large diatonic harp against two violins, vihuela and guitarra de golpe, with a second player drumming the harp's soundbox as percussion; the repertoire of sones and gustos rides a 6/8 against 3/4 hemiola with shouted verses and falsetto-tipped duet singing. It differs from mariachi in its harp-centered rather than trumpet-centered texture and slower gusto forms, and from Sinaloan banda in remaining a string ensemble rather than a brass one.

items.name: Muziek voor Kinderen (Dutch children's song)
items.lineage: Dutch-language children's popular song professionalized by VARA television from 1980 through the Kinderen voor Kinderen project and by cabaret songwriters such as Herman van Veen and Annie M.G. Schmidt's earlier lyric tradition — bright major-key verse-chorus pop at 100-130 BPM sung by unschooled child choirs in unison or thirds over a session band of piano, acoustic guitar, electric bass, drum kit, and glockenspiel, with witty spoken-Dutch phrasing and topical, non-moralizing lyrics.
items.description: Muziek voor kinderen is the Dutch broadcast tradition of purpose-written children's pop, distinct from inherited nursery rhyme, that took its modern shape with the annual VARA series Kinderen voor Kinderen from 1980 onward and with Annie M.G. Schmidt's and Harrie Geelen's lyric school before it. Musically it is straight studio pop — clean session band, tight tempo grid, glockenspiel and recorder colouring, choruses doubled by a large untrained child chorus — carrying lyrics that treat divorce, bullying, and homework in plain conversational Dutch. It differs from international kids' entertainment franchises by its cabaret-derived wordplay and refusal of babytalk, and from traditional kinderliedjes by being newly composed each season for television.

items.name: Odia Pop
items.lineage: Odisha's Odia-language popular song, moving from HMV Cuttack and Odia cinema playback in the 1960s-80s into a cassette and now YouTube-driven album industry — verse-refrain songs at 90-130 BPM with lightly ornamented melodic lines derived from Odissi and bhajan phrasing, harmonium and bansuri counterlines over dholak, mardala, or programmed kit, and a bright forward-placed lead vocal doubled in the chorus.
items.description: Odia pop is the non-film and film-adjacent popular song of Odisha, grown from Akashvani Cuttack broadcasts and Odia cinema playback into a cassette-era album market in the 1980s-90s and a YouTube single economy after 2010. Its sound keeps the melodic ornament and phrase-ending gamak of Odissi and Jagannath bhajan repertoire but sets it on a tempered pop chassis of programmed drums, keyboard pads, and harmonium or bansuri obbligato, with the vocal mixed far forward. It is distinguished from Bengali adhunik and Bollywood filmi pop by language, by the mardala's presence in the percussion bed, and by an album-and-video rather than film-soundtrack release path.

items.name: Trap Colombiano
items.lineage: Colombian Spanish-language trap centred on Medellín's barrio studios from roughly 2015, downstream of Puerto Rican Latin trap but locally inflected by paisa slang and reggaetón session culture — 130-145 BPM half-time beats over long tuned 808 slides, triplet hi-hat rolls, minor-key piano or plucked-synth loops, and heavily Auto-Tuned melodic verses that slip between sung hook and rapped bar.
items.description: Trap colombiano emerged in Medellín and Cali after 2015 as producers and singers who had come up through reggaetón sessions adopted the Atlanta half-time template with Spanish melodic delivery. The records are sparse — sub-heavy 808 glides, rolled hi-hats, a two-bar minor loop, and stacked Auto-Tuned vocals with the ad-lib layer as an instrument in itself — and lean toward sung hooks rather than dense rapping. It differs from Puerto Rican trap latino chiefly in accent, slang, and its constant crossover back into reggaetón and guaracha rhythms, and from Colombian boom-bap rap in tempo feel and its melodic rather than lyrical centre of gravity.

items.name: Funk Viral
items.lineage: Rio and São Paulo baile funk variant shaped after 2018 by TikTok and YouTube Shorts circulation — 130-150 BPM beat-viral patterns built from stacked tamborzão and beatbox-derived samples, extreme sub-bass drops, chopped shouted MC phrases looped as hooks, abrupt beat switches every eight bars, and mixes optimised for phone speakers rather than paredão sound systems.
items.description: Funk viral is the short-video-native strain of Brazilian funk that consolidated around 2019-2021, produced almost entirely in FL Studio on home machines in Rio and São Paulo peripheries and released straight to YouTube and TikTok. Its grammar is the beat-viral montage: layered tamborzão and vocal-percussion samples, a punishing sub drop, an MC phrase chopped into a rhythmic loop, and structural beat switches timed to fit a fifteen-second clip. It is distinguished from earlier funk carioca and from funk ostentação by that clip-length editing logic and by mixes tuned for lossy phone playback rather than for wall-of-speaker bailes, and from Brazilian rap by having no sustained verse.

items.name: Medieval Rock (Mittelalter-Rock)
items.lineage: German Mittelalter-Rock, formed in the 1990s when medieval-market ensembles such as Corvus Corax were joined to an amplified rock rhythm section by In Extremo and Subway to Sally — mid-tempo 4/4 riffs on downtuned humbucker guitars doubled by shawm, bagpipe and hurdy-gurdy playing modal Dorian and Aeolian melodies, thunderous davul and floor-tom patterns, and declaimed German or Middle-High-German lyrics.
items.description: Medieval rock is a German-speaking scene that grew out of the 1980s Mittelaltermarkt circuit, where drone-pipe and drum ensembles played reconstructed repertoire, and out of its collision with metal when In Extremo and Subway to Sally added distorted guitars in the mid-1990s. The sound places loud reeded instruments — shawm, various bagpipes, hurdy-gurdy — in the lead role a guitar would normally occupy, doubling riffs in unison over a heavy backbeat, with declamatory German vocals and frequent 6/8 dance sections. It differs from Nordic folk metal by drawing on market-medievalist rather than Viking imagery and by keeping clean rather than harsh vocals, and from historically informed early music by being written new for amplification.

items.name: Turkish Pop
items.lineage: Türk pop müziği, running from the 1960s aranjman craze of foreign melodies with Turkish lyrics through Sezen Aksu's songwriting school and the 1990s Tarkan-era boom — 95-130 BPM verse-chorus songs with darbuka and programmed kit under Western pop harmony, bağlama or kanun countermelodies, synth pads and horn stabs, and a melismatic, makam-inflected but tempered lead vocal.
items.description: Turkish pop began as aranjman — imported French and Italian melodies refitted with Turkish lyrics in the 1960s — and became a self-sustaining songwriting industry through Sezen Aksu, whose circle wrote much of the canon that Tarkan, Sertab Erener, and Hande Yener later carried to Europe. The records marry Western pop harmony and 1990s dance production to Anatolian melodic contour and to a percussion bed where darbuka and bendir sit beside the drum machine, with vocals ornamented in makam style even over tempered accompaniment. It is distinguished from arabesk by its cosmopolitan, non-fatalistic register and lighter orchestration, and from Anadolu rock by foregrounding the singer and the dance groove rather than the electric guitar.

items.name: Turkish Folk (Türk Halk Müziği)
items.lineage: Anatolian village repertoire codified for broadcast by the Ankara Radio and TRT collecting programmes from the 1930s under Muzaffer Sarısözen — long-metre free-rhythm uzun hava and metred kırık hava forms, aksak 9/8 and 5/8 dance metres, bağlama family lutes fretted to makam commas, outdoor davul-and-zurna pairing, and âşık bardic singing with heavy vibrato and glottal breaks.
items.description: Türk halk müziği is the village and âşık repertoire of Anatolia and Thrace, systematically collected from the 1930s by state radio teams and standardised into a broadcast repertoire with fixed notation and regional ensemble arrangements. Its core is the bağlama family, fretted in unequal makam commas and played with drone strings and percussive şelpe or plectrum technique, alongside free-rhythm uzun hava lament singing and metred kırık hava dances in aksak 9/8, 7/8, and 5/8. It differs from Ottoman makam art music in being modal-monophonic without the classical fasıl suite structure, and from arabesk in rejecting orchestral strings and the studio ballad frame.

items.name: Turkish Trap
items.lineage: Istanbul and Berlin-diaspora Turkish-language trap that broke through around 2017 with Ezhel's Müptezhel and the Kabus Kerim / Uzi generation — 130-145 BPM half-time 808 productions, triplet hi-hats and rolled snares, minor-key loops frequently sampling or replaying bağlama, kanun, and arabesk string lines, and Turkish verses that alternate melodic Auto-Tuned hooks with fast rapped bars.
items.description: Turkish trap took hold after 2016 as producers in Istanbul, Ankara, and the German-Turkish diaspora adopted the Atlanta half-time template and fed Anatolian material into it, reaching national scale with Ezhel and later Uzi, Motive, and Blok3. The beats are sparse and 808-centred with triplet hat rolls, but their melodic loops routinely replay bağlama, kanun, or arabesk string figures in makam-flavoured minor, and vocals swing between Auto-Tuned melodic hooks and dense Turkish rhyme. It differs from the earlier Turkish boom-bap of Ceza and Sagopa Kajmer in tempo feel, sung delivery, and streaming-native release, and from Turkish pop in keeping the rap verse and street-register lyric at the centre.

items.name: Arab Pop
items.lineage: Pan-Arab commercial pop consolidated in Cairo and Beirut from the late 1980s onward — Amr Diab's 1996 'Nour El Ain' fixing the template — setting maqam-inflected melody and Egyptian-dialect lyric over a 100-130 BPM four-on-the-floor bed with programmed darbuka/riq maqsum and baladi patterns, synth-doubled qanun and violin unisons, and a lightly ornamented mid-register chest vocal.
items.description: Arab pop is the pan-regional commercial song style built in Cairo and Beirut studios from the late 1980s and dominant across Arabic-language media since the 1990s. Its signature is the collision of maqam melody and quarter-tone-capable violin/qanun unisons with a fully programmed dance rhythm section, the darbuka and riq figures sequenced rather than played, and vocals tracked close and dry with light ornament. Unlike the golden-age tarab orchestral repertoire it descends from, songs run three to five minutes with fixed verse-chorus form and no extended improvised layali.

items.name: Egyptian Pop
items.lineage: Cairo's al-jeel ('generation') pop, formed circa 1980 around Hamid El Shaeri and Egyptian-Libyan cassette-kiosk production, layering Casio/Roland preset keyboards and drum machines over maqsum and baladi patterns at 110-125 BPM with darbuka, riq, accordion and mizmar interjections and a nasal, forward-placed street vocal in colloquial Egyptian Arabic.
items.description: Egyptian pop in its defining al-jeel form emerged in Cairo around 1980 as cheap cassette production put synthesizers and drum machines in the hands of producers working outside the state-radio orchestral apparatus. The sound is bright, compressed and slightly overloaded: preset keyboard brass and strings, mechanical maqsum programming, live darbuka and riq on top, and hooky colloquial refrains built for wedding PA and microbus playback. It differs from broader Arab pop by its rawness and from shaabi proper by keeping a smoother, more melodic vocal rather than the shouted mahraganat delivery that later grew from the same kiosks.

items.name: Moroccan Pop
items.lineage: Casablanca and Marrakech commercial chaabi-pop, professionalized from the early 1970s through Nass El Ghiwane's political song and the later cassette-label boom, combining 6/8 and 12/8 Berber-Gnawa cycles with guembri ostinato, qraqeb clatter, bendir and darbuka, unison violin and oud lines, and call-and-response chorus vocals over synthesizer pads.
items.description: Moroccan pop is the studio-mediated descendant of urban chaabi and Gnawa ritual music, built in Casablanca from the 1970s and carried nationwide by cassette. Its defining features are the guembri's low three-string ostinato and metal qraqeb against bendir frame drums, accelerating 6/8 cycles that break into faster closing sections, and a chorus that answers the lead singer in short unison phrases. Compared with Algerian rai it stays closer to Berber and Gnawa rhythmic cycles and uses less pop-rock harmony, and compared with Andalusi nuba it abandons the fixed suite architecture entirely.

items.name: Israeli Pop
items.lineage: Tel Aviv commercial song from the 1970s onward, formed when the Ashkenazi-European Shirei Eretz Yisrael tradition was overtaken by Mizrahi cassette culture from the Yemenite and Iraqi neighbourhoods — bouzouki and oud tremolo lines, darbuka doubling a rock kit, Hebrew lyric sung with Arabic-derived melisma, and 100-130 BPM verse-chorus forms.
items.description: Israeli pop is the mainstream Hebrew-language song style of Tel Aviv radio and the central bus station cassette stalls, decisively reshaped between the 1970s and 1990s as musika mizrahit moved from the margins to the charts. The defining sound pairs a Western rock rhythm section with bouzouki and oud tremolo, darbuka on the backbeat, and vocals that carry Yemenite or Iraqi ornamentation over major-minor or hijaz harmony. It is distinguished from Arab pop by Hebrew text and greater use of Greek-Anatolian bouzouki timbre, and from earlier Israeli folk-song by its dance-oriented rhythm and unashamed Middle Eastern melisma.

items.name: South African Pop
items.lineage: Johannesburg commercial pop from the 1980s Soweto 'bubblegum' boom of Brenda Fassie and Yvonne Chaka Chaka through post-1994 kwaito-pop, running 100-115 BPM four-on-the-floor synth-bass grooves with mbaqanga-derived lead guitar lines, gospel-thick group harmony in isiZulu and English, and drum-machine kits mixed over live bass.
items.description: South African pop as a continuous studio tradition runs from the Gallo-era township bubblegum records of the 1980s to the kwaito-adjacent chart pop of the 2000s. It keeps the cyclical two- or four-chord vamp and interlocking high guitar line of mbaqanga but replaces the live jive rhythm section with synth bass and programmed drums, and it carries choral group singing inherited from isicathamiya and church into pop hook writing. Against gqom and amapiano, which strip the arrangement down to drum and bass elements, South African pop stays song-shaped, sung end to end, and harmonically warm.

items.name: Brazilian Reggae
items.lineage: Reggae maranhense, formed in São Luís do Maranhão from the mid-1970s around radiola sound systems playing imported Jamaican 45s, later joined by Rio and Brasília bands in the 1990s — one-drop and steppers kits at 70-90 BPM, bubbling organ, deep melodic bass, skanking off-beat guitar, and Portuguese lyrics sung in a smooth, unhurried mid-register.
items.description: Brazilian reggae originated as a listening and dancing culture rather than a recording one: from the mid-1970s São Luís do Maranhão built enormous radiola sound systems around Jamaican imports, spawning a local dance style and eventually local bands. The recorded style keeps Jamaican one-drop and steppers architecture — bass carrying the melody, guitar and organ on the off-beats, drums dropping the downbeat — but softens the mix, brightens the harmony toward Brazilian pop, and sings in Portuguese with none of the patois toasting. It is distinct from Jamaican roots reggae in its lyrical romanticism and from MPB reggae dabbling in that it is a full regional scene with its own dance halls.

items.name: Brazilian Gospel
items.lineage: Música gospel brasileira, industrialized from the early 1990s around São Paulo evangelical labels and the Universal and Assembleia de Deus congregations — 65-80 BPM power-ballad forms and 120 BPM congregational anthems with grand piano and pad foundations, stacked choir responses in Portuguese, belted modulating final choruses, and rock kit with electric guitar climaxes.
items.description: Brazilian gospel is the commercial worship music of Brazil's Pentecostal and neo-Pentecostal churches, which grew from a niche hymn market into one of the country's largest recording sectors after 1990. The template is the arena worship ballad: sustained piano and synth pads, a slow build to a modulated final chorus, a large multitracked choir answering the soloist, and a vocal style that prizes wide vibrato and a belted top. It borrows US contemporary Christian production wholesale and shares little with African-American gospel's blues-derived harmony or with Brazilian folk-Catholic song, which stays acoustic and processional.

items.name: Mexican Rock
items.lineage: Mexico City rock en español, codified between 1986 and 1996 by Caifanes, Maldita Vecindad, Café Tacvba and Molotov after the Rock en tu Idioma marketing push — post-punk and ska-inflected guitar bands at 90-150 BPM using jarana, requinto and son jarocho or bolero quotations inside distorted 4/4 arrangements, with theatrical, regionally accented Spanish vocals.
items.description: Mexican rock became a mass idiom in the late 1980s, when labels rebranded Spanish-language guitar music as Rock en tu Idioma and Mexico City bands turned from imitation toward local material. The defining records set goth-inflected or ska-punk guitar arrangements against explicit Mexican citation — jarana strumming, bolero cadences, mariachi horn quotes, danzón interludes — with vocals delivered in a declamatory, chilango-accented register. That collage instinct separates it from Argentine rock nacional, which stayed closer to a straightforward Anglo-American band template and to lyrical introspection.
exemplars: Maldita Vecindad y los Hijos del Quinto Patio

items.name: Mexican Pop
items.lineage: The Mexico City balada-pop industry built by RCA, Musart and Televisa from the 1960s through the 1990s — Armando Manzanero's bolero writing, then Juan Gabriel and Luis Miguel — slow 2/4 and 4/4 romantic ballads with orchestral string beds, nylon guitar and piano arpeggios, mariachi trumpet obbligatos on the ranchera-leaning numbers, and a large, vibrato-rich chest voice carrying the melody.
items.description: Mexican pop is the balada romántica tradition of the Mexico City recording industry, running from the bolero-derived writing of the 1960s through the televised superstar era of Juan Gabriel, Luis Miguel and Thalía. Its sonic identity is the orchestral arrangement — sectional strings, nylon guitar figures, tube-warm close vocal — around a slow-building romantic lyric that resolves in a key change and a sustained high note. It is separated from ranchera by the absence of mariachi as the default ensemble and by its through-composed ballad form, and from Anglo pop by the sheer weight given to the singer's vibrato and rubato.

items.name: Argentine Rock (Rock Nacional)
items.lineage: Rock nacional, born in Buenos Aires in 1967 with Los Gatos' 'La Balsa' and codified by Almendra, Sui Generis, Charly García and Luis Alberto Spinetta, then Soda Stereo in the 1980s — Spanish-language songwriting insisting on local idiom, mid-tempo 4/4 band arrangements with piano or 12-string acoustic foundations, extended harmonic progressions borrowed from tango and jazz, and intimate, unshouted vocals.
items.description: Rock nacional is the Argentine rock tradition that began in Buenos Aires in the late 1960s with the deliberate decision to sing rock in Spanish, and became a coded language of resistance under the 1976-83 dictatorship. Musically it leans literary and harmonically dense — Spinetta and García wrote with tango-inflected voice leading and jazz extensions over comparatively restrained band arrangements — before Soda Stereo pushed the scene toward gleaming 1980s new wave production. It is more introspective and songwriterly than Mexican rock's carnivalesque genre-collage, and its canonical records were cut on British-style analog chains in Buenos Aires rather than abroad.
exemplars: Patricio Rey y sus Redonditos de Ricota

items.name: Chilean Rock
items.lineage: Chilean rock formed in two waves — Los Jaivas' Andean progressive fusion from 1970, using charango, quena and tarka inside long-form rock suites, and the 1984-90 Santiago new-wave of Los Prisioneros, whose 120-135 BPM drum-machine-and-guitar songs carried sharply political Spanish lyrics against the Pinochet dictatorship, later joined by Los Tres' bolero-and-blues band writing.
items.description: Chilean rock is defined by two distinct formations: the early-1970s Andean progressive fusion of Los Jaivas and Congreso, who ran charango, quena and Andean percussion through extended rock suites in dialogue with the Nueva Canción movement, and the mid-1980s Santiago new-wave scene led by Los Prisioneros, built on cheap drum machines, trebly guitar and blunt anti-dictatorship lyrics. The later scene's thin, punchy, deliberately unpolished production is its most recognizable trait. Against Argentine rock nacional it is more overtly political and less harmonically ornate, and against Mexican rock it draws its local color from Andean instruments rather than from son and bolero.
exemplars: Los Jaivas — Alturas de Machu Picchu
Los Prisioneros — La Voz de los '80

items.name: Spanish rock (rock urbano and rock andaluz)
items.lineage: Spanish-language rock formed in Madrid, Barcelona and Seville between the late 1960s and the 1980s — Smash and Triana grafting flamenco compás and Phrygian cadences onto blues-rock in Andalusia while Madrid's rock urbano (Leño, Barón Rojo) and La Movida bands (Radio Futura, Nacha Pop) worked mid-tempo 4/4 riff rock at 110-150 BPM with declamatory Castilian vocals, single-coil guitars through Marshall stacks, Hammond organ pads and hand-clap palmas or cajón accents carried over from flamenco.
items.description: Spanish rock consolidated after the loosening of Francoist censorship, splitting into an Andalusian branch that fused flamenco modality and 12-beat compás with progressive blues-rock and an urban Madrid branch of blunt riff rock and, later, the pop-leaning bands of La Movida Madrileña. The sound is guitar-forward and mid-scooped, with Castilian lyrics sung in a chesty, consonant-heavy declamation and frequent nylon-string or palmas textures inside an otherwise standard rock kit arrangement. It differs from Anglo hard rock in its Phrygian harmonic gravity and from flamenco proper in its fixed strophic song forms and backbeat drum kit.

items.name: German Rock (Deutschrock)
items.lineage: German-language rock that formed in West Berlin, Cologne and the Ruhr from the early 1970s — codified by Ton Steine Scherben's agitprop street-rock and later by BAP's Kölsch-dialect songs, Herbert Grönemeyer's piano-driven anthems and the punk-descended Die Toten Hosen and Die Ärzte — built on straight-eighth 4/4 at 120-160 BPM, distorted rhythm guitar doubling, four-on-the-floor or plain backbeat kit, and gruff, front-of-mouth German diction that pushes consonants over melisma.
items.description: Deutschrock is the mainstream German-language rock tradition that grew out of the political squat-scene bands of the 1970s and hardened through the punk generation of the 1980s into stadium-scale anthem rock. Its defining marks are unornamented diatonic melody, heavy guitar-and-bass unison riffing, and a vocal delivery closer to shouted speech than to soul phrasing, with lyrics treated as the load-bearing element. It is distinct from krautrock, which is instrumental, motorik and studio-experimental, and from Anglo hard rock in its plainer harmony and text-first mixing.

items.name: German drill
items.lineage: German-language drill emerging in Berlin, Frankfurt and Hamburg from roughly 2019, importing the UK drill template through producers working in FL Studio — sliding 808 sub-bass, triplet and rolled hi-hats over a 138-144 BPM half-time feel, sparse minor-key bell, flute or plucked-string loops, and a flat, on-beat German delivery mixing Turkish, Arabic and Kiezdeutsch slang, tracked dry on a dynamic mic in home and project studios.
items.description: German drill is the Deutschrap adaptation of the UK drill sound, arriving via Berlin and Frankfurt at the end of the 2010s and quickly absorbed into the mainstream German rap charts. Sonically it keeps the pitch-glide 808, the syncopated hat rolls and the two-bar minor loop of its London source, but the vocals sit further forward, doubled and lightly tuned, with a heavier rhythmic emphasis on the downbeat than the off-kilter British flows. It differs from German trap in tempo feel and from UK drill mainly in diction, harder consonant attack, and a cleaner, more compressed commercial master.

items.name: German Baroque
items.lineage: North- and central-German art music of roughly 1650-1750 codified by Buxtehude in Lübeck and brought to its summit by J.S. Bach in Weimar, Köthen and Leipzig alongside Telemann and Handel — dense contrapuntal writing over a continuo of organ or harpsichord with cello and violone, Lutheran chorale melodies as structural cantus firmus, dance-suite meters, terraced dynamics, and gut-strung violins, oboes, natural trumpets and recorders played in circulating well temperaments at low chamber pitch.
items.description: German Baroque names the Lutheran-centred repertoire of organ preludes and fugues, cantatas, passions, concertos and dance suites written in the German lands between the mid-seventeenth century and Bach's death in 1750. Its signature is relentless imitative counterpoint anchored by a figured-bass continuo, chorale tunes carried as long-note scaffolding, and ornamentation that is written out rather than left to the player as often as in the Italian style. Compared with the French and Italian Baroque it is denser in voice-leading, less driven by solo vocal display, and inseparable from the sound of a large church organ in a stone acoustic.

items.name: German Romanticism
items.lineage: German and Austrian art music of roughly 1815-1900, opened by Schubert's Lieder and carried by Schumann, Mendelssohn, Brahms, Wagner and Wolf — chromatically extended functional harmony with deferred cadences and enharmonic modulation, expanded orchestras built around a valve-horn and clarinet core, the piano-and-voice Lied cycle as a central form, wide dynamic terracing, and rubato-inflected phrasing at slow-to-moderate tempos in equal temperament.
items.description: German Romanticism covers the nineteenth-century Austro-German mainstream, from Schubert's song cycles through Brahms's symphonies to Wagner's music dramas and Wolf's late Lieder. It is marked by chromatic harmony that keeps postponing resolution, motivic development stretched across long spans, an orchestra weighted toward warm brass and low strings, and an aesthetic of interiority in which text and instrumental line are treated as a single expressive unit. Against the German Baroque it trades counterpoint-first construction for harmonic colour and dynamic drama, and against French Romanticism it is denser in texture and darker in orchestral weighting.

items.name: Nederpop (Dutch pop)
items.lineage: Dutch pop and pop-rock built in Amsterdam, The Hague and Hilversum studios from the mid-1960s — Nederbeat groups like Shocking Blue and Golden Earring working English-language beat and hard rock, Focus adding progressive organ-and-flute instrumentals, and the late-1970s Doe Maar generation switching to Dutch lyrics over ska and reggae-inflected upstrokes at 100-140 BPM, with bright close-miked drum kits, chorused guitars and tight two- and three-part vocal harmony.
items.description: Nederpop is the Dutch national pop-rock tradition, running from the English-singing Nederbeat exports of the late 1960s through Focus and Golden Earring's international hits to the Dutch-language turn of Doe Maar and its 1990s and 2000s descendants. Its house sound is clean, harmony-forward and radio-oriented, with organ or synth pads under compact guitar riffs, prominent vocal doubling, and arrangements built from tight, verse-chorus repeats. What separates it from British pop-rock of the same years is a lighter rhythmic touch, an early absorption of ska and reggae feel, and after 1980 the deliberate use of Dutch as a chart language.

items.name: Irish rock
items.lineage: Rock made in Dublin, Belfast and Derry from about 1970, codified by Thin Lizzy's twin-harmony lead guitars and Phil Lynott's narrative singing, Horslips' grafting of jigs and reels onto amplified band instrumentation, and U2's early-1980s delay-drenched arpeggio guitar over open-tuned drone chords — mostly straight 4/4 at 110-150 BPM but frequently borrowing Dorian and Mixolydian modal melody, whistle or pipe countermelodies, and a rhetorical, chest-voice vocal delivery.
items.description: Irish rock is the amplified band tradition that emerged from Ireland's showband and ballad-group circuit around 1970 and became a global export through Thin Lizzy, U2 and the punk-era Undertones. Its recurring markers are modal melody inherited from trad session repertoire, harmonised twin lead guitar or, in the U2 lineage, rhythmic dotted-delay arpeggios over sustained root drones, and a declamatory storytelling vocal. It differs from British rock of the same decades by that modal melodic pull and by the routine presence of trad instruments — whistle, bodhrán, bouzouki — inside an otherwise conventional rock line-up.

items.name: Scottish rock
items.lineage: Rock from Glasgow, East Kilbride and Edinburgh from the late 1970s onward — Simple Minds and Big Country building wide, reverberant anthem rock with e-bowed or MXR-processed guitars imitating pipe drones, The Jesus and Mary Chain burying doo-wop melody under feedback in 1985, and later Primal Scream, Mogwai and Franz Ferdinand working dance-rock and instrumental crescendo forms, typically 110-150 BPM 4/4 with big gated snares, chorused bass and plain-spoken Scottish vocal accent.
items.description: Scottish rock is the post-punk-descended guitar tradition centred on Glasgow, spanning the arena-scale anthems of Simple Minds and Big Country, the noise-pop of The Jesus and Mary Chain, and the later instrumental post-rock of Mogwai. The common thread is scale and space rather than a fixed harmonic dialect: long reverbs, sustained ringing guitar figures often shaped to evoke pipe drones, and dynamics built from slow accumulation. Compared with Irish rock it is less modal and less trad-instrumented, and compared with English indie it leans harder on texture, distortion, and delayed release.

items.name: British blues
items.lineage: London-centred electric blues of roughly 1962-1970, codified by Alexis Korner and Cyril Davies at the Marquee and by John Mayall's Bluesbreakers, whose 1966 sessions with Eric Clapton set the template — Chicago-derived twelve-bar and eight-bar forms at 80-160 BPM, shuffle and 12/8 slow-blues feels, amplified harmonica, overdriven single-coil and Les Paul guitar through cranked combo amps, walking or riff bass, and a strained, imitative white-English vocal reaching for Delta and Chicago phrasing.
items.description: British blues was the mid-1960s London revival of Chicago and Delta repertoire by young British players who learned it from imported records, and which fed directly into hard rock through Cream, Fleetwood Mac and Led Zeppelin. Its sonic signature is a louder, more distorted and more soloistic reading of the American source: extended lead guitar improvisation over strict twelve-bar frames, amplifier saturation used as a tone in its own right, and horn sections mostly replaced by organ. It is distinguished from Chicago blues by that guitar-hero foregrounding and thinner rhythm-section groove, and from the British R&B of the same clubs by its slower tempos and lack of pop song-form ambition.

items.name: British soul
items.lineage: Soul and R&B made in Britain from the mid-1960s onward — Dusty Springfield's Atlantic-styled orchestral soul, the Northern Soul club circuit's uptempo four-on-the-floor imports, and the decisive 1980s London wave of Soul II Soul, Loose Ends and Mica Paris working out of Black community studios in Brent and Brixton, using swung 90-110 BPM breakbeat programming, dubwise bass weight, lush string and Rhodes pads, and a restrained, melisma-light lead vocal over stacked group harmony.
items.description: British soul runs from the mid-1960s Anglo readings of American R&B through to the 1980s London sound that fused soul singing with reggae bass, jazz-funk chords and hip-hop-derived breakbeat programming. Its defining qualities are a cooler, less gospel-declamatory lead vocal, heavy sub-weighted low end inherited from Jamaican sound-system practice, and arrangements that let a single sampled drum loop carry the whole track under strings and Rhodes. Against American soul it is more understated in vocal delivery and more sound-system-shaped in its bass, and against UK lovers rock it is less strictly reggae in rhythm.

items.name: Japanese idol pop (aidoru kayō)
items.lineage: Japanese teen-idol pop formalised by talent agencies and TV variety programming in Tokyo from the early 1970s — Momoe Yamaguchi and then Seiko Matsuda in the 1980s establishing the template, extended by Onyanko Club and later Morning Musume and AKB48 — bright 120-145 BPM major-key songs with Brill-Building-style key-change choruses, session-band backing with syncopated slap bass and gated snare, sweetened brass and synth-string beds, and a deliberately thin, high, unrehearsed-sounding solo or unison-group vocal recorded very close.
items.description: Aidoru kayō is the agency-managed Japanese teen-idol pop that dominated television-driven Japanese charts from the 1970s and reorganised itself around large group formats after 2000. Musically it is written and played by elite session professionals — the arrangements carry city-pop-grade chord substitutions and horn writing — while the vocal is intentionally kept youthful, light and imperfect, mixed loud and dry at the front. That contrast between polished backing and untrained-sounding lead is precisely what separates it from J-pop's adult vocal tradition and from the harder-produced dance vocabulary of K-pop.

items.name: Japanese technopop (electropop)
items.lineage: Tokyo synthesizer pop launched by Yellow Magic Orchestra in 1978 with Haruomi Hosono, Ryuichi Sakamoto and Yukihiro Takahashi sequencing a Roland MC-8 microcomposer against live drums, joined by Hikashu and P-Model, and revived from the mid-2000s by Yasutaka Nakata's work with capsule and Perfume — 110-135 BPM four-on-the-floor or stiff sixteenth-note sequences, pentatonic and exotica-derived melodic hooks, vocoder and heavy formant-shifted or pitch-corrected vocals, and analogue polysynth stabs later replaced by sidechained in-the-box production.
items.description: Japanese technopop began with Yellow Magic Orchestra's late-1970s use of microprocessor sequencing as a compositional method rather than a studio convenience, and became a continuous national lineage through 1980s new-wave bands and the 2000s Nakata-produced idol-electro of Perfume. The sound is deliberately mechanical: quantised sequencer lines, clipped synthetic percussion, vocoded or aggressively processed voices, and bright pentatonic hooks that read as playful rather than austere. It differs from European synthpop in its lighter, exotica-tinged melodic vocabulary and from Detroit or Berlin electronic music in remaining firmly a vocal pop form.

items.name: Japanese soundtrack scoring
items.lineage: Japanese screen and game scoring consolidated from the 1950s onward — Toru Takemitsu's sparse modernist film scores for Kobayashi and Teshigahara, Joe Hisaishi's minimalist ostinato-and-melody writing for Miyazaki from 1984, Ryuichi Sakamoto's synth-and-orchestra hybrids, and the game lineage of Koichi Sugiyama and Nobuo Uematsu whose chiptune themes were later rescored for full orchestra — built on long-breathed diatonic or yo-scale themes, ostinato piano or harp figuration, restrained rubato, and orchestral colour weighted toward strings, woodwind solos and celesta.
items.description: Japanese soundtrack scoring is the composed screen music of Japanese cinema, anime and video games, running from Takemitsu's postwar modernism through Hisaishi's Ghibli scores to the orchestral game repertoire now performed in concert halls. Its recurring traits are a strong, singable principal theme stated and restated over a repeating accompaniment figure, transparent orchestration that leaves individual instrumental colours audible, and pentatonic or modal inflections folded into otherwise Western tonal harmony. Compared with Hollywood scoring it is thinner in texture, less driven by brass, and far more willing to leave silence and single-line writing exposed.

items.name: T-pop (Thai idol and mainstream Thai pop)
items.lineage: Bangkok mainstream pop consolidated in the mid-1980s around the Grammy Entertainment and RS Promotion label system — Thongchai 'Bird' McIntyre and Asanee-Wasan set the template of string (สตริง) band-pop sung in central Thai over 100-125 BPM programmed backbeats — and re-formed after 2015 as idol-group T-pop (BNK48, 4EVE, PROXIE) built on K-pop-style synth-and-808 arrangements, tight unison choreography vocals, and occasional luk thung phrasing or khaen and ranat timbres dropped into otherwise Western-harmonised choruses.
items.description: Thai-language mainstream pop from Bangkok, industrialised by Grammy and RS from the mid-1980s and relaunched as idol-driven T-pop after 2015. The sound is heavily programmed — sub-weighted 808 kicks, bright supersaw and plucked-synth hooks, hard-tuned lead vocals with stacked group harmony — with Thai tonal-language phrasing shaping melodic contour and occasional khaen, ranat or phin colour marking it as Thai rather than imported. It differs from luk thung and luk krung, its parents, by abandoning their live-band and orchestral arrangements and their rural or crooner vocal delivery for grid-locked electronic production.

items.name: Taiwanese Mandopop (Taipei ballad industry)
items.lineage: Taipei became the centre of Mandarin-language pop after 1980 when Rock Records, UFO and later Sony Music Taiwan built an export industry aimed at the whole Chinese-speaking world — Teresa Teng's soft-voiced ballad style, Lo Ta-yu's songwriter turn and Jonathan Lee's producer-arranger school established the canonical form: 60-90 BPM piano-and-string ballads in 4/4, verse-prechorus-chorus with a modulated final chorus, close-miked breathy chest-voice Mandarin delivery, and from the 1990s an R&B-inflected Jay Chou variant with mumbled syncopated phrasing and pentatonic 'China wind' hooks.
items.description: The Taipei-centred Mandarin pop industry that dominated Chinese-language popular music from the 1980s through the 2000s. Its signature is the mid-tempo ballad: piano and sustained string pad foundation, restrained drum kit, wide reverb on a close, breathy solo vocal, and a semitone key lift into the last chorus, with lyric-first craft and virtually no improvisation. Against Hong Kong Cantopop it is less orchestrally lush and more songwriter-driven, and against mainland C-pop it kept an independent label ecology and a stronger indie-crossover strand.

items.name: Mainland Chinese pop (neidi liuxing yinyue)
items.lineage: Mainland Chinese popular song revived after 1978 as gangtai imports met domestic tongsu singing, hardened into the 1994 Beijing 'new music' generation (Na Ying, Sun Nan, Gao Feng) and then into the post-2005 televised-talent and streaming era dominated by Hunan TV, Modern Sky and Tencent Music — the mainstream form is a 70-100 BPM 4/4 ballad with piano, string pad and programmed kit, declamatory wide-vibrato tongsu vocal projection over Western functional harmony, often with erhu, dizi or guzheng overdubs signalling 'guofeng' national style.
items.description: Mandarin-language popular music produced inside the PRC, distinct from the Taipei and Hong Kong industries that seeded it. The dominant register is a big-voiced ballad — full-throated tongsu projection with pronounced vibrato, dense string-and-piano beds, heavy bus compression and mastering loudness — shaped by television singing competitions that reward sustained high notes. Its guofeng subcurrent layers erhu, dizi, guzheng and pentatonic hooks over the same Western harmony, a nationalist colouring largely absent from Taiwanese Mandopop's more understated songwriter aesthetic.

items.name: Malaysian pop (pop Melayu / muzik pop Malaysia)
items.lineage: Kuala Lumpur's Malay-language pop industry grew out of 1950s-60s P. Ramlee film song and 1970s pop yeh yeh guitar bands, then codified in the 1980s-90s through EMI Malaysia, BMG and the Anugerah Juara Lagu competition — Sheila Majid's jazz-inflected balada, Search and Wings' rock kapak power ballads, and Siti Nurhaliza's irama Malaysia recordings that set florid melismatic cengkok ornament over 60-100 BPM 4/4 or 6/8 with gendang, kompang, accordion and string pads.
items.description: Malay-language mainstream pop centred on Kuala Lumpur, running from 1980s balada and rock kapak through the irama Malaysia revival of the late 1990s. Its most distinctive feature is vocal: dense cengkok ornamentation and long melismatic tails inherited from asli and ghazal singing, laid over Western-harmonised ballad arrangements with string pads, and in irama Malaysia over gendang, kompang and rebana patterns in zapin, joget or inang rhythms. Compared to Indonesian dangdut it is slower, less percussion-forward and far more ballad-weighted; compared to Mandopop it carries much heavier melodic ornament.

items.name: Pinoy R&B
items.lineage: Manila-based Filipino R&B emerged in the early 1990s as OPM absorbed American new jack swing and quiet-storm soul — Jaya, Kyla and later Nyoy Volante and Jay-R built it on 65-95 BPM swung sixteenth programmed kits, electric-piano and pad-heavy chord beds, and a heavily melismatic belt-and-riff vocal culture nurtured by nationwide karaoke and church choirs — with a 2010s neo-soul and alt-R&B turn through Careless Music and the Manila indie scene.
items.description: Filipino R&B made in Metro Manila, sung in English, Tagalog or a code-switching mix. It is defined by vocal maximalism — runs, melisma, full-belt climaxes and gospel-derived ad-libs over the last chorus — sat on soft-attack electric piano, warm sub bass and swung programmed drums, with the 2010s wave trading gloss for hazier neo-soul chords and looser rhythmic placement. Where mainstream OPM ballads foreground the songwriter and a straight-eighth piano arrangement, Pinoy R&B foregrounds groove and improvised vocal embellishment.

items.name: Pinoy trap
items.lineage: Filipino trap formed after 2015 in Metro Manila and the provincial bedroom-producer scene — Ex Battalion, Shanti Dope, Al James and the Ownmuzik and Uprising collectives built it on 130-150 BPM half-time 808 patterns with long pitched sub-glides, triplet hi-hat rolls, dark minor-key plucked or bell loops, and Taglish rap alternating rapid triplet flows with sung Auto-Tuned hooks, circulated first through YouTube and SoundCloud rather than radio.
items.description: Trap-derived Filipino rap made largely in bedrooms around Metro Manila from the mid-2010s. The beats follow the Atlanta template — sustained 808 sub with glide, snare or clap on the third beat of a half-time bar, stuttering hi-hat triplets, sparse minor loops — but the rapping is Taglish, and the hooks lean on heavily Auto-Tuned melodic singing shaped by Filipino balladry. It is distinguished from earlier Pinoy rap, which used boom-bap breaks and Francis Magalona's declamatory social-commentary delivery, by its cyclic loop structure and vocal processing.

items.name: Punjabi pop
items.lineage: Punjabi-language pop crystallised in the early 1990s across Jalandhar, Delhi and the UK diaspora as folk boliyan and tappe were set to programmed beats — Malkit Singh, Gurdas Maan and Daler Mehndi's cassette-era hits established the form of a driving 100-140 BPM dhol chaal with tumbi or algoza riff, harmonium or synth chord stabs, and an open-throated declamatory tenor with sharp gamak-like grace notes — remade after 2010 by Diljit Dosanjh and the Punjabi-Canadian axis into a slick DAW production still anchored to the dhol pattern.
items.description: Non-film Punjabi popular song from Indian Punjab and the diaspora, commercially formalised in the cassette boom of the early 1990s. Its constant is the dhol: a loud, sharply accented chaal or bhangra pattern, doubled by programmed kick and clap, under a tumbi or algoza ostinato and a loud unornamented-but-gamak-inflected male lead with call-and-response chorus shouts. It differs from UK bhangra, which foregrounds reggae and house production, and from Punjabi filmi playback, which subordinates the dhol to an orchestral arrangement.

items.name: Punjabi hip hop
items.lineage: Punjabi rap grew from mid-2000s UK and Canadian diaspora records (Bohemia's Delhi-Punjabi Urdu rap, RDB's bhangra-rap fusions) into a mass Indian form after 2017 through Sidhu Moose Wala, Karan Aujla and the Brampton-Ludhiana production axis — 90-160 BPM tracks that graft trap 808s and half-time snares onto dhol chaal accents and tumbi riffs, with rapped or half-sung Punjabi verses in a hard, chest-forward register and lyric matter running from village pride to gangster narrative.
items.description: Punjabi-language rap made across Indian Punjab and the Canadian and British diaspora, mass-market since the late 2010s. Production hybridises trap — sustained 808 sub, triplet hats, sparse minor loops — with live or sampled dhol accents and tumbi or algoza motifs, and the vocal sits between rapping and the declamatory bhangra tenor rather than committing to either. Against mainstream Punjabi pop it is slower, darker and lyric-forward; against US trap it retains folk instrumentation and a folk-derived melodic phrasing.

items.name: Bhojpuri pop
items.lineage: Bhojpuri-language commercial song exploded in the 1980s-90s cassette economy of eastern Uttar Pradesh and Bihar — T-Series and small Varanasi and Patna labels mass-pressed devotional, wedding and double-entendre albums by Bharat Sharma Vyas, Manoj Tiwari and later Pawan Singh — built on 110-150 BPM dholak and nagara patterns in kaharwa and dadra tal, harmonium and reedy synth doubling the tune, and a nasal high-register folk vocal carried straight over from birha, kajri and chaita repertoire.
items.description: Commercial popular song in Bhojpuri from Bihar and eastern Uttar Pradesh, built on the cheap cassette-duplication economy of the 1980s onward and later on video and YouTube. Musically it stays close to its folk sources: dholak-led kaharwa grooves, harmonium and a thin synth reed doubling a repetitive pentatonic-leaning tune, minimal harmonic movement, and a piercing nasal vocal that projects like open-air folk singing. Unlike Hindi filmi pop it is regionally self-contained, arranged for speed and low cost rather than orchestral scale, and its lyric registers — Chhath devotional, wedding, and frank double-entendre — have no filmi equivalent.

items.name: Gujarati pop
items.lineage: Gujarati commercial pop grew out of the Navratri garba and raas industry of Ahmedabad, Vadodara and Surat, professionalised from the late 1980s by cassette labels and by the arena-scale garba productions of Falguni Pathak and Atul Purohit — the core form is a hemiola-free but relentlessly cyclic garba pattern at 90-160 BPM on dhol and dholak with clap accents, tabla or programmed kit doubling, harmonium or synth chords, and a bright female-led vocal in call-and-response with a mass chorus, accelerating across a long single cycle.
