items.lineage: Western art-music practice of one player per part for small rooms, standardized between Haydn's Op. 33 quartets (1781) and the Beethoven-Schubert generation and extended by Brahms, Debussy, Bartók and Shostakovich — string quartet, piano trio, quintet and wind serenade formats, fully notated sonata-cycle movements, tempi from grave adagio to presto finales, motivic dialogue traded between equal parts, and a dynamic and articulation vocabulary calibrated to a salon or shoebox hall rather than an orchestra pit.
items.description: Chamber music is the repertoire written for small ensembles playing without a conductor, one instrument to a line, which Haydn's quartets established as the discipline's central testing ground for motivic development. Its recorded sound is defined by minimal miking in a resonant but tight hall, near-total dynamic control, blend achieved by ensemble listening rather than mixing, and textures where every voice is independently audible. Against orchestral music it trades mass for transparency and rhetorical intimacy; against solo recital repertoire it is fundamentally conversational, with thematic material passed between equal partners.
exemplars: Schubert, String Quintet in C D. 956

items.name: Choral (Western art choral singing)
items.lineage: Western tradition of multi-voice ensemble singing on notated parts, running from Renaissance polyphony through Bach's motets and the nineteenth-century amateur choral society to the twentieth-century professional chamber choir — SATB and divisi scoring, a cappella or organ-accompanied, blend achieved through vibrato restraint and vowel matching, tuning pulled toward pure thirds and fifths in unaccompanied writing, tempi generally moderate, and a large resonant acoustic treated as part of the instrument.
items.description: Choral music is the notated multi-part vocal repertoire of the Western church and concert hall, from Palestrina and Byrd through Bach, Brahms and Poulenc to Pärt and Whitacre, sung by ensembles that prize blend and intonation over individual timbre. Recordings typically use a distant stereo pair in a stone building so that the reverberant tail carries the harmony, and unaccompanied writing drifts toward just intonation as singers tune chords by ear. It differs from gospel and folk group singing in its fixed written parts and suppressed vibrato, and from solo art song in that no single voice is meant to emerge from the texture.
exemplars: J.S. Bach, motet Jesu meine Freude BWV 227

items.name: Concerto Grosso
items.lineage: Late-seventeenth-century Italian orchestral form opposing a small concertino of soloists to the full ripieno string body, codified by Corelli in Rome (Op. 6, published 1714) and carried into Northern Europe by Handel's Op. 6 and Bach's Brandenburg Concertos — multi-movement slow-fast alternation, ritornello construction, walking continuo bass under harpsichord and theorbo, terraced dynamics achieved by adding or dropping the ripieno, and brisk detached Baroque articulation at dance-derived tempi.
items.description: The concerto grosso is the Baroque orchestral genre built on contrast of ensemble size: a concertino of two violins and cello trades ritornello material with the full string ripieno, all over a continuo realized at the harpsichord or organ. Corelli's Roman sets fixed the model, Handel expanded it and Bach stretched it toward the solo concerto by giving individual instruments virtuosic display. Its terraced rather than graded dynamics and continuo-anchored texture distinguish it from the Classical concerto that replaced it, and its instrumental ritornello writing from the vocally driven cantata of the same decades.

items.name: Early Music
items.lineage: Historically informed performance tradition covering Western medieval, Renaissance and early Baroque repertoire, revived from Arnold Dolmetsch's 1900s instrument-building through the 1950s-70s work of Noah Greenberg, David Munrow and Gustav Leonhardt — gut strings, unkeyed winds, meantone and other pre-equal temperaments, low pitch standards around A=415 or 466, small one-per-part vocal ensembles with straight tone, tactus-based flexible pulse, improvised ornamentation and continuo realization, and church or chapel acoustics used as the natural performing space.
items.description: Early music names both a repertoire — plainchant, ars nova, Renaissance polyphony, and the early Baroque — and the twentieth-century performance movement that reconstructed how it might have sounded, using period instruments, historical temperaments and sources rather than modern editorial practice. The result is a distinctly reedy, transparent timbral palette of viols, lutes, recorders, cornetts and sackbuts with straight-toned voices, sung and played at flexible tactus with improvised division and ornament. It differs from mainstream classical practice not in notation but in reconstructed sound ideals: no vibrato as default, unequal temperament, lower pitch, and small forces recorded in resonant stone rooms with minimal microphones.
exemplars: David Munrow / Early Music Consort of London
Guillaume de Machaut, Messe de Nostre Dame

items.name: Expressionist (Art Music)
items.lineage: Central European art-music idiom crystallized in Vienna and Berlin roughly 1908-1925 by Arnold Schoenberg, Alban Berg and Anton Webern, marked by free atonality before serialism, extreme registral leaps and dynamic swings from ppp to fff within a bar, Sprechstimme half-sung declamation, splintered chamber-orchestra timbres (bass clarinet, celesta, muted brass, harmonium), fluctuating tempo without stable meter, and texts of dread, hysteria and nocturnal isolation.
items.description: Expressionism in music emerged in Vienna and Berlin between roughly 1908 and 1925, abandoning functional tonality before any systematic replacement existed. Its signature is violent contrast: whispered flutter-tongued flutes against shrieking trumpets, Sprechstimme that hovers between speech and song, and chamber textures where each instrument is a distinct dramatic character rather than part of a blended section. Unlike the twelve-tone method that grew out of it, Expressionist writing is intuitively atonal with no governing row, and unlike Impressionism it treats dissonance as psychological rupture rather than colour.
exemplars: Anton Webern - Six Pieces for Orchestra Op. 6

items.name: Impressionist (Art Music)
items.lineage: French art-music current of roughly 1890-1925 centred on Claude Debussy and Maurice Ravel in Paris, defined by whole-tone and octatonic collections, unresolved parallel ninth and eleventh chords, modal borrowings from plainchant and Javanese gamelan heard at the 1889 Exposition, veiled orchestration favouring divided muted strings, harp glissandi, celesta and flute in its lowest register, and rubato-heavy pacing that suppresses downbeat articulation.
items.description: Impressionism formed in Paris in the 1890s as Debussy and his circle turned harmony from a syntax of tension and resolution into a medium of colour, letting sevenths and ninths sit unresolved and planing whole chords in parallel. Orchestrationally it favours transparency over mass: muted divisi strings, harp, celesta, and woodwinds in unusual registers, with percussion used as tint rather than pulse. It differs from late Romanticism in its avoidance of goal-directed climax, and from Expressionism in that its dissonance is sensuous rather than traumatic.
exemplars: Claude Debussy - Prelude a l'apres-midi d'un faune
Lili Boulanger - D'un matin de printemps
Frederick Delius - On Hearing the First Cuckoo in Spring

items.name: Requiem Mass
items.lineage: Latin Mass for the Dead as an art-music genre, developing from the Gregorian Missa pro defunctis into large-scale concert settings between Ockeghem's 15th-century polyphonic Requiem and the 19th-century monuments of Mozart, Berlioz, Verdi, Faure and Durufle, built on a fixed liturgical text sequence (Introit, Kyrie, Dies irae, Offertorio, Sanctus, Agnus Dei, Lux aeterna, In paradisum), scored for SATB chorus, vocal soloists and orchestra, with the Dies irae typically the fastest and loudest movement and the Introit and In paradisum the quietest.
items.description: The Requiem is the funerary Mass treated as a large concert form, its text fixed by liturgy while its musical scale expanded from a cappella Renaissance polyphony to Berlioz's four antiphonal brass bands. The sonic signature is massed choir in long reverberation, with the Dies irae sequence supplying the dramatic centre of gravity and unaccompanied or organ-only passages framing it. It differs from the oratorio in having a prescribed sacred text rather than a narrative libretto, and from ordinary Mass settings in the Dies irae and the omission of the Gloria and Credo.
exemplars: W. A. Mozart - Requiem in D minor K. 626
Hector Berlioz - Grande Messe des morts

items.name: Organum
items.lineage: Earliest notated Western polyphony, documented from the Musica enchiriadis around 900 CE and brought to its high form at Notre-Dame de Paris circa 1160-1240 by Leonin and Perotin, in which a plainchant tenor is stretched into immensely sustained drone notes while one to three upper voices move above in rhythmic modes, cadencing on perfect fifths, octaves and unisons within a Pythagorean tuning, sung by small male ensembles in stone church acoustics.
items.description: Organum is the first repertory of Western polyphony, running from ninth-century parallel doubling of chant at the fifth to the florid three- and four-voice settings of the Notre-Dame school around 1200. Its defining sound is an extremely slow chant tenor held under melismatic upper voices that lock into repeating rhythmic-modal patterns, all resolving to open fifths and octaves in Pythagorean intonation inside a long stone reverberation. Against later Ars Nova polyphony it is harmonically austere and metrically unbarred, and against monophonic plainchant it introduces measured rhythm and vertical consonance as compositional concerns.

items.name: Oratorio
items.lineage: Unstaged sacred dramatic work for soloists, chorus and orchestra, originating in Filippo Neri's Roman oratory devotions around 1600 and codified by Carissimi, then transplanted to Protestant England by Handel from Esther (1732) through Messiah (1741) and to Vienna by Haydn, built from recitative-aria-chorus chains on a biblical libretto, with da capo arias, fugal choruses, continuo-supported secco recitative and no staging, costume or action.
items.description: The oratorio is opera's sacred, unstaged twin: a full-evening narrative on a religious subject sung by soloists and chorus with orchestra, but performed in concert without sets or action. Handel's English oratorios established the balance that defines the genre, giving the chorus a commenting and dramatic role far larger than in opera seria, framed by continuo recitative and da capo arias with singer-supplied ornamentation. It differs from the Mass and Requiem in using a freely written libretto rather than liturgical text, and from the Lutheran Passion in its concert rather than devotional-service function.
exemplars: G. F. Handel - Israel in Egypt
Edward Elgar - The Dream of Gerontius

items.name: Sonata (Classical Instrumental Form)
items.lineage: Instrumental genre and formal principle consolidated in Vienna and Mannheim between about 1750 and 1830 by C. P. E. Bach, Haydn, Mozart, Clementi and Beethoven, in which a multi-movement work for solo keyboard or solo instrument with keyboard opens with an exposition presenting contrasting first and second themes in tonic and dominant, develops them through remote keys, and recapitulates both in the tonic, typically followed by a slow movement, a minuet or scherzo, and a rondo or sonata-rondo finale.
items.description: The Classical sonata is chamber-scale instrumental music organized around tonal departure and return: an exposition that establishes a key and then contradicts it, a development that destabilizes both themes through modulation and fragmentation, and a recapitulation that resolves everything into the home key. Textures are lean, usually one or two players, with dynamics articulating structure rather than mood. It is distinguished from the symphony and concerto by its intimate forces and from Baroque suite movements by its dramatic, thematically argued architecture rather than dance-derived binary form.
exemplars: Ludwig van Beethoven - Piano Sonata No. 29 'Hammerklavier'
W. A. Mozart - Piano Sonata in A minor K. 310
Joseph Haydn - Piano Sonata in E-flat Hob. XVI:52
C. P. E. Bach - Wurttemberg Sonatas
Franz Schubert - Piano Sonata in B-flat D. 960

items.name: Twelve-tone (Dodecaphony)
items.lineage: Compositional method announced by Arnold Schoenberg in Vienna in 1923 and extended by Webern, Berg, Krenek, Dallapiccola and later Boulez and Babbitt, in which all twelve chromatic pitches are ordered into a row deployed in prime, inversion, retrograde and retrograde-inversion forms at any of twelve transpositions, producing music without tonal centre, generally in chamber or orchestral scoring with pointillistic register distribution, Klangfarbenmelodie timbral rotation, and precisely notated dynamics and articulation on nearly every note.
items.description: Twelve-tone composition, formulated by Schoenberg in the early 1920s, replaced tonal hierarchy with a fixed ordering of the chromatic aggregate, transformed by inversion, retrograde and transposition. In sound it favours wide leaps, isolated attacks, rapid changes of instrumental colour on successive notes, and scores annotated to the level of individual dynamics and attacks. It grew directly out of free-atonal Expressionism but is systematic rather than intuitive, and it is narrower than the total serialism of the 1950s, which extended row control to rhythm, dynamics and articulation as well as pitch.
exemplars: Arnold Schoenberg - Variations for Orchestra Op. 31
Milton Babbitt - Three Compositions for Piano

items.name: Novelty Song
items.lineage: Anglo-American comic popular song tradition running from Tin Pan Alley sheet music of the 1900s through its commercial peak in the 1940s-60s with Spike Jones, Sheb Wooley, David Seville and Ray Stevens, built on thirty-two-bar AABA or twelve-bar frames at bright dance tempi, deliberately absurd lyrics, sound effects (gunshots, cowbells, whistles, anvils), cartoon vocal treatments including sped-up tape voices, and instrumental gimmicks such as kazoo, slide whistle and tuba glissandi.
items.description: The novelty song is comic popular song engineered for a single memorable gag, dominant on American radio and jukeboxes from the 1940s through the 1960s. Musically it borrows standard Tin Pan Alley and dance-band forms but loads them with sound effects, character voices, tape-speed manipulation and absurd instrumental substitutions, with production gimmickry treated as the hook rather than the arrangement. It differs from vaudeville comic song in being a studio artifact built around recording tricks rather than a stage routine, and from parody song in that the tune is usually original.
exemplars: Spike Jones and His City Slickers - Cocktails for Two
Sheb Wooley - The Purple People Eater
Napoleon XIV - They're Coming to Take Me Away, Ha-Haaa!

items.name: Vaudeville
items.lineage: American variety-theatre circuit music of roughly 1881-1932, standardized by Tony Pastor and the Keith-Albee booking chain, in which songs were performed between comedy, acrobatic and dance acts by belting stage singers over small pit bands of piano, banjo, cornet, trombone, tuba and traps, using Tin Pan Alley thirty-two-bar and verse-chorus forms with spoken patter interludes, march and cakewalk two-step tempi, and a projecting unamplified delivery captured on acoustic-horn 78s until the mid-1920s.
items.description: Vaudeville was the dominant American popular-entertainment format from the 1880s to the early 1930s, and its songs were written to carry across a large hall without amplification: front-loaded hooks, patter verses, and a chorus pitched for a big chest-voice or nasal comic delivery. Accompaniment came from a small pit ensemble of piano, banjo, brass and traps playing march, cakewalk and early ragtime rhythms, and surviving recordings are acoustic-horn 78s with the singer pressed close to the cone. It is distinguished from minstrelsy by its family-oriented, ethnically varied bills and from cabaret by its rapid multi-act circuit format rather than a single intimate room.

items.name: Jingles (Advertising)
items.lineage: Commercial broadcast micro-song form born with the 1926 Wheaties radio spot and industrialized from the 1950s by Chicago and Dallas jingle houses such as PAMS and later Steve Karmen and Barry Manilow's ad work, engineered as 15, 30 or 60-second cues with an immediately singable hook in the first two bars, close-stacked session-singer harmony, bright big-band or synth-pop backing tracks, a brand-name payoff on the final cadence, and mixes optimized for AM radio and small television speakers.
items.description: The advertising jingle is popular song compressed to broadcast-slot length and written backwards from a brand payoff line. Its craft markers are an unmissable hook stated within the first few seconds, tightly doubled session-vocal stacks, arrangements that resolve exactly on the spot's out-point, and mastering pushed loud and midrange-forward to survive AM radio and television speakers. It differs from the TV theme in being sold rather than scene-setting, and from ordinary pop in that repetition and mnemonic clarity outrank development.
exemplars: Steve Karmen - I Love New York
Barry Manilow - State Farm 'Like a Good Neighbor'
Ginny Redington - McDonald's 'You Deserve a Break Today'
Bill Backer - Coca-Cola 'I'd Like to Teach the World to Sing'
Tom Dawes - Alka-Seltzer 'Plop Plop Fizz Fizz'

items.name: TV Themes
items.lineage: American and British television title-music tradition running from the late 1940s through the present, shaped by Henry Mancini, Lalo Schifrin, Mike Post, Nelson Riddle and Ron Grainer, written to fixed title-sequence durations of roughly 30 to 90 seconds with an immediate melodic statement, no long introduction, a hard button ending cut to picture, and stylistic markers tracking the era: jazz combos and big band in the 1960s, funk and wah guitar in the 1970s, LinnDrum and gated synth brass in the 1980s.
items.description: Television theme music is short-form scoring built to a stopwatch: the melody must arrive within a few seconds, establish the show's genre and tone, and land a decisive button on the last frame of the titles. Because the form is so constrained, composers lean on strong hooks over simple ostinatos, with instrumentation dating each era precisely, from Mancini's jazz combos and Schifrin's odd-metre brass to Mike Post's synth-and-gated-drum signatures. It differs from advertising jingles in selling atmosphere rather than a product, and from film scoring in reusing one fixed cue weekly rather than developing material across a feature.
exemplars: Ron Grainer & Delia Derbyshire - Doctor Who

items.name: Bakersfield Sound
items.lineage: California honky-tonk style codified in Bakersfield, Kern County, between 1955 and 1970 by Buck Owens with guitarist Don Rich and by Merle Haggard with the Strangers, recorded largely at Capitol Studios in Hollywood, defined by trebly Fender Telecaster leads through amp reverb, pedal steel, a driving 2/4 shuffle or freight-train backbeat with slap-hard snare, minimal or no string sweetening, high tenor harmony doubling the lead vocal a third above, and dance-hall tempos around 120-150 BPM.
items.description: The Bakersfield sound emerged among Dust Bowl migrant communities in California's Central Valley in the late 1950s as a hard-edged answer to Nashville's smooth countrypolitan production. Its core is the bright, compressed Telecaster tone of Don Rich and Roy Nichols, pedal steel, a loud dance-hall backbeat, and vocals sung with rockabilly attack rather than crooned, tracked live with minimal overdubbing and no orchestral sweetening. Compared with the Nashville Sound of the same years it is louder, drier and rhythmically stiffer; compared with rockabilly it keeps steel guitar and country song structure intact.
exemplars: Buck Owens and the Buckaroos - Act Naturally
Merle Haggard and the Strangers - Mama Tried
Wynn Stewart - It's Such a Pretty World Today

items.name: Progressive Bluegrass
items.lineage: American acoustic string-band style that opened bluegrass instrumentation to jazz and rock materials from the late 1960s onward, driven by the Country Gentlemen, New Grass Revival with Sam Bush and Bela Fleck, David Grisman's 'Dawg' quintet and Tony Rice, retaining banjo, mandolin, fiddle, dreadnought guitar and upright bass while adding extended and modal harmony, long improvised solos over non-tonic vamps, rock and reggae backbeats, electric bass and amplification, odd-metre passages, and repertoire drawn from Beatles, Dylan and bebop sources.
items.description: Progressive bluegrass, or newgrass, formed in the late 1960s and 1970s when younger players kept Monroe's instrumentation but discarded its harmonic and repertoire limits. The result is virtuoso acoustic string-band music with extended chords, modal vamps that support long solos, rock and reggae grooves, occasional odd metres, and covers pulled from outside country entirely. It is distinguished from traditional bluegrass by amplification, drums or electric bass, and improvisation that leaves the chord changes behind, and from jam-band music by its unbroken commitment to acoustic string-band technique and tone.

items.name: Reactionary Bluegrass
items.lineage: Late-1960s and 1970s US topical bluegrass strain in which the standard Monroe-derived instrumentation — banjo, fiddle, mandolin, guitar, upright bass at 130-160 BPM with driving offbeat mandolin chop and high-lonesome tenor stacked above the lead — carried explicitly conservative, pro-military, anti-counterculture lyrics, circulated on Rebel, County and Starday singles and at the emerging festival circuit.
items.description: A topical branch of bluegrass that hardened during the Vietnam era, when traditional-minded bands used the genre's fixed instrumental frame — five-string banjo in Scruggs roll, chopping mandolin, twin-fiddle or single fiddle break, doghouse bass on one-and-three — as a delivery vehicle for flag-and-faith lyrics aimed against hippies, draft resisters and urban modernity. Musically it is deliberately conservative: no drums, no electric instruments, breaks traded in strict rotation, harmony stacked as tenor-above-lead with a baritone third on choruses. It differs from mainstream festival bluegrass only in lyric stance, and from country's Nashville Sound of the same years by refusing strings, drums and pedal steel entirely.

items.name: Cajun Fiddle Tunes
items.lineage: South Louisiana Acadian instrumental dance repertoire — two-steps, waltzes and one-steps documented from the 1920s Vocalion/Bluebird sides through Alan Lomax's 1934 field cylinders — built on twin fiddles in cross tuning or unison-with-drone, diatonic Cajun accordion in C, triangle and later frottoir keeping the shuffle, at brisk 120-140 BPM two-step tempos with strongly bowed downbeats and no vocal in the instrumental strains.
items.description: The instrumental core of Cajun music as played for dancing in Acadiana halls and house fais do-do from the late nineteenth century onward, carried orally as a fixed tune repertoire ("Jolie Blonde", "Grand Mamou", "Bosco Stomp") rather than a songbook. The sound is two fiddles — one carrying the melody, one bowing a rhythmic seconding drone below — locked to a push-pull diatonic accordion, with triangle or rubboard marking a shuffling backbeat and guitar strumming bass-chord. It is distinguished from Creole zydeco by its fiddle-led, less syncopated groove and slower harmonic turnover, and from Anglo-American old-time fiddling by its accordion-anchored two-step and waltz forms.

items.name: Christian Country
items.lineage: US commercial format consolidated in the late 1980s and 1990s around Nashville's inspirational-country labels and the Christian Country Music Association, applying full contemporary country production — pedal steel, Telecaster, drum kit, 70-100 BPM ballad and mid-tempo shuffle feels — to explicitly evangelical first-person testimony lyrics sung in a clean, unornamented mainstream country baritone or soprano.
items.description: Christian country is a radio format rather than a folk practice: mainstream Nashville arrangement conventions — steel-and-fiddle pads, tight rhythm section, big-chorus vocal stacks, key-change final refrain — carrying devotional lyrics addressed to God or narrating conversion. Production is glossy and centered on lyric intelligibility, with a strong preference for ballad tempos and major-key I-IV-V harmony. It differs from Southern gospel by using a soloist-plus-band format instead of male quartet close harmony, and from country gospel by its contemporary, post-1985 production values rather than a hymn-derived repertoire.

items.name: Close Harmony (Country Brother Duet)
items.lineage: American Southeastern vocal-duet practice recorded intensively from the early 1930s by Bluebird and ARC — two voices, most often siblings, singing parallel thirds and sixths within a narrow tessitura with matched timbre and no vibrato, accompanied by mandolin and guitar at 80-120 BPM, a repertoire of sentimental ballads and hymns codified by the Monroe, Delmore and Bolick brothers.
items.description: Close harmony in the country sense means two voices spaced a third or a sixth apart, blended so tightly that the second part reads as a coloring of the first rather than a separate line — a sound built on shared family timbre, matched vowel placement and near-total absence of vibrato. Accompaniment is deliberately thin: tremolo mandolin over flatpicked or thumb-brushed guitar, sometimes a fiddle countermelody, with the whole ensemble balanced live to a single ribbon microphone. It differs from Southern gospel quartet singing by using two parts instead of four and from later bluegrass duet singing by its slower tempos and lack of banjo drive.

items.name: Country Gospel
items.lineage: Sacred repertoire of white rural America as recorded commercially from the 1927 Bristol sessions onward — shape-note and Stamps-Baxter hymn tunes reset for guitar, autoharp, fiddle and later steel, sung in family-group harmony or solo at 70-110 BPM with plain diatonic delivery and testimony lyrics, later institutionalized through the sacred albums of Nashville stars.
items.description: Country gospel is the sacred wing of white Southern country music: hymnal and convention-book songs plus original testimony numbers, performed with country instrumentation and delivered in a conversational, ornament-free voice that prizes lyric clarity over vocal display. Arrangements favor family or duet harmony over the chorus, guitar-and-fiddle accompaniment with steel filling behind the vocal, and steady walking-bass or waltz motion. It is separated from Black gospel by its narrower melismatic range and absence of call-and-response with a shouting congregation, and from Southern gospel proper by its solo-or-duet format rather than the professional male quartet with piano.

items.name: Country Rap
items.lineage: US Southern hybrid consolidated after 2008 through Colt Ford, Bubba Sparxxx and the Average Joes label — rapped verses in a rural Southern accent over 808-driven trap or boom-bap programming at 75-95 BPM, alternating with sung country hooks, acoustic guitar and slide or banjo loops, and lyrics about trucks, dirt roads and small-town life.
items.description: Country rap grafts Southern hip-hop's programmed rhythm section — long-decay 808 kick, rolling hi-hat triplets or a half-time boom-bap kit — onto country signifiers: strummed dread guitar, banjo rolls, slide licks and a big sung chorus. Verses are rapped in an unhurried drawl, usually with less rhythmic density than mainstream trap and with rhyme schemes closer to country storytelling. It differs from hick-hop's rock-leaning cousins by keeping the beat programmed rather than played, and from mainstream Southern rap by its rural lyric world, pentatonic country hooks and live-string overdubs.

items.name: Country Soul
items.lineage: Mid-1960s recordings made at Muscle Shoals, American Sound in Memphis and Fame by integrated house bands — country song forms and pedal-steel voicings played with a gospel-derived rhythm-section pocket, tambourine on the backbeat, Wurlitzer or tonewheel organ pads, at 60-100 BPM, sung with the melisma and rasp of Southern soul over three-chord country changes.
items.description: Country soul names the mid-South studio idiom in which country repertoire and soul phrasing met inside the same rhythm section: the songs are country ballads and shuffles, but the drums sit behind the beat with a gospel triplet feel, the bass is melodic and Motown-adjacent, and the lead vocal bends, cries and delays the melody. Pedal steel and Telecaster share the arrangement with organ swells and horn punches. It differs from Nashville countrypolitan by replacing strings and vocal choirs with a live soul band, and from Memphis soul proper by its country song structures and steel guitar.

items.name: Cowboy
items.lineage: Anglo-American cattle-trail song repertoire documented by John Lomax in 1910 and reshaped for radio and film in 1930s Hollywood — modal and pentatonic ballads and waltzes at 70-110 BPM, sung in an open unforced tenor over strummed guitar, with trio yodel-tinged harmony and desert-imagery lyrics narrating trail work, loneliness and the range.
items.description: The cowboy song began as unaccompanied or guitar-backed work-and-leisure singing among cattle-drive hands in the late nineteenth-century American West, its melodies often borrowed from British Isles ballads and Anglo hymn tunes and its lyrics narrating specific trail incidents. Commercial recording from the 1920s added guitar-trio close harmony, high thirds and the smooth crooned delivery of the singing-cowboy films. The idiom is defined by wide-open phrasing, free rubato in ballad performance, absence of percussion, and lyric geography; it differs from Western swing by having no dance-band rhythm section and from honky-tonk by its pre-electric, narrative rather than barroom subject matter.

items.name: Western
items.lineage: The Western half of the mid-century "country and western" trade category — Texas, Oklahoma and California music of the 1930s-50s spanning cowboy song, Western swing and border-influenced dance music, marked by fiddle-and-steel front lines, 2/4 and 4/4 dance tempos of 110-180 BPM, swung eighths, and clear diction over four-to-the-bar rhythm guitar.
items.description: Western is the trans-Mississippi wing of country music as the record trade defined it before the terms split: cowboy ballads, Western swing dance sets and Southwestern honky-tonk sharing a fiddle-and-steel instrumentation, dance-hall function and a plainer, less mountain-inflected vocal than Southeastern hillbilly music. Steel guitar carries the signature glissando fills, twin fiddles harmonize the heads, and rhythm guitar chunks four to the bar under a walking bass. It differs from Appalachian old-time by its swing feel and amplified steel, and from Nashville country by its dance-band orientation and Texas-California recording base.
exemplars: Bob Wills and His Texas Playboys

items.name: Cowpunk
items.lineage: Early-1980s Los Angeles and Nashville hybrid — punk tempos of 150-200 BPM and distorted barre-chord guitars welded to country song forms, pedal steel or Telecaster twang, upright or driving eighth-note bass and shouted-then-drawled vocals, codified by Jason & the Scorchers, Rank and File and the Los Angeles Paisley-adjacent club scene.
items.description: Cowpunk emerged around 1981-83 when American hardcore and post-punk musicians turned to honky-tonk, rockabilly and Bakersfield country for material, playing it at punk velocity with overdriven amps and a slamming backbeat while keeping country's verse-chorus forms, twangy bends and harmony vocals. Records are typically cut fast and live, with mid-forward guitars and a dry, close-miked kit. It differs from later alt-country and Americana by its aggression and short song lengths, and from rockabilly revival by its punk rather than 1950s rhythmic vocabulary.

items.name: Dansband
items.lineage: Swedish social-dance popular style formalized in the late 1960s and 1970s out of the folkpark circuit — foxtrot, bugg and waltz tempos around 100-130 BPM played by five- or six-piece bands with electric guitar, bass, drums, saxophone and heavy use of Hammond or synth pads, singing Swedish-language sentimental lyrics in smooth major-key harmony.
items.description: Dansband is Sweden's dedicated couple-dancing pop: bands play sets built around the bugg and foxtrot, keeping tempos and rhythmic feel steady enough for social dancing across an entire evening, with untroubled major-key harmony, a saxophone or guitar obbligato, and lead vocals doubled in thirds. Production is clean, mid-forward and reverb-rich, closer to schlager than to rock. It differs from Anglo country covers it often absorbs by its Swedish lyrics and stricter dance-tempo discipline, and from Eurodisco by its live band instrumentation and absence of four-on-floor club energy.

items.name: Franco-Country
items.lineage: French-language country music of Québec and Acadian New Brunswick, established from the late 1940s by Willie Lamothe and Paul Brunelle — American honky-tonk and cowboy-song templates with yodel, steel guitar, fiddle and 2/4 shuffle or waltz at 90-130 BPM, sung in Québécois French with a nasal front-placed delivery and strong turlutte and reel inflections.
items.description: Franco-country is the francophone Canadian adaptation of American country and western, built on the same steel-and-fiddle instrumentation and three-chord shuffles but sung entirely in French and inflected by Québécois folk practice — yodeling, mouth-reel turlutte phrasing, and occasional foot-tapping podorythmie under the beat. Repertoire mixes translated American standards with original cowboy narratives set in Canadian geography. It is distinguished from Cajun music by language variety, honky-tonk band format and absence of diatonic accordion lead, and from Anglo honky-tonk by its vocal placement and folk-reel ornaments.

items.name: Gulf and Western (Trop Rock)
items.lineage: US coastal songwriter style codified by Jimmy Buffett's Key West recordings of the mid-1970s — country and folk-rock song forms at relaxed 90-120 BPM, acoustic guitar and pedal steel augmented by steel pan, marimba-like percussion, calypso-tinged shuffles and saxophone, with conversational baritone vocals narrating beaches, boats, bars and escape.
items.description: Gulf and Western, later marketed as trop rock, is Caribbean-flavored American country-folk: Nashville session craft and country song structure loosened by calypso and soca rhythmic borrowings, steel pan and hand percussion in the arrangement, and lyrics organized around coastal leisure and mild escapism. Tempos stay mid, the harmony is diatonic and major, and the vocal is deliberately conversational rather than belted. It differs from mainstream country by its island percussion palette and beach imagery, and from actual calypso by keeping the melodic and harmonic language of Anglo-American songwriting.

items.name: Hellbilly Music
items.lineage: American horror-country hybrid crystallized in the late 1980s-1990s around Reverend Horton Heat's Sub Pop sides and Unknown Hinson's Charlotte club act, later popularized as a term by Rob Zombie — upright-bass slap and rockabilly shuffle at 150-190 BPM welded to overdriven baritone-heavy guitar, tremolo surf figures, graveyard/moonshine narratives and a leering, growled or howled baritone vocal delivery.
items.description: Hellbilly emerged in the American South and Southwest in the late 1980s as rockabilly instrumentation pushed through punk-volume amplification and horror-movie iconography. The sound centers on slapped upright bass, reverb-drenched twang guitar with surf tremolo, and a theatrical baritone that alternates between croon and snarl over minor-modal changes. It differs from psychobilly in keeping country song forms, pedal-steel-adjacent phrasing and Southern-gothic storytelling rather than adopting the British punk attack.
exemplars: Hank Williams III - Straight to Hell

items.name: Instrumental Country
items.lineage: Nashville and Bakersfield studio-musician tradition formalized in the 1950s-60s by Chet Atkins, Merle Travis, Speedy West and Jimmy Bryant, and by the A-Team session players — melody-lead pedal steel, fingerstyle or Telecaster electric guitar and fiddle trading choruses over a 2/4 train-beat or shuffle at 100-160 BPM, with no vocal and 32-bar or 12-bar forms carrying the tune.
items.description: Instrumental country is the wordless branch of the Nashville and West Coast country session economy, running from Chet Atkins' fingerstyle sides through Speedy West and Jimmy Bryant's steel-and-Telecaster duels to Bakersfield instrumentals and later Danny Gatton. The defining sound is a clean, compressed single-coil or pedal-steel lead carrying a singable head over brushed shuffle drums and walking bass, with tightly arranged solo trades rather than open blowing. It differs from western swing in its smaller rhythm section and absence of horns, and from bluegrass instrumentals in using electric amplification and drums.
exemplars: Speedy West & Jimmy Bryant - Stratosphere Boogie

items.name: Lubbock Sound
items.lineage: West Texas songwriter school formed in Lubbock in the early 1970s around the Flatlanders (Joe Ely, Butch Hancock, Jimmie Dale Gilmore) and visual-artist-songwriter Terry Allen, extending Buddy Holly's local legacy — flatpicked acoustic guitar, musical saw or dobro drones, honky-tonk piano and fiddle under conversational nasal high-plains vocals at moderate 2/4 and waltz tempos, with literary, place-fixed lyrics.
items.description: The Lubbock Sound names the songwriting circle that came out of the Texas South Plains in the early 1970s, centered on the Flatlanders and Terry Allen and running through Joe Ely's band and later Lubbock emigres. Musically it is sparse honky-tonk and country-folk instrumentation — acoustic guitar, fiddle, tack-toned piano, occasional musical saw — behind plainspoken, wide-vowel West Texas vocals and narrative lyrics rooted in specific landscape. It is distinguished from Nashville outlaw country by its art-school literary bent and thinner, less rock-driven arrangements.
exemplars: The Flatlanders - More a Legend Than a Band

items.name: Neotraditional Country
items.lineage: Mid-1980s Nashville corrective movement led by George Strait, Randy Travis, Ricky Skaggs, Dwight Yoakam and Patty Loveless, produced by figures like Kyle Lehning and Pete Anderson — restored fiddle and pedal steel to the front of the mix over shuffle and train-beat rhythms at 90-140 BPM, with dry baritone vocals, minimal string sweetening and honky-tonk three-chord forms.
items.description: Neotraditional country arose in Nashville around 1981-1989 as a deliberate rejection of the countrypolitan strings and Urban Cowboy pop of the preceding decade. Its markers are audible steel and fiddle, twin-fiddle shuffles and Bakersfield Telecaster tone, clean 24-track separation, and unornamented baritone singing that references Lefty Frizzell and Merle Haggard. Unlike the honky-tonk it revives, it is recorded with modern studio polish and headroom rather than mono dance-hall immediacy.
exemplars: Dwight Yoakam - Guitars, Cadillacs, Etc., Etc.
Keith Whitley - Don't Close Your Eyes

items.name: Psychobilly
items.lineage: London-centred fusion codified at the Klub Foot in Hammersmith 1980-1986 by The Meteors, Guana Batz, Demented Are Go and Frenzy — 1950s slap-bass rockabilly propulsion at 160-200 BPM welded to punk downstroke guitar and drum kit with minimal or no ride, snarled or hiccupped horror-film lyrics, and heavy slapback reverb on both voice and guitar.
items.description: Psychobilly took shape in early-1980s London, with The Meteors and the Klub Foot scene fixing the template of double-bass slap driving a punk rhythm section at rockabilly tempos. The signature texture is a percussive upright bass functioning as both bass and secondary drum, distorted barre-chord guitar with tape-echo slapback, and shouted B-movie horror lyrics; drums are often stripped to snare, kick and floor tom. It diverges from neo-rockabilly by its aggression and tempo, and from straight punk by retaining the slapped acoustic bass and 12-bar chassis.

items.name: Punkabilly
items.lineage: Late-1970s to 1980s Anglo-American crossover — Stray Cats' rockabilly revival, The Clash's rooted covers, Social Distortion and later Reverend Horton Heat — pairing rockabilly's walking bass line, hollow-body twang and 12-bar shuffle with punk's downstroke electric guitar, snare-heavy 4/4 backbeat at 150-190 BPM, and flat, shouted vocals rather than hiccup-and-echo crooning.
items.description: Punkabilly names the looser transatlantic overlap where punk bands absorbed 1950s rockabilly changes and rhythms without the horror theatrics of psychobilly. It runs on a walking or slapped bass line, trebly single-coil guitar with light overdrive, and a hard punk backbeat, with vocals delivered as declaimed street singing rather than the reverb-soaked Sun Records style. Compared to psychobilly it is slower, more song-oriented and often retains electric rather than upright bass; compared to neo-rockabilly it sacrifices period-correct tone for punk drive.
exemplars: The Cramps - Songs the Lord Taught Us

items.name: Truck-Driving Country
items.lineage: American honky-tonk subgenre codified 1963-1976 by Dave Dudley's 'Six Days on the Road', Red Sovine, Dick Curless and C.W. McCall — a driving 2/4 or 4/4 train beat at 120-150 BPM with a fuzz or baritone-guitar riff hook, prominent pedal steel, walking electric bass, and plainspoken or recited baritone vocals narrating highway, CB-radio and long-haul life.
items.description: Truck-driving country is the trucker-themed honky-tonk vein that ran through Nashville studios from the early 1960s into the CB-radio craze of the mid-1970s. Its stock elements are a relentless train-beat shuffle, a fuzz-toned or muted low-string guitar riff standing in for engine noise, weeping pedal steel fills, and a conversational or spoken-recitation baritone lead. It differs from general honky-tonk chiefly in subject matter and in the mechanical, unswinging insistence of its rhythm section, and from countrypolitan in avoiding string sections entirely.
exemplars: Dave Dudley - Six Days on the Road
Dick Curless - A Tombstone Every Mile

items.name: Urban Cowboy (Country-Pop)
items.lineage: Nashville and Los Angeles country-pop peak of 1978-1984, named for the 1980 John Travolta film and its Gilley's Club setting, delivered by Mickey Gilley, Johnny Lee, Kenny Rogers, Ronnie Milsap and Barbara Mandrell — mid-tempo 4/4 with soft rock drums, electric piano and synth pads, string sweetening, muted pedal steel far back in the mix, and smooth crossover-radio vocals.
items.description: Urban Cowboy is the countrypolitan-to-soft-rock crossover that dominated country radio between the 1980 film's release and the neotraditional backlash of the mid-1980s. Sonically it is a pop-rock rhythm section with big reverberant drum sounds, Fender Rhodes and early polysynth beds, orchestral or synthetic strings and heavily compressed lead vocals, with fiddle and steel reduced to occasional colour. It stands opposite neotraditional country, which explicitly rejected this production, and differs from countrypolitan proper by trading orchestral arrangement for contemporary AOR instrumentation.

items.name: 4-Beat (UK Hardcore)
items.lineage: UK hardcore variant named for its steady four-on-the-floor kick, consolidated 1996-2002 around Slammin' Vinyl, Hardcore Heaven and producers Brisk, Ham, Sy & Unknown and Force & Styles — 165-180 BPM distorted or reverse-bass kick on every beat, pitched-up diva or MC vocal hooks, piano-riff breakdowns and offbeat Hoover stabs, with breakbeats reduced to fills rather than the main pulse.
items.description: 4-beat is the late-1990s UK hardcore style that replaced breakbeat hardcore's chopped Amen drive with an unbroken four-on-the-floor kick, becoming the mainstream of the British rave circuit around 1997-2002. It is built from a saturated kick, offbeat or reverse bass, sped-up vocal hooks and euphoric piano or supersaw breakdowns, produced largely in-the-box or on hardware samplers. Distinguished from happy hardcore mainly by its rhythmic footing and harder kick processing, and from continental hardstyle by its faster tempo and pop-vocal orientation.

items.name: Acid Breaks
items.lineage: Late-1990s British and American breaks hybrid developed by Rennie Pilgrem, Lee Coombs, Hyper and Baby Anne — a 130-140 BPM funky or chopped breakbeat underpinning a resonance-swept Roland TB-303 line as the primary melodic voice, with dubby delay throws, heavy sidechained sub-bass and sparse sampled vocal stabs.
items.description: Acid breaks fused the 303 vocabulary of Chicago acid house with breakbeat rhythm in the late 1990s, mostly through the London Thursday Club Recordings circle and parallel Florida producers. The music sits near 135 BPM, driven by a syncopated sampled break rather than a four-on-the-floor kick, with a filter-swept squelching acid line carrying the hook and sub-bass reinforcing the downbeats. It differs from acid techno in its broken rhythm and lower tempo, and from nu skool breaks in placing the 303 rather than electro synth stabs at the centre.

items.name: Breakbeat Hardcore
items.lineage: UK rave style of 1990-1993 built at Shut Up and Dance, Suburban Base and Reinforced by The Prodigy, 4hero, Acen and Altern-8 — 125-145 BPM Amen and Think breaks chopped on Akai S950 samplers, sped-up soul and ragga vocal snippets, Hoover and piano riffs, and 808/909 sub-bass, cut to dubplate for pirate radio and warehouse sound systems.
items.description: Breakbeat hardcore was the dominant British rave sound between roughly 1990 and 1993, the direct bridge from acid house to jungle and drum and bass. It layers sampler-chopped funk breaks — above all the Amen and Think breaks — over house-derived piano and Hoover riffs, pitched-up vocal fragments and heavy sub-bass, mixed loud and bright for dubplate cutting. It differs from earlier bleep techno in its breakbeat foundation and from jungle proper in its slower tempo, major-key euphoria and retention of four-to-the-floor kick elements.

items.name: Florida Breaks
items.lineage: Orlando, Tampa and Miami club style of the mid-1990s codified by DJ Icey, Baby Anne, Rabbit in the Moon and the Zone label — 128-135 BPM electro-funk breakbeat with a hard clipped kick and snare, dominant filtered sub or acid bassline, Miami-bass-derived 808 low end, minimal melodic content and short chanted vocal drops.
items.description: Florida breaks, sometimes called funky breaks, developed in central Florida clubs from about 1993 as DJ Icey and the Orlando scene grafted Miami bass low end onto UK-derived breakbeat. The tracks are deliberately spare: a punchy chopped break, an enormous 808-weighted sub-bass, occasional acid filter sweeps and a repeated vocal or siren hook, arranged as long DJ-friendly loops with few chord changes. It is harsher and more bass-forward than UK nu skool breaks and far less melodic than big beat.

items.name: Nu Skool Breaks
items.lineage: London breaks style codified 1998-2004 by Adam Freeland, Rennie Pilgrem, Stanton Warriors, Plump DJs and the Marine Parade and TCR labels — 128-135 BPM two-step-influenced chopped breakbeat with a techno-tight kick, growling filtered or reese basslines, dub-siren effects and heavy sidechain compression, arranged with long tension-building filter sweeps rather than song forms.
items.description: Nu skool breaks emerged in London at the end of the 1990s as a self-conscious modernisation of breakbeat, absorbing UK garage's two-step swing, techno's mixdown discipline and drum and bass's bass design. Its signature is a tightly quantised, heavily processed break at around 130 BPM under a snarling modulated bassline, with dub sirens, vocal cuts and long filtered risers structuring the track for club mixing. Compared to big beat it is leaner and less rock-sampling; compared to Florida breaks it is more melodically and harmonically developed.

items.name: Chillstep
items.lineage: Melodic downtempo offshoot of UK dubstep that coalesced online circa 2010-2013 through Blackmill, Phaeleh and Seven Lions, keeping the 140 BPM half-time snare-on-three skeleton and sub-bass weight of dubstep but replacing wobble aggression with sustained major-key pad washes, arpeggiated piano figures, long reverb tails and wordless or breathy female topline vocals.
items.description: Chillstep formed on YouTube and Bandcamp between roughly 2010 and 2013 as producers stripped the aggression out of UK dubstep while keeping its 140 BPM half-time rhythmic grid and deep sub-bass. The sound is defined by sustained diatonic pad chords, delicate piano or plucked-synth motifs, heavy convolution reverb and airy sung or sampled vocal fragments floating above a restrained two-step drum pattern. Unlike brostep or deep dubstep it avoids mid-range modulation entirely, and unlike ambient it retains a strict, danceable beat and a clear sub-bass line.

items.name: Electro Swing
items.lineage: European club hybrid crystallised in Paris and Vienna in the mid-2000s around Parov Stelar, Caravan Palace and the Freshly Squeezed label, layering four-on-the-floor house or breakbeat drums at 110-130 BPM under sampled 1920s-40s shellac jazz — clarinet, muted trumpet, tenor banjo, slap bass and crackly crooner vocals — with the swung eighths of the source loop set against straight electronic kick and clap.
items.description: Electro swing emerged in continental European clubs in the mid-2000s, built by sampling 78-era jazz and swing recordings over house and breakbeat production. Its signature is the collision of a shellac-noise, band-limited acoustic loop — clarinet, muted brass, slap bass, banjo comping — with a clean modern kick, clap and sidechained bass, often augmented by live horn overdubs. It differs from jazz-house in that the swing source is foregrounded rather than chopped into anonymity, and from nu-jazz in its dance-floor tempo and lack of extended improvisation.

items.name: Glitch Hop
items.lineage: Late-1990s/2000s fusion of hip-hop tempo and IDM digital error, developed by Prefuse 73, Dabrye and Edit and later by the 110 BPM bass-heavy West Coast strain of Opiuo and Koan Sound, characterised by half-time boom-bap drum programming shredded with buffer stutters, bit-crushing and granular resampling, filthy modulated synth basslines and abrupt rhythmic gating.
items.description: Glitch hop grew from the Warp/Anticon end of instrumental hip-hop around 1999-2005 and mutated into a heavier 110 BPM bass-music form in the late 2000s. It keeps hip-hop's swung, half-time drum feel while treating every element with buffer repeats, bit reduction, granular smears and hard gating, so that digital artifacts function as rhythmic content rather than error. Against straight instrumental hip-hop it is far more processed and asymmetric; against IDM proper it retains a fixed danceable groove and a dominant, aggressively modulated bassline.

items.name: Glitch Pop
items.lineage: Turn-of-the-2000s song-form offshoot of clicks-and-cuts electronica, shaped by Múm, Lali Puna, The Postal Service and later Björk's Vespertine sessions, setting conventional verse-chorus vocal melodies and diatonic harmony over micro-edited digital percussion built from clicks, vinyl crackle and truncated samples, with brittle sine and bell timbres replacing a drum kit.
items.description: Glitch pop appeared around 1999-2003 in Reykjavik, Munich and Seattle as producers working in the clicks-and-cuts idiom began writing conventional pop songs on top of it. Intimate, close-miked and often untrained vocals carry a diatonic melody while the rhythm section is assembled from clicks, crackle, cut-off sample tails and tiny percussive artefacts, softened by melodica, toy-piano and bowed-string textures. It differs from IDM by centring the sung song and from indietronica generally by using audible digital malfunction as its main percussive vocabulary.

items.name: Bouncy House
items.lineage: Northern English club style of the late 1990s and 2000s, developed in Wigan, Bolton and Blackpool by producers such as the Blackout Crew and DJ Rob Tissera out of scouse house and hard house, running 138-150 BPM over a four-on-the-floor kick with an off-beat detuned 'donk' cowbell-like stab, filtered rave hoover leads, Italo-style piano riffs and shouted rap or diva vocal samples.
items.description: Bouncy house, known in Britain as donk, formed in the North West of England in the late 1990s from scouse house and hard house and peaked commercially around 2008. Its identity rests on a hard four-on-the-floor kick at roughly 140 BPM with a metallic, heavily pitched off-beat donk stab filling every upbeat, plus rave hoover leads, piano vamps and MC'd or pitched-up vocal hooks. Compared with UK hard house it is faster, simpler and more melodically hooky; compared with bouncy techno it uses a house kick pattern rather than breakbeat residue.

items.name: Bouncy Techno
items.lineage: Scottish rave subgenre of 1992-1996 centred on Glasgow, Ayrshire and labels like Clubscene and Twitch, driven by Scott Brown, Q-Tex and Ultra-Sonic — 150-170 BPM distorted four-on-the-floor kicks with a heavily syncopated bouncing offbeat bass, chopped Amen-derived breaks, hoover and organ stabs, rave piano and pitched-up diva or MC vocal samples.
items.description: Bouncy techno emerged in central Scotland around 1992 as local producers pushed UK hardcore faster and stripped out its jungle-leaning breakbeat complexity. The template is a saturated 150-170 BPM kick, a springy detuned offbeat bassline that gives the style its name, rave hoover and organ stabs, and short sped-up vocal or Amen fragments. It sits between happy hardcore and gabber: less melodic and less sugary than happy hardcore, less distortion-dominated and more melodically hooked than Rotterdam hardcore.

items.name: Doomcore
items.lineage: Slow, apocalyptic branch of European hardcore techno that formed in Germany and the Netherlands in the mid-1990s around Low Entropy, The Kotzaak Klan and Fifth Era, running 140-170 BPM with distorted but ponderous kicks, sustained minor-mode drones and orchestral or choral pads, heavily reverbed film and horror dialogue samples, and near-absent hi-hat activity.
items.description: Doomcore crystallised in the mid-1990s German and Dutch hardcore underground as a deliberately slowed, bleak counterpart to gabber. It keeps the overdriven, clipped kick drum of hardcore but sets it at a heavy 140-170 BPM under long minor drones, choral and orchestral sample beds, and cavernous spoken-word or horror-film dialogue. Where gabber and terrorcore chase speed and density, doomcore trades them for weight, space and sustained dread, and unlike industrial techno it stays rooted in the distorted Roland kick.

items.name: Dubstyle
items.lineage: Late-2000s Dutch and Australian crossover between hardstyle and dubstep, pushed by Zatox, The Prophet and Bass Kleph around 2009-2011, halving the hardstyle framework to a 140 BPM half-time feel while retaining the reverse-bass kick-and-offbeat pattern, screeching pitched hardstyle leads and LFO-wobbled dubstep sub-bass under a snare on beat three.
items.description: Dubstyle appeared around 2009 when Dutch hardstyle producers began writing at dubstep's 140 BPM half-time grid. Tracks combine hardstyle's distorted kick and pitch-bent reverse bass with dubstep's LFO-modulated wobble sub-bass and snare on the third beat, plus the screeching detuned hardstyle lead over the drop. It is distinguishable from brostep by that reverse-bass hardstyle kick pattern and euphoric major-key melodic breaks, and from mainstream hardstyle by its half-time rather than four-on-the-floor drop.

items.name: Jumpstyle
items.lineage: Belgian and Dutch dance-and-music style codified in Flanders in the early 2000s and mainstreamed by Patrick Jumpen and Kartoon Jumpen around 2006-2008, built at 140-150 BPM on a hard four-on-the-floor kick with a detuned offbeat bass stab, simple minor-key square-wave riffs, hoover accents and shouted or sampled vocal hooks, all keyed to the scissor-kick footwork dance.
items.description: Jumpstyle developed in Belgian clubs from late-1990s hardcore and jump-up hard trance and became a Low Countries mass phenomenon around 2006-2008, inseparable from its scissor-kick dance. Musically it is spare: a hard 145 BPM kick, an offbeat detuned bass hit that supplies the bounce, a short square or saw riff in minor, and vocal shouts or chopped pop hooks. Compared with hardstyle it is thinner and faster in feel with no reverse bass, and compared with jumpstyle's parent hard trance it drops long builds for immediate loop-based repetition.

items.name: Makina
items.lineage: Catalan hard dance style that grew out of the Barcelona bakalao and Ruta Destroy scenes in the early 1990s at clubs such as Chasis and Pont Aeri, running 150-180 BPM with a relentless four-on-the-floor kick, sharp offbeat bass, bright hoover and trance-derived arpeggio riffs, rave piano stabs and Spanish or English MC chants, later re-exported to North East England as UK makina.
items.description: Makina formed around Barcelona in the early 1990s out of the Valencian bakalao circuit, with Pont Aeri and Chasis as its defining clubs. It runs faster than most European hard dance — 150-180 BPM — over a driving kick, a stabbing offbeat bass, hoover and arpeggiated trance leads and euphoric piano breaks, usually topped by an MC. Its Newcastle-area UK offshoot from the late 1990s kept the tempo and riff style but leaned harder on MC chat and vocal-trance melodies, distinguishing it from Scottish bouncy techno and Dutch hardstyle.

items.name: Terrorcore
items.lineage: Extreme hardcore techno strain from Rotterdam, Frankfurt and Berlin from about 1993, driven by DJ Skinhead, Ultraviolence, Nasenbluten and the Fifth Era circle, running 200-300 BPM with brutally overdriven and clipped kick drums, screamed or pitch-shifted vocal samples, sirens, chopped horror-film dialogue and dissonant noise stabs over minimal melodic material.
items.description: Terrorcore split from Rotterdam gabber around 1993 by pushing tempo past 200 BPM and treating distortion as the primary compositional material. Kicks are clipped into square-wave tones, samples are screamed, sirened or lifted from horror cinema, and melody is largely refused in favour of noise stabs and rhythmic assault. It is faster and more abrasive than mainstream gabber, and the mirror image of doomcore, which uses the same distorted kick source at a fraction of the speed.

items.name: Hard Dance
items.lineage: Umbrella British club idiom of the late 1990s and 2000s consolidated around London's Trade and Frantic nights and labels like Tidy Trax and Nukleuz, at 145-155 BPM with a punchy four-on-the-floor kick, offbeat bass, long filtered risers, hoover and stab leads, sharp snare rolls and diva or shouted vocal hooks over rigid sixteen-bar build-and-drop structures.
items.description: Hard dance is the British umbrella term that settled in the late 1990s over hard house, hard trance and NRG as they converged in London clubs and on Tidy Trax and Nukleuz. Records run near 150 BPM with a compressed four-on-the-floor kick, an offbeat bass or donk, filter sweeps and hoover stabs, snare rolls into every drop and vocal hooks either sung by a diva or shouted. It is more song-shaped and melodically euphoric than hardcore and slower and cleaner than gabber, while remaining harder-edged and faster than mainstream house.

items.name: Diva House
items.lineage: New York and New Jersey club style of the late 1980s and 1990s associated with Frankie Knuckles, Junior Vasquez and Masters at Work, pairing a 120-128 BPM four-on-the-floor garage groove, open hi-hats, gospel-rooted piano chords and organ bass with a full-throated belted or melismatic female lead in the mould of Martha Wash and Ultra Naté, arranged around a hook-driven twelve-inch club edit.
items.description: Diva house is the vocally maximal wing of US garage house, developed in New York and New Jersey clubs from the late 1980s through the 1990s and central to the era's twelve-inch remix economy. Its markers are a 122-128 BPM four-on-the-floor kick with swinging open hats and claps, gospel-derived piano chording and organ bass, and a powerful gospel-trained female voice belting a chorus hook with melismatic runs. It differs from deep house by pushing the vocal to the front with anthemic choruses, and from Eurodance by keeping live-feeling gospel harmony and an American club arrangement rather than rap-verse formatting.

items.name: Dutch House
items.lineage: Netherlands club and festival style of roughly 2007-2012, codified by Chuckie, Afrojack, Sidney Samson and Laidback Luke out of Rotterdam and Amsterdam bubbling-and-house crossover, built on 128 BPM four-on-the-floor kicks with heavily sidechained tails, pitch-bent squelch leads voiced on a single detuned saw, tuned filtered toms borrowed from bubbling, near-total absence of sustained pads, and short shouted vocal stabs used as rhythmic punctuation rather than melody.
items.description: Dutch House emerged from Rotterdam and Amsterdam producers around 2007 who fused Antillean bubbling percussion with big-room house, and dominated main-stage EDM programming until about 2012. Its signature is the dry, pad-free arrangement: a clipped kick, tuned tom rolls, and a monophonic pitch-bending lead riff that carries the entire hook. Against electro house it is markedly thinner in the midrange and more percussion-driven, and against progressive house it refuses long harmonic build-ups in favour of abrupt drops.

items.name: Freestyle House
items.lineage: Late-1980s to mid-1990s New York, New Jersey and Miami hybrid in which Latin freestyle songwriting was re-tracked over 120-126 BPM house drum programming, worked out by producers such as Todd Terry, Little Louie Vega and Carlos Berrios, marked by TR-909 kick and open hat over syncopated 808 cowbell and tumbao-derived bass figures, glassy FM piano and brass stabs, and belted Nuyorican and Italian-American lead vocals with dense stacked harmony choruses.
items.description: Freestyle House is the club-remix lineage of Latin freestyle, in which the genre's melodramatic Nuyorican vocal writing was rebuilt over straight house drums for the New York and New Jersey dancefloors of roughly 1988-1995. It keeps freestyle's minor-key hooks, cowbell syncopation and stacked chorus harmonies but swaps the mid-tempo 808 shuffle for a 909 four-on-the-floor and a longer, DJ-usable arrangement. Compared with Latin house it is far more song-led and Anglophone; compared with classic freestyle it is faster, drier, and mixed for a big room rather than a car system.
exemplars: Little Louie Vega productions for Nu Groove

items.name: French House
items.lineage: Paris-centred style of roughly 1995-2003 codified by Daft Punk, Cassius, Etienne de Crecy, Alan Braxe and Stardust, built from short looped disco and boogie vinyl samples at 115-128 BPM, driven by aggressive resonant band-pass filter sweeps and phaser motion across the whole loop, hard bus compression that pumps against a 909 kick, and vocals used as pitched, chopped, vocoded or talkbox texture rather than as verse-chorus lead.
items.description: French House, or French touch, formed in Paris in the mid-1990s around the Roule, Solid and Source labels, and defined itself by treating a two- or four-bar disco sample as the whole composition. The filter sweep and the pumping sidechain are the compositional events; harmonic material stays fixed while timbre opens and closes across sixteen or thirty-two bars. It is warmer and more sample-dependent than progressive house and less vocal-forward than US garage, and its heavy limiting gives it a saturated, radio-loud texture unusual for 1990s club records.
exemplars: Stardust - Music Sounds Better With You

items.name: Funky House
items.lineage: UK and US club style of roughly 1997-2005 associated with Defected, Cr2 and DJs such as Roger Sanchez, Bob Sinclar, Full Intention and Basement Jaxx, running 125-130 BPM with pitched-up disco and soul-guitar loops, slap or filtered funk basslines, live-feel conga and shaker overdubs, brass and Rhodes stabs, and gospel-inflected sung hooks placed over a plain four-on-the-floor kick with open hi-hat on the upbeat.
items.description: Funky House is the disco-sampling commercial wing of late-1990s house, built in London and New York around the Defected and Subliminal catalogues. Its markers are pitched-up 1970s guitar and horn loops, a bouncy filtered bass, real percussion overdubs, and a short soulful vocal hook engineered for daytime radio as much as for the club. It is brighter and more literal in its sampling than French house, and considerably more up-tempo and chord-driven than the deep house it grew out of.
exemplars: Bob Sinclar - I Feel For You

items.name: Hardbag
items.lineage: Short-lived UK club style of roughly 1993-1996 bridging commercial handbag house and hard house, driven by Tony De Vit, Steve Thomas and the Hooj Choons and Tripoli Trax catalogues, running 135-145 BPM with a hard-clipped kick, offbeat stabbed bass, ravey piano riffs, filtered hoover and organ leads, siren risers, and diva vocal snippets sampled from Italo-house and garage records rather than sung in full.
items.description: Hardbag names the mid-1990s British compromise between handbag house, the euphoric piano-and-diva end of commercial club music, and the harder, faster hard house being played at Trade and similar venues. It keeps the major-key piano riff and sampled vocal hook but sets them over a distorted 909 kick at rave tempo with offbeat bass stabs. It is less relentless and more melodic than the UK hard house that superseded it, and considerably faster and more abrasive than the Italo-derived handbag records it borrowed from.

items.name: Hip House
items.lineage: Chicago and New York style of 1988-1991 in which rapped verses were set over house tracks, codified by Fast Eddie, Tyree Cooper, the Jungle Brothers with Todd Terry, and Doug Lazy, running 118-125 BPM with a TR-909 or TR-707 four-on-the-floor, chopped James Brown breakbeat overlays, acid or sampled sub bass, minimal chordal material, and a straight-eighth party-rap delivery locked to the kick rather than to a swung boom-bap grid.
items.description: Hip House appeared almost simultaneously in Chicago and New York in 1988 as house producers put rappers on their tracks and hip-hop crews adopted 909 four-on-the-floor programming. The rap sits on the beat in straight eighths, chanted and hook-heavy rather than dense, and the backing is stripped to kick, hats, a sampled break and a single bass figure. It differs from contemporaneous hip-hop in its lack of swing and its DJ-length arrangements, and from Chicago house proper in that the voice, not the track, is the lead instrument.
exemplars: Fast Eddie - Yo Yo Get Funky
Tyree Cooper - Turn Up the Bass
Rob Base & DJ E-Z Rock - Joy and Pain

items.name: Progressive House
items.lineage: British style crystallising around 1992 in the Guerilla and Junior Boy's Own catalogues with Leftfield, Sasha, John Digweed and Fluke, running 126-132 BPM with long evolving filter and reverb automation, rolling sixteenth-note bass, dub-inflected delay throws, tribal tom and shaker layers, and sparse wordless vocal pads, later re-formed in a 2008-2013 festival variant around Deadmau5 and Eric Prydz built on sustained sidechained supersaw chords.
items.description: Progressive House began in Britain in 1992 as a deliberately unhurried alternative to hard rave, prizing gradual timbral evolution over hooks: an eight-minute track might change only through filter opening, layer accretion and delay feedback. A second wave from roughly 2008 kept the long build but rebuilt it from sidechained supersaw chords for festival systems. It is more linear and less loop-locked than funky house, and warmer and more melodic than the techno it borders.

items.name: Swing House
items.lineage: European club style of roughly 2008-2016 associated with Parov Stelar, Caravan Palace, Wolfgang Lohr and the Freshly Squeezed and Electro Swing Club circuits, in which 1920s-40s shellac jazz with muted trumpet, clarinet, banjo comping and crooned or scatted vocal is sampled, pitch- and time-corrected, and set over a 120-128 BPM house kick with swung sixteenth hats, filtered upright-bass loops and a sidechained sub reinforcing the sampled walk.
items.description: Swing House, the house-tempo wing of electro swing, took hold on the European festival circuit from about 2008 by mounting sampled interwar jazz on a four-on-the-floor frame. The defining tension is metric: the sampled material swings while the kick and bass do not, and producers reconcile them with swung hi-hats and time-stretched horn loops. Compared with funky house it draws on shellac-era rather than disco-era sources, and compared with nu-jazz it is loop-based and contains almost no live improvisation.

items.name: Tropical House
items.lineage: Style consolidated around 2013-2016 by Kygo, Thomas Jack, Klingande and Matoma out of Norway and northern Europe, running a slow 100-115 BPM four-on-the-floor with soft rounded kick, off-beat plucked marimba, steelpan and flute-like synth leads, wide reverberant pads, filtered saxophone hooks, and breathy singer-songwriter vocals mixed forward with pop rather than club balance.
items.description: Tropical House emerged from Scandinavian bedroom producers around 2013 as a deliberately low-energy, radio-facing deep house: the tempo drops to roughly 105 BPM, the drop is carried by a soft marimba or steelpan pluck rather than a synth surge, and the whole mix is bathed in long reverb. It is far softer in transient and lower in tempo than progressive house, and unlike deep house proper it is arranged as a three-minute pop song with a named featured vocalist.
exemplars: Robin Schulz - Prayer in C remix

items.name: UK Hard House
items.lineage: London-centred style of roughly 1995-2005 built at Trade and Sundissential and on the Tidy Trax, Nukleuz and Vicious Circle labels by Tony De Vit, the Tidy Boys, BK and Lisa Lashes, running 145-155 BPM with a distorted overdriven kick, hard offbeat bass stab, gated hoover and reverse-siren risers, long breakdown build-ups on white-noise sweeps, chopped diva or shouted MC vocal snippets, and a driving offbeat rhythm derived from hardbag and Belgian new beat.
items.description: UK Hard House is the faster, harder successor to hardbag, formalised at Trade's after-hours sessions and on Tidy Trax from the mid-1990s. Its grammar is a clipped distorted kick, an offbeat bass stab filling every gap, and long tension-and-release breakdowns built from sirens, noise sweeps and hoover stabs; melody is minimal and hooks are usually sampled shouts. It is straighter and more percussive than hard trance, and unlike Dutch hardstyle it retains the offbeat bass rather than the reverse-bass kick tail.
exemplars: Tony De Vit - Give Me Life

items.name: US Garage
items.lineage: New York and New Jersey style of roughly 1979-1992 named for the Paradise Garage and shaped by Larry Levan, Tony Humphries, Timmy Regisford and the Salsoul, West End and Nu Groove catalogues, running 118-124 BPM with live-feel drum programming that keeps disco's open hi-hat and tambourine, warm electric-bass and Rhodes comping, real percussion overdubs, gospel-trained lead vocals with full verse-chorus writing, and long dub-style breakdowns cut for twelve-inch play.
items.description: US Garage is the New York and New Jersey continuation of disco into the drum-machine era, carried by Larry Levan's residency at the Paradise Garage and by Tony Humphries at Zanzibar. It keeps live bass, Rhodes and percussion under the machine drums and centres a gospel-schooled lead singer, giving it a warmth and songfulness that Chicago house of the same years largely forgoes. Its extended dub breakdowns are structural, built for the DJ, and distinguish it from the later UK garage that borrowed its name.
exemplars: Larry Levan remixes for West End Records
Ten City - That's the Way Love Is

items.name: Vocal House
items.lineage: Transatlantic house strand running from the late 1980s onward and codified by Frankie Knuckles' and David Morales' Def Mix productions, Marshall Jefferson, Robert Owens and later Defected releases, at 120-128 BPM, in which a full sung lyric with verse, bridge and gospel-derived melisma sits over four-on-the-floor kick, open-hat upbeat, sustained seventh and ninth pad chords, and piano or organ comping arranged so the vocal, not the groove, defines the form.
items.description: Vocal House is the song-centred branch of house, running continuously from Chicago and New York in the late 1980s through Def Mix and Defected into the present. It is identified by a complete sung lyric delivered with gospel technique, extended pad harmony beyond simple triads, and an arrangement in which drops and breakdowns serve the vocal's phrase structure. Against funky house it relies on original topline writing rather than sampled hooks, and against US garage it is typically cleaner and more studio-constructed in its backing.
exemplars: Robert Owens - I'll Be Your Friend

items.name: Liquid Dub
items.lineage: Late-1990s onward UK and northern-European studio strand joining liquid drum-and-bass to dub techno production practice, associated with Calibre, Fanu, Rhythm & Sound-influenced producers and the Basic Channel lineage, marked by long tape and spring delay throws on single sustained chords, filtered sub bass under 170 BPM rolling breaks that feel half-time, mixing-desk performance in which parts are muted and reintroduced live, melodica and organ stabs, and wordless or heavily echoed vocal fragments.
items.description: Liquid Dub is the dub-engineering wing of smooth, atmospheric bass music, in which Jamaican mixing-desk technique - long delay throws, abrupt drop-outs, spring reverb, filtered bass drops - is applied to liquid drum-and-bass and dub-techno material. Texture and space are the subject; harmony is usually a single sustained minor chord treated as a drone. It is sparser and slower-feeling than mainstream liquid drum-and-bass, and unlike Jamaican dub proper it is built from synthesised and sampled parts rather than a re-mixed band multitrack.

items.name: Free Tekno
items.lineage: European free-party sound-system music formed 1992-1995 when UK travellers' rigs (Spiral Tribe, Bedlam, Circus Warp) relocated to France, Italy and the Czech Republic after the Criminal Justice Act, codified at teknivals as 150-180 BPM hardware-sequenced 4/4 with a distorted overdriven kick, dry stabbing acid and metallic percussion loops, no vocal, and hour-long DJ-less live sets played on self-built rigs.
items.description: Free tekno emerged from the mid-1990s European free-party circuit, made by and for travelling sound systems playing unlicensed teknivals in warehouses, quarries and fields. Its sonic signature is a heavily saturated, near-square kick drum at 150-180 BPM, relentlessly looped acid and noise-percussion layers with almost no harmonic movement, and a deliberately raw mix optimised for enormous outdoor stacks rather than club monitors. It is faster and dirtier than Detroit or Berlin techno, and unlike gabber it stays rhythmically austere rather than anthemic, with tracks pressed to white-label vinyl or traded on unmarked CDs outside any commercial industry.

items.name: Ghettotech
items.lineage: Detroit club style codified 1995-2000 by DJ Assault, Mr. De' and DJ Godfather on the Assault Rifle and Databass labels, fusing Chicago ghetto house's 707/808 tracks with Miami bass sub-drops and Detroit techno tempo — 145-160 BPM, four-on-floor kick with hyper-syncopated hats and clap rolls, chopped-and-repeated profane vocal chants, and fast blend-heavy DJ mixing behind booty-shake dancing.
items.description: Ghettotech crystallised in mid-1990s Detroit as the city's answer to Chicago ghetto house, taking that music's stripped drum-machine tracks and pushing them to 145-160 BPM with Miami-bass low end and techno-derived edit density. Tracks are typically two or three elements deep — a hard kick, ticking closed-hat triplet figures, a sub-bass drop and a looped shouted vocal hook — arranged for rapid DJ blending rather than long builds. It is faster and more percussion-driven than ghetto house, more vocally explicit and dance-functional than Detroit techno proper, and it fed directly into the Chicago juke and footwork tempo range that followed.

items.name: Nortec
items.lineage: Tijuana border style formed 1999-2001 by the Nortec Collective (Bostich, Fussible, Panóptica, Hiperboreal, Clorofila), built from sampled tambora and banda sinaloense brass offcuts and norteño accordion/bajo sexto phrases sequenced over 120-130 BPM house and minimal-techno grids, with tuba basslines doubling synth sub and no lead vocal on the canonical early records.
items.description: Nortec was assembled in Tijuana around 1999 when a group of local electronic producers were handed reels of discarded banda and norteño rehearsal tape and began sequencing the fragments against techno and house programming. The result keeps the acoustic grain of tambora drums, sousaphone bass and accordion trills intact but locks them to a rigid 4/4 machine pulse at club tempo, so the timbral palette is unmistakably northern Mexican while the form is electronic. Unlike cumbia digital or later NAAFI-era rebajada it is instrumental, mid-tempo and deliberately clean-sounding, and unlike straight minimal techno its melodic material is quoted rather than synthesised.

items.name: Schranz
items.lineage: German hard-techno subgenre named by Chris Liebing in Frankfurt around 1997 and developed by Liebing, Arkus P. and the Wavescape/Bonzai hard circuit — 140-160 BPM, a distorted rolling kick with heavy sidechain pumping, aggressive looped saw and metallic percussion stabs, near-total absence of melody or vocal, and three-deck vinyl mixing that layers tool tracks into a continuous grinding wall.
items.description: Schranz was codified in late-1990s Frankfurt as the hardest, most functional strain of German techno, its name a coinage suggesting the scraping, grinding quality of the sound. Tracks run 140-160 BPM around a saturated kick that is compressed until the whole mix breathes with it, with looped distorted percussion and short metallic stabs replacing any melodic content; most releases are explicitly DJ tools built for stacking. It is more rigidly four-on-floor and less breakbeat-inflected than hardcore or gabber, and considerably more distorted and monochrome than Berlin's dub-techno or minimal lineages.

items.name: Toytown Techno
