items.lineage: UK novelty offshoot of breakbeat hardcore that peaked in 1992-1993 with Smart E's, Urban Hype and Shaft, built on chart sampling of children's television themes and nursery melodies over 140-150 BPM sped-up Amen and Think breaks, cartoon-pitched vocal samples, rave stabs and simple major-key riffs aimed squarely at the singles chart.
items.description: Toytown techno was a short-lived 1992-93 UK strain of breakbeat hardcore that leaned entirely on recognisable childhood samples — Sesame Street, Trumpton, nursery rhymes — pitched up over fast chopped breaks and rave stabs. Musically it retains hardcore's sampler-and-breakbeat construction and 140-150 BPM tempo but replaces the darker sub-bass and menace with bright major-key hooks and helium vocals engineered for daytime radio. It is distinguished from happy hardcore, which followed it, by its breakbeat rather than four-on-floor foundation, and from mainstream hardcore by its openly novelty intent, which prompted the scene's rapid turn toward jungle and darkside.

items.name: Acid Trance
items.lineage: European hybrid formed 1992-1995 in Germany, the Netherlands and the UK (Hardfloor, Union Jack, Choci, Dave Angel), joining Chicago-derived TB-303 resonant filter sweeps to trance's 135-145 BPM four-on-floor pulse, long breakdown-and-build arrangement, sustained minor-key pad chords and a squelching 303 line whose cutoff automation is the track's principal melodic event.
items.description: Acid trance took shape in the early 1990s as European producers grafted the Roland TB-303's resonant filter squelch onto trance's long-form 135-145 BPM structures. The defining gesture is a single repeating 303 pattern whose cutoff, resonance and accent are performed live across many minutes, rising through a breakdown and returning over 909 kick and open hats and a bed of minor-key pads. Compared with Chicago acid house it is faster, more harmonically padded and built around a single climactic build; compared with classic trance it substitutes filter movement for supersaw melody, and it later fed directly into Goa and psytrance production practice.

items.name: Classic Trance
items.lineage: German-centred style codified 1993-1999 through Frankfurt and Berlin labels (Eye Q, Harthouse, MFS, Superstition) by Paul van Dyk, Oliver Lieb, Cosmic Baby, Jam & Spoon and Sven Väth — 135-142 BPM four-on-floor with rolling offbeat sixteenth bass, layered detuned saw arpeggios, a long instrumental breakdown with a sustained pad chord progression, and a snare-roll build into the main melodic drop.
items.description: Classic trance is the mid-1990s German template that established the genre's architecture: a 135-142 BPM kick with sixteenth-note offbeat bass, sequenced arpeggios in a minor key, a filtered pad breakdown lasting a minute or more, and a snare-roll release into a euphoric detuned lead. Arrangements are long and directional rather than loop-based, which sets it apart from techno, and the harmonic language is genuinely chordal — moving progressions, not static drones. It predates the vocal-led, radio-length uplifting trance of the 2000s and carries more Frankfurt techno grit than the polished Dutch productions that succeeded it.

items.name: Dream Trance
items.lineage: Italian variant launched 1995-1997 by Robert Miles, Gigi D'Agostino, DJ Dado and the BXR/Media label axis in Brescia and Rome, defined by a foregrounded acoustic or sampled grand-piano melody over 132-140 BPM four-on-floor with soft-attack strings and pads, minimal percussion, frequent absence of vocals, and an arrangement designed as a chill-out closer for Italian clubs.
items.description: Dream trance, sometimes called dream house, was an Italian invention of 1995-96 whose signature is a lyrical piano theme carried across the whole track rather than confined to a breakdown. Tempos sit slightly below standard trance at 132-140 BPM, percussion is restrained, and lush string pads and reverb give the productions an almost soundtrack quality; Robert Miles's "Children" defined the formula as an anti-anthem intended to calm drivers leaving clubs at dawn. It differs from classic trance in its melodic instrument, its softer dynamics and its avoidance of an aggressive drop, and from Italo house in its slower harmonic rhythm and absence of a diva vocal.

items.name: Dark Psytrance
items.lineage: Post-Goa strain codified circa 1999-2005 through European and Russian labels (Parvati, Hydrogen, Osom) by Kindzadza, Psykovsky, Xenomorph and Penta, running 145-165 BPM over a rigid kick-and-rolling-offbeat-bass triplet with dissonant chromatic FM leads, horror-film speech samples, granular metallic textures and no harmonic resolution across a through-built ten-minute arc.
items.description: Dark psytrance emerged around the turn of the 2000s in Russia, Germany and the European forest-party circuit as Goa trance's melodic euphoria was replaced by dissonance and dread. Its foundation is the standard psy engine — kick on every beat, sixteenth-note rolling bass, offbeat kick-bass interlock — at an elevated 145-165 BPM, over which producers stack detuned FM screeches, pitch-bent voice samples and dense metallic granular layers with no tonal centre. It is faster and far more atonal than full-on or progressive psy, and unlike forest psytrance it foregrounds industrial noise design over organic squelch, with arrangements that build tension without ever offering an uplifting release.

items.name: Full On (Psytrance)
items.lineage: Israeli psytrance style codified 1997-2002 by Astrix, GMS, Infected Mushroom, Skazi and the Phonokol/HOMmega labels, running 142-148 BPM with a punchy short kick, a triplet rolling bass figure syncopated against it, bright major-key supersaw and pluck leads, big filtered breakdowns with spoken-word samples, and a peak-time arrangement built for large outdoor festival systems.
items.description: Full-on is the Israeli reformation of Goa trance, consolidated in the late 1990s around Tel Aviv producers who traded Goa's long modal arpeggios for a tighter, louder, melody-forward peak-time sound. The engine is a short compressed kick at 142-148 BPM interlocking with a triplet rolling bassline, above which sit bright major-key supersaw leads, staccato plucks and heavily automated filter risers into a sample-laden breakdown. Compared with dark or forest psytrance it is tonal, euphoric and mixed for maximum loudness; compared with progressive psy it is faster, busier and structured around explicit drops rather than gradual layering.

items.name: Psybreaks
items.lineage: UK-Australian hybrid formed circa 2000-2006 (Hedflux, Kick Bong, Tegma, Beatsystem, Elektroniikan Sanansaattaja) placing psytrance's rolling sixteenth bass, acid squelch and FM lead vocabulary over a syncopated broken 130-145 BPM breakbeat drawn from nu-skool breaks rather than a four-on-floor kick, with long filtered builds and dub-style delay throws.
items.description: Psybreaks developed in the early 2000s among UK and Australian producers moving between the breaks and psytrance circuits, keeping psy's synthesis palette — acid lines, FM screeches, granular risers, heavy stereo modulation — while swapping its relentless four-on-floor kick for a swung, syncopated breakbeat at 130-145 BPM. The result is looser and funkier in the low end than full-on, with space for dub delay throws and half-time sections. It differs from nu-skool breaks by its psychedelic sound design and long trance-style builds, and from progressive psy by its broken rather than straight drum foundation.

items.name: Progressive Psytrance
items.lineage: European-Israeli style codified 2002-2010 through Iboga, Digital Structures and Zenon-adjacent labels (Ace Ventura, Liquid Soul, Atmos, Perfect Stranger), slowing psytrance to 130-138 BPM with a deep round kick, a minimal two-or-three-note rolling bass, sparse morphing modular textures introduced one layer at a time, minor-key pads and very few breakdowns across an eight-minute groove-first arc.
items.description: Progressive psytrance, usually shortened to psyprog, took shape in the 2000s around Scandinavian and Israeli labels seeking a warmer, slower alternative to full-on's peak-time assault. It runs 130-138 BPM on a deep sustained kick and a minimal rolling bass, with the interest carried by slowly morphing filtered textures and modular blips that enter and exit gradually rather than by melodic hooks or drops. Against full-on it is quieter, sparser and harmonically static; against progressive house it retains the psy kick-bass interlock and psychedelic layering, and against dark psy it stays tonal and unhurried.

items.name: Suomisaundi
items.lineage: Finnish freeform psytrance codified 1997-2005 by Texas Faggott, Squaremeat, Salakavala, Haltya and the 6equj5/Exogenic circle, running 140-150 BPM over a standard psy kick-and-rolling-bass but abandoning genre structure for cartoonish detuned lead patches, absurd Finnish speech samples, sudden tempo and key ruptures, live jamming and deliberately amateur mixing.
items.description: Suomisaundi — literally "Finnish sound" — grew out of late-1990s forest parties in Finland as a wilfully eccentric mutation of Goa trance. It keeps the 140-150 BPM psy rhythm section but fills the upper register with squelching detuned leads, chirping cartoon effects, spoken Finnish absurdities and sudden unannounced changes of key, tempo or texture, often captured from live hardware jams with little mixdown polish. Where full-on is engineered and euphoric and dark psy is menacing, suomisaundi is playful, harmonically wandering and structurally unpredictable, valuing humour and improvisation over dancefloor function.

items.name: Hard Trance
items.lineage: German and Dutch trance hardened circa 1994-1999 in Frankfurt, Cologne and Rotterdam through labels like Overdose, Tracid Traxxx and Blutonium and producers Kai Tracid, DJ Scot Project and Yoji Biomehanika, running 140-155 BPM over a hard offbeat-bass 4/4 kick, heavily distorted and hoovered supersaw stabs, gated 16th-note arpeggios, long filtered white-noise risers into breakdowns, and rolling acid-303 or reverse-bass sections with no vocal beyond short chopped shouts.
items.description: Hard trance formed in mid-1990s Germany and the Netherlands as trance's aggressive wing, pushing tempos to 140-155 BPM and replacing the style's plush pads with distorted hoover leads, saturated offbeat bass and reverse-bass patterns. Arrangements are strictly cyclic and DJ-functional: sixteen- and thirty-two-bar blocks, an extended noise-swept breakdown, and a hard drop back into the kick. It is distinguished from uplifting trance by the absence of major-key euphoric string melodies and by its distortion-first sound design, and from hardstyle by retaining trance's straight kick and 303 acid lineage rather than the pitched, screwed hardstyle kick.

items.name: Tech Trance
items.lineage: Emerging around 1999-2005 across the UK, Netherlands and Germany via Bedrock, Yoshitoshi and later Coldharbour and Pharmacy, tech trance welded techno's rolling, dry drum programming to trance's 138-142 BPM arpeggios — codified by Marco V, Sander van Doorn, Simon Patterson and John Askew with pumping sidechained basslines, minor-key rolling 16th sequences, minimal breakdowns and almost no vocal presence.
items.description: Tech trance crystallised around the turn of the 2000s as trance producers absorbed techno's dry, percussive kick-and-hat programming while keeping the genre's rolling minor arpeggios and sidechained bass. The result runs 138-142 BPM with tight, tunnelling 16th-note sequences, short functional breakdowns and a deliberately cold, unmelodic surface. It differs from uplifting trance by refusing the big supersaw chord anthem and the vocal hook, and from techno proper by retaining trance's arpeggiated melodic engine and breakdown-and-build arrangement architecture.

items.name: Elevator Music (Muzak functional background programming)
items.lineage: Industrialised from 1934 onward by George Owen Squier's Muzak Corporation in New York and later Seattle, elevator music is purpose-recorded instrumental background scoring — light string orchestra, muted brass, celeste, vibraphone and organ playing popular standards at deliberately even dynamics, no vocals, no drum accents, arranged in fifteen-minute 'stimulus progression' blocks of graded tempo and distributed by leased telephone line and tape cartridge to lobbies, factories and lifts.
items.description: Elevator music is the commercially engineered background repertoire produced by Muzak and its imitators from the 1930s through the 1980s, written and mixed specifically not to be listened to. Its signature is a narrow dynamic range, legato string-and-woodwind voicing of familiar melodies, suppressed percussion and bass, and programming sequenced in ascending-energy quarter-hour blocks intended to modulate worker productivity. It is separable from easy listening and lounge records by its distribution model and its refusal of soloists, hooks or vocal presence — the arrangement is engineered as acoustic furnishing rather than as a record to be bought.

items.name: Furniture Music (musique d'ameublement)
items.lineage: Coined and composed by Erik Satie with Darius Milhaud in Paris 1917-1923, first performed at the Galerie Barbazanges in 1920 — short modal cells for small mixed ensemble (piano, clarinet, trombone, strings) repeated unchanged for the duration of an interval, deliberately unresolving, dynamically flat and written to be ignored, with Satie shouting at the audience to keep talking.
items.description: Musique d'ameublement is Satie's early-twentieth-century proposal for music as literal furnishing: brief notated cells for chamber ensemble looped without development for as long as the social occasion lasts, with flat dynamics and no cadential resolution. Titles like Tapisserie en fer forge and Tenture de cabinet prefectoral name domestic objects rather than musical forms. It anticipates ambient music by six decades but differs from it in medium and means — it is fully notated for acoustic players and depends on human repetition rather than tape loop, synthesis or studio process.

items.name: Lounge (cocktail-bar mood music)
items.lineage: Consolidated in American hotel bars and Las Vegas rooms circa 1954-1966 and captured on Capitol, RCA and Command LPs by Martin Denny, Esquivel, Henry Mancini and Jackie Gleason — small combo of vibraphone, muted trumpet, organ, brushed kit and upright bass playing standards and originals in slow-to-medium swing and bossa, drenched in chamber reverb, with exaggerated stereo panning and novelty percussion for the hi-fi demonstration market.
items.description: Lounge is the mid-century American bar-and-hotel repertoire of small-combo mood records, sitting between cocktail jazz and orchestral easy listening. Its markers are vibraphone and muted trumpet lead, Hammond or electric-organ pads, brushes on the kit, Latin percussion colour, and the extreme stereo staging and echo-chamber depth that made these LPs stereo-demonstration objects. It differs from elevator music by being sold as records with named bandleaders and audible soloing, and from cool jazz by prioritising exotic timbre, novelty effects and atmosphere over improvisational development.
exemplars: Jackie Gleason – Music for Lovers Only

items.name: Middle of the Road (MOR adult radio pop)
items.lineage: A US and UK radio-format category hardened between 1968 and 1980 in Los Angeles, Nashville and London studios around Karen Carpenter, Neil Diamond, Barry Manilow and Anne Murray — mid-tempo 4/4 ballads and soft shuffles at 70-110 BPM, close-miked unstrained lead vocal over acoustic guitar and electric piano, sweetened with orchestral strings, flugelhorn and stacked backing harmonies, brushes or restrained kit, and a key-change final chorus.
items.description: Middle of the road is the adult-oriented pop that dominated late-1960s to 1970s AM and easy-listening radio, built on unhurried tempos, immaculate multitrack production and a warm, unstrained lead vocal carrying a hummable melody. Orchestral strings and horn sweetening, layered backing vocals and a modulating final chorus are near-constant; distortion, extended solos and rhythmic aggression are absent. It differs from soft rock in leaning on arranger-driven orchestration rather than the band as unit, and from easy listening or elevator programming in that the vocal is the foreground and the song is the product.

items.name: Ambient Dub
items.lineage: Named by Birmingham's Beyond label with the Ambient Dub compilations of 1992-93 and developed across the UK and New York by The Orb, Bill Laswell, Rockers Hi-Fi and Dreadzone — Jamaican dub's bass-and-drum skeleton at 70-95 BPM stripped of vocals and stretched into long ambient washes, with tape and digital delay feedback, spring reverb blooms, melodica and dubwise mixing-desk drop-outs replacing conventional arrangement.
items.description: Ambient dub emerged in the early 1990s UK as producers applied Kingston dub-mixing technique to ambient's slow, atmospheric time-scale. Sub-bass and a sparse one-drop or steppers pulse anchor the track while everything above is submerged in cascading delay, reverb tails and filtered drop-outs, with the mixing desk treated as the lead instrument. It differs from Jamaican dub by discarding the vocal riddim source and stretching structures to eight or ten minutes without a song underneath, and from ambient house by keeping bass weight and dub processing rather than four-on-floor kicks and rave samples.

items.name: Ambient House
items.lineage: Invented in London 1988-1992 in the chill-out rooms of acid-house parties, codified by The KLF's Chill Out and The Orb's Adventures Beyond the Ultraworld — house's 110-125 BPM four-on-floor kick and dub bassline slowed and softened under long sampled beds of field recordings, radio talk, choral pads and Mellotron, arranged as extended twenty-minute suites rather than DJ tools.
items.description: Ambient house was the chill-out-room music of the British acid house era, keeping a gentle house pulse and dub bass while foregrounding sampled speech, birdsong, weather, choral pads and Mellotron flutes. Tracks are long, sectional and collage-like, often built from found audio as much as from synthesis. It differs from ambient techno by retaining a recognisable house kick and a sunny, pastoral-psychedelic sample palette, and from ambient proper by never abandoning the beat entirely.
exemplars: The Orb – Adventures Beyond the Ultraworld

items.name: Ambient Techno
items.lineage: Formed 1991-1995 around Warp's Artificial Intelligence series, Detroit's Carl Craig and Berlin's Basic Channel — Detroit techno's machine sequencing at 110-135 BPM with the dance-floor function removed, favouring dubby chord stabs, deep reverb, evolving analogue filter movement and 909 or 808 patterns mixed low beneath pads, intended for home listening rather than DJ use.
items.description: Ambient techno developed in the early 1990s between Sheffield, Detroit and Berlin as the listening-room counterpart to club techno, keeping precise machine rhythm but pushing it under washes of reverberant chords and slowly modulating filters. Structures evolve by gradual timbral change across seven or eight minutes rather than by breakdown and drop. It is distinguished from ambient house by its colder, more synthetic Detroit palette and absence of found-sound collage, and from dub techno by less exclusive reliance on the delayed offbeat chord as sole material.
exemplars: Aphex Twin – Selected Ambient Works Volume II

items.name: Dark Ambient (cavernous ritual drone)
items.lineage: Consolidated 1988-1996 through Lustmord's Heresy, Raison d'Etre and the Cold Meat Industry and Soleilmoon labels in Los Angeles, Sweden and the Netherlands — beatless subterranean drone built from processed field recordings of caves, crypts and industrial spaces, detuned low synth beds, bowed metal and gong resonance, distant treated choir, extreme long reverb and near-subsonic bass, with no pulse, melody or vocal line.
items.description: Dark ambient took shape in the late 1980s and early 1990s out of industrial culture, replacing rhythm and song with sustained low drone, cavernous artificial space and processed environmental recording. Its sound is defined by sub-bass floor, slowly shifting inharmonic texture, metallic and ritual resonance, and reverb long enough to erase any sense of attack. It differs from ambient techno and ambient house by rejecting pulse altogether, and from power electronics or noise by working at low intensity and long duration rather than through saturation and assault.

items.name: Illbient
items.lineage: Named in mid-1990s Brooklyn around DJ Spooky, DJ Olive, We, Byzar and the Soundlab loft parties — hip-hop turntablism and sampler collage fused with dub bass and ambient drone, running slow broken breakbeats at 70-95 BPM under multiple simultaneous vinyl layers, tape hiss, city field recording, spoken-word fragments and heavy delay, mixed live on multiple decks in an installation setting.
items.description: Illbient was a mid-1990s Brooklyn scene built around loft parties and multi-turntable performance, layering murky sampled breakbeats, dub bass and ambient drone into dense, deliberately smeared collage. Recordings favour saturated low-fidelity texture, overlapping unsynchronised loops, urban field recording and dubwise delay over clean beat-matching. It differs from trip-hop by its improvised multi-deck performance practice and refusal of song structure, and from ambient dub by keeping hip-hop's broken breakbeat and turntable manipulation at the centre.
exemplars: DJ Spooky – Songs of a Dead Dreamer

items.name: Isolationism
items.lineage: Named by Kevin Martin for the 1994 Virgin compilation Ambient 4: Isolationism, gathering British, American and European artists such as Thomas Koner, Main, Scorn, Paul Schutze and Aphex Twin — beatless or near-beatless ambient stripped of consonance and warmth, built from corroded guitar drones, processed metal, tape decay and sub-bass hum, with static harmonic fields, minimal event density and a bleak, depopulated affect.
items.description: Isolationism is a mid-1990s critical grouping rather than a scene, defined by Kevin Martin's Ambient 4 compilation and describing ambient music emptied of comfort. Its sound is corroded and static: heavily processed guitar and metal resonance, tape and digital decay, subsonic hum, and long stretches in which almost nothing happens. It overlaps dark ambient but is more rooted in post-industrial rock and studio degradation of instrumental sources than in synthesised cave-drone, and unlike ambient techno it has no pulse, grid or dance-music inheritance at all.

items.name: Lowercase
items.lineage: Formulated around 1998-2004 by Steve Roden in Los Angeles, Bernhard Gunter in Germany and Richard Chartier and the 12k and Line labels in New York — extreme-quiet composition built from close-miked microsound (paper, water, insects, small objects) and digital silence, presented near the noise floor at levels that force the listener to raise playback volume, with long silences, no beat, no harmony and near-total absence of dynamic gesture.
items.description: Lowercase is a turn-of-the-millennium practice named by Steve Roden in which amplified, close-miked micro-events and digital near-silence become the entire material of a piece. Recordings sit only a few decibels above the noise floor, with sparse clicks, grains and room tone separated by long empty passages, so that playback level and listening environment become part of the work. It is distinguished from dark ambient and isolationism by its refusal of drone mass and low-end weight, and from glitch by using acoustic microsound and silence rather than digital error as its rhetoric.
exemplars: Bernhard Gunter – Un Peu de Neige Salie

items.name: Asian Underground
items.lineage: London club-scene fusion formed 1995-2000 around Talvin Singh's Anokha nights at the Blue Note and Nitin Sawhney's Outcaste circle, welding 160-175 BPM jungle and breakbeat programming to live tabla tarang, sitar and sarangi with Hindustani raga melody and Punjabi/Bengali vocal lines sung over sampled amen edits and long dub-delayed sub-bass.
items.description: Asian Underground emerged in London between 1995 and 2000 from second-generation British South Asian musicians and DJs, chiefly Talvin Singh's Anokha residency and the Outcaste and Nation Records labels. Its signature is live tabla and sitar improvisation played against sequenced drum-and-bass breaks, with raga-derived melodic lines and dub-scale reverb and delay treatments on both the acoustic and sampled layers. Unlike bhangra crossover, which keeps the dhol-driven Punjabi song form intact, Asian Underground foregrounds the club rhythm track and treats Hindustani classical material as improvised soloing over it; unlike ordinary jungle it retains microtonal, non-tempered melodic phrasing.

items.name: Bassline
items.lineage: Sheffield and the East Midlands, roughly 2002-2008, codified at the Niche club and by DJs Jamie Duggan, DJ Q and producers behind T2's 'Heartbroken' — a 4/4 UK garage derivative at 135-142 BPM built on a hard offbeat kick-and-clap grid, an aggressive square- or reese-toned mid-bass riff carrying the hook, and soulful female topline vocals or MC chat over sparse organ stabs.
items.description: Bassline (also called niche or 4x4 bassline) formed in Sheffield's Niche club in the early 2000s as northern England's answer to speed garage after London garage had turned toward 2-step. It keeps a rigid four-to-the-floor kick with an offbeat clap or snare while the entire melodic identity is delegated to a distorted, heavily modulated mid-range bass riff, over which R&B-derived female vocals or MC bars ride. Against UK garage proper it is faster, harder and abandons swung 2-step displacement; against grime it stays 4/4 and song-shaped rather than 140 BPM and MC-first.

items.name: Bitpop
items.lineage: Northern European home-computer scene music turned pop, roughly 1998-2010 in Sweden, Germany and the northeastern United States, made by routing Commodore 64 SID and Game Boy LSDJ chip voices through conventional pop songwriting — verse-chorus forms, 120-160 BPM four-on-the-floor or breakbeat drums, arpeggiated square-wave leads, and sung vocals or guitars layered against the 8-bit timbres.
items.description: Bitpop crystallised in the demoscene-adjacent circles of Sweden and Germany in the late 1990s and spread through American chip labels such as 8bitpeoples in the 2000s. It differs from pure chiptune by refusing to stay inside the chip: fast arpeggios and pulse-width leads from a SID or Game Boy sit inside conventional pop arrangements alongside sampled drums, electric guitar and sung choruses. Against nintendocore it is melodic and dance-oriented rather than hardcore-derived, and against 8-bit tracker music it prioritises hooks and mixdown over hardware purism.

items.name: Nintendocore
items.lineage: United States, roughly 2000-2010, named from Horse the Band's Long Beach output and extended by Sky Eats Airplane and Genghis Tron — metalcore and post-hardcore instrumentation (down-tuned humbucker riffing, double-kick blasts, screamed vocals) interleaved with lead lines voiced on chiptune and FM synths in the melodic register of 8-bit video-game music, with abrupt tempo cuts between 90 and 200 BPM.
items.description: Nintendocore is a 2000s American hybrid in which metalcore and screamo bands built keyboard leads out of deliberately video-game-like square and FM timbres, most influentially Horse the Band, who coined the term half-jokingly. The sound alternates chugged low-tuned riffing and blast sections with bright chiptune melodies that carry the hook, and structures are through-composed and spasmodic rather than verse-chorus. It differs from bitpop by taking hardcore rather than pop as its host body, and from synth-driven metalcore generally by the specific low-bit-depth, non-orchestral synth palette.

items.name: Yorkshire Bleeps and Bass
items.lineage: Sheffield and Leeds, 1988-1991, codified on Warp and Bassic by Forgemasters, Unique 3, LFO and Nightmares on Wax — 120-130 BPM electro-derived programmed drums under stark sine-wave and square 'bleep' motifs, with an enormous sustained sub-bass borrowed from Jamaican sound-system practice and near-empty midrange, cut for maximum system pressure.
items.description: Bleep, or bleep-and-bass, was the first distinctly British techno idiom, made in Sheffield and Leeds between 1988 and 1991 by producers who had grown up on both Detroit electro and West Indian sound systems. Its method is subtraction: a hard electro or house drum pattern, one or two pure-toned synth bleeps as the entire melody, and a very low, very long bass note that dominates the mix. It is distinguished from Detroit techno by that sub-bass emphasis and its sparser harmony, and from the rave hardcore that followed it by its slower tempo and refusal of breakbeats and chopped vocal stabs.

items.name: Balearic Beat
items.lineage: Ibiza, mid-1980s, codified by DJ Alfredo Fiorito's open-air sets at Amnesia and carried to Britain in 1987 by Paul Oakenfold and Danny Rampling — a 100-120 BPM eclectic mode joining dub-delayed guitar, nylon-string and slide figures, warm analogue pads and loose live-feel drum machine programming, with long unhurried arrangements and sun-facing major-key harmony.
items.description: Balearic beat began as a DJ practice rather than a production style, in Ibiza's open-air clubs of the mid-1980s where Alfredo Fiorito mixed Euro-pop, dub, new-age, Italo and rock records at a mid tempo for an all-night outdoor crowd. As producers began writing for it, the style settled into slow-to-mid tempo grooves with nylon-string or chorused electric guitar, wide pads, congas and generous delay, favouring atmosphere over dancefloor pressure. Against acid house, which shares its 1987-88 UK moment, Balearic is slower, more harmonically open and organic in instrumentation; against deep house it is looser and less club-functional in arrangement.

items.name: Dubtronica
items.lineage: European and North American studios from the mid-1990s onward, growing out of Basic Channel's Berlin work and Bill Laswell's New York dub projects — 120-140 BPM electronic productions built on Jamaican mixing-desk technique: one-drop or steppers kick placement, spring and tape echo throws, filtered chord stabs on the offbeat, melodica or dubbed guitar fragments, and a sustained sine sub-bass as the harmonic floor.
items.description: Dubtronica names the broad post-1995 practice of building electronic dance records by dub methodology rather than sampling reggae records: the mixing desk itself is played, with echo sends, filter sweeps and channel drops treated as performance. Typical tracks run long, hold two or three chords, and let a chorused stab and a deep sine bass carry everything while percussion and fragments fade in and out of the delay. It is distinguished from roots dub by its programmed rather than session-band rhythm bed, and from dub techno proper by admitting downtempo, psychedelic and world-percussion material rather than staying tied to a Berlin four-to-the-floor.

items.name: Darkcore
items.lineage: London and the Home Counties, 1992-1993, made by 4hero, Rufige Kru, Doc Scott and Origin Unknown as breakbeat hardcore turned menacing — 150-160 BPM chopped and time-stretched Amen and Think breaks, minor-key stab and string pads, horror-film and sci-fi vocal samples, deep detuned sub-bass, and the piano and euphoric riffs of 1991 rave stripped out entirely.
items.description: Darkcore is the 1992-93 turn in UK breakbeat hardcore, when producers reacting against the happy-rave saturation of the previous year replaced piano riffs and diva samples with dissonant pads, horror dialogue and heavily time-stretched breaks. It is the direct bridge from hardcore to jungle: the drum programming becomes intricate and the bass drops below the break, but the tempo and the rave-era sampler workflow remain. It is separable from jungle proper by its retention of four-to-the-floor kick underlays and hardcore stabs, and from later techstep by its sample-collage rather than synthesised sound sources.

items.name: Darkstep
items.lineage: UK, Germany and the Netherlands from roughly 1997 onward, developed by Panacea, Technical Itch, Dylan and Current Value out of techstep — 170-180 BPM drum and bass with saturated and distorted Amen edits, atonal noise-based reese and screech bass, near-total absence of chordal harmony, and long unresolved builds with no vocal presence.
items.description: Darkstep took shape in the late 1990s as techstep's harsher continuation, driven by continental European producers as much as British ones. It runs faster and dirtier than mainstream drum and bass, using distortion and clipping as compositional material, with breakbeats layered until they read as texture and bass timbres derived from noise and detuned saw stacks rather than pitched notes. Against neurofunk it is less clinically engineered and far more abrasive; against darkcore, its ancestor, it is fully synthesised and tempo-elevated rather than sample-collaged.

items.name: Drumfunk
items.lineage: UK, from the late 1990s onward around Paradox, Fanu and Macc, a drum-and-bass idiom in which the whole composition is the break — 165-175 BPM Amen, Apache and rare funk breaks chopped to single hits and re-sequenced into constantly varying non-looping patterns, over minimal warm sub-bass and sparse Rhodes or ambient pads with almost no riff content.
items.description: Drumfunk is the breakbeat-purist wing of drum and bass, established in Britain from the late 1990s by producers who treated jungle's early cut-up ethic as the point rather than a stage. Tracks are built from finely edited funk and soul breaks resequenced so that the drum pattern rarely repeats identically, with bass and harmony deliberately kept minimal so the percussion carries the whole arrangement. It differs from jump-up and neurofunk by having essentially no bass hook, and from liquid drum and bass by rejecting sustained chordal beds and vocal toplines.

items.name: Drumstep
items.lineage: UK and North America, roughly 2010-2015, emerging where dubstep producers met drum and bass on festival stages — tracks nominally at 170-175 BPM but with kick and snare placed on a half-time 85-BPM grid, wobbling LFO-modulated mid-bass in the dubstep manner, EDM-scale supersaw or vocal build-ups, and full drum-and-bass hi-hat and break fills between drops.
items.description: Drumstep is the early-2010s hybrid that plays a drum-and-bass tempo with dubstep's half-time backbeat, so the track feels like 87 BPM while the hats and fills run at 174. It arrived with the brostep boom and shares that music's tools: heavily modulated growl bass, sidechained supersaws, and a build-drop-build arrangement designed for large festival systems. Against drum and bass it sacrifices the rolling break for a heavy backbeat, and against dubstep it doubles the underlying pulse and restores the genre's rapid percussion detail.

items.name: Hardstep
items.lineage: London, 1995-1997, defined on dubplate by Ed Rush, Trace, Lemon D, Dillinja and Nico as jungle stripped of its ragga chatter — roughly 170 BPM two-step drum patterns using tight programmed kicks and snares rather than rolling Amen loops, hard filtered sub and reese bass, dark minimal stabs, and a percussive, mechanical feel aimed at big-room systems.
items.description: Hardstep is the mid-1990s London style in which jungle's chopped-break density was replaced by a spare, hard two-step drum pattern and the ragga vocal sampling was dropped altogether. Producers built rhythm from tightly programmed kicks and heavily compressed snares over sustained reese and sub bass, producing a track that reads as functional and mechanical rather than exuberant. It is the immediate parent of techstep, from which it differs by using cleaner, less distorted sound design, and it is separable from jump-up by having no bouncy melodic bass hook.

items.name: Jump-Up
items.lineage: London, from about 1995 and revived from the mid-2000s by Aphrodite, DJ Hype, Shy FX, Hazard and Original Sin — 172-176 BPM drum and bass built on a short, bouncy, heavily pitch-modulated mid-range bass hook, tight two-step kick-and-snare programming, funk and reggae vocal samples used as punctuation, and simple call-and-response arrangements written for immediate crowd reaction.
items.description: Jump-up split from jungle around 1995 as the deliberately fun, crowd-facing side of drum and bass, driven by Aphrodite, DJ Hype and Shy FX and later renewed by a mid-2000s London generation. Its defining device is a short looping mid-bass riff, usually squelchy and pitch-bent, which acts as the tune's melody and hook, set over uncomplicated two-step drums with big snares and cut-in vocal samples. It contrasts with hardstep and techstep, which suppress melodic bass in favour of texture, and with liquid drum and bass, which uses sustained chords and full sung vocals instead of the riff.

items.name: Oldschool Jungle
items.lineage: Formed in London and Bristol 1992-94 out of hardcore rave's acceleration, codified by Rebel MC, Shy FX, Congo Natty and DJ Hype on white-label 12-inches — 155-170 BPM chopped Amen and Apache breakbeats time-stretched over halftime 80 BPM sub-bass and Jamaican dancehall samples, with ragga toasting and pitched-up diva vocals cut to dubplate for pirate-radio play.
items.description: Jungle in its 1992-94 form, when hardcore rave producers began chopping the Amen break into intricate 16th-note edits over reggae basslines, creating a music with two simultaneous tempos: frantic percussion and a slow, dub-derived low end. Ragga vocal samples, timestretch artefacts and sirens define the palette, and tracks were pressed to dubplate for immediate pirate-radio testing. It is warmer and more melodic than the darkside and techstep strains that followed, retaining rave's piano stabs and euphoric diva hooks.

items.name: Darkside Jungle
items.lineage: London 1992-93 reaction against happy hardcore, driven by 4hero, Doc Scott, Goldie's Metalheadz circle and Reinforced Records — 155-165 BPM breakbeats stripped of piano and diva hooks, replaced by minor-key horror-film pads, detuned Reese basslines, reversed cymbals and sparse dread-laden atmospheres cut to dubplate.
items.description: The darkcore strain that split from rave euphoria in 1992-93, keeping hardcore's tempo and break-chopping while draining out the major-key hooks. Its markers are the detuned Reese bass, horror-soundtrack string pads, time-stretched screams and long tension-building intros with the drums held back. Compared to ragga-led oldschool jungle it is largely instrumental and minor-modal; compared to techstep it is still sample-collage rather than distorted synthesis.
exemplars: Doc Scott - Here Comes The Drumz

items.name: Raggacore
items.lineage: Emerged in Berlin and London around 2003-07 from breakcore's collision with dancehall, codified by Bong-Ra, Aaron Spectre, DJ Scotch Egg and the Wasted Sound / Death$ucker circles — 170-200 BPM distorted Amen and Mentasm edits under looped ragga toasting and dancehall riddim samples, produced entirely in-the-box with heavy clipping and abrupt cut-and-paste structure.
items.description: A mid-2000s European breakcore offshoot that laid ragga and dancehall vocal samples over extremely fast, heavily distorted chopped breakbeats. It keeps jungle's Jamaican vocal source material but pushes tempo past 180 BPM and saturates the drums into clipping, with sudden edits and metal-adjacent aggression. Where jungle rides a sub-bass groove, raggacore treats the break itself as the distorted lead instrument.
exemplars: Aaron Spectre - Lost Tribe of the Bassline

items.name: Sambass
items.lineage: Developed in Sao Paulo and Rio de Janeiro from 1997, codified by DJ Marky, XRS Land, Patife and the Sambaloco label — 170-175 BPM drum and bass programming fused with samba and bossa nova, using surdo and pandeiro layers, tamborim patterns, nylon-string guitar comping, Rhodes chords and Portuguese-language female vocals over rolling two-step breaks.
items.description: Brazilian drum and bass, formed in Sao Paulo in the late 1990s when local DJs began layering live samba percussion and bossa harmony over 174 BPM liquid breaks. Pandeiro and tamborim sit inside the programmed drum pattern rather than beside it, and the harmonic language comes from bossa's extended seventh and ninth chords, giving it a lighter, jazz-inflected feel than UK liquid funk. Portuguese vocals and nylon guitar are the clearest markers separating it from its British parent form.

items.name: Techstep
items.lineage: London 1995-97, codified by Ed Rush, Trace, Nico and No U-Turn Records with Optical and Bad Company following — 170-175 BPM drum and bass stripped of samples and rebuilt from distorted Reese and Hoover synthesis, two-step drum patterns with heavily compressed processed snares, and bleak industrial-metallic sound design mixed loud onto DAT.
items.description: The mid-1990s techno-facing turn in drum and bass, in which producers abandoned chopped funk breaks for synthesised and heavily processed drums and made the distorted Reese bassline the central voice. Tracks are near-instrumental, minor or atonal, built on a rigid two-step pattern with a snare on the third beat and long, austere arrangements. It is far more mechanical and sparse than darkside jungle, and its industrial timbral palette is what later hardstep, neurofunk and drumfunk grew from.

items.name: Electro Backbeat
items.lineage: New York and Detroit 1982-86, following Afrika Bambaataa's Planet Rock and codified by Man Parrish, Hashim, Cybotron and Egyptian Lover — 115-130 BPM TR-808 programming in which the snare falls squarely on beats two and four rather than in syncopated electro-funk clusters, over cold synth-bass ostinati, vocoder or talkbox vocals and Kraftwerk-derived monophonic riffs.
items.description: The strand of early-1980s electro that keeps a plain rock-and-funk backbeat under 808 programming instead of the broken, syncopated snare placement of Planet Rock-style electro-funk. The result is a stiffer, more four-square groove that made the style easy to rap and breakdance over, with vocoded robot vocals, hand-clap layers and stark monophonic bass lines. It is a direct ancestor of Detroit techno and of Miami bass, and its rigidity is what distinguishes it from the looser electro-funk and boogie records of the same years.
exemplars: Man Parrish - Hip Hop Be Bop

items.name: Electro-Grime
items.lineage: East London 2002-05, the electro-facing wing of grime shaped by Wiley's eskibeat, Ruff Sqwad, Jammer and Terror Danjah — 138-140 BPM instrumentals built in Fruity Loops from icy square-wave and sine leads, 8-bar loops, sparse 808-derived kicks with an offbeat snare, and heavy sub-bass, cut to dubplate for pirate radio and MC clashes.
items.description: The synth-led, sample-averse branch of grime that emerged in East London around 2002, closest to Wiley's eskibeat template of glassy square-wave melodies and near-empty space between the kick and the sub. Where garage-derived grime carried swung shuffle and vocal chops, this strain is rigid, cold and largely built from preset synth tones in cheap software, leaving wide gaps for MCs. It sits between early-80s electro's synthetic minimalism and UK sound-system bass weight.
exemplars: Ruff Sqwad - Died in Your Arms

items.name: Computer Music
items.lineage: Institutional art-music practice begun at Bell Labs in 1957 with Max Mathews's MUSIC I and extended at Stanford CCRMA, IRCAM and CCRMA-adjacent centres by John Chowning, Jean-Claude Risset and Barry Truax — sound synthesised or algorithmically composed by computer, using FM and granular techniques, spectral analysis-resynthesis, non-tempered frequency structures and fixed-media multichannel diffusion rather than live instrumental performance.
items.description: The academic tradition of composing with digitally synthesised sound, running from Max Mathews's MUSIC programs at Bell Labs through Chowning's FM synthesis at Stanford and IRCAM's spectral and analysis-resynthesis work. Its output is typically fixed-media, multichannel and through-composed, with timbre itself treated as the primary compositional dimension and pitch often derived from inharmonic spectra rather than a scale. Unlike tape music it generates sound rather than transforming recordings, and unlike live electronics the computation happens before the concert.
exemplars: Paul Lansky - Six Fantasies on a Poem by Thomas Campion
Max Mathews - Bicycle Built for Two

items.name: Field Recording (Phonographic Practice)
items.lineage: Grew from ethnographic cylinder collecting around 1890 into an autonomous listening practice after R. Murray Schafer's World Soundscape Project in Vancouver in the early 1970s, extended by Chris Watson, Annea Lockwood, Hildegard Westerkamp and Francisco Lopez — unaccompanied environmental sound captured with stereo or hydrophone arrays to portable recorders, presented with minimal edit, no metre and no pitch centre, structured only by the duration and dynamics of the place itself.
items.description: The presentation of recorded environmental sound as music in its own right, distinct from field recording as an ethnographic collecting method. Practitioners use matched stereo pairs, contact microphones and hydrophones into portable recorders, and the compositional decisions are microphone placement, duration and framing rather than notes. It differs from musique concrete in that the material is generally left untransformed, and from soundscape composition in refusing narrative montage.
exemplars: Annea Lockwood - A Sound Map of the Hudson River
Toshiya Tsunoda - Extract from Field Recording Archive

items.name: Live Coding
items.lineage: Formalised in Sheffield and London from 2003 by the TOPLAP collective — Alex McLean, Nick Collins and Adrian Ward — and spread through algorave events after 2012, with SuperCollider, TidalCycles and Sonic Pi as the primary tools: performers write and rewrite executing code onstage with the screen projected, generating pattern-based dance music at 120-170 BPM from sample banks and synthesis, with structure emerging from edits made in real time.
items.description: A performance practice in which musicians improvise by writing and modifying running program code onstage, with the projected screen part of the show. Output ranges from algorave dance floors built on cyclic sample patterns to abstract generative textures, but the shared markers are audible discontinuity at each code evaluation, layered polymetric loops and gradual accretion of parts. Its notation is executable rather than descriptive, which separates it from both DJ practice and studio-composed electronic music.

items.name: Live Electronics
items.lineage: Post-war European and American art music from the late 1950s, codified by Karlheinz Stockhausen's Mikrophonie and Mixtur, John Cage and David Tudor's Cartridge Music, Luigi Nono's Milan work and later IRCAM real-time systems — acoustic instruments and voices transformed onstage by ring modulators, tape delay networks, live filtering and spatialisation, from graphic or verbal scores with substantial performer latitude over timing and gesture.
items.description: Art music in which electronic transformation happens in the concert hall rather than in the studio, so the processing is a performed act. Characteristic techniques are ring modulation of a live instrument, feedback and delay networks, contact-miked amplification of small sounds, and multi-loudspeaker spatial diffusion, usually notated in scores that fix process while leaving detail open. It is distinguished from tape music by the presence of performers and from computer music by real-time, hall-dependent decision-making.
exemplars: John Cage & David Tudor - Cartridge Music
Alvin Lucier - I Am Sitting in a Room

items.name: Tape Music
items.lineage: Born in Paris in 1948 with Pierre Schaeffer's studio at RTF and in Cologne in 1951 at the WDR Studio fur elektronische Musik under Herbert Eimert and Stockhausen, with Vladimir Ussachevsky and Otto Luening establishing the American branch at Columbia in 1952 — compositions assembled by splicing, varispeed, reversal and tape-loop layering of recorded material onto magnetic tape as the finished, fixed work, with no performers and no metric pulse.
items.description: The 1950s studio practice of composing directly onto magnetic tape, where the razor blade, the varispeed capstan and the loop replace the score and the performer. Its sonic signatures are audible splice edges, pitch-shifted acoustic sources, reversed envelopes and superimposed loops of differing length, all fixed at the moment the master is cut. It overlaps musique concrete in method but names the broader practice, including Cologne's purely oscillator-generated elektronische Musik and the Columbia-Princeton school.
exemplars: Pierre Schaeffer - Etude aux chemins de fer

items.name: Berlin School
items.lineage: West Berlin and Dusseldorf 1971-79, codified by Tangerine Dream, Klaus Schulze and Ashra — long-form sequencer music built on 16-step analogue sequencer ostinati at roughly 100-130 pulses per minute, layered Mellotron and string-synthesiser pads, slow filter sweeps and gradual additive arrangements running fifteen to twenty-five minutes without vocals, tracked to multitrack tape in self-built studios.
items.description: The German sequencer-driven electronic style of the 1970s, in which a hypnotic analogue step pattern is set running and the composition proceeds by slowly changing filter, register and added layers over twenty minutes or more. Mellotron choirs and string machines supply the harmonic bed, and drums are usually absent or sparse. It differs from Dusseldorf's motorik rock in having no rhythm section, and from later ambient in retaining a constant audible pulse.
exemplars: Michael Hoenig - Departure from the Northern Wasteland

items.name: Folktronica
items.lineage: British and North American style crystallizing circa 1999-2005 through Four Tet, Tunng, Múm and Beth Orton, splicing acoustic fingerpicked guitar, glockenspiel, dulcimer and hand percussion with chopped-sampler beats, edited breakbeats at 85-115 BPM and granular texture beds, sung in soft close-mic'd untrained voices over cyclic modal loops.
items.description: Folktronica emerged around the turn of the millennium in British and American home studios, pairing the intimate acoustic timbres of folk revival — fingerpicked steel-string, hammered tuned percussion, breathy unforced singing — with sampler editing, glitch artefacts and looped breakbeats. Its textures are warm and pastoral rather than clinical, distinguishing it from the colder IDM it borrows production technique from, and its beats are chopped and quantized rather than played, distinguishing it from acoustic indie folk. Arrangements are cyclic and additive: a short loop accrues layers instead of moving through verse-chorus form.
exemplars: Tunng — Mother's Daughter and Other Songs
Múm — Finally We Are No One
The Books — The Lemon of Pink

items.name: Laptronica
items.lineage: Late-1990s European and Japanese live-computer performance idiom named around 2001 and practiced by Oval, Ryoji Ikeda, Christian Fennesz and Kim Cascone, in which the laptop running Max/MSP or SuperCollider is the sole instrument, producing beatless or arrhythmic fields of sine tones, CD-skip artefacts, clicks and DSP feedback at extreme dynamic contrast with no vocals and no fixed meter.
items.description: Laptronica names the practice, consolidated in the late 1990s around the Mego and Raster-Noton labels, of performing electronic music live entirely from a computer using custom software patches. The sonic signature is digital error made compositional: pure sine tones, quantization noise, buffer glitches and abrupt silences, arranged as slowly evolving fields rather than tracks. Unlike glitch-inflected IDM it usually abandons beat and song form altogether, and unlike concrète it works from synthesized or algorithmically mangled data rather than recorded objects.

items.name: Skweee
items.lineage: Nordic microgenre named in Stockholm and Helsinki circa 2007 by Daniel Savio, Pavan and the Flogsta Danshall / Harmönia circles, built from cheap monophonic synth leads squeezed with pitch-bend and filter over slow 70-100 BPM funk drum-machine patterns, deliberately thin and unmastered, entirely instrumental and released on short vinyl.
items.description: Skweee was coined in Sweden and Finland around 2007 for a deliberately minimal electronic funk: one squeezed monosynth melody line, a bassline, and a bare drum-machine pattern, with almost nothing else in the mix. Tempos sit in slow funk territory and the lead voice is expressive through pitch-bend and filter sweep rather than harmonic movement. It differs from Detroit electro and from wonky hip-hop in its extreme sparseness and its refusal of studio polish — the tracks sound like unfinished sketches by design.

items.name: Sound Art
items.lineage: Gallery-and-installation practice consolidated in New York and Europe from the late 1970s through Max Neuhaus, Bill Fontana, Alvin Lucier and Christina Kubisch, using site-specific field recording, resonating architecture, feedback, long-duration drones and electromagnetic induction rather than metered composition, presented as spatial installation without stage, beat or vocal line.
items.description: Sound art names work that treats sound as a spatial and sculptural material rather than as music unfolding in performance time, formalized as a category from the late 1970s onward in galleries, public squares and architectural sites. Typical materials are field recordings, room resonance, feedback loops, induction coils and very long durations with no discernible pulse. It is distinguished from musique concrète by being installed rather than fixed to a playback format, and from ambient music by having no listener-facing song object at all — the site itself is the piece.
exemplars: Alvin Lucier — I Am Sitting in a Room
Janet Cardiff — The Forty Part Motet

items.name: Synthcore
items.lineage: Late-1990s and 2000s hybrid, worked out by Refused, The Blood Brothers' peers and later Enter Shikari, fusing hardcore punk's screamed vocals, downpicked distorted guitar and blast-adjacent drumming with foregrounded analog and digital synthesizers, trance-derived arpeggios and breakdown-to-drop structures at 150-180 BPM.
items.description: Synthcore describes hardcore punk and post-hardcore that places synthesizers on equal footing with guitars rather than using them as garnish, developing from the late 1990s through bands who imported rave and trance material wholesale into screamed, breakdown-driven songs. Arpeggiated synth leads, gated pads and outright EDM drops sit inside riffing built on downpicked power chords and shouted group vocals. It differs from electronicore in leaning on played synth parts and punk song structure rather than programmed metalcore breakdowns, and from synthpop in its distortion and vocal aggression.
exemplars: Enter Shikari — Take to the Skies
Refused — The Shape of Punk to Come

items.name: Baggy (Indie-Dance)
items.lineage: British indie-dance sound of 1989-1992, exported from Manchester by The Stone Roses, Happy Mondays, The Charlatans and Flowered Up, marrying loose swung breakbeat drumming and wah-inflected funk guitar to jangling indie melody at 105-120 BPM, with drawled deadpan lead vocals, prominent congas and tambourine, and dub-length grooving outros.
items.description: Baggy is the British indie-dance idiom of roughly 1989 to 1992, named for the loose clothing of its audience, in which guitar bands adopted the swung breakbeat feel and extended groove structures of acid house. The rhythm section plays a loose, behind-the-beat funk shuffle under wah guitar and hand percussion, topped by flat, unstrained vocals. It is broader than Madchester, which names the specific city scene, and it differs from big beat in being played by a live band rather than sequenced.
exemplars: Happy Mondays — Pills 'n' Thrills and Bellyaches

items.name: Madchester (Manchester Scene)
items.lineage: Manchester city scene of 1988-1992 centred on the Haçienda and Factory Records, with The Stone Roses, Happy Mondays, 808 State and A Guy Called Gerald, blending acid-house 4/4 and sampled breakbeats with psychedelic guitar, Northern-drawled vocals and Latin hand percussion at 110-125 BPM, produced by Martin Hannett and Paul Oakenfold.
items.description: Madchester names the Manchester scene of roughly 1988 to 1992 in which the city's guitar bands, ecstasy culture and the Haçienda's acid-house DJ programming fused into a single sound. Tracks combine four-to-the-floor or swung sampled breaks with psychedelic wah guitar, dub-influenced bass, hand percussion and laconic vocals, often extended into long remix-friendly grooves. Where baggy names the wider national style, Madchester is the geographic and institutional scene that produced it, and it includes purely electronic acts alongside the bands.
exemplars: The Stone Roses — The Stone Roses
A Guy Called Gerald — Voodoo Ray

items.name: Dance-Punk
items.lineage: New York and London style running from the 1979-1982 post-punk disco crossover of ESG, Liquid Liquid and Gang of Four into the 2001-2006 revival of The Rapture, LCD Soundsystem and !!!, built on a dry syncopated sixteenth-note hi-hat groove, popped or picked funk bass carrying the hook, scratchy trebly guitar and shouted or yelped vocals at 120-135 BPM.
items.description: Dance-punk is punk and post-punk played on a disco rhythm section: a hard, dry, tightly-locked drum-and-bass groove with sixteenth hi-hats, hand percussion and cowbell, over which guitar functions as a percussive treble scrape rather than a chord bed. It formed in downtown New York and Britain around 1979-1982 and returned in the early 2000s New York revival. Unlike baggy's loose swung feel it is rigid and quantized-tight, and unlike disco proper it keeps punk's shouted vocals, minimal harmony and abrasive guitar tone.

items.name: Electroclash
items.lineage: New York, Berlin and Paris scene of 1998-2004, named by promoter Larry Tee and defined by Fischerspooner, Miss Kittin & The Hacker, Peaches and Ladytron, pairing stiff 808/909 electro beats and cheap analog monosynth basslines at 120-130 BPM with deadpan spoken-sung vocals, heavy new-wave pastiche and vocoder, deliberately cold and campy.
items.description: Electroclash was the club-and-art-scene style of the turn of the 2000s in New York, Berlin and Paris that revived early-1980s electro and synthpop with intentional cheapness and sexual provocation. Its tracks are built on rigid drum-machine electro patterns, a single fat analog bassline and almost no harmonic development, fronted by flat spoken vocals delivered in an ironic register. It is distinguished from synthpop by its four-to-the-floor club function and from electro-house by its lo-fi, retro gear palette and performance-art framing.
exemplars: Miss Kittin & The Hacker — First Album
Felix da Housecat — Kittenz and Thee Glitz

items.name: Electronicore (Metalcore Hybrid)
items.lineage: Late-2000s American and British metalcore hybrid codified circa 2007-2012 by Attack Attack!, Asking Alexandria and Crossfaith, layering trance supersaw leads, sidechained pads and dubstep-style wobble drops over drop-tuned breakdown riffing, blast beats and triggered kick drums at 130-175 BPM, alternating screamed verses with heavily tuned clean choruses.
items.description: Electronicore is the late-2000s fusion of metalcore with mainstream EDM, in which trance supersaw leads, sidechained synth pads and dubstep bass drops are welded onto drop-tuned breakdowns and triggered blast drumming. Vocals alternate between screams and pitch-corrected clean choruses, and mixes are maximally loud and grid-locked. It differs from synthcore in that the electronics are programmed dance-genre material dropped in as sections rather than played synth parts, and from trancecore in its heavier reliance on breakdown-centred metalcore riffing.

items.name: Electropunk
items.lineage: Style running from Suicide's 1977 New York duo format through Alec Empire and Le Tigre in the 1990s, using a distorted drum machine and a screaming monophonic synth in place of a rhythm section, with shouted or slap-back-echoed vocals over relentless one-chord ostinatos at 130-160 BPM and no guitar solos or harmonic development.
items.description: Electropunk is punk played on electronic instruments: a primitive drum machine and one overdriven synth carrying both riff and bass, with vocals delivered as shout, chant or slap-echoed croon. It begins with Suicide in mid-1970s New York and recurs through 1990s digital hardcore and riot-grrrl electronics. Where electroclash is cold and club-functional, electropunk is abrasive and confrontational, keeping punk's one-chord aggression, distortion and short songs rather than aiming at the dancefloor.

items.name: Ethereal Wave
items.lineage: British gothic-rock offshoot of 1983-1990 defined by Cocteau Twins, This Mortal Coil and Dead Can Dance on 4AD under producers John Fryer and Ivo Watts-Russell, built from chorused and heavily reverberant guitar, fretless or chorused bass, drum machine, and wordless soprano vocals stacked in cathedral-scale reverb over slow modal 60-100 BPM cycles.
items.description: Ethereal wave is the luminous branch of British gothic rock that developed on 4AD in the mid-1980s, replacing goth's bass-forward menace with washes of chorused, reverberant guitar and soaring, often wordless female vocals layered many tracks deep. Rhythm is usually a soft drum machine or restrained live kit, and harmony drifts through modal suspensions rather than resolving. It is distinguished from darkwave by its brightness and vocal centrality, and from shoegaze by its cleaner, non-distorted guitar tone and its debt to medieval and world-music modality.
exemplars: This Mortal Coil — It'll End in Tears
Dead Can Dance — Within the Realm of a Dying Sun

items.name: New Rave
items.lineage: British scene of 2006-2008 named by NME around Klaxons, Shitdisco and Hadouken!, layering early-1990s rave synth stabs, air-horns and acid basslines onto indie guitar band instrumentation at 130-145 BPM, with shouted call-and-response vocals, sidechained pumping and neon club presentation.
items.description: New rave was a short-lived British scene of 2006-2008 in which indie guitar bands adopted the sonic furniture of early-1990s rave — piano and organ stabs, acid squelch, air-horn samples, pumping sidechain compression — while keeping live drums and shouted vocals. Songs are bright, fast and hook-driven, closer to indie rock structure than to DJ-oriented dance tracks. It differs from dance-punk in tempo and in drawing on hardcore rave rather than disco, and from electroclash in its band format and lack of irony-cold delivery.
exemplars: Klaxons — Myths of the Near Future
Hadouken! — Music for an Accelerated Culture
Test Icicles — For Screening Purposes Only
Late of the Pier — Fantasy Black Channel

items.name: Synthpunk
items.lineage: Late-1970s American punk offshoot (Los Angeles, Akron, New York, 1977-1981) in which cheap monophonic synthesizers, combo organs and primitive drum machines replaced guitars entirely — codified by The Screamers, Suicide, Nervous Gender and The Units, running 140-170 BPM with buzzing sawtooth ostinati, no cymbals, hammering eighth-note machine pulses and shouted, hectoring, close-miked vocals delivered flat and unmelodic.
items.description: Synthpunk emerged in the American punk underground between 1977 and 1981 when bands substituted ARP, Korg and Farfisa keyboards for electric guitar while keeping punk's tempo, brevity and confrontational delivery. The sound is harsh and thin: unfiltered sawtooth leads, dry rhythm-box pulses with no reverb tail, and vocals shouted just off pitch. Unlike synthpop it refuses melodic sweetening and studio polish, and unlike industrial it keeps conventional verse-chorus song form and two-minute running times.

items.name: Bubblegum Dance
items.lineage: Scandinavian and Benelux late-1990s commercial eurodance variant (Denmark, Sweden, Netherlands, 1996-2002) built by producers such as Søren Rasted and Claus Norreen of Aqua and the Toy-Box and Daze teams — 130-140 BPM four-on-the-floor, offbeat sawtooth stabs, cartoonishly high female lead vocals answered by pitched-down comic male spoken lines, and relentless major-key hooks with no rap verse in the classic eurodance sense.
items.description: Bubblegum dance is the children's-television-bright branch of eurodance that dominated Northern European charts from about 1996 to 2002. It keeps eurodance's 135 BPM kick, offbeat bass and supersaw stabs but swaps the genre's tough MC verse for helium-pitched female leads and comic character voices, with lyrics about toys, candy and cartoon romance. Against mainstream eurodance it is faster in hook turnover, thinner in low end and deliberately juvenile in vocal casting.

items.name: Eurobeat
items.lineage: Italian-produced, Japan-exported hi-NRG dance style codified from 1990 onward by Milanese and Roman studios (A-Beat C, Delta, Time Records) for the Super Eurobeat compilation series — 150-160 BPM, driving straight kick and octave-jumping synth bass, twin-lead sawtooth riffs in the eight-bar break, English-language power vocals sung by session singers under stage aliases, and a rigid intro-verse-break-chorus template.
items.description: Eurobeat is a closed production system: Italian studios manufacturing hi-NRG derived dance tracks almost exclusively for the Japanese market from the early 1990s to the present, distributed through the long-running Super Eurobeat series and popularized further by arcade rhythm games and street-racing anime. Its markers are the 155 BPM straight kick, relentless sixteenth octave bassline, and a mandatory instrumental break of dual sequenced lead lines. It is faster and more formulaic than eurodance, and unlike hi-NRG it is sung almost entirely by anonymous vocalists over producer-owned aliases.

items.name: Hard NRG
items.lineage: UK hard-house derivative of the early 2000s centred on the Tidy Trax and Nukleuz labels and the Leeds/Birmingham club circuit — 150-160 BPM, distorted offbeat 'donk' bass stab, hoover-style detuned leads, long filtered noise risers and hard-panned reverse cymbal drops, with vocals reduced to chopped one-shot shouts rather than sung lines.
items.description: Hard NRG (also nu-NRG) is the accelerated, heavily distorted end of British hard house as it developed around 2000-2005 in Tidy Trax and Nukleuz club culture. Tracks sit near 155 BPM with a saturated kick, the signature offbeat donk stab, and structures organised entirely around riser-and-drop tension rather than song form. Compared with hardstyle it lacks the reverse-bass kick pattern, and compared with hard house proper it drops the vocal diva hooks in favour of pure percussive drive.

items.name: New Beat
items.lineage: Belgian club style formed in Ghent and Antwerp in 1987-1989 when DJs played EBM and Italo 45s at 33 rpm with the pitch raised, producing a 100-115 BPM half-speed groove — codified by Confetti's, A Split-Second, Erotic Dissidence and the Antler/Subway label roster, marked by a dry gated kick, clipped sequenced bass, sampled orchestral or spoken stabs, and slowed, sinister male vocal fragments.
items.description: New Beat was a short, intense Belgian scene between 1987 and 1989, born from the accidental discovery that EBM and Italo records slowed to 33 rpm produced an eerie, dragging dancefloor groove. Producers then wrote to that tempo directly: hard gated drum-machine kicks around 105 BPM, terse monophonic bass sequences, sampled stabs and pitched-down vocal menace, always dry and mid-forward. It is slower and colder than the acid house running parallel in Chicago and Britain, and less song-oriented than the eurodance that eventually absorbed its producers.

items.name: Vaportrap
items.lineage: Internet-born hybrid formed around 2013-2016 on Bandcamp and SoundCloud, merging vaporwave's pitched-down 1980s corporate and R&B samples with Atlanta trap drum programming — 60-75 BPM half-time feel over 808 kicks with long pitch-glide sub tails, rolling triplet hi-hats, chopped and screwed vocal fragments drowned in hall reverb, and lush pad washes lifted from smooth-jazz and mall-music sources.
items.description: Vaportrap appeared in the mid-2010s online music underground as vaporwave producers began building their slowed sample collages on top of trap drum kits rather than looped elevator music alone. The result pairs 808 sub-bass glides and triplet hi-hat rolls with heavily reverbed, pitch-lowered snippets of 1980s soft rock, anime soundtracks and advertising audio. It differs from vaporwave in having a foreground rhythm section and from trap proper in having no rapper and no clean mix — everything is smeared, detuned and deliberately lossy.

items.name: Vaporhop
items.lineage: Online-scene fusion of vaporwave sampling with boom-bap hip-hop production, circulating from roughly 2012 onward on Bandcamp and Tumblr — 80-95 BPM swung breakbeats, dusty filtered loops taken from 1980s Japanese city pop, muzak and corporate video libraries, MPC-style chopping with audible sample truncation, and instrumental-first tracks where any vocal is a looped, unintelligible fragment rather than a rapped verse.
items.description: Vaporhop is the boom-bap wing of the vaporwave family, built after 2012 by producers who kept the genre's nostalgic corporate-audio sources but grounded them in swung 90 BPM hip-hop drums. Loops are chopped short, low-pass filtered and left slightly out of time, with tape hiss and MP3 artefacts treated as texture. Unlike vaportrap it avoids 808 sub-bass and triplet hats, and unlike lo-fi hip hop it foregrounds recognisable, ironically framed commercial samples instead of anonymous jazz chords.

items.name: Protovapor
items.lineage: The 2009-2011 American experimental precursor stratum to vaporwave — hypnagogic-pop and plunderphonic cassette work by Daniel Lopatin (as Chuck Person), James Ferraro and Ford & Lopatin — using slowed, looped and echo-drenched fragments of 1980s soft rock, VHS library music and early digital synth demos, with no fixed tempo grid, degraded cassette speed drift, and structures built from a single repeated four-bar cell.
items.description: Protovapor names the small body of work made in the United States between roughly 2009 and 2011 that established vaporwave's method before the genre had a name: cassette and CD-R releases of slowed, echo-flooded loops drawn from 1980s consumer audio. The sound is unstable in pitch, heavy in tape wow and hiss, and rhythmically loose or beatless. Compared with the vaporwave that followed it is less ironic and less visually branded, and compared with musique concrète it keeps whole recognisable pop phrases intact rather than atomising them.

items.name: British Folk Revival
items.lineage: The second British folk revival, formed in London and the industrial north from 1951 onward around Ewan MacColl, A.L. Lloyd and the Topic Records catalogue and spread through the folk-club circuit — repertoire drawn from Child ballads, broadsides and Cecil Sharp collections, performed largely unaccompanied or with anglo concertina, fiddle and guitar in modal Dorian and Mixolydian settings, free or loosely metered on the long ballads, with plain non-vibrato regional-accented delivery.
items.description: The British Folk Revival is the movement that ran from the early 1950s through the late 1960s to restore traditional English, Scottish and Welsh song to public performance, organised around folk clubs, the BBC radio ballads and Topic Records. Its aesthetic was deliberately austere: unaccompanied or lightly accompanied singing, regional accents preserved, ballads sung at length without dramatised delivery. It differs from the concurrent American revival in repertoire and in its resistance to guitar-driven arrangement, and it precedes the electric folk-rock that Fairport and Steeleye later built from the same songs.

items.name: Filk Music
items.lineage: Science-fiction and fantasy fandom's own song tradition, established at American conventions from the 1950s (the name a typo for 'folk' in a 1953 fanzine) and codified through late-night convention filksings and the Off Centaur and Firebird cassette labels — guitar-accompanied or unaccompanied strophic singing at moderate tempo, contrafacta set to existing folk and pop tunes alongside original songs, prizing lyric wit and narrative clarity over vocal polish.
items.description: Filk is the participatory song culture of English-language science-fiction fandom, performed mainly in hotel-room and function-room circles at conventions from the 1950s onward and documented largely on self-released cassettes. Musically it borrows wholesale from Anglo-American folk revival practice — strophic verses, alternating-bass guitar, group choruses — but its content is fannish: space travel, computing, Tolkien, and parodies fitted to borrowed tunes. What distinguishes it from the folk revival is the primacy of lyric and community participation over repertoire authenticity or performance craft.

items.name: Industrial Folk
items.lineage: The body of English and Scottish work song from the coalfields, mills, foundries and shipyards, written from the early nineteenth century by pitmen-poets such as Tommy Armstrong and Joe Wilson and brought into performance from 1951 by A.L. Lloyd's Come All Ye Bold Miners collection and Ewan MacColl's radio ballads — strophic modal tunes in steady walking tempo, sung unaccompanied or with concertina and melodeon, in broad regional dialect with narrative verses on accident, strike and wage.
items.description: Industrial folk is the occupational song of Britain's industrial workforce — mining, weaving, iron and shipbuilding communities from the 1800s onward — largely unrecorded until Lloyd, MacColl and the BBC radio ballad team collected and staged it in the 1950s and 1960s. The songs are strophic and modal, carried by a single strong voice with chorus answers, often unaccompanied so the dialect text stays intelligible. Unlike rural balladry it deals with wage, machinery and disaster in named places and dates, and unlike protest song proper it was written from inside the workforce rather than for a movement.
exemplars: A.L. Lloyd — Come All Ye Bold Miners

items.name: Neofolk
items.lineage: European post-industrial acoustic style formed in England in the mid-1980s as members of Crisis and Death in June turned from industrial electronics to acoustic guitar — codified by Death in June, Current 93 and Sol Invictus and extended in Germany and Scandinavia through the 1990s — with strummed nylon and steel guitar in Aeolian and Phrygian modes, martial snare and bass-drum patterns at slow marching tempo, drones from hurdy-gurdy and string machine, and declaimed baritone vocals over sparse, reverberant arrangements.
items.description: Neofolk grew out of the British post-industrial underground after 1984, when musicians from the industrial and death-rock scenes adopted acoustic guitar, marching percussion and European folk imagery while keeping tape loops, drones and studio reverb from their earlier work. Songs are slow, cyclic and declamatory, built on a repeating minor-modal guitar figure with a martial drum underneath. It is distinguished from the folk revival by its non-traditional repertoire and studio construction, and from gothic rock by its acoustic instrumentation and absence of a rock rhythm section.

items.name: Progressive Folk
items.lineage: British and American folk of roughly 1965-1975 that extended revival repertoire into long-form, harmonically ambitious arrangement — Pentangle, the Incredible String Band, Roy Harper, Bert Jansch and Tim Buckley — using open and altered guitar tunings, jazz-derived double bass and brushed kit, modal and chromatic harmony, extended instrumental sections, and free-metred introductions before settling into a sung strophic body.
items.description: Progressive folk describes the late-1960s and early-1970s wing of the Anglo-American folk world that treated the song as a frame for extended composition and improvisation rather than a fixed traditional text. Its signatures are altered-tuning fingerstyle guitar, upright bass and brushed drums borrowed from jazz, unusual timbres such as recorder, sitar and dulcimer, and pieces running well past five minutes. It separates from folk-rock by keeping acoustic instrumentation and avoiding backbeat drive, and from the earlier revival by writing new material with modern harmony.

items.name: Sung Poetry (Poezja Śpiewana)
items.lineage: Polish art-song form crystallized in the Kraków and Warsaw student cabarets of the early 1960s (Piwnica pod Baranami, Ewa Demarczyk, Marek Grechuta) and carried through the martial-law years by Jacek Kaczmarski, setting canonical literary verse by Baczyński, Leśmian and Wysocki-derived texts to through-composed piano-and-guitar accompaniment at free rubato tempos, with declamatory diction, no drum kit, and dynamics driven entirely by the syllabic weight of the poem.
items.description: Poezja śpiewana is the Polish practice, formalized in the Kraków student-cabaret scene of the early 1960s and institutionalized by the Studencki Festiwal Piosenki in Kraków, of setting published literary poetry to composed song rather than writing lyrics. The sonic signature is a solo declamatory voice given absolute foreground, sparse piano or fingerpicked guitar with occasional bass and cello, rubato phrasing that follows the poem's line breaks instead of a fixed bar count, and complete absence of percussion. It differs from Western singer-songwriter confessionalism in that the singer is usually not the author of the text, and from chanson in its heavier reliance on canonical national literature and its wartime and dissident political charge.

items.name: Techno-Folk
items.lineage: European fusion consolidated in Scotland and London in the early-to-mid 1990s through Martyn Bennett, Shooglenifty and Afro Celt Sound System, laying live fiddle, Highland pipes and whistle over programmed 125-140 BPM breakbeat and four-on-floor sequencer grooves, with modal jigs and reels looped as riffs, sampled Gaelic waulking and puirt-a-beul vocals, and sub-bass replacing the traditional drone.
items.description: Techno-folk emerged in the early 1990s from Celtic-fringe musicians who had grown up in club culture, most decisively in Martyn Bennett's Edinburgh work and the Shooglenifty and Afro Celt Sound System records that followed. It keeps the melodic material of session tradition — dorian and mixolydian dance tunes, piped ornamentation, sean-nós vocal samples — and rebuilds the accompaniment as a sequenced dance track with sub-bass, breakbeats and filtered pads. Unlike folk-rock, which substitutes a rock band for the ceilidh band but preserves song form, techno-folk imposes loop-and-build DJ architecture; unlike world-fusion pop, the tunes themselves remain repertoire pieces rather than newly written hooks.

items.name: German Folk (Volksmusik)
