Its sound is defined by the cajón as lead drum, the scraped donkey-jaw quijada, a syncopated nylon-string guitar tumbao, and shouted responsorial choruses at roughly 110-130 BPM. Unlike the slower, rubato landó or the melancholic vals criollo, festejo is relentlessly cyclic, percussion-forward and made for stamped zapateo competition.

items.name: Música llanera
items.lineage: Plains music of the Orinoco llanos straddling Venezuela and Colombia's Arauca-Casanare, professionalized from the 1940s onward through radio and the Festival Internacional del Joropo, built on arpa llanera or bandola llanera lead, strummed cuatro golpes, driving capachos maracas and a 3/4-6/8 hemiola at breakneck tempo under a high, declamatory copla voice.
items.description: Música llanera is the cattle-country repertoire of the Orinoco floodplain, sung in strophic coplas over harp-cuatro-maracas trios and given national profile in Venezuela and eastern Colombia by mid-century radio. Its markers are the extremely fast right-hand harp bordón, the percussive cuatro strum that carries both chord and pulse, dry capacho maracas articulating the hemiola, and a strained high tenor delivery with long held notes and contrapunteo improvised verse duels. It is broader than the dance form joropo alone, taking in slow pasajes and unaccompanied cattle-calling tonadas de ordeño.

items.name: Gaita zuliana
items.lineage: Christmas-season protest and devotional dance-song of Maracaibo and Zulia state, Venezuela, commercialized from the 1960s by groups such as Cardenales del Éxito and Maracaibo 15, driven by the friction drum furro, tambora, scraped charrasca and cuatro at a brisk 4/4 with dense unison choruses alternating with a soloist's topical verses to the Virgin of Chiquinquirá.
items.description: Gaita zuliana is Maracaibo's seasonal music, flooding Venezuelan airwaves from October through Epiphany with topical, often sharply political verses set against devotional refrains. The core sound is the barking furro friction drum on the downbeat, tambora and charrasca filling the offbeats, cuatro chording throughout, and a massed male chorus answering a lead singer in short, shouted phrases. Despite the shared Spanish-Caribbean root it is unrelated to the Colombian gaita flute traditions and far denser and more choral than llanera or joropo.

items.name: Cuatro venezolano (solo concert tradition)
items.lineage: Solo and small-ensemble concert repertoire for the four-string Venezuelan cuatro, lifted from accompaniment to art instrument by Fredy Reyna from the 1950s and extended by Cheo Hurtado and Jorge Glem, using re-entrant A-D-F#-B tuning, thumb-and-finger charrasqueo strum with muted rasgueo, and joropo, vals and merengue caraqueño forms at hemiola-heavy 3/4 and 5/8.
items.description: The Venezuelan cuatro began as a strummed accompaniment engine for joropo and gaita, but a solo literature grew around it after Fredy Reyna's mid-century recordings recast the instrument as a melodic and harmonic voice. Modern players combine damped percussive strums with plucked counterpoint, extended jazz voicings and the characteristic 3/4-against-6/8 displacement of the merengue caraqueño and vals venezolano. Recorded close and dry with a small-diaphragm pair, it is far more transparent and chamber-like than the ensemble llanera or gaita contexts the instrument grew out of.

items.name: Porro
items.lineage: Colombian Caribbean savanna dance form from Sucre and Córdoba, carried both by rural banda pelayera brass and by 1940s-60s Barranquilla and Medellín orquestas on Discos Fuentes, marked by a 2/4 cut-time bombo-and-redoblante pulse, clarinet-led melody over trumpets and bombardino, and the bozá section where brass riffs answer the drums.
items.description: Porro is the brass-band dance music of Colombia's Sabana region, existing in a rural banda pelayera form built on bombo, redoblante, platillos and massed winds, and an urban big-band form arranged for saxes and trumpets by orquestas from Barranquilla and Medellín. Its identity rests on the clarinet's high obbligato line, the bombo player striking both head and shell, and the alternation of the danza-like first section with the riff-driven bozá. Compared to cumbia it is faster, more strictly duple and almost entirely instrumental.

items.name: Folclor afrocolombiano (Pacific and Atlantic Afro-Colombian folklore)
items.lineage: Afro-descendant ritual and festive repertoire of Colombia's Pacific littoral (Chocó, Cauca, Nariño) and Atlantic coast, documented from the 1960s by Delia Zapata Olivella and later by Petronio Álvarez festival ensembles, built on marimba de chonta ostinati, cununo and bombo cross-rhythms, guasá shakers and interlocked female chorus over currulao's 6/8 and bullerengue's hand-drum 2/4.
items.description: This is the collective label for Colombia's Afro-descendant village traditions: Pacific currulao, juga and arrullo built around the palm-wood marimba de chonta and cununo drums, and Atlantic-coast bullerengue, chalupa and lumbalí carried by hand drums and unaccompanied female chorus. The music is overwhelmingly cyclic and responsorial, with singers entering in overlapping call-and-response over a fixed percussion interlock and no harmonic movement. Field recordings capture it outdoors in patios and funerary wakes rather than in the arranged, chord-based settings of coastal commercial cumbia or porro.

items.name: Música costeña (Colombian Caribbean coastal popular)
items.lineage: Umbrella commercial idiom of Colombia's Caribbean coast consolidated between the 1940s and 1970s by Discos Fuentes and Codiscos in Cartagena, Barranquilla and Medellín, joining accordion-and-caja conjuntos with saxophones and electric bass across cumbia, paseo, puya and porro at a mid-tempo 4/4 with guacharaca scrape and llamador on the offbeat.
items.description: Música costeña names the recorded coastal sound of Colombia rather than a single rhythm: the label output that fused rural accordion conjuntos, gaita flute ensembles and urban dance orchestras into a portable 45-rpm idiom exported across Latin America and West Africa. Its signature is the accordion or sax carrying melody over guacharaca and a two-drum alegre-llamador bed, with electric bass added from the 1960s and a warm, mid-forward Fuentes tape sound. It is broader than vallenato, which is one of its constituent repertoires, and more studio-shaped than the outdoor Afro-Colombian folklore that feeds it.

items.name: Champeta (Colombian Caribbean picó style)
items.lineage: Cartagena and Palenque dance style born when 1970s-80s picó sound systems spun imported Congolese soukous and highlife, then localized from the late 1980s by Viviano Torres and Louis Towers into a 4/4 style with cascading single-coil guitar seben lines, syncopated bass, timbal-and-conga kit patterns and shouted Spanish-Palenquero lyrics.
items.description: Champeta grew out of Cartagena's picó culture, where enormous painted sound systems built local followings on African imports whose labels were scratched off to protect exclusives, and the response was homegrown records in the same rhythmic mould. The mature style pairs a bright, ringing lead guitar derived from Congolese seben with hard-panned programmed drums, a heavy sub bass and a hectoring vocal alternating chorus hooks with picó shout-outs. It is more African-guitar-driven and less clave-bound than cumbia or salsa, and its digital-era champeta urbana form leans further toward reggaeton and dancehall production.

items.name: Chicha (Peruvian Amazonian psychedelic cumbia)
items.lineage: Peruvian working-class cumbia hybrid formed circa 1968-1980 between Lima's Andean migrant barrios and the oil-boom Amazon towns of Pucallpa and Moyobamba, codified by Los Destellos, Juaneco y su Combo and Los Mirlos, joining Colombian cumbia's 4/4 güiro pattern to surf-fuzz Farfisa-and-guitar timbres and huayno-derived pentatonic melodies.
items.description: Chicha is what happened when the cumbia records circulating through Peru in the late 1960s met Andean migrant melody, Amazonian dance-band electric guitar and cheap spring reverb and fuzz. Tracks are typically instrumental or lightly sung, built on a two-guitar interlock with tremolo and delay, a Farfisa-style combo organ, timbales and güiro over a plain root-fifth bass, with melodies that fall into minor pentatonic huayno shapes rather than Colombian modal ones. Its rawer studio sound and Andean melodic accent distinguish it from Colombian cumbia and from later Lima technocumbia's synthesized production.

items.name: Música andina (pan-Andean folkloric)
items.lineage: Pan-Andean folkloric repertoire of highland Peru, Bolivia and Ecuador, consolidated as a stage and record idiom from the 1950s-60s by Los Kjarkas, Savia Andina and Los Chalchaleros-era conjuntos, joining quena and siku panpipe melodies, charango tremolo, bombo andino downbeat and duple huayno or slow 6/8 yaraví forms with paired-parallel vocal harmony.
items.description: Música andina covers the highland Quechua and Aymara song and dance repertoire — huayno, wayño, yaraví, sikuri panpipe ensembles, carnival tunes — as performed in village fiestas and as reworked for the twentieth-century conjunto stage. Its markers are breathy notched-flute quena tone, interlocking hocketed siku pairs where two players share one melody, fast charango tremolo strumming, and vocals in parallel thirds with a strained high placement. Field settings favour a thin outdoor acoustic and mixed ensemble balance, unlike the reverberant studio productions of nueva canción groups that draw on the same instruments.

items.name: Música andina chilena (Norte Grande / nueva canción Andean)
items.lineage: Andean-instrument repertoire of Chile's Norte Grande and its adoption by Santiago nueva canción groups from the mid-1960s — Violeta Parra's collecting, then Inti-Illimani, Quilapayún and Illapu — combining quena, zampoña, charango, bombo and guitar in arranged, harmonized settings of huaynos, trotes and cachimbos with political texts.
items.description: In Chile the Andean instrumentarium of the far north — quena, zampoña, charango, bombo — was carried south by folklorists and then made the signature timbre of nueva canción in the years around the Popular Unity government, with exile-era recording continuing in Europe after 1973. The style is arranged rather than traditional: fixed multi-part instrumental writing, blended choral harmony, guitar and tiple counterlines, and through-composed sections that abandon village cyclicity. That arrangement and its explicit political text set it apart from the Peruvian-Bolivian huayno practice it borrows its instruments from.

items.name: Chilena (Costa Chica)
items.lineage: Dance-song of the Costa Chica of Guerrero and Oaxaca, Mexico, seeded by Chilean and Peruvian sailors passing through Acapulco during the 1850s gold-rush traffic and localized among Afro-mestizo communities, performed by guitar-and-violin conjuntos or wind bandas in a fast 6/8-against-3/4 sesquialtera with coplas, zapateado footwork and shouted interjections.
items.description: The chilena is the Costa Chica's regional descendant of the Chilean-Peruvian cueca/zamacueca, absorbed on the Pacific coast of Guerrero and Oaxaca in the nineteenth century and now inseparable from Afro-mestizo fiesta life there. It is sung in short rhyming coplas over a sesquialtera guitar strum, with violin or requinto ornamenting between verses and, in the banda version, trumpets and tuba carrying the same figures at dance-hall volume. Compared with the Chilean cueca it is faster, less handkerchief-formalized and harmonically simpler, and compared with the neighbouring son jarocho it is more strophic and less improvisatory.
exemplars: Los Cotorros de la Costa Chica

items.name: Tonada chilena
items.lineage: Central-Chilean strophic song of the countryside, documented and reshaped from the 1940s-60s by Margot Loyola and Violeta Parra, sung solo or in parallel thirds by women over rasgueado guitar in a 6/8-3/4 hemiola at moderate tempo, with pandero tambourine and hand claps and a closing repeated coda phrase rather than a refrain.
items.description: The tonada is the sung, non-danced counterpart to the cueca in central Chile's rural repertoire: lyric, devotional or seasonal texts carried by one or two female voices in thirds over a guitar playing the sesquialtera rasgueo, sometimes with pandero and clapping. Its structural fingerprint is the coda or 'despedida' tacked onto each strophe rather than a chorus, and its free-ish opening guitar introduction. Violeta Parra's collected and original tonadas became the foundation of Chilean nueva canción, but the traditional form is quieter, unaccompanied by Andean winds and closer to Spanish parlour song than to the highland repertoire.

items.name: Música Mapuche
items.lineage: Ceremonial and social music of the Mapuche people of the Araucanía region of southern Chile and Neuquén in Argentina, documented ethnographically from the late nineteenth century onward and carried unbroken through the ngillatun and machitún rites — built on the machi's kultrun, a shallow shamanic frame kettledrum struck in a steady duple pulse against wada gourd rattles and pifilka whistles, with narrow-range, heavily glissando'd solo singing (ül) and the long trutruka horn braying over the top, all at slow processional walking tempo.
items.description: The ritual and social music of the Mapuche of southern Chile and southwestern Argentina, still practiced at ngillatun harvest-renewal ceremonies and machi healing rites and recorded ethnographically since the early twentieth century. Its sound is austere: the kultrun's dry, damped duple beat, wada rattles, pifilka whistles blown in interlocking pairs, and unaccompanied ül singing with a range of a few tones, heavy portamento and speech-inflected delivery. Unlike Andean highland music to the north, it has no panpipe consorts, no charango or European string borrowings, and no harmonic accompaniment at all; the pitch material is narrow and untempered rather than pentatonic-melodic.

items.name: Folklore Chileno
items.lineage: The codified rural song-and-dance repertory of central Chile — cueca, tonada, refalosa, sajuriana — collected and professionalized from the 1940s by Violeta Parra, Margot Loyola and the Cuncumén and Huasos Quincheros ensembles, marked by cueca's 6/8-against-3/4 hemiola strummed on guitar and arpa, tambourine and handclaps, brisk 120-140 BPM dance tempo, and parallel-thirds duet singing in a bright, nasal chest register.
items.description: Chile's national folkloric repertory, gathered from the central valley countryside and standardized for stage and record between the 1940s and 1960s by Violeta Parra, Margot Loyola and the Chilean Folklore Society. Cueca dominates it — a courtship dance in a sung 6/8 that constantly slips into 3/4, driven by guitar rasgueo, harp, tambourine, handclaps and shouted interjections — alongside the slower, lyric tonada. It differs from Andean folklore to the north in its Iberian string basis and absence of panpipes, and from the later nueva canción chilena, which took this material as raw source and rewrote it with political texts and Andean instrumentation.

items.name: Polca Paraguaya
items.lineage: Paraguay's national dance form, crystallized in the late nineteenth century after the Triple Alliance war from European polka rhythms reworked in Guaraní-speaking bandsmanship and codified on record by José Asunción Flores' contemporaries and by Luis Alberto del Paraná from the 1950s — a fast 6/8 melody riding a 3/4 accompaniment (sesquiáltera), 120-160 BPM, arpa paraguaya arpeggiating over strummed guitar, with paired tenor voices in parallel thirds singing bilingual Spanish-Guaraní texts.
items.description: The dominant Paraguayan dance-song genre, formed in the late 1800s and carried worldwide by touring trios from the 1950s. Its signature is sesquiáltera: a melody phrased in 6/8 over an accompaniment felt in 3/4, so the beat continuously reinterprets itself, played fast and bright with the diatonic Paraguayan harp filling every gap with cascading arpeggios. It is faster and more metrically ambiguous than the guarania, the slow lyrical form invented by José Asunción Flores from the same material, and unlike the Venezuelan joropo it is percussion-free, relying on harp and guitar alone for drive.
exemplars: Luis Alberto del Paraná y Los Paraguayos

items.name: Arpa Paraguaya (Paraguayan Harp Tradition)
items.lineage: The solo and lead tradition of the Paraguayan diatonic harp, descended from Jesuit mission harps of the seventeenth-century Guaraní reductions and rebuilt in the twentieth century as a light 36-38 string cedar instrument played with fingernails, virtuosically codified by Félix Pérez Cardozo in the 1930s-40s and by Digno García and Luis Bordón after him — right-hand tremolo and glissando figuration over left-hand 3/4 bass in polca and galopa, with showpiece programmatic imitations such as Pájaro Campana.
items.description: The instrumental art of the Paraguayan harp, a fingernail-plucked diatonic instrument with no pedals, tuned by hand-levers or by retuning between pieces. Repertoire centers on polcas, galopas and guaranias arranged for the harp as lead voice, with a dense right-hand tremolo, sweeping glissandi and rapid arpeggio filigree over a bass that swings between 3/4 and 6/8. Distinct from the Venezuelan arpa llanera, which is percussive, tuned differently, and locked into a maraca-and-cuatro ensemble; the Paraguayan style is legato, ornamental and often solo.

items.name: Folklore Paraguayo
items.lineage: Paraguay's broader traditional repertory — polca, galopa, chamamé-adjacent rasguido, the danza de la botella, and above all the guarania invented by José Asunción Flores in 1925 — sung in bilingual Guaraní-Spanish and performed by harp-and-guitar conjuntos with paired parallel-third voices, spanning slow rubato guaraniás around 60-70 BPM to fast sesquiáltera dances above 130 BPM.
items.description: The national traditional-music complex of Paraguay, unusual in Latin America for being sung largely in an Indigenous language, Guaraní, by a mestizo population rather than a separate Indigenous minority. It couples the fast polca paraguaya with the guarania, a slow, melancholic ballad form devised by José Asunción Flores in 1925 by stretching polca rhythm into a lyrical 6/8, both scored for harp, guitars and close two- or three-part male vocal harmony. Where the polca record is bright and dance-driven, the wider folklore repertory foregrounds lament and rural nostalgia, and it stays free of the drums and horns that define neighbouring Brazilian and Argentine folk forms.

items.name: Folklore Boliviano
items.lineage: The Aymara and Quechua highland music of Bolivia, staged and recorded as national folklore from the 1960s by Los Jairas, Ernesto Cavour and Gilbert Favre in La Paz peñas — huayño in a driving 2/4 around 120 BPM and slow yaraví laments, with siku panpipe consorts played in interlocking hocket pairs, quena, charango tremolo, bombo andino on the downbeat, and high, tight, nasal unison or parallel-fifth singing.
items.description: The Andean highland tradition of Bolivia, rooted in Aymara and Quechua community ensembles of the altiplano and reformatted for concert and record in 1960s La Paz. Its core rhythm is the huayño, a stamping 2/4 with a long-short melodic cell, played by siku panpipe troupes whose two halves alternate notes so no player sounds a complete melody, plus quena, charango and bombo. Compared with Peruvian huayno it favours larger breath-driven panpipe consorts, rougher airy tone and community-wide participation, and it lacks the harp-and-violin mestizo layer that dominates Peru's central sierra.

items.name: Folklore Ecuatoriano
items.lineage: The mestizo and Kichwa traditional music of the Ecuadorian sierra — sanjuanito's insistent 2/4 stomp at around 110-130 BPM, the slower albazo and yumbo, and the elegiac pasillo in 3/4 — codified on record from the 1930s onward by duos such as Dúo Benítez-Valencia and by Otavalo Kichwa ensembles, scored for rondador and quena over strummed guitar and requinto, with plaintive parallel-third duet singing in a high male register.
items.description: Ecuador's highland traditional repertory, split between the Kichwa-community sanjuanito — a minor-pentatonic dance in a hammering 2/4 driven by rondador panpipe and bombo — and the mestizo pasillo, a slow waltz-derived song of loss carried by guitar, requinto and two close-harmony voices. Julio Jaramillo's mid-century recordings made the pasillo an international lament style. It is gentler and more song-centred than Bolivian folklore, with smaller panpipes played by one performer rather than interlocking consorts, and it keeps a stronger Iberian guitar and bel-canto vocal inheritance.

items.name: Folklore Venezolano
items.lineage: The traditional music of Venezuela's llanos and coast — joropo llanero above all, a fast 3/4 sesquiáltera at 130-180 BPM built from fixed harmonic corridos and golpes, with arpa llanera or bandola llanera taking the lead, cuatro strumming a percussive four-string chord chop, capachos maracas playing a continuous rustling subdivision, and shouted, high-register contrapunteo singing improvised in rhyming décimas.
items.description: Venezuela's national folkloric complex, centered on joropo llanero from the cattle plains shared with eastern Colombia, plus coastal Afro-Venezuelan tambor drumming and the Andean bambuco-adjacent repertory of the west. Joropo runs on a hemiola between 3/4 and 6/8 at very high tempo, with harp or bandola improvising over cyclic golpe patterns while cuatro and maracas supply an almost continuous rhythmic wash and singers trade improvised décimas in duel form. Unlike Paraguayan harp music it is percussive, maraca-locked and competitively improvised rather than lyrical and legato.

items.name: Folklore Panameño
items.lineage: The traditional music of the Panamanian interior provinces of Herrera, Los Santos and Veraguas — the mejorana, a five-string guitar accompanying sung décimas and the socavón; the tamborito, a call-and-response women's song over three hand drums in a brisk 2/4; and cumbia panameña with accordion, violin, churuca scraper and tambor, all danced at village patronal festivals and codified for stage from the 1940s.
items.description: The rural festival music of Panama's central provinces, performed at tunas, patron-saint fiestas and the Azuero carnival. Three strands define it: the tamborito, in which a lead woman singer trades short cyclic phrases with a female chorus over caja and two hand drums and dense handclapping; the mejorana, a small five-course guitar accompanying sung décimas and the shouted saloma; and the accordion-and-violin cumbia panameña with its churuca scraper. It is faster and more drum-forward than Colombian cumbia, and its vocal core is female chorus response rather than a solo singer with brass.

items.name: Folklore Uruguayo
items.lineage: Uruguay's traditional repertory joining the pampa's guitar forms — milonga and cifra sung over a syncopated 2/4 ostinato — with Afro-Uruguayan candombe from Montevideo's Barrio Sur conventillos, whose three drums chico, repique and piano play interlocking clave-anchored patterns behind carnival comparsas, codified in song by Alfredo Zitarrosa, Los Olimareños and Rubén Rada from the 1960s.
items.description: The traditional music of Uruguay, defined by two distinct lineages that twentieth-century songwriters fused. From the countryside come milonga and cifra, guitar-accompanied narrative songs over a lurching 2/4 bass ostinato; from Montevideo's Black neighbourhoods comes candombe, a drum tradition of three tuned barrel drums whose interlocking parts and rolling madera stick pattern power the carnival llamadas. Alfredo Zitarrosa's grave baritone over four guitars typifies the first; Rubén Rada's candombe-beat songcraft the second. It is separated from Argentine folklore by candombe's presence and by the milonga's darker, slower delivery.

items.name: Huapango
items.lineage: The son of the Huasteca region of northeastern Mexico, formed in the eighteenth-nineteenth centuries from Spanish fandango and local mestizo practice and standardized on record from the 1940s — a fast sesquiáltera alternating 6/8 and 3/4 at roughly 120-150 BPM, with an improvising violin taking the lead between sung coplas, jarana and quinta huapanguera supplying strummed chords and bass, and two men trading verses in a piercing falsetto-break delivery.
items.description: The dance-song of Mexico's Huasteca, played by a three-piece string trio for zapateado dancers stamping on a wooden tarima that functions as the ensemble's percussion. Its defining features are the sesquiáltera swing between 6/8 and 3/4, extended improvised violin passages between vocal coplas, and a vocal style that breaks abruptly into falsetto at phrase peaks. Huapango huasteco is leaner and more improvisatory than the orchestrated huapango arrangements mariachi groups later adopted, and unlike son jarocho it centres a violin rather than a harp and requinto.

items.name: Trío Huasteco
items.lineage: The standard performing ensemble of the Huasteca — violin, jarana huasteca and quinta huapanguera — professionalized in Mexico City recording studios from the 1940s by groups such as Trío Armonía Huasteca and Los Camperos de Valles, in which the violinist improvises florid double-stopped variations over a fixed son harmony while the two guitarists split rasgueo and bass roles and alternate falsetto-broken vocal coplas.
items.description: The instrumental format that carries huapango huasteco: one violin plus jarana huasteca and the deeper five-string quinta huapanguera, with all three members singing. The violinist's role is virtuosic and improvised, spinning new variations on the son's fixed cycle each time through, while the huapanguera's low strummed bass line and the jarana's off-beat chop create the ensemble's characteristic dry, treble-forward rattle. Recorded catalogues from Mexican labels in the 1940s-60s fixed the repertory of sones such as El Querreque and La Petenera; the trío is distinguished from mariachi by its lack of trumpets, harp and guitarrón and by its improvisational rather than arranged conception.

items.name: Son Mexicano (Mexican Son)
items.lineage: The family of regional Mexican string-band dance forms descended from the seventeenth-century Spanish son and fandango — son jarocho in Veracruz, son jalisciense in the mariachi heartland, son huasteco, son calentano and son istmeño — sharing sesquiáltera 6/8-3/4 metre, cyclic harmonic cells with improvised coplas, communal zapateado stamping on a tarima, and locally distinct rosters from jarana and requinto jarocho to vihuela, guitarrón and violins.
items.description: The umbrella tradition of Mexican regional string-band dance music, formed across New Spain from the 1600s onward and still the basis of mariachi, fandango jarocho and huapango. All its branches share a rhythmic engine of alternating 6/8 and 3/4, short repeating chord cycles, improvised or traded sung coplas, and dancers' zapateado on a resonant wooden platform as the percussion. What varies is the roster and dialect: harp, requinto and jaranas with son montuno-like call-and-response in Veracruz; vihuela, guitarrón, violins and later trumpets in Jalisco; violin trio in the Huasteca. It differs from Caribbean son cubano, with which it shares a name, in metre, instrumentation and Iberian rather than African-derived rhythmic organization.

items.name: Tololoche norteño
items.lineage: Northern Mexican and Texan conjunto practice formed in Nuevo León, Tamaulipas and the Rio Grande valley in the 1930s–50s, in which the tololoche — a three-quarter-size slapped upright bass — supplies the walking-and-slapped two-beat under diatonic button accordion and bajo sexto at 90–130 BPM in polka, redova and vals rhythms, with paired parallel-third male vocals delivered plainly and loudly.
items.description: The pre-drumkit norteño conjunto sound, built on the slapped tololoche upright rather than the electric bass and tarola that displaced it from the 1960s onward. Its markers are the percussive bass slap standing in for a drummer, dry accordion bellows articulation, and bajo sexto strummed on the offbeat. Compared to modern norteño it is thinner, faster-decaying and more rhythmically exposed, and compared to Tejano conjunto it stays closer to the Mexican polka repertoire.

items.name: Tamborazo zacatecano
items.lineage: Rural wind-and-drum band tradition of Zacatecas and Jalisco codified in the late nineteenth century out of village municipal bands, in which two or three clarinets and trumpets carry the melody over trombone and tuba bass while a single huge double-headed tambora, struck with a mallet on one head and a stick on the shell, drives 2/4 marches and 3/4 valses outdoors at ceremonial volume with shouted gritos.
items.description: A loud, unamplified processional band music from the Zacatecas highlands played at saints' feasts, weddings and funerals, named for the tambora that dominates its texture. It differs from banda sinaloense in its smaller roster, its harsher clarinet-led melodic writing and its lack of a vocalist in much of the repertoire, and from mariachi in having no strings at all. Intonation is deliberately wide and the ensemble plays essentially flat-out from start to finish.

items.name: Banda guanajuatense
items.lineage: Wind-band tradition of the Bajío state of Guanajuato consolidated after the 1870s municipal-band expansion, using a compact roster of clarinets, two trumpets, alto horn or trombone and tuba with tambora and platillos, playing sones abajeños, valses, marchas fúnebres and polkas at village fiestas in 2/4 and 3/4 with a lighter, more song-derived phrasing than the Sinaloan bandas.
items.description: The Bajío's regional wind band, smaller and softer than Sinaloan banda, keeping a repertoire of sones abajeños and processional pieces tied to the Guanajuato religious calendar. Its identity comes from clarinet-doubled melody in thirds, a tuba playing simple root-fifth rather than the aggressive Sinaloan countermelody, and a much lower dynamic ceiling. It is more likely to be heard in funeral cortèges and church processions than at dances.
exemplars: Banda de Viento Los Hermanos Vargas

items.name: Banda de viento (Mexican wind band)
items.lineage: Umbrella Mexican brass-and-reed band tradition seeded by nineteenth-century military and municipal band reforms under Maximilian and the Porfiriato, standardized on clarinets, cornets or trumpets, alto horns, trombones, tuba, tambora and platillos, playing marchas, valses, pasodobles and sones at 2/4 and 3/4 with the tuba supplying a bass line that later became the harmonic engine of every regional banda style.
items.description: The generic Mexican wind band from which banda sinaloense, tamborazo and the Bajío bandas all descend, still active as a civic and ceremonial ensemble across the country. Its sound is defined by written parts rather than improvisation, European march and waltz forms filtered through local sones, and a tuba bass instead of any string bass. Unlike its commercial descendants it is usually instrumental and reads from parts, giving it a stiffer, more bandstand character.
exemplars: Banda de Música del Estado de Michoacán

items.name: Norteño-sax
items.lineage: Monterrey and Tamaulipas variant of norteño consolidated in the 1950s–70s when alto and tenor saxophone were added to or substituted for the button accordion, giving a conjunto of sax, bajo sexto, electric bass and drum kit playing polkas, huapangos norteños and cumbias at 100–140 BPM with breathy, heavily-vibratoed saxophone lines doubling the vocal in thirds.
items.description: A norteño subvariant in which saxophone rather than accordion carries the instrumental hook, associated with the Linares and Monterrey scenes and with the huapango norteño repertoire. The sax plays with a wide slow vibrato and slurred lower-register phrasing that gives the music a warmer, more legato character than accordion norteño's staccato bellows attack. It sits between conjunto norteño and Tejano orquesta without adopting the latter's horn-section arrangements.
exemplars: Ramón Ayala y sus Bravos del Norte

items.name: Corridos bélicos
items.lineage: Militarized narco-corrido strain that emerged in Sinaloa, Michoacán and Guerrero in the mid-2000s and hardened through the 2010s, sung over tuba-and-charchetas banda or a guitar-tololoche-requinto conjunto at 80–120 BPM in 3/4 vals and 2/4, with gunfire and radio-chatter samples, chanted gritos naming commanders, and a declamatory shouted-tenor vocal that abandons the older corrido's narrative distance for first-person boasting.
items.description: The most aggressive branch of the corrido, built around cartel enforcement narratives and circulated primarily through YouTube and streaming rather than radio, which largely bans it. Sonically it is marked by heavily compressed loud tuba, sampled weapon and vehicle sound effects, and a strained, near-shouted vocal recorded close on a dynamic mic. It differs from corridos tumbados in rejecting trap drums and R&B phrasing, staying with acoustic banda and conjunto instrumentation played at maximum intensity.

items.name: Corridos alternativos
items.lineage: Melancholic Mexican-American offshoot of the corrido that surfaced around 2020–2022 in Southern California and Texas among bedroom-producing teenagers, slowing the requinto-led sierreño trio to 70–95 BPM, drenching nylon-string lead and doubled vocals in reverb and delay, borrowing bedroom-pop and emo chord motion, and replacing narco narrative with first-person heartbreak sung in a soft, breathy, close-miked head voice.
items.description: A sad-boy reinvention of the sierreño corrido made by young US-born Mexican-Americans, where the form's requinto arpeggios and tololoche pulse remain but the subject matter and vocal manner come from bedroom pop. The recordings are quiet, reverb-heavy and vocally intimate, the opposite of corridos bélicos' compressed shout. It also stays acoustic where corridos tumbados add 808s and trap hi-hats.

items.name: Conjunto de arpa grande
items.lineage: Tierra Caliente tradition of Michoacán and southern Jalisco documented from the late nineteenth century, in which a large diatonic arpa grande plays bass and melody while a player drums the tapping rhythm on its soundbox, joined by two violins, vihuela and guitarra de golpe in fast 6/8 sones and jarabes with hemiola cross-accent and high, tightly-pitched shouted vocals.
items.description: The regional string ensemble of Michoacán's hot lowlands, defined by the arpa grande functioning simultaneously as bass, melody instrument and drum through the tamboreo struck on its body by a second player. Violins trade improvised variations over cyclic son forms while the vihuela and guitarra de golpe hold the 6/8 against 3/4 cross-rhythm. It is the direct ancestor of mariachi but retains the harp that mariachi discarded for trumpets, and never adopted brass.
exemplars: Beto Pineda y su Conjunto de Arpa Grande

items.name: Marimba mexicana (Chiapas)
items.lineage: Chiapanecan marimba tradition consolidated in Chiapa de Corzo and Tuxtla Gutiérrez after the 1890s invention of the chromatic marimba doble by the Nandayapa and Borraz families, pairing a large marimba grande and smaller requinta played by four to six mallet players in parallel thirds and sixths over a double bass and light trap kit, in danzón, vals, son chiapaneco and bolero at moderate tempos.
items.description: The Mexican branch of the Central American marimba, centered on Chiapas and largely instrumental, with multiple players sharing one or two large gourd- or box-resonated keyboards. Its signature is dense parallel-interval voicing across the full range with a warm buzzing resonator timbre from the tela membranes. Compared with Guatemalan marimba it leans harder on Mexican salon repertoire — danzón, vals, bolero — and less on the son chapín.

items.name: Marimba orquesta
items.lineage: Guatemalan and Chiapanecan dance-band format that emerged in the 1930s–50s when marimba doble ensembles added saxophones, trumpets, trombone, double bass and drum kit to play foxtrot, danzón, cumbia, bolero and merengue for urban ballrooms, keeping the marimba's four-to-eight-mallet block chords as the rhythmic core while the horns supply riffs and the kit a straight dance backbeat.
items.description: The commercial dance-orchestra form of the Central American marimba, distinguished from the pure marimba pura ensemble by its full horn section and drum kit and from a standard Latin big band by keeping the marimba as lead voice. Repertoire is international ballroom and tropical dance rather than folkloric son. Vocals appear on cumbias and boleros but much of the book is instrumental.

items.name: Marimba de Guatemala
items.lineage: National instrumental tradition of Guatemala running from the colonial-era gourd-resonated marimba de tecomates through the nineteenth-century marimba sencilla to Sebastián Hurtado's 1894 chromatic marimba doble, played by three to seven mallet players sharing one or two keyboards in sones chapines, guarimbas and the anthem-like 'Luna de Xelajú', with mirliton-buzzed cedar keys and steady 6/8 or 3/4 pulse.
items.description: Guatemala's declared national instrument and its associated repertoire, spanning indigenous Maya highland ceremonial use and ladino urban salon pieces. The characteristic sound comes from tuned wooden box or gourd resonators fitted with pig-gut or membrane mirlitons that add a nasal buzz to every note, plus the physical presence of several players standing at one instrument. It differs from marimba orquesta in having no horns or kit, and from the orchestral concert marimba in tuning practice, resonator design and rolled block-chord idiom.
exemplars: Marimba de Concierto de Bellas Artes

items.name: New Tejano
items.lineage: Post-1990 South Texas revitalization of Tejano music led from San Antonio and Corpus Christi, blending the accordion-and-bajo-sexto conjunto core with DX7-era synth pads, slap electric bass, programmed and live drums, and cumbia rather than polka as the default groove at 95–110 BPM, with polished bilingual lead vocals and pop-song forms modeled on contemporary US radio production.
items.description: The 1990s commercial peak of Tejano, when the genre briefly crossed into the US mainstream with major-label budgets and gloss. Its markers are the accordion mixed as a pop hook rather than a folk signifier, glossy chorused synth pads, gated snare or programmed kit, and cumbia-based grooves replacing the older polka. It splits from traditional conjunto in production values and from Tejano orquesta in dropping the big horn charts for keyboards.

items.name: Nuevo folklore mexicano
items.lineage: Art-song reinterpretation of Mexican regional repertoire that took shape in Mexico City and Oaxaca from the late 1990s through the 2010s, in which conservatory- and rock-trained songwriters rebuild son jarocho, huapango, bolero ranchero and Oaxacan folk material with jarana and requinto alongside chamber strings and sparse studio production, at slower tempos, in through-composed forms, with restrained close-miked vocals in place of the traditional shouted delivery.
items.description: A curatorial, songwriter-led rereading of Mexican folk traditions aimed at urban and international audiences, closer to chamber pop than to any village practice. It keeps the instrumental colors — jarana, requinto, harp, marimba — but rearranges them with harmonic substitutions, dynamic shaping and audiophile recording that the source traditions do not use. It is distinct from son jarocho revival groups in prioritizing the individual authored song over communal fandango participation.

items.name: Mexican Traditional (Son y Canción Mexicana)
items.lineage: The umbrella of regional Mexican string-and-voice repertoires — son jalisciense, son huasteco, son jarocho, canción ranchera — consolidated between the late colonial period and the 1930s-50s XEW radio and Peerless/Musart record era, built on 6/8-against-3/4 sesquiáltera hemiola, zapateado footwork on a wooden tarima, close two-voice falsete harmony, and a plucked-string core of vihuela, guitarrón, harp, jarana and violin, with the mariachi trumpet added only after 1930s broadcasting demanded it.
items.description: The core regional song traditions of Mexico, formed across the nineteenth century from Spanish string practice, indigenous and African rhythmic layers, and codified commercially by Mexico City radio and the Peerless/Musart labels from the 1930s onward. Its signature is sesquiáltera — 6/8 melody riding 3/4 accompaniment — with strummed vihuela mánico, walking guitarrón bass on the strong beats, and paired vocals in parallel thirds pushed to a shouted falsete break. It differs from the norteño and tejano border traditions in having no accordion or bajo sexto, and from banda in being a string ensemble rather than a wind ensemble.

items.name: Música Purépecha
items.lineage: The song and ensemble music of the Purépecha (Tarascan) people of the Meseta and Lake Pátzcuaro region of Michoacán, whose central form is the pirekua — a slow 3/4 or 6/8 strophic love-and-protest song in Purépecha language sung in close parallel thirds by two or three voices over nylon-string guitar and vihuela, expanded since the late nineteenth century into the orquesta purépecha of clarinets, trumpets and saxophones and recognized by UNESCO in 2010.
items.description: Indigenous Michoacán music centred on the pirekua, a lyrical strophic song in the Purépecha language carried by pireris (singer-composers) and traditionally performed at fiestas, weddings and community assemblies. The texture is unhurried: a lilting 3/4 or 6/8 pulse, guitar and vihuela arpeggios, and two tightly blended voices in parallel thirds with almost no percussion. Unlike mariachi son from neighbouring Jalisco it avoids hemiola drive and trumpet fanfare, and unlike Oaxacan banda it keeps the ensemble small and string-led even when the orquesta version adds winds.

items.name: Música Mixteca
items.lineage: The wind-band and waltz tradition of the Mixteca region spanning Oaxaca, Guerrero and Puebla, formed after mid-nineteenth-century military bandmasters and church maestros seeded reed-and-brass instruction in Mixtec villages — its repertoire runs from the chilena in 6/8 with hemiola to the sentimental 3/4 vals (Alfredo Colín's 1912 'Canción Mixteca' becoming its anthem), played by community bandas de viento of clarinets, trumpets, trombones, tuba and bass drum at patron-saint fiestas and funerals.
items.description: The village banda de viento music of the Mixteca highlands, taught by ear and by hand-copied parts within municipal bands that sustain fiestas, processions and funerals across Oaxaca and Guerrero. Chilenas in 6/8 with cross-rhythmic hemiola sit alongside slow waltzes and dirges, with clarinets carrying the melody, trumpets answering, tuba walking the bass and a bass drum marking the frame. It is distinguished from Sinaloan banda by its slower, more processional and often funereal repertoire and its Mixtec-language song adaptations, and from mariachi by the total absence of strings.
exemplars: Banda de Música del Estado de Oaxaca
Banda Filarmónica de San Juan Mixtepec

items.name: Música Wixárika (Huichol)
items.lineage: The ceremonial and social music of the Wixárika (Huichol) of the Sierra Madre Occidental in Jalisco and Nayarit, comprising the shaman-mara'akame's long night-long chanted narrations accompanied by the tepu log drum and the xaweri/kanari — a locally built miniature violin and five-string guitar pair — whose 'minuete' dance pieces run in a bright 3/4 with fast bowed ostinati at peyote and maize ceremonies, unnotated and transmitted entirely by apprenticeship.
items.description: Ceremonial music of the Wixárika people, split between the mara'akame's hours-long sung recitation of ancestral journeys over a single skin-headed log drum and the instrumental xaweri-and-kanari duo that plays cyclic 'minuetes' for dancing. The homemade violin is small, high and buzzy, tuned by ear rather than to a fixed standard, and the guitar supplies a scrubbing rhythmic drone rather than functional harmony. It differs from mestizo Mexican son in having no bass instrument, no hemiola architecture and no commercial repertoire, and from Native American Church peyote song in retaining European-derived string instruments.
exemplars: Cantos Huicholes de Nayarit (INAH field recordings)

items.name: Música Indígena Mexicana
items.lineage: The collective pre-Hispanic-descended and syncretic musics of Mexico's indigenous peoples — Nahua, Maya, Zapotec, Otomí, Rarámuri, Totonac and others — documented systematically by the INAH and INI from the 1960s onward, spanning conch-trumpet and clay-flute ceremonial signalling, teponaztli/huehuetl slit-and-skin drum patterns for danza, and post-conquest string and wind adaptations, with vocal delivery ranging from narrow-range ritual chant to festival song in indigenous languages.
items.description: An umbrella for the ceremonial and community music of Mexico's indigenous nations, most of it functional — tied to agricultural cycles, patron-saint days, danza de concheros, healing and mortuary rites. The sonic signature is cyclic repetition over a single drum or drum pair, aerophones of clay, cane and shell used as signals rather than melody carriers, and singing in indigenous languages with limited melodic range. It differs from mestizo Mexican traditional music in its absence of European harmonic function and from Andean indigenous music in its drum-and-shell rather than panpipe orientation.
exemplars: Antología del Son de México (Discos Corasón)
INAH Testimonio Musical de México series
Danza de los Concheros de la Gran Tenochtitlan

items.name: Merengue Típico (Perico Ripiao)
items.lineage: The rural accordion merengue of the Cibao valley in the Dominican Republic, formed in the late nineteenth century when the German-imported diatonic button accordion displaced the string tres and codified by mid-twentieth-century players such as Ñico Lora and Tatico Henríquez — a fast 2/4 with the tambora's driving pa'l medio and jaleo patterns, the guira's continuous scraped sixteenths, an interlocking accordion right-hand ostinato, and shouted, nasal call-and-response vocals.
items.description: The countryside form of Dominican merengue, played by a three-to-five-piece conjunto built around a diatonic accordion, double-headed tambora struck with hand and stick, and metal güira. Tempos routinely exceed 160 BPM, the jaleo section spins a two-chord vamp indefinitely under accordion and saxophone improvisation, and the vocal is a hoarse, forward-placed shout trading with a chorus. It is distinguished from the orchestrated merengue de orquesta of Johnny Ventura and Wilfrido Vargas by its accordion lead, absent horn section arrangements and rougher, faster feel.

items.name: Perreo
items.lineage: The dance-floor core of Puerto Rican reggaeton, named for the grinding dance that emerged in early-1990s San Juan marquesinas and caserío parties and codified on DJ Playero and DJ Nelson underground mixtapes before Luny Tunes' 2000s productions standardized it — 90-100 BPM Dem Bow riddim with the 3+3+2 kick-snare tresillo, filtered synth bass, sparse minor-key melodic loops, and chanted, mid-register call-and-response vocals aimed squarely at the dance.
items.description: Perreo is the rhythm-first, explicitly dance-directed strand of reggaeton that took shape in San Juan's underground cassette scene around 1993-1996 and never abandoned the Dem Bow loop as its organizing principle. Productions stay near 95 BPM with a dry, tight kick-snare tresillo, one repeated minor synth or sampled hook, and vocals that alternate a chanted hook with short rapped verses. Compared to the pop-facing reggaeton of the 2010s it uses fewer chords, less sung melody and a harder, drier drum balance, and compared to Dominican dembow it is slower and rounder in the low end.

items.name: Bomba (Puerto Rico)
items.lineage: Afro-Puerto Rican drum-and-dance tradition rooted in seventeenth- and eighteenth-century sugar-plantation communities of Loíza, Mayagüez, Ponce and Santurce, sustained by families such as the Cepedas and Ayalas — a call-and-response song over two or more barriles de bomba, with the buleador drums holding the sicá, yubá or holandés rhythm, a cuá stick pattern on the drum shell, maraca, and the lead subidor drummer improvising in direct dialogue with a single dancer's piquetes.
items.description: Bomba is the oldest documented Afro-Puerto Rican music, a batey circle in which a soloist's call is answered by a fixed chorus while barrel drums hold one of roughly a dozen named rhythms. Its defining feature is the inversion of the usual dancer-musician hierarchy: the lead subidor drummer follows and marks the dancer's improvised gestures rather than the reverse. It is distinct from plena in having no melodic instruments, no pandereta frame drums and no topical newspaper-style narrative, and from Cuban rumba in its barrel drum construction and dancer-led cueing.

items.name: Bomba y Plena
items.lineage: The paired-repertoire ensemble practice that fused Puerto Rico's two Afro-descendant folk forms into a single performance and recording format from the 1950s onward, driven by Rafael Cortijo y su Combo with Ismael Rivera bringing barril and pandereta patterns into a horn-and-conga dance band — sets alternate sicá-based bomba numbers with duple plena refrains, joined by shared call-and-response chorus practice and the same barrio lyric register.
items.description: The combined stage and studio presentation of bomba and plena, standard in Puerto Rican folkloric groups and on the island's mid-century dance records. A single ensemble covers both idioms: barriles and cuá for the bomba rhythms, graduated panderetas and güiro for the plena, with cuatro or horns added for melodic material. It is not a third genre so much as a programming convention, and it is what distinguishes commercially recorded folklórico groups from the strictly separate community batey and street-plena contexts.
exemplars: Cortijo y su Combo con Ismael Rivera

items.name: Música Jíbara
items.lineage: The mountain peasant music of Puerto Rico's interior, descended from Andalusian and Canarian song brought in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries and codified on record from the 1930s-50s by Ramito and Chuíto el de Bayamón — built on the seis and aguinaldo in duple and triple metres, sung as improvised décimas in ten-line espinela rhyme with a high nasal tenor, over strummed cuatro puertorriqueño, guitar, bordonúa, güiro and maracas.
items.description: Música jíbara is the rural Hispanic-descended song tradition of Puerto Rico's central highlands, associated with the jíbaro smallholder and preserved through Christmas parranda, velorio and trovador competition. The trovador improvises décimas on a given topic in real time over a fixed seis melody while the cuatro answers each vocal phrase with rapid double-course fills. Compared with bomba and plena it is European in harmony and melodic contour with minimal percussion, and compared with Cuban punto guajiro it centres the ten-string cuatro rather than the tres.

items.name: Cuatro Puertorriqueño (Instrumental Tradition)
items.lineage: The instrumental art tradition built on Puerto Rico's national instrument — a five-double-course chordophone standardized in its modern form in the late nineteenth century and raised to virtuoso solo status by Ladislao Martínez and Yomo Toro in the mid-twentieth century — featuring rapid plectrum tremolo and cascading scalar runs over seis and aguinaldo forms, danzas, and later boleros and salsa sessions, taught by apprenticeship and now by conservatory method.
items.description: The solo and lead-instrumental practice of the Puerto Rican cuatro, which grew out of accompaniment to jíbaro song into a repertoire of concert pieces, danzas and showcase seis variations. Its sonic hallmarks are the doubled steel courses played with a plectrum, sustained tremolo on long notes, and fast diatonic runs answered by a guitar-and-bass rhythm section. It differs from música jíbara proper by removing the improvising décima singer and placing the instrument itself in the foreground, and from the Venezuelan cuatro tradition, which is a four-string strummed rhythm instrument rather than a plucked melodic one.

items.name: Kompa Gouyad
items.lineage: Haitian dance-band style that crystallized in Port-au-Prince and the Haitian diaspora (Miami, New York, Montreal) through the late 1990s and 2000s, slowing classic konpa to roughly 88-110 BPM over a hip-swiveling 'gouyad' (grind) groove built on a syncopated tanbou/kit pattern with a heavy snare-and-hi-hat push, a repeated clean single-coil guitar arpeggio, a walking-melodic electric bass, sustained synth pads and a lead vocal that alternates crooned Kreyol verses with call-and-response 'chante pwen' choruses.
items.description: Kompa gouyad is the slow-grind branch of Haitian konpa that took shape in the diaspora dance circuit from the late 1990s onward, tailored to close partner dancing rather than the brisker carnival tempos of classic kompa direk. Its signature is a hypnotic mid-tempo groove: dry syncopated drum kit doubled by hand tanbou, a looping clean guitar figure, warm sustained synth pads and long-breathed Kreyol vocals. Against Nemours-era kompa it is slower, more keyboard- and studio-shaped, and far less horn-driven; against zouk it keeps the Haitian tanbou accent and Kreyol ayisyen phrasing.

items.name: Twoubadou (Haitian guitar-and-accordion ballad)
items.lineage: Haitian acoustic song tradition formed in the early twentieth century when cane-cutters returning from Cuba brought the son/trova guitar idiom home, settling into a moderate 2/4 meringue-derived lilt carried by strummed nylon guitar, piano accordion, a plucked bass or tanbou, maracas and a scraped guiro, with paired male voices singing bawdy, satirical or sentimental Kreyol lyrics in close harmony.
items.description: Twoubadou is Haiti's acoustic troubadour song, descended from Cuban son brought back by migrant sugar workers and settled into a Haitian meringue lilt. Small ensembles of nylon guitar, accordion, hand drum and shaken percussion back one or two singers whose Kreyol texts run from ribald double entendre to lament and social commentary. It differs from konpa by being acoustic, small-group and lyric-driven, and from Cuban trova by its meringue rhythmic accent and Haitian Kreyol prosody.

items.name: Raboday
items.lineage: Port-au-Prince street-carnival electronic style that emerged in the 2000s and dominated Haitian youth dance music through the 2010s, taking the fast rara/petwo percussion cell out of the street band and rebuilding it in software at roughly 105-125 BPM as looped tanbou samples, hard programmed kick and hand-clap, cheap synth stabs and shouted, often obscene Kreyol MC vocals traded over a two-bar cycle.
items.description: Raboday is Haiti's laptop-made carnival music, translating the drum batteries of rara and vodou petwo rhythm into looped samples, distorted kicks and thin synth stabs produced on cheap home rigs and circulated by MP3 and sound truck. Vocals are shouted, chant-like and deliberately crude, built for street processions and block parties rather than radio. Against rara it is electronic, fixed-tempo and MC-fronted; against konpa it discards harmony and melody almost entirely in favour of percussive drive.

items.name: Rara
items.lineage: Haitian Lenten processional music from the rural Artibonite and Cul-de-Sac plains, documented from the nineteenth century and tied to vodou societies, in which bands walk the roads between Ash Wednesday and Easter playing interlocking single-note bamboo vaksin trumpets and tin cornets in hocket over tanbou and cylindrical drums, adja bells, scraped iron and conch, with a chorus answering a lead singer's Kreyol pwen in fast duple time.
items.description: Rara is the Lenten walking-band music of rural and peri-urban Haiti, sponsored by vodou societies and moving through villages on foot during Holy Week. Its defining sound is hocketed vaksin: stopped bamboo tubes each sounding one pitch, locking into an interlocking melody over layered hand drums, struck iron and clattering bells, with sung and shouted Kreyol commentary. Unlike Trinidadian carnival music it is unamplified, single-pitch-per-instrument and religiously framed; unlike raboday it is wholly acoustic and processional.
exemplars: Rara La Belle Fraicheur de l'Anglade
Alan Lomax Haitian Diary field recordings

items.name: Nyahbinghi
items.lineage: Rastafarian ritual drumming and chanting codified in Kingston's Wareika Hills camps in the 1950s by Count Ossie and the Mystic Revelation of Rastafari out of Burru and Kumina drum practice, using a three-drum battery — bass drum struck on one and three, mid-range funde holding a steady two-beat pulse, and an improvising akete repeater — under slow modal chanting of psalms and Rasta hymns at roughly 60-80 BPM.
items.description: Nyahbinghi is the ceremonial drum-and-chant music of Rastafari, played at grounations and formalized by Count Ossie's Wareika Hills community in 1950s Kingston. Three drums stratify the groove: a heartbeat bass drum, a metronomic funde and a soloing akete repeater, over slow congregational chanting of psalms and hymn melodies. It is the rhythmic ancestor of reggae's one drop but stands apart from it in having no bass guitar, no chord instruments and a devotional rather than commercial function.
exemplars: Count Ossie and the Mystic Revelation of Rastafari
Ras Michael and the Sons of Negus

items.name: Early Reggae (1968-1972)
items.lineage: Jamaican style that appeared in Kingston studios around 1968 as rocksteady accelerated, driven by producers Lee Perry, Bunny Lee and Joe Gibbs and the Upsetters and Hippy Boys bands, marked by a bubbling organ shuffle, scratchy quaver guitar chops on the offbeat, a busy melodic bass, a snapping one-drop or four-beat kit at roughly 85-100 BPM, and vocal-group or DJ toasting over cheaply cut mono mixes for the sound systems.
items.description: Early reggae, also called skinhead reggae, is the brief transitional phase between rocksteady and roots reggae in Kingston from 1968 to about 1972. Faster and more manic than rocksteady, it foregrounds a chattering organ shuffle and rapid double-time guitar chops over a bass line that has become the lead melodic voice, all cut fast and cheap for sound-system release. It lacks the deep, slow one-drop and Rasta lyricism of the roots era that followed, and the horn-led swing of ska that preceded it.
exemplars: Toots and the Maytals, Pressure Drop
The Pioneers, Long Shot Kick De Bucket
Dave and Ansel Collins, Double Barrel

items.name: Traditional Ska (early-60s instrumental)
items.lineage: Jamaican style codified in Kingston between 1960 and 1966 by the Skatalites and the studio bands of Clement Dodd and Duke Reid, welding mento and American jump-blues shuffle into a fast 2/4 at 130-160 BPM with a walking upright or electric bass, a hard piano-and-guitar chop on the upbeat, a swinging shuffle kit, and long modal-jazz horn lines from Don Drummond's trombone and Tommy McCook's tenor.
items.description: Traditional ska is the first-wave Jamaican dance music of the early 1960s in its instrumental, horn-led form, played by session players steeped in bebop and Caribbean mento. The rhythm section stamps an emphatic offbeat chop against a walking bass and shuffling kit while trombone and tenor saxophone carry extended, often minor-modal melodies and take real solos. It is distinguished from vocal ska by the absence of a fronted singer, and from later 2-Tone revivals by its jazz phrasing, tape-era mono mixes and slower harmonic turnover.

items.name: Jamaican Ska (vocal sound-system style)
items.lineage: Vocal branch of Jamaica's first-wave ska, cut for Kingston sound systems between 1961 and 1966 by producers Coxsone Dodd, Duke Reid and Leslie Kong, pairing the same 140-plus BPM upbeat chop and shuffle kit with American-influenced close-harmony vocal trios and belting solo singers, boogie piano, and short punchy horn riffs answering the vocal line rather than carrying it.
items.description: This is the sung side of Jamaican ska as it circulated on dubplate and 45 through the island's sound systems in the first half of the 1960s. Harmony trios and solo shouters sing gospel- and doo-wop-derived lines over the genre's stamping upbeat guitar chop, boogie piano and shuffling kit, with horns reduced to short riffing punctuation. Where Skatalites-era instrumental ska builds around jazz soloing, this branch is song-form, chorus-led and cut for maximum impact on a single mono speaker stack.
exemplars: The Maytals, Six and Seven Books of Moses

items.name: Old School Dancehall (early-1980s Kingston)
items.lineage: Jamaican style that emerged in Kingston dancehalls around 1979-1984 as roots reggae receded, built by producers Henry Junjo Lawes and Linval Thompson with the Roots Radics at Channel One and Volcano, slowing the tempo to a stark 'rockers-to-rub-a-dub' 70-90 BPM with a dry gated kit, an enormous minimal bass line, sparse skank guitar and deejays like Yellowman toasting and singers chanting over recycled Studio One riddims.
items.description: Old school dancehall is the rub-a-dub music of early-1980s Kingston, made when the Roots Radics stripped roots reggae to a slow, dry, bass-dominated skeleton and producers recycled classic riddims under deejays and singjays. The mixes are spare and heavily gated, with the bass carrying nearly all the harmonic information and the vocal front and centre in slack or boastful patois toasting. It precedes the fully digital ragga of Sleng Teng onward, and differs from roots reggae in its secular, competitive lyricism and near-total loss of horn and harmony-vocal layers.

items.name: Dancehall Queen (1990s digital ragga dance style)
items.lineage: Jamaican dancehall strain built around the 1990s Kingston female dance scene and the 1997 film of the same name, running fully digital riddims from Steely and Clevie, Dave Kelly and Bobby Digital at 90-105 BPM with sampled kick-and-snare grids, staccato synth bass, brittle sampled percussion, and stacked female or duet vocals over 'juggling' riddims cut for competitive dance-floor performance.
items.description: Dancehall queen names the 1990s Jamaican dancehall aesthetic organized around female dancers and singers competing in the yard sessions, and by extension the hard digital riddims cut for them. Riddims are wholly sequenced: sharp programmed kick and snare, clipped synth bass, and metallic sampled percussion supporting bright, rhythmically aggressive female vocal delivery. It differs from 1980s rub-a-dub by its machine-tight grid and higher tempo, and from later reggaeton by keeping the one-drop-derived Jamaican riddim rather than the dembow cell.

items.name: Zimdancehall
items.lineage: Zimbabwean adaptation of Jamaican dancehall that formed in Harare's Mbare ghetto studios around 2010-2012 through producers Levels, Oskid and the Chillspot Records crew, running riddim-based digital productions at 95-110 BPM with programmed kick-snare grids, deep synth bass, and rapid Shona-and-English chatting delivered in a patois-inflected accent over communal 'riddim albums' released for free download.
items.description: Zimdancehall is Zimbabwe's dominant youth music since the early 2010s, made in small Harare township studios that release shared riddims voiced by dozens of chanters. Productions are entirely in-the-box: hard programmed drums, sub-heavy synth bass, sparse melodic stabs, and vocals that mix Shona, Zimbabwean street slang and imitated Jamaican patois. It follows the Jamaican riddim-economy model closely but is distinguished by Shona-language wordplay, local topical lyricism, and occasional imported hosho or mbira-derived melodic figures.

items.name: Vincy Soca
items.lineage: Soca variant developed in St Vincent and the Grenadines from the 1990s onward around the Vincy Mas carnival calendar, favouring very fast power-soca tempos of roughly 155-175 BPM with driving four-on-the-floor kick, snare rolls into the drop, bright synth brass stabs, iron and cowbell patterns, and hoarse commanding lead vocals issuing jump-and-wave instructions in Vincentian dialect.
items.description: Vincy soca is the St Vincent branch of the Eastern Caribbean soca circuit, built for the Vincy Mas road and for the regional power-soca competition season. It runs at the fastest end of soca tempos, with a relentless four-on-the-floor kick, rolling snare fills, clattering iron, synthetic brass hits and shouted call-and-response commands. Against Trinidadian soca it leans harder on power tempos and crowd-instruction lyrics rather than groovy soca's mid-tempo winein feel, and against Bajan soca it is rougher-edged and less melody-driven.

items.name: Bajan Soca
items.lineage: Barbadian soca style shaped around the Crop Over festival since the 1980s and codified by Square One, Krosfyah and later producers such as Nicholas Brancker and Stiffy's circle, mixing 130-155 BPM soca grooves with the local 'ragga soca' and bashment-soca accents, live or sampled horn sections, tuk-band snare-and-bass-drum inflections, and melodic sung hooks alongside chanted crowd calls.
items.description: Bajan soca is the Barbadian carnival music of Crop Over, running from the live horn-band sound of Square One and Krosfyah in the 1990s to today's bashment-soca productions. It keeps a strong melodic and harmonic profile — real or sampled horn sections, sung choruses, richer chord movement — over a soca kick-and-iron groove that often carries the local tuk band's marching snare accent. Compared with Vincy power soca it sits at lower tempos and prizes hooks over shouted commands, and compared with Trinidadian soca it retains a distinct ragga-soca vocal inflection.

items.name: Grenada Soca
items.lineage: Grenadian branch of soca consolidated from the late 1970s Spice Mas carnival circuit and codified by Ajamu, Mr Killa, and Lil Natty & Thunda, running 145-165 BPM over a four-on-floor kick with heavy offbeat iron and jab-jab tempo-drop breaks, brass or synth-brass stabs, and hoarse shouted lead vocals delivering call-and-response ramajay commands to a road crowd.
items.description: Grenada soca is the Spice Isle variant of Trinidadian soca, distinct since the 1980s and dominant in Caribbean road-march competition since the 2010s through Mr Killa and Lil Natty & Thunda. It runs faster and rawer than Trinidad power soca, foregrounds the jab-jab devil-mas aesthetic with clanking chain-and-iron percussion, abrupt tempo drops, and shouted rather than sung lead vocals aimed at instructional crowd choreography. Where Trinidadian groovy soca leans melodic and mid-tempo, Grenadian soca is built almost entirely for the jouvert road at 150+ BPM with minimal harmonic movement.

items.name: Trinibad
items.lineage: Trinidadian street-rap style that emerged around 2018 in Port of Spain and Laventille as a local reworking of Jamaican trap-dancehall, codified by Rebel Sixx, Prince Swanny, and Jahllano over 95-105 BPM programmed 808 kicks, rolling triplet hats, minor-key synth or plucked-guitar loops, and half-sung Trinidadian Creole vocals detailing gang and hardship narratives.
items.description: Trinibad formed in Trinidad and Tobago from roughly 2018 as young producers and deejays adapted Jamaican trap-dancehall to local speech and local subject matter. It is sparse: long sub-808 kicks, skittering triplet hi-hats, one repeating minor loop, and a semi-melodic Trinidadian Creole toast whose diction rather than rhythm marks it as Trinidadian. It differs from Jamaican trap-dancehall in accent and slang, and from soca entirely in tempo, drum feel, and its refusal of carnival celebration.

items.name: Steelpan (Trinidad steel orchestra)
items.lineage: Trinidadian idiom born in 1930s-40s Laventille and Port of Spain when tamboo bamboo bands were replaced by tuned oil-drum idiophones, codified by Ellie Mannette, Winston 'Spree' Simon, and Bertie Marshall into the modern steel orchestra of tenor, double-second, guitar, cello and bass pans backed by an engine-room of iron, scratcher and drum kit, playing calypso and arranged concert works at Panorama.
items.description: The steel orchestra is Trinidad's national ensemble form, developed from the 1940s out of banned skin-drum and tamboo-bamboo processions using discarded oil drums sunk and tuned into chromatic instruments. A full band of eighty to over a hundred players stacks tenor pans on melody, double-seconds and guitar pans on strumming inner harmony, cello and bass pans on the low line, with an engine room of brake iron, scratcher and kit driving the pulse; the tone is bright, harmonically rich and heavily beating from the pans' inharmonic partials. Unlike carnival soca it is largely instrumental and closely arranged, with Panorama arrangements notated or drilled by rote over months.

items.name: Dennery Segment
items.lineage: Saint Lucian dance style that emerged around 2013-2015 out of the fishing village of Dennery, codified by Motto, Subance, and Ricky T over 100-115 BPM programmed patterns that graft dancehall kick-and-snare placement onto soca's offbeat iron, with sparse synth-brass stabs, a thin repeated melodic hook and terse Kwéyòl chants rather than sung verses.
items.description: Dennery segment formed in Saint Lucia in the mid-2010s and became the island's carnival sound, exported through Motto and Subance to the wider Antilles and to French-Caribbean shatta. Its signature is a dancehall-derived kick and snare under soca's offbeat metallic pattern at a slower tempo than Trinidadian power soca, with extremely reduced harmony, a single looping synth motif and clipped Kwéyòl vocal chants. It is distinguished from soca by the halved tempo and dancehall drum grid, and from shatta by its Saint Lucian Kwéyòl delivery and comparatively dry, brass-tinged production.

items.name: Zouk
items.lineage: Guadeloupean-Martinican dance music codified in Paris in 1984 by Kassav' (Pierre-Édouard Décimus, Jacob Desvarieux, Jocelyne Béroard), fusing gwo ka and biguine rhythmic cells with Haitian kompa's guitar and Dominican cadence-lypso into a 120-130 BPM machine-driven groove featuring DX7 electric-piano pads, slap or synth bass, staccato horn hits, and multi-tracked Kréyòl lead-and-chorus vocals.
items.description: Zouk was assembled in Paris studios by Antillean migrant musicians in the early 1980s, with Kassav's Yélélé and Zouk Is the Only Medicine We Have setting the template. It is defined by drum-machine and sequenced production, bright FM keyboard chords, a percussive guitar chank inherited from kompa, punchy arranged horn lines and richly stacked Kréyòl choral harmony. It differs from Haitian kompa by faster tempo and fully electronic rhythm section, and from the later zouk love ballad style by its uptempo carnival drive.

items.name: Zouk Riddim
items.lineage: French Antillean and Cape Verdean-diaspora producer style of the 2010s, in which digital zouk instrumentals are built as reusable open riddims at 88-100 BPM around a half-time kick, a syncopated kompa-derived hi-hat shuffle, wide detuned pad chords and a heavy sub-bass, cut for multiple singers and deejays in the Paris-Pointe-à-Pitre studio circuit.
items.description: Zouk riddim names the 2010s practice, common across Guadeloupe, Martinique and the Cape Verdean and Angolan diasporas in Paris and Lisbon, of producing digital zouk backing tracks as shared riddims that multiple vocalists version. Tempos sit near half the classic zouk pulse, sub-bass carries the low end, and the kompa guitar chank is replaced by clipped synth plucks and slow chord pads. It is distinguished from 1980s zouk by its Jamaican-style riddim economy and sub-bass weight, and from shatta by staying romantic and mid-tempo rather than aggressive.

items.name: Shatta
items.lineage: Guadeloupe- and Martinique-centred dance style consolidated around 2014-2018 from Jamaican dancehall, Saint Lucian dennery segment and gwo ka accents, codified by Kalash, Jahyanaï and Bamby over 100-110 BPM tracks with a hard four-on-floor kick, offbeat iron and clave-like snare, minimal minor synth riffs, and shouted Kréyòl deejay vocals cut heavily with sirens and drops.
items.description: Shatta is the French Antilles' contemporary dancehall, taking shape in Guadeloupe and Martinique after 2014 and reaching France through Kalash and Jahyanaï. Its rhythm section is denser and more four-on-floor than Jamaican dancehall, with soca-derived offbeat metal, snapping snares on the offbeat, near-absent harmony and aggressive Kréyòl toasting punctuated by air-horn and rewind effects. It sits between dennery segment, from which it takes its drum grid, and Jamaican dancehall, from which it takes its vocal posture, while keeping a distinctly Antillean Kréyòl identity.

items.name: Gwoka
items.lineage: Guadeloupean drum-and-voice tradition formed among enslaved and post-emancipation Africans on the sugar plantations and codified as a seven-rhythm system (léwòz, kaladja, toumblak, graj, woulé, padjanbèl, mendé) played on goatskin ka drums, with a boula holding the base pulse, a makè improvising against the lead dancer, chacha rattle, and a call-and-response Kréyòl chantè answered by a répondè chorus and hand-clapping in the léwòz night circle.
items.description: Gwoka is Guadeloupe's core Afro-Creole drum tradition, continuous since the plantation era and inscribed by UNESCO in 2014, organised around seven named rhythms and performed in the léwòz circle where singer, drummers and dancer negotiate in real time. The boula drums lock a repeating cell while the makè lead drum answers the dancer's feet phrase by phrase; the chantè's Kréyòl calls are met by an unaccompanied répondè chorus over chacha and clapping. Unlike zouk it is entirely acoustic and improvisational, and unlike Haitian vodou drumming it is secular and organised around dancer-drummer dialogue rather than liturgy.

items.name: Kaseko
items.lineage: Surinamese Creole urban dance music that crystallised in Paramaribo in the 1930s-50s from kawina drumming, Dutch military brass bands and Trinidadian calypso, codified by Lieve Hugo and Max Nijman over a 2/4 groove driven by the booming skratji bass drum with cymbal, a rattling snare, and unison horn riffs supporting Sranan Tongo lead vocals with chorus responses.
items.description: Kaseko is Suriname's Afro-Creole popular music, formed in Paramaribo between the 1930s and 1950s and brought to a national and Dutch-diaspora audience by Lieve Hugo in the 1960s-70s. The sound is anchored by skratji, a large bass drum with mounted cymbal, played against a dry snare in a driving 2/4, with brass or saxophone riffs and Sranan Tongo call-and-response singing; later bands added electric bass, guitar and congas. It differs from calypso by its heavier drum-corps low end and Sranan Tongo lyrics, and from kawina by the addition of brass and Western harmony.

items.name: Musique Guadeloupéenne (biguine-mazouk salon tradition)
items.lineage: Guadeloupean Creole salon and ballroom repertoire of the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries — biguine, mazouk, valse créole and haute-taille — codified in Pointe-à-Pitre and in 1930s Paris recordings, played by clarinet lead with trombone counterline, banjo or guitar chording, string bass and chacha rattle in a lilting 2/4 or dotted 3/4 with heavily syncopated clarinet ornament.
items.description: This is the older Creole dance-orchestra music of Guadeloupe and its Paris diaspora, running from the 1890s bal salons through the 1930s Antillean cabarets of Montmartre and surviving today in revival ensembles. Its markers are a highly ornamented clarinet lead over a tailgate trombone counterline, banjo or guitar strum, plucked bass and chacha, in biguine's syncopated 2/4 and mazouk's swung triple metre. It is distinguished from Martinican biguine mainly by repertoire and local mazouk variants, and from later zouk by its acoustic wind-band instrumentation and European ballroom harmony.

items.name: Garifuna Folk Music
items.lineage: Ritual and social song tradition of the Garifuna of Belize, Honduras, Guatemala and Nicaragua, descended from the 1797 St Vincent exile and maintained in genres such as hunguhungu, paranda, wanaragua and the dügü ancestral ceremony, sung in Garifuna over primero and segunda skin drums, sisira shakers, turtle-shell strikes and, in paranda, an acoustic guitar, with a lead singer answered by a women's chorus.
items.description: Garifuna folk music is the ceremonial and communal repertoire of the Afro-Indigenous Garifuna, carried from St Vincent to the Central American coast after 1797 and inscribed by UNESCO in 2001. Its constants are a two-drum core of high primero improvising against a steady segunda, sisira gourd rattles, and a woman-led call-and-response in the Garifuna language; the paranda subgenre adds a Spanish-guitar accompaniment, hunguhungu a swaying triple pulse, and wanaragua a masked Christmas dance. It differs from neighbouring Afro-Caribbean drumming by its Arawakan-derived language and its women's-chorus foreground rather than an all-male battery.

items.name: Punta (Honduras Garifuna traditional)
items.lineage: Garifuna wake-and-celebration dance of the Honduran and Belizean coast, sung in Garifuna at a brisk 2/4 with the segunda drum holding a steady low pulse against the primero's improvised high strokes, sisira shakers, hand-clapping and a woman lead singer answered by chorus, the fertility-themed hip-driven dance performed at beluria wakes and at community festivals.
items.description: Punta is the best-known Garifuna dance rhythm, traditionally performed at beluria wakes on the Honduran and Belizean coast as an affirmation of life against death. Two drums carry it: a segunda locking a driving duple ostinato while the primero improvises against the dancer's hips, with sisira rattles, clapping and a woman's lead vocal in Garifuna answered by chorus. It is the acoustic ancestor of 1980s Belizean punta rock, and differs from that electrified form by its exclusively drum-and-voice texture and ceremonial context.

items.name: Old School Highlife (Ghana dance band era)
items.lineage: Ghanaian and Nigerian dance-band idiom of the 1940s-60s, grown from coastal palm-wine guitar and colonial brass bands and codified by E.T. Mensah's Tempos, Ramblers and Broadway Dance Band, built on a mid-tempo 4/4 with clave-inflected offbeat clips, gently rolling guitar arpeggios, unison trumpet-and-saxophone riffs, congas and claves, and relaxed Twi, Ga or Pidgin vocals with a light chorus.
items.description: Old-school highlife is the dance-band phase of Ghanaian highlife, dominant from the 1940s through the 1960s in Accra ballrooms and on Decca and HMV West African sessions, with E.T. Mensah and the Tempos as its central figures. It is defined by horn-section riffs shaped by Caribbean calypso and swing phrasing, a clean interlocking guitar line derived from palm-wine picking, conga and claves under a light kit, and easy conversational singing in Twi, Ga or Pidgin.
