items.lineage: Tagalog art song of the Philippines, folk in origin and elevated to concert form in the 1920s-30s by Nicanor Abelardo, Francisco Santiago and Francisco Buencamino, cast in a slow 3/4 that opens in the minor and modulates to the parallel major, with elevated Tagalog love poetry sung legato over piano or rondalla accompaniment and a strongly rubato, sentimental delivery.
items.description: The Philippine art song, a triple-metre love lyric whose formal signature is a minor-key opening resolving into the parallel major. Abelardo and Santiago transformed a rural courtship song into a conservatory genre with through-composed piano writing and trained bel canto delivery, though rondalla-accompanied popular versions remained current. Where the rondalla repertoire is ensemble-led and strophic, kundiman is soloistic, notated, rubato and text-driven.

items.name: Manila Sound
items.lineage: Mid-1970s Metro Manila pop movement launched by Hotdog's Ikaw Ang Miss Universe Ng Buhay Ko and Manila and carried by VST & Company, Cinderella, Rico J. Puno and Hagibis, blending soft-rock and disco-funk rhythm sections at 100-120 BPM with Taglish lyrics, sweet close-harmony backing vocals, clean single-coil guitar, Rhodes or clavinet comping, congas and occasional horn stabs, recorded on multitrack in Manila studios for the local label boom.
items.description: The commercial Manila pop style of roughly 1973-1980, the first mass-market Filipino-language pop wave. It runs on light soft-rock and disco grooves with clean electric guitar, electric piano, congas and glossy group backing vocals, and its lyrics mix Tagalog and English in a conversational, often comic register. It is distinguished from the concurrent Pinoy rock scene by its polish and dance orientation, and from kundiman by its urban vernacular text and full rhythm-section production.

items.name: Bisrock
items.lineage: Cebuano-language rock movement launched in Cebu City in the late 1990s and named around 2002 by Missing Filemon and the Bisrock compilations, applying alternative-rock and ska-punk arrangements — distorted humbucker guitar, driving 4/4 kit and electric bass at 130-170 BPM, shouted-to-sung Visayan vocals — to lyrics of local humour, protest and provincial identity, produced cheaply in Cebu and Davao project studios.
items.description: Cebuano-language rock centred on Cebu City from the late 1990s, a deliberate regional counterweight to Tagalog-dominated Manila pop-rock. Musically it is standard guitar-band alternative rock with ska and pop-punk inflections, cut in modest DAW-era studios, but the Visayan text and colloquial, often satirical delivery define it. It is rougher and cheaper-sounding than mainstream Pinoy rock and explicitly language-political in a way Manila Sound never was.

items.name: Luk Thung
items.lineage: Thai rural popular song named in the 1960s but shaped from the 1950s by Suraphon Sombatcharoen and later dominated by Pumpuang Duangjan and Sodsai Rungphothong, characterized by slow-to-mid tempos, heavy behind-the-beat phrasing, extravagant vocal vibrato and Thai-language ornamental slides, molam-derived khaen and phin colour beside Western horns, electric bass, kit and synth, and lyrics of village hardship and migration, spread nationally by the 1970s-80s cassette industry.
items.description: Thailand's rural popular song, the country's dominant working-class genre since the 1960s. Its markers are a dragging, deliberately delayed vocal placement, wide theatrical vibrato and heavy Thai melodic ornament, set against arrangements that mix brass and Western rhythm section with khaen and phin. Compared with molam it is slower, more song-form and more orchestrated; compared with Bangkok string pop it is pentatonic, ornamented and explicitly provincial in subject matter.

items.name: Molam
items.lineage: Lao-Isan sung poetry of northeast Thailand and Laos, traditionally performed by a mo lam expert declaiming rhymed klon verse in rapid syllabic patter against the free-reed khaen mouth organ, and modernized from the 1960s-70s into lam sing and the electrified molam band with phin lute, electric bass, kit and ching timekeeping, running fast anhemitonic pentatonic lines over a driving cyclic groove in the khaen's near-equal heptatonic tuning.
items.description: The sung-poetry tradition of the Lao-speaking Isan region, built on a virtuoso vocalist delivering rhymed verse in fast syllabic patter over the continuous drone-and-figure of the khaen. Its electrified form from the 1970s adds phin lute, bass and drums while keeping the pentatonic khaen mode, ching cymbal pulse and relentless cyclic drive. Unlike luk thung it is faster, more improvised and text-dense, closer to a bardic recitation than to a composed pop ballad.

items.name: Phleng Phuea Chiwit
items.lineage: Thai "songs for life" protest rock formed among Bangkok student activists around the 1973-76 uprisings and codified by Caravan and later Carabao, welding mid-tempo 4/4 folk-rock strumming and country-rock backbeats to Isan reed timbres (khaen, phin), plainspoken baritone lead vocals in unison group choruses, and lyrics on rural poverty, labor and dictatorship.
items.description: Phleng phuea chiwit emerged in Thailand in the mid-1970s as the soundtrack of the student left, initially acoustic and semi-clandestine, then arena-scaled in the 1980s under Carabao. Its signature is a Western folk-rock band chassis colored by Isan instruments — the free-reed khaen drone and the buzzing phin lute — under declamatory, grainy male vocals delivered close to speech. Unlike luk thung, which stays inside melismatic Thai popular-song phrasing and sentimental themes, songs-for-life keeps melody plain and subordinates it to text.

items.name: Thai Folk (Village Traditions)
items.lineage: Village song traditions of Thailand's Central, Northern and Isan regions — repartee genres such as lam klon, phleng choi and so phrae — carried by itinerant singers into the twentieth century and documented by mid-century field collectors, built on free-reed khaen drone-and-ostinato, plucked phin or sueng, hand-drum and ching cymbal timekeeping, and rapid syllabic call-and-response verse improvised over a single mode.
items.description: Thai rural song is regional and functional — courtship duels, harvest songs, ordination processions — rather than a single repertoire, and outside the court it uses roughly equidistant seven-tone tuning without fixed Western pitch. Texture is thin and cyclic: a khaen or fiddle sustains a modal drone while a solo voice spins improvised verse in fast syllabic patter, answered by a partner or the crowd. It differs from Thai classical piphat in having no fixed composition, no gong-circle ensemble, and no fixed instrumental hierarchy.

items.name: Thai Traditional (Piphat and Mahori)
items.lineage: Court and ceremonial ensemble music of Siam, formalized under Ayutthaya and Bangkok-era royal patronage and standardized in the early twentieth century by Luang Pradit Phairoh and the Fine Arts Department, using piphat (ranat xylophones, khong wong gong circles, pi nai quadruple reed, taphon and klong that drums) or mixed mahori with fiddles and khim, in stratified heterophony over a colotomic ching cycle and a seven-tone near-equidistant tuning.
items.description: Thai classical music organizes a fixed melodic skeleton into simultaneous variation: each instrument realizes the same tune at its own idiomatic density, the lead ranat ek in rapid octave tremolo, the khong wong yai in the plainer core version, with the ching hand cymbals marking the metric cycle and drums articulating the phrase. Tuning is roughly seven equidistant steps per octave, which places it audibly outside both Western temperament and Javanese pelog. Against Khmer pinpeat, which shares ancestry and instrument types, Thai practice is faster, more ornate on the xylophones, and more extensively notated by state conservatories.
exemplars: The Thai Fine Arts Department Orchestra

items.name: Khmer Court Music (Pinpeat)
items.lineage: Cambodian royal ceremonial and dance-accompaniment tradition traceable to Angkorian temple reliefs and maintained at the Phnom Penh palace until the Khmer Rouge, then rebuilt after 1979 by surviving masters such as Chek Mach and the Royal University of Fine Arts, scored for roneat xylophones, kong vong gong circles, the sralai quadruple reed and skor thom barrel drums in stratified heterophony over a chhing cymbal cycle.
items.description: Pinpeat is the loud ceremonial ensemble of Cambodia, played for masked lakhon khol and robam dance, temple ritual and royal occasion, with the sralai reed cutting over bright bronze gong-circles and hard-mallet xylophones. Its tuning is a roughly equidistant seven-tone system shared with Thai practice, and its texture is the same stratified heterophony, but tempos sit lower, the drum language is weightier, and repertoire is tied to dance-drama cues rather than concert suites. Post-1975 the tradition survives through a small number of transmitted lineages, making living masters unusually load-bearing.
exemplars: Royal University of Fine Arts Phnom Penh Pinpeat Ensemble

items.name: Cambodian Rock (Phnom Penh Psych)
items.lineage: Phnom Penh popular music of roughly 1963-1975, made by Sinn Sisamouth, Ros Serey Sothea, Pen Ran and Yol Aularong for radio and nightclub, grafting surf-reverb and fuzz guitar, combo organ, Farfisa-and-saxophone bandstand arrangements and a-go-go or slow-rock backbeats onto Khmer ramvong and romvong dance rhythms, with high, nasal, heavily ornamented Khmer vocal delivery on top.
items.description: Cambodian rock formed when American Forces radio and French yé-yé records reached Phnom Penh nightclubs, and it kept Khmer melodic ornament and vocal placement intact while borrowing wholesale from surf, garage and soul instrumentation. Recordings are dry-to-slapback, often small-room and lightly overdubbed, with organ and reverbed guitar sharing the top and horns arranged in unison stabs. What separates it from Thai string and Vietnamese kích động nhạc of the same years is the vocal line: intensely melismatic, high-set, and phrased against the beat rather than with it. The scene ended abruptly in 1975, and most of its principals were killed.

items.name: Cambodian Traditional (Village and Wedding)
items.lineage: Rural Khmer repertoires outside the court — the phleng kar wedding cycle, arak spirit-possession music, ayai sung repartee and the solo chapei dang veng bardic tradition — carried orally through village ceremony and codified in the late twentieth century largely through Kong Nay and post-genocide revival projects, built on chapei long-necked lute, tro fiddles, khim dulcimer, skor daey hand drum and chhing cymbals under speech-rhythm vocal narration.
items.description: Village Khmer music is small-ensemble and event-bound: the multi-movement phleng kar suite paces a three-day wedding, arak music summons healing spirits, and chapei dang veng is one man with a two-string lute improvising rhymed social commentary between instrumental refrains. Textures are sparse and heterophonic, fiddles and dulcimer trailing the singer, with cymbals rather than a drum kit holding time. Against pinpeat it is quiet, indoor, non-bronze, and improvisatory — the singer's text, not a fixed dance cue, drives the form.

items.name: Vietnamese Bolero (Nhạc Vàng)
items.lineage: Slow sentimental Vietnamese popular song crystallized in Saigon from the late 1950s through 1975 by writers such as Trúc Phương, Lam Phương and Trần Thiện Thanh, using the Latin bolero's slow duple pulse and dotted bongo-and-guitar rhythm under minor-mode, pentatonically inflected melodies, guitar phím lõm scalloped-fret bends, and a high, nasal, heavy-vibrato solo vocal; banned in the North after 1975 and sustained on cassette by the overseas diaspora.
items.description: Vietnamese bolero borrows the Cuban-by-way-of-Mexico bolero tempo and accompaniment pattern but sets it to Vietnamese-language melodies that lean on pentatonic contour and the vọng cổ tradition's ornamental sighs, most audibly in the scalloped-fret guitar's deep between-note bends. Arrangements stayed modest — nylon guitar, bass, brushed or light kit, later home-organ and synth pads on diaspora cassettes and Paris By Night video productions. Its nearest neighbour, tân cổ, folds the same songs into cải lương recitative; bolero proper keeps strophic verse-chorus form throughout.

items.name: Tân Cổ Giao Duyên
items.lineage: Southern Vietnamese hybrid form invented in Saigon in the early 1960s, credited to lyricist Viễn Châu, that alternates strophic modern popular song (tân nhạc) with the six-phrase vọng cổ recitative of cải lương theatre, accompanied by đàn tranh zither, đàn bầu monochord, đàn nguyệt moon lute and scalloped-fret guitar over free-breathing phrases that cadence together on the song bar with trống chầu punctuation.
items.description: Tân cổ is deliberately bilingual in musical idiom: a verse of Western-harmonized Vietnamese pop hands off, mid-track, to unmeasured vọng cổ, where the singer drifts ahead of and behind the accompanists until the whole ensemble lands together on the phrase-ending song beat. The instrumental writing is heterophonic and highly ornamented, with the đàn bầu's whole-tone pitch bends and the guitar's scalloped-fret vibrato imitating vocal inflection. It is distinguished from straight bolero by that recitative section and from full cải lương by having no staged drama around it.

items.name: Nhạc Thiếu Nhi
items.lineage: Vietnamese children's song repertoire built from the 1950s onward for schools, Young Pioneer organizations and state radio and television, composed by figures such as Phạm Tuyên and Hoàng Long, in bright major keys and simple duple or 6/8 meters, sung by unison children's choir over piano, accordion, glockenspiel and later home-keyboard backing, with short strophic forms and didactic, patriotic or animal-themed texts.
items.description: Unlike inherited nursery rhymes, nhạc thiếu nhi is largely a composed and institutionally distributed body of songs, taught in classrooms and broadcast, with named authors and printed sheet music. Its sound is deliberately clean and legible: unison or simple two-part children's voices, tonal Western harmony, tempos steady enough to march or clap to, and thin accompaniment that never obscures the words. Later commercial recordings replace the accordion-and-piano radio texture with preset keyboard and drum-machine backing, but the melodic and formal simplicity is unchanged.

items.name: Kayōkyoku
items.lineage: Mainstream Japanese popular song of roughly 1950-1990, produced by label-and-agency systems (Nippon Columbia, Victor, Watanabe Productions) with composers such as Hachidai Nakamura and Kyōhei Tsutsumi, joining Western pop and jazz-orchestra arranging — full string sections, brass, drum kit, electric bass — to yonanuki pentatonic melody, sentimental strophic AABA forms and a controlled, vibrato-forward solo vocal at mid-tempo.
items.description: Kayōkyoku is the broad postwar Japanese hit-song category from which enka and later J-pop separated, and its defining sound is a lush arranged backing — strings, horn section, electric rhythm section, occasionally shamisen for period color — supporting a single foregrounded vocalist recorded close and compressed. Melodies favor the yonanuki pentatonic scales, giving even fully tonal arrangements a distinctly Japanese contour. Against enka, kayōkyoku is lighter, more jazz- and Western-pop-derived, and less committed to the heavy kobushi vocal ornament; against city pop it is more orchestral and less funk-inflected.

items.name: Ryūkōka
items.lineage: Japanese popular song of the Taishō and early Shōwa eras, roughly 1914-1945, spread by Nippon Victor and Columbia shellac discs and composers such as Masao Koga and Shinpei Nakayama, mixing Western salon-orchestra scoring — violin, mandolin, accordion, Hawaiian steel guitar, light brass — with yonanuki minor melodies and a restrained, throat-forward vocal delivery over slow waltz, foxtrot and duple march tempos.
items.description: Ryūkōka is the first mass-mediated Japanese popular song, born with electrical recording, radio and the record industry, and audible today through the bandwidth-limited midrange of 78rpm shellac. Arrangements are chamber-scale — a handful of strings, reeds and plucked instruments, often with no drum kit at all — behind a single vocalist whose delivery sits between shinnai narration and Western light-opera singing. It is the direct ancestor of both kayōkyoku and enka, differing from them in its thinner, pre-amplified ensemble and its unmistakably prewar salon-orchestra harmony.

items.name: Min'yō
items.lineage: Japanese regional folk song — work, festival, dance and celebration repertoires such as Esashi Oiwake, Sōran Bushi and Tsugaru jongara — transmitted orally by locality, then standardized in the twentieth century through iemoto teaching lineages, NHK broadcast and contest culture, sung with strong nasal-forward tone and kobushi ornament over shamisen, shakuhachi, shinobue and taiko, some pieces in free unmeasured rhythm and others in strict festival duple.
items.description: Min'yō divides sharply between free-rhythm songs, where the shamisen or shakuhachi trails a singer stretching phrases at will, and metrical bon-odori and festival songs locked to taiko and hand-clapping. Vocal production is tight, high and nasal, with kobushi — rapid pitch flicks around the melody note — as the central expressive device, and scales are usually anhemitonic yo or hemitonic in scale depending on region. Compared with enka, which imported kobushi into composed pop, min'yō keeps the anonymous, locality-bound repertoire and the sparse plucked-and-drum accompaniment intact.

items.name: Denpa-kei
items.lineage: Japanese otaku-culture song style crystallized around 2000s bishōjo-game and doujin circles (I've Sound, Momoi Halko, Under17), built on very fast 150-190 BPM four-on-the-floor or happy-hardcore kicks, saturated FM and supersaw synth stacks, chopped vocal samples and rapid modulating chord loops beneath a deliberately childlike, hyper-high, nonsense-syllable vocal delivered with exaggerated affect.
items.description: Denpa-kei — named for the slang for someone receiving strange radio waves — is a deliberately overloaded, cognitively noisy style associated with visual-novel theme songs, Akihabara idol acts and Nico Nico doujin releases. Its markers are extreme tempo, dense layered synth leads with near-constant modulation, abrupt structural cuts, and vocals pitched and processed into a cartoon register with heavy retuning. Where anison and J-pop retain conventional song pacing, denpa maximizes stimulus density and treats intelligibility as optional.

items.name: Oshare kei
items.lineage: Bright, candy-colored offshoot of Japanese visual kei that crystallized in Osaka and Tokyo indies venues circa 2001-2003 around bands on the Peace & Smile Committee and Indie PSC circuit, trading gothic black for pastel layered hair, plastic accessories and polka dots while musically leaning on 170-200 BPM pop-punk and emo eighth-note downstrokes, bubblegum major-key choruses, gang-vocal 'oi' backings and high nasal boyish lead vocals over chorus-drenched clean guitar verses and octave-riff bridges.
items.description: Oshare kei emerged in the early 2000s Japanese indies scene as the deliberately cheerful inverse of visual kei's gothic wing, keeping the elaborate costuming and makeup but discarding the minor-key theatricality. The sound is fast pop-punk and emo with major-key hooks, clipped downstroke guitars, brief synth stabs and a thin bright mix that favors vocal and cymbal top end. It differs from mainstream visual kei in tempo and mode, and from Western pop-punk in its high boyish vocal placement, key-change final choruses and heavy use of unison gang shouts.
exemplars: Ando Yuko / Antic Cafe circle releases

items.name: Shakuhachi (sankyoku ensemble repertoire)
items.lineage: Chamber practice in which the shakuhachi joined the koto-and-shamisen jiuta-sokyoku trio, displacing the bowed kokyu across the late Edo and Meiji periods (roughly 1830-1900) as Kinko-ryu and then Tozan-ryu players entered secular concert life, playing heterophonic lines that shadow and decorate the koto melody in the in-scale with meri-kari microtonal shading, at slow to moderate free-breathing tempi articulated by the koto's plectrum attacks rather than a drum.
items.description: Sankyoku is the three-part Japanese chamber ensemble of koto, shamisen and shakuhachi that became standard in the nineteenth century when the flute took over the kokyu's role. Texture is heterophonic rather than harmonic: all parts trace one melody, the koto supplying the metrical spine while the shakuhachi bends around it with meri-kari pitch inflection and breath noise, and a singer often carries the jiuta text. It is distinct from solo honkyoku in being metered, ensemble-bound, notated and secular rather than a Zen breathing discipline.

items.name: Tsugaru-jamisen
items.lineage: Percussive virtuoso shamisen style of the Tsugaru plain in Aomori, northern Honshu, developed from the 1870s by itinerant blind bosama beggar-musicians — Nitabo (Akimoto Nitaro) is the traditional founder — using the heavy futozao thick-necked instrument with a thick-skinned body struck rather than plucked by a large bachi, built on the fast triplet-driven Jongara-bushi, Yosare-bushi and Aiya-bushi tune families with extended improvised maebiki preludes and rough, forced min'yo vocal delivery.
items.description: Tsugaru-jamisen turned an accompanying instrument into a solo attack vehicle: the bachi strikes the skin as well as the strings, producing an audible drum thud under every note, and players compete in speed, dynamic contrast and improvised preludes. Repertoire centers on a handful of Tsugaru folk-song frameworks that function like blues heads, over which the soloist elaborates before the singer enters with a strained, high, heavily ornamented delivery. Compared with nagauta or jiuta shamisen it is louder, thicker-necked, rhythmically aggressive and improvisatory rather than notated.

items.name: Taiko (North American kumi-daiko)
items.lineage: Diasporic drum-ensemble tradition founded in California — San Francisco Taiko Dojo under Tanaka Seiichi in 1968, Kinnara Taiko at Senshin Buddhist Temple in Los Angeles in 1969, San Jose Taiko in 1973 — adapting Japanese kumi-daiko to Japanese-American identity work with wine-barrel-built nagado drums, choreographed full-body stances, shime-daiko keeping the ji base pulse under odaiko solos, unison kiai shouts and pieces built as sectional grooves at 100-160 BPM rather than festival-cycle accompaniment.
items.description: North American taiko began in 1960s California as a Japanese-American community practice rather than an import, with groups building their own drums from wine barrels because instruments were unavailable. Musically it foregrounds composed multi-section ensemble pieces, visible choreography, and a layered rhythmic texture in which shime-daiko holds a fast ji ostinato while nagado and odaiko players trade phrases and kiai shouts. It differs from Japanese matsuri-bayashi in being concert-framed, composed and detached from shrine calendar function, and from Japanese kumi-daiko groups in its explicit civil-rights-era identity politics.

items.name: Ryukyu koten ongaku (Okinawan classical court music)
items.lineage: Court repertoire of the Ryukyu Kingdom at Shuri, systematized in the eighteenth century when Yakabi Choki (1716-1775) devised the kunkunshi tablature and the music was formalized for reception of Chinese sappushi envoys and for kumiodori dance-drama created by Tamagusuku Chokun in 1719 — very slow, sung in courtly Okinawan to the ryukyu scale on sanshin with kutu koto, kucho spike fiddle, fue flute and sparse taiko punctuation, in ryuka thirty-syllable verse form.
items.description: Ryukyu koten ongaku is the aristocratic sanshin song repertoire of the former Ryukyu Kingdom, notated in Yakabi Choki's kunkunshi tablature and preserved through the Nomura and Afuso schools. Tempos are extremely slow, the singing is restrained and nasally focused with long sustained syllables, and the heterophonic ensemble of sanshin, koto, kucho and fue moves in near-unison with wide spaces between events. It is sharply distinct from Okinawan min'yo in tempo, diction and social setting, and from mainland Japanese sokyoku in its ryukyu scale with its raised fourth and seventh.

items.name: Okinawan min'yo
items.lineage: Village folk-song tradition of the Ryukyu islands, transmitted orally through work, festival and awamori-party settings and commercially codified from the 1950s by singers such as Kadekaru Rinsho and Fukuhara Tsuneo, based on the ryukyu pentatonic with its raised fourth and seventh, sanshin accompaniment with the singer playing his own part, interjected hayashi shout-calls of hiyamiaachi and iyasasa, and the fast open-ended kachashi finale in a driving duple pulse with paranku frame drums and hand claps.
items.description: Okinawan min'yo is the everyday song repertoire of the Ryukyus, sung in the Okinawan language over self-accompanied sanshin, covering work songs, love songs, laments for the 1945 battle and celebration numbers. Its identifying marks are the ryukyu scale, the bright snakeskin-bodied sanshin timbre, shouted hayashi interjections from the room, and the kachashi ending in which tempo doubles and everyone dances with raised hands. It differs from mainland Japanese min'yo in scale and instrument, and from Ryukyu court music in its fast tempi, colloquial diction and communal participation.

items.name: Uchina pop (Okinawan pop)
items.lineage: Okinawan popular-music hybrid launched by Kina Shoukichi and Champloose's 1977 'Haisai Ojisan' and consolidated through the 1990s by Rinken Band, Nenes and BEGIN, setting the ryukyu scale and sanshin against electric guitar, bass, drum kit and synthesizers at mid-tempo rock and reggae pulses, retaining hayashi calls, kachashi double-time codas and Okinawan-language refrains inside verse-chorus pop structures.
items.description: Uchina pop is the electrified Okinawan popular style that carried island melody and language into the Japanese national market from the late 1970s onward. The sanshin stays audible as a lead colour over a full rock rhythm section, choruses lean on the ryukyu scale's raised fourth and seventh, and many tracks accelerate into a kachashi coda with paranku and clapping. It differs from mainland J-pop in modal vocabulary and instrumentation, and from Okinawan min'yo in its studio production, drum kit and fixed song forms.

items.name: Ainu upopo and rimse (song and dance)
items.lineage: Communal song-and-dance repertoire of the Ainu of Hokkaido and formerly Sakhalin, performed seated in a circle around a lidded shintoko container beaten as a drum for upopo round-songs sung in short overlapping canon, and standing for rimse circle dances such as the crane dance sarorun rimse and the sword dance emush rimse, with tonkori zither and mukkuri bamboo jaw harp providing instrumental colour; documented in Pilsudski's 1902-1905 cylinders and revived from the 1960s through preservation societies at Shiraoi and Akan.
items.description: Upopo are short strophic Ainu songs sung by seated women in staggered entries so that the phrases overlap in a rough canon, while rimse are the accompanying circle dances performed standing. Textures are narrow in range, strongly cyclic and driven by a lid-beaten container or handclaps rather than a membrane drum, with the tonkori five-string zither and the buzzing mukkuri adding timbral rather than melodic weight. It differs from Ainu yukar epic recitation, which is solo, narrative and stick-marked, and from Sami yoik in its group canonic overlap.
exemplars: Ainu Museum Shiraoi Poroto Kotan ensembles

items.name: Trot (contemporary revival)
items.lineage: Twenty-first-century Korean revival of trot triggered by Hong Jin-young and Jang Yoon-jeong's crossover hits and detonated commercially by TV Chosun's Miss Trot (2019) and Mr. Trot (2020), keeping the genre's duple ppongjjak backbeat, minor pentatonic melodies and heavily inflected kkeokk-neun vocal breaks while replacing the analog band with programmed drums, synth bass, EDM-adjacent risers and semi-trot arrangements that borrow K-pop production gloss at 110-135 BPM.
items.description: The trot revival of the late 2010s brought a genre associated with older listeners back to the top of the Korean charts through audition television, producing arena-scale stars in Lim Young-woong and Song Ga-in. The music keeps trot's characteristic two-beat ppongjjak feel and the ornamented, sob-inflected vocal delivery, but sits on modern programmed drums, sub bass and bright mastered mixes, with semi-trot tracks folding in dance-pop and even brass-band figures. It differs from mid-century trot in production and tempo, and from K-pop in its minor pentatonic melody, vocal ornamentation and solo-singer format.

items.name: Korean minyo (regional folk song)
items.lineage: Korean folk-song repertoire transmitted orally by village and professional singers and codified into regional tori dialects during the twentieth century — Gyeonggi minyo with its light, clear sesetgarum triple-shake, Namdo minyo of Jeolla with the heavy yukjabaegi wide vibrato and downward slides, Seodo minyo of the northwest with nasal tremulous delivery, and Dongbu minyo of the east — typically in 6/8 or 12/8 jangdan cycles played on the janggu hourglass drum, with call-and-response between a lead singer and chorus.
items.description: Korean minyo is the country's folk-song body, sorted by regional tori — melodic dialects defined less by scale than by which notes are shaken, bent or approached from above. Gyeonggi songs like Arirang and Doraji are bright and evenly ornamented; Namdo songs such as Yukjabaegi use a broad slow vibrato and a heavy descending slide that carries into pansori. Accompaniment is usually a janggu marking a compound-metre jangdan with optional melodic instruments doubling the voice heterophonically; unlike pansori it is strophic, communal and short-form rather than epic narrative.

items.name: Korean jeongak (court and literati music)
items.lineage: Aristocratic Korean repertoire of the Joseon court and yangban literati, notated in jeongganbo mensural tablature devised under King Sejong in the fifteenth century and preserved through the Jangagwon court music bureau and its successor the National Gugak Center, comprising ritual aak, banquet suites such as Sujecheon and Yeongsan hoesang, and the vocal jeongga forms gagok, gasa and sijo — extremely slow, in long 20-beat and 10-beat cycles marked by janggu and buk, with geomungo, gayageum, daegeum, piri, haegeum and ajaeng in heterophony.
items.description: Jeongak is the 'correct music' of the Korean court and scholar class, standing opposite the folk minsogak repertoire in nearly every parameter. Tempos are among the slowest in world practice, individual tones swell and are shaped by nonghyeon left-hand pressure vibrato, and the ensemble proceeds heterophonically with the piri's reedy double-reed cutting above the string body while the janggu marks very long cycles. Against sanjo or minyo it is notated, restrained in dynamics and emotionally cool rather than virtuosic; against Japanese gagaku it is more linear and less chordal, lacking the sho's cluster harmony.
exemplars: National Gugak Center Court Music Orchestra

items.name: Gayageum byeongchang (self-accompanied gayageum song)
items.lineage: Korean solo form in which a performer sings pansori excerpts and short folk-derived songs while simultaneously accompanying herself on the twelve-string gayageum, developed in the late nineteenth century out of the sanjo circle around Kim Chang-jo and carried into the twentieth by Oh Tae-seok, Park Gwi-hui and Kang Jeong-suk — the zither punctuating rather than doubling the vocal line, both parts riding a janggu jangdan cycle in jinyang, jungmori or jajinmori, with the gruff pansori chest voice and wide yukjabaegi vibrato intact.
items.description: Byeongchang is the practice of singing and playing the gayageum at once, drawing texts from pansori episodes such as the Chunhyangga and from short danga and folk numbers. The zither does not simply shadow the voice: it fills the gaps between vocal phrases and reinforces cadences, while the left hand's nonghyeon pressure vibrato mirrors the singer's ornamentation. It differs from sanjo, which is purely instrumental and improvisatory, and from full pansori, which is a solo voice with only a barrel-drum accompanist and runs to several hours.

items.name: Joseon pop
items.lineage: Korean fusion style named around LEENALCHI's 2020 album Sugungga and its single 'Tiger Is Coming', in which pansori-trained singers deliver Sugungga narrative text over a rhythm section of two electric basses, drum kit and no harmony instrument, at steady mid-tempo post-punk and disco pulses, so that the sori vocal's yukjabaegi bends and jangdan phrasing sit against a Western groove; developed in Seoul indie circles alongside Ssing Ssing's earlier shaman-song glam-rock experiments from 2017.
items.description: Joseon pop is the label attached to the pansori-meets-post-punk sound that LEENALCHI made internationally visible in 2020. The defining arrangement is deliberately hollow — twin basses and drums, no chordal instrument — leaving space for two to four sori singers to trade narrative lines with full traditional ornamentation over a locked eight-note groove. It differs from earlier gugak fusion in refusing orchestral padding, and from K-pop in using unamplified traditional vocal technique and Joseon-era narrative texts rather than contemporary lyric writing.

items.name: Xinyao
items.lineage: Singaporean Mandarin campus-folk movement formed 1979-1985 among junior-college and university students (Liang Wern Fook, Eric Moo, Billy Koh, and the Hocktone/Ocean Butterflies circle), built on strummed steel-string guitar at unhurried 70-100 BPM ballad tempos, diatonic verse-chorus songwriting with light piano and fretless-toned bass, and a conversational untrained-sounding Mandarin vocal delivery singing local Singaporean subject matter rather than Taiwanese or Hong Kong romantic convention.
items.description: Xinyao ('Singapore songs') emerged around 1979 from Chinese-medium school and junior-college songwriting clubs in Singapore and was commercially codified through the early-1980s Ocean Butterflies compilations. Its sound is deliberately plain: acoustic guitar or piano foundation, restrained rhythm section, no vocal ornament, and lyrics in colloquial Mandarin about school life, national service, and Singaporean places. It differs from contemporaneous Taiwanese campus folk by its explicit local-identity subject matter, and from Cantopop by its amateur, un-glossed production posture.

items.name: Zhongguo Feng (China Wind Mandopop)
items.lineage: Taiwanese-led Mandopop substyle codified 2003-2008 by Jay Chou with lyricist Vincent Fang and arranger Chung Hsing-min, setting gong-mode pentatonic melodies and guzheng, erhu, pipa and dizi timbres over 80-100 BPM R&B and hip-hop programmed drums, with breathy half-sung Mandarin delivery, classical-allusion lyrics, and string-pad arrangements that fold Chinese instrumental heterophony into Western pop verse-chorus form.
items.description: Zhongguo feng ('China wind') crystallised in Taiwan in the mid-2000s around Jay Chou's 'East Wind Breaks' and 'Blue and White Porcelain', then spread across mainland and Malaysian Mandopop. Its signature is a pentatonic vocal line and traditional Chinese lead instruments layered onto contemporary R&B or hip-hop production, with classical-poetry lyric registers. Unlike guofeng-adjacent traditional revival, the Chinese instruments here are colour on a Western pop chassis, and unlike ordinary Mandopop ballad it commits to modal pentatonicism rather than functional major-key writing.

items.name: Chinese Minyao (Mainland Indie Folk)
items.lineage: Mainland Chinese indie-folk current formed in Beijing bar circuits (D-22, School, Jianghu) from the late 1990s through the 2010s around Zhou Yunpeng, Wan Xiaoli, Li Zhi, Song Dongye and Zhao Lei, built on fingerpicked or lightly strummed steel-string guitar at 70-110 BPM, plain-spoken narrative Mandarin diction close to the microphone, sparse upright bass, cello or accordion colour, and city-name lyric geographies rather than rural folk-song sources.
items.description: Minyao in its contemporary sense denotes mainland Chinese singer-songwriter folk rather than traditional folk song, taking shape in Beijing's late-1990s bar scene and reaching mass audiences after 2013 via televised covers of songs like 'Chengdu' and 'An Herb'. The sound is guitar-and-voice first, dry and close-miked, with narrative lyrics naming specific cities, trains and rented rooms. It is distinguished from state-sponsored minge folk-song performance by its untrained, unamplified vocal manner, and from Chinese rock by the absence of distortion and backbeat drive.

items.name: Chinese Traditional Music (Han Instrumental & Vocal)
items.lineage: Han Chinese instrumental and vocal repertoire transmitted from the Tang-Song court and literati eras through regional sizhu, chuida and qin lineages and codified into conservatory practice after 1949 by the Central Conservatory and China Record Company, characterised by gong-mode pentatonic frameworks with expressive passing tones, heterophonic ensemble texture where each instrument ornaments a shared melody, free-tempo openings tightening into metered ban-yan cycles marked by paiban clapper, and timbral extremes from the whisper of guqin to the outdoor blare of suona.
items.description: Chinese traditional music covers the Han instrumental and narrative-song repertoire preserved through regional chamber ensembles (Jiangnan sizhu, Chaozhou string music), solo literati traditions (guqin, pipa), and loud outdoor wind-percussion bands, systematised into conservatory teaching and state recording from the 1950s. Its defining traits are heterophony rather than harmony, a pentatonic gong-system core with mode-specific inflected tones, and extremely wide timbral contrast between silk, bamboo, and reed families. It differs from Chinese opera traditions by the absence of staged dramatic vocal roles, and from the modern guoyue orchestra by keeping small ensembles and untempered ornament intact.

items.name: Pipa Repertoire
items.lineage: Solo repertoire for the four-string pear-shaped fretted lute that entered China via Central Asia by the Tang dynasty, held upright and played with five fingernail plectra since the Ming, codified in the 1819 Hua Qiuping handbook and the Pudong and Pinghu school lineages and modernised by Liu Tianhua and Liu Dehai, split between martial wu pieces such as 'Ambush from Ten Sides' with rolling lunzhi tremolo, snapped strings and drum-imitating strikes, and civil wen pieces in slow rubato with heavy left-hand bending and vibrato over gong-mode pentatonic lines.
items.description: The pipa tradition is the solo art-music practice of the Chinese plucked lute, transmitted through named regional schools whose handbooks fix the repertoire while leaving ornament and tempo to the player. Its sonic identity comes from the continuous lunzhi finger-tremolo that sustains melody, aggressive left-hand pitch bending and portamento, and percussive body and string effects used programmatically in the martial pieces. Compared to guzheng repertoire it is more linear and narrative than resonant and arpeggiated, and unlike ensemble sizhu it is a single-voice, through-composed programmatic form.

items.name: Guzheng Repertoire
items.lineage: Solo and ensemble practice of the Chinese movable-bridge half-tube zither, documented since the Qin dynasty and carried through the Shandong, Henan, Chaozhou, Hakka and Zhejiang regional schools before the twentieth-century standardisation to 21 steel-wound nylon strings tuned in pentatonic gong mode, defined by right-hand arpeggiated glissando sweeps and tremolo and by left-hand pressing behind the bridges that supplies the mode's inflected fourth and seventh degrees through slow bends and vibrato.
items.description: Guzheng repertoire is the zither art of the Chinese movable-bridge zheng, historically divided into northern schools with heavy left-hand pressing and southern Chaozhou and Hakka schools with lighter, faster figuration; the modern concert version was standardised in the 1960s. Its recognisable sound is the wide arpeggiated glissando across an open pentatonic tuning, tremolo-sustained melody notes, and bend-produced non-tuned scale degrees. It differs from pipa music by favouring resonance and washes over percussive attack, and from the older guqin by its brighter, louder, concert-projected tone.
exemplars: 'Yu Zhou Chang Wan' (Fisherman's Song at Eventide)

items.name: Erhu Repertoire
items.lineage: Solo repertoire for the two-string snakeskin-membrane spike fiddle, elevated from folk and opera accompaniment to art-music status by Liu Tianhua's 1918-1932 conservatory etudes and pieces and by the recorded improvisations of the blind Wuxi street musician Abing in 1950, defined by a bow permanently threaded between the strings, fingering with no fingerboard so pitch is produced by string tension, continuous sliding portamento, wide expressive vibrato, and a nasal, vocally-inflected tone over pentatonic melodies in slow lament tempos.
items.description: The erhu solo tradition dates from the early twentieth century, when Liu Tianhua wrote graded concert works for an instrument previously confined to opera pits and street playing, and it gained its emotional archetype from Abing's 'Erquan Yingyue', recorded shortly before his death. The characteristic sound is a thin, reedy, almost human two-string voice with unbroken portamento between notes and no fixed intonation reference, typically accompanied only by yangqin. It is distinguished from other huqin members by its lower, softer register and lyrical rather than brilliant role, and from Western violin repertoire by its melodic single-line, ornament-driven construction.

items.name: Dizi Repertoire
items.lineage: Repertoire for the transverse bamboo flute with its distinctive dimo reed membrane over a sixth hole, split into the bright fast-tonguing northern bangdi style of Feng Zicun and the lyrical breathy southern qudi style of Zhao Songting, codified as solo concert music from the 1950s and marked by flutter-tonguing, rapid grace-note taps, wide glissando bends, circular-breathing long tones and a buzzing membrane overtone that no keyed flute produces.
items.description: Dizi solo repertoire was built in the 1950s from northern bangzi-opera and southern sizhu flute practice into a conservatory concert genre. The instrument's signature is the dimo membrane, which adds a bright buzzing edge and lets the flute cut through an ensemble, played with flutter-tongue, finger-tremolo and pitch bends drawn from opera vocal ornament. Northern pieces are rhythmic and virtuosic with staccato double-tonguing; southern pieces are slow, legato and heavily ornamented, which separates dizi music from the softer, membraneless xiao repertoire.

items.name: Huqin Ensemble (Chinese Bowed-Fiddle Family)
items.lineage: The family of Chinese bowed spike lutes — jinghu, erhu, gaohu, zhonghu, banhu — that entered China from Central Asian nomadic sources by the Song dynasty and became the melodic backbone of regional opera pits and southern chamber ensembles, standardised into fixed pitch registers by twentieth-century conservatories, all sharing bow hair fixed between two strings, a resonator of snakeskin, wood or coconut, tension-stopped fingering with no fingerboard, and a shared role of shadowing and ornamenting the singer's line in metered ban-yan opera cycles.
items.description: Huqin names the whole class of Chinese two-string bowed fiddles rather than one instrument, ranging from the piercing high jinghu that leads Beijing opera to the coconut-bodied gaohu of Cantonese music and the loud wood-faced banhu of northern bangzi opera. Played as a group they produce dense heterophony, each register bending and sliding around the same tune with different attack and nasality. The tradition is defined by its accompanimental function — tracking and cushioning the opera singer — which separates it from the concert solo erhu repertoire that grew out of it in the twentieth century.
exemplars: Jing Opera Company of Beijing orchestras

items.name: Mongolian Folk Music
items.lineage: Herding-society vocal and instrumental tradition of the Mongolian steppe and Inner Mongolia, transmitted orally through family and regional lineages and documented by Soviet-era and post-1990 fieldwork, built on the free-rhythm urtyn duu long song with enormous sustained melismas over a five-tone scale, the metered bogino duu short song, morin khuur horsehead-fiddle accompaniment mixing bowed drone and melody, plucked tovshuur and shudraga, yatga zither and limbe flute with circular breathing, and khoomei overtone singing used as colour rather than centrepiece.
items.description: Mongolian folk music is the pastoral repertoire of Mongolia and Inner Mongolia, centred on the urtyn duu long song, whose few words are stretched across minutes of unmetered, heavily ornamented melody with shurankhai falsetto leaps, and its metered counterpart the short song. The morin khuur, bowed on horsehair string bundles and often tuned in fourths, supplies both drone and heterophonic doubling; texture is thin, usually one or two players. It differs from Tuvan practice by making the ornamented open-throat song rather than overtone singing the central technique, and from Mongolian state-composed song by remaining unnotated and free in tempo.

items.name: Zohioliin Duu (Mongolian Authored Song)
items.lineage: Mongolian 'authored song' repertoire created from the 1930s through the 1980s by state-trained composers such as Bilegiin Damdinsuren, Sembiin Gonchigsumlaa and Dashdorjiin Luvsansharav under the Mongolian People's Republic, notated in Soviet-derived staff practice and recorded for state radio and Melodiya, setting patriotic and lyrical Mongolian texts to pentatonic long-song-derived melodies harmonised with functional Western chords and arranged for morin khuur, yatga, yoochin, accordion, piano and mixed choir at steady moderate tempos.
items.description: Zohioliin duu is the body of composed, credited Mongolian song written under the socialist state from the 1930s onward, taught in conservatories and broadcast on Mongolian state radio. It keeps the pentatonic contour and wide vocal leaps of folk long song but fixes them in metre, adds Western triadic harmony and orchestral or choral arrangement, and is sung with a trained projecting voice. This notated, authored status is precisely what separates it from anonymous oral urtyn duu, while the Mongolian modal and morin-khuur colour separates it from ordinary Soviet estrada.

items.name: Throat Singing (Overtone Singing)
items.lineage: Inner Asian overtone vocal technique practised across Tuva, Mongolia, Altai, Khakassia and Bashkortostan and paralleled in Tibetan monastic chant, transmitted orally among herders and formalised into named styles (khoomei, sygyt, kargyraa, borbangnadyr, ezengileer) by Tuvan and Mongolian state ensembles from the 1960s, produced by constricting the ventricular folds or false vocal folds over a fixed low fundamental and shaping the mouth and tongue to isolate harmonics 6-12 into an audible whistled melody, usually in free or slow duple time against igil or morin khuur drone.
items.description: Throat singing is the family of Inner Asian techniques in which a single singer sounds a sustained low fundamental and simultaneously amplifies individual upper partials into a separate melodic line. Named Tuvan and Mongolian styles differ by mechanism: kargyraa uses subharmonic ventricular-fold vibration an octave below the sung note, sygyt produces a piercing flute-like whistle, khoomei sits between them. The music is essentially static harmonically, built on drone and harmonic series rather than chord change, which separates it from every scalar vocal tradition, and from Tibetan dzokar chant by its melodic use of the overtones rather than sheer depth of tone.

items.name: Tuvan Folk Music
items.lineage: Herding and hunting music of the Republic of Tuva in south Siberia, transmitted orally in the Tuvan pastoral nomadic community and brought to international documentation from 1987 onward through Ted Levin's fieldwork and the ensemble Huun-Huur-Tu, characterised by khoomei, sygyt and kargyraa overtone singing over the two-string horsehair igil fiddle and plucked doshpuluur, khomus jaw harp, tsuur end-blown flute, sound-mimesis of rivers, wind and horses, walking-horse duple rhythms around 90-110 BPM, and a pentatonic melodic frame anchored on unchanging drone.
items.description: Tuvan folk music is the herder repertoire of south Siberia, where overtone singing is not a curiosity but the ordinary way of making music alongside the igil fiddle and doshpuluur lute. Songs run over a fixed drone in a slow or ambling duple gait that imitates horse movement, with lyric texts about animals, rivers and home valleys, and a strong aesthetic of sound-mimesis in which instrument and voice imitate the landscape. Compared to Mongolian folk it puts overtone technique at the centre rather than long-song melisma, and compared to concert throat-singing showcases it stays song-shaped, cyclic and modest in range.
exemplars: Tuva: Voices from the Center of Asia (Smithsonian Folkways, 1990)

items.name: Sami yoik (Sápmi vocal tradition)
items.lineage: Circumpolar Sápmi vocal art across northern Norway, Sweden, Finland and the Kola Peninsula, documented from the 17th-century missionary suppression records and revived from the 1960s-70s by Nils-Aslak Valkeapää and later Mari Boine — short cyclic melodic cells of narrow ambitus repeated with subtle variation, non-lexical vocables (loi-la-loi) carrying more weight than text, glottal catches and pulsing chest attacks, no fixed metric frame, historically unaccompanied though the noaidi's oval frame drum survives in ritual and revival use.
items.description: Yoik is the Sámi vocal tradition of the European Arctic, a practice of singing a person, animal, or place rather than singing about it — the yoik is understood as belonging to its subject. Its sonic markers are short repeated melodic cells of narrow range, heavy use of non-lexical syllables, free unmetered phrasing that follows breath rather than pulse, and a pressed, forward chest tone with glottal onsets. It differs from Inuit katajjaq in being solo and melodic rather than a paired throat game, and from Nordic folk song in its cyclic non-strophic form and absence of harmonic accompaniment.

items.name: Kaneka (Kanak New Caledonia)
items.lineage: New Caledonian Kanak popular music codified in the mid-1980s around the independence movement, with bands Bwanjep, Gurejele and Edou fusing customary pilou dance rhythm and bwanjep bamboo-stamping patterns with Jamaican reggae backbeat — mid-tempo 4/4 around 80-100 BPM, one-drop or half-time kit under offbeat guitar chops, electric bass carrying the melodic weight, unison male choruses in Drehu, Paicî and French, lyrics on land, custom and independence.
items.description: Kaneka emerged in New Caledonia in the mid-1980s as the sound of the Kanak independence struggle, deliberately built by musicians who wanted a modern idiom rooted in customary rhythm rather than imported wholesale. The music sets reggae's offbeat guitar and one-drop kick against pilou-derived stamping patterns and log-percussion, with bass-forward mixes and unison male choral refrains sung in Kanak languages alongside French. It is distinguished from Caribbean reggae by its rhythmic underpinning and vernacular choral texture, and from Tahitian or Polynesian pop by its overtly political lyric content and reggae skeleton.

items.name: Waiata (Māori song tradition)
items.lineage: Aotearoa New Zealand Māori sung repertoire carried on the marae from pre-contact times and reshaped after the 19th century by mission hymnody, spanning waiata ā-ringa, waiata aroha and waiata tangi — narrow-ambitus recitational melody built on two or three pitches with a characteristic falling cadence, unmetered phrasing tied to breath groups and whakaeke entries, communal unison or drone-plus-melody texture, and post-contact strophic harmonised settings sung in te reo Māori.
items.description: Waiata is the sung layer of Māori marae practice in Aotearoa, ranging from ancient recitational mōteatea to the harmonised strophic songs that followed missionary hymn contact in the nineteenth century. Older strata use a very narrow melodic range around a reciting tone, free breath-governed phrasing, and communal unison with a sustained drone under the leader, while the post-contact layer adopts diatonic four-part harmony over guitar. It is separated from kapa haka by being sung rather than performed with choreographed action and stamped percussion, and from Polynesian himene by its recitational rather than stacked-chord basis.
exemplars: Archive of Māori and Pacific Sound (University of Auckland)

items.name: Kapa haka
items.lineage: Māori performing-arts discipline formalised through 20th-century concert parties and the biennial Te Matatini national competition founded in 1972 — a fixed bracket of whakaeke, mōteatea, waiata ā-ringa, poi, haka and whakawātea, with unison group chant in te reo Māori, sharply stamped foot percussion and thigh slaps supplying the pulse, declaimed leader calls answered by the full rōpū, and pūkaea or pūtātara conch calls opening the set.
items.description: Kapa haka is the competitive and ceremonial Māori group performance form codified across the twentieth century and standardised by Te Matatini's bracket structure since 1972. Sonically it alternates full-throated unison chant and declamation with harmonised waiata ā-ringa, all driven by body percussion — stamped feet, slapped thighs, and the rhythmic hiss of breath — rather than by instruments, with a leader's kaea call cueing each entry. It is distinguished from waiata sung on the marae by its choreographed, drilled ensemble discipline and far higher dynamic intensity, and from Polynesian dance forms elsewhere by its absence of a standing drum battery.

items.name: Himene tārava (Society Islands village choir)
items.lineage: Tahitian and Cook Islands congregational choral form that crystallised after London Missionary Society hymn contact from 1797 onward and is now judged annually at the Heiva i Tahiti — large unaccompanied village choirs stacked in six or more parts, a continuously grunted low-male ostinato (the tuki or perepere) under the texture, high women's ha'u lines sliding into the chords, sustained non-diatonic clusters that drift in pitch across a verse, and abrupt unison cadential drops.
items.description: Himene tārava is the massed unaccompanied choral polyphony of the Society and Cook Islands, a hybrid of missionary hymnody with pre-contact Polynesian vocal practice, still contested competitively at the Heiva. Its signature is a thick six-to-ten-part stack over a continuous grunted male bass ostinato, women's voices entering with portamento above the chord, tuning that drifts upward across a verse rather than holding equal temperament, and no instrumental support at all. It differs from European hymn singing in its rhythmic ostinato layer and non-tempered intonation, and from Tahitian drum dance in being wholly vocal and largely static in pulse.
exemplars: Heiva i Tahiti choral competition recordings

items.name: Polynesian traditional music (pan-Pacific)
items.lineage: Pre-contact and continuing repertoire across the Polynesian triangle — Tonga, Sāmoa, Hawaiʻi, Aotearoa, Tahiti and the Cooks — documented ethnographically from Cook's voyages onward and systematically from the mid-20th century by researchers such as Mervyn McLean and Adrienne Kaeppler: sung poetry over sharp-edged idiophone percussion (slit gong, sharkskin pahu, struck bamboo, body slaps), narrow-range recitational melody widening into stacked polyphony after mission contact, conch-shell calls framing ceremony, and rhythm organised in fast even subdivisions rather than harmonic cycles.
items.description: This is the shared traditional layer of the Polynesian triangle: sung poetry bound to dance and ceremony, carried by voices over wooden idiophones rather than membranophone ensembles or melodic instruments. Across island groups the constants are recitational melody of small range, dense fast percussion subdivision on slit gong and standing sharkskin drum, body percussion integrated into the rhythm, conch calls as ceremonial punctuation, and texts whose genealogical or dedicatory content outranks musical elaboration. It is distinguished from Melanesian and Micronesian practice by the slit-gong and pahu combination and by the post-contact choral polyphony layered on top, and from Southeast Asian traditions by the absence of tuned metallophone ensembles.
exemplars: Tongan Royal Corps of Musicians recordings
Smithsonian Folkways Music of Polynesia series

items.name: Tahitian traditional music (ʻōteʻa and pāʻōʻā)
items.lineage: French Polynesian dance-and-drum repertoire revived from the 1950s through the Heiva competitions after decades of missionary prohibition — the tōʻere slit-gong battery driving fast unison patterns at 160-200 BPM with the pahu tūpaʻi and small faʻatete drum layered beneath, sudden ensemble breaks and tempo shifts cueing choreography, unaccompanied vocal pāʻōʻā and rhythmic hissed chant interludes, and hīmene choral blocks separating the drum sections.
items.description: Tahitian traditional performance centres on the ʻōteʻa, a drum-driven dance whose sound is dominated by a battery of tōʻere slit gongs struck with hardwood beaters at extreme speed, underpinned by the deep pahu and the tight faʻatete. Sections are cyclic and rehearsed to the beat, with sharp full-ensemble stops, tempo escalations, and vocal pāʻōʻā call-and-response or hissed rhythmic chant filling the gaps between drum figures. It differs from Hawaiian hula in its far higher tempo and slit-gong-forward timbre rather than gourd and sharkskin, and from himene tārava in being percussion-led with vocals subordinate.
exemplars: Heiva i Tahiti ʻōteʻa competition recordings

items.name: Hula (mele hula dance-chant)
items.lineage: Hawaiian chant-and-dance tradition transmitted through the hālau system, suppressed after 1830 and restored publicly from Kalākaua's reign in the 1880s, then reasserted in the 1970s Hawaiian Renaissance and the Merrie Monarch Festival — hula kahiko sets oli and mele over the ipu heke gourd struck-and-thumped pattern, pahu sharkskin drum for temple repertoire, puʻili split-bamboo rattles and ʻiliʻili stones, with a chanter's sustained ʻiʻi vibrato, narrow melodic range, and text-governed unmetered phrase lengths.
items.description: Hula is the Hawaiian dance form whose music is chant: the kumu hula's oli or mele carried on a very narrow set of pitches with a distinctive trembling ʻiʻi sustain, timed to the gourd ipu heke's alternating thump-and-slap or to the pahu drum in sacred repertoire. Phrase lengths follow the poetic line rather than a bar count, and the percussion is a steady frame rather than an elaborated groove. It is distinguished from the guitar-and-steel hula ʻauana of the hapa haole era by having no Western harmony or melodic instruments at all, and from Tahitian ʻōteʻa by its slower tempo and voice-first hierarchy.

items.name: Slack-key guitar (kī hōʻalu instrumental)
items.lineage: Hawaiian fingerstyle guitar idiom developed after Mexican paniolo vaqueros brought guitars to the islands in the 1830s, kept largely within families until Gabby Pahinui's 1946 recordings and the 1970s Renaissance releases on Panini — the six strings slackened to open major or wahine tunings (taro-patch G, F-wahine, C-mauna-loa), thumb holding an alternating bass while the fingers pick melody above, chimed natural harmonics, slides and hammered ornaments imitating vocal ʻiʻi, at unhurried tempi in loose rubato.
items.description: Kī hōʻalu is the Hawaiian solo fingerstyle guitar tradition built on slackened open tunings, in which the thumb maintains a bass-and-chord pulse while the fingers carry the melody, decorated with chimed harmonics, slides, and ornaments modelled on chant vibrato. Tunings were family property and often kept secret; the repertoire is largely instrumental settings of mele and hapa haole songs at relaxed, elastic tempi. It differs from the Hawaiian steel guitar in being fretted and fingerpicked rather than bar-slid, and from American folk fingerstyle in its open-tuning vocabulary, slower rubato, and its ornamental vocabulary derived from vocal chant.

items.name: Vintage Hawaiian (hapa haole steel-guitar era)
items.lineage: Mainland-facing Hawaiian popular style running from the 1915 Panama-Pacific Exposition craze through the 1920s-40s Victor and Columbia sides and the Hawaii Calls broadcasts — Joseph Kekuku's bar-slid steel guitar carrying the melody with wide portamento and tremolo, ukulele and tenor guitar chording a gentle two-beat, string bass on the downbeats, English-and-Hawaiian hapa haole lyrics in close crooned harmony, at leisurely 70-100 BPM.
items.description: Vintage Hawaiian is the commercial hapa haole sound that swept the American mainland after 1915 and was fixed on 78s and radio through the 1940s. Its defining timbre is the acoustic steel guitar played with a bar — sustained, sliding, heavily tremoloed melody lines over ukulele and tenor-guitar strums, string bass on one and three, and softly crooned English-language lyrics with Hawaiian tags. It differs from slack-key in being ensemble popular song rather than solo fingerstyle instrumental, and from hula kahiko in using full Western diatonic harmony and no traditional percussion whatsoever.
exemplars: Ray Kinney and the Hawaii Calls Orchestra

items.name: Inuit traditional music (drum-dance and pisiq)
items.lineage: Circumpolar Inuit repertoire of Nunavut, Nunavik, Greenland and Alaska, documented from Knud Rasmussen's Fifth Thule Expedition of the 1920s and revived after mission-era bans — the qilaut single-membrane frame drum struck on its rim by a rotating soloist while an aya-yaa chorus answers, personal pisiq songs of hunt and weather sung in narrow descending phrases over the drum's uneven triple stroke, plus the paired katajjaq breath-game exchanged face to face until one singer breaks.
items.description: Inuit traditional music across the North American and Greenlandic Arctic centres on two practices: the drum dance, in which a soloist rotates a large rim-struck frame drum while singing a personally owned pisiq answered by a seated chorus of vocables, and katajjaq, the women's paired throat game of interlocked voiced and unvoiced breath patterns. Melodies are of very narrow range with descending contours, the drum stroke is uneven and asymmetrical rather than metronomic, and there are no melodic instruments. It is distinguished from Sámi yoik by the drum's structural role and by the existence of the competitive breath game, and from Plains powwow singing by its solo drum and much lower dynamic ceiling.
exemplars: Knud Rasmussen Fifth Thule Expedition recordings

items.name: Navajo traditional song (Diné)
items.lineage: Diné repertoire of the Four Corners Southwest documented from the 1890s by Washington Matthews and continuing in ceremony today — Yeibichai and Nightway chant sung in a tense high falsetto with sudden octave leaps and pulsating breaks, gourd or hoof rattle marking an even pulse, water-drum and gourd accompanying Native American Church peyote songs at fast even tempo with a distinctive closing formula, plus secular skip-dance and social songs in tighter mid-range unison.
items.description: Navajo traditional song spans the long ceremonial chantway cycles of the Diné Southwest and the shorter social and Native American Church repertoires that grew alongside them. Its most recognisable sound is the Yeibichai voice — extremely high, tense falsetto with abrupt octave breaks and pulsed vibrato over a steady rattle — while peyote songs move faster and lighter on water-drum and gourd with a fixed cadential tag. Melody is strictly monophonic with rigid, memorised text, and improvisation is essentially absent because ceremonial accuracy is the point. It differs from Plains powwow singing in vocal placement and the absence of a large communal bass drum, and from Apache repertoire in its chantway architecture.

items.name: Native American traditional music (pan-tribal)
items.lineage: Indigenous North American repertoire spanning Plains, Woodlands, Southwest and Northwest Coast nations, recorded from Frances Densmore's cylinder work of 1907 onward and consolidated in the intertribal powwow circuit after the 1950s — terraced descending melodic contours in strict monophony, vocables carrying most songs, a communal bass drum struck in even pulse with the honor-beat accent pattern, seated singers around one drum in unison and octaves, and rattles, whistles and cedar flute in ceremonial and courting contexts.
items.description: This is the shared body of Indigenous North American song as documented on cylinder from 1907 and as practised on the modern intertribal powwow circuit. The consistent markers are strict monophony, terraced melodic descent from a high entry to a low cadence, vocable rather than lexical text in most songs, and a single large communal drum struck by seated singers in even pulse with periodic honor beats. Northern-style singing sits very high and tense, Southern-style lower and broader. It is distinguished from Inuit drum dance by the shared bass drum and multi-singer unison, and from Mesoamerican and Andean Indigenous traditions by the absence of melodic wind ensembles and harmonic accompaniment.

items.name: Native American courting flute music
items.lineage: Plains and Woodlands North American end-blown duct flute tradition (Lakota siyotanka, Kiowa, Anishinaabe) used for courting and personal songs from at least the 18th century, near-extinguished by mid-20th-century assimilation policy and revived from the 1960s-80s by Doc Tate Nevaquaya and R. Carlos Nakai — free-rhythm unmetered breath-length phrases on a two-chamber cedar flute whose block tuning yields an untempered minor-pentatonic scale, played rubato with heavy diaphragm pulse, finger-slur ornaments, and terminal breath vibrato.
items.description: The solo cedar duct flute repertoire of Plains and Great Lakes peoples, historically a private courting and personal-song instrument, revived from the 1960s onward into a recorded solo-instrumental idiom. Its sound is a breathy, slightly buzzing tone from the fetish-block air channel, unmetered phrasing shaped entirely by breath length, and a pentatonic scale whose intervals sit noticeably wide of equal temperament. Unlike powwow or peyote singing, it is instrumental, soft-dynamic, and non-communal; unlike revival new-age flute records it retains audible finger-slide ornament and irregular phrase lengths rather than metric backing.

items.name: Australian Aboriginal clan song and manikay
items.lineage: Ceremonial song traditions of Aboriginal Australia, most fully documented in Arnhem Land manikay and Central Desert inma from the mid-20th century through recordings by A.P. Elkin, Alice Moyle and later community song-men such as Djalu Gurruwiwi — paired singer and clapstick beat in strict fast isochronous pulse against a continuously circular-breathed yidaki drone, with descending terraced melodic contours, texted ancestral songlines in clan languages, and short repeated song items separated by spoken cueing.
items.description: The ceremonial song repertoire held by Aboriginal Australian clans, in which songlines encoding country and ancestral law are performed as short, repeated song items. Sonically it is defined by a rasping harmonic drone from the yidaki, a hard clapstick pulse that fixes tempo without subdivision, and a strained-chest male vocal on stepwise descending contours ending in glottal drops. It differs from solo didgeridoo playing by the primacy of the sung text and clapstick, and from later Aboriginal rock or country in retaining unaccompanied language singing with no harmonic accompaniment.

items.name: Australian bush ballad
items.lineage: Australian narrative folk-song form emerging from 1880s Bulletin-era verse by Banjo Paterson and Henry Lawson and set to music commercially from the 1930s by Buddy Williams, Tex Morton and later Slim Dusty — moderate 2/4 and 3/4 strummed guitar with brushed snare, plain flat-vowel Australian diction on long strophic narratives of drovers, shearers and drought, sparse fiddle, accordion or harmonica fills between verses, and repeated singalong choruses.
items.description: The Australian rural narrative song tradition, rooted in 1890s bush verse and recorded commercially from the 1930s onward. It is built on strophic multi-verse storytelling delivered in an unadorned broad-Australian accent over three-chord strummed guitar, with fiddle, harmonica or button accordion decorating the turnarounds and a light two-beat bass. It differs from American country of the same era in vocabulary, flatter and less nasal vocal placement, and near-absence of blue notes or steel guitar; it differs from the older unaccompanied bush song by its studio instrumentation and fixed choruses.

items.name: Didgeridoo drone practice (yidaki and mago technique)
items.lineage: Northern Australian aerophone tradition of Arnhem Land (yidaki) and western Arnhem (mago), documented from the 1930s and internationally disseminated from the 1980s — a termite-hollowed eucalypt tube sounded by lip buzz with continuous circular breathing, producing a fixed fundamental around D-to-F, a superimposed second overtone 'toot', and rhythm generated entirely by tongue, cheek, diaphragm and vocalized calls layered into the drone at fast isochronous cycle lengths.
items.description: The instrumental technique tradition of the Australian didgeridoo, centred on Yolngu yidaki and Kunwinjku mago practice and later taken up worldwide. The music is a single unbroken fundamental sustained by circular breathing, articulated into fast repeating rhythmic cells by tongue and diaphragm pulses, punctuated by an overblown toot a tenth above and by vocalized animal calls that beat against the drone. Unlike clan song performance, no sung text or fixed songline governs it; unlike Western drone minimalism, its variation is entirely timbral and rhythmic rather than harmonic.

items.name: Yiddish folksong (Ashkenazi secular repertoire)
items.lineage: Secular song repertoire of Yiddish-speaking Eastern Europe, collected from the 1890s by S. An-sky, Y.L. Cahan and Moshe Beregovski and carried to New York by mass migration — mostly strophic solo song in Ahava Raba and natural-minor modes, free rubato in lyric and lament types against duple dance rhythms in tanzlider, with sighing appoggiaturas, krekhts catch-sobs borrowed from cantorial delivery, and optional fiddle, tsimbl or accordion doubling the vocal line heterophonically.
items.description: The secular song tradition of Ashkenazi Eastern Europe, systematically collected around 1900 and preserved through immigrant recordings and postwar revival. It centres on solo strophic singing in minor and Ahava Raba modes, alternating rubato lyric and lament songs with metric dance and work songs, and carries a distinctive ornament vocabulary of sobbing catches and upper-neighbour sighs. It differs from klezmer in being vocal and text-led rather than instrumental and dance-functional, and from Hasidic niggunim in its worldly subject matter and fully texted lyrics.

items.name: Jewish cantorial recitative (golden-age hazzanut)
items.lineage: Synagogue solo-prayer art of Eastern and Central Europe, professionalized in the 19th century and reaching its recorded golden age in 1900-1940 Warsaw, Vilna and New York through Yossele Rosenblatt, Zavel Kwartin and Gershon Sirota — unmetered recitative on liturgical Hebrew set in the nusach prayer modes (Ahava Raba, Magen Avot, Adonai Malach), with extended melismatic coloratura, deliberate krekhts sobs and falsetto breaks, and either unaccompanied delivery or a male choir supplying sustained chordal support.
items.description: The virtuoso solo prayer-leading art of the Ashkenazi synagogue, at its peak in early twentieth-century Europe and immigrant America and preserved on acoustic and early electrical discs. Its defining sound is free-rhythm Hebrew recitative in fixed prayer modes, elaborated with long florid melismas, register leaps into a piercing falsetto, and a cultivated weeping catch in the tone. It differs from congregational nusach in its improvisatory extravagance and trained operatic technique, and from Hasidic niggun in being texted liturgy sung by a single professional rather than wordless communal melody.

items.name: Chabad-Lubavitch niggunim
items.lineage: Wordless devotional melody repertoire of the Chabad Hasidic movement, formed in Belarusian Lyubavichi from the early 19th century and codified in the printed Sefer HaNigunim under the sixth and seventh Rebbes from 1948 — melodies attributed to specific Rebbes, sung communally at farbrengen gatherings in slow rubato dveykus meditation form building through fixed repeated sections into fast duple rikud dance versions, on syllables like 'ai-ai-ai' and 'bim-bam', with table-banging and clapping the only percussion.
items.description: The wordless melody tradition of the Chabad-Lubavitch Hasidic movement, transmitted from early-nineteenth-century Belarus and catalogued in the twentieth century as an authored corpus tied to individual Rebbes. Musically it is unison male communal singing on nonsense syllables, moving from slow, free-tempo contemplative statements through repeated multi-section forms into accelerating duple-time dance repetitions, with clapping and table-pounding as the sole accompaniment. It differs from other Hasidic courts' niggunim by its documented authorship and doctrinal ordering of melody types, and from cantorial hazzanut by having no text and no soloist.

items.name: Chasidic pop (Orthodox Jewish popular music)
items.lineage: Orthodox Jewish popular idiom created in late-1960s New York by Shlomo Carlebach and the Rabbis' Sons and industrialized from the 1980s through Mordechai Ben David, Avraham Fried and the arranger Yisroel Lamm — Hebrew liturgical and biblical verse texts set to major-key or Ahava Raba pop melodies at moderate 4/4, with synth-and-brass big-band arrangements, boys'-choir doubling of the hook, and a fast 'freilach' double-time section built for wedding dancing.
items.description: The commercial popular music of Ashkenazi Orthodox communities in New York and Israel, launched by Shlomo Carlebach's melodies in the late 1960s and turned into a studio industry in the 1980s. It sets Hebrew scriptural and prayer texts to hook-driven pop tunes with layered synths, session brass, and a children's choir doubling the chorus, usually accelerating into a duple-time dance strain for weddings. It is distinguished from klezmer by its pop-song form and absence of instrumental improvisation, and from communal niggunim by fully texted lyrics, professional arrangement, and studio production.

items.name: Byzantine ecclesiastical music (papadic and sticheraric styles)
items.lineage: Liturgical monody of the Eastern Roman church, notated from the tenth century in neumatic systems and reformed in 1814 by Chrysanthos, Chourmouzios and Gregorios into the New Method still taught in Constantinople, Athens and Athos — a solo protopsaltis chanting in the eight-mode Oktoechos over a sustained ison drone, unmetered and text-governed in the syllabic heirmologic style, expansively melismatic in the slow papadic style, with microtonal intervals and prescribed ornamental formulas.
items.description: The chant of the Greek Orthodox rite, continuously transmitted through a written neumatic notation and reformed into its present analytical system in 1814. It is sung by a cantor or small choir over an ison drone held on the mode's base, in one of eight modes with non-tempered intervals, and shifts between fast syllabic delivery for hymns and vastly extended melismatic settings for slow papadic pieces. It differs from Gregorian chant in retaining microtonal modality, the drone, and an unbroken living pedagogy, and from Slavic Orthodox chant by rejecting Western harmonization.

items.name: Orthodox chant (Slavonic obikhod and znamenny)
items.lineage: Church Slavonic liturgical singing of the Russian, Ukrainian and Serbian Orthodox churches, from eleventh-century znamenny neumes through the seventeenth-century shift to staff notation and the nineteenth-century Obikhod harmonizations of Bortniansky, Lvov and Bakhmetev — unaccompanied mixed or male choir in four parts with the melody in the tenor, deep octavist basses, unmetered text-driven declamation in the eight-tone system, and no instruments of any kind.
items.description: The unaccompanied liturgical singing of the Slavonic Orthodox churches, descending from monophonic znamenny chant and standardized in the nineteenth century as four-part Obikhod harmony. Its sound is a wholly a cappella choir with the chant melody carried in an inner voice, close triadic harmony beneath it, and octavist basses extending below the staff, phrased by the prose text rather than by meter. Unlike Byzantine chant it uses functional harmony and a tempered scale with no ison drone; unlike Western choral polyphony it forbids instruments and subordinates counterpoint to syllabic text delivery.

items.name: Coptic hymnody (Alexandrian Tasbeha)
items.lineage: Hymn repertoire of the Coptic Orthodox Church of Egypt, transmitted purely orally by blind cantors of the Institute of Coptic Studies and first transcribed by Ragheb Moftah with Ernest Newlandsmith from the 1920s — long melismatic Coptic-language hymns in free rhythm over a congregational drone, marked by microtonal inflection, extremely extended vocalises on single syllables in pieces such as the Golgotha hymn, and punctuation by hand cymbals and triangle in the metrical Tasbeha praises.
items.description: The chant tradition of the Coptic Orthodox Church, sung in Coptic and Arabic and preserved by memory through generations of cantors until twentieth-century transcription efforts. It is characterized by very long melismas over a few syllables of text, microtonally inflected melody with no harmonization beyond a held congregational drone, and small hand cymbals with triangle marking the pulse of the metrical praise hymns. It differs from Byzantine chant in lacking a notated modal theory and in its heavier percussion, and from Ethiopian zema in language, cymbal type, and the absence of drum and sistrum dance.

items.name: Syro-Aramaic chant (Beth Gazo modal cycle)
