items.lineage: Liturgical chant of the Syriac churches of Tur Abdin, Mosul and Kerala, organized since the sixth-century hymnody of Jacob of Serugh and Ephrem into the eight-mode Beth Gazo treasury codified by Patriarch Yacoub III in 1913 — unaccompanied antiphonal singing in Syriac by two half-choirs, strictly syllabic strophic qole in fixed poetic meters of five, seven or twelve syllables, alternating with free unmetered melismatic sections, over an occasional held drone.
items.description: The chant of the Syriac Orthodox and related Aramaic-language churches of upper Mesopotamia and the Malabar coast, whose melody treasury was fixed in print in the early twentieth century after long oral transmission. It is sung a cappella by two alternating half-choirs in eight modes with Near Eastern microtonal intervals, most of the repertoire being syllabic strophic hymns bound to counted-syllable poetic meters, opening out into freer melismatic passages at key liturgical moments. It differs from Byzantine chant in its syllable-counting metrical hymnody and antiphonal alternation, and from Coptic chant in its shorter melismas and absence of percussion.
exemplars: Beth Gazo of Patriarch Yacoub III
Assyrian Church of the East cantors

items.name: Gregorian dance (chant-sampling dance pop)
items.lineage: European studio pop subgenre of 1990-1997 launched by Michael Cretu's Enigma project in Munich and extended by Era, Gregorian and Deep Forest — plainchant or chant-styled male choir loops laid over slow 90-100 BPM downtempo or mid-tempo four-on-floor breakbeats, sampled shakuhachi and pan-flute leads, reverb-drenched synth pads, and whispered or breathy female vocals doubling the modal chant line in an ambient, heavily gated mix.
items.description: The early-1990s continental European studio genre that placed Gregorian or pseudo-Gregorian male chant over programmed dance beats, defined commercially by Enigma's 1990 debut and its many imitators. It relies on looped monophonic chant, a slow steady kick with reverse-reverb and gated snare, sustained modal pad harmony, and ethnic-flute samples, with the chant treated as texture rather than liturgy. It differs from ambient house by its foregrounded choral hook and song-length pop structure, and from actual plainchant recordings by fixed tempo, tempered pitch, and multitrack studio construction.

items.name: Spirituals (arranged concert tradition)
items.lineage: Concert-arranged branch of the African-American spiritual formed when the Fisk Jubilee Singers took plantation songs on tour from 1871 and codified by Harry T. Burleigh's solo-voice-and-piano settings (1916), Hall Johnson's and William Dawson's choral arrangements, and Roland Hayes and Marian Anderson's recital performances — slow-to-moderate rubato tempos, SATB four-part homophony with dialect text, call-and-response refrains flattened into written verses, and trained legit vocal delivery replacing the ring-shout's foot-stamped polyrhythm.
items.description: The notated, recital-hall form of the African-American spiritual, created in the decades after 1871 as Fisk Jubilee tours and then Burleigh, Hall Johnson and Dawson fixed orally transmitted songs into published SATB and voice-with-piano settings. It keeps the modal-pentatonic melodies and dialect texts but replaces the ring shout's stamping polyrhythm and heterophonic congregational blend with blended choral tone, conductor-controlled rubato and dynamic shaping. That written fixity is what separates it from the congregational spiritual and from later black gospel, which reintroduced improvised soloing, piano vamps and rhythm section.

items.name: Shape-note singing (fasola tradition)
items.lineage: American singing-school practice begun with Little and Smith's The Easy Instructor (1801), which assigned four notated head-shapes to fa-sol-la-mi so rural congregations could sight-read; carried south and west through The Southern Harmony (1835), The Sacred Harp (1844) and the seven-shape Christian Harmony and Stamps-Baxter books, sung a cappella in a hollow square at loud open-throated chest voice, one loud beat-marking arm stroke per singer, dispersed harmony with open fifths and octaves, fuging-tune imitative entries, and the syllables sung through once before the words.
items.description: A notated but wholly participatory American sacred singing tradition running from the 1801 singing schools through the four-shape Sacred Harp and Southern Harmony books and the later seven-shape Southern gospel convention books. Singers sit in a hollow square facing inward, take turns leading, beat time with the arm, sing the solfege syllables before the text, and produce a deliberately unblended, hard-edged full-chest sound over open-fifth dispersed harmony and modal tunes. It differs from choral church music in having no audience, no conductor-shaped dynamics and no vibrato, and from Southern gospel quartet singing in its refusal of instruments and soloists.
exemplars: The Sacred Harp (1844, B.F. White and E.J. King)
Cold Mountain soundtrack Sacred Harp sessions

items.name: Appalachian folk song
items.lineage: Unaccompanied and lightly accompanied song repertoire of the southern Appalachian highlands, descended from British and Scots-Irish balladry and documented by Cecil Sharp and Olive Dame Campbell's 1916-18 collecting and by the Library of Congress field campaigns — free-rhythm or loosely metered delivery, modal Dorian-Mixolydian-Aeolian melodies in a narrow tessitura, hard nasal unornamented-to-lightly-slid solo voice, long strophic narrative texts, and drone accompaniment from mountain dulcimer, banjo or autoharp when instruments appear at all.
items.description: The song side of southern mountain tradition: Child ballads, native murder ballads, lyric love songs and lullabies carried orally in the Blue Ridge, Cumberland and Great Smoky ranges and first systematically transcribed by Cecil Sharp in 1916-18. The defining sound is a single hard nasal voice in modal melody with almost no harmony, phrases stretched or contracted to fit the words rather than a bar count, sometimes over a static dulcimer or banjo drone. It is distinguished from old-time string band and fiddle music by its non-dance, vocal-first orientation and free rhythm, and from commercial country by its lack of chord progression.

items.name: Old-time fiddle
items.lineage: Southern American dance-fiddle tradition crystallized in the 19th century and preserved in regional strains — Round Peak (Galax-Mount Airy, NC), West Virginia's Hammons family, Missouri and Texas breakdown styles — built on short repeated AABB tunes at 110-130 BPM for square dances, cross-tunings such as AEae and GDgd for open-string drone, a short shuffle bowstroke with doubled notes and heavy bow rhythm rather than long slurs, and a strict unvarying groove designed for dancers rather than solos.
items.description: The fiddle-led core of pre-bluegrass southern dance music, played in scordatura cross-tunings that let drone strings ring under the melody and driven by a short choppy shuffle bow that supplies its own percussion. Tunes are two short strains repeated for as long as the dance lasts, with variation confined to bowing and note placement rather than improvised solos. Against bluegrass fiddling it is rhythmically flatter, melodically more static and modal, with no break-taking format; against Irish or Cape Breton fiddling it uses far less finger ornamentation and much more bow-driven drive.

items.name: Clawhammer banjo
items.lineage: Downstroking five-string banjo technique carried from West African plucked-lute practice into the antebellum American South and through blackface minstrelsy's stroke style into Appalachian home and dance music, documented from the 1920s Round Peak players onward — the striking nail of the index or middle finger brushes down onto the melody string while the thumb catches the fifth-string drone on the off-beat, producing a bum-ditty ostinato in open gDGCD, gCGCD or gDGBD tunings on a fretless or open-back gut- or nylon-strung banjo at dance tempo with almost no dynamic variation.
items.description: A downstroke, non-picking banjo idiom in which the hand strikes rather than plucks, so melody, rhythm chop and a constant high fifth-string drone are produced in one motion. Retuning the whole instrument to the key rather than moving up the neck keeps open strings ringing, giving the modal, drone-anchored sound of Round Peak and West Virginia players. It is the direct opposite of Scruggs-style three-finger bluegrass banjo in attack, tuning practice and rhythmic feel, and unlike classic minstrel-era stroke style it is played at dance tempo with a percussive brushing hand.

items.name: String band (Southern pre-war)
items.lineage: Commercially recorded southern American ensemble format of the 1920s-30s in which fiddle carries melody, banjo and guitar supply the bum-ditty and bass-run rhythm, and mandolin or string bass fill out the middle — codified by the 1923-31 Okeh, Victor and Columbia field trips including Ralph Peer's 1927 Bristol sessions, with Gid Tanner's Skillet Lickers, Charlie Poole's North Carolina Ramblers and the Carter Family setting the templates of dance breakdowns, ballads and comic skits at steady 2/4 and 4/4 with heavy bass-string runs on guitar.
items.description: The ensemble that carried old-time music onto commercial 78s between the mid-1920s and the Depression, pairing lead fiddle with rhythm banjo, guitar bass runs and often mandolin or bass fiddle. Recorded in one take into a single electrical microphone in hotel rooms and warehouses, it balances dance breakdowns against vocal ballads and hokum comedy in a way solo fiddle or banjo traditions do not. It differs from bluegrass, which came a generation later, in having no rotating solo breaks, no high tenor stack and no mandolin-chop backbeat; it is the direct ancestor of both bluegrass and early commercial country.
exemplars: Gid Tanner and the Skillet Lickers
Charlie Poole and the North Carolina Ramblers
Dr. Humphrey Bate and the Possum Hunters

items.name: Hot jazz
items.lineage: Small-group jazz of roughly 1923-1935 that moved the New Orleans collective idiom toward the virtuoso solo, codified by King Oliver's Creole Jazz Band (Chicago, 1923) and above all Louis Armstrong's Hot Five and Hot Seven (1925-28) with parallel work by Jelly Roll Morton's Red Hot Peppers and Bix Beiderbecke — 180-240 BPM two-beat or early four-beat swing, front line of cornet, clarinet and trombone trading collective polyphony for chorus-length improvised solos, tenor banjo and tuba rhythm section giving way to guitar and string bass, all cut direct to 78 in three-minute takes.
items.description: The Chicago and New York recording style of the mid-1920s in which the New Orleans front line's simultaneous improvisation gave way to the individually featured solo chorus, with Armstrong's Hot Five sides as the pivot. Ensembles stay small, tempos are brisk with a two-beat banjo-and-tuba pulse modulating toward walking four, and the aesthetic value is the 'hot' individual break rather than ensemble counterpoint. It is distinguished from classic New Orleans jazz by that shift to soloist-centred form, and from the swing era that followed by its small combo size, absence of written section arrangements, and stiffer two-beat rhythm.
exemplars: Louis Armstrong and His Hot Five
Jelly Roll Morton's Red Hot Peppers

items.name: Stride
items.lineage: Harlem solo-piano idiom of the 1920s-40s that turned ragtime's written left hand into a virtuoso improvised engine — James P. Johnson's Carolina Shout (1921) as its founding text, extended by Willie The Lion Smith, Fats Waller and Art Tatum — with the left hand leaping a tenth or more between low bass note on beats 1 and 3 and mid-register chord on 2 and 4 at 200-280 BPM, the right hand running broken-octave and arpeggio figures over 32-bar AABB and popular-song forms, and rent-party cutting contests as the training ground.
items.description: A complete self-accompanying solo piano language developed in Harlem rent parties and theatre pits between the wars, where the leaping left hand supplies bass, chord and pulse while the right improvises at high velocity. It keeps ragtime's sectional forms and steady march pulse but adds swing eighths, blues inflection, richer substitute harmony and improvised variation from chorus to chorus. It is heavier and more metrically strict than the later bebop-derived left-hand comping styles, and unlike boogie-woogie its left hand outlines full harmony rather than a repeated bass ostinato.

items.name: Barrelhouse piano
items.lineage: Rough solo blues piano of southern juke joints, logging and turpentine camps and Texas-Louisiana barrelhouses from roughly 1900, first recorded in the late 1920s through Cow Cow Davenport, Little Brother Montgomery, Roosevelt Sykes and Cripple Clark Bell — heavy percussive left hand alternating walking bass, slow-drag 12/8 shuffle and eight-to-the-bar figures on badly maintained upright pianos, right hand playing blue-note tremolos and crushed seconds, hollered blues vocals over 12-bar forms and constant loud dynamics to carry over a drinking crowd.
items.description: The rough juke-joint ancestor of boogie-woogie and of blues piano generally, played loud and hard on out-of-tune uprights for dancing and drinking crowds in the early-century South. Its markers are a hammered percussive left hand, blue-third crushes and tremolos in the right, 12-bar and slow-drag forms and a shouted vocal, with no concern for dynamic shading. Boogie-woogie narrows it to a fixed eight-to-the-bar bass ostinato and a faster tempo; stride, by contrast, is harmonically fuller and formally tied to popular song rather than the blues.

items.name: Second line
items.lineage: New Orleans street-parade practice in which the hired brass band is the first line and the following neighborhood crowd is the second, formalized through 19th-century Afro-Creole benevolent and social aid and pleasure club funerals and Sunday parades and still weekly in Treme and Central City — bass drum with attached cymbal marking a syncopated three-over-two street beat, snare rolling loose press patterns, sousaphone walking a two-beat bassline, trumpets and trombones riffing hymns and pop tunes over roughly 90-110 BPM, with the crowd's handclaps, whistles and dance steps as an active layer.
items.description: The moving, participatory parade tradition of black New Orleans, in which a brass band leads and the dancing crowd behind it is a constituent part of the music rather than an audience. The rhythmic signature is the bass drummer's syncopated street beat with a cymbal bolted to the drum, against a loose press-roll snare and a two-beat sousaphone, over which horns trade riffs and hymn heads. Distinct from the funeral procession's slow dirge portion that often precedes it, and from studio New Orleans funk, which abstracted this drum pattern into a fixed kit groove.

items.name: New Orleans funk
items.lineage: Studio-band funk that formed in New Orleans between about 1965 and 1975 around Allen Toussaint's writing and production and The Meters as house band, with Eddie Bo, Lee Dorsey and the Neville family in orbit — Ziggy Modeliste's parade-derived kit patterns displacing the backbeat with second-line bass-drum syncopation and ghost-note snare, George Porter Jr's melodic sixteenth-note bass, Leo Nocentelli's clipped single-coil scratch guitar, Toussaint's rolling tresillo piano, mid tempos around 90-105 BPM and short vamp forms with laconic call-and-response vocals.
items.description: A regional funk built in Crescent City studios in the late 1960s and early 1970s, in which the street parade's bass-drum syncopation is transplanted onto the trap kit and everything else is arranged around that displaced pulse. Textures stay sparse and dry, tempos moderate, forms reduced to two-chord vamps, with vocals often understated or absent. It is looser, slower and more polyrhythmically internal than James Brown's one-driven funk, and far less horn-arranged than Memphis soul; its drum patterns became among the most heavily sampled in hip-hop.

items.name: Go-go
items.lineage: Washington DC funk subgenre invented by Chuck Brown and the Soul Searchers in the mid-1970s and built out by Trouble Funk, Rare Essence and E.U. — its defining device is the pocket beat, a swung 4/4 with syncopated snare and heavy cowbell, conga and timbale layer at roughly 96-108 BPM, kept running continuously between songs so a set becomes one unbroken groove, with an MC leading call-and-response crowd chants and roll calls over horn riffs and organ, and the music circulating primarily on live PA-board cassettes rather than studio records.
items.description: A live, city-specific funk that has remained largely local to Washington DC since the mid-1970s, organized around an unbroken percussion-heavy pocket beat that never stops for the length of a performance. Congas, timbales and cowbell sit as high in the mix as the drum kit, and an MC works call-and-response chants and neighborhood roll calls into the groove, making crowd response part of the arrangement. Unlike most funk it is a set-length continuous form rather than discrete songs, and its canonical documents are audience and soundboard cassettes rather than studio albums.
exemplars: Chuck Brown and the Soul Searchers

items.name: Atlanta bass
items.lineage: Atlanta variant of Southern bass music running from the late 1980s through the mid-1990s on labels such as Ichiban, Bassment and So So Def, with Kilo Ali, MC Shy D, Raheem the Dream, DJ Smurf and Ghost Town DJs as its principal makers — 808 kick tuned to long decaying sub tones and Miami-style rapid hi-hat rolls at 130-145 BPM, sparse synth stabs and cheap sampler hits, chanted party and dance-instruction hooks over minimal verses, mixed with extreme low end for car audio and skating-rink systems.
items.description: Atlanta's take on the 808-driven bass music that spread up from Miami in the late 1980s, made for skating rinks, strip clubs and car systems and centred on a long-decay sub kick with rapid hi-hat rolls at uptempo dance speeds. Arrangements are deliberately thin above the low end, with chanted crowd-response hooks and dance-instruction lyrics carrying the record. It is slower and more song-shaped than Miami bass at its fastest, and it is the direct precursor to snap, crunk and Atlanta trap, which inherited its 808 tuning and hi-hat rolls while dropping the tempo.

items.name: Freestyle (Latin Freestyle)
items.lineage: Latino and Italian-American dance-pop that crystallized in New York and Miami between 1983 and 1989 out of Afrika Bambaataa-era electro, built on TR-808 and TR-909 programming at 110-120 BPM with the signature syncopated kick-and-tom 'freestyle break', DX7 and Juno bell/brass stabs, minor-key chord loops, and high, emotive Spanish-inflected female lead vocals with heavy reverb, codified by producers Andy 'Panda' Tripoli, Mickey Garcia and Elvin Molina, Lewis Martineé, and the Fever/Cutting Records twelve-inch economy.
items.description: Freestyle formed in New York and Miami club and radio culture in the mid-1980s, mostly among Puerto Rican, Dominican, Cuban and Italian-American teenagers working out of small twelve-inch labels. Its sound is drum-machine-first: an 808 or 909 kit with a distinctive syncopated tom-and-kick break, glassy FM synth stabs, a synth bassline, and a soaring melodramatic lead vocal about heartbreak. Unlike contemporaneous electro it is fully song-form with verse-chorus pop writing, and unlike Latin house it keeps a broken, non-four-on-the-floor kick and lives at a slower tempo.

items.name: Minneapolis Sound
items.lineage: Minneapolis funk-rock-synth hybrid developed 1979-1986 by Prince and his circle (The Time, Jimmy Jam and Terry Lewis, Jesse Johnson, Alexander O'Neal, Sheila E.), defined by a gated LM-1 / Linn drum machine replacing live drums, staccato single-note synth basslines instead of electric bass, choked rhythm guitar on the sixteenth-note offbeats, Oberheim brass stabs, tempos around 108-124 BPM, and falsetto-to-scream lead vocals over minor-pentatonic funk vamps.
items.description: The Minneapolis Sound is the funk dialect Prince built at his Kiowa Trail and Paisley Park home studios and exported through The Time and the Jam & Lewis production shop between 1979 and the mid-1980s. Its signature is subtractive: no bass guitar, no live drum kit, a hard-gated Linn snare, sparse choked guitar, and glossy Oberheim keyboard pads carrying the harmony, all cut by one or two people playing every part. Compared with contemporaneous P-Funk or Gap Band records it is thinner, colder, more rock-guitar-inflected, and built around synthesized rather than horn-section arrangements.

items.name: Philly Soul
items.lineage: Philadelphia orchestral soul codified 1971-1979 by Kenny Gamble, Leon Huff and arranger Thom Bell at Sigma Sound Studios with the MFSB house band, built on Earl Young's four-on-the-floor kick with open hi-hat on the upbeats (the proto-disco pattern), Ronnie Baker's melodic bass, Norman Harris and Bobby Eli's clean rhythm guitar, sweeping violin and harp lines, Vince Montana's vibraphone, and smooth gospel-tenor or falsetto group vocals at 100-120 BPM.
items.description: Philly soul is the lush, string-heavy studio soul that Gamble, Huff and Thom Bell built at Sigma Sound in the 1970s, with MFSB as an in-house orchestra of forty-plus players. Its defining traits are Earl Young's four-on-the-floor hi-hat pattern that directly seeded disco, ornate violin and harp countermelodies, vibraphone glitter, and restrained, silky vocal groups. Where Memphis soul is dry, sparse and gospel-raw, Philly is wet, arranged, and orchestrally dense, and it stays closer to song form than the extended vamps of the funk that ran alongside it.
exemplars: Billy Paul - 360 Degrees of Billy Paul

items.name: Memphis Soul
items.lineage: Memphis studio soul of 1962-1975 built at Stax on McLemore Avenue and at Hi Records on Willie Mitchell's watch, with Booker T. & the M.G.'s and the Hi Rhythm Section playing behind-the-beat 12/8 and mid-tempo 4/4 grooves, Al Jackson Jr.'s dead-flat backbeat, single-coil rhythm guitar on damped triads, Hammond B-3 pads, and the unison Memphis Horns riffing in place of strings, under raw gospel-shouting or intimate breathy leads.
items.description: Memphis soul is the sound of two racially integrated house bands cutting live to four- and eight-track in a converted cinema and a small Hi studio between the early 1960s and mid-1970s. It is defined by an unhurried, slightly behind-the-beat backbeat, minimal arrangement, muted horn stabs voiced in unison rather than block harmony, and vocals delivered with full gospel weight. It is markedly drier and sparser than Philadelphia or Detroit soul, and its arrangements are riff-based head charts rather than written orchestral scores.
exemplars: Booker T. & the M.G.'s - Green Onions
Sam & Dave - Hold On, I'm Comin'
Ann Peebles - I Can't Stand the Rain

items.name: Chicago Soul
items.lineage: Chicago soul of 1962-1973 developed at Chess, Vee-Jay, OKeh, Brunswick and One-derful by Curtis Mayfield, Carl Davis, Johnny Pate and Willie Henderson, marked by gospel quartet-derived close harmony, Mayfield's open F-sharp tuned guitar with high triadic figures, Latin-tinged bolero and cha-cha rhythm patterns under mid-tempo 12/8 ballads, brass-and-flute charts rather than string beds, and light, high tenor leads carrying civil-rights-era lyric content.
items.description: Chicago soul grew out of the city's Black gospel quartet circuit and its blues-label infrastructure in the 1960s, with Curtis Mayfield and arranger Johnny Pate as the central creative pair. It leans on interlocking three-part male harmony, brightly voiced brass and flute arrangements, Latin percussion figures, and a lighter, more buoyant rhythm feel than Southern soul. Against Detroit's assembly-line pop hooks it is more sermonic and message-driven, and against Memphis it is more harmonically arranged and less raw.
exemplars: Jerry Butler - The Ice Man Cometh

items.name: New Orleans Soul
items.lineage: New Orleans soul of the 1960s built at Cosimo Matassa's studios by Allen Toussaint, Wardell Quezergue and Harold Battiste, carrying second-line street-parade drumming (Smokey Johnson and Zigaboo Modeliste's syncopated, rolling snare-and-bass-drum figures) under rolling triplet piano in the Professor Longhair line, thin punchy horn riffs, and conversational, humorous vocal delivery at mid tempos.
items.description: New Orleans soul is the 1960s R&B produced almost entirely within a few blocks of the French Quarter, with Allen Toussaint writing, arranging and playing piano on most of it. The rhythmic core is the second line: a limping, heavily syncopated snare and bass drum lifted from brass-band street parades, which pulls the groove off the straight backbeat that governs Memphis and Detroit records. Harmonically simple and horn-light, it privileges rhythmic play and wry vocal personality over gospel catharsis or orchestral sweetening.
exemplars: Irma Thomas - Wish Someone Would Care
Aaron Neville - Tell It Like It Is

items.name: Souldies
items.lineage: A listening and revival tradition rather than a production era: slow 1960s soul and doo-wop ballads canonized by Mexican-American lowrider and oldies-radio culture in East Los Angeles, San Antonio and the Southwest from the 1970s onward and later re-recorded by Chicano revival acts since the 2000s — 6/8 and slow 12/8 triplet ballads at 55-75 BPM, tremolo guitar, triplet piano, close male group harmony behind a high aching tenor lead, and heavy plate reverb.
items.description: Souldies is the Chicano oldies canon: slow soul and doo-wop ballads from roughly 1958 to 1972 that became the permanent soundtrack of Southern California and Texas lowrider car culture, sustained by oldies radio, dedication shows and compilation LPs. Musically it favors 12/8 triplet ballads on I-vi-IV-V changes, sighing background harmony, tremolo guitar, and a plaintive high lead. It differs from generic doo-wop in being a curated, later-defined repertoire skewed toward slow soul ballads and sweet soul rather than uptempo jump numbers, and it has since generated new recordings in deliberate period style.
exemplars: Sunny & the Sunliners - Talk to Me
The Delfonics - La-La Means I Love You

items.name: Rare Groove
items.lineage: A UK-defined canon rather than a scene of origin: obscure American funk and soul 45s and album cuts from roughly 1969-1976 excavated by London DJs Norman Jay, Judge Jules and the Kiss FM pirate circuit at warehouse parties in 1985-1988 — mid-tempo 90-105 BPM one-chord funk vamps, dry unprocessed drum breaks, clavinet and Rhodes comping, punchy small-section horns, and gritty gospel-shout vocals, all cut fast and cheaply on small independent labels.
items.description: Rare groove names the body of low-selling early-1970s American funk and soul that London warehouse-party DJs rediscovered in the mid-1980s and turned into a working repertoire, which in turn fed the sample libraries of hip-hop and acid jazz. The typical record is a modestly budgeted, dry-sounding one-chord funk vamp with an exposed drum break, chicken-scratch guitar, and a shouted lead. It is distinguished from mainstream 1970s funk not by musical technique but by obscurity and by the breakbeat-forward, extended-vamp cuts that collectors selected for.
exemplars: Maceo & the Macks - Cross the Tracks
Bobby Byrd - I Know You Got Soul
Charles Wright & the Watts 103rd Street Rhythm Band

items.name: Brit Funk
items.lineage: British Black dance-band funk of 1978-1984 centred on London's Acton, Wembley and Southall youth-club circuit and the Ealing/Crackers jazz-funk dancefloors, made by Light of the World, Hi-Tension, Freeez, Level 42, Beggar & Co and Incognito — jazz-schooled slap and thumb bass, tight brass sections, Rhodes and Prophet pads, Latin percussion, tempos of 105-120 BPM, and a lighter, more instrumental-led approach than American funk with chanted group vocals.
items.description: Brit funk was the first substantial British-made Black dance music, produced between the late 1970s and mid-1980s by young London bands who had grown up on imported American jazz-funk records and on the Caribbean sound-system circuit. Its markers are virtuosic slap bass, crisply arranged horn lines, Latin percussion, and long instrumental sections with vocals used as chanted hooks. Compared with contemporaneous American funk it is brighter, jazzier and less vocal-centred, and it fed directly into the UK's later acid jazz and street soul.
exemplars: Light of the World - Round Trip

items.name: Modern Funk
items.lineage: A Los Angeles-centred 2008-onward revival of early-1980s boogie and synth-funk led by Dâm-Funk, XL Middleton, Zackey Force Funk, Moniquea and the MoFunk and Peanut Butter Wolf label circles — programmed LinnDrum and 808 patterns at 98-112 BPM, Moog and Juno synth basslines in place of electric bass, glassy poly-synth chords, talkbox and vocoder leads, and hazy, deliberately lo-fi analogue mixes produced largely by one person in a home studio.
items.description: Modern funk is a self-described scene that emerged in Los Angeles around 2008, rebuilding the sound of 1981-1985 boogie and synth-funk with vintage drum machines and analogue synths but a contemporary DAW workflow. Tracks are typically the work of a single producer-performer: programmed drums, synth bass, warm pad chords, talkbox hooks, and a soft, low-slung mix. It differs from the boogie originals in its slower, hazier feel and one-man-band construction, and from vaporwave or nu-disco in that it plays the idiom straight rather than as pastiche or sample collage.

items.name: Traditional Funk
items.lineage: The foundational funk idiom codified by James Brown's bands at King Records in Cincinnati and on the road between 1965 and 1974 (Jabo Starks, Clyde Stubblefield, Bootsy Collins, Fred Wesley, Maceo Parker) and paralleled by Dyke & the Blazers and the Meters — single-chord vamps with all parts locked to 'the One', sixteenth-note damped guitar, staccato horn punctuation, syncopated melodic bass, and shouted, percussive lead vocals at 95-115 BPM, cut live to tape with minimal overdubs.
items.description: Traditional funk is the mid-1960s to early-1970s core of the genre, in which R&B song form gave way to extended one-chord vamps with every instrument treated as a percussion part and the downbeat of bar one carrying the accent. James Brown's bands defined the grammar; the Meters and Dyke & the Blazers supplied parallel dialects. It is played live in a room with little studio construction, which separates it from the multitracked, synth-heavy funk of the later 1970s and from P-Funk's psychedelic layering, and its harmonic stasis distinguishes it from the chord-driven soul it grew out of.
exemplars: The J.B.'s - Doing It to Death

items.name: Country Boogie (Hillbilly Boogie)
items.lineage: Hillbilly-boogie idiom that ran from about 1945 to 1955 across Nashville, Cincinnati and the Los Angeles Western scene, codified by the Delmore Brothers, Arthur 'Guitar Boogie' Smith, Merle Travis, Tennessee Ernie Ford and the Maddox Brothers & Rose — eight-to-the-bar boogie-woogie bass lines transferred from piano to slapped doghouse bass and low-string electric guitar, twelve-bar blues form at 150-190 BPM, hot lead breaks traded between electric guitar, harmonica and steel, and brash, half-shouted vocals.
items.description: Country boogie was the postwar collision of boogie-woogie piano bass figures with hillbilly string bands, running from Freddie Slack and the Delmore Brothers' late-1940s sides through the Western swing and West Coast honky-tonk circuits into the early 1950s. Its constant is the eight-to-the-bar walking bass, usually played by slapped upright bass or a guitarist's thumb, under twelve-bar blues verses at brisk dance tempos with instrumental breaks passed around the band. It is faster and bluesier than mainstream honky-tonk, less orchestrated and less jazz-harmonic than Western swing, and it fed directly into rockabilly a few years later.
exemplars: The Delmore Brothers - Freight Train Boogie

items.name: Old West frontier music
items.lineage: Nineteenth-century Anglo-American frontier repertoire of the trans-Mississippi West (roughly 1840s-1890s), carried by soldiers, freighters, miners and trail crews and later salvaged by collectors John A. Lomax (Cowboy Songs, 1910) and N. Howard 'Jack' Thorp — solo or duo performance of parlor sentimental songs, broadside ballads and Anglo-Celtic fiddle tunes on fiddle in cross-tuning, gut-strung parlor guitar and harmonica, sung in an unforced declamatory chest voice with free rubato in ballads and a hard-driving 2/4 or 6/8 in the dance tunes.
items.description: The working repertoire of the nineteenth-century American frontier: trail ballads, camp songs, parlor sentimental numbers and Anglo-Celtic dance tunes played on whatever travelled well — fiddle, cheap parlor guitar, harmonica, banjo. Textures are thin and often unaccompanied, with long strophic narratives sung in free time and a plain, non-vibrato voice. Unlike the later studio-made cowboy Western style it fed, it has no close harmony, no orchestration and no fixed arrangement; what survives comes from cylinder collecting and printed songsters rather than commercial sessions.
exemplars: John A. Lomax, Cowboy Songs and Other Frontier Ballads
N. Howard 'Jack' Thorp, Songs of the Cowboys

items.name: Cowboy Western (singing-cowboy style)
items.lineage: Commercial Western music codified in Hollywood and on network radio from the early 1930s through the late 1940s by Gene Autry, Roy Rogers and the Sons of the Pioneers (Bob Nolan, Tim Spencer, the Farr brothers), taking frontier ballad texts and setting them in slow 3/4 waltzes and easy 4/4 canters at 80-110 BPM over close three- and four-part male harmony, smooth crooned lead, nylon and steel-string guitar, hot jazz-inflected fiddle and, from the 1940s, accordion and light bass, all cut for 78 release and radio transcription.
items.description: The studio-and-screen Western style built in 1930s-40s Los Angeles, where frontier subject matter was reworked into smoothly arranged songs with close male harmony, crooned solo leads and a soft guitar-fiddle-bass backing. Waltz tempos, sustained vocal blend and pictorial lyrics about mesas, tumbleweed and cattle define its sound; the fiddle plays written harmony lines rather than breakdown figures. It differs from honky-tonk in having no drums, no shuffle and no barroom edge, and from actual frontier song in being fully arranged and professionally voiced.

items.name: Jamgrass
items.lineage: American acoustic hybrid that emerged from the 1990s Colorado and southeastern festival circuit — Leftover Salmon, String Cheese Incident and later Yonder Mountain String Band and Greensky Bluegrass — applying jam-band structure to a bluegrass roster: open-ended modal vamps and extended round-robin solos over a bluegrass backbeat at 100-160 BPM, mandolin and banjo played through effects and amplification, drums or percussion added to the traditionally drumless lineup, and songs stretched from three minutes to fifteen with segues between them.
items.description: A festival-born fusion of bluegrass instrumentation with jam-band form, consolidated in Colorado during the 1990s. Tunes function as launch pads: heads give way to long modal stretches where mandolin, banjo and fiddle trade choruses over a vamp, often with a drum kit and amplified or effected acoustic instruments that traditional bluegrass excludes. It is looser and more rock-influenced than progressive bluegrass, and unlike bluegrass proper it prizes groove continuity and segue over tight breaks and high-lonesome trio harmony.

items.name: Neo-traditional bluegrass
items.lineage: Conservative revival strain that took shape in the mid-1970s and 1980s around the Johnson Mountain Boys, Larry Sparks and Del McCoury, deliberately restoring the 1946-48 Monroe-Flatt-Scruggs template — five-string banjo in Scruggs three-finger roll, chopping mandolin backbeat, walking upright bass, no drums, and tenor-above-lead trio harmony sung high and hard into a single central condenser at 130-180 BPM, with modern recording fidelity but period repertoire, tempos and vocal placement.
items.description: A revivalist bluegrass practice that emerged in the 1970s-80s and consciously rejects the additions of newgrass: no drums, no electric bass, no jazz harmony, and strict adherence to the first-generation instrumental roles and repertoire. Its signature is a piercing high tenor stacked above a hard-driving lead, banjo rolls and mandolin chop locked to a fast steady backbeat, and ensembles that still work a single microphone on stage. Distinct from jamgrass and progressive bluegrass in structure and from 1940s originals only in recording clarity.

items.name: Instrumental bluegrass
items.lineage: Voiceless branch of bluegrass established by Earl Scruggs's banjo showpieces and Bill Monroe's mandolin instrumentals in the late 1940s and extended from the 1960s by Kenny Baker, Tony Rice, Bela Fleck and Sam Bush — tunes built on fiddle-tune and blues forms taken at 140-220 BPM, with banjo roll, mandolin cross-picking, flatpicked guitar lead and long fiddle shuffles trading breaks over an unamplified bass-and-chop rhythm section, and no sung text at all.
items.description: Bluegrass stripped of singing, where the whole weight falls on the instrumental break. Forms are short and cyclic — fiddle-tune AABB or twelve-bar blues — cycled while banjo, mandolin, fiddle and flatpicked guitar take successive solos at high tempo over a chop-and-walking-bass pulse. It differs from jamgrass in staying inside strict tune form rather than opening into modal vamping, and from newgrass in keeping the harmonic language diatonic and the roster acoustic.

items.name: Sean-nós singing (Conamara tradition)
items.lineage: Unaccompanied solo Irish-language song tradition of Conamara, west Munster and Donegal, documented from the early twentieth century and carried into the recording era by Joe Heaney and the Oireachtas na Gaeilge competitions — long strophic ballads and love songs delivered with no fixed pulse, the line breathing to the text, heavily ornamented with melismatic runs, glottal stops and nasalisation, with intonation that departs from equal temperament, sung inward at conversational volume and without vibrato.
items.description: The unaccompanied Irish-language solo song of the western Gaeltachtaí, sung entirely without instruments, harmony or metric pulse. Its identity lies in ornamentation — melismatic turns, glottal articulations, sliding intonation and variation of the melody at every verse — and in a restrained, undramatised delivery that puts the narrative text first. It is more melodically elaborate and rhythmically free than Scots ballad singing, and its non-tempered intervals separate it from any revival arrangement with accompaniment.

items.name: Puirt-à-beul (Gaelic mouth music)
items.lineage: Scottish Gaelic 'mouth tunes' from the Hebrides and Highlands, documented in the nineteenth century and sustained through Cape Breton and the Mòd — dance tunes (strathspey, reel, jig) sung instead of played, using nonsense-heavy or bawdy Gaelic verse chosen for consonant attack, delivered at strict dance tempo (reels around 110-120 BPM in cut time) with the Scotch snap and the strathspey dotted figure articulated by the tongue, usually solo or in unison with foot-tapping and no instruments.
items.description: Gaelic vocal dance music from the Hebrides and Cape Breton, sung to supply reels, jigs and strathspeys when no piper or fiddler was present. The words are chosen for their percussive syllables rather than their sense, so the voice functions as a rhythm instrument, snapping the strathspey dotted figures and driving strict dance tempo with foot-tapping. Unlike sean-nós or Gaelic ballad singing, which are free in time and richly ornamented, puirt-à-beul is metrically rigid, fast and functionally dance music.

items.name: Jig and reel (Irish dance tune repertoire)
items.lineage: Core Irish instrumental dance repertoire consolidated in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries and fixed in print by O'Neill's Music of Ireland (1903), then standardised for session play by the 1960s Ceoltóirí Chualann and Tulla/Kilfenora circles — reels in cut time at 110-120 BPM and double jigs in 6/8 at 120-130, cast in binary AABB form with each part eight bars, played heterophonically in unison by fiddle, flute, whistle, box and pipes with cuts, rolls and crans supplying the ornament and the bodhrán or foot marking the pulse.
items.description: The backbone tune types of Irish traditional music — the duple-time reel and the 6/8 double jig — played in eight-bar AABB strains, repeated and strung into sets of two or three tunes. Ensemble texture is heterophonic unison rather than harmonised: everyone plays the melody, and individuality shows in ornamentation (cuts, rolls, crans, triplets) and phrasing rather than in solos. It differs from the ceilidh band in lacking a fixed rhythm section and arrangement, and from slow airs in its strict, unyielding dance pulse.

items.name: Céilí / ceilidh band music
items.lineage: Social dance band format standardised in Ireland and Scotland from the 1920s-30s, driven by the Gaelic League's céilí and the Scottish dance-band broadcasts of Jimmy Shand — fixed sets of jigs, reels, polkas and Strip-the-Willow figures played at unvarying dance tempo by a front line of fiddles, accordion and flute or whistle over piano vamp, string bass and drum kit, with arranged unison melody, hard on-beat piano chording and tunes counted in strict eight-bar blocks to match caller-directed figures.
items.description: The amplified social-dance band of Ireland and Scotland, built in the interwar decades to fill halls rather than kitchens. A unison melody front line of fiddles, accordion and whistle is nailed to a rhythm section of vamping piano, bass and drum kit playing rock-steady dance tempo, with tune sets pre-arranged to fit the length of a called figure. It is louder, more regimented and more harmonically fixed than a pub session, and unlike concert-stage folk groups it is functional music subordinate to the dancers.

items.name: Irish tenor banjo playing
items.lineage: Melody style developed on the four-string tenor banjo in Irish-American dance bands of the 1920s (Mike Flanagan of the Flanagan Brothers) and brought back into Irish session play by Barney McKenna of The Dubliners in the 1960s — the instrument tuned GDAE an octave below the fiddle, played with a plectrum in single-note lines with tight triplet ornamentation replacing the fiddle's rolls, short sustain from the skin head, and reels and jigs taken at full session tempo as a percussive lead voice.
items.description: A distinct plectrum melody idiom on the four-string tenor banjo, tuned GDAE and pitched an octave under the fiddle, established by Irish-American dance bands and popularised by Barney McKenna. Because the skin-headed instrument has almost no sustain, ornamentation shifts from fiddle-style rolls to fast plectrum triplets and the line reads as half-percussive. It sits inside the same jig-and-reel repertoire as the pub session but is defined by attack, tone and the ornament vocabulary the instrument forces, and shares nothing with five-string bluegrass banjo technique.

items.name: Uilleann piping (Irish pipe tradition)
items.lineage: Irish bellows-blown pipe tradition developed from the union pipes of the late eighteenth century and codified by the Taylor and Rowsome making families and by Leo Rowsome, Willie Clancy and Séamus Ennis in the twentieth century — a two-octave chanter in D over three drones and three regulators, played seated on the knee with staccato 'tight' or legato 'open' fingering, crans and popping, supplying dance tunes at session tempo and free-time slow airs shaped to the sung Irish-language line.
items.description: The bellows-blown Irish pipes, quieter and more chromatic than the Highland bagpipe, playing a two-octave chanter over sustained drones with regulators used for chordal punctuation. Two contrasted styles govern the repertoire: crisply staccato 'tight' or 'close' fingering with crans and popping in dance tunes, and legato, heavily ornamented free-time slow airs modelled on sean-nós vocal phrasing. Its indoor volume, second-octave range and regulator harmony distinguish it sharply from Highland and border piping.

items.name: Scottish fiddle tradition
items.lineage: Scottish violin tradition codified in eighteenth-century printed collections by Niel and Nathaniel Gow, William Marshall and James Scott Skinner and sustained through Shetland, North-East and Cape Breton streams — built on the strathspey with its dotted rhythms and inverted 'Scotch snap', plus reels, jigs, marches and free-time slow airs and laments, played with a driving detached bow, double-stop drones on open strings and pipe-derived grace figures, at reel tempos near 120 BPM.
items.description: The fiddle music of Scotland and its Cape Breton diaspora, whose signature form is the strathspey — a duple tune driven by dotted figures and the short-long Scotch snap, executed with a sharply articulated bow. Alongside it sit reels, jigs, marches and unmetered pibroch-influenced airs and laments, with open-string drones and pipe-style grace notes borrowed from the bagpipe. It differs from Irish fiddling in bow attack, snap rhythm and the strathspey itself, and from the North-East concert style in favouring dance function over Skinner's virtuoso showpieces.

items.name: Scottish Gaelic folk song
items.lineage: Gàidhlig song tradition of the Highlands, Hebrides and Cape Breton, collected by Frances Tolmie, Marjory Kennedy-Fraser and the School of Scottish Studies from the 1900s onward — waulking songs (òrain luaidh) with call-and-response leader and chorus locked to the beat of cloth on the board, plus laments, love songs, milking songs and precented psalm lines, sung mostly unaccompanied in narrow-range pentatonic and hexatonic modes with vocable refrains and modest ornamentation, and since the 1970s arranged with clàrsach, guitar and fiddle by revival groups.
items.description: Song in Scottish Gaelic from the Hebrides and Highlands, historically tied to work and community: waulking songs with a soloist answering a fixed vocable chorus over the rhythm of fulling tweed, along with laments, love songs, lullabies and the long unmetered lines of Gaelic psalm precenting. Melodies are narrow-range and modal, delivery is plain and communal rather than declamatory, and vocable refrains carry as much weight as the text. Compared with Irish sean-nós it is far more often choral, more metrically regular and much less ornamented.

items.name: Pibroch (ceòl mòr Highland piping)
items.lineage: The Scottish Highland 'great music' of the Great Highland bagpipe, codified by the MacCrimmon hereditary pipers of Skye and the MacArthurs from roughly 1600 onward and fixed in the Campbell Canntaireachd and Angus MacKay's 1838 collection — a slow ground (ùrlar) in free, elastic pulse followed by fixed variation sets (siubhal, taorluath, crunluath) built from named grace-note gestures over an unbroken two-octave-plus-drone texture, typically fifteen to twenty minutes for a single tune.
items.description: Ceòl mòr, the classical repertoire of the Great Highland bagpipe, took its present shape in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries around hereditary piping families in Skye and the Western Isles and was frozen into notation in the nineteenth century. A single tune states a slow modal ground over the fixed drone-and-chanter sound world, then rebuilds it through obligatory variation levels in which the melody note count stays constant while embellishment doubles and redoubles. It is distinguished from ceòl beag — the marches, strathspeys and reels of competition and pipe-band piping — by its unmeasured, breathing pulse and its enormous single-tune duration.

items.name: Scottish smallpipe music
items.lineage: Bellows-blown Lowland and Border pipe music revived in Scotland from the late 1970s and early 1980s — Colin Ross's 1981 cylindrical-bore smallpipe design gave players a quiet, indoor, A-pitched drone instrument that could sit in tune with fiddle, cittern and accordion, so the repertoire became the session tunes of the Borders and Lowlands (jigs, reels, hornpipes, slow airs) played at dance tempo with lighter, less obligatory gracing than Highland practice.
items.description: A late-twentieth-century revival tradition built on the reconstructed bellows-blown smallpipe and its louder cousin the Border pipe, both keyed to concert pitch so they can play with other instruments — the decisive break from the Highland pipe, which sits sharp and alone. The sound is soft, sustained and mid-range, with a two- or three-drone bed under strathspey, jig and reel repertoire taken from Lowland manuscripts and modern composition. Against ceòl mòr it is fast, metrical, ensemble-oriented and largely a recording-studio and folk-club music rather than an outdoor solo one.

items.name: Orkney and Shetland folk
items.lineage: Northern-isles fiddle tradition of the Norse-settled Scottish archipelago, collected and taught into the modern era by Tom Anderson from the 1940s onward — Shetland reels and 'trowie' tunes with heavy ringing-string double stops and off-beat bowing, wedding and Up Helly Aa dance repertoire, Orkney's slower strathspey-inflected airs, backed by vamping piano or guitar rather than by pipes.
items.description: The fiddle music of Orkney and Shetland, shaped by Norn-era Scandinavian contact and by nineteenth-century Scottish dance repertoire, and preserved through Tom Anderson's collecting and his Shetland schools fiddle teaching from 1973. Shetland playing is driving and rhythmic, full of open-string ringing, sustained double stops and short crisp bow strokes for reels; Orkney tends slower and more song-like. Unlike mainland Highland tradition it is fiddle-and-piano rather than pipe-led, and its modal colouring and drone double stops sit closer to Norwegian practice than to Irish.

items.name: Northumbrian folk
items.lineage: Border-county tradition of north-east England centred on the closed-chanter Northumbrian smallpipes standardised in the nineteenth century by the Reid family of North Shields and carried forward by the Northumbrian Pipers' Society from 1928 — staccato detached-note pipe variation sets, hornpipes and rants at dance tempo, Tyneside industrial songs and Border ballads sung with plain unornamented delivery, backed by fiddle, concertina and melodeon.
items.description: The regional music of Northumberland and Tyneside, defined sonically by the Northumbrian smallpipes — bellows-blown, keyed, and uniquely able to stop the chanter dead, giving a crisp staccato line no other bagpipe produces. Its dance repertoire runs to rants and hornpipes rather than the reels of Scotland, and its song side runs from the Border ballads to Tyneside music-hall and pit songs. It is quieter, more even-tempered and more indoor than either Highland piping or Irish session music.

items.name: Traditional English folk
items.lineage: The vernacular song and dance repertoire of rural England as documented by Cecil Sharp, Ralph Vaughan Williams and the Folk-Song Society from 1898 and re-recorded from source singers in the 1950s by Peter Kennedy and Alan Lomax — unaccompanied strophic ballads in Dorian and Mixolydian modes sung in a straight, forward-placed voice with minimal vibrato, plus melodeon- and fiddle-led morris and country-dance tunes and pub harmony carolling.
items.description: The song tradition carried by English agricultural and fishing communities, collected in two great waves — the Edwardian manuscript collectors and the postwar tape collectors who caught singers like Harry Cox and Sam Larner in their own kitchens. Its core sound is a solo unaccompanied voice delivering long narrative ballads to a repeating modal tune, with ornament confined to small slides and note-splitting rather than the melisma of Gaelic sean-nós. It differs from the 1960s britfolk revival that grew out of it by having no guitar, no arrangement and no stage.

items.name: Cornish folk
items.lineage: Traditional music of Cornwall documented from the 1820s Sandys and Gilbert carol collections and revived from the 1970s alongside the Cornish-language movement — four-part west-gallery Christmas carols sung by male-heavy village choirs, harbour shanties from the Port Isaac and Padstow coast, the Furry Dance and Obby Oss processional tunes on melodeon and accordion, and Kernewek-language song set to modal fiddle and pipe accompaniment.
items.description: The music of Cornwall as it survived in carol-singing, mining and fishing communities and was rebuilt from the 1970s by the Celtic-revival movement around Lowender Peran and the Cornish Language Board. Its most distinctive strand is loud unaccompanied male-led harmony — pub carols and shanties sung in thirds and open fifths with a bass line — alongside processional dance tunes tied to specific calendar customs in Helston and Padstow. Compared with English folk further east it is more choral and more festival-anchored, and compared with Breton folk it lacks the kan ha diskan call-and-response form despite the shared language family.

items.name: Welsh folk
items.lineage: Traditional music of Wales preserved through the eisteddfod system and the Welsh Folk Song Society (founded 1908) — cerdd dant penillion in which a singer improvises a counter-melody against a harper's set tune, plygain pre-dawn Christmas carols sung in unaccompanied three- and four-part male harmony, and modal dance tunes for triple harp, crwth and fiddle recovered from eighteenth-century manuscripts such as Blodeugerdd and the Morris brothers' collections.
items.description: Welsh traditional music was carried more by institutions — chapel, eisteddfod, harp societies — than by isolated rural singers, which gives it an unusually harmonic and part-singing character for a Celtic tradition. Cerdd dant is its signature: the triple harp plays a fixed melody while the voice weaves a different, metrically offset line above it, a form of controlled improvisation with no close parallel elsewhere. The plygain carol repertoire adds dense unaccompanied male harmony sung in parish churches before daybreak, and the instrumental side centres on the three-rank Welsh triple harp and the bowed lyre crwth rather than on pipes.

items.name: Manx folk
items.lineage: Traditional music of the Isle of Man, collected by Dr John Clague and the Gill brothers in the 1890s and revived from the 1920s by Mona Douglas and again from the 1970s around the Yn Chruinnaght festival — Manx Gaelic carvals and lullabies sung in a plain narrow-range style, plus jigs, reels and the distinctive Manx hop-tu-naa and dance tunes played on fiddle, whistle and harp with light accompaniment.
items.description: The smallest of the Gaelic traditions, nearly extinguished by the collapse of Manx as a spoken language and reconstructed largely from the 1890s Clague and Gill manuscripts. Song repertoire is dominated by long carvals, ballads and cradle songs with short repeating tunes and syllabic, lightly ornamented delivery; the dance side draws on jigs and reels sharing stock with Ireland and Scotland but with local hop-tu-naa and Mollag Band material. Modern Manx bands play it with contemporary session instrumentation, so the tradition today is audibly a revival rather than a continuous line.

items.name: Galician folk
items.lineage: Traditional music of Galicia in north-west Spain, collected from the 1920s by the Seminario de Estudos Galegos and revived from the mid-1970s by Milladoiro and the pandereteira singing groups — the two-drone gaita galega leading muiñeiras in fast 6/8 and alalás in free rhythm, driven by rows of women singing in nasal parallel harmony over hand-struck pandeiretas and bombo, with hurdy-gurdy and later bouzouki filling harmony.
items.description: Galician traditional music pairs a loud outdoor bagpipe repertoire — muiñeira, alborada, pasodoble — with an equally loud women's tambourine-and-voice tradition that carries the older song layer. The pandeireta groups sing in strident parallel thirds and seconds over an insistent tambourine pattern, a texture quite unlike anything in Anglo-Celtic music despite the shared 'Celtic' branding of the 1980s revival. Against Asturian practice next door the gaita galega sits at a different pitch and the percussion is heavier and more central.

items.name: Asturian folk
items.lineage: Traditional music of Asturias in northern Spain, documented by Eduardo Martínez Torner's 1920 Cancionero musical and revived from the 1980s by Llan de Cubel and the Xixón folk scene — the single-drone gaita asturiana in B-flat playing giraldillas and muñeiras against snare-and-bass-drum tamboriteru, and the tonada or asturianada, a solo unmetred song delivered at full chest voice with long melismatic ornaments and heavy portamento.
items.description: Asturian tradition runs on two separate engines: the paired gaita and drum that supply outdoor processional and dance music, and the tonada, a fiercely competitive solo vocal art judged at concursos, sung without accompaniment in free rhythm with sustained high notes and elaborate melismatic descents. The gaita asturiana carries one drone rather than the Galician two and is pitched higher, giving a brighter and thinner sound. The tonada's rhetorical, near-shouted intensity marks it off sharply from the collective tambourine singing of Galicia.

items.name: Jota aragonesa
items.lineage: The fast triple-metre dance-song of Aragón in north-east Spain, crystallised in the nineteenth century around Zaragoza and Calatayud and institutionalised through the certamen oficial de jota from 1912 — brisk 3/8 or 3/4 at roughly 130-160 beats per minute, a rondalla of bandurrias, laúdes and guitars strumming a hard I-V-I ostinato, castanets on the dance, and coplas of four octosyllabic lines sung at extreme volume in a high open chest register with long held cadential notes.
items.description: The Aragonese jota is the loudest and most athletic of the Spanish regional jotas, a competition music as much as a village one, judged on vocal power and on the leaping, high-kneed dance. Musically it is harmonically plain — an unchanging tonic-dominant strum from the plucked-string rondalla — with all the interest thrown onto the singer's ornamented, forcefully projected copla and onto the dancers' castanets. It differs from the Valencian and Castilian jotas in tempo and in the sheer declamatory pressure of the vocal delivery, and from flamenco in being metrically square, major-mode and non-modal.

items.name: Sevillanas
items.lineage: Andalusian dance-song derived from the Castilian seguidilla and fixed in its modern four-copla form in nineteenth-century Seville, becoming the mass repertoire of the Feria de Abril and the El Rocío pilgrimage — a bright 3/4 at about 120-140 beats per minute in four short linked coplas each danced as a separate figure, with strummed nylon-string guitar rasgueado, palmas, castanets and paired male-female or group vocals in parallel thirds.
items.description: Sevillanas is the social dance music of Andalusian fairs and romerías, sold in enormous quantities on record every spring since the 1970s by groups like Cantores de Híspalis and Los Romeros de la Puebla. Its form is rigid: four coplas of identical length, each with a fixed introduction and a fixed stopping point matched to a memorised dance figure, in bright major or minor with conventional tonal harmony. Although it uses flamenco guitar technique and palmas, it is not flamenco — it has no twelve-beat compás, no cante jondo vocal production and essentially no improvisation.

items.name: Cante flamenco (the vocal art)
items.lineage: The sung core of flamenco, formed among Andalusian Roma and payo communities in Seville, Jerez and Cádiz in the early nineteenth century, professionalised in the cafés cantantes from the 1860s and canonised by Antonio Mairena's mid-twentieth-century recordings and the 1922 Concurso de Cante Jondo — palo-specific twelve-beat and free-rhythm forms sung in a rasping, high-pressure chest voice with microtonal Phrygian melisma over guitar falsetas, palmas and jaleo shouts.
items.description: Cante is the centre of flamenco — the guitar and dance historically served the singer, not the reverse. Its repertoire divides into palos, each with its own compás, mode and emotional register, from the unmetred martinete and toná to the twelve-beat soleá, siguiriya and bulería, and the singer works a fixed set of inherited melodic tercios, bending pitches microtonally around the Phrygian cadence and stretching phrases against the clap pattern. What separates it from the wider flamenco spectacle and from Andalusian light music like sevillanas is the vocal production itself: constricted, hoarse, deliberately effortful, and evaluated on afición rather than beauty of tone.

items.name: Flamenco guitar (toque solo tradition)
items.lineage: Andalusian solo guitar practice (toque) that separated from song accompaniment in Seville, Jerez and Madrid cafés cantantes around 1900 and was codified by Ramón Montoya, Niño Ricardo and Sabicas before Paco de Lucía's 1970s rearmament — cypress or rosewood nylon-string guitar with low action and golpeador, played rasgueado, picado, alzapúa and tremolo over the twelve-beat compás of soleá, seguiriya, bulería and tangos at 60-220 BPM, with palmas and cajón marking accents and falsetas alternating with strummed compás.
items.description: The instrumental branch of flamenco, in which the guitar carries a full palo on its own rather than accompanying a cantaor. Defined by the percussive golpe on the tapping plate, thumb-driven alzapúa, machine-gun picado runs, and rasgueado strumming that articulates the twelve-beat compás, with composed falsetas strung between passages of pure rhythm. Distinguished from cante-led flamenco by the absence of a singer and from classical nylon-string repertoire by its oral transmission, percussive right hand and compás-bound rather than bar-line phrasing.

items.name: Pasodoble
items.lineage: Spanish two-step march that crystallized in early-nineteenth-century military bands and became the fixed music of the bullring paseíllo and of village banda repertoire, codified by Pascual Marquina ('España Cañí', 1921) and Santiago Lope — brisk 2/4 at roughly 110-130 BPM, bass drum and cymbal on the beat with off-beat brass punches, a strident cornet or trumpet melody often in Phrygian-inflected minor, dulzaina or clarinet counterlines, and a contrasting trio in the parallel major.
items.description: A Spanish march form for wind band, fixed as ceremonial music for bullfights, processions and municipal fiestas from the nineteenth century onward and later exported as a ballroom dance. Its sonic signature is a hard 2/4 tread from bass drum and low brass, snappy off-beat accompaniment, and a piercing trumpet or dulzaina cantabile that borrows the Andalusian cadence without flamenco's rhythmic elasticity. Distinguished from the sardana by its fixed march meter and brass-band scoring rather than cobla instrumentation, and from copla by being wholly instrumental and notated.

items.name: Copla (Spanish copla andaluza)
items.lineage: Spanish popular-song genre built in Seville and Madrid theatres of the 1930s-40s by the writing team of Rafael de León, Antonio Quintero and Manuel Quiroga and sung by Concha Piquer, Estrellita Castro, Juanita Reina and later Rocío Jurado — strophic narrative lyrics of thwarted love, jealousy and social scandal declaimed in a chest-heavy, near-spoken Andalusian delivery, over pit orchestra with guitar, castanets and pasodoble or zambra rhythms at moderate tempo, each verse capped by a rubato held note.
items.description: Spain's mid-century theatrical popular song, associated with the revue stage and, after 1939, with Franco-era mass entertainment, though its lyrics repeatedly smuggled in unsanctioned female desire and marginal lives. The sound is an orchestrated Andalusian idiom: guitar and castanets riding a pasodoble or zambra pulse under a big, unamplified-sounding contralto that swings between declamation and melisma. Distinguished from flamenco cante by its notated composition, fixed strophic form and orchestral backing, and from zarzuela by its single-song rather than theatrical-score scale.

items.name: Zarzuela género chico (one-act Madrid tradition)
items.lineage: The one-act, hour-long branch of Spanish lyric theatre that dominated Madrid's Teatro Apolo from the 1870s to about 1910, codified by Federico Chueca ('La Gran Vía', 1886), Tomás Bretón ('La verbena de la Paloma', 1894) and Ruperto Chapí — spoken dialogue alternating with sung numbers built on urban Madrid dance rhythms (chotis, mazurka, habanera, pasodoble, seguidillas), scored for small pit orchestra with prominent clarinet and cornet, chorus of neighbourhood types, and a comic-declamatory vocal style close to speech.
items.description: Género chico is the short, cheap, hourly-turnover form of zarzuela that made Madrid working-class street life its subject during the teatro por horas boom of the late nineteenth century. Musically it is a chain of self-contained dance numbers — chotis, habanera, seguidilla, pasodoble — for pit orchestra and chorus, framed by spoken Madrid slang, with singing that stays close to declamation rather than operatic line. It differs from the three-act zarzuela grande in scale and from Italian operetta in its reliance on specifically Spanish urban dance rhythms and costumbrista dialogue.
exemplars: Tomás Bretón - La verbena de la Paloma
Gerónimo Giménez - La boda de Luis Alonso

items.name: Tuna universitaria (Spanish student serenade troupe)
items.lineage: Iberian university student serenading tradition descended from the medieval sopistas of Salamanca and Coimbra and reorganized as faculty tunas from the late nineteenth century — plucked bandurria and laúd melody lines doubled in thirds above strummed guitars, pandereta and hand-clapping, sung in unison male chorus in cloaks and beribboned capes, repertoire of jotas, boleros, pasodobles and serenading coplas at brisk 3/4 or 2/4, performed outdoors in courtyards and beneath windows.
items.description: A living student-fraternity music of Spanish and Portuguese universities in which a cloaked troupe performs serenades in streets and courtyards. Its sound rests on the tremolando bandurria and laúd carrying the tune in parallel thirds over massed strummed guitars, with pandereta and clapping supplying a light dance pulse and a rough unison male chorus on the refrains. Unlike the estudiantina concert ensembles it grew from, the tuna is amateur, ceremonial and outdoor, and unlike the Portuguese fado de Coimbra it is collective, extroverted and dance-derived rather than solitary and melancholic.

items.name: Catalan folk (música tradicional catalana)
items.lineage: Traditional music of Catalonia, the Balearics and Valencia documented by the Obra del Cançoner Popular de Catalunya from 1922 and revived from the 1970s by Grup de Folk and later Coetus and Sílvia Pérez Cruz — modal strophic songs (cançons de treball, goigs, nadales, havaneres), the outdoor gralla-and-timbal cobla de tres quartans for castells and dances, and dance repertoire of ball de bastons, jota and contrapàs in duple and 6/8, sung in open-throated unison Catalan with tambourine, accordion and guitar accompaniment.
items.description: The vernacular song and dance repertoire of the Catalan-speaking lands, spanning work songs, carols and goigs, coastal havaneres sung by male groups, and the shrill outdoor gralla-and-drum music that accompanies castells and stick dances. Voices are typically unison and unornamented, harmonic language is modal with frequent Phrygian and Aeolian colouring, and instrumental accompaniment stays light — guitar, accordion, tambourine — except in the loud outdoor genres. It differs from the sardana in being neither cobla-scored nor fixed-choreography, and from the Nova Cançó in being anonymous and orally transmitted rather than authored protest song.
exemplars: Obra del Cançoner Popular de Catalunya (Higini Anglès field archive)

items.name: Nova Cançó (Catalan singer-songwriter movement, 1960s)
items.lineage: Catalan-language song movement launched in Barcelona in 1961 by the Els Setze Jutges collective around Miquel Porter, Josep Maria Espinàs and Delfí Abella, modelled on French chanson rive gauche and radicalized by Raimon's 'Al vent' (1963) — solo voice with nylon-string guitar or piano, later widened to string and wind arrangements, setting Catalan and Valencian poetry (Espriu, Estellés) in strophic through-built forms with declamatory, non-vibrato delivery and slow crescendo builds toward anthemic refrains.
items.description: An authored singer-songwriter movement that used the Catalan language itself as political statement under Franco, spreading from Barcelona to Valencia and Mallorca through the 1960s and 70s and recording heavily in Paris and Barcelona studios. Its sound is chanson-derived: an unornamented, forward, almost recited baritone or alto over fingerpicked nylon guitar or piano, with orchestral strings and winds added for the long-form anthems. It is distinguished from anonymous Catalan folk by its literary authorship and studio arrangement, and from Castilian cantautor song by its minority-language repertoire and Mediterranean-poetic sources.
exemplars: Joan Manuel Serrat - Ara que tinc vint anys

items.name: Basque folk (Euskal Herriko musika tradizionala)
items.lineage: Traditional music of the Basque Country on both sides of the Pyrenees, catalogued by Resurrección María de Azkue and Aita Donostia in the 1910s-20s and revived from the 1970s by Oskorri and Kepa Junkera — narrow-range modal melodies sung in Euskara, txistu-and-tamboril one-man pipe-and-drum for processional dances, double-reed alboka with circular breathing, txalaparta plank duo in interlocking irregular strokes, and dance repertoire (aurresku, fandango, arin-arin) alternating 6/8 and 2/4 with strong stepped accents.
items.description: The pre-commercial dance, processional and song repertoire of Euskal Herria, performed largely outdoors at romerías, village squares and festival processions. Its most identifiable timbres are the three-hole txistu played with one hand while the same player strikes the tamboril, the raucous horn-belled alboka sustained by circular breathing, and the txalaparta, two players hammering wooden planks in interlocking asymmetric patterns. Compared with Basque bertsolaritza it is instrumental and dance-bound rather than improvised verse, and compared with Galician or Asturian piping traditions it lacks bagpipe drones and favours stepped, irregular accentuation.
exemplars: Resurrección María de Azkue - Cancionero popular vasco

items.name: Trikiti (Basque diatonic accordion dance music)
items.lineage: Basque dance music built on the diatonic button accordion introduced to Gipuzkoa and Bizkaia by Alpine railway and forestry workers in the 1880s, formalized as the trikitixa-and-pandero duo and modernized from the 1980s by Joseba Tapia, Elena Bergara and Kepa Junkera — fast fandango in 6/8 followed by arin-arin in 2/4 at 130-170 BPM, right-hand melody in parallel thirds with bisonoric bellows articulation, left-hand tonic-dominant bass, tambourine keeping continuous rolls and thumb accents, with optional shouted irrintzi and sung couplets.
items.description: Trikiti is the accordion-and-tambourine duo music of Basque romerías, weddings and village dances, once condemned from the pulpit as the 'devil's bellows' and now a competition and festival tradition with its own championships. The sound is relentless and bright: bisonoric diatonic accordion running melody in thirds with the push-pull articulation of the bellows, over a driving pandero that shifts the pair from lilting 6/8 fandango to the sprint of arin-arin. It differs from Basque txistu and alboka music in being harmonized and chordal, and from French or Italian folk accordion styles in its fixed fandango-arin-arin pairing and tambourine-only percussion.

items.name: Polyphonies corses (Corsican ensemble polyphony)
items.lineage: The staged and recorded ensemble form of Corsican polyphony that emerged from the 1970s riacquistu cultural revival through Canta u Populu Corsu and was refined by A Filetta, Tavagna and Barbara Furtuna — three to seven male voices in close-position chords derived from paghjella practice, with bassu, secunda and terza roles expanded, cadences on unstable seconds and near-just thirds, heavy melismatic ricuccata ornamentation, straight non-vibrato tone, and slow free-pulse declamation of sacred Latin-Corsican and secular texts in resonant stone acoustics.
items.description: The concert-hall and record-label expression of Corsican vocal polyphony, developed by revival ensembles who took village paghjella and confraternity chant onto festival stages and into church-acoustic recordings from the late 1970s onward. Its markers are tight clustered male voices tuned toward beatless just intervals, floating unmeasured pulse, and profuse melismatic ornament on the upper terza line, captured with long natural reverb and minimal processing. Unlike unaccompanied village paghjella it is arranged, rehearsed and often newly composed, and unlike Sardinian cantu a tenore it uses no guttural bass timbre and no fixed dance-rhythmic ostinato.

items.name: Corsican folk (canti corsi)
items.lineage: Village song repertoire of Corsica documented by Félix Quilici's 1948-63 field recordings and revived after 1970 — the free-rhythm solo genres (lamentu, voceru, nanna lullaby, tribbiera threshing calls, chjam'è rispondi improvised verse duels) alongside three-voice paghjella and accompanied dance songs, sung in Corsican with heavy nasal ricuccata ornament, non-vibrato chest tone, and accompaniment by cetera-derived plucked strings, guitar or button accordion in duple mountain dance rhythms.
items.description: The full village repertoire of Corsica beyond its famous polyphony: pastoral and work calls, keened laments, lullabies, improvised verse contests and accompanied dance songs collected largely in the Niolu, Castagniccia and Sartenais. The voice is nasal, straight-toned and densely ornamented with fast melismatic turns, often unmeasured and shaped by breath rather than beat, with modest plucked-string or accordion backing on the social repertoire. It sits between the unaccompanied ensemble tradition of paghjella and the Italian-facing song of neighbouring Sardinia and Tuscany, sharing their modal language but keeping Corsican-language texts and the chjam'è rispondi improvisation practice.
exemplars: Félix Quilici - Musique corse de tradition orale

items.name: Canti alpini (Alpine male-choir song)
items.lineage: Northern Italian male-choir repertoire of Trentino, Veneto and Friuli codified by the Coro della SAT of Trento from 1926 and its arranger Antonio Pedrotti, drawing on Alpine village song and First World War Alpini regimental repertoire — four-part TTBB harmonization of modal or major folk melodies, sung a cappella in slow to moderate duple time with straight tone, strict blend, whispered pianissimi and swelling crescendi, texts on mountains, emigration, love and the war dead.
items.description: The male-voice choral song of the Italian Alps, formalized in the twentieth century when mountaineering clubs and Alpini veterans' associations turned village and regimental tunes into arranged four-part repertoire. Its sound is a cappella and tightly blended: melody usually in the second tenor, close chordal harmony with just-tuned thirds, extreme dynamic range from breathed pianissimo to full unison declamation, and unhurried duple phrasing that follows the text. Unlike Corsican or Sardinian polyphony it is notated, conductor-led and functionally harmonic, and unlike alpine yodel it avoids register-break vocalise entirely.
exemplars: Bepi De Marzi - Signore delle Cime

items.name: Tarantella (pan-southern Italian dance complex)
items.lineage: The family of fast southern Italian couple and ritual dances documented from seventeenth-century Neapolitan tarantism accounts and revived from the 1970s by Nuova Compagnia di Canto Popolare and later Officina Zoè — driving 6/8 or 12/8 at 110-160 BPM propelled by tamburello frame drum with continuous thumb-roll and rim slaps, organetto or mandolin and guitar cycling two-chord modal vamps, castanets and shouted vocal refrains, in regional variants from Neapolitan tammurriata to Salentine pizzica and Calabrian tarantella.
items.description: An umbrella term for the fast compound-meter dances of the Italian Mezzogiorno, historically tied to the tarantism healing rite in Puglia and now the core of the southern folk revival and of summer festivals like La Notte della Taranta. The engine is the tamburello, whose unbroken thumb roll and hard rim accents sit under an accelerating two-chord modal vamp on organetto, mandolin or guitar, with raw open-throated vocal refrains and long ecstatic accelerandi. It differs from the Neapolitan tarantella of the salon and canzone repertoire by being un-notated, harmonically static and rhythm-driven rather than melodically composed, and from northern Italian dance music by its Greek-Salentine modal colour and frame-drum dominance.
exemplars: Alan Lomax and Diego Carpitella - Southern Italy field recordings 1954
Ernesto De Martino - La terra del rimorso (Salento documentation)

items.name: Zampogna
items.lineage: Southern Italian double-chantered mouth-blown bagpipe tradition of Molise, Abruzzo, Campania, Calabria and Sicily, documented from the 17th century and carried by shepherd-pipers (zampognari) who descend to towns for the Christmas novena, playing paired-chanter harmony with two drones against the ciaramella shawm at brisk 6/8 pastorale tempi, with untempered scales and heavy nasal reed-driven ornamentation.
items.description: The zampogna is the bagpipe family of southern Italy, played by shepherd musicians whose Christmas novena rounds preserved the repertoire into the recording era. Its defining sound is two chanters sounding simultaneously in parallel thirds and drone-anchored counterpoint, plus one or two constant bass drones, and it is almost always paired with the loud conical ciaramella shawm carrying the tune above. Unlike Highland or Galician piping it is untempered, double-voiced, and pastorale rather than martial in function.

items.name: Organetto (Italian Diatonic Accordion Music)
items.lineage: Central and southern Italian dance repertoire built on the diatonic button accordion that spread through Abruzzo, Lazio, Marche and Campania after 1870, driving saltarello, tarantella and quadriglia at fast 6/8 and 2/4 tempi with continuous bellows-shake drive, left-hand bass-chord alternation, and tammorra or tamburello frame drum marking the beat under call-and-response village singing.
items.description: Organetto music is the accordion-led festa dance tradition of the Italian centre-south, where a single player supplies melody, bass and chords for hours of open-air dancing.
