Iskelmä is lighter and more varied in tempo than Finnish tango and less deliberately comic and fast than humppa, though the same composers and singers moved freely between all three.

items.name: Humppa
items.lineage: Finnish dance-hall style crystallized in the 1950s from foxtrot and German oom-pah playing, running at roughly 210-260 BPM in fast duple time with a relentless alternating bass-note/offbeat-chord accordion or brass vamp and a two-step lavatanssit dance step, popularized by Dallapé and above all by Antti Hammarberg's Humppa-Veikot from 1965, whose LPs of humppa-ized standards fixed the genre's clipped clarinet, muted trumpet and shouted-cheerful vocal.
items.description: A very fast Finnish couple-dance music built on an unvarying oom-pah alternation between bass note and offbeat chord, with accordion carrying the melody and clarinet or trumpet answering. Tempos sit far above ordinary foxtrot, giving the style its breathless, slightly absurd forward drive, and its repertoire is largely existing tunes rearranged into the pattern. It is the up-tempo, comic-toned counterpart to the slow melancholy of Finnish tango within the same dance-pavilion circuit.

items.name: Rautalanka
items.lineage: Finnish instrumental guitar-band style of 1961-1965, taking its name ('iron wire') from The Shadows' and The Spotnicks' sound and adapting it to Finnish and Karelian folk melodies — clean single-coil guitar with heavy spring reverb and tremolo carrying the tune in the middle register, second guitar on chords, electric bass and drums in plain 4/4 or fast 2/4, launched commercially by The Sounds' 'Emma' (1963) and consolidated by The Strangers and Agents in later revivals.
items.description: Finland's early-1960s instrumental guitar-group music, essentially the Shadows template turned toward minor-key Nordic and Karelian melody. The defining sound is an undistorted single-coil lead soaked in spring reverb and amp tremolo, played with clean picking and no blues bending, over an unfussy rhythm section. It differs from American surf rock in melodic source material and mood — modal, minor and melancholy rather than aggressive — and from beat groups in being almost entirely instrumental.

items.name: Danseband (Nordic dance-band pop)
items.lineage: Swedish and Norwegian ballroom dance-band idiom crystallized in the late 1960s-70s out of gammaldans and Anglo-American schlager, codified by Sven-Ingvars, Vikingarna and Ole Ivars — steady 100-130 BPM foxtrot, bugg and waltz grooves with a brushed or lightly rock backbeat, chorused electric guitar and Nordic-accented saxophone or accordion filling between phrases, and warm unaffected baritone lead vocals over major-key three-chord verses with tight thirds harmony on the refrain.
items.description: Danseband is the Nordic ballroom-dance pop that dominated Swedish and Norwegian folkparks from the 1970s onward, built for couples' social dancing rather than listening. Its signature is metronomic mid-tempo foxtrot and waltz rhythm, clean chorused guitar, accordion or saxophone obbligato, and an unstrained conversational male lead voice singing sentimental Swedish or Norwegian lyrics. Unlike Eurodisco or schlager proper it keeps a live rhythm-section feel and rural repertoire ties, and unlike gammaldans it uses a full drum kit and electric bass.

items.name: Trallpunk
items.lineage: Swedish melodic hardcore subgenre named for its 'tralla' singalong melodies, formed in the mid-1980s around Uppsala and Stockholm and codified by Asta Kask, Strebers, Charta 77 and later Coca Carola and De Lyckliga Kompisarna — fast 180-220 BPM d-beat and straight-eight punk drumming, major-key twin-guitar lines drawn from Swedish visa and folk tunes, chanted gang-vocal choruses, and blunt Swedish-language social lyrics.
items.description: Trallpunk emerged in mid-1980s Sweden as a distinctly melodic strand of punk, grafting the singable diatonic contours of Swedish visa onto fast d-beat drumming and buzzsaw power chords. Recordings are typically cheap, mid-forward and dry, with the guitars panned hard and unison shouted refrains carrying the hook. It differs from Swedish d-beat and käng punk in that the melody, not the distortion, is the point, and from pop-punk in its Swedish-language leftist lyrics and rougher production.

items.name: Norwegian folk music (norsk folkemusikk)
items.lineage: Rural Norwegian instrumental and vocal tradition documented systematically from Ludvig Mathias Lindeman's 1840s collecting through the 20th-century kappleik contest circuit — asymmetric springar and gangar dance rhythms with unevenly long beats, Hardanger fiddle and ordinary fiddle slåtter over sympathetic-string drones, herding calls (lokk) and stev sung in free rhythm, plus lur and bukkehorn signalling instruments and the drone zither langeleik.
items.description: Norwegian folk music covers the rural repertoire of fiddle dance tunes, herding calls and solo song preserved in valley communities and revived through 20th-century kappleik contests. Its defining traits are the uneven three-beat springar, heavy double-stop drones, dense ornamentation with microtonally raised or lowered thirds and sevenths, and free-rhythm vocal genres like kulning and stev. It is distinguished from Swedish polska tradition by the specific Norwegian beat asymmetries and by the central role of the Hardanger fiddle and its resonant sympathetic strings.

items.name: Hardingfele (Hardanger-fiddle practice)
items.lineage: Instrument-centred Norwegian tradition of the eight- or nine-string Hardanger fiddle, traced to Ole Jonsen Jaastad's 1651 instrument and consolidated in Telemark, Setesdal and Hardanger by 19th-century masters such as Myllarguten and Håvard Gibøen — solo dance slåtter in springar, gangar and halling, played in scordatura tunings across four to five bowed strings above four to five sympathetic strings, with continuous double-stop drone, foot-stamp pulse and richly ornamented microtonal intonation.
items.description: Hardingfele denotes the solo repertoire and technique of the Norwegian Hardanger fiddle, whose sympathetic strings produce a constant shimmering resonance under the bowed melody. Performance is overwhelmingly solo and unaccompanied except for the player's own stamping foot, using scordatura retunings chosen per tune and a heavy bow arm that keeps two strings sounding almost throughout. It differs from the plain Norwegian flatfele tradition in tuning variety, sympathetic resonance and denser ornamentation, and from Swedish fiddle music in its markedly uneven springar beat lengths.

items.name: Nyckelharpa (keyed-fiddle tradition)
items.lineage: Uppland-centred Swedish keyed-fiddle tradition attested since the 14th century and rebuilt in the 20th by Eric Sahlström, who standardized the chromatic three-row instrument in the 1930s-40s — bowed melody strings stopped by wooden key tangents over twelve sympathetic strings, playing polska, schottis and gånglåt in moderate 3/4 and 2/4, with legato bowing across drone strings and a soft, reverberant, organ-like sustain.
items.description: The nyckelharpa tradition centres on the Swedish keyed fiddle of Uppland, a bowed instrument whose pitches are stopped by wooden keys and whose sympathetic strings give a continuous halo of resonance. Repertoire is dance music — polska above all, plus schottis, vals and walking tunes — played with long slurred bow strokes and a nasal, sustaining timbre unlike any violin. Compared with Swedish fiddle playing generally it is more legato and more harmonically padded, and compared with Hardanger fiddle it is chromatic and evenly metred rather than scordatura-based and asymmetric.

items.name: Swedish fiddle tradition (spelmanslag)
items.lineage: Swedish fiddle practice codified through 19th-century parish spelmän, the 1908 spelmansstämma revival movement and the Zorn medal system from 1933 — polska in uneven 3/4 with the second or third beat shortened, plus schottis, vals and polketta, played with heavy double-stops, drone-fifth accompaniment, second-fiddle stämma harmony a third below, and swung foot-driven pulse in unison spelmanslag ensembles.
items.description: Swedish fiddle tradition is the regional dance-tune practice of Dalarna, Hälsingland, Jämtland and beyond, carried by named spelmän and since 1908 by the annual spelmansstämma gatherings. The core is the polska, a triple-time couple dance whose beats are unequal in ways specific to each parish, played with drone double-stops and an improvised second-fiddle harmony line. It is distinguished from Norwegian slått playing by its more even but still lilting polska, its ensemble stämma harmony practice, and its greater use of the nyckelharpa alongside the violin.

items.name: Folkmusik (Swedish folk revival)
items.lineage: Swedish folk-music revival that ran from the 1970s 'gröna vågen' youth turn to tradition through the 1990s Falun and Umeå scenes, codified by Groupa, Filarfolket, Hedningarna and Väsen — traditional polska and vallåt melodies reharmonized with modal chords, nyckelharpa and Hardanger d'amore fiddle joined by bouzouki, hand percussion and later samplers, at moderate dance tempi with close-miked chamber clarity.
items.description: Folkmusik in its revival sense is the Swedish art-folk movement that took parish polska and herding repertoire into concert halls and studios from the 1970s onward. Its sound is deliberately produced: wide-imaged close-miked nyckelharpa and fiddle, added bouzouki or guitar drones, discreet percussion, and modal reharmonization far beyond what village practice used. It differs from traditional spelmanslag playing in arrangement ambition and studio construction, and from Nordic folk-rock in keeping acoustic instrumentation and traditional tune shapes intact.

items.name: Icelandic traditional music (þjóðlagatónlist)
items.lineage: Icelandic oral tradition documented by Bjarni Þorsteinsson's 1906-09 collection and later Hallgrímur Helgason and Iceland State Radio field work — rímur epic chant in stemma melodies of narrow range sung in strict rhyme-and-alliteration stanzas, tvísöngur two-part singing in parallel fifths surviving from medieval organum, plus the bowed drone-boxes langspil and fiðla, with hard consonantal delivery and free declamatory rhythm.
items.description: Icelandic traditional music is overwhelmingly vocal, dominated by rímur — long narrative poems chanted to short recycled melodic formulas called stemmur — and by tvísöngur, a two-voice parallel-fifth singing preserved from medieval organum long after it vanished elsewhere in Europe. Instruments are few and drone-based: the fretted langspil and the two-string fiðla, both bowed against open strings. It is distinguished from Norwegian and Swedish folk by having almost no fiddle dance repertoire and by the parallel-fifth harmony that most Nordic traditions lack entirely.

items.name: Faroese folk music (føroysk fólkatónleikur)
items.lineage: Faroe Islands oral tradition centred on the kvæði ballad chain-dance, documented from V.U. Hammershaimb's 19th-century collecting and the Corpus Carminum Færoensium — hundreds of stanzas sung unaccompanied by a lead skipari with the whole ring answering the refrain, propelled by heavy synchronized foot-stomping in a steady two-beat step, plus the shorter Danish-derived vísur and religious kingosálmar heterophonic hymn singing.
items.description: Faroese folk music is defined by the kvæði, an unaccompanied ballad chain-dance in which a ring of dancers stamps a steady two-beat step while a lead singer delivers stanza after stanza and the ring answers with a fixed refrain. The only percussion is the floor under the dancers' feet, and the melody is a short narrow-range formula repeated for hours. It differs from other Nordic ballad traditions in surviving as a living communal dance rather than a concert repertoire, and from Icelandic rímur in being danced, choral and refrain-driven rather than solo-chanted.
exemplars: Traditional Faroese ballad singers of Sandoy

items.name: Nordic folk (pan-Scandinavian umbrella)
items.lineage: Pan-Scandinavian traditional-music complex spanning Norway, Sweden, Denmark, Finland, Iceland and Sápmi, consolidated as a shared category by the 20th-century revival and festival circuit (Førde, Falun, Kaustinen) — uneven-beat polska and springar dance tunes, drone-heavy bowed strings, narrow-range herding calls and yoik-adjacent vocal styles, modal melodies with raised fourths and neutral thirds, and minimal or foot-supplied percussion.
items.description: Nordic folk is the umbrella term for the shared traditional-music practices of Scandinavia, Finland and the Faroes as they circulate on the modern festival and recording circuit. Common markers are asymmetric triple-time dance rhythms, sympathetic-string and open-string drones, modal scales with unstable thirds and sharp fourths, and vocal genres pitched between song and call. It is broader than any single national tradition and, unlike folk-rock or world-fusion, keeps acoustic bowed and plucked strings at the centre rather than a rhythm section.

items.name: Siberian folk music (Sakha, Tuva, Altai)
items.lineage: Indigenous South and East Siberian traditions of the Sakha, Tuvan, Altai and Khakas peoples, documented from Aleksei Anokhin's early-1900s expeditions through Soviet Melodiya ethnographic issues — overtone throat singing in khöömei, kargyraa and sygyt styles, the khomus jaw harp played with breath-shaped resonance, bowed igil and byzaanchy over pentatonic long-song melodies, epic olonkho and kai narration in free rhythm, and horse-gait rhythmic imitation.
items.description: Siberian folk music covers the Turkic and Mongolic traditions of Tuva, Sakha, Altai and Khakassia, where the defining technique is overtone-selective throat singing that isolates a whistling harmonic above a low drone. Alongside it sit the khomus jaw harp, the two-string bowed igil and doshpuluur lute, the Khakas chatkhan zither, and long free-rhythm epic narration. It is distinguished from Mongolian long song by its stronger emphasis on the sygyt whistle register and jaw-harp repertoire, and from Sámi yoik by being instrumentally accompanied and overtone-based rather than purely vocal.

items.name: Tatar folk music (Volga Tatar)
items.lineage: Volga-Tatar tradition of Kazan and the middle Volga, collected from the 1920s by Soltan Gabashi and Ghazi Almuhammetov and issued through Soviet Melodiya and Tatar Radio — anhemitonic pentatonic melodies, long ornamented ozyn köy lyric songs in free rhythm, brisk 2/4 kyska köy dance songs, the quray reed flute and kubyz jaw harp, and after the 19th century the talyanka button accordion carrying both melody and chordal pulse.
items.description: Tatar folk music is the Turkic-Muslim tradition of the middle Volga, built on anhemitonic pentatonic scales shared across the Volga-Ural region. The core genres are the ozyn köy, a slow lyric song sung in free rhythm with dense melismatic ornament, and the kyska köy, a fast duple dance song; the talyanka accordion, quray flute and kubyz jaw harp are the standard instruments. It differs from Russian village song in its pentatonicism and absence of thick chordal polyphony, and from Central Asian maqam traditions in having no extended modal suite form.

items.name: Uyghur folk music (Xinjiang village and meshrep song)
items.lineage: Turkic-Muslim tradition of the Tarim Basin oases — Kashgar, Khotan, Turpan and Ili — documented in state collecting campaigns from the 1950s and on China Record Corporation issues, distinct from the courtly On Ikki Muqam: strophic love songs and meshrep gathering songs in 7/8, 6/8 and 5/8 aksak patterns, plucked rawap and dutar with wire sympathetic strings, bowed ghijek, kalun struck zither, and the dap frame drum's dum-tek accents driving communal dance, sung in a bright nasal chest voice with heavy neighbour-tone ornament.
items.description: Uyghur folk music is the village and meshrep-gathering repertoire of the Tarim Basin oases, separate from the formal Twelve Muqam suites though drawing on the same modal vocabulary. Plucked rawap and dutar carry the melody in heterophony with the bowed ghijek while the dap frame drum lays down limping aksak patterns in 7/8 or 5/8, under a bright, forward, heavily ornamented vocal line. Compared with Central Asian shashmaqam it is shorter-formed, dance-driven and more percussive; compared with Han Chinese folk song it is modal in a Middle Eastern sense with neutral intervals.

items.name: Kazakh Traditional Music
items.lineage: Steppe song-and-lute tradition of the Kazakh nomads codified in the 19th century by the composer-performers Kurmangazy Sagyrbaiuly, Dauletkerei and the singer-poets (änshi/aqyn) Birzhan Sal and Akhan Seri — solo two-string dombyra strumming continuous 6/8 and 2/4 driving figures under a wide-ranged, chest-forward declamatory voice, with qobyz horsehair fiddle supplying breathy overtone-rich shamanic küy and sybyzgy end-blown flute doubling at the octave.
items.description: The song and instrumental repertory of the Kazakh steppe, formalized during the 19th-century flourishing of named küy composers and aqyn singer-poets and preserved through Soviet-era conservatory transcription. Its sound is dominated by the fretted two-string dombyra played with a continuous strummed right hand that fuses melody, drone and pulse, and by the bowed qobyz whose unstopped horsehair strings produce a hoarse, harmonic-saturated timbre. Unlike Mongolian long song it keeps a firm dance-derived metre and favours a bright forward vocal placement rather than sustained overtone singing.

items.name: Dombra Küy
items.lineage: Kazakh solo instrumental art form for the fretted long-necked two-string dombyra, crystallized in the 19th century in two regional schools — the western tökpe style of Kurmangazy and Dina Nurpeisova with fast continuous alternating strums across both strings, and the eastern shertpe style of Tättimbet using plucked, sparser, rubato phrasing — each küy a three-to-six-minute programmatic piece built from a low bass-string drone, a rising climb through the register (buyn) and a return.
items.description: Purely instrumental Kazakh lute music, distinct from the sung repertory in that a küy narrates its story through register and rhythmic drive alone. The dombyra's gut or nylon strings and thin resonant soundbox give a dry, buzzing attack; the constant strum makes the instrument simultaneously melody, drone and drum. Where the eastern shertpe school breathes and pauses, the western tökpe school is relentless — the closest analogue in the region to a moto perpetuo etude, and the reason Kurmangazy's pieces became the Soviet-era orchestral canon.

items.name: Kyrgyz Traditional Music
items.lineage: Tien Shan mountain-nomad tradition of Kyrgyzstan, transmitted by manaschy epic reciters of the Manas cycle and by küü composers such as Toktogul Satylganov, Karamoldo Orozov and Muratali Kurenkeev — unaccompanied hypnotic recitation in fast trochaic verse alternating with three-string fretless komuz pieces whose right hand throws the instrument in the air mid-phrase, plus kyl kyiak horsehair fiddle laments and temir komuz jaw-harp overtone melodies.
items.description: Kyrgyz music divides between the manaschy's unaccompanied epic declamation — hours of memorized verse delivered in a trance-inducing accelerating chant with no instrument at all — and the komuz küü, short character pieces whose fretless neck permits sliding microtonal inflection and whose theatrical performance gestures are part of the form. The kyl kyiak's two horsehair strings, bowed without a fingerboard, produce a whistling harmonic tone unlike any bowed instrument to its west. It is sparser and more rubato than the Kazakh dombra tradition next door, and drumless throughout.

items.name: Uzbek Traditional Music
items.lineage: Classical and regional music of the Uzbek khanates centred on Bukhara, Samarkand, Khorezm and Ferghana, codified in the 19th-20th centuries through the Khorezm tanbur notation and the teaching of Yunus Rajabiy — long-necked tanbur and dutar heterophony with ghijak spike fiddle and doira frame drum marking the usul cycle, over a strained, high-tessitura ornamented vocal delivery that climbs through the awj climax and descends.
items.description: An urban Central Asian art tradition of the oasis cities, sitting between Persian modal practice and Turkic lute technique. Instruments play the same line in loose heterophony rather than harmony, the doira's fixed usul pattern supplies the metric frame, and the singer is judged by how high and how intensely the awj apex is sustained. It differs from Persian dastgah by its strict drum-cycle governance and from Turkish makam by its darker, more nasal vocal placement and its metal-strung tanbur plucked with a wire plectrum.

items.name: Tajik Traditional Music
items.lineage: Persian-language music of Tajikistan spanning the Bukharan classical falak and shashmaqam repertory and the Pamiri highland maddoh devotional song, transmitted through hereditary ustod lineages and documented from the 1930s by Soviet folklorists — sato bowed long-necked lute and rubab plucked lute with ghijak, doira and daf, over a plaintive high-register solo voice whose falak laments use free-rhythm melisma before settling into a fast doira usul.
items.description: Tajik practice shares the Bukharan classical repertory with Uzbek musicians but keeps Persian text and a strong highland vernacular layer: the falak, a mountain lament sung in an aching upper register, and the Pamiri maddoh, a hours-long devotional cycle that accelerates from sung poetry into ecstatic rubab-and-daf sections. The sato — a tanbur played with a bow rather than plucked — gives a sustained, keening timbre found almost nowhere else. Compared to Uzbek court style it is rougher, more openly devotional and less conservatory-polished.

items.name: Turkmen Pop
items.lineage: State-adjacent popular song of Turkmenistan formed in the late Soviet 1980s and consolidated after 1991 in Ashgabat television studios — synthesizer string pads and DX-style presets over programmed 4/4 or aksak-inflected drum-machine patterns, with the gijak fiddle and dutar sampled or played live as national signifiers, and a nasal, heavily ornamented male or female lead voice carrying Turkmen-language lyrics with reverb-drenched doubling.
items.description: Turkmenistan's mainstream popular music, shaped by state broadcasting and by cassette-kiosk distribution rather than an independent industry. Its texture is thin and synthesizer-forward — factory keyboard presets, gated reverb, machine drums — but the melodic language and vocal ornamentation stay tied to the bagshy singer tradition and the dutar's rapid tremolo figures. It is more overtly electronic and more melodically Turkic-ornamented than Uzbek estrada, and unlike Turkish arabesk it avoids orchestral strings almost entirely.

items.name: Shashmaqam
items.lineage: Six-maqam classical suite cycle of Bukhara and Samarkand, formalized at the Bukharan emir's court in the 18th-19th centuries and notated in the 1920s-50s by Viktor Uspensky and Yunus Rajabiy — each maqam opening with an instrumental mushkilot section on tanbur and dutar in fixed doira usul cycles, then a vocal nasr section whose successive shu'ba climb stepwise to the awj apex on Persian and Hebrew-inflected Chagatai poetry before the descent (furovard).
items.description: The classical suite tradition of the Bukharan oasis, carried jointly by Uzbek, Tajik and Bukharan Jewish musicians — the latter dominating its performance in the 20th century and carrying it to Queens and Tel Aviv after the 1970s emigration. The form is a strict architecture: fixed usul cycles, a mandated ascent to the awj, and cadential formulas that close each shu'ba. Its notation under Soviet institutionalization makes it more fixed and less improvised than Persian dastgah or Turkish makam performance, though the ornamental surface remains dense.

items.name: Central Asian Folk
items.lineage: Village and pastoral repertory across Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan, Tajikistan and Turkmenistan documented by Soviet ethnographic expeditions from the 1920s onward — wedding and lament song, work and cradle song, and dance tunes carried on dutar, komuz, dombyra, ghijak and doira, mostly solo or in unison duo, in short strophic forms with free-rhythm openings and pentatonic or narrow-range modal melodies over an unstopped drone string.
items.description: The non-courtly layer of Central Asian music: songs tied to labour, marriage, mourning and the seasonal round, recorded mostly on portable tape by ethnographers rather than in studios. Textures are thin — one voice, one lute, occasionally a frame drum — and forms are strophic and repetitive, with melodies confined to a narrow range and decorated by grace-note slides rather than the extended melisma of the urban maqam tradition. It is the shared substrate from which the Kazakh küy, the Kyrgyz manas and the Bukharan shashmaqam each specialized.
exemplars: Smithsonian Folkways Music of Central Asia series

items.name: Persian Traditional Music (Radif)
items.lineage: Iranian classical system organized as the radif, a canonical body of some 250 gusheh melodic models distributed across seven dastgah and five avaz, assembled and taught in Qajar Tehran by Mirza Abdollah and Aqa Hoseinqoli around 1900 — an unmetred avaz section in which a solo voice and tar or santur trade phrases in strict heterophony, punctuated by metered tasnif songs and fast chaharmezrab etudes over tombak goblet-drum patterns.
items.description: The classical art music of Iran, built on memorized melodic models rather than notated pieces: a performer learns the radif exactly, then improvises a unique path through a dastgah's gusheh in performance. The characteristic sound is the tar or setar's plucked, decaying tone answered by a voice using tahrir, a rapid yodel-like break between registers, over long unmetred stretches with no drum. It differs from Arab maqam in its intervals (the koron three-quarter flat), its avoidance of ensemble homophony, and its far greater proportion of free rhythm.

items.name: Persian Neo-Traditional
items.lineage: Iranian classical revival current formed in Tehran from the late 1960s around the Center for Preservation and Propagation of Traditional Music and the Chavosh collective, driven by Mohammad Reza Lotfi, Hossein Alizadeh, Parviz Meshkatian and Shajarian — enlarged unison ensembles of tar, setar, santur, kamancheh, ney and daf performing newly composed pieces in radif idiom, with arranged introductions, fixed metric sections and a concert-hall dynamic arc replacing the intimate solo-plus-voice format.
items.description: The post-1970s composed wing of Persian classical music, which kept the modal language and instrumentation of the radif but moved the practice into concert halls and studio albums with written ensemble parts. Daf and larger string sections give it a fuller, more dynamically shaped sound than the traditional solo format, and pieces are through-composed with recurring themes. Purists distinguish it from the radif proper precisely because improvisation is bounded and the ensemble plays arranged unison rather than free heterophony.

items.name: Santur (Persian Hammered Dulcimer)
items.lineage: Solo repertory for the Iranian trapezoidal 72-string hammered dulcimer, raised from ensemble accompaniment to a concert instrument in mid-20th-century Tehran by Habib Somai and above all Faramarz Payvar, who wrote its first method books — light wooden mezrab hammers producing rapid tremolo rolls (riz) under free-rhythm avaz, and driving sixteenth-note chaharmezrab passages whose fixed movable bridges force a dastgah-specific retuning before every piece.
items.description: Persian santur playing is defined by the tension between a struck instrument with no sustain control and a modal system that demands long expressive lines — solved by the riz, a continuous hammer tremolo that turns discrete strikes into sustained tone. Because the bridges must be repositioned for each dastgah, a santur performance is committed to one mode throughout. Its bright metallic bloom and long decay set it apart from the tar's drier plucked attack and from the Iraqi and Indian santoor traditions, which use heavier hammers and different tunings.

items.name: Tar (Persian Classical Lute)
items.lineage: Repertory for the double-bowl mulberry-body, lambskin-faced Iranian long-necked lute with adjustable gut frets, made the primary radif-carrying instrument by Mirza Abdollah and Aqa Hoseinqoli in late-Qajar Tehran and extended technically by Jalil Shahnaz and Hossein Alizadeh — a brass-plectrum attack with a distinctive metallic buzz, riz tremolo, glissando between quarter-tone frets, and open bass strings sounding as an intermittent drone under the melody.
items.description: The tar is the instrument on which the Persian radif is canonically taught, and its solo repertory is the reference recording of the system. Its skin soundboard and figure-eight body give a nasal, biting tone with a fast decay, and the plectrum's brass tip adds an audible click that outlines every articulation. Against the setar's whispered fingertip sound and the santur's ringing wash, the tar is the most percussive and rhetorically declamatory of the Persian classical instruments, closest in role to the singer it usually shadows.

items.name: Setar (Persian Solo Lute)
items.lineage: Intimate solo tradition for the small four-string Iranian long-necked lute plucked with the nail of the right index finger, historically the instrument of Sufi khaneqah practice and of private radif study, brought to the concert stage by Ahmad Ebadi, Dariush Talai and Mohammad Reza Lotfi in 20th-century Tehran — extremely low volume, sympathetic-resonating open strings, a continuous nail tremolo for sustain, and long unmetred avaz explorations of a single dastgah with minimal metric material.
items.description: The quietest instrument in Persian classical music, so soft that its traditional setting is a single listener or a Sufi gathering rather than a hall. Its thin wooden soundboard and fingernail plucking produce a fragile, breathy tone in which the fourth (bass) string rings as a constant sympathetic drone. Setar performance leans further toward free rhythm and contemplative pacing than tar or santur playing, dispensing with chaharmezrab display passages and often with percussion altogether.

items.name: Ney taksim (Ottoman-Sufi reed improvisation)
items.lineage: Ottoman-Turkish and Arab art-music practice for the end-blown rim-edge reed flute, codified in Mevlevi lodges and Istanbul mesk pedagogy from the 16th-19th centuries and carried into 20th-century state conservatories by players such as Niyazi Sayin and Aka Gunduz Kutbay, marked by unmetered taksim in a single makam, breathy overblown octave leaps, comma-inflected perde tuning, glissando finger-slides and portamento, and the long-breathed ascending-then-descending seyir arc preceding the metered pesrev.
items.description: Ney taksim is the unmetered solo improvisation tradition of the Ottoman-Arab end-blown reed flute, formalized in Mevlevi dervish lodges and transmitted through the master-apprentice mesk system before entering Turkish state conservatories in the 20th century. Its sound is defined by an audible breath-noise component at the lip-rim, microtonal perde positions that do not map to equal temperament, sliding portamento between degrees, and a free-rhythm melodic exposition that establishes and modulates a makam before resolving to the tonic. Distinguished from Persian dastgah ney playing by makam theory and Turkish comma tuning rather than the dastgah radif, and from metered pesrev or sema repertoire by its absence of usul cycle.

items.name: Qanun taqsim (Arab-Turkish plucked zither art music)
items.lineage: Trapezoidal 72-81-string plucked box zither central to the Arab takht and Ottoman fasil from the 19th century, standardized with the mandal lever system in early-20th-century Cairo and Istanbul workshops and codified by players such as Muhammad al-Aqqad, Abraham Salman and Ruhi Ayangil, marked by tortoise-shell plectrum rings, dense tremolo and rapid descending runs, mid-phrase mandal shifts that retune quarter-tone degrees for maqam modulation, and unmetered taqsim alternating with heterophonic ensemble accompaniment.
items.description: Qanun taqsim is the solo and takht-leading practice of the Arab-Ottoman plucked box zither, which acquired its modern identity when metal mandal levers were fitted in the early twentieth century, letting a player retune individual courses by fractions of a tone mid-phrase. The sound is bright and metallic with heavy tremolo, cascading scalar runs, and rapid maqam modulation that would be impossible on a fixed-fret instrument. Distinguished from the Persian santur by plucking rather than hammering and by the mandal apparatus, and from the oud by fixed pitch-per-string and a far denser note rate.

items.name: Oud taqsim (Arab short-neck lute art music)
items.lineage: Fretless short-necked pear-bodied lute at the center of Arab, Turkish and Iraqi art music, its modern courses and risha technique settled in Cairo and Baghdad between the 1900s and 1930s and codified by Sharif Muhieddin Haydar, Riyad al-Sunbati, Farid al-Atrash, Munir Bashir and Jamil Bashir, marked by eagle-feather or plastic plectrum tremolo, fretless microtonal sliding within maqam, unmetered taqsim exposition, and characteristic rest-stroke accents against low open-string drones.
items.description: Oud taqsim is the improvised solo tradition of the fretless Arab lute, whose modern performance idiom crystallized in Cairo and Baghdad in the first third of the twentieth century. Its markers are the risha plectrum's fast tremolo on sustained tones, sliding intonation across quarter-tone maqam degrees that no fretted instrument can reproduce, drone-and-melody interplay with open bass courses, and free-rhythm phrase architecture that builds through modulation before descending to the qarar. Distinguished from the Turkish ud by lower tuning, heavier bass emphasis and Arab rather than Ottoman makam theory, and from the fretted buzuq or saz by continuous pitch.

items.name: Darbuka solo (goblet-drum virtuoso tradition)
items.lineage: Goblet-drum practice of Egypt, Turkey and the Levant, transformed by the mid-20th-century shift from clay-and-skin tabla baladi to aluminium shells with tunable synthetic heads, codified through Cairo film-orchestra percussionists and Turkish soloists such as Misirli Ahmet and Hossam Ramzy, marked by doum-tek finger technique, split-hand and clarinet-finger rolls, iqa cycles such as maqsum, baladi, sa'idi, chiftetelli and 10/8 curcuna, and cadenza-like solos that fragment the cycle before restoring it.
items.description: Darbuka solo is the virtuoso goblet-drum idiom of Egypt, Turkey and the Levant, which acquired its modern high-pitched, ringing voice when metal shells and tunable plastic heads replaced clay and goatskin around the 1960s. It is built on a vocabulary of doum (bass center) and tek (rim) strokes elaborated with finger rolls, slaps and split-hand technique, deployed over Arab and Ottoman iqa cycles and in unaccompanied solo displays that deliberately destabilize the cycle before snapping back to it. Distinguished from the frame-drum idioms of riq and bendir by the goblet body's sharp bass-to-rim contrast, and from Turkish davul-zurna street percussion by fingertip rather than mallet technique.

items.name: Afghan traditional (klasik and Kabuli art music)
items.lineage: Art and regional music of Afghanistan centered on the Kharabat quarter of Kabul, where Hindustani musicians brought from India in the 1860s under Amir Sher Ali Khan established hereditary ustad lineages, later broadcast nationally by Radio Kabul from the 1940s through figures such as Ustad Sarahang, Ustad Rahim Bakhsh and Ustad Mohammad Omar, marked by the plucked rubab with sympathetic strings, tabla and zerbaghali accompaniment, raga-derived naghma-e-kashal instrumental forms, and ghazal singing in Dari and Pashto.
items.description: Afghan traditional art music took shape in Kabul's Kharabat musicians' quarter after Hindustani ustads were installed at the royal court in the 1860s, producing a hybrid of North Indian raga practice with local instruments and Dari-Pashto poetry. Its signature is the rubab's short sustaining plucked tone against sympathetic-string resonance, tabla or the clay-bodied zerbaghali marking cycles, an instrumental naghma form that moves from free introduction into accelerating metered sections, and ghazal singing on Hafez and Bedil texts. Distinguished from Hindustani classical proper by rubab-and-zerbaghali timbre, shorter development and Persianate song forms, and from Pashto regional folk by its court pedigree and raga theory.

items.name: Dambora (Hazara long-neck lute song)
items.lineage: Hazarajat highland tradition of central Afghanistan built on the fretless two-string long-necked dambora lute, sustained orally by village and shrine singers and brought to recording through Dawood Sarkhosh and Sarwar Sarkhosh from the 1980s exile period onward, marked by strummed drone-plus-melody right-hand patterns, no fixed fretting, moderate duple pulse, and Hazaragi-dialect poetry of exile, love and mourning delivered in a nasal high-tessitura solo voice.
items.description: Dambora music is the song tradition of the Hazara people of central Afghanistan, named for the fretless two-string lute that carries it. A single player strums a continuous drone-and-melody figure with the whole hand while singing Hazaragi quatrains, often about displacement, massacre and longing, in a high, nasal, unornamented-to-lightly-ornamented voice; a frame drum or clay zerbaghali may join for dance pieces. It differs from Kabuli rubab art music in having no raga framework, no tabla and no court pedigree, and from Central Asian dutar traditions across the border by its Hazaragi text repertoire and cyclic single-strain melodies.

items.name: Balochi folk
items.lineage: Music of Balochistan across southwestern Pakistan, southeastern Iran and southern Afghanistan, transmitted by hereditary Luri and Domb musician castes and documented from the 1960s onward by Radio Pakistan Quetta and researchers such as Jean During, marked by the bowed spike-fiddle suroz shadowing the voice heterophonically, the plucked tanburag lute, double-flute nal and donali, dholak or dohol accompaniment, and repertoires spanning zahirig laments, epic sherwandi narrative and the trance-healing guati ceremony.
items.description: Balochi folk is the music of the Baloch of Pakistan, Iran and Afghanistan, historically performed by hereditary professional musician groups for weddings, mourning and healing rather than by the wider community. Its defining sound is the bowed suroz doubling and answering the singer a fraction behind the beat, plucked tanburag providing a rhythmic drone, and dholak or the large dohol driving dance and trance pieces; the zahirig modal family carries the characteristic melancholic laments. It is distinguished from Persian dastgah art music by oral caste transmission and absence of radif theory, and from Sindhi and Saraiki neighbours by the suroz-led heterophony and the guati trance repertoire.

items.name: Pashto pop
items.lineage: Commercial popular music in Pashto emerging from Peshawar and Kabul radio and film industries in the 1960s-70s with Ahmad Zahir-era orchestration and Nashenas, then reshaped by the Peshawar cassette and Pashto-film boom of the 1980s-90s around Nazia Iqbal, Gul Panra and Rahim Shah, marked by rubab and harmonium hooks doubled by synth, attan-derived duple dance grooves with mangey clay-pot and tabla, and belted duet vocals over cassette-era saturated mixes.
items.description: Pashto pop is the commercial song idiom of the Pashto-speaking regions of Pakistan and Afghanistan, running from 1960s-70s radio and film orchestration through the Peshawar cassette industry of the 1980s-90s to present-day digital releases. It keeps the rubab and harmonium as identifying melodic voices while layering synthesizers, drum machines and the mangey clay pot over attan-derived duple dance grooves, with strongly ornamented, high-belted lead vocals and frequent male-female duets. Distinguished from Urdu filmi pop by language, rubab timbre and the attan rhythm, and from Pashto folk proper by studio arrangement and fixed song form.

items.name: Saraiki pop
items.lineage: Popular music in Saraiki from the southern Punjab belt of Multan, Dera Ghazi Khan and Bahawalpur, professionalized through Radio Pakistan Multan from the 1970s and the Lahore cassette-and-VCD trade of the 1980s-2000s with Attaullah Khan Esakhelvi, Pathanay Khan and Abida Parveen, marked by dholak-and-tabla duple grooves, alghoza double-flute and harmonium riffs, kafi and doha poetic texts of Khwaja Ghulam Farid, and long melismatic laments in a plaintive high register.
items.description: Saraiki pop is the cassette-era commercial song tradition of Pakistan's southern Punjab, built on the region's Sufi kafi poetry and its plaintive vocal aesthetic. Recordings pair dholak and tabla duple grooves with harmonium, alghoza twin flutes and later keyboards, under a solo voice that stretches long melismatic phrases over sustained tones, a style Attaullah Khan Esakhelvi turned into a mass-market idiom. It is distinguished from Punjabi bhangra pop by slow-to-mid tempos, lament affect and the absence of dhol-driven dance rhythm, and from formal qawwali by solo delivery and short commercial song form.

items.name: Sindhi (Sufi kalam and folk of Sindh)
items.lineage: Music of Sindh in southern Pakistan anchored in the Shah jo Risalo of Shah Abdul Latif Bhittai (18th century) and its surs sung nightly at the Bhit Shah shrine by faqirs on the five-string tambooro, plus Sachal Sarmast and Jhulelal repertoire, carried to broadcast by Radio Pakistan Hyderabad from the 1950s and to cassette by Abida Parveen and Allan Faqir, marked by yaktaro drone, borrindo and narr flutes, surando bowed lute, chapri clappers and dholak, and slow declamatory melismatic singing.
items.description: Sindhi music is centered on the sung poetry of Shah Abdul Latif Bhittai, whose thirty surs are performed continuously at his Bhit Shah shrine by hereditary faqirs accompanied by the tambooro drone-lute they credit to the saint himself. The wider tradition adds the clay whistle-flute borrindo, the long narr flute, bowed surando, wooden chapri clappers and dholak, with singing that is slow, declamatory and heavily melismatic over an unwavering drone. It differs from Punjabi qawwali by its lack of clapped party chorus and rhythmic acceleration, and from Saraiki kafi by repertoire, the tambooro's specific tuning, and shrine-liturgical rather than commercial framing.
exemplars: Bhit Shah faqirs (Shah jo Raag ensemble)

items.name: Nohay (Shia Muharram elegy)
items.lineage: Shia mourning elegy sung during Muharram in South Asia and the Gulf, formalized in Lucknow and Hyderabad majlis practice from the 18th-19th centuries in Urdu marsiya-noha poetics and diffused globally by the Pakistani cassette industry from the 1980s through Nadeem Sarwar and Farhan Ali Waris, marked by unaccompanied or minimally accompanied voice, chest-beating matam supplying the pulse, unison responsorial refrains, slow duple or 6/8 processional meters, and rising modal laments on the martyrdom of Husayn at Karbala.
items.description: Nohay are the elegies sung in Shia Muharram gatherings and processions commemorating the killing of Husayn ibn Ali at Karbala, developed as a distinct form in the Urdu poetic culture of Lucknow and Hyderabad and now a global cassette-and-video repertoire in Urdu, Punjabi, Sindhi, Arabic and Farsi. Melodic instruments are usually avoided; the rhythmic foundation is matam, the synchronized chest-beating of the assembly, over which a lead reciter alternates with a massed unison refrain in slow duple or lilting 6/8 processional meter. It is distinguished from marsiya by shorter strophic form and communal refrain, and from naat by its elegiac rather than laudatory subject and its percussive body-beating pulse.

items.name: Naat (South Asian Prophetic praise recitation)
items.lineage: South Asian devotional poetry in praise of the Prophet Muhammad, sung in Urdu, Punjabi, Arabic and Persian and codified in the Barelvi mehfil-e-naat culture of the Punjab and Deccan from the 19th century, transformed into a mass genre by Pakistani radio and the T-Series and Lahore cassette trades through Qari Waheed Zafar Qasmi, Marghoob Hamdani and Junaid Jamshed, marked by unmetered opening hamd, harmonium and tabla or wholly voice-only rendition, responsorial durood refrains, and ornate raga-inflected melisma at deliberate tempo.
items.description: Naat is the South Asian tradition of sung poetry praising the Prophet Muhammad, performed in mehfil-e-naat assemblies, at mawlid observances and on Ramadan broadcasts across Pakistan, India and their diasporas. A soloist delivers Urdu or Punjabi verse in ornamented raga-derived melody, typically opening in free rhythm before settling into a moderate cycle, supported by harmonium and tabla or, in stricter circles, sung entirely a cappella with a congregational durood refrain. It differs from qawwali by its slower tempo, absence of clapped ensemble drive and lack of ecstatic acceleration, and from nohay by its celebratory rather than mourning register.

items.name: Mappila paattu
items.lineage: Song tradition of the Mappila Muslims of Malabar in northern Kerala, written in Arabi-Malayalam script from at least the 17th century with Muhyiddin Mala (1607) as its founding text and Moyinkutty Vaidyar as its great 19th-century poet, revived commercially from the 1970s through V. M. Kutty and cassette-era singers, marked by isal melodic templates blending Arabic maqam contour with Malayalam prosody, duff frame-drum and kolkali stick rhythms, oppana wedding hand-clap accompaniment, and responsorial group singing.
items.description: Mappila paattu is the Arabi-Malayalam song literature of the Muslim communities of Malabar in northern Kerala, spanning devotional mala texts, martyrdom ballads such as the Malappuram padappattu, wedding oppana songs and riddle-and-love genres. Musically it runs on isal, a set of inherited melodic-metric templates whose contours carry Arabic and Persian inflection over Malayalam-Arabic hybrid verse, delivered responsorially with duff frame drums, ringing elathalam cymbals, and the clapping and stick-striking of oppana and kolkali dance. It is distinguished from Kerala's Hindu temple and Carnatic repertoires by language, Islamic subject matter and duff-based rhythm, and from Urdu naat by its Malayalam prosody and dance-linked communal performance.

items.name: Zikir (Southeast Asian Islamic dhikr)
items.lineage: Communal Islamic remembrance chanting as practiced across Aceh, the Malay Peninsula and Java from the spread of Sufi tariqa in the 16th-17th centuries onward, led by a syeikh who intones the tahlil formula while seated ranks of men answer in accelerating unison, the pulse driven by body percussion, hand-claps and rebana/kompang frame drums that tighten from a slow swaying tempo to a hard 160+ BPM shout at the climax.
items.description: Zikir is the Southeast Asian communal form of Islamic dhikr, sung by seated male ranks in mosque halls and village meunasah across Aceh, Malaysia and Java. A leader chants melismatic Arabic phrases in a maqam-inflected line while the group answers with short repeated formulas over accelerating hand-claps and frame drums, the texture built entirely from voices and body sound. Unlike Arab Sufi hadra it favors tight collective unison and a hypnotic accelerando rather than instrumental ensemble accompaniment, and unlike sholawat it is remembrance of God rather than praise of the Prophet.

items.name: Sholawat (Indonesian praise of the Prophet)
items.lineage: Indonesian devotional genre of sung blessings on the Prophet Muhammad, rooted in Hadrami Arab maulid texts (Barzanji, Simtud Durar) brought to Java in the 19th century and mass-popularized from the 1990s by pesantren majelis and cassette/television broadcast — a solo munsyid sings ornamented Arabic verse in maqam over a hadrah bank of rebana and marwas frames at a swaying 90-110 BPM, answered by massed male congregational refrains.
items.description: Sholawat is the Indonesian tradition of singing blessings on the Prophet, performed by hadrah groups and huge majelis gatherings from Java to Kalimantan. A lead munsyid delivers heavily ornamented Arabic text in a maqam contour, with a congregation answering fixed refrains over interlocking rebana frame-drum patterns and reverberant PA. It is distinguished from zikir by its textual focus on the Prophet and its stable song-form melodies, and from Arab inshad by its Javanese vocal timbre and dense frame-drum interlock.
exemplars: Habib Syech bin Abdul Qadir Assegaf

items.name: Nasyid (Malay-Indonesian Islamic vocal song)
items.lineage: Malaysian and Indonesian Islamic popular song that emerged from 1970s-80s campus dakwah movements and went commercial in the 1990s with Raihan and Snada — originally a cappella four-to-five-part male harmony with only frame drum and hand percussion permitted, later expanding to full pop arrangement, in clean twelve-tone diatonic pop melodies at 70-100 BPM with Malay and Arabic lyrics of moral exhortation.
items.description: Nasyid is the Malay-world genre of Islamic popular song, built on close male vocal harmony and frame-drum percussion and produced to full commercial studio standards since Raihan's 1996 breakthrough. Its sound is diatonic, verse-chorus, and tightly multitracked, with layered backing stacks and restrained pop-ballad instrumentation. It differs from sholawat and zikir in being composed songwriting for record release rather than congregational liturgy, and from mainstream Malay pop in its lyrical remit and voice-forward, percussion-light arrangements.

items.name: Qur'an murattal (measured devotional recitation)
items.lineage: The slow, measured style of Qur'anic recitation codified in the tajwīd manuals of the classical era and standardized through 20th-century Egyptian and Saudi broadcast and cassette masters such as Mahmoud Khalil Al-Husary and Abdul Basit — unaccompanied solo male voice at roughly 40-60 syllables per minute, strict elongation (madd) rules governing duration, restrained maqam contour, and long breath-defined phrases separated by silence.
items.description: Murattal is the deliberate, teaching-oriented register of Qur'anic recitation: one unaccompanied voice, no metric pulse, phrase durations dictated by tajwīd elongation rules rather than melody, sometimes with students or congregation repeating after the reciter. Recorded canonically in dry studio rooms for radio and mushaf-cassette sets, it is sparse, mid-range and close-miked, with silence functioning as structure. It is distinguished from mujawwad recitation by its lower ornamental density and narrower maqam range, and from all sung Islamic devotional genres by the prohibition on instruments and on treating the text as song.

items.name: Islamic recitation (adhān and mujawwad tilāwa)
items.lineage: The ornate melodic register of Islamic vocal recitation — the call to prayer and mujawwad Qur'anic tilāwa — as perfected by Cairo's radio reciters from the 1930s onward and disseminated through Egyptian state broadcast, in which a solo unaccompanied voice moves through a full maqam modulation cycle (bayati to saba to hijaz and back), sustains extreme melismatic elongation, and shapes each phrase to a single long breath with no fixed meter.
items.description: Mujawwad recitation and the adhān constitute the melodic, publicly performed face of Islamic vocal art: one voice, no instruments, no pulse, but a full traversal of the Arab maqam system with elaborate melisma, dramatic register leaps and audience-responsive repetition of a single verse, often with a live congregation audible in response. The classic recorded sound is Egyptian radio — tube microphone, valve chain, tape, and the natural reverberation of a mosque or a large studio. Against murattal it is far more ornamented and improvisatory; against Sufi inshad it stays strictly solo and unaccompanied.

items.name: Tibetan traditional secular song (nangma-töshé and dranyen song)
items.lineage: Urban courtly and social song of Lhasa and central Tibet, consolidated in the 17th-19th centuries around the Nangma Kyidug guild with clear Central Asian and Chinese influence, performed by singers accompanying themselves on the dranyen long-necked lute with piwang fiddle, lingbu flute and yangqin — slow pentatonic nangma introductions opening into brisk duple töshé dance sections around 120-140 BPM with stamped footwork marking the beat.
items.description: Nangma and töshé are the secular song-and-dance repertoire of Tibetan towns, sung in a bright high-tessitura voice with dense grace-note ornament over dranyen lute, bowed piwang and transverse lingbu. Performances pair a slow, freely ornamented nangma section with a fast metrical töshé for stamping dance. It sits apart from monastic Tibetan chant in its pentatonic melodic idiom and stringed accompaniment, and from ache lhamo opera in having no narrative or masked-theatre frame.

items.name: Tibetan mantra recitation (mani and vajra mantra)
items.lineage: Vajrayana mantra practice of Tibet and the Himalayan monastic world, formalized from the 11th-century second diffusion onward, in which assembled monks or laypeople repeat a fixed syllable formula such as om mani padme hum thousands of times in a low collective drone at roughly 40-70 repetitions per minute, punctuated in ritual settings by tingsha, damaru, rolmo cymbals and long dung chen blasts.
items.description: Mantra recitation is the most repetitive stratum of Tibetan Buddhist sound: a short fixed syllable string cycled without variation, usually on a narrow low pitch band, by one practitioner or a whole assembly whose slight tuning spread produces a beating drone. Ritual instruments punctuate section boundaries rather than keep time. Compared with yang liturgical chant it has almost no melodic contour or notated shape, and compared with thödröl recitation it is non-textual formula rather than read scripture.

items.name: Himalayan folk (trans-Himalayan hill song)
items.lineage: Village song of the mid-Himalayan belt from Kumaon and Nepal through Sikkim and Bhutan, transmitted orally and documented by ethnographers from the mid-20th century — seasonal, agricultural and wedding songs in narrow-range modal melody with heavy nasal vocal placement, accompanied by madal or damphu hand drum, murali/bansuri flute and sarangi, in walking-tempo duple or free-metered outdoor calls.
items.description: Himalayan folk covers the village repertoire of the hill belt spanning Uttarakhand, Nepal, Sikkim and western Bhutan: harvest, herding, wedding and pilgrimage songs carried orally in narrow modal ranges with a bright nasal delivery that projects across valleys. Accompaniment is minimal — a madal or damphu keeping a lilting duple, plus flute or sarangi doubling the vocal line. It is broader and more rural than the staged lok dohori duet form and lacks the Tibetan monastic chant idiom of the higher plateau.

items.name: Lok dohori (Nepali call-and-response duet)
items.lineage: Nepali competitive improvised duet song, rooted in village courtship exchanges of the hill districts and commercialized through Radio Nepal and the 1980s-90s cassette industry, in which male and female singers trade extemporized rhyming couplets in a fixed melodic frame over a driving madal ostinato at roughly 100-130 BPM with sarangi, bansuri and later harmonium and keyboard filling the responses.
items.description: Lok dohori is the improvised Nepali duel-song, a male and female singer alternating freshly invented couplets over a repeating madal groove until one is stumped. Recorded output from the cassette era onward keeps the competitive structure but adds sarangi, flute, harmonium and eventually keyboard pads over a bright compressed mix. It differs from general Himalayan folk by its verbal contest form and fixed refrain frame, and from Nepali pop by keeping the improvised text and folk instrumentation at the centre.

items.name: Nepali pop (adhunik geet and Kathmandu pop)
items.lineage: Kathmandu-based popular song developed from Radio Nepal's adhunik geet of the 1950s-70s and turned into a guitar-and-keyboard pop industry after the 1990 democracy movement by bands such as Nepathya and 1974 AD — mid-tempo 80-120 BPM verse-chorus songs in Nepali, diatonic and lightly Hindustani-inflected, with clean electric guitar, layered synth pads, programmed or acoustic kit, and madal added for national colour.
items.description: Nepali pop is the Kathmandu-centred popular-song mainstream, running from lyrical adhunik geet ballads to the folk-rock of Nepathya and modern DAW-produced singles. Arrangements are diatonic and vocal-led, with clean guitars, synth pads and a mixed acoustic-programmed rhythm section, and madal or sarangi used as identifying colour rather than structural drive. It differs from lok dohori in being composed and non-improvised, and from Bollywood-facing South Asian pop in its Nepali-language melodic phrasing and lighter orchestration.

items.name: Bhutanese pop (rigsar)
items.lineage: Bhutan's modern popular song style, named rigsar and dated by convention to the 1960s song 'Zhendi Migo', which took shape through the 1980s-90s as electric keyboards, drum machines and Bollywood-derived arrangement templates were fitted to Dzongkha lyrics — mid-tempo 90-115 BPM verse-chorus songs, sweet high nasal vocal delivery, preset synth strings and rhythm boxes, with dranyen retained as a traditional signature.
items.description: Rigsar is Bhutan's contemporary popular song, built on cheap keyboard workstations and rhythm presets carrying Dzongkha or Tshangla lyrics, and dominant in Bhutanese film soundtracks since the 1990s. The sound is thin, bright and highly synthetic — preset string pads, boxy programmed drums, doubled high vocals — with dranyen or piwang dropped in as cultural marker. It is set apart from Bhutan's zhungdra and boedra court repertoire by its metric regularity and Western harmony, and from Nepali pop by its Tibetan-derived vocal timbre and heavier reliance on keyboard presets.

items.name: Burmese traditional song (thachin gyi and village repertoire)
items.lineage: Court-derived and village song repertoire of central Myanmar, its canon fixed after the 18th-century Ayutthaya contact and preserved through the Konbaung palace and 20th-century state ensembles — heptatonic near-equal tuning, sharply syncopated melody with the vocal line deliberately offset from the instruments, saung gauk arched harp or pattala xylophone accompaniment, and time marked strictly by si bell and wa clapper rather than by drums.
items.description: Burmese traditional song joins the classical thachin gyi canon to the folk and devotional repertoire of the Irrawaddy valley, sung in a tense, sharply articulated voice over saung gauk harp or pattala xylophone. Its defining trait is rhythmic dislocation: the singer and the instrument stagger against each other while si and wa hand percussion hold an unyielding cycle. Compared with the loud outdoor hsaing waing drum-circle it is intimate and chamber-scaled, and its heptatonic tuning and offbeat phrasing set it apart from Thai and Khmer court music.
exemplars: Hsaing Waing Traditional Music Ensemble of Yangon

items.name: Lao traditional music (sep ensembles and lam song)
items.lineage: The traditional music of Laos and the Lao-speaking Isan plateau, comprising the courtly sep nyai and sep noi ensembles of Luang Prabang codified under the Lan Xang kingdoms and the village lam sung-poetry tradition — khaen free-reed mouth organ supplying a continuous drone-plus-melody, phin lute and so u fiddle in heterophony, seven-near-equal tuning, and a rapid syllabic vocal recitation over a lilting duple pulse.
items.description: Lao traditional music spans the gong-and-xylophone sep ensembles inherited from the Luang Prabang court and the khaen-accompanied lam vocal poetry of the villages and Isan plateau. The khaen is the defining sound — a bamboo mouth organ producing a continuous drone with an interlocking melodic line — under a fast, speech-derived vocal delivery that follows Lao tonal contours. It is thinner and more drone-based than Thai piphat, and its lam singing is more syllabic and improvisatory than Burmese classical song.

items.name: Sinhala Pop (Sri Lankan)
items.lineage: Colombo-centred Sinhala-language popular song codified from the late 1960s by Clarence Wijewardena's Moonstones and Super Golden Chimes and carried into the 1980s cassette era by Milton Mallawarachchi, Sunil Perera's Gypsies and Bathiya & Santhush, welding Portuguese-descended baila's 6/8 kaffrinha lilt and rabana-derived hand-drum patterns to electric guitar-bass-kit combo instrumentation, 100-130 BPM, diatonic major-key refrains and a light nasal-forward tenor delivery with Hindi-filmi-influenced string sweetening.
items.description: Sinhala pop is the Sri Lankan mainland popular-song mainstream that emerged around 1968 when Clarence Wijewardena replaced imported English-language covers with Sinhala lyrics over guitar-combo backing, and dominated Colombo radio and the cassette-kiosk economy through the 1990s. Its sonic signature is a bright, thin-mixed guitar band with prominent hand percussion, sweetened by synth strings or small violin sections, carrying strophic verse-chorus melodies in plain major keys and clearly enunciated Sinhala. It differs from baila proper by its slower ballad register and studio polish, and from Indian filmi pop by its guitar-band rather than orchestra-and-playback foundation.

items.name: Maldivian Pop (Dhivehi)
items.lineage: Dhivehi-language popular song developed in Malé from the late 1970s around Voice of Maldives broadcasts and the Zero Degree Atoll and Fasgandu circles, setting Dhivehi lyrics and bodu-beru-derived hand-drum patterns against Hindi-filmi melodic contour, nylon and electric guitars, cheap polysynth pads and drum-machine backbeats at 90-120 BPM, with an unforced mid-range male tenor and heavy reverb typical of the island cassette studios.
items.description: Maldivian pop is the small-scale Dhivehi popular-song idiom of Malé and the atolls, consolidated in the 1980s cassette economy and given an art-conscious wing by Zero Degree Atoll's 1997 album Dhoni. Its texture is sparse — guitar, bass, a programmed backbeat and a synth pad — over bodu beru's rolling hand-drum figures and clapped accents, with melodies that borrow Hindi film ornamentation but stay in short strophic forms. Compared to Sinhala pop it is thinner, more synth-dependent and more openly filmi-derived; compared to bodu beru itself it is metrically regular and harmonised rather than accelerating and purely percussive.

items.name: Zeuhl (Kobaïan movement)
items.lineage: Paris, 1970 onward: drummer Christian Vander's Magma codified zeuhl as a rock idiom built on Coltrane-derived modal fervour and Orff-like massed choral chant in the invented Kobaïan language, over relentless minor-mode ostinati, distorted-and-clanking fuzz bass carrying the principal riff, marcato Fender Rhodes and piano clusters, jazz-schooled polyrhythmic drumming and long crescendo forms, extended by Univers Zéro, Art Zoyd, Eskaton and later Japanese followers Ruins and Koenjihyakkei.
items.description: Zeuhl is the French progressive-rock lineage that Magma founded in 1970 and named in its own invented Kobaïan tongue, in which massed unison chanting and militaristic ostinati replace the verse-chorus song entirely. The characteristic sound is a saturated, growling bass playing the lead melodic figure, hammered Rhodes and piano chords, jazz-trained drums driving long accelerating vamps, and choral voices used as a brass-like block rather than for lyrics in any real language. It is distinguished from Canterbury progressive by its lack of whimsy and its ritual, minor-key relentlessness, and from Rock in Opposition by its trance-inducing repetition where RIO prefers discontinuity.

items.name: Rock in Opposition
items.lineage: A movement declared at Henry Cow's March 1978 London festival, when Fred Frith and Chris Cutler allied Univers Zéro, Stormy Six, Samla Mammas Manna and Etron Fou Leloublan against the record industry, producing a through-composed chamber-rock of shifting odd meters, dissonant reed-and-string writing, Bartók- and Weill-derived harmony, notated scores fused with free-improvisation blocks, and pointedly leftist texts sung in several European languages.
items.description: Rock in Opposition began as a 1978 mutual-support pact among five European avant-rock groups shut out of the commercial circuit, and hardened into a recognisable style: notated chamber-rock scored for reeds, strings and voice alongside a rock rhythm section, with abrupt sectional cuts, chromatic and cluster harmony, and blocks of free improvisation embedded in written material. Texts are political and delivered plainly rather than theatrically. It is distinguished from symphonic progressive rock by its refusal of grandeur and tonal resolution, and from zeuhl by its through-composed discontinuity rather than ostinato trance.

items.name: Neue Deutsche Welle
items.lineage: West German new wave of 1979-1983, sparked in Düsseldorf and Hamburg by Der Plan, DAF, Fehlfarben and Abwärts and pushed into the charts by Nena, Trio and Ideal, defined by deadpan German-language vocals, cheap monophonic and polyphonic synths, sequenced or metronomic drum-machine and motorik-derived 4/4 at 120-145 BPM, trebly clipped guitar, and a minimal, dry, self-produced small-studio sound.
items.description: Neue Deutsche Welle was the West German answer to punk and new wave, running from the 1979 independent-label wave to its exhausted chart phase in 1983. Its sound is deliberately cheap and rigid: sequenced or drum-machine pulse, one or two thin analogue synth lines, staccato guitar chops, almost no reverb, and flat, spoken-adjacent German vocals delivering ironic or absurdist texts. It differs from British new wave chiefly in insisting on German, and from krautrock in its short pop forms and abandonment of extended improvisation.

items.name: Hamburger Schule
items.lineage: Hamburg indie-rock circle of roughly 1989-1997 around the L'Age d'Or and What's So Funny About labels, with Blumfeld, Tocotronic, Die Sterne and Kolossale Jugend applying American post-punk and Sonic Youth guitar textures to dense, theory-inflected German lyrics, at mid-tempo 100-140 BPM with jangling or scraped single-coil guitars, plain unadorned four-piece rhythm sections, and speech-rhythm vocal delivery that subordinates melody to text.
items.description: Hamburger Schule names the German indie-rock scene of the early and mid 1990s centred on Hamburg's L'Age d'Or label, where bands paired conventional guitar-bass-drums post-punk with unusually literary, politically self-conscious German lyrics. Sonically it is deliberately plain: dry unlayered guitars ranging from clean jangle to controlled feedback, a mid-forward vocal that half-speaks long syntactically complex lines, and little studio ornament. It separates itself from Neue Deutsche Welle by rejecting synths and irony for guitars and earnestness, and from Anglo-American indie rock by treating the lyric as the primary compositional material.

items.name: Ostrock (GDR rock)
items.lineage: East German rock produced from the late 1960s to 1990 under the state Amiga label and the mandatory 60-percent domestic-repertoire rule, with Puhdys, City, Karat, Silly and Pankow writing German-language songs that fold Anglo hard-rock riffing and progressive keyboard arrangements into radio-length forms, using Hammond and string-machine pads, folk violin colour, restrained heavy-rock guitar and lyrics coded to slip past censors.
items.description: Ostrock is the rock repertoire made inside the GDR between the late 1960s and reunification, shaped as much by Amiga's monopoly, state licensing of musicians and airplay quotas as by musical choice. The result is a well-drilled, conservatively engineered hard rock with prominent organ and string-machine, competent but unshowy guitar solos, and German lyrics whose ambiguity was the point — City's Am Fenster and Karat's Über sieben Brücken became standards on both sides of the border. It is distinguished from West German Deutschrock by its state-studio uniformity and metaphorical lyricism, and from Soviet magnitizdat rock by being officially released rather than clandestinely taped.

items.name: Deutschrock (German-language rock mainstream)
items.lineage: West German-language rock consolidated from the mid-1970s by Udo Lindenberg's Panikorchester and extended through BAP's Cologne dialect songs, Herbert Grönemeyer's 1984 Bochum and later Böhse Onkelz and Die Toten Hosen, applying Anglo-American hard-rock and heartland-rock arrangements — driving mid-tempo 4/4, riff-plus-piano backing, saxophone and horn accents, arena-scaled backing choruses — to plainspoken, regionally accented German lyrics about everyday and political life.
items.description: Deutschrock is the mainstream German-language rock idiom that Udo Lindenberg made commercially viable in the mid-1970s and that BAP, Grönemeyer and later punk-descended acts carried into stadiums. Musically it is straightforward heartland rock — mid-tempo backbeat, chorused rhythm guitar over piano or organ, big unison singalong choruses, occasional sax — with the identity carried by the voice: gravelly, accented, conversational, and always in German or dialect. It differs from Ostrock in its market rather than state formation and its blunter lyricism, and from Neue Deutsche Welle in rejecting synths and irony for band-played rock sincerity.

items.name: Liedermacher (German songwriter tradition)
items.lineage: West and East German art-of-song tradition named by Wolf Biermann in the early 1960s after Brecht's Stückeschreiber, developed at the Burg Waldeck festivals from 1964 by Franz Josef Degenhardt, Hannes Wader, Reinhard Mey and Konstantin Wecker, setting long politically or satirically pointed German texts to fingerpicked steel-string guitar, cabaret piano or small accordion accompaniment in strophic ballad form, sung in an unhurried near-spoken baritone with rubato tied to the words.
items.description: The Liedermacher tradition is the German singer-songwriter practice that grew out of the Burg Waldeck festivals in the mid-1960s, deliberately descended from Brecht and Tucholsky rather than from Anglo-American folk revival. Recordings are sparse — one voice, fingerstyle guitar or cabaret piano, sometimes a bass or clarinet — with the words placed forward and rhythm bent freely to the line, over many-versed narrative or agitational strophes. It is separated from Anglo folk revival by its cabaret harmony and literary rather than balladic diction, and from Deutschrock by having no band, no backbeat and no chorus.

items.name: Variété française
items.lineage: The French mainstream popular-song industry from the 1950s onward, built around Paris labels and the Olympia stage and defined by Charles Aznavour, Michel Sardou, Sylvie Vartan, Michel Berger and Jean-Jacques Goldman, characterised by orchestral or later synth-and-band arrangements written by contracted arrangers, mid-tempo 4/4 or slow ballad meters, wide string and brass swells behind a strongly enunciated French lead vocal, and a chorus-forward song architecture aimed at television and radio.
items.description: Variété française is the commercial French popular-song mainstream, distinct from chanson as a professional industry rather than an authorial stance: staff arrangers, orchestral sessions, television promotion and a repertoire of ballads and mid-tempo numbers sung in careful, front-of-mouth French. Its sound moves from 1960s string-and-rhythm-section orchestration to 1980s synth-pad, gated-drum and saxophone production without changing the melodic priority given to the vocal line. It is distinguished from chanson classique by the diminished role of the singer as author and by the scale of its arrangements, and from yé-yé by its adult address and slower tempos.

items.name: Yé-yé
items.lineage: French and francophone teen-pop of roughly 1962-1968 named from the English 'yeah yeah', promoted by Salut les copains radio and centred on Françoise Hardy, France Gall, Sylvie Vartan and Jacques Dutronc with Serge Gainsbourg supplying material, combining Brill Building and beat-group templates — 120-160 BPM shuffle or straight backbeat, tambourine and hand claps, twangy reverbed guitar, walking or eighth-note bass — with light untrained girlish French vocals and small string or horn overdubs cut at Pathé-Marconi and Barclay.
items.description: Yé-yé was the French adaptation of Anglo-American teen pop between about 1962 and 1968, marketed through the Salut les copains magazine and radio show and sung mostly by young women in a deliberately slight, breathy, untrained voice. Records are short and bright: reverbed single-coil guitar, tambourine and claps on the backbeat, a beat-group rhythm section, and a quick string or brass sweetener, with lyrics often ironic or double-edged when Gainsbourg wrote them. It is separated from American girl-group pop by its thinner vocal ideal and wittier lyric register, and from variété française by its youth address, brevity and beat-band instrumentation.

items.name: Bal-musette (Parisian dance-hall practice)
items.lineage: Parisian dance-hall music of the 1880s-1930s, begun in Auvergnat immigrant bals of the Bastille and Italie quarters where the bellows-blown cabrette bagpipe led bourrées, then reshaped after 1900 as Italian immigrant accordionists took over and standardised the repertoire of valse, java, polka and paso doble in fast 3/4 and 2/4, played by accordion with banjo and drums for a paying, close-packed dancing crowd.
items.description: Bal-musette is the working-class Parisian dance-hall practice that began with Auvergnat migrants dancing bourrées to the cabrette in the 1880s and mutated when Italian accordionists entered the same halls after 1900, producing the accordion-led valse and java repertoire that became a Paris emblem. The music is functional and fast: strongly marked triple or duple pulse, a driving banjo chop, brushed or stick drums, and a bellows-shaken accordion vibrato carrying a diatonic melody, all recorded raw onto 78s. It differs from the later valse musette of the 1930s by its rougher, pre-virtuoso playing and lingering bagpipe presence, and from chanson by having no lyric centre at all.

items.name: Valse musette (accordion virtuoso repertoire)
items.lineage: The refined accordion repertoire that grew out of bal-musette from the mid-1930s when Gus Viseur, Tony Murena and Jo Privat absorbed the harmony and swing feel of the Paris manouche jazz scene, giving the fast valse — typically 180-220 beats per minute in 3/4 with the accordion's shimmering wet-tuned tremolo — chromatic passing chords, sixth and ninth voicings, rhythm-guitar la pompe and virtuoso right-hand runs, cut for Odéon and Pathé and later maintained by Yvette Horner and Marcel Azzola.
items.description: Valse musette is the virtuoso, jazz-inflected accordion repertoire that separated from the rough bal-musette dance practice in the mid-1930s, when players such as Gus Viseur and Tony Murena took the harmonic language of Django Reinhardt's circle into the waltz. Its markers are extreme tempo, a wet tremolo-tuned accordion tone, rapid ornamented right-hand figuration, swung rhythm-guitar comping and altered chord substitutions under otherwise simple melodies, usually purely instrumental. It differs from bal-musette proper in polish, harmonic ambition and jazz phrasing, and from gypsy jazz in placing the accordion rather than the guitar at the centre.

items.name: Canzone d'Autore
items.lineage: Italian literary songwriting tradition formed circa 1958-62 around the Genoa school (Luigi Tenco, Gino Paoli, Bruno Lauzi) and codified by Fabrizio De André, Francesco Guccini, Lucio Dalla and Paolo Conte through RCA Italiana and Ricordi sessions — moderate 4/4 or 3/4 ballad tempos, nylon or steel acoustic guitar and piano over discreet string and woodwind arrangements, sung in a low conversational baritone that privileges dense anticlerical, political and narrative lyric text over vocal display.
items.description: Canzone d'autore emerged in northern Italy at the turn of the 1960s as a deliberate literary answer to the Sanremo light-song industry, taking French chanson's writer-performer model and grafting it onto Italian poetic tradition. The sound is restrained: fingerpicked guitar or piano, upright bass, chamber strings, and an unornamented mid-range male voice mixed forward so the text stays intelligible. Unlike Neapolitan canzone or Italian schlager it avoids melisma and big cadential climaxes, and unlike Anglo folk revival it keeps professional orchestrators in the room.
exemplars: Fabrizio De André - Non al denaro non all'amore né al cielo
Lucio Dalla - Com'è profondo il mare

items.name: Neomelodici
items.lineage: Neapolitan working-class pop that crystallized in the Naples suburbs during the late 1980s and 1990s around Nino D'Angelo's successors — Gigi D'Alessio, Mauro Nardi, Tommy Riccio, Gianni Celeste — built on cheap MIDI keyboard-and-drum-machine backing at 90-115 BPM, string-pad and mandolin patches, minor-key melodic hooks, and a piercing high-tenor dialect voice singing love, jail and neighbourhood narratives distributed on locally pressed cassettes and CDs sold outside the national label system.
items.description: The neomelodica scene formed in Naples in the late 1980s as a cassette-economy successor to classic canzone napoletana, produced in small home studios and circulated through street kiosks, weddings and local TV rather than national radio. Sonically it is defined by programmed drum machines, sequenced string pads and synthetic mandolin timbres under a very high, heavily emotive Neapolitan-dialect tenor with fast narrow vibrato. It differs from canzone napoletana in its wholly electronic backing and from Italian mainstream pop in its dialect text and informal distribution.

items.name: Beat Italiano
items.lineage: Italian beat boom of 1965-69, launched by Piper Club Rome and the Milan scene and codified by Equipe 84, The Rokes, I Nomadi, I Camaleonti and Le Orme — mid-tempo 4/4 backbeats at 110-140 BPM, jangling twelve-string and fuzz-toned single-coil guitars, Vox and Farfisa combo organ, and close two- and three-part harmony over Italian-language lyrics, much of it Italianized cover versions cut at RCA Italiana and Ricordi with heavy tape echo and orchestral overdubs.
items.description: Beat italiano was Italy's absorption of British beat between 1965 and 1969, centred on Rome's Piper Club and the Milanese label studios, and often performed by British expatriate groups singing in Italian. The records pair Merseybeat guitar-and-organ instrumentation with the reverb-drenched, string-sweetened arranging habits of the Italian pop studio, giving a fuller, more orchestral texture than their UK models.
