Its sonic signature is the fully sequenced arrangement — no recorded performance anywhere in the chain — carrying a synthesised lead pushed past human limits: extreme syllable density, wide leaps, and stepwise pitch-bend automation used as expression. It is distinguished from J-pop by the absence of a singer and from Western EDM-vocal production by its rock-band instrumentation, modulating J-pop harmony and its fan-remix-and-cover economy rather than club play.

items.name: Chipmusic (LSDj and Game Boy live scene)
items.lineage: Post-2000 international scene playing 1980s-90s consumer sound chips as live instruments, codified by Johan Kotlinski's Little Sound Dj (2000) and Oliver Wittchow's Nanoloop for the Nintendo Game Boy plus NES/Famicom NSF and Amiga trackers, spread through 8bitpeoples, Blip Festival (NYC, 2006-2012) and micromusic.net — 140-190 BPM patterns programmed step-by-step on four voices (two pulse, one wave, one noise), fast arpeggio 'chords' from single-channel note-cycling, pulse-width and vibrato modulation as the only timbral controls, and a live set played from handheld hardware straight into a PA.
items.description: Chipmusic in this sense is not nostalgia scoring but a live performance practice, consolidated around 2000-2010 when LSDj and Nanoloop turned the Game Boy into a gigging sequencer and Blip Festival gave the scene an annual centre. The sound is defined by hard limits: three or four monophonic voices, square and noise waveforms, no reverb, so melody, bass and drums are interleaved in time and 'chords' exist only as ultra-fast arpeggios, with pulse-width sweeps supplying colour. It differs from soundtrack chip music by being written for a dancefloor rather than a game, and from demoscene tracker music by using the original chips as the actual sound source instead of samples on a general-purpose computer.

items.name: Demoscene tracker module music
items.lineage: European computer-demo subculture music, formed on the Commodore Amiga after Karsten Obarski's Ultimate Soundtracker (1987) and carried onto PC by ProTracker, Scream Tracker, FastTracker II and Impulse Tracker — composed by Purple Motion, Skaven, Jesper Kyd, Lizardking and Necros for Future Crew, Triton and Renaissance demos and shown at Assembly and The Party — 120-165 BPM four-to-thirty-two-channel patterns of short looped samples entered as hexadecimal note tables, with heavy use of volume/pitch effect columns, sample offset tricks and slot-sharing to fake extra voices inside a few hundred kilobytes.
items.description: Demoscene music is the tracker-module repertoire written from 1987 onward to soundtrack real-time computer demos, first on the Amiga's four-channel Paula chip and then on PC soundcards. The idiom is shaped by file-size ceilings: a handful of one-shot samples reused across bass, lead and pads, aggressive per-row effect commands standing in for envelopes and filters, and multi-part structures that develop over five or six minutes rather than looping. Unlike chipmusic proper it is sample-based rather than chip-synthesised, and unlike game soundtracks it is through-composed for a fixed non-interactive visual sequence, which is why its arrangements build and modulate like concert pieces.
exemplars: Jesper Kyd — The Silents / Amiga demos

items.name: Commodore 64 SID music
items.lineage: British and Northern European game-music practice of 1983-1992 written for the MOS 6581/8580 SID chip in the Commodore 64, codified by Rob Hubbard, Martin Galway, Ben Daglish, Jeroen Tel and Chris Huelsbeck via hand-written 6502 assembly players — three voices only, so chords are rendered as 50Hz arpeggio cycling, bass and lead share a channel through rapid note interleaving, and colour comes from pulse-width modulation, hard sync, ring modulation and the chip's resonant analog filter, over driving 130-160 BPM patterns whose drums are the noise oscillator with a fast pitch envelope.
items.description: SID music is the body of Commodore 64 game and demo soundtracks written between roughly 1983 and 1992, when a handful of composers turned a three-voice chip with one shared analog filter into a recognisable compositional style. Its hallmarks are the chirping fast arpeggio used as a chord substitute, channel-stealing that makes three voices sound like five, filter sweeps and ring-modulated metallic timbres, and long loopable cues that develop through variation rather than a chorus. Compared to Famicom/NES writing it is far more timbrally varied because of the filter and pulse-width control, and compared to later chipmusic it was produced commercially under deadline for cassette- and disk-loaded games rather than for live performance.
exemplars: Rob Hubbard — Monty on the Run

items.name: Algorave (live-coded algorithmic dance music)
items.lineage: UK-originated live-coding dance practice named by Alex McLean and Nick Collins in 2011-2012 out of Sheffield, Nottingham and the TOPLAP live-coding movement — performers write and rewrite code on stage in TidalCycles, SuperCollider, Sonic Pi or Hydra with the editor projected behind them, generating 120-180 BPM sample-and-synthesis patterns whose Euclidean rhythms, polymetric cycle-lengths and probabilistic substitutions mutate audibly with each evaluated line, over techno-derived kick foundations and glitch-heavy percussive grain.
items.description: Algorave is dance music generated by code written live in front of the audience, named in 2012 by Alex McLean and Nick Collins and spreading from UK warehouse nights into an international network of events. Musically it sits on a techno chassis but the material is pattern algebra: Euclidean and polymetric cycles of differing lengths drifting in and out of phase, randomised sample substitution, and abrupt structural jumps that happen when a line of code is re-evaluated rather than at bar 16. It is distinguished from DJ sets and hardware-jam techno by the absence of pre-made tracks and by the projected source code, which makes the compositional decision-making part of the performance.

items.name: Trip hop
items.lineage: Bristol, England, 1991-1998, growing out of the Wild Bunch sound-system and codified by Massive Attack, Portishead, Tricky and producers Nellee Hooper and Geoff Barrow — 70-100 BPM sampled or replayed hip-hop breakbeats slowed and swung, dub-derived deep bass with long tape-style delay throws, minor-key Rhodes, film-library strings and Mellotron pads, deliberate vinyl surface noise and turntable scratching, and a torch-singer or half-spoken vocal delivered close to the mic.
items.description: Trip hop formed in Bristol in the early 1990s where Jamaican sound-system culture, punk-era studio pragmatism and American sampling collided, and was consolidated by Massive Attack's Blue Lines (1991) and Portishead's Dummy (1994). Its defining sound is a slow, heavy, swung breakbeat under sub-heavy dub bass, with minor-key keyboard and string samples treated for grain and hiss, delay used as an arranging tool, and vocals that are intimate and unhurried rather than declamatory. It differs from instrumental hip-hop by centring sung female or murmured male lead lines and full song form, and from downtempo/chillout by its dub bass weight and noir emotional register.

items.name: Psydub (psychedelic dub)
items.lineage: Mid-2000s downtempo offshoot of the psytrance chillout room, codified by Ott (Hallucinogen in Dub, 2002; Blumenkraft, 2003), Kaya Project, Bluetech and Kalya Scintilla on Twisted and Interchill — 70-110 BPM half-time dub drum patterns with heavy siren-tail delay and spring-style reverb on every hit, deep sine sub-bass, phased and filter-swept psytrance lead patches slowed to a crawl, and sampled tabla, hand percussion and South Asian or Middle Eastern vocal fragments layered as texture.
items.description: Psydub is the dub-processing branch of psychedelic chillout, consolidated in the UK and North America in the mid-2000s when Ott's remix work applied Jamaican mixing-desk technique to psytrance sound design. The result runs at 70-110 BPM with skanking half-time drums drenched in feedback delay, a clean sine sub, and slow-modulating resonant synth lines that are recognisably psytrance patches stretched out, threaded with sampled tabla, frame drums and world-vocal fragments. Against classic dub it is entirely constructed in-the-box with no live band, and against psychill it keeps a hard rhythmic backbone and dub's echo-throw performance gestures rather than dissolving into ambient pads.

items.name: Psychill (psychedelic chillout)
items.lineage: Chillout-tent music of the 1990s-2000s psytrance festival circuit, codified by Shpongle (Simon Posford and Raja Ram, from 1996), Entheogenic, Carbon Based Lifeforms and the Twisted, Ultimae and Interchill catalogues — 80-120 BPM loose downtempo or beatless passages, long evolving pad beds and reverse-reverb swells, phrase-length arrangements that move by texture rather than chorus, sampled bansuri, didgeridoo, throat singing and spoken-word fragments, and pitch-shifted wordless vocals used as timbre.
items.description: Psychill is the ambient wing of psytrance culture, formalised in the late 1990s by Shpongle and the chillout rooms of Goa-descended festivals across Europe and Australia. It runs at 80-120 BPM or drifts beatless, favouring wide stereo pad beds, slow filter and phaser movement, sampled acoustic ethnic instruments and treated vocal fragments arranged as a continuous psychedelic narrative rather than verse-chorus. It is separated from generic downtempo by the psytrance sound-design lineage — the same resonant, heavily modulated synth voices in slow motion — and from psydub by its lack of dub's delay-throw discipline and skank rhythm.

items.name: Zenonesque
items.lineage: Mid-tempo psychedelic style named for Melbourne's Zenon Records (founded 2007 by Sensient), codified through the 2010s by Grouch, Kliment, Zen Mechanics and Way Out West festival culture — 125-140 BPM with a rolling but non-relentless kick-bass relationship, offbeat and swung hi-hat and shaker layers borrowed from techno and tribal house, granular and field-recording textures placed as percussion, dark modal or near-atonal micro-motifs instead of trance melody, and long eight-to-sixteen-bar morphs as the main structural device.
items.description: Zenonesque is the mid-tempo, groove-led branch of psytrance that grew around Australia's Zenon Records after 2007 and became the default sound of daytime and sunrise floors at European and Australian outdoor festivals. It sits at 125-140 BPM, replacing full-tilt psytrance drive with a swung, percussion-rich groove closer to tribal techno, and puts sound design — granular textures, resonant blips, field recordings used rhythmically — where trance would put melody. Against progressive psytrance it is darker, drier and less harmonically resolved; against techno it retains psytrance's continuously morphing modulation and its dedicated outdoor-festival audience.

items.name: Forest psy
items.lineage: Night-forest offshoot of psytrance formed in Finland, Russia and Denmark from the late 1990s around Parvati Records, Insomnia and the Fungus Funk / Psykovsky / Ka-Sol axis — 145-165 BPM with a tight short kick and continuous rolling 16th-note offbeat bass, FM and ring-modulated squelch leads that gurgle and pitch-bend organically rather than sing, no chord movement and only fragmentary minor motifs, dense stacking of ten or more short modulated layers, and outdoor woodland night-floor mixing that keeps the low mids scooped for open-air rigs.
items.description: Forest psy is the woodland night variant of psytrance, consolidated from the late 1990s in Finland, Denmark and Russia and given its canonical catalogue by Parvati Records. It runs at roughly 145-165 BPM over a relentless rolling bassline and a short punchy kick, with lead material made of organic-sounding FM and ring-modulated squelches, insect chirps and voice-like formant sweeps rather than melody, layered so densely that the texture reads as a continuous chattering organism. Compared to darkpsy it is generally slower, more organic and less atonally violent; compared to full-on psytrance it discards uplifting melodic hooks and the big-room build-and-drop entirely.

items.name: Nitzhonot
items.lineage: Israeli late-1990s Goa-trance variant (from nitzachon, 'victory'), built on the Phonokol and Krembo Records compilation series and the post-army Sinai and Negev party circuit — 145-155 BPM with a hard four-on-floor kick and continuous 16th-note offbeat bass, extended uplifting lead melodies in harmonic minor and Hijaz with Middle Eastern ornament and rapid trills, stacked supersaw and PPG-style digital lead layers, and long two-to-four-minute breakdowns that strip to pad and melody before an anthemic full return.
items.description: Nitzhonot is the Israeli 'victory trance' style of roughly 1996-2001, a faster and more overtly melodic reading of Goa trance carried by domestic compilation series and the Sinai desert party scene. It is identified by 145-155 BPM tempos, an unbroken rolling offbeat bass under a hard kick, and long singable lead melodies in harmonic-minor and Hijaz modes decorated with Middle Eastern trills and grace notes, arranged around euphoric extended breakdowns. Against classic Goa trance it is faster, brighter and more harmonically direct with less acid squelch; against later full-on psytrance it is melody-first rather than bassline-and-sound-design-first.

items.name: Hi-tech psytrance
items.lineage: Fastest branch of psytrance, formed in Russia, Israel and Japan from the mid-2000s around labels such as Anomalistic, Hi-Tech Doctor and the Indian and Israeli underground circuits — 190-230 BPM with a very short clicky kick and a sixteenth-note bass so fast it fuses into a drone, granular and FM-generated micro-leads chopped and re-triggered every sixteenth, glitch edits and pitch-jumped speech samples used as rhythm, near-total absence of harmony or sustained melody, and bright treble-forward mastering built for high-powered outdoor rigs.
items.description: Hi-tech psytrance is the extreme-tempo wing of the psytrance family, emerging in the mid-2000s in Russia, Israel and Japan and pushing 190-230 BPM. Its material is almost purely rhythmic sound design: a short dry kick, a sixteenth-note bass that reads as a continuous tone at speed, and constantly retriggered granular and FM fragments, glitch stutters and mangled speech placed with sample-level precision, with harmony reduced to a single implied root. It is distinguished from darkpsy by speed and by a cleaner, brighter, more digitally surgical texture, and from forest psy by discarding organic squelch and forest ambience in favour of machine-like precision.

items.name: Acid Techno
items.lineage: Formed in London and Chicago between 1988 and 1993 and codified by Liberator DJs, Chris Liberator, Lochi and the Stay Up Forever label out of the UK squat-party circuit, built on a 135-150 BPM four-on-the-floor TR-909 kick with open-hat offbeats and one or more overdriven Roland TB-303 lines whose cutoff, resonance and accent are performed live over long single-chord loops with little or no vocal.
items.description: Acid techno emerged around 1990 when UK free-party producers pushed the Chicago acid house 303 sound to faster tempos and harder distortion. The music is almost entirely instrumental: a relentless 909 kick and hats under stacked, screaming resonant basslines whose filter sweeps carry all the drama. It is faster and more abrasive than Chicago acid house and more monotimbral and loop-locked than Detroit techno.

items.name: Italo Disco
items.lineage: Italian and West German studio-producer dance music of 1979-1988, codified by Giancarlo Meo, Claudio Simonetti and the ZYX and Discomagic labels, using a 118-128 BPM electronic four-on-the-floor with LinnDrum or TR-808 claps, arpeggiated Juno/Prophet basslines, glossy string-machine pads and lightly accented English vocals often doubled by vocoder.
items.description: Italo disco formed in Italian and German studios as American disco collapsed, replacing live orchestras with drum machines and polysynths on small budgets. Its signature is a bright arpeggiated synth bass, spacious reverbed claps and earnest, melodically simple vocals in heavily accented English. Compared with post-disco boogie it is whiter in rhythm and more melodic, and unlike Hi-NRG it sits slower and leans on song hooks rather than pure propulsion.

items.name: New Italo Disco
items.lineage: A 2007-2015 revivalist scene centred on Dutch, Italian and Scandinavian net-labels such as Bordello a Parigi and Slow Motion, reconstructing early-1980s Italo templates at 115-125 BPM using vintage Juno-106 and TR-808 hardware or emulations, long instrumental intros, deep-reverb claps and deliberately cold, deadpan vocals.
items.description: New Italo disco is the reconstructed, DJ-oriented descendant of 1980s Italo, produced almost entirely in home studios from roughly 2007 onward. It keeps the Juno arpeggios, gated claps and analogue sequencer basslines but strips the pop-song scaffolding in favour of long, mixable instrumental structures and drier, more melancholic vocals. It is slower and more nostalgic than nu-disco proper and far less song-driven than the original Italo it imitates.

items.name: Euro Hi-NRG
items.lineage: European gay-club dance music of 1982-1990 built on the San Francisco Hi-NRG template and codified in London by Stock Aitken Waterman and in Italy by producers for ZYX, running 128-140 BPM with a hammering octave-jumping synth bass, four-on-the-floor kick with sixteenth open hats, orchestra-hit stabs and belted, heavily double-tracked female lead vocals.
items.description: Euro Hi-NRG carried Patrick Cowley's San Francisco disco formula into British and continental European chart pop through the mid-1980s. Its defining features are a driving octave synth bass, unrelenting sixteenth-note hats and an emotionally maximal, gospel-adjacent female vocal delivery. It runs faster and harder than Italo disco and, unlike Eurobeat's later Japanese variant, was made for domestic European clubs and singles charts.
exemplars: Divine - You Think You're a Man
Dead or Alive - You Spin Me Round
Miquel Brown - So Many Men, So Little Time

items.name: Super Eurobeat
items.lineage: Italian-produced, Japanese-marketed dance music codified from 1990 by Avex Trax's Super Eurobeat series and the A-Beat C and Delta studios in Rome, running a strict 150-160 BPM four-on-the-floor with sixteenth-note bass arpeggios, orchestra hits, a fixed intro-verse-chorus-break-chorus form and high, hard-belted English vocals by Italian session singers.
items.description: Super Eurobeat is Hi-NRG industrialised: Italian producers writing to a rigid formula for Japanese compilation albums, parapara dance clubs and later the Initial D soundtracks. Every track shares the same tempo band, chord-loop logic and rapid-fire arpeggiated bass, with vocals mixed forward and pitched near the top of the singer's range. It is faster, more formulaic and more melodically saturated than the Euro Hi-NRG it descends from.

items.name: Disco Polo
items.lineage: Polish provincial dance-pop that formed at rural wedding halls and roadside markets in the late 1980s and was codified on cassette by Blue Star and Green Star labels around 1992-1996, using 125-140 BPM preset drum-machine beats, cheap keyboard brass and accordion patches, simple I-V-vi-IV loops and plain-toned male vocals singing sentimental or bawdy Polish lyrics.
items.description: Disco polo grew out of Polish wedding-band repertoire in the last years of the communist period and boomed on cheap cassettes after 1989. It pairs generic Euro-dance drum machine patterns with keyboard imitations of accordion and brass, and its centre of gravity is the unadorned, folk-inflected Polish vocal rather than the groove. Unlike Eurodance it is sung entirely in Polish, keeps village dance-band harmony, and never adopted rap verses or club production values.

items.name: Melodipop
items.lineage: A late-1980s-to-1990s melodic electronic pop current documented across Eastern Europe and the post-Soviet space, descended from Italo disco via ZYX-style imports, built on 110-125 BPM drum-machine four-on-the-floor, minor-key diatonic melodies carried by monophonic synth leads, sparse arpeggiated bass and untrained, plaintive lead vocals in the local language.
items.description: Melodipop names the melody-first strain of synthesizer dance-pop that spread through Eastern and Southeastern Europe as Italo records reached the region in the 1980s. Its productions are thin by Western standards, foregrounding a single memorable minor-key synth hook and an emotionally direct vocal over rudimentary machine rhythm. It differs from Italo disco in its minor-mode local-language songwriting and from Eurodance in having no rap breaks and far less low-end weight.

items.name: Space Disco
items.lineage: French, Italian and German disco of 1977-1981 codified by Jean-Marc Cerrone, Didier Marouani's Space and Giorgio Moroder's Munich productions, using a 115-125 BPM sequenced Moog bass pulse under four-on-the-floor kick and open hats, vocoder and synthesized choir textures, phased string washes and long instrumental suites with sci-fi sound effects in place of verses.
items.description: Space disco is the European branch of late-1970s disco that traded orchestral soul for synthesizer futurism, most visibly on French and Munich twelve-inches built around sequencer pulses and vocoded voices. Tracks are long, instrumental and sectional, with elaborate synth arrangements and cosmic effects rather than sung choruses. Against Philadelphia disco it is machine-locked and largely wordless, and against Italo it retains live drums and full-scale studio orchestration.
exemplars: Giorgio Moroder - From Here to Eternity
Droids - Do You Have the Force

items.name: Post-Disco
items.lineage: New York and Chicago black dance music of 1980-1985 made after the disco backlash, codified by producers such as Kashif, Leon Sylvers III and the Prelude and West End labels, running 100-118 BPM with a slapped or synth-doubled electric bassline, LinnDrum and TR-808 programming, brittle syncopated electric-piano and clavinet comping and conversational soul lead vocals with group answer parts.
items.description: Post-disco, later called boogie, is what New York dance-floor R&B became once orchestras and strings were cut from budgets in 1980. Drum machines and synth bass replaced the rhythm section, tempos dropped below disco's, and space opened around a funk-derived syncopated groove and a foregrounded soul vocal. It is slower and more song-oriented than the electro that grew beside it and warmer and more R&B-rooted than Italo disco.
exemplars: D Train - You're the One for Me
Peech Boys - Don't Make Me Wait

items.name: Electro
items.lineage: New York electro-funk of 1982-1986 codified by Afrika Bambaataa and Arthur Baker on 'Planet Rock' and by Tommy Boy, Streetwise and Sunnyview, built on a syncopated TR-808 breakbeat at 110-130 BPM with tuned 808 kick bass, Kraftwerk-derived synth melodies, vocoder and talkbox vocals and turntable scratching in place of live drums.
items.description: Electro crystallised in 1982 when New York hip-hop producers replaced live funk bands with the Roland TR-808 and Kraftwerk's synthetic melodic vocabulary. Its rhythmic signature is the broken, non-four-on-the-floor 808 pattern with a long tuned kick doing bass duty, topped by robotic vocoded or talkbox voices and scratched samples. Unlike post-disco boogie it abandons the human rhythm section and sung chorus, and unlike techno it stays breakbeat-based rather than four-to-the-floor.
exemplars: Afrika Bambaataa & Soulsonic Force - Planet Rock
Man Parrish - Hip Hop, Be Bop

items.name: Miami Electro (Miami Bass)
items.lineage: Miami and Fort Lauderdale bass music of 1984-1995 codified by MC ADE, Amos Larkins II, Luke Skyywalker Records and the 2 Live Crew, running 120-145 BPM over a TR-808 pattern with extreme long-decay tuned kick, rapid sixteenth hi-hats and hand-clap fills, terse synth stabs and call-and-response party chants recorded loud for car subwoofer playback.
items.description: Miami bass took New York electro's 808 template south and reoriented the entire mix around the kick's sub-frequency decay, tuned and stretched to shake car systems. Tempos climbed toward 140 BPM, hi-hats became continuous sixteenths, and the vocals turned into raunchy or exhortatory crowd chants rather than narrative rap. It is faster, bass-heavier and less melodic than the New York electro it descends from and became the direct ancestor of booty bass and Atlanta bass.

items.name: Techno Bass
items.lineage: Detroit hybrid of electro and techno codified 1991-1998 by Underground Resistance, Aux 88, Will Web and DJ Assault on Direct Beat and 430 West, running 125-140 BPM with a syncopated 808/909 electro breakbeat carrying a deep detuned sub-bass line, cold sequenced synth motifs, vocoded vocals and militant sci-fi track titles.
items.description: Techno bass is the Detroit answer to Miami bass, formed in the early 1990s when Underground Resistance and Aux 88 fused 808 electro syncopation with techno's sequencer discipline and sub-heavy mixing. Tracks keep the broken electro drum pattern rather than a straight four-four, but their synth writing, tempo and austerity are Detroit techno's. It is colder and more machine-abstract than Miami bass and rhythmically broken where Detroit techno proper is four-on-the-floor.

items.name: Bleep Techno
items.lineage: Yorkshire dance music of 1989-1992 codified by Unique 3, LFO, Nightmares on Wax and Warp Records in Sheffield and Leeds, running 118-130 BPM with sparse sine-wave 'bleep' melodies, enormous sound-system sub-bass drops derived from local reggae culture, dry 808/909 drums and occasional ragga or house vocal samples.
items.description: Bleep techno, sometimes called bleep and bass, was Britain's first indigenous techno idiom, made in northern English cities where Jamaican sound-system bass culture met imported Detroit records. Its arrangements are extremely spare: a few pure-tone bleeps, hard dry drums and a sub-bass so low it registers as pressure rather than pitch. It is emptier and more bass-defined than Detroit techno and far more restrained than the breakbeat hardcore that grew out of it a year or two later.

items.name: Proto-Techno
items.lineage: Detroit and its suburbs 1981-1987, codified by Juan Atkins, Derrick May and Kevin Saunderson (the Belleville Three) plus Atkins' Cybotron work with Rick Davis — 118-128 BPM machine funk built on TR-808 and TR-909 patterns, Roland SH-101 and Juno bass, cold string-synth pads borrowed from Kraftwerk and Italo disco, largely instrumental with occasional vocoded or deadpan spoken vocals, sequenced live to two-track in bedroom home studios before vinyl mastering.
items.description: Proto-techno covers the Detroit records made between roughly 1981 and 1987 — Cybotron's 'Clear', Model 500's 'No UFO's', Rhythim Is Rhythim's 'Nude Photo' — before the word techno was applied commercially by the 1988 Virgin compilation. The sound is drum-machine funk at mid-tempo with sequenced monosynth basslines, glassy detuned pads and almost no vocal, mixed dry and released on small local labels cut straight to vinyl. It differs from Chicago house of the same years in its cooler, futurist, science-fiction framing and its preference for synthesized melody over disco and gospel sample sources, and from later techno in its slower tempo and audible electro/Italo inheritance.

items.name: Minimal Techno
items.lineage: Detroit and Berlin from the mid-1990s, codified by Robert Hood's Minimal Nation (1994), Daniel Bell, Basic Channel and later the Berlin Hardwax/Perlon axis — 125-135 BPM four-on-the-floor with a stripped kit, a single evolving loop, heavy use of subtractive filtering and sends, near-total absence of melody or vocal, arranged as long slow-mutating DJ tools inside a DAW or hardware sequencer.
items.description: Minimal techno emerged in the mid-1990s from Robert Hood's Detroit reduction of techno to kick, hat and one figure, and was consolidated in Berlin studios through the 2000s. Its defining features are extreme subtraction — a handful of elements looped for eight or more minutes, changes made through filter and send automation rather than new parts — plus sidechain-pumped kick relationships and very controlled sub-bass. It differs from Detroit techno by discarding chordal and string-pad melody, from microhouse by lacking that style's clicky swing and vocal fragments, and from industrial techno by its clean, low-distortion mixdown.

items.name: Outsider House
items.lineage: New York, Glasgow and London circa 2011-2015 around L.I.E.S., Mister Saturday Night and Trilogy Tapes, with Ron Morelli, Legowelt, DJ Slugo-influenced raw-hardware producers and Huerco S. — 118-126 BPM house tracked live from drum machines and cheap samplers to cassette or one-take stereo, deliberately overdriven and detuned, with hiss, clipping and mis-timed loops kept in the mix.
items.description: Outsider house is the raw hardware-house current that formed around Ron Morelli's L.I.E.S. label in New York from 2011 and spread through Glasgow and London tape labels. Tracks are jammed live on cheap drum machines and monosynths, printed with saturation, tape hiss and audible clipping, and structured as one long unquantized take rather than an arranged record. It is distinguished from lo-fi house proper by its harsher, more industrial and less nostalgic palette, and from deep house by its refusal of clean mixdowns and jazz chords.

items.name: Gospel House
items.lineage: Chicago and New York 1988-1996, codified by Marshall Jefferson and Curtis McClain, Frankie Knuckles with Robert Owens and Jamie Principle, and by Kerri Chandler and Tony Humphries at Club Zanzibar — 118-124 BPM four-on-the-floor with piano vamps, organ pads, hand claps and tambourine, topped by full-throated Black church belting, testifying ad-libs and choir-response stacks tracked in New York and Chicago commercial rooms.
items.description: Gospel house is the strain of late-1980s and 1990s American house that carried Black church vocal practice intact onto the dance floor — sustained organ, gospel piano vamps over the 909, and lead singing full of melisma, testimony and call-and-response with a stacked choir. It grew from the Chicago house scene and the New York/New Jersey garage clubs, and stayed a working-church-singer idiom rather than a sampled one. It differs from garage house generally by making the vocal, not the groove, the centre of the record, and from deep house by its major-key uplift and explicitly devotional lyrics.
exemplars: Marshall Jefferson & Curtis McClain – Move Your Body

items.name: Hard House
items.lineage: London and the UK club circuit 1994-2003 (Trade, Tidy Trax, Nukleuz), codified by Tony De Vit, Ian M and the Tidy Boys out of NRG and Belgian hoover techno — 145-155 BPM with a hard offbeat bassline, gated hoover stabs, filtered white-noise risers, drum-roll breakdowns and pitched-up diva vocal snatches, produced on hardware and early DAWs and mastered loud for large club rigs.
items.description: Hard house is the UK club style of the mid-1990s and early 2000s built on a hammering offbeat bass, the Belgian hoover stab, and long noise-sweep breakdowns resolving into drum rolls. Tempos of 145-155 BPM and heavy limiting made it a large-room and after-hours music, championed by Tony De Vit at Trade and released in volume by Tidy Trax and Nukleuz. It is distinguished from hard trance by its offbeat bass drive and absence of long melodic arpeggios, and from hardstyle by its earlier date, cleaner kick and house rather than gabber ancestry.

items.name: Funky Breaks
items.lineage: UK and US clubs circa 1994-2003 (Bomb the Bass and Freestylers in London, Rennie Pilgrem's TCR, Florida breaks in Orlando) — 130-140 BPM chopped funk and hip-hop breakbeats over a heavy syncopated synth or sampled bassline, with turntable scratching, ragga and old-school rap samples and filtered disco stabs, assembled from vinyl samples in hardware samplers and early DAWs.
items.description: Funky breaks — also called nu-skool breaks or big beat's dancefloor cousin — is the mid-1990s breakbeat style built on chopped funk drums at 130-140 BPM rather than a four-on-the-floor kick, with a fat syncopated bassline and scratched vocal samples on top. It ran through London labels like TCR and Freskanova and through Florida's club-oriented breaks scene. It differs from drum and bass by running roughly half the drum tempo without a time-stretched Amen, from big beat by its DJ-tool functionality over rock-sample bombast, and from house by the broken rather than straight kick pattern.

items.name: Balearic
items.lineage: Ibiza 1985-1990, codified by Alfredo Fiorito's open-air sets at Amnesia and carried to Britain by Danny Rampling, Paul Oakenfold and Trevor Fung — not a production template but a curated 95-120 BPM mixture of Italo disco, dub reggae, European synth-pop, soft-rock ballads and early house, marked by warm analogue keyboards, congas and shakers, dubbed-out delays and sunlit major-key melody.
items.description: Balearic began as a DJ sensibility rather than a genre: at Amnesia in the late 1980s Alfredo mixed Italo disco, dub, Cure and Woodentops records, soft-rock and nascent Chicago house into one open-air set, and returning British DJs turned it into the founding aesthetic of UK acid house. The recognisable sound is mid-tempo and unhurried — warm poly-synth chords, live percussion, echoing guitar, a melodic and often sung top line. It is distinguished from house proper by its eclectic tempo and instrumentation and its lack of a fixed drum programme, and from chill-out by being dancefloor music rather than lounge listening.

items.name: Harsh Noise Wall
items.lineage: Emerging from Japanese and European harsh noise around 2003-2008 and named through Vomir, The Rita and the Hospital Productions/Turgid Animal cassette networks — a single static, unvarying mass of amplified distortion and crushed low-mid frequency held for twenty to sixty minutes with no rhythm, event, dynamic change or vocal, generated by chained pedals, contact mics and feedback loops recorded direct to cassette or CD-R.
items.description: Harsh noise wall is the reductionist extreme of noise music, consolidated in the mid-2000s cassette underground around Romain Perrot's Vomir and Sam McKinlay's The Rita. A piece is one continuous unmodulated block of distortion — no gestures, no build, no silence — held at fixed amplitude for the whole running time, so that all musical incident is displaced into micro-texture. It is distinguished from Japanoise and power electronics, which are violently dynamic and often vocal, precisely by its stasis and its ideological refusal of change or performance.

items.name: Martial Industrial
items.lineage: Central and Northern Europe from the early 1990s (Cold Meat Industry in Sweden, Der Blutharsch in Austria, Les Joyaux de la Princesse in France) — slow processional 60-80 BPM marching-snare and timpani patterns, synthesized brass and orchestral samples, tolling bells, male choir pads and archival wartime speech samples, mixed dark and reverberant in DIY studios onto CD.
items.description: Martial industrial developed in the 1990s European post-industrial scene, chiefly on Sweden's Cold Meat Industry, as a slow, ceremonial style built from marching snare rolls, timpani, synthetic brass fanfares, bells and choral pads, frequently over sampled interwar speech and film dialogue. The mood is funereal-triumphal and the arrangements are through-composed rather than looped for a dancefloor. It differs from EBM by its slow processional tempo and absence of sequenced bass, and from neofolk by using orchestral and electronic sources rather than acoustic guitar and voice.

items.name: Dark Folk
items.lineage: Britain and Central Europe from the mid-1980s, codified by Douglas P. of Death in June, Tony Wakeford's Sol Invictus and David Tibet's Current 93 out of the post-industrial scene — slow minor and Phrygian-modal songs on strummed and picked acoustic guitar with hurdy-gurdy, bowed strings and tolling percussion, chanted or intoned baritone vocals with declamatory apocalyptic texts, tracked live to tape in small independent studios.
items.description: Dark folk, overlapping with what is usually called neofolk, formed in the mid-1980s when British industrial musicians moved to acoustic instruments while keeping industrial's bleak subject matter and tape collage. Songs are slow, modal and largely strophic, with strummed steel-string guitar, hurdy-gurdy or bowed drone, martial drum figures and low intoned vocals delivering apocalyptic, mythological or wartime texts. It is distinguished from the British folk revival by its post-industrial provenance and absence of traditional repertoire, and from martial industrial by being guitar-and-voice song rather than orchestral processional.
exemplars: Death in June – But, What Ends When the Symbols Shatter?

items.name: Drone Folk
items.lineage: North America and Britain from the late 1990s, associated with Charalambides, Pelt, Six Organs of Admittance and the Jewelled Antler circle — open-tuned acoustic and 12-string guitar, bowed dulcimer, shruti box and harmonium sustaining a fixed tonic under free-tempo modal melody and wordless voice, recorded in rooms and cabins with minimal miking and long natural decay.
items.description: Drone folk takes the modal fingerstyle vocabulary of American primitive guitar and Appalachian song and stretches it over a continuous sustained tonic supplied by shruti box, harmonium, bowed dulcimer or open bass strings. Formed in the late 1990s underground around Texas duo Charalambides, Virginia's Pelt and Ben Chasny's Six Organs of Admittance, it favours slow free tempo, wordless or barely articulated voice and unedited long takes in resonant rooms. It differs from free folk by keeping a fixed tonal centre and a legible melody rather than collective improvisation, and from drone metal by acoustic sources and folk melodic material.
exemplars: Six Organs of Admittance – Dark Noontide

items.name: Free Folk
items.lineage: New England and the American Northeast circa 1998-2008 around Sunburned Hand of the Man, No-Neck Blues Band and the Brattleboro/Ecstatic Peace and Time-Lag circles — collectively improvised, largely unmetered sessions on acoustic guitar, hand percussion, harmonium, flute and untrained group voice, captured in one take on cassette or portable recorder in houses and lofts and issued in tiny CD-R editions.
items.description: Free folk names the loose American collective-improvisation scene of the early 2000s, centred on Massachusetts and Vermont communes and lofts, in which folk instruments were played with the ethos of free jazz and the Japanese psychedelic underground. Sessions are group jams without fixed song, meter or key, drifting between hand-drum ritual, acoustic guitar clusters and chanted group vocals, and were released almost entirely on self-dubbed cassettes and CD-Rs. It differs from freak folk, which retains written songs and studio arrangement, and from drone folk, which holds a single tonic rather than roaming freely.

items.name: New Weird America
items.lineage: US underground folk current named by David Keenan in a 2003 Wire feature and centered on the Brattleboro/Providence axis (Sunburned Hand of the Man, Six Organs of Admittance, Josephine Foster, the Jewelled Antler collective), fusing Appalachian modal ballad and open-tuned fingerpicking with free-improvised drone, unmetered group ritual jams, tape-hiss home recording, and untrained keening or whispered vocal delivery over droning harmonium and bowed banjo.
items.description: A loose American underground folk movement that crystallized around 2000-2006 in New England and the Pacific Northwest, taking its name from a 2003 Wire magazine piece. It couples Appalachian and British-revival ballad materials with free-improv drone, communal untracked jams, and deliberately lo-fi home tape recording. Unlike the songwriter-centered indie folk it overlaps with, it privileges texture, ritual duration and collective noise over verse-chorus form.

items.name: Psychedelic Folk
items.lineage: Late-1960s British and American acid-folk, codified 1967-1971 by the Incredible String Band, Vashti Bunyan, Comus and Pearls Before Swine, applying modal fingerstyle guitar in altered tunings to raga-derived drone (sitar, tanpura, hand percussion), free-floating tempo, chamber-string and recorder overdubs, and high, unforced close-miked vocals treated with tape flange and reverse tape.
items.description: Emerging in Britain and California between 1966 and 1971, psychedelic folk grafted Indian drone instruments, medieval and Middle Eastern timbres, and studio tape manipulation onto acoustic ballad forms. Its signature is a suspended, tempo-free floating feel with layered exotic overdubs and childlike or declamatory vocal delivery. It differs from electric folk-rock in refusing drum-kit propulsion, and from straight revival folk in its studio artifice.
exemplars: The Incredible String Band - The Hangman's Beautiful Daughter
Vashti Bunyan - Just Another Diamond Day

items.name: Chamber Folk
items.lineage: Anglo-American acoustic songwriting recorded with classical chamber forces, traceable to Robert Kirby's string arrangements for Nick Drake (1969-70) and revived from the late 1990s by Sufjan Stevens, Andrew Bird and Ólöf Arnalds — slow-to-moderate tempo, aeolian and phrygian modal harmony, fingerpicked or nylon guitar doubled by cello, violin, clarinet and harmonium, brushed or absent drums, and close, breathy, low-vibrato vocal delivery.
items.description: Chamber folk sets singer-songwriter material in a written classical chamber setting rather than a rock band, with strings, winds and reed organ arranged rather than jammed. It descends from Nick Drake's late-sixties Robert Kirby charts and re-emerged as an indie idiom around 2000. Against psychedelic folk's tape haze and drone, it is precisely notated, dry, and dynamically restrained.

items.name: Exotica
items.lineage: American instrumental mood music of 1957-1963 codified by Martin Denny at the Hawaiian Village and by Les Baxter and Arthur Lyman on Capitol and HiFi Records — languid rumba and bolero tempos, pentatonic and whole-tone melodies carried on vibraphone, marimba and celesta over congas and bongos, with bird calls, gongs, wordless soprano vocalise, and extravagant stereo reverb evoking an imagined Polynesia.
items.description: Exotica was a Hollywood and Honolulu studio genre of the stereo-hi-fi boom, roughly 1957 to 1963, built for domestic listening rather than dance. Vibraphone and mallet lead lines float over Afro-Cuban percussion, punctuated by animal calls, gongs and wordless vocalise, all bathed in the Capitol Tower echo chambers. It is distinguished from lounge and easy listening by its percussion-forward, quasi-ethnographic sound design, and from genuine Pacific traditions by being wholly a studio invention.
exemplars: Les Baxter - Ritual of the Savage
Yma Sumac - Voice of the Xtabay

items.name: Library Music (Production Music)
items.lineage: European production-music industry of 1959-1980 centred on KPM, De Wolfe, Bruton and Italy's Cometa, where staff composers (Keith Mansfield, Alan Hawkshaw, Brian Bennett, Piero Umiliani, Janko Nilović) cut short cue-length instrumentals to brief — brisk funk drum-kit breaks, fuzz and wah guitar, Hammond and early synthesizer leads, flute and string sweeteners — recorded fast in London and Rome sessions and pressed to catalogue LPs for broadcast licensing.
items.description: Library music is instrumental production music written on spec for film, television and radio licensing, at its creative peak in London and Rome between the mid-1960s and late 1970s. Cues are short, tightly arranged, mood-labelled, and recorded by top session players in single fast dates, spanning funk breaks, bossa, jazz-rock, easy listening and early electronics. It differs from soundtrack composition in that no picture exists: the music is written to abstract categories, which is exactly why its drum breaks became prime hip-hop sampling stock.

items.name: Music Hall
items.lineage: British urban variety song of roughly 1850-1920, born in London public-house saloon theatres and codified by Marie Lloyd, Gus Elen, Harry Champion and Vesta Tilley — brisk 2/4 and 6/8 comic patter and waltz choruses, cockney or regional dialect delivery pitched between speech and song, chorus lines written for mass audience singalong, backed by pit piano with cornet, trombone and tuba, and preserved on acoustic-horn 78s.
items.description: Music hall was the dominant popular song form of Victorian and Edwardian Britain, performed in licensed variety theatres between 1850 and the First World War. Its songs are comic or sentimental character pieces in working-class dialect, with simple diatonic tunes and hook choruses built for the audience to bellow back. It differs from American vaudeville and Tin Pan Alley in its class-specific dialect comedy and from operetta in its unaccompanied-chorus, pit-piano economy.

items.name: Song-Poem
items.lineage: American vanity-record industry from the 1950s to the early 1980s, in which mail-order firms (Preview, Halmark, Film City, MSR) set amateurs' submitted lyrics to music for a fee — house bands and singers such as Rodd Keith, Gene Marshall and Bobbi Blake cutting one- or two-take tracks in Hollywood, Nashville and Los Angeles rooms, over generic three-chord country, twist or Chamberlin-organ backing, with awkward scansion and unedited lyric text as the defining marker.
items.description: Song-poems are commercial vanity recordings made from lyrics mailed in by amateurs who answered magazine adverts, produced in bulk by small US firms from the 1950s into the 1980s. Sessions were cut in a single pass with a hired band, so the tracks pair slick professional playing with unsingable, uncut amateur text and hasty melodic fitting. What distinguishes the form from ordinary demo pop is that the customer, not the label, was the market, and no revision was ever possible.
exemplars: The American Song-Poem Anthology: Do You Know the Difference Between Big Wood and Brush

items.name: Salon Music
items.lineage: European domestic art music of roughly 1820-1900, cultivated in bourgeois and aristocratic drawing rooms of Paris, Vienna and Leipzig and codified by Field, Chopin, Fanny Hensel, Gottschalk and Cécile Chaminade — short character pieces, nocturnes, waltzes, romances without words and parlour songs for piano alone or piano with violin, cello or voice, written for amateur hands with rubato-rich cantabile melody over broken-chord accompaniment.
items.description: Salon music is the nineteenth-century repertoire of the private drawing room: short, self-contained character pieces and romances published for amateur performers rather than the concert stage. Its idiom is singing right-hand melody, arpeggiated left-hand support, expressive rubato, and modest technical demands with maximum sentimental effect. It is separated from the concert-hall Romantic repertoire by scale and intent, and from popular parlour song by its notated, conservatory-derived harmonic language.

items.name: Minnesang
items.lineage: German-language courtly love-song tradition of circa 1150-1350 at the Hohenstaufen courts, codified by Walther von der Vogelweide, Neidhart and Heinrich von Morungen and preserved in the Manesse and Jena codices — monophonic strophic song in Pythagorean-tuned church modes, Bar form (Stollen-Stollen-Abgesang), largely unmeasured declamatory delivery by a solo male voice, sometimes doubled by vielle, psaltery or portative organ in modern reconstruction.
items.description: Minnesang is the German courtly song tradition of the high Middle Ages, roughly 1150 to 1350, transmitting texts of idealized love, political satire and pastoral parody. Surviving sources give text far more often than notation, and the melodies that do survive are monophonic, modal and in Bar form, so performance rests on strophic repetition and speech-shaped delivery. It parallels the troubadour and trouvère repertoires but in Middle High German, with a stronger later strain of rustic dance-song (Neidhart) absent from the Occitan corpus.

items.name: Trouvère Song
items.lineage: Northern French langue d'oïl courtly song of circa 1180-1300, centred on Arras, Champagne and the royal court and codified by Thibaut de Champagne, Adam de la Halle, Blondel de Nesle and Gace Brulé — monophonic strophic chansons courtoises alongside rondeaux, motets and pastourelles, notated in largely unmeasured neumes in the chansonniers, sung by solo voice in Pythagorean modal tuning with optional vielle or harp doubling.
items.description: The trouvère repertoire is the northern French counterpart to the Occitan troubadours, flourishing between about 1180 and 1300 and far better preserved musically, with over two thousand melodies in the chansonniers. Its songs are modal, monophonic and strophic, though Arras figures such as Adam de la Halle extended the tradition into polyphonic rondeaux and the sung play Le Jeu de Robin et Marion. Compared with troubadour song it is later, more urban and bourgeois in patronage, and it hands the repertoire directly into thirteenth-century motet practice.
exemplars: Adam de la Halle - Le Jeu de Robin et Marion

items.name: Troubadour Song (Occitan)
items.lineage: Occitan courtly lyric of circa 1100-1290 in Aquitaine, Provence and Toulouse, begun by Guilhem IX of Aquitaine and codified by Bernart de Ventadorn, Raimbaut de Vaqueiras, Guiraut Riquier and the trobairitz Comtessa de Dia — monophonic strophic cansos, sirventes and albas in church modes, only about 250 melodies surviving in unmeasured notation, delivered by solo voice with vielle, harp or Mediterranean plucked-lute accompaniment.
items.description: Troubadour song is the earliest documented European vernacular art-song tradition, composed in Occitan at southern French and Catalan courts between about 1100 and the Albigensian collapse of the thirteenth century. The surviving melodies are monophonic, modal and strophic, notated without rhythm, so realization depends on text declamation and on debated Andalusi-influenced instrumental accompaniment. It precedes and models the trouvère and Minnesang traditions, but with far fewer surviving tunes and a stronger Mediterranean-Arab performance hypothesis.
exemplars: Bernart de Ventadorn - Can vei la lauzeta mover
Comtessa de Dia - A chantar m'er

items.name: Ars Subtilior
items.lineage: Late-fourteenth-century Franco-Cypriot courtly polyphony of circa 1370-1420 around Avignon, Foix and the Aragonese court, written by Baude Cordier, Solage, Jacob de Senleches and Matteo da Perugia and preserved in the Chantilly and Modena codices — extreme rhythmic notation with simultaneous mensurations, syncopation across the tactus, chromatic inflection, eye-music heart- and circle-shaped scores, and three- or four-voice ballades and rondeaux for solo voices with vielle, harp and lute.
items.description: Ars subtilior is the hyper-refined secular polyphony written for a handful of southern French, Cypriot and Aragonese courts between about 1370 and 1420, in the wake of the papal schism. It pushes Ars Nova mensural notation to its limit, layering conflicting mensurations, proportional shifts and cross-rhythms so dense that the surface sounds nearly free, and it delights in visually elaborate manuscript notation. Against the contemporaneous Italian trecento it is far more rhythmically complex and less melodically cantabile, and it marks the end of the mannerist medieval line before Dufay's smoothing.
exemplars: Jacob de Senleches - La harpe de melodie

items.name: Italian Trecento Polyphony
items.lineage: Fourteenth-century Italian secular polyphony centred on Florence, Bologna and Padua and codified by Jacopo da Bologna, Francesco Landini, Gherardello and Niccolò da Perugia in the Squarcialupi Codex — two- and three-voice madrigals, cacce and ballate in Italian mensural notation with divisiones, long florid melismatic upper-voice openings and closes, cantabile stepwise motion, canonic hunting cacce, and the under-third Landini cadence.
items.description: The Italian trecento is the fourteenth-century secular polyphonic tradition of northern and central Italy, its main forms the madrigal, the canonic caccia and the ballata, with Francesco Landini as its central figure and the illuminated Squarcialupi Codex as its great source. Its idiom is lyrical and vocal: long melismas at phrase beginnings and endings, mostly consonant two-voice writing, and the distinctive Landini cadence. It contrasts with the contemporaneous French Ars Nova and Ars Subtilior in favouring melodic sweetness and clear text-setting over rhythmic complexity.
exemplars: Jacopo da Bologna - Non al suo amante
Gherardello da Firenze - Tosto che l'alba

items.name: Madrigal
items.lineage: Secular vocal polyphony that emerged in Italian courts around 1530 (Verdelot, Arcadelt) and peaked with Marenzio, Wert and Monteverdi by 1600 — three to six unaccompanied voices, one singer per part, setting Petrarchan and pastoral verse in through-composed sections where each poetic image gets its own point of imitation, with word-painting, chromatic cross-relations and unmeasured declamatory freedom over a flexible duple tactus.
items.description: The madrigal formed in 1530s Italy as a learned setting of vernacular poetry for a small consort of solo voices, and by the 1590s had become the laboratory for extreme chromaticism in Marenzio, Gesualdo and the early Monteverdi books. Its signature is through-composed structure: no repeating stanza, each line of text receiving fresh imitative material and pictorial gesture. It is distinguished from the sacred motet by its secular text and expressive licence, and from the later English madrigal by its denser chromatic syntax and Italian declamation.

items.name: Franco-Flemish School
items.lineage: Sacred and secular polyphony of the Low Countries and northern France c.1450-1560, carried across Europe by Ockeghem, Josquin, Willaert and Lassus — four to six equal voices in continuous pervading imitation over cantus firmus or paraphrase tenors, mensural notation with proportional canons, long-breathed overlapping phrases avoiding cadential coincidence, and Latin mass and motet texts sung one or two per part in resonant chapel acoustics.
items.description: The dominant European compositional style from roughly 1450 to 1560, exported by singers trained in Cambrai, Bruges and Antwerp to courts and chapels from Rome to Vienna. Its sound is a seamless woven texture of independent equal voices in pervading imitation, with cadences deliberately elided so the flow rarely stops, and a preference for smooth Pythagorean-leaning intervals and long modal spans. Against the Italian madrigal it is text-neutral and structural rather than pictorial; against earlier Burgundian song it is denser, longer-breathed and technically canonic.

items.name: English Renaissance (Tudor Polyphony)
items.lineage: Tudor and early Stuart music c.1500-1620 — Taverner, Tallis, Byrd, Gibbons and Weelkes — built on a distinctly English taste for full sonority: broad florid melismatic Latin votive antiphons, then post-Reformation vernacular anthems and services in clear syllabic declamation, alongside consort songs, viol fantasias and lute ayres, using false relations, a rich thirds-and-sixths harmony and mean-tone keyboard temperament.
items.description: English composition between the Eton Choirbook generation and the death of Gibbons, spanning Latin votive polyphony, Anglican anthems and services, viol consort fantasias and lute ayres. It is recognisable by full-textured harmony rich in thirds, the characteristic false relation between simultaneous major and minor thirds, and long melismatic upper lines over slow-moving lower voices. Compared with contemporary Franco-Flemish writing it is less canonic and more vertically sonorous; compared with the Italian madrigal it is more restrained in chromaticism even in its secular repertoire.

items.name: Italian Baroque
items.lineage: Italy c.1600-1750 — Monteverdi's seconda pratica, then Corelli in Rome codifying the trio sonata and concerto grosso, Vivaldi in Venice fixing the ritornello concerto and Scarlatti-era opera seria — driven basso continuo of cello plus harpsichord or theorbo, sequential tonal harmony, terraced dynamics, motoric semiquaver figuration at brisk steady tempo, and violin-idiomatic solo writing with improvised cadential ornamentation.
items.description: The Italian strand of Baroque practice, running from the Florentine and Venetian monodists through Corelli's Roman string school to Vivaldi's Venetian concertos and Neapolitan opera. Its markers are a functional bass line realised in continuo, ritornello form alternating tutti refrain with solo episodes, propulsive unbroken rhythmic drive and violin writing that treats sequence and arpeggio as primary material. It is separated from French Baroque by its speed, sequential harmony and vocal bel canto, and from later Galante music by continuo texture and unbroken motoric surface.

items.name: French Baroque
items.lineage: Music of the French court from Lully at Versailles in the 1670s through Couperin and Rameau to c.1760 — the ouverture with dotted grand rhythm and fugal fast section, tragedie lyrique with recitative bent to French prosody, dance suites of allemande, courante, sarabande and gigue, notes inegales performance of even quavers, a dense codified agrement ornament table, and a wind-rich orchestra of transverse flutes, oboes and bassoons over string band.
items.description: The court-centred French style consolidated by Lully under Louis XIV and extended by Couperin, Marais and Rameau. It is identified by the French overture's double-dotted opening, the dance suite as primary architecture, notes inegales swing applied to written-even quavers, and an exhaustively notated ornament vocabulary of ports de voix, tremblements and coules. Where Italian Baroque prizes sequence and virtuoso momentum, French Baroque prizes dance metre, ornament and instrumental colour, with the viol and harpsichord repertoire especially deliberate and rhetorically slow.

items.name: Spanish Baroque
items.lineage: Iberian and colonial Hispanic music c.1600-1750 — Juan Hidalgo and Sebastian Duron at the Madrid court, Correa de Arauxo and Cabanilles at the organ, Jose de Nebra and the New World chapelmasters — vernacular Castilian villancicos in refrain-and-copla form, hemiola-heavy 6/8 against 3/4 dance metres, guitar and cross-strung harp continuo instead of harpsichord, tiento organ writing on split-keyboard horizontal reeds, and zarzuela's mix of sung and spoken theatre.
items.description: The Baroque as practised in Spain, Portugal and the Spanish Americas, notable for keeping vernacular and dance idioms inside sacred institutions long after Italy had Latinised its repertoire. Its hallmarks are the villancico with estribillo refrain, persistent 6/8 against 3/4 hemiola inherited from the folia and jacara, plucked guitar and harp as continuo, and Iberian organs with horizontal trumpet stops used in tiento partido. It differs from Italian Baroque in its lighter, more percussive continuo and dance-derived metre, and from French Baroque in its comparatively plain ornamentation.

items.name: Galante Era
items.lineage: European transitional style c.1720-1770 centred on Naples, Dresden, Mannheim and Berlin — Pergolesi, Johann Christian Bach, Sammartini and the Mannheim school under Stamitz — short periodic phrases in balanced two- and four-bar antecedent-consequent units, thin melody-and-accompaniment texture with Alberti bass replacing contrapuntal continuo, slow harmonic rhythm, graceful appoggiatura ornamentation, and the fortepiano and clarinet entering the orchestra alongside crescendo effects.
items.description: The galant and empfindsam style that displaced late Baroque counterpoint between roughly 1720 and 1770, cultivated in Neapolitan opera buffa, the Mannheim orchestra and the Berlin circle around C.P.E. Bach. Its defining sound is deliberate lightness: symmetrical periodic phrasing, a single singing melody over Alberti or repeated-note accompaniment, sparse harmony that changes slowly, and expressive sighing appoggiaturas. It is thinner and more sectional than Italian Baroque, and less developmentally ambitious than the Viennese Classical style that grew directly out of it.

items.name: Viennese Classical Era
items.lineage: Vienna c.1770-1820 — Haydn, Mozart, early Beethoven and Schubert — codified sonata form with exposition, development and recapitulation across four-movement symphony, quartet and sonata cycles, clear tonic-dominant polarity and long-range modulation, motivic development from small cells, dynamic contrast including sudden sforzando and orchestral crescendo, and a standardised orchestra of paired winds, natural horns and trumpets, timpani and string body.
items.description: The Viennese Classical style of Haydn, Mozart and the young Beethoven, roughly 1770 to 1820, in which sonata form became the governing architecture of instrumental music. It is marked by balanced periodic phrasing carried into large-scale tonal drama, motivic economy where whole movements grow from a few bars, and a fixed orchestral apparatus with clearly graded dynamics. Against the Galante it is structurally far more ambitious and contrapuntally re-engaged; against early Romanticism it keeps formal proportion and tonal clarity above personal expressive rhetoric.

items.name: Early Romantic Era
items.lineage: European art music c.1820-1850 shaped by Schubert's late works, Berlioz, Chopin, Schumann and Mendelssohn — expanded chromatic harmony with third-related key relations and unresolved dissonance, character pieces and Lieder cycles replacing formal cycles, rubato-inflected tempo, the iron-framed double-escapement piano as central medium, greatly enlarged orchestra with valved brass and idee fixe thematic recurrence, and literary programmatic narrative.
items.description: The first Romantic generation, roughly 1820 to 1850, in which the Classical inheritance was bent toward personal and literary expression. Characteristic traits are chromatic harmony that loosens functional cadence, flexible rubato tempo, the intimate piano character piece and the German Lied as major genres, and in Berlioz an orchestra of unprecedented size and colouristic imagination. Compared with Viennese Classicism it subordinates formal symmetry to expressive contour; compared with the late Romantic era its harmony still resolves and its orchestral forces remain smaller.

items.name: Late Romantic Era
items.lineage: Roughly 1850-1900 across Germany, Austria, Russia and France — Wagner's Tristan chromaticism and leitmotif music drama, Liszt's symphonic poem, Brahms's developing variation, Bruckner and Tchaikovsky's massive symphonies — continuous unresolved chromatic harmony weakening tonal centre, enormous orchestras with Wagner tubas and extended brass and percussion, long-span thematic transformation, extreme dynamic range and slow harmonic rhythm under soaring string cantilena.
items.description: The maximal phase of nineteenth-century Romanticism, from Wagner's Tristan through Bruckner, Brahms, Tchaikovsky and Franck. Its sound is defined by dense chromatic harmony that postpones resolution across enormous spans, an orchestra swollen to a hundred players with divided strings and heavy low brass, and thematic transformation binding hour-long structures. It is distinguished from the early Romantic era chiefly by scale and harmonic saturation, and from post-Romanticism by still asserting, however remotely, a governing tonic.

items.name: Post-Romantic Era
items.lineage: c.1890-1930 in Vienna, Munich, Paris and Helsinki — Mahler, Richard Strauss, Scriabin, Szymanowski, Zemlinsky and late Sibelius — tonality stretched to breaking with mystic and quartal chords, polytonal superimposition and floating unresolved suspensions, gigantic orchestras deployed chamber-like for isolated soloistic colour, ironic collage of marches and folk tunes, extreme registral extremes, and vast multi-movement symphonies and tone poems with vocal and choral finales.
items.description: The generation that pushed Romantic tonality to its structural limit between about 1890 and 1930, centred on Mahler, Strauss and Scriabin. Its hallmarks are harmony hovering at the edge of atonality through quartal and mystic sonorities, orchestras of enormous size treated as a reservoir of soloistic chamber colours rather than blended mass, and an ironic, quotation-laden expressive register that admits banality alongside the sublime. It is separated from the late Romantic era by that irony and by harmony that frequently fails to resolve at all, and from serialism by retaining tonal reference points.

items.name: Serialism
items.lineage: Devised by Arnold Schoenberg in Vienna around 1921-23 and extended to rhythm, dynamics and attack by Boulez, Stockhausen and Babbitt at Darmstadt after 1949 — a fixed ordering of all twelve chromatic pitches deployed in prime, inversion, retrograde and retrograde-inversion forms with no pitch privileged, pointillistic Webernian textures of isolated attacks across extreme registers, irregular non-repeating rhythm, and precisely notated dynamics changing note by note.
items.description: Twelve-tone composition, invented by Schoenberg in the early 1920s and generalised into total serialism at Darmstadt after 1949. All twelve pitch classes circulate in a fixed row order and its transformations so no key can assert itself, and in the postwar integral variant duration, dynamic and articulation are governed by analogous series. The audible result is athematic, metrically unpredictable and often pointillistic, with wide leaps and constantly shifting timbre. It differs from post-Romantic free atonality by its systematic ordering, and from aleatoric or minimalist modernism by leaving nothing to chance or repetition.

items.name: Totalism
items.lineage: New York downtown movement of the late 1980s and 1990s — Michael Gordon, Julia Wolfe and David Lang with Bang on a Can, plus Mikel Rouse, Rhys Chatham and critic Kyle Gann — steady fast pulse with conflicting tempo layers stacked as 3:4 or 5:7 rhythmic dissonance over it, harmony richer and more dissonant than minimalism, amplified mixed ensembles of electric guitar, bass, drums, piano and winds played at rock volume but with through-composed formal scale.
items.description: Totalism named the second-generation downtown New York style of the late 1980s and 1990s, associated with Bang on a Can and theorised by Kyle Gann. It keeps minimalism's constant pulse and audible process but layers mutually dissonant tempos over it and admits far more chromatic and sometimes just-intoned harmony, performed by amplified mixed ensembles at rock dynamic levels. Against classic minimalism it is harmonically restless and rhythmically conflicted rather than gradually phasing; against serialism it is pulse-driven, consonance-tolerant and physically loud.

items.name: Post-Minimalism
items.lineage: Emerging in New York and Britain circa 1975-1990 as composers including John Adams, Michael Nyman, Louis Andriessen, Arvo Pärt and the Bang on a Can circle absorbed Reich-Glass pulse technique back into functional harmony, expressive phrase-shape and long-form architecture — steady eighth-note motor pulse, additive but audibly directional harmonic rhythm, mixed amplified chamber forces (piano, mallets, electric guitar, saxophones, strings), fully notated with no improvisation and dynamic arcs the earlier minimalists refused.
items.description: Post-minimalism formed in the late 1970s and 1980s when composers who had absorbed Reich and Glass reintroduced goal-directed harmony, contrast and dramatic climax into pulse-based music. The sound is a driving amplified chamber ensemble — piano and mallet percussion locked to a constant subdivision, electric guitar and saxophones cutting through strings — with harmonic changes that arrive as events rather than as slow process. It is distinguished from classic minimalism by audible cadence and phrase-shape, and from mainstream orchestral modernism by its rock-derived rhythmic literalism and amplification.

items.name: Xenharmonic Music
items.lineage: Named by Ivor Darreg in the 1970s out of the Harry Partch and Erv Wilson lineage in California and consolidated online from the 1990s through the Alternate Tuning List and Xenharmonic Wiki, it is composition built explicitly on non-12-TET lattices — 19-, 22- and 31-note equal divisions, Bohlen-Pierce, and rank-2 temperaments — realized on refretted guitars, retuned synthesizers and purpose-built instruments, with harmony judged by comma-pump and consonance behaviour rather than by common-practice function.
items.description: Xenharmonic music is a post-1970s composer-theorist practice defined by deliberate use of tuning systems outside 12-tone equal temperament — equal divisions such as 19-, 22- and 31-EDO, the Bohlen-Pierce scale, and just-intonation-derived temperaments. Its sonic signature is chords that sound consonant yet unplaceable, beating-free thirds or intervals with no 12-TET analogue, usually realized on refretted guitars, retuned software synths and custom keyboards. It differs from historical microtonal composition in being tuning-system-first — the temperament is the compositional premise, and the community is a distributed online theory culture rather than a concert-hall lineage.

items.name: Microtonal Music (interval-scale practice)
items.lineage: Twentieth-century concert practice codified by Alois Hába in Prague from 1923 with quarter-tone piano and clarinet, Ivan Wyschnegradsky in Paris, Julián Carrillo in Mexico and later Ligeti, Haas and the spectral school, using intervals smaller than the semitone — quarter- and sixth-tones, beating dyads and slow glissando drift — on retuned pianos, specially fingered winds and unfretted strings, fully notated with accidental systems invented for the purpose.
items.description: Microtonal music as a notated concert tradition runs from Hába's Prague quarter-tone school of the 1920s through Wyschnegradsky and Carrillo to Ligeti, Georg Friedrich Haas and the spectralists. Its hallmark is intervals smaller than a semitone used structurally — beating dyads, gradual pitch drift, harmonies tuned toward or away from the overtone series — on paired detuned pianos, quarter-tone clarinets and unfretted strings. It is more score-bound and orchestral than xenharmonic practice, which starts from a chosen temperament, and unlike just-intonation drone music it retains through-composed form and rapid textural change.

items.name: Wandelweiser
items.lineage: Founded in Germany in 1992 by Antoine Beuger and Burkhard Schlothauer as a composers' collective and publishing house, extending Cage's 4'33" into a full practice — long durations built mostly of measured silence, single quiet sustained tones on flute, clarinet, strings, piano or sine tone placed at notated intervals, near-static dynamics at the edge of audibility, and performance rooms where ambient sound is treated as part of the score.
items.description: The Wandelweiser group formed in Germany in 1992 around Antoine Beuger and Burkhard Schlothauer and has since spread through Jürg Frey, Michael Pisaro and Radu Malfatti. Pieces are mostly silence: isolated quiet tones — a bowed string, a breath-thin clarinet note, a sine tone — are placed at notated time points across durations that can run an hour, so room tone and incidental noise become audible content. Unlike free improvisation's quiet end, everything here is scored and counted, and unlike ambient electronics the material is acoustic, unprocessed and deliberately sparse rather than continuous.

items.name: Acousmatic Music (loudspeaker concert practice)
items.lineage: Named by François Bayle at the GRM in Paris in 1974 for fixed-media work composed directly onto tape or disk and diffused live over a loudspeaker orchestra such as the Acousmonium — no performers on stage, source recordings of objects, voices and environments transformed by filtering, time-stretching and spatial trajectory, organized by spectromorphology rather than pitch or metre.
items.description: Acousmatic music is the fixed-media concert tradition named at the Groupe de Recherches Musicales in 1974 and carried on at Bourges, INA-GRM and Birmingham's BEAST. Works exist only as a finished stereo or multichannel file, built from recorded sound transformed beyond recognition and shaped by gesture, texture and spatial motion; in performance a composer diffuses the piece live across dozens of loudspeakers. It differs from early musique concrète in scale and in its developed theory of listening, and from ambient electronica in its dramatic, through-composed form and refusal of pulse.

items.name: Sound Collage
items.lineage: Running from Cage's Imaginary Landscape No. 5 (1952) and the Buchanan-Goodman break-in records through the Residents, Negativland, John Oswald's Plunderphonics (1985) and the tape-trading underground, it assembles finished music into new work by splice, turntable, sampler and radio capture — abrupt cuts between unrelated sources, recognizable fragments left legible, speech and broadcast material foregrounded, and no continuous metre unless a host loop imposes one.
items.description: Sound collage is the practice of building music out of other recordings left audibly intact — radio broadcasts, advertisements, commercial records, found speech — spliced or sampled into abrupt juxtaposition. It runs from Cage's radio pieces and 1950s break-in novelty singles through Negativland, John Oswald and the Bomb Squad's densest work, and is bound up with copyright confrontation. Unlike acousmatic music it keeps its sources recognizable and often satirical, and unlike sample-based hip hop it usually refuses a steady beat, treating the cut itself as the rhythmic event.
exemplars: The Avalanches — Since I Left You

items.name: ECM-style Jazz
items.lineage: Codified by Manfred Eicher and engineer Jan Erik Kongshaug at Oslo's Rainbow Studio from ECM's founding in 1969, it is a European chamber-jazz manner — slow to medium tempos, modal or folk-derived material, brushed or mallet-led drums, arco double bass, piano and saxophone recorded with long artificial and room reverb, wide dynamic range, minimal overdubbing and an editorial preference for space over density.
items.description: ECM-style jazz is the sound established by Manfred Eicher's label from 1969, most of it cut with Jan Erik Kongshaug in Oslo. Its markers are audible before any note of harmony: enormous decaying reverb around piano and cymbals, arco bass sitting close and dry, saxophone with almost no vibrato, and arrangements that leave long silences. Compared with American post-bop it trades swing propulsion and blues inflection for Nordic and folk modality, rubato phrasing and studio space treated as a compositional element.
exemplars: Eberhard Weber — The Colours of Chloë

items.name: Avant-Garde Jazz
items.lineage: Formed in New York and Chicago from 1959 onward through Ornette Coleman, Cecil Taylor, late Coltrane, Albert Ayler and the AACM, it abandons fixed chord changes and often steady tempo — collective simultaneous improvisation, saxophone in the altissimo and overblown register, arco and pizzicato bass freed from walking, drums playing pulse-free wash, and pieces framed by short unison heads or open notated cells.
items.description: Avant-garde jazz emerged around 1959-1965 as Ornette Coleman, Cecil Taylor, Albert Ayler and the late Coltrane quartet dropped functional chord progressions, then broadened through Chicago's AACM and the New York loft scene. The texture is dense collective improvisation at high intensity: multiphonics and screaming altissimo saxophone, piano played in tone clusters, bass and drums generating turbulence rather than time. It differs from modal jazz in discarding the underlying scale-frame entirely, and from European free improvisation in retaining blues cry, gospel shout and often a stated theme.

items.name: Jazz-Funk
items.lineage: Consolidated 1969-1977 in New York and Los Angeles around Creed Taylor's CTI, Blue Note's later roster and Herbie Hancock's Headhunters, it fuses jazz soloing with a sixteenth-note funk rhythm section — electric bass playing composed slap or fingered ostinatos, drums locked to a syncopated one-drop backbeat around 95-110 BPM, Fender Rhodes and clavinet comping, and horn or saxophone leads over static two-chord vamps with congas layered on top.
items.description: Jazz-funk crystallized between 1969 and 1977 as soul-jazz organ grooves gave way to electric bass, Rhodes and clavinet and to James Brown's sixteenth-note rhythmic vocabulary. Tracks sit on one or two chords for minutes at a time while a written bassline and tight syncopated drums hold the floor and horns or saxophone improvise above; production is close, compressed and punchy rather than airy. Against jazz-rock fusion it is groove-first and rarely uses odd metres or distorted guitar, and against instrumental funk it keeps extended improvised solos and jazz harmony in the comping.

items.name: Afro-Cuban Jazz
items.lineage: Created in New York in 1947-1949 when Dizzy Gillespie hired Chano Pozo and Mario Bauzá and Machito's Afro-Cubans commissioned Cubop charts, it welds bebop horn writing and improvisation onto Cuban clave — son and rumba clave underpinning a full percussion section of congas, timbales, bongos and bell, piano montuno and tumbao bass, with mambo and moña shout sections behind the solos.
items.description: Afro-Cuban jazz was made in New York in the late 1940s by Mario Bauzá, Machito, Chano Pozo and Dizzy Gillespie, and continued through Tito Puente, Cal Tjader and Chucho Valdés. Everything is organized by clave: piano montuno and bass tumbao interlock against congas, timbales and bongo bell while bebop-voiced brass plays riff-based mambo sections and soloists improvise across the two-bar cell. It is distinct from Brazilian-derived Latin jazz in its percussion battery and clave discipline, and from commercial salsa in foregrounding extended instrumental improvisation over sung coro-pregón.

items.name: West African Jazz
items.lineage: Developed in Lagos, Accra, Bamako and Dakar from the late 1950s through the 1970s in the dance-band highlife orbit — Fela Kuti's pre-Afrobeat Koola Lobitos, Guy Warren, Manu Dibango, the Bembeya and Rail Band circles — setting bebop and hard-bop horn language over highlife and Mande grooves: 4/4 or 12/8 clave-adjacent patterns, tenor and trumpet lead lines, clean single-coil guitar arpeggios, kora or balafon lines, and long vamp-based solo sections.
items.description: West African jazz grew out of the Ghanaian and Nigerian dance-band highlife scene and the Malian and Senegalese state orchestras between roughly 1957 and 1978, when musicians who had absorbed Parker, Coltrane and Blakey applied that vocabulary to local rhythm. Horn sections play riff heads over cyclic highlife or Mande vamps while clean electric guitar, kora or balafon supplies the interlocking ostinato and hand drums carry the pulse.
