It represents one early Norwegian electronic-dance branch while the geographic category also includes harder, less ambient producers. Synthetic space is a production choice, not an asserted sonic effect of climate or landscape.

items.name: Dutch trance
items.lineage: Netherlands-centered trance production network. Armin van Buuren’s theme-led work provides the representative studio branch: a recurring keyboard melody, synthesized bass and carefully arranged programmed drums, with vocal collaborations optional.
items.description: The authored default uses an unfolding arpeggiated synthesizer theme, clear harmonic motion and steady programmed percussion. Phrase variations and a long dynamic build are central to the selected approach. It is a regional category, not a requirement that every Dutch trance recording be vocal, uplifting, or made on one hardware brand.

items.name: German trance
items.lineage: German trance production network, represented by Paul van Dyk’s melodic club recordings and his documented Roland-machine lineage. This default selects a classic hardware-inspired arpeggio, acid-bass and programmed-kick arrangement.
items.description: A regional trance category rather than an alternative name for all classic trance. This authored model combines broad sustained synth harmonics with repeated acidic figures and a firm machine kick. It chooses an instrumental, hardware-inspired branch; software emulations, vocals and less acid-oriented arrangements are equally possible within the broader scene.

items.name: Deep techno
items.lineage: An Every Noise discovery cluster spanning melodic, atmospheric club techno. This representative branch follows Stephan Bodzin’s live interplay of an expressive monophonic synthesizer and prepared electronic percussion. The classifier label does not imply a universally agreed historical genre boundary.
items.description: The authored arrangement foregrounds a sustained, manually inflected synth melody over a steady programmed beat. Filter movement and gradual phrase development supply motion without filling every frequency band. Bodzin’s documented Moog-centered performance is the reference, while Minimoog lineage and sample settings are catalog approximations rather than an exact Sub37 patch or a specification for the whole cluster.

items.name: Destroy techno
items.lineage: An Every Noise discovery label joining electro-, techno- and fidget-adjacent club artists rather than a literal instruction to maximize distortion. Siriusmo supplies the selected keyboard-and-sampler branch, supported by his own descriptions of synthesis, electric piano and sampled beat making.
items.description: Short synthetic figures, rhythmically edited samples and a lightly driven electric-piano ostinato form this authored arrangement. It emphasizes the playful keyboard and beat-making side of the roster, allowing irregular fills within a danceable structure. The source label is preserved without inventing a single industrial lineage or asserting that every included artist plays electric piano.

items.name: Spanish techno
items.lineage: Spain-centered techno producers and club networks, represented here by Paco Osuna’s Barcelona-associated, groove-oriented branch. His documented studio combines Ableton and plug-ins with a Waldorf Pulse; a Roland909 is available but, by his own account, used only occasionally.
items.description: This authored compact hardware option uses a short low synth figure, dry kick-led percussion and small changes in phrasing. It selects the occasional909 side of Osuna’s documented setup for a transparent two-instrument model; it does not imply that his primarily computer-based production always uses that machine. The geographical category also includes harsher and more atmospheric branches beyond this lean, house-adjacent groove.

items.name: Danish techno
items.lineage: Denmark-centered techno networks range from Kölsch’s melodic club work to the harder Copenhagen underground. This default selects the former’s documented combination of modular synthesis and drum-machine rhythm, rather than treating the national category as one tempo or mood.
items.description: An authored melodic studio branch: arpeggiated modular tones evolve over articulated machine percussion, with spacious reverb and clear repeating phrases. The model leaves room for live adjustment rather than specifying a fixed modular patch. Rawer and faster Danish productions are part of the broader label but are not forced into this particular setup.

items.name: Chilean techno
items.lineage: Chile-connected techno networks include artists working locally and in diaspora. Ricardo Villalobos provides a documented minimal, rhythm-oriented branch, with synthesis, drum machines and sampling shaped by his transnational musical background.
items.description: The authored model pairs an understated synth bass figure with small sample fragments and finely articulated electronic percussion. Repetition, spacing and evolving microdetail are favored over a large melodic refrain. This is a representative minimal branch, not a claim that Chilean techno must use folk instruments, Latin-percussion loops or one European studio location.

items.name: Russian techno
items.lineage: Russia-connected techno production and label networks, represented here by Nina Kraviz’s compact synthesizer-centered practice. The selected branch crosses the house/techno boundary; neither a single city nor one artist defines the full national category.
items.description: A restrained authored arrangement of low repeated synth figures and dry programmed drum hits, leaving space for a hypnotic groove. These settings model one lean production branch. Vocals, noisier sound design and much faster styles remain optional, while a geographical label does not justify stereotyped national timbres.

items.name: Finnish techno
items.lineage: Finland-centered techno practice. This default selects Mika Vainio’s sparse hardware rhythm-and-tone branch, associated with the Turku/Sähkö network, rather than proposing one national sound.
items.description: The authored arrangement places short electronic tones against a sharply delimited sampled rhythm, leaving substantial silence between gestures. It is a beat-oriented representative branch; melodic dance tracks and beatless pieces also occur in Finnish electronic practice, and no national folk instrumentation is prescribed.

items.name: Experimental techno
items.lineage: Techno experimentation that reworks machine rhythm, sound-source behavior and formal expectations. Pan Sonic and Mika Vainio supply one documented hardware-focused branch; the label is broader than this Finnish lineage.
items.description: A deliberately exploratory recording model: fragmented sample loops, noisy synthetic transients, irregularly changing articulation and contrasting gaps. These choices explore the techno/noise boundary rather than fixing a universal beat or chord recipe. The representative setup remains playable with familiar sampler and synthesis categories.

items.name: Arabic jazz
items.lineage: Arab-music and jazz encounters, represented by Anouar Brahem’s drummerless Thimar trio. Oud, bass clarinet and plucked double bass keep their separate voices while sharing composed melodies and improvisation. This is one branch of a much wider transnational category.
items.description: The authored trio gives ornamented oud melody room to converse with low reed lines and a flexible bass pulse. No drum kit or compulsory piano is added. The maqam24EDO setting is only a catalog approximation to flexible modal intonation, not a claim that these musicians uniformly played equal quarter-tones. Exact woods, string brand and reed range are representative choices.

items.name: Austrian jazz
items.lineage: Austria-connected jazz musicians working in international ensembles. Wolfgang Muthspiel’s Rising Grace quintet supplies this selected branch: electric guitar, trumpet and piano converse above acoustic bass and drums.
items.description: An authored lightly amplified quintet balances sustained guitar phrases, lyrical unmuted trumpet and responsive piano voicings. Bass and brushed/stick percussion support overlapping exchanges rather than a rigid sequence of solos. The acoustic-guitar side of the reference album remains optional; exact guitar construction, piano model and drum materials are authored choices.

items.name: Danish modern jazz
items.lineage: Contemporary Denmark-connected improvised music, represented by Jakob Bro’s open-form electric-guitar trio on Gefion. Guitar, acoustic bass and drums develop parallel, responsive lines with spacious dynamics.
items.description: The authored trio places clean, lingering guitar fragments over loosely articulated bass and delicate mixed brush/stick percussion. The focus is on space, timbral decay and interaction rather than a fixed walking-bass swing pattern. Single-coil construction and gentle delay are selected implementation choices; the source credits electric guitar without requiring one pickup design.

items.name: Indie jazz
items.lineage: Indie/electronic-informed jazz; selected GoGo Penguin acoustic trio
items.description: The authored trio translates repetitive electronic-style sketches into piano, double bass and drums. Short piano cells, plucked bass and tightly articulated stick rhythms create a propulsive ensemble rather than a conventional walking-bass standard. Software used to compose sketches is not silently added as an audible sampler or synthesizer. Exact room, materials and rock-backbeat kit setting are authored ways to realize the acoustic/electronic tension described by the musicians.
exemplars: GoGo Penguin — A Humdrum Star (2018), acoustic core

items.name: Italian contemporary jazz
items.lineage: Contemporary Italian improvisation; selected Stefano Bollani solo-piano branch
items.description: The authored solo performance treats short melodic ideas as material for spontaneous transformation, with changes of texture and register rather than a fixed accompaniment pattern. It follows the freely improvised miniatures on Piano Solo; ragtime, tango and standard-song pieces on the same recital are contextual alternatives, not simultaneous genre requirements. Piano brand/build and clean capture are representative defaults, not an exact studio reconstruction.
exemplars: Stefano Bollani — Piano Solo (2006), selected Impro miniatures

items.name: Classic Japanese jazz
items.lineage: Historical Japanese jazz recording; selected Akiyoshi 1953 quartet
items.description: The authored quartet places bebop-oriented piano ahead of lightly amplified jazz guitar, plucked bass and acoustic drums. It follows the Tokyo debut-session personnel rather than importing Akiyoshi’s later big-band sections or Japanese traditional instruments. The guitar’s archtop construction, steel bass strings and piano make are representative choices. A modern clean playback/capture model is used deliberately, so the source recording date does not falsely imply a verified vintage studio chain.

items.name: Italian jazz fusion
items.lineage: Italian jazz-rock fusion; selected Trio Bobo electric trio
items.description: The authored trio uses electric-guitar lines, a fingerstyle electric-bass groove and strong stick-driven drums. It follows the core performing group rather than automatically adding piano or voice from guest appearances on Sensurround. The source describes jazz/progressive-rock interaction and rhythmic influences; no extra African or Latin percussion instrument is inferred from those influences. Pickup type, materials and clean guitar branch are authored representative choices.
exemplars: Trio Bobo — core concert trio: Alessio Menconi, Faso and Christian Meyer

items.name: German jazz
items.lineage: German jazz scenes; selected Berlin composition-led acoustic quartet
items.description: The authored quartet allows piano and tenor saxophone to exchange melody and accompaniment while bass and drums respond flexibly. It draws on the leader’s first-person description of shifting roles and collective listening. The source’s post-bop/modal context supports open solo space without assuming fully free playing. The wood, brass, reed, piano model and clean recording choices are authored representatives, not session equipment claims.

items.name: Greek jazz
items.lineage: Greek jazz scenes; selected Vassilis Tsabropoulos international trio
items.description: The authored Achirana trio uses spacious piano phrases, singing plucked bass and restrained drums. The documented post-Bill-Evans improvising context permits fluid pacing and open dynamic space. Tsabropoulos’s classical training does not turn this ensemble into an orchestra, and Greek geography does not require bouzouki or folk percussion. Exact sustain, materials and room are representative implementation choices.
exemplars: Arild Andersen, Vassilis Tsabropoulos and John Marshall — Achirana (2000)

items.name: Danish jazz
items.lineage: Danish jazz scenes; selected Copenhagen Kenny Drew/NHØP ballad trio
items.description: The authored title-piece branch of Dark Beauty alternates composed piano melody with freer improvised sections, supported by plucked bass and light drums. Sustained arpeggiated piano gestures provide an opening and closing frame. It is deliberately a ballad branch rather than assuming all Copenhagen jazz swings at a fast tempo. The American-born leader’s long Copenhagen career and Danish bassist ground the local connection.
exemplars: Kenny Drew — Dark Beauty, 1974 trio recording with Niels-Henning Ørsted Pedersen and Albert Heath

items.name: Japanese jazz
items.lineage: Japanese jazz scenes; selected Hiromi solo-piano composition and improvisation branch
items.description: The authored Kaleidoscope branch of Spectrum uses repeated piano cells that expand into melodic and harmonic variation, with wide dynamic contrast. It selects a genuinely documented solo format: no bass, drum kit, synth or string quartet is imported from Hiromi’s other bands. Exact concert-grand construction and the clean room model are authored choices. A keyboard visible in the illustrative photo does not change the source album’s selected acoustic-piano role.

items.name: Japanese jazz fusion
items.lineage: Japanese jazz-rock fusion; selected Hiromi Sonicbloom piano/electric quartet
items.description: The authored quartet contrasts acoustic-piano attack with overdriven electric-guitar lead, fingerstyle electric bass and emphatic kit playing. The leader explicitly describes how electric guitar pushed this band toward rhythmic, groove-oriented music. Additional electronic keyboards remain an optional doubling instead of a mandatory fifth player. Humbuckers, neck construction, alder bodies and generic long-scale bass are author-selected implementations, not reconstructions of Fiuczynski’s specialist guitars or Grey’s Fodera instruments.
exemplars: Hiromi’s Sonicbloom — Time Control (2007), piano-centered quartet branch

items.name: Brazilian modern jazz
items.lineage: Contemporary Brazilian jazz; selected Recife piano-trio branch
items.description: The authored trio uses interlocking piano figures, mobile double-bass lines and sharply articulated kit responses. It leaves room for asymmetric phrases, changing meters and contrasting quieter passages. Freitas’s discussion of Black Brazilian history and regional rhythmic inheritance contextualizes this recording; it does not license automatically adding a samba percussion battery. Piano construction, room, kit materials and the balance of brushes and sticks are representative choices.

items.name: British jazz
items.lineage: Contemporary British jazz; selected London tenor-and-electric-piano quartet
items.description: The authored Inner Game branch pairs a tenor saxophone line with reed-electric-piano harmony, plucked double bass and responsive drums. The 200A, medium cane reed and clean signal path are authored realizations, not verified equipment used at the session. The catalog’s Ray Charles Wurlitzer-use selector represents a modeled soulful keyboard role, not a claim of direct stylistic influence on Garcia.

items.name: Dutch jazz

items.description: The authored Freya branch combines alto saxophone and trumpet with piano, double bass and drums. Lyrical themes and layered group responses can open into less prescribed improvisation. Soprano saxophone and electric bass are credited alternatives, not additional simultaneous players. The saxophone model, mouthpiece, piano build and trumpet construction are representative catalog choices; this does not assert a uniform Dutch national timbre.

items.name: Estonian jazz
items.lineage: Estonia-connected jazz, represented by Kristjan Randalu’s Absence trio with electric guitarist Ben Monder and drummer Markku Ounaskari. This bassless ensemble opens carefully structured piano compositions to improvised color and interplay.

It does not automatically add a double bass to a documented bassless trio. Semi-hollow construction and subtle delay are chosen ways to realize the electric-guitar role; no exact Monder guitar model is asserted.

items.name: Finnish modern jazz
items.lineage: Contemporary Finland-connected improvised music, represented by Verneri Pohjola’s Bullhorn quartet. Trumpet, piano, acoustic bass and drums balance memorable compositions, lyrical lines and bursts of rougher energy.

Piano voicings, mobile bass and responsive kit playing support changing intensity rather than a fixed atmospheric wash. The album’s guest saxophone, trombone and cello are optional colors and are not stacked into the four-player default. Exact instrument makes and materials are author-selected.

items.name: Finnish jazz
items.lineage: Finland-connected jazz lineages, represented by Iiro Rantala’s solo-piano homage project Lost Heroes. The selected branch draws together improvised jazz phrasing, songlike melody and references to the pianist’s musical influences.
items.description: An authored solo performance moves between quietly sustained arpeggios, melodic variation and resonant lower-register responses. The piano supplies all voices; no electric bass is added merely because one piece pays tribute to a bassist. This reflective selection is one Finnish jazz branch, not a claim that the wider scene or Rantala’s trio work shares the same mood.

items.name: Jazz accordion
items.lineage: Accordion-centered jazz practice, represented by Richard Galliano’s drummerless Mare Nostrum collaboration with Paolo Fresu and Jan Lundgren. Accordion, trumpet and piano share melodic and harmonic roles.

It selects accordion and trumpet from documented instrumental doublings rather than stacking bandoneon, accordina and flugelhorn as simultaneous extra players. Reed configuration and cassotto are representative timbral choices, not a claim about the exact recording instrument.

items.name: Australian jazz

items.description: An authored solo arrangement lets one piano move between lyrical melodic statements, dense chord voicings and freer transitions. The pianist provides both pulse and counterline, so no bass or drum kit is automatically added. A full-size concert grand with clear attack and generous headroom is the chosen recording model, not an assertion of the reference instrument’s exact brand or construction.

items.name: Italian jazz

It selects the core quartet rather than presenting every guest doubling as compulsory. Pickup design, trumpet make and all materials are representative options, not exact album-session specifications.

items.name: French jazz

items.description: The authored quartet sets a chromatic accordion line against clean hollow-body guitar, plucked bass and light drums. It represents the jazz-oriented New Musette collaboration rather than making a waltz rhythm compulsory for all French jazz. The guitarist’s credited role is realized with an authored archtop model; no exact Catherine guitar construction is claimed. items.name: Israeli jazz
items.lineage: Israel-connected contemporary jazz; selected Avishai Cohen bass-led trio
items.description: The authored trio gives plucked double bass a foreground melodic and rhythmic role, with piano figures and close drum interaction. Repeated cells can support shifting phrase lengths and more expansive improvisation. It follows the instrumental Gently Disturbed group rather than importing voice, Middle Eastern percussion or orchestral strings from the leader’s other projects. Exact piano make, steel strings, room and clean chain are authored defaults.

items.name: Jazz blues

items.description: The authored instrumental trio uses blues-derived piano phrases, a steady plucked-bass foundation and swung kit responses. Night Train supplies a documented blues-form theme in a jazz-trio interpretation; no vocalist or electric blues guitar is required. The model allows chorus-based improvisation rather than claiming every track on the album uses the same form. Modern clean capture and Steinway-like construction are explicit modeling choices, not the 1962 studio’s verified equipment.

items.name: Canadian modern jazz
items.lineage: Canada-connected contemporary jazz; selected Ingrid Jensen tribute quintet
items.description: The authored quintet pairs trumpet and tenor saxophone over piano, plucked bass and drums, following the documented live Foxy Trot group. Written themes provide material for improvisation rather than fixing every player to an accompaniment role. Guest voice and soprano saxophone elsewhere on the album remain optional; they are not added to the live quintet. Trumpet effects, equipment makes and exact materials are not inferred from the general album credit.

items.name: Contemporary vocal jazz
items.lineage: Current-era jazz song interpretation; selected voice-and-piano duo
items.description: The authored duo foregrounds a single singer and responsive piano, with freedom to stretch time, reshape phrases and reinterpret harmony. It follows The Window’s documented format rather than adding a standard bass/drums section. Variable vocal register and phonation remain unspecified where the evidence describes expressive range rather than a stable mechanism. Moderate effort, a neutral tract setting and an unprocessed single lead are modest authored defaults, not a physiological analysis of Salvant.
exemplars: Cécile McLorin Salvant with Sullivan Fortner — The Window (2018)

items.name: Faroese jazz
items.lineage: Faroe Islands jazz scenes; selected Yggdrasil drummerless mixed ensemble
items.description: The authored Duologues branch combines piano, tenor saxophone, flute, electric guitar and double bass, with occasional non-lexical vocal expression by the pianist. items.name: Jazz guitar trio

items.description: The authored three-player arrangement makes clean guitar the only chordal lead, with plucked bass and delicate drums responding in open space. It follows Gefion’s actual trio rather than adding piano by habit. Single-coil pickups and a gentle delay are representative choices; the source does not identify one required pickup construction. Guitar-trio labels can also describe other three-guitar or drummerless groups, which are not represented by this selected branch.

items.name: Jazz trio

items.description: The authored trio gives piano both melody and harmony, double bass a steady plucked foundation and drum kit a responsive swung pulse. The Night Train group supplies a concrete three-player example without making this the only possible jazz-trio instrumentation. The source’s historical date is retained in the exemplar, while the clean modern capture and detailed piano materials are explicitly authored alternatives.

items.name: Jazz quartet

items.name: Jazz guitar

items.name: Jazz clarinet

items.description: The authored duet gives clarinet the sustained melodic line while piano answers with harmonic and rhythmic choices. Articulation choices describe a connected jazz line without assigning a klezmer or doina tradition.

items.name: Jazz harp

items.description: The authored duet lets harp supply ringing harmony and melodic figures against a plucked double-bass line.
